t:
THE HYPNEROTOMACHIA OF POLIPHILO, WHEREIN HE TEACHES THAT ALL HUMAN THINGS ARE NOTHING BUT A
DREAM. AND ALONG THE WAY HE RECOUNTS VERY MANY THINGS THOROUGHLY WORTHY OF KNOWING.

IT IS PROVIDED THAT NO ONE WITHIN THE DOMINION OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS SIGNORY OF VENICE MAY PRINT
THIS BOOK WITH IMPUNITY.
pages.note: The title page. Latin.

t: LEONARDO CRASSO OF VERONA SENDS MUCH GREETING TO GUIDO, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS DUKE OF URBINO.

Since I have always honoured and regarded you, most unconquered Duke, for the singular virtues
and the fame of your name — and most of all since my brother served under your auspices at the
siege of [?Bibbiena] — whatever was then bestowed by you upon him (and he often recalls it was
much, reporting your kindness and humanity toward him), all of that we have reckoned to belong
to all the Crassi; and what one received, we all count as received by us from you, nor do we
now concede to him that he is more yours than we all are. But my brothers await an occasion to
expose for your sake not only all they have, but their lives as well.

I myself, who so far as my strength allows think often — and shall go on thinking, until I have
done it — by what means I may [?open myself to] you, now come into some hope of my wish. For since
I know that with you one can do no more by the goods of fortune than (as the saying goes) by
water with the sea, and that letters and virtues alone have power with you, I have tried
letters as a ford, for a way of approach to you.

There came lately into my hands a certain new and admirable work of Poliphilo (for that is the
name given to the book), which — that it should not lie hidden any longer in darkness, but
should profit mortals in good time — I have seen to the printing and publishing of at my own
expense. But lest that book, bereft of its parent, should seem to be like a ward without
guardian or any patronage, I have chosen you as its present patron, in whose name it might go
forth [?a little more boldly]: so that as I now use it as the servant and messenger of my love and
regard toward you, so you may often use it as a companion to your studies and your manifold
learning.

**For there is in it not only such knowledge but such abundance that, when you have seen this
book, you will seem to have seen not so much all the books of the ancients as the hidden things
of nature herself.**

There is one thing in it to marvel at: that although it speaks in our own tongue, one has no
less need of Greek and Latin to understand it than of Tuscan and the vernacular. For that most
wise man reckoned that, if he spoke so, there was one road and one method by which nobody could
plead his own negligence as excuse for learning nothing. Yet he tempered himself so that none
but the most learned could penetrate into the sanctuary of his doctrine, while one who came to
it unlearned should not despair even so.

Add to this, that if any matters were by their own nature difficult, they are declared and
brought out in sweet speech with a certain pleasantness — as though a garden of every kind of
flower were unlocked — and they lie open and are set before the eyes in figures and images.
These are not things set out for the crowd and to be chanted at the crossroads, but such as,
drawn from the storehouse of philosophy and drunk from the fountains of the Muses, polished
with a certain novelty of speaking, may deserve the favour of every wit.

Take up then, most humane prince, our Poliphilo, with the brow you are wont to show the
learned; and take him up so that, since he is the little gift of a grateful mind, you may read
him the more willingly for being reminded of your Leonardo Crasso. And if you do this (as I
hope), then he will fear no one's censure, having undergone yours; and he will be read the more
often by others, who will be thought to have been read by you; and I shall hope that in some
part I have attained what I had wished for.
pages.note: Leonardo Crasso's dedicatory letter to Guidobaldo da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino. Latin. It runs over onto page 3.

t: …Farewell, and number your Crassi, with me, among your own.
pages.note: The end of Crasso's letter; then Giovanni Battista Scita's poem to him; then the beginning of the anonymous elegy to the reader, which runs over onto page 4. Latin.

> — symmetry, and whatever makes proud roofs.
> Here you will see the cultivated palaces of kings, the adornments
>    of nymphs, fountains, and outstanding feasts.
> Here is the two-coloured dance of robbers, and the whole life
>    of men set out in labyrinthine darkness.
> Here read what he says of the threefold majesty of the Thunderer,
>    and what he himself performed at the three gates.
> What form Polia had, how adorned; then behold
>    the four heavenly triumphs of Jove.
> Besides these, he tells the various affections of love,
>    and its works, and how fiercely that God rages.
> Here Pomona triumphs together with Vertumnus.
>    Here too are rites performed to the Lampsacan god.
> Here is a huge temple, more perfect than any art,
>    and the manifold rites of the ancient sacred things.
> Soon you will see another temple, spoiled by the teeth of time;
>    and here very many things pleasing to your mind:
> the seats of Tartarus, many epitaphs, and the boat
>    in which the boy of Venus is carried over the vast straits;
> and the highest honours reverently shown to him
>    by all the gods, as many as the waters hold.
> Here see Cythera, marked out with gardens and meadows,
>    in the middle of which curved theatres lie open.
> And here you may behold the triumph of Cupid.
>    Here is the fountain, and the venerable form of the Paphian Goddess;
> and what is celebrated around the tomb of beloved Adonis
>    yearly by Venus — and you shall read the Naiads' laws.
> This is the series of matters contained in the first volume:
>    these are the new dreams of the divine Poliphilo.
> Where she was born, of what stock, of what parents sprung,
>    is Polia — the book that follows sets out thereafter.
> And who first founded the walls of Treviso.
>    From there it has the whole sequence of a long love.
> Lastly the book is furnished with a long appendix,
>    which I do not think, reader, it will be thankless to read.
> There are very many things besides; it wearied me to report them all.
>    Take what the horn of plenty has generously given.
> Behold, the book delights and profits. If you scorn both,
>    believe the fault is not the book's, but yours.
>
>                         *The end.*
pages.note: The rest of the anonymous elegy to the reader, begun on page 3. Latin.

t:
Reader, if you wish briefly to understand what is contained in this work, know that Poliphilo
tells of having seen wondrous things in sleep; which work he calls, by a Greek word, *the strife
of love in a dream*. Wherein he feigns to have seen many antique things worthy of memory, and
all that he says he saw he describes point by point and by their proper terms, in an elegant
style: pyramids, obelisks, the greatest ruins of buildings; the difference of columns, their
measure, the capitals, bases, epistyles — that is, straight beams — bent beams, zophori, that is
friezes, cornices with their ornaments. A great horse. A very great elephant. A colossus. A
magnificent gate, with its measures and its ornaments. A terror. The five senses in five nymphs.
An excellent bath, fountains, the palace of the queen who is Free Will. A royal and most
excellent feast. The variety of jewels, or rather precious stones, and their nature. A game of
chess danced to three measures of music. Three gardens: one of glass, one of silk, one in a
labyrinth which is human life. A brick peristyle, in the middle of which the Trinity was set out
in hieroglyphic figures — that is, sacred Egyptian carvings. The three gates, at which he stayed
behind with Polia. How she was in habit and in bearing. Polia leads him to look upon four
wondrous triumphs of Jove, the loves of the gods, those of the poets, the various affection and
effect of love. The triumph of Vertumnus with Pomona. The sacrifice to Priapus in the antique
manner. A marvellous temple, described by its art, where sacrifices were made with wonderful
rites and religion. How Polia and he went to the shore to await Cupid, where there was a
destroyed temple; in which Polia persuades Poliphilo to go in and look upon the antique things.
And there he saw many epitaphs, and a hell painted in mosaic. How for terror he departed thence
and came to Polia. And as they stood there Cupid came with the little ship rowed by six nymphs,
into which both entered, and Love made sail with his wings. And there honour was done to Cupid
by the sea-gods and goddesses, and by the nymphs and monsters; and they came to the Cytherean
island, which Poliphilo describes fully, laid out in groves, meadows, gardens, rivers and
fountains; and the presents that were made to Cupid, and how he was received by the nymphs; and
how upon a triumphal car they went to a wondrous theatre, all described, in the middle of the
island. In the midst of which is the Venereal fountain of seven precious columns, and all that
was done there. And, Mars coming, they departed thence and went to the fountain where was the
sepulchre of Adonis. And here the nymphs tell of the anniversary that Venus kept in his memory.
Then the nymphs persuade Polia to tell her origin and her falling in love. And this is in the
first book. In the second, Polia tells her parentage, the building of Treviso, the difficulty of
her falling in love and its happy issue; and, the history being completed with infinite and most
worthy accessories and corollaries, at the song of the nightingale he awoke. Farewell.
pages.note: The summary of the whole work, addressed to the reader. Italian — and, unlike everything around it, plain Italian. One unbroken sentence-chain of about five hundred words.

> Leonardo Crasso, my revered doctor,
>    prelate accomplished in the liberal arts
>    and, as I understand it, in every excellent virtue:
> he merits the highest and immortal praise
>    for the expense and the undertaking he has assumed
>    to furnish us with such a compendium.
> Polished reader, then — listen, listen
>    to the dreams of Poliphilo as he tells them,
>    sent down from heaven with much sweetness.
> You will not waste your time extravagantly;
>    rather you will rejoice at having heard
>    the work, exuberant with various things.
> If, grim, you scorn the new erotic
>    invitation, then do not scorn the well-disposed
>    sequence, with its fine and exquisite style.
> If the grave discourse and well-composed learning
>    should not please you, then look at the figures,
>    ancient in geometry — which costs little.
> The many signs, with their measures,
>    kept beside the Nile by the Egyptians;
>    the ancient pyramids, sepulchres,
> with the obelisks set upright on top of them;
>    the therms and baths and statues of colossi,
>    such that whoever looks on them is left undone.
> Here are diverse bases and thick arches,
>    various columns proportioned to them,
>    with capitals and beams that can bear them,
> and the cornices with their quadrants,
>    the symmetries, the zophori, epistyles,
>    which have shown us proud roofs.
> There you will see palaces cultivated and fair
>    of kings and lords, and the nymphal fountains,
>    and the banquets befitting them.
> There you will see diverse chessmen joined
>    in a game of robbers, and human acts
>    conjoined in labyrinth and darkness.
> Here you will read of threefold and not idle
>    deeds, and the majesty of the great Thunderer
>    in the three gates and his sound counsels.
> Who Polia was, fair and triumphant,
>    you will see thereafter; and of Jove the celestial —
pages.note: An Italian poem in terza rima, addressed to Leonardo Crasso and then to the reader. It is the anonymous Latin elegy of pages 3–4 done over again in the vernacular, for readers who have no Latin — which is itself an argument about who the book was for. It runs over onto page 7.

t: ANDREA MARONE OF BRESCIA.

> *Whose work is it, Muse, say?* — It is mine, and the eight sisters'.
>    *Why then was the title given to Poliphilo?*
> — He earned still more from us, our common foster-child.
>    *But I ask: who is Poliphilo, by his true name?*
> — We do not wish him to be known. *Why?* — It is settled to see first
>    whether rabid envy devours even things divine.
> If it spares him, [?what will he be? He will be known]. But if not, we do not
>    think you worthy of Poliphilo's true name.

> O how happy beyond all mortals you alone are,
>    Polia, who live though dead — and better so.
> While Poliphilo lies buried in deep sleep,
>    you make the man keep watch, through learned lips.
pages.note: Two Latin epigrams by Andrea Marone of Brescia. The first is a dialogue with the Muse; the second is addressed to Polia.

t:
THE HYPNEROTOMACHIA OF POLIPHILO, WHEREIN HE SHOWS THAT ALL HUMAN THINGS ARE NOTHING BUT A
DREAM, AND ALONG THE WAY RECOUNTS VERY MANY THINGS THOROUGHLY WORTHY OF KNOWING.
pages.note: The half-title, repeating page 1 with one word changed. Latin.

t: POLIPHILO SENDS MUCH GREETING TO POLIA.

MANY TIMES, POLIA, CONSIDERING THAT the ancient authors fittingly dedicated their works to
princes and magnanimous men — some for a price, others for favour, some for praise — for none of
such causes, then, but for the middle one, I offer this my *Hypnerotomachia*, finding no worthier
prince to whom to dedicate it than to you, my high Empress: whose excellent condition and
incredible beauty, and venerable and greatest virtues, and most illustrious manners, holding
sovereignty over whatever nymph there is in our centuries, have exceedingly inflamed, burned and
consumed me with your signal Love.

Receive then this little gift — you, suffused with the splendour of beauties, and adorned with
every comeliness, and conspicuous of glorious aspect. Which gift you yourself have industriously
made and fashioned, painted with gilded arrows in my amorous heart and marked with your angelic
likeness; so that you possess it singularly as its Patroness.

Which gift I thereafter commit to your diligent and ingenious judgement, leaving the style I
began in and translating it into this one at your instance. Whence, if a fault appear, and if in
some part you find it barren and meagre, falling short of your elegant worth, then you shall be
the one accused — you, best of workwomen, and sole key-bearer of my mind and of my heart.

Therefore I esteem and desire no prize of greater talent or price, especially, than your gracious
love; and, for this, your kind favour. Farewell.
pages.note: Poliphilo's dedication of the work to Polia. Italian — and here the book's own voice begins: the Latinate, clause-heaped style that will run for another four hundred and fifty pages.

t:
POLIPHILO BEGINS HIS HYPNEROTOMACHIA, DESCRIBING THE HOUR AND THE SEASON WHEN IT APPEARED TO HIM IN
SLEEP THAT HE FOUND HIMSELF UPON A QUIET AND SILENT SHORE, DESERTED OF ALL CULTIVATION. THEREAFTER,
UNAWARES, IN GREAT FEAR HE ENTERED A PATHLESS AND SHADOWED WOOD.
HYPNEROTOMACHIA POLIPHILI
DESCRIPTION OF THE DAWN

At that hour when Phoebus, issuing forth, was whitening the brow of Matuta Leucothea, he did not yet
show, risen clear of Ocean's waves, his rolling wheels held aloft. But diligent with his winged
horses — Pyrous first, and Eous somewhat appearing — he did not delay in painting the pale-lit
four-horse chariot of the daughter of vermilion roses, following after her most swiftly. And already,
glittering above the cerulean and restless wavelets, his beams came curling. At which arrival, in
that instant, the un-horned Cynthia gave herself over to her setting, urging on the two horses of her
vehicle together with the Mule — the one white, the other dusky — drawing her to the last Horizon
that divides the Hemispheres; and having come there, the day being kindled by the star that runs
before it, she yielded and fled.

In that season when the Riphaean mountains were at peace, and the chill and frost-bearing Eurus no
longer shook the tender branches with such rigour in its sidelong blowing, nor troubled the swaying
rushes and the pointed reeds and the frail Cyperus, nor harried the pliant withies, nor stirred the
slow willows, nor bowed down the brittle fir beneath the horns of the wanton Bull — as much, that is,
as it is wont to blow in the season of winter. And likewise the boastful Orion, weeping, left off
pursuing the adorned shoulder of the Bull and the seven sisters.

In that very hour when the coloured flowers no longer feared the heat of Hyperion's coming son as a
thing that harms them, but were bedewed and flowing with the fresh tears of the Dawn, and the meadows
green; and the Halcyons, above the levelled waves of a tranquil calm and a becalmed sea, appeared to
be nesting on the sandy shores. Then, therefore, when the grieving Hero

warmly sighed, upon the gnawed shores, for the sorrowful and thankless departure of Leander the
swimmer: I, Poliphilo, lying upon my little bed, that timely friend of the weary body, with no one in
the room that knew my secret save my dear watcher Agrypnia — who, after she had held various converse
with me to console me, and I had made plain to her the cause and the origin of my deep sighs,
mercifully urged me to temper such a disturbance; and, perceiving the hour at which I ought by now to
sleep, asked leave to go. Whereupon, left alone in the high cogitations of love, consuming the long
and tedious night without sleep, all unconsoled by my barren fortune and my adverse and unjust star,
and weeping for an importunate and unprospering love, I turned over point by point what a thing
unequal love is; and how one may fitly love who does not love in return; and with what protection the
fluctuating soul, besieged by unaccustomed and repeated assaults and surrounded by hostile battle,
may resist at all, being so unarmed — the seditious battle being above all an inward one, and
ceaselessly ensnared by anxious, unstable and ever-new thoughts.

Having grieved bitterly and at length over a state so made and so wretched, and the wandering spirits
being already worn out with thinking to no purpose, and fed upon a false and feigned pleasure — yet
rightly and without fail upon an object not mortal but rather divine, upon Polia, whose venerable
Idea lives deeply impressed in me and more inwardly carved still, and holds me. And already the
trembling and glittering stars were beginning to pale their splendour, when, the tongue falling
silent, that desired enemy from whom proceeds this so great and unceasing contest, impatiently urging
the wounded heart, called upon it tirelessly for a profitable and effectual remedy — which was
nothing other than the renewal of my torment, without interval, cruel.

Musing too upon the quality of wretched lovers, by what condition they choose sweetly to die in order
to please another, and, pleasing themselves, to live ill; and to feed a spear-like desire upon
laborious and sigh-laden imagining, and upon nothing else. Then, like a man weary after long labours,
just so and no otherwise, the sorrowful outward weeping being scarcely at all abated, and the course
of the streaming tears shut in, my cheeks hollowed with the languor of love, I now desired the
natural and timely quiet. Now, my wet eyes a little closed within their reddened lids, without
lingering between bitter life and gentle death, that part was invaded and possessed and pressed down
by a sweet sleep which is not united with the mind, nor with the loving and wakeful spirits, nor
shares in operations so high.

O high-thundering Jupiter! Happy, or wonderful, or terrifying shall I call this unaccustomed vision,
which leaves in me no atom that does not tremble and burn to think upon it. To me

it seemed that I was in a spacious plain, which showed itself all green and much adorned, painted
variously with manifold flowers. And with kindly airs there was there a certain silence. Nor yet did
any noise, nor any formed voice, come to ears most ready to hear. But with the gracious rays of the
Sun the temperate season passed.

In which place I, wandering with timid wonder, said within myself: here no humanity appears to the
desiring gaze, nor yet any wild thing of the woods, nor forest-dweller, nor creature of the glade,
nor any tame beast. No country house, no cottage of the fields, no shepherd's roof, no hut nor
shieling is to be seen. Nor likewise, in these grassy places, did I see any keeper of sheep, nor
goatherd, nor oxherd, nor groom, nor any straying flock and herd, with their rustic two-mouthed
Syrinx, nor with their sounding pipes of bark. But confident, because of the quiet shore and the
kindliness of the place, and going forward almost made secure, I looked this way and that, and saw
the tender leaves resting unmoved, discerning no other work.

And so, straight before me, I turned my unknowing journey towards a thick wood. Into which, having
entered somewhat, I did not perceive that I had thus incautiously left — I know not in what manner —
the path itself. Whereupon a sudden fear at once invaded my suspended heart, spreading itself through
my pale limbs with a quickened beating, my cheeks become bloodless of their colour. Seeing that to my
eyes no trace whatever was granted to be seen, nor any turning aside. But in that thorny wood there
appeared only close thickets, pricking brakes, the woodland Ash that is hateful to vipers, rough Elms
grateful to the fruitful vine, the corky Cork-oak fit for a woman's adding, hard Turkey-oaks, strong
oaks, and acorn-bearing Oaks and Holm-oaks, and so abounding in branches that they did not permit the
rays of the gracious Sun to reach the dewy ground entire. But, as beneath a vaulted roof covered over
with thickening leaves, the kindly light did not penetrate. And in this manner I found myself in the
cool shade, the humid air, and the dusky wood.

For which cause I began thereafter, and with reason, to suspect and to believe that I had come into
the vastest Hercynian forest; and that there was nothing there but the lairs of harmful beasts, and
the caves of noxious animals and of raging brutes. And therefore, with the greatest terror, I feared
that, being without any defence, I should be torn without warning by some bristled and tusked Boar,
as Charidemus was; or by a raging and starved wild Ox; or by a hissing serpent; or that I should see
my flesh miserably dismembered and gulped down by wolves rushing upon me and howling.

Fearing this, and terrified, I resolved there — all sloth being condemned — to linger no longer, but
to find a way out and escape the perils that offered, and to urge on my steps, already halting and
disordered; stumbling often on the roots laid bare from the earth, wandering here and there astray,
now to the right hand and now to the left, at one time going backwards and at another forwards,
ignorant, and not knowing where to pass; having come into a woodland glade and a thicket and a place
full of briars, all scratched by the branches, and my face injured by the thorny sloes and by their
intractable fruit. And by the sharp-pointed thistles and other thorns my gown was torn, and, held
back, it hindered and made sluggish my attempted flight.

Beyond this, seeing no sign of instructive footprints, nor the worn line of any path, in no small
measure mistrustful and doubting, I hastened the more anxiously. So that, what with my swift steps
and what with the midday heat, made hot also by the motion of my body, all moistened with sweat the

cold breast. Not knowing any longer what to do, I held my mind bound and intent upon terrible
thoughts alone. And so at last, to my sighing voice, Echo alone, rival of the voice, offered herself
newly in answer; scattering my resounding sighs, together with the hoarse chirping of the lover of
the dewy Dawn, and with the shrill Crickets. At last, in this rough and pathless wood, I desired only
the succour of the merciful Cretan Ariadne — who, being privy to the killing of her monstrous
brother, held out to the deceiving Theseus the masterly and guiding thread, that he might come forth
out of the wayward labyrinth. And I the like, that I might come out of the dark Wood.

POLIPHILO, FEARING THE PERIL OF THE DARK WOOD, MADE PRAYER TO DIESPITER; HE CAME FORTH ANXIOUS AND
THIRSTING; AND, WISHING TO RESTORE HIMSELF WITH WATER, HE HEARD A SWEET SINGING, WHICH, FOLLOWING AND
REFUSING THE WATERS, HE CAME INTO GREATER ANXIETY STILL.

MY UNDERSTANDING HAVING NOW BEGUN to be darkened, so that it could not discern, and my senses to be
clouded as to which choice I ought to take — whether to meet hateful death, or to hope for safety
wavering in that shadowy and dark grove — running this way and that, I bent all my strength and
striving to get out. Into which, the further I penetrated in my wandering, the darker it grew. And
being already made feeble by great terror, I only waited, fearing it from some quarter or other, for
some most savage beast to fall upon me and begin to devour me; or else, stumbling blindly and without
forethought, to fall into some abysmal pit and trench, or to be thrown headlong into some vast gape
of the earth; and by now to end this wearisome life like Amphiaraus, or like Curtius swallowed by the
mephitic gulf of the earth, and to fall from a greater height than the witless Pyreneus did.

In this manner, almost without hope, my mind was troubled on every side, yet still attempting,
lawlessly wandering, some way out. Whereupon, trembling more than the moving leaves in the
must-scented Autumn under the raging North winds, stripped of their green and of the juicy weight of
their moisture, I said within myself, praying thus: O Diespiter, Greatest, Best, Almighty and
Helping, if by the divine suffrages the

prayer that deserves it by just petition ought to be heard: now, grieving under every fragile injury,
I call upon thee as suppliant, highest father of the gods above, the middle and the below, eternal
ruler, that it may please thy immense Deity to free me from these my mortal perils and this present
horror, and to end this doubtful life of mine by some better end. And there, like the bristling
Achaemenides pleading with Aeneas in anxious and beseeching words to be saved from the horrifying
Cyclops — desiring rather to die at the hands of enemy men than by so horrid a destruction — so, and
in no other way, did I pray.

Scarcely had I finished those devout prayers, sincerely made, with the heart united in prayer,
contrite and shaken, and bathed in tears — holding firmly that the gods come to the aid of a good
mind — when without delay I found myself, unawares, outside that narrow, harsh and overshadowing
wood. And as if come forth into a new day out of the humid night, my shadowed eyes could not for a
while endure the lovely light. All wan and mournful and anxious, it seemed to me nonetheless that I
had come to the light I had longed for, as one might come out of a blind prison, stripped of heavy
and troubling chains, and issue from murky darkness.

All thirsting, torn, my face and hands bloodied and blistered by the biting Nettle, feeling myself
half dead, I counted nothing else as anything against the gracious light. So thirsty was I that the
fresh airs could not cool me, nor fitly satisfy my dry heart; most greedy to swallow the empty saliva
that had dried within me. But when I had somewhat reassured myself, and recalled a little spirit into
me — my breast parched with repeated sighs and with anxiety of spirit and with bodily labour — I
resolved by every means to quench that arid thirst. And therefore, searching carefully over that
shore to find some water, and seeking long and very wearily, there offered itself to me most timely a
most joyful spring, with a great vein of water freshly rising up. The place of it the marsh Acorus
and the Silvan's beard disclosed to me, and the flowering Loosestrife, and the musky Masterwort.

From it there was born a most limpid stream, which, running off in little rills through the middle of
the deserted wood in a wayward and winding channel, widened as it took increase from many other
flowing channels. And against the hindering Rocks and fallen trunks the currents rose up in sounding
waves. And thereafter it received great increase from impetuous and wave-sounding torrents fallen
from the melted snows of the alpine and rigid mountains, which appeared to stand not too far off,
made white in the freezing monster of Pan. To which, having come many times in my fearful flight, I
found there a little dusky light, where the lofty trees were somewhat

wedged apart at their tops above the muddy river, and where I saw the sky torn by the hindering leafy
branches — some of them dry — a place of horror for a man to find himself in alone, with no crossing
anywhere; the farther banks appearing still darker and more tangled than the nearer.

There was my terror to hear from that quarter, now and again, the hissing ruin of trees, and a crash
of branches, and the crackling splitting of wood, with a doubled and horrid-sounding din, held long
in the density of the trees and the enclosed air.

Wishing therefore, I Poliphilo, terrified and afflicted, having escaped so much horror, to drink up
the longed-for waters upon those green banks, I lowered myself upon my knees; and drawing my hands
together into an enclosure, with the palm hollowed, I made of them a most welcome drinking vessel.
Which, dipped in the spring and filled with water, I made ready to offer to my raging and panting
mouth, and to cool the dryness of my burning breast. More welcome then to me than the Hypanis and the
Ganges to the Indians, than the Tigris and Euphrates to the Armenians; nor is the Nile so welcome to
the Ethiopian peoples, nor to the Egyptians its flooding that drinks into the baked soil; nor yet
Eridanus to the Ligurian peoples, as those most acceptable and fresh banks offered themselves to me.
Nor was the spring shown by the fleeing Ram so exceedingly welcome to Father Liber.

It happened that no sooner was I about to bring the awaited and desirable waters, enclosed in my
hollowed hand, to my open mouth, than in that instant I heard a Dorian singing — which I cannot
persuade myself Thamyras the Thracian ever found — penetrating through the little caverns of my ears,
and passing through to my restless heart so sweet, so soft and so harmonious. With a voice not of
earth, with such harmony, with such incredible sonority, with such unaccustomed proportion. Alas, how
could it ever be imagined? For without doubt this thing exceeds the power of telling.

The sweetness of it and the delight offered me far more pleasure than the little draught that was
offering itself. So much so that the water drawn up, held within the enclosure of the intervals of my
teeth — my understanding as it were senseless and already stupefied, and my appetite laid to sleep,
no faculty gainsaying it — the knots being loosed, was spilt upon the moist earth.

Now, like an animal that for the sweet bait does not weigh the hidden trap, setting aside my natural
need, I went without delay, hastening vehemently on the way, after that more-than-human strain. And
when I reasonably judged that I had come to it, I heard it in another quarter; and when I had hurried
to that place, it appeared to have settled somewhere else. And so, as it changed its places, so
likewise it changed to a voice more sweet and more delightful, with heavenly harmonies.

Therefore, by this empty labour, and having run so far with troublesome thirst, I so weakened myself
that I could scarcely sustain my weary body. And my panting spirits being no longer able to bear up
the body, gravely wearied as it was — what with the terror now past, what with the urgent thirst,
what with the long wandering search, and also with my heavy anxieties and with the hot hour — I was
left defenceless and abandoned by my own powers, desiring and craving nothing whatever save quiet
rest for my weakened limbs.

Wondering at the chance that had befallen, stupefied by that mellifluous voice, and much more at
finding myself in a region unknown and uncultivated, though a country pleasant enough. Beyond this it
grieved me sorely that the flowing spring, found with such labour and sought out with such care, had
been taken away and lost from my eyes. For all which things I stood with my mind entangled in
ambiguity, and much perplexed. At last, seized by so great a weariness, my whole body

and languid. Beneath a rough and most ancient oak, abounding in its cupped or tufted fruit, despised
by fertile Chaonia, in the midst of a spacious and grassy meadow — an oak leafy with knotted and
spreading branches, making a cool shade, its trunk gaping — I laid myself down upon the dewy herbs.
Resting upon my left side, lying there, I drew in the fresh airs with my thinned spirits, more
constantly with my parted lips than the weary Stag that has been driven and bitten in the flanks by
biting and fierce hounds, and wounded in the breast by the arrow, and that at the last, propping his
heavy head with its branching horns upon his weakened back and no longer able to stand, sinks down
dying and weary upon his buckling knees.

Whence, lying in this like agony, I ran over anxiously in my mind the most tangled quarrels of
infirm fortune, and the enchantments of the maleficent Circe — whether by chance I had been knotted
into her verses, or the magic wheel had been used against me. To these and so many attendant terrors:
alas then, where could I find here, among herbs so various, the Mercurial Moly with its black root,
for my help and my medicine? Then I said: this is not that; but what is it, if not a malign deferring
of the death I long for?

Standing thus in these pernicious agitations, my powers dwindled little by little, and I could
think of no other Safety than to draw in and receive frequently and diligently the fresh airs, and,
having warmed them in my breast where a little vital heat still gathered and beat, to breathe them
out again through my parched throat. Finding myself therefore in no other way than half alive, for a
last refreshment I took the moist dew-laden leaves kept beneath the leafy oak, and offered them to my
pale and harsh lips, sucking them dry with the greediest avidity, licking at them ravenously, and
cooling a little my thirsty palate. Desiring then that Hypsipyle might show me too the spring of
Langia, as she did to the Greeks. For I anxiously suspected that perhaps in the vast wood I had been
bitten unawares by the serpent Dipsas, so unbearable was my thirst.

At last, renouncing and proscribing this wearisome life, whatever might come of it, astonished and
estranged by the gravest cogitations, and reeling as though in madness, once again beneath this
oaken shade, wanton with the spreading darkness of its branches, I was overcome by an overpowering
sleep; and the sweet drowsiness being spread through my limbs, it seemed to me that I slept again.
pages.wcap: Poliphilo in a Garden with Palms

t:
POLIPHILO HERE RELATES THAT IT SEEMED TO HIM THAT HE SLEPT AGAIN, AND THAT ELSEWHERE, IN SLEEP, HE
FOUND HIMSELF IN A VALLEY WHICH AT ITS END WAS CLOSED BY A MARVELLOUS BARRIER WITH A PORTENTOUS
PYRAMID, WORTHY OF ADMIRATION, AND A LOFTY OBELISK ABOVE IT; WHICH WITH DILIGENCE AND PLEASURE HE
CONSIDERED SUBTLY.

THE FEARFUL WOOD AND THE CROWDED grove being escaped, and those first other places left behind
through the sweet sleep that had spread itself over my broken and prostrate limbs, I found myself
anew in a place far more delightful than the one before. It was not girdled about with horrid
mountains and sheer crags, nor scythed with knotted ridges, but was composed of pleasant little
hills of no great height; wooded with young oaklings, with oaks, ashes and Hornbeams, and with leafy
Italian oaks and Holm-oaks, and with tender Hazels, and Alders, and Limes, and Maples, and with
barren wild Olives, disposed according to the aspect of those tree-bearing Hills. And down on the
level there were pleasant little woods of other woodland

saplings, and of flowering Brooms, and of manifold most green herbs. There I saw the Cytisus, the
Sedge, the common Honeywort, the musky All-heal, the flowering buttercup, and hartwort, or Elaphium,
and the sawwort, and many various noble kinds, and many other useful simples, and unknown herbs and
flowers dispensed about the meadows. All this glad region offered itself richly adorned with
greenery.

Then, a little beyond its middle, I came upon a sandy place, or gravelled stretch, though in some
parts scattered with some tufts of herbage. There a most joyful Palm-grove presented itself to my
eyes, with leaves of knife-like point, of such usefulness to the Egyptians, fruitful and abounding in
their most sweet fruit. Among which clustered palms, some were small, and many middling, and the
others were straight and lofty — the chosen Sign of victory, because of the way they resist a
pressing weight.

Here again in this place I found no inhabitant, nor any other animal whatever. But wandering
solitary among those palms — not thickly set, but standing apart, and most worth the seeing — I
thought that the palms of Rachelais, of Phaselis and of Libya were perhaps not comparable to these.
Behold, then, a famished and flesh-eating wolf appeared to me on the right hand, with its mouth full.

At the sight of which my hairs at once stood up on end, and, wishing to cry out at it, I had no
voice. And it immediately fled. And I, then somewhat returned to myself, lifting my eyes towards
that quarter where the wooded hills appeared to join, saw far off, in a deep recess, an incredible
height in the figure of a tower, or of a most lofty watch-tower; and near it a great building
appearing still unfinished, yet a work and structure of antiquity.

Where, towards this building, I saw the gracious little hills of the valley rising ever higher, which
I saw joined to the aforesaid edifice; and it was a closure between the one mountain and the other,
and made an enclosed valley. Judging this thing shrewdly to be most worthy of beholding, I turned my
already hastened journey eagerly towards it without delay. And the nearer I came to it as I went, the
more I discovered a work huge and magnificent, and the desire to look upon it multiplied. For it no
longer appeared a lofty watch-tower, but rather a high Obelisk, founded upon a vast heap of stones.

The height of which incomparably exceeded the summits of the mountains on either side, however
famous a mountain I might reckon Olympus, or Caucasus, or Cyllene, to be. Having come eagerly even to
this deserted place, surrounded with a pleasure beyond imagining at beholding freely so great an
insolence of the builder's art, and a structure so immense, and an eminence so stupendous, I halted
quietly.

Looking upon and considering the whole mass and thickness of this fragmented and half-ruined
structure of white Parian marble: the squared and four-angled blocks fitted together without the glue
of cement, and equally set and placed, so polished and so exquisitely reddened at their edges as
could ever be done — so much so that between the one edge and the other, that is at the joints, no
thinness whatever, however sharpened, could have resisted being thrust in and yet have penetrated in
the least.

Here, then, I found so noble a colonnade, of every figuration, lineament and material as any man
could ever suppose: part broken down, part still in its place, and part preserved unhurt, with their
Architraves and with capitals excellent in device and in rough carving; Cornices, Zophori or
Friezes, arched Beams. Great fractures of statues, many of their bronzed and finished members struck
off. Basins, and Shells, and vases, of Numidian stone and of Porphyry and of various marble and
ornament. Great washing-basins. Aqueducts, and almost infinite other fragments of noble sculpture,
wholly deprived of any knowing what they had been when whole, and reduced as it were to their first
rough beginning; fallen and cast down to the earth here and there. Above

and among which broken ruins many woodland shoots had sprung: chiefly the unshaken Bean-trefoil with
its bundled pods, and Mastic of one kind and the other, and Bear's-foot and Cynocephalus, and the
stinking Iris and the rough Bindweed, and Centaury, and many others germinating amid the ruins. And
upon the fretted walls many House-leeks, and the hanging Ivy-leaved Toadflax, and thickets of
pricking brier. Among which certain lizards crept, and crawled too upon the shrubbed walls, often in
those deserted and silent places bringing no small horror to me at their first motion, as I stood all
suspended.

Great fragments in many parts of plane rounding, and of Ophite and of Porphyry, and of a Coralline
colour, and of many other pleasing colourings. Fragments of various storied work in high relief and
half relief, in finished and in half-finished carving; declaring its excellence, which unfailingly
accuses our own times, and shows that of such an art the perfection is fallen asleep.

Having come therefore near the middle front of that great and illustrious work, I saw an entire
portal, wonderful and conspicuous, and proportioned to the whole building. Which fabric I saw
continuous, set between the one and the other of the mountains with their sheared-off slopes, so that
I could reasonably conjecture its dimension to be twenty paces and six stadia. The joining of these
mountains was made level perpendicularly from the summit right down to the floor.

For which cause I stood pondering within myself with what iron instruments, and with how much wearing
of men's hands, and what numbers of them, so great an artifice had been forcibly brought to pass —
so incredibly laborious, and with so great a grinding away of time. Here, then, with the one mountain
and the other, this admirable structure joined itself in knowing adhesion. By which joining, as is
said above, the valley was fortified with a closure, so that no one could go out from there, or turn
back, or enter, save through this open gate.

Now above this so huge work of building — whose height from the topmost cornices to the footing and
base could easily be conjectured at a fifth of a stadium — there was founded an adamantinely
pinnacled and most portentous Pyramid. Whereupon I reasonably judged that not without inestimable
expense, and time, and the greatest multitude of mortals, could such an incredible artifice ever have
been devised and set up. And if I rightly judged its excess, beyond belief, to be a thing
unimaginable to look upon — which in the beholding wearied the visual power not a little, and thinned
the other spiritual senses — how much more to make it? Therefore, so far as the grasp of my
understanding will grant it me, in this manner I now briefly describe it.

Each face of the squared base of the mass, below the beginning of the stepping of this admirable
Pyramid set above the aforesaid building, was in length six stadia. Multiplied by four in
circumference, the said equilateral footing took up, all told, four and twenty stadia. Then in
height, raising the lines from each angle by measure — as far as the lowest line of the plinth
extends — all four running together and meeting at the middle of the summit constituted the perfect
Pyramidal figure. The middle perpendicular, above the centre where the diagonals of the Plinth cross,
was one part less in six than the ascending lines.

Which immense and terrible Pyramid, rising by steps adamantine with wonderful and exquisite Symmetry,
contained one thousand four hundred and ten steps, or stairs, wrought in relief — apart from ten
steps needed to finish the tapering. In place of these was set and substituted a stupendous Cube,
solid and firm and monstrous in its thickness, offering itself beyond belief as a thing carried up
and appointed to that summit; of that same Parian stone of which the steps were made.

The said square was set beneath as the base and support of the obelisk that is to be spoken of. This
most huge stone — such as was never the block quarried by Titis — had a falling-away in its
circumference of six parts, two in the descent and one in the pointed level; and it remained on the
topmost plane four paces broad by diameter. In the levelling of which there rose four Harpy's feet of
metal, with their pads and clawed talons cast, fixed into the great stone towards the angles, along
the diagonal lines, and firmly leaded in; of proportioned thickness, and of the height of two paces.
Which, knotting themselves most beautifully together, encircled and bound the lowest Socle of a great
Obelisk, cast in wonderful foliage, and fruits, and flowers of fitting greatness. Upon which the
Obelisk pressed, most firmly set above them. Its breadth two paces, and seven times as much in
height, artificially sharpening itself, of Theban fire-flecked stone. On the faces of which were
Egyptian Hieroglyphs excellently carved, smooth, and brightly polished like a mirror.

On the topmost pinnacle of it, set above with the utmost diligence and art, rested a settled base of
brass. In which there was besides a turning engine, or broad-brimmed cap, fixed upon a stable pivot
or pole. Which held up an image of a Nymph, an elegant work of the material already named — enough to
turn to stupefaction anyone who considered it most carefully and with fixed gaze. Of such and so
made a proportion that she allowed herself to be seen perfectly from below, in the air, at the common
stature. And

further, the magnitude of that statue was a wonderful thing to consider: with what temerity, carried
up to such a loftiness — nay, into the air — such a work had been brought, with its flying garment,
part of the fleshy calves showing themselves uncovered. And two open wings were fastened at the space
between her shoulders, showing the act of flight. Her most beautiful face and propitious aspect were
turned towards the wings. She had, moreover, above her tressed brow the braids flying free, and the
part of the Crown, or Skull, bared and as it were unhaired — which were as though stretched out
towards the flying.

In the right hand, at the object of her gaze, she held an artificial horn of plenty, stuffed with
every good thing, turned towards the earth. And the other hand she held pressed and closed upon her
naked breast. This statue, then, turned easily at whatever breeze blew, with such a whirring of the
rubbing of the hollow metal engine as was never heard from the Roman treasury. And where the figure
rested with its feet, rubbing upon the little altar beneath, there sounded such a ringing as the
Bell at the magnificent Baths of Hadrian never gave out, nor that of the five Pyramids standing upon
the square.

Which most lofty Obelisk allows me still not the least belief that another showed any conformity to
it, or any likeness. Not the Vatican one. Not the Alexandrian. Not the Babylonian. It held in itself
such a heaping-up of wonder that I stood senseless with stupefaction at the considering of it. And
far more still, the immensity of the work, and the excess of the subtlety of that opulent and most
acute genius, and the great care and exquisite diligence of the Architect.

With what daring invention of art, then; with what power and human strength, and order, and
incredible expense, was so great a weight carried up and set so high in the air, in emulation of the
heavens? With what Windlass, and with what wheeled Pulleys, and with what Crabs, or Block-and-tackle,
and other hauling Engines, and framed Scaffoldings? Let every other incredible and greatest structure
keep silence here.

t:
Let us return, then, to that vastest Pyramid, beneath which lay a huge and solid Plinth, or block, or
square set under it, of fourteen paces in height and in extension, or length, six stadia. Which made
the footing of the lowest step of the massive Pyramid. And this I shrewdly judged had not been
brought there from elsewhere, but carved out of the mountain itself by human labours into that figure
and Scheme, and reduced to so great a mass in its own place. The remainder of the steps was made
compositely of separate blocks.

Which immense square did not adhere to the flanking mountains of the valley, but was set apart and
separated on the one side and the other by ten paces. On the right-hand side, as I went, of the
aforesaid Plinth, in the middle of it, the viperous head of the fearful Medusa was fearsomely and
perfectly carved, shown in furious act, crying out and snarling; with terrifying eyes, hollowed
beneath the pressed-down brows, and with wrinkled forehead, and the mouth gaping open. Which,
excavated with a straight passage, its top vaulted, penetrating as far as the centre — or as far as
the middle perpendicular central line of the topmost Cap of that portent-bearing Pyramid — made a
most ample entrance and approach.

To which opening of the mouth one ascended by way of her twisted hairs, expressed with an
inconceivable subtlety of understanding, and art, and studied thought of the craftsman; with such
rule and reduction that they aptly made climbing steps up to the open mouth. And in place of curling
tresses I gazed astonished at vipers and twisted serpents, in living and huge coils, wrapping
themselves confusedly about the monstrous head with the swiftest turnings. Whereupon the face and the
scaly quarrelling serpents were so exactly counterfeited in the working that they struck no little
horror and terror into me. In the eyes of which were most conveniently enclosed the brightest little
stones — so much so that, had I not been certain the material was marble, I should not have dared
approach so easily.

The above-named passage, carved within the solid rock, led to where the stairs were, with a winding
course, in the centre, by spiral turnings; by which one climbed to the highest summit of that Pyramid,
onto the surface of the square Cap. Upon which was founded the eminent Obelisk.

Beyond all this illustrious and stupendous work, I certainly judged this the most excellent: that the
aforesaid spiral stairs were everywhere clearly lit. For the ingenious and most acute architect had
shrewdly made certain light-stealing passages, with great and most exquisite investigation of the
understanding. Which, in respect of the wandering of the Sun, corresponded directly to three parts:
the lowest, the middle, and the upper. The lower one by the

light-wells; the upper was lit by the down-shafts; and with certain reflections from the opposite
sides they gave sufficient light. So great was the calculated rule of the exquisite disposition of
that artificial mathematician, in the three faces — Eastern, Southern and Western — that at every
hour of the day the winding stair was lit and clear. Which breathing-holes were defined
symmetrically in different placings of that greatest Pyramid, and distributed here and there.

I came to the part of the aforesaid opening of the mouth by climbing another solid and straight
stair, which at the Airy footing of the building, towards the right-hand side flanking the
sheared-off mountain, was excavated within the rock itself, where the interval of the ten paces was.
By which — more curious, certainly, than perhaps was lawful — I climbed. Where, having come to the
going-in by the mouth to the stair, and having at last climbed by innumerable steps or stairs,
circling about, not without grave labour and dizziness of the head, above so unimaginable a
loftiness: my eyes could not fitly bear to look down at the level ground, so much so that everything
below appeared to me imperfect. And for this I did not dare to leave the middle floor.

And there, round about the circular and topmost exit — that is, the end of the winding stair and its
opening — many spindled posts of metal were neatly disposed and fixed in a circuit, the spacing of
which, from centre to centre, divided one foot, and half a pace in height. Girded above with a little
waving cornice going round about, of the said cast material, which surrounded and fenced the lip of
the opening and gape of the upper exit of the said stair — excepting that part by which one went out
onto the surface. Rightly judged, so that no one less cautious should fall headlong into the opening
of the winding cave; seeing that the immoderate height induced a reeling.

Beneath, then, the sloping level of the Obelisk, a bronze tablet was leaded in, lying face upward,
with ancient writing in letters of our own, and in Greek and Arabic; by which I fully understood that
it was dedicated to the highest Sun. And of the whole vast structure the measurement also was
entirely noted and described. And the name of the architect, above the Obelisk, noted in Greek:
LICHAS THE LIBYAN, STONE-BUILDER, SET ME UP.

Let us return for the present to the Base, or Block, set beneath the Pyramid; in the front of which I
beheld an elegant and magnificent sculpture of a cruel Battle of the Giants, wanting only the breath
of life, excellently carved in wonderful relief; with its movements, and with so much

of those tall bodies as could ever be told. The imitating rival of nature was so properly expressed
that the eyes, wearying together with the feet, forced themselves eagerly now to one part and now to
another. No less did it appear in the lifelike Horses: some prostrate, some stumbling and falling;
many wounded and struck, showing that they breathed out their gracious life; and their hooves
planting themselves ill upon the fallen bodies, furious and unbridled.

And the Giants, their armour cast off, closely embracing one another; some carried along with their
feet caught in the trappings; others crushed beneath their own bodies; and some falling headlong with
their wounded horses. Some, laid flat upon the ground on their backs, fought protecting themselves
with the shield. Many girt with side-swords and with belted blades, and with antique Persian
broadswords and manifold instruments of deadly shaping. The greater part on foot, fighting confusedly
with darts and bucklers. Some in corslets and helmets, marked with varied crests; and others naked,
showing that they attacked with a lively heart, intent upon death. Some breastplated, adorned with
various and most noble military ornaments. Many with the fearful look of men crying out; some with
the semblance of obstinacy and fury.

Those who were about to die, with a thread rivalling nature, expressed the effect; and others dead,
with hateful and manifold engines of war and slaughter. They showed the robust limbs and the swelling
muscles, and gave the eyes to see the office of the bones, and the hollows where the hard sinews
drew. Which conflict and duel appeared so fearful and horrible that you would say it was bloody and
arms-mighty Mars himself about to fight in single combat with Porphyrion and Alcyoneus; and the
flight they had at the braying of the ass came into my memory to see.

All these images exceeded the natural tallness and stature, and the carving was in deep relief of
most illustrious and polishable marble, the flat space between introduced of the blackest stone for
the comeliness and grace of the white stone and for the setting-off of the statuary work; and they
stood out perfectly. Here, then, were infinite tall bodies, last strivings, intent acts, breastplated
habits, and various death, with doubtful victory. Alas, my wearied spirits, and my understanding
confused by such continual variety, and my disordered senses, cannot fitly bear not only to tell the
whole, but they are not able to express even a part, with completeness, of so polished a
stone-carving.

And whence then was born so great a boasting, and so burning a lust, to heap up stones by joining
them into so great a mass, a pile, a pinnacle? And with what Waggon? with what Bearers? and Dray?
with what Rollers was so great and such a vastness of stones forced along? And upon what propping
were they joined and confederated? And upon what mound of cemented rough-work? And of so great an
immensity, the loftiest Obelisk, and the immense Pyramid? So that never did Dinocrates more boastfully
propose to Alexander the Great the

matter of his loftiest conceit of Mount Athos. For this most ample structure without fail exceeds the
Egyptian insolence. It surpasses the marvellous labyrinths. Let Lemnos be quiet. Let the Theatres
fall dumb. The dignified Mausoleum is not its equal. For this was certainly not known to him who
wrote of the seven miracles, or spectacles, of the world. Nor in any age was such a thing ever seen
or conceived — passing over in silence even the wonderful sepulchre of Ninus.

At the last I considered discreetly what opposed and obstinate resistance of vaults could ever
sustain or support beneath it, and what Hexagonal and four-square Piers, and what smallness of
columning could firmly, set beneath, endure so great a heaviness and intolerable weighing. By which
reasoning I judged rightly that either the whole remained solid and massive, the mountain being
subject beneath it, or else it was one compacted heap of glued cement and gravel and rough stonework.
By such consideration I explored through the ample gate. And I saw that within there was thick
darkness and hollowness. Which gate, together with the wonderful and proud building — things worthy of
an eternal monument — will be somewhat described in what follows, as it was excellently disposed.

POLIPHILO, AFTER HE HAS TOLD PART OF THE IMMENSE STRUCTURE, AND THE VASTEST PYRAMID WITH ITS
WONDERFUL OBELISK, DESCRIBES IN THE FOLLOWING CHAPTER GREAT AND MARVELLOUS WORKS, AND CHIEFLY A
HORSE, A LYING COLOSSUS, AN ELEPHANT, BUT ABOVE ALL A MOST ELEGANT GATE.

MOST JUSTLY MIGHT IT BE FREELY granted me to say that in the universal world there were never other
like most magnificent works, neither conceived nor yet seen by human gaze. So that I would almost
freely judge that from human knowledge and the highest and most virtuous power no like insolence of
building and of artifice could fitly be raised up, nor defined by invention. Whereupon my senses were
so captivated at this intent and obstinate sight, together with excess of pleasure and with
stupefaction, that nothing else came into my ravished memory that was solacing and most joyful,
except when I looked applying myself, and curiously all the parts to the comely

t:
fitting composition, examining those excellent and choice stone statues of maidenly making, so that,
stirred at once, I sighed warmly and sobbing.

So that my loving and sounding sighs echoed in this solitary and deserted place, in air made thick,
recalling to me my Goddess and immeasurably longed-for Polia. Alas, scarcely a little pause was
granted in which that loving and heavenly Idea was not figured in my mind, and a diligent companion
of my strange and unknown journeying. In which, firmly nested, my soul lay contentedly, as in the
safest garrison and an inviolate Asylum, secure.

Being therefore come in this manner to such a place, where my eyes were stolen and taken up with such
a sight by the copious and choice work of antiquity, above all I beheld a most beautiful gate, so
stupendous and of such incredible artifice, and so elegant in every lineament, as could ever be
wrought and polished. Which without fail I do not feel that I have knowledge enough in me to describe
perfectly, or even sufficiently. Chiefly because in our age the vernacular, proper and native words,
and those peculiar to the art of building, are buried and extinguished together with the true men.

O execrable and sacrilegious barbarism, how despoilingly have you invaded the noblest part of the
precious treasure and sanctuary of Latin, and that art so dignified, at present darkened and ruinously
injured by accursed ignorance! Which, associated together with raging, insatiable and perfidious
avarice, has blinded that most high and excellent part which made Rome both sublime and a wandering
Empress.

Before this excellent gate — judging this the first thing to say — there was left open to the sky a
four-square courtyard, thirty paces by its diameter. With a notable pavement of marble squares,
divided by one foot, set between with tessellation in various interlacings and bindings and
colourings. In many parts broken up by the fall of stones, and grown over with shrubs.

And at the extremities of the said courtyard, on the right and on the left, towards the mountains,
there were two orders of columns set to the level, with the exquisite interval of the wide-spaced
manner set between, according to the fitting requirement from one column to another. Where the first
run, or order, on both the one side and the other, began level with the edge, or outermost bound, of
the pavement at the front of the great gate. And between the one colonnade and the other was a space
of fifteen paces.

Of which columns some, and the greater part in number, were seen whole; with their Doric, or
cushioned, capitals, with the bark-like, or spiral, volutes outside the ringed echinus, with the
astragals beneath, hanging here and there, exceeding by a third part its own base — that is, of the
capital, which was of a thickness equal to the half-diameter of the column set beneath it. Upon which
lay the Architrave, or straight beam,

continuous, but for the greater part broken and interrupted. Many columns widowed of their capitals,
and buried amid the ruins up to their topmost part and the projection of the Astragal and the neck
and the foot. Near which runs of columning there still endured ancient Plane-trees, and a wild
Laurel-grove, and cone-bearing Cypresses, and thorny Brambles. I supposed it a Hippodrome, or a
covered walk, or a running-track, or Ambulatories — that is, walking-places — or an ample breadth of
uncovered porticoes, or the place of a seasonal water-channel.

Upon this courtyard, ten paces in from the beginning towards the gate, I saw a prodigious horse and
winged Vaulting-steed, with its wings spread, of bronze, of excessive magnitude. The hoof of which
occupied, upon the level of the base, in the outermost line of the rounding of one shoe, five feet.
And from this outermost circuit of the hoof up to beneath the breast I found it, by due reckoning,
nine feet high.

With its head loose and unbridled, with two little ears, the one thrust forward and the other drawn
back. With waving and flowing mane hanging down over the right of the neck. Upon which many striplings
were attempting to ride astride. Not one of them was able to hold himself firmly upon it, because of
its unchecked swiftness and hard jolting. Whereupon some were falling, some stood on the point of
falling headlong. Some on their backs, and some thrown over backwards, and others were climbing up
leaning on it; some, tumbled over, held vainly to the long hairs caught in their gripping hands.
There were some fallen, and then in the act of rising, slipped beneath the body of the shaker-off.

In the surface of the base there was fixed and leaded a plate of the same cast material — as much as
the shoes stood held fast and the young men thrown down — the whole one composition and mass cast
together, by a wonderful art of founding. In the end one could not tell whether any rider of such a
swift horsemanship was yet content, so far as I could judge. For which cause the statues appeared
sorrowful and wearied, without lament — which was not heard because they lacked it: only because the
maker could not breathe the breath of life into them, so excellently did they imitate the truth of
nature. Let the sharp genius of the imprudent Perillus give way here, and of Hiram the Jew, and of
every founder of statues whatsoever. It gave one to understand that those striplings were being
brought so ill towards the opened gate.

The Pedestal, or marvellous base, was of solid marble — of a thickness, height and length proportioned
to sustaining the machine fixed upon it — of flooding veins many-coloured, and of pleasing markings
grateful to the eyes, disposed confusedly in infinite mixtures.

In the front of the aforesaid stone, towards the gate, I saw set a crown of green marble of leaves of
bitter Parsley, with mixed fennel-like leaves of Hog's-fennel. Within which there was moreover
fastened a rounding of white stone, in which, carved, it held a writing in Latin capitals.
On the opposite face likewise, in a crown of leaves of deadly Aconite, was such a note.

On the right-hand side thereafter were carved certain figures of men and of damsels dancing, with two
faces apiece — the one in front laughing, the hinder one weeping. And they danced in a ring, holding
one another by the arms, man with man and woman with woman: the one arm of a man
pages.note: In the 1499 the inscription itself is given as a woodcut and is not carried by the source transcription.

t:
beneath that of the woman, and the other above that of the next. And so, holding one another, they
went forward, one after another, so that always a glad face was turned to meet the mournful face of
the one before. These were seven and seven, so perfectly feigned in comely carving, with lifelike
movements, with the veiling garments flying, that they accused the excellent craftsman of no other
defect save that he had not given the voice to the one and the tears to the other. The aforesaid
dance was excellently cut in a figure of two semicircles with a partition set between.
Beneath which Half-round figure I saw this word inscribed: TIME.

Then I saw besides, on the other side, many striplings — the work of the aforesaid craftsman,
altogether perfect, in a figure uniform with the one just recited, most beautifully waved, and the
waving of both figures clothed with exquisite foliage — intent upon gathering flowers among many
herbs and shrubs; while together many merry Nymphs, jesting playfully, coaxingly snatched them away.
And in the manner recited above, beneath the figure were certain hollowed Capitals which said this
one word: LOSS. And they were choice letters, exactly made, their thickness a ninth part, and a
little more, of the diameter of the square.

Not a little stupefied, therefore, turning it over and looking with the greatest curious delight upon
that huge machine cast into an animal by human genius, most worthily imagined — so that in every
member it shared unfailingly the excellent harmony and joining — there came into my retaining memory
the ill-fated horse of Seianus.

Then, dazzled by such an artificial mystery, there offered itself to my eyes a spectacle no less
wonderful, a very great Elephant, and with it the greatest desire to hasten towards it. But behold, I
hear from another quarter a human groan as of sickness. I stood at once, my hair rising, and without
further deliberation, hurrying towards the groan, I climbed a heap of ruins of great fractures and
marble cuttings. And having gone forward fitly from there — behold, I see a most Vast and wonderful
colossus, with the feet hollowed out and without soles, and all the Shin-bones open and empty.

And coming from there to the head, gazing with horror, I conjectured that the air let in through the
gaping soles, by a divine invention, caused the groan to be moderately expressed. Which lay silent,
reclining on its back, cast of metal by a wonderful artifice, of middle age, holding its head raised a
little upon a cushion. With the semblance of a sick man, with the mouth showing that it sighed and
groaned. Gaping, of a tallness of sixty paces. And by the hairs one could climb up over the breast,
and by the matted and tormented hairs of the thick beard, to the lamenting mouth. Which by passages
was all void and empty. Through that, then, driven by the stimulus of curious searching, without other
counsel, into the throat by little steps

and thence into the stomach, and from there by hidden ducts to all the other parts of the inner
viscera, I came, somewhat afraid. O wonderful conception! I beheld all the parts intimately, as they
lie open in a human body. And at each one I beheld carved, in three tongues — Chaldean, Greek and
Latin — the name of that part, so that in each natural body one might see the intestines, sinews and
bones, veins, muscles and flesh; and what disease is engendered in it, and the cause, and the cure and
remedy. Wherefore through all the coiled viscera there was a little approach and a convenient entry,
with breathing-holes variously distributed through the body, lighting the fitting places. In no part
less than it stands in nature.

And when I came to the heart, I saw, reading, how of love the little sighs are engendered, and where
love grievously wounds. And there, wholly moved, I drew from the depth of my heart a bellowing sigh,
invoking Polia; so that I felt the whole brazen machine resound, with no little horror. An art
invented above every exquisite thing, that a man should make himself without an excelling anatomy.

O illustrious wits of the past! O truly golden age, when virtue kept concert with fortune! To this
age alone you left ignorance and rival avarice as an inheritance.

I saw, standing out in another part of the aforesaid thickness, the brow of a woman's head somewhat
uncovered among the ruins, the rest buried by the greatest breakages. For which cause, judging a like
workmanship to be there, and fearing the disordered and unequal ruins, I left off looking at it and
returned to the first place.

Where also, not too far distant from the great horse, there offered itself at the level a very great
Elephant of blackening stone, more than Obsidian, sparkling with gold and with silvery flecks
copiously scattered like a fine dust, and glittering through the stone. The stubborn hardness of which
plainly showed its clear lustre; for in it every object represented itself and was sent back most
properly to that quarter — except where the metal had spread its greenish rust.

And this fittingly, because on the summit of its most ample back it had a marvellous Bronze
saddle-cloth, with two tight Girths carried round the monstrous bulk. Between which very great
bindings, fastened with buckles of the same stone, there was held a quadrangle answering to the
thickness of the Obelisk set above; so that no perpendicular of weight should have air, or rather
void, beneath it. For being hollow within, it is not solid, nor lasting.

Which quadrangular part was beautifully lined on each of its three faces with Egyptian characters.
This burden-bearing monster, then, expressed and finished most diligently and not without wonder — as
well as by rule one could artificially feign and set up in statue — and in the aforesaid saddle,
approvedly adorned with many seals and bosses and little histories and figures, sustained most firmly
founded an Obelisk of greening Laconian stone. Of a breadth in its levelled faces equal to the lowest
diameter of one pace, and multiplied by seven, so much was it to the sharpened summit

. On the pinnacle of which, fixed, there stood out a most round Triangle, of a material clear and
translucent.

This greatest beast stood therefore in fitting composition, so nobly figured, upon the levelled plane
of a vast base of hardest Porphyry, most smoothly lined. With two great projecting tusks of a most
white and shining stone, set on and fastened. And from the bronze saddle there hung, buckled, an
excellent breast-piece of various ornament, of the material of the saddle, in the middle of which was
written in the Latin tongue: *The brain is in the head.*

And likewise, carried round by the end of the neck and joined to the great head, there went a
masterly binding. From which an ambitious ornament, most notable, of bronze, hung thrown over its most
ample brow, composed of two squares, with elegant lineaments. In the flat of which — surrounded with
waving foliage — I saw certain Ionic and Arabic letters.

Now its voracious trunk did not keep to the level of the base, but raised and hanging it stood, turned
somewhat towards the front, with the furrowed ears very widely let down, or barred. Which image in its
vastness showed itself not one whit less than the natural. And in the oblong circuit of the base were
carved hieroglyphs, or Egyptian characters. Decently polished, with the due base-course, with the
block, gorge, torus and roundel, with their Astragals or little bindings, with the reversed Cyma at
the footing. And above no less, with the projecting Cyma turned back, and the collar of the scotia and
the dentils with the Astragals; excellently Symmetried according as the thickness required. The
length, breadth and height: twelve paces, five, and three. The extremities of which were formed in a
half-circle.

In the hinder half-round part of the base just described, I found a stepped ascent of seven steps
carved for climbing upon the flat surface. By which, eager for novelty, I mounted. And towards the
reserved quadrangle, set beneath the perpendicular of the saddle-cloth, I saw a little door hollowed
out. A thing of great admiration, that in so stubborn a material so apt a hollow was afforded; so that
by certain posts of metal fixed after the manner of a ladder, by which was a convenient ascent, one
