t: might enter into the disembowelled Elephantine machine.
pages.wcap: Monument with Female Figure, Lamp, and Trilingual Inscriptions

t:
For which cause, greatly stirred by curious eagerness, I entered and climbed. Where I found the
greatest and most prodigious monster all hollow and void, and made a cavern — save that the same solid
mass was left within, which stood beneath as the ballast. And it had as much passage, both towards the
head and towards the hinder part, as a natural man could make his way through.

And there, hung in the vault of the back, there burned with brazen chains an inextinguishable lamp,
with a prison's lighting. By which, in this hinder part, I beheld an ancient sepulchre granted to the
stone itself, with a perfect image of a man, naked, of the common natural size, crowned, of the Stone,
most black. With the teeth, eyes and nails covered in shining silver. Standing above the arched
sepulchral cover, clothed in scale-work and other exquisite lineaments. It showed the forepart with a
gilded sceptre of bronze, the arm stretched out. And in the left hand it held a keel-shaped shield,
its form taken exactly from the skull-bone of a horse, inscribed in three tongues with little letters
— Hebrew, Attic and Latin — to this sense:
*I should be naked, had not the beast covered me. Seek, and you shall find. Let me be.*

At which unaccustomed thing I stood not a little stupefied, and with some horror. Whereupon, without
delaying too long, turning to go back, I saw likewise another lamp burning and shining, as is said
before. And crossing over the opening by which one climbs, there towards the head of the animal, in
this side too I found a like making of a most ancient burial. And the

statue standing above the whole, like the other, save that this one was a queen; which, having raised
the right arm, pointed with the forefinger to the part behind her shoulders, and with the other held a
tablet, held fast with its cover and with her hand undivided. On which likewise was inscribed this
epigram in three tongues:

*Whoever you are, take as much of this treasure as you please. But I warn you: take away the head. Do
not touch the body.*

At so great a novelty, worthy of the telling, and reading over the riddles again and again, I remained
wholly ignorant, both of the interpretation and of the sophistical meaning, which was very ambiguous.
Nor did I dare therefore to attempt anything. But being struck as it were with fear in this dark and
unlighted place — for all that there was the lamp's light there — nevertheless the anxious desire to
contemplate the triumphal gate, urging me on, was a more lawful cause for my not lingering there than
any other.

Whereupon, without doing anything else, with the thought and purpose of returning there once more by
every means after the contemplation of that wonderful gate, and of considering more tranquilly such a
magnificence of invention from human wits, I came most swiftly to the opening. And going down I came
out of the disembowelled monster.

An invention unimaginable and beyond estimation, an excess of labour and of rash human daring: what
Auger could bore through so great a hardness and stubbornness of stone, and hollow out so great a
hardness of material, or what other builder's engines could do it? The hollowing within agreeing
harmoniously with the outward form. At last, having returned onto the courtyard, I saw in this

base carved round about most worthily with these hieroglyphs. First a horned skull-bone of an ox, with
two instruments of husbandry knotted to the horns, and an Altar founded upon two goat's feet, with a
little burning flame, in the face of which was an eye and a vulture. Then a Basin, and a ewer for
pouring; following, a ball of thread fixed upon a spindle-pin, and an Antique vase with the mouth
stopped. A Sole with an eye, with two fronds laid across, the one of olive and the other of palm,
neatly strapped. An anchor, and a goose. An Antique lamp, with a hand holding it. An ancient Rudder,
girt about with a branch of fruit-bearing Olive. Then two Hooks. A Dolphin, and last a closed Ark.
These hieroglyphs were of the best carving in these markings.
Which most ancient and sacred writings, considering them, I interpreted thus:

*From your labour sacrifice liberally to the god of nature; little by little you will bring back a
mind made subject to god. He will hold a firm guard over your life, governing it mercifully, and will
keep it unharmed.*

Leaving this most excellent and mysterious and unimaginable making, I returned again to look upon the
prodigious Horse. Which had a bony head, and lean, and proportionately small; it appeared an excellent
figuring of standing unquiet and impatient of delay, and one saw almost the trembling of its flesh,
and it was more alive than feigned. With a Greek word hollowed in its brow: GENEA.

Then many other great pieces and fragments of every lineament, among the greatest broken heaps of
ruin. And of all of them, devouring and flying time had kindly spared these four stupendous things
only, untouched: the Gate, the Horse, the colossus, and the Elephant. O holy fathers, ancient
craftsmen, what savagery invaded so great a virtue of yours, that you carried with you into the
sepulchre the disinheriting of us from such riches?

Having come, then, to this most ancient gate, of work most notable, and marvellously constructed with
exquisite rule and art, and with illustrious ornaments of carving and of various lineament — for all
which things, being studious and inflamed with the desire to understand the fertile understanding and
the keen searching-out of that perspicacious Architect, both his dimension and his lineament and his
practice — I set about examining it subtly, and did thus.

I diligently measured a square set beneath the columns, two to a side. From which measuring I easily
grasped the whole symmetry of the aforesaid gate. Which, explaining, I shall run over briefly. A
four-sided figure A.B.C.D., divided by three straight lines and three cross lines equally distant,
will be sixteen squares. Then, adding to the figure as much as its half, and dividing the addition by
those same partitions, there are found twenty-four squares. This figure of little cords offers itself
ready to hand, and how useful and fitting it is for reducing to a smaller scale, in cutting, or in
fine work and in painting.

Drawing again in the first figure A.B.C.D. two diagonals; and marking in it besides two lines, a
straight and a cross one, mutually intersecting, four squares were made. Likewise in that empty space
above the equal sides, four middle points being made, and lines drawn from one to the other, the
Rhombus is constituted.

The aforesaid figures being described in such a way, I considered fitly: what reason have the blind
moderns, who esteem themselves in the art of building, not knowing what the thing is? So enormously
still they order their false little buildings, sacred as well as profane, public and private,
dishonouring the parts that proceed from the middle, neglectful of that which nature teaches by
showing. It being a golden and heavenly saying and lesson that in that consists virtue — and the poet
sings of blessedness — which, being deserted and neglected, must needs come out disordered, and
everything with it.

For any part that does not agree with its chief is base. The order and the norm being removed,
however, what convenient, or pleasing, or worthy thing could be afforded? The cause, then, of such
unfitting error is born of negative ignorance, and has its origin in want of letters.

Nevertheless, although the perfection of that most worthy art does not stray from rightness, yet the
shrewd and industrious Architect, to make the object gratify the gaze, may lawfully polish his work
with addition and subtraction. Above all preserving the whole solid entire, and reconciled with the
universal. Which solid I call the whole body of the fabric, that being the principal intent and
invention and forethought and Symmetry of the Architect; which, well examined and carried through
without the accessories, shows (if I do not deceive myself) the excellence of his genius — because the
adorning afterwards is an easy thing.

Granted that its distribution also matters, and that one should not set the cornice at the feet but at
the head; and so the ovolo, and the dentil, and the rest, must be destined to their fitting place. The
ordering, then, and the chief invention are shared among the few; the ornaments offer themselves to be
worked by the many, and the common or unlearned sort. And therefore the handworking craftsmen are the
architect's ministers.

Which architect must in no manner succumb to accursed and perfidious avarice. And beyond his learning
let him be good, not talkative, kindly, well-wishing, gentle, patient, pleasant, copious, a curious and
universal searcher-out, and slow. Slow, I say, so as not to be hasty afterwards in mending. Of this
let it be enough.

Reducing finally the last three figures shown into one, and adding the second from the sixteen squares
contained in it, this figure will be produced. From which, then, removing the rhombus and the
diagonals, and leaving the three perpendiculars and the three straight lines, except the middle one —
which, cut off, ends inclusively between the perpendiculars — and by this rule two perfect squares are
found, the one above and the other below, each containing in itself four squares.

In the lower square, making the diagonal, which set upright in a perpendicular towards the straight
line A.B. will readily be found, by what it falls short of reaching, to be exactly the thickness of the
arch and of the Antae. So then the line A.B. will be the due place of the extended, or straight, Beam.
The middle point of the truncated line E.F. will be the point from which to bend the arch-beam into a
half-circle. Which must have as much addition at its turned-back horns as is the half-diameter of its
thickness. Otherwise, such a falling-short being there, I do not call it perfect. But this was most
beautifully and exquisitely and diligently observed by the best and most skilled of the ancients in
their arches, to give the arch elegance and fitting resistance, and to avoid the encroachment of the
projections of the Abaci.

manner: beneath the paired columns on this side and on that, the square, or little Altar, or Podium,
began from a Plinth level with the paved Area, raised one foot. Which was also the continued
boundary. From this the turned-back Cymas, tori and channels with the Astragals stepped neatly
towards the Podium. And with due and requisite binding they made the Socles for the Antae, that is to
say the bases. And consequently, above the Podium, the cornice was stretched out with the Cyma turned
up, and the other concurring linings.

Between the line A.B. and the last line of the master square M.N. I found that it was taken up by a
third — that is, divided into four partitions, three of which are attributed to the straight Beam, the
Zophorus, and the cornice. Which cornice claimed one part more than the Beam and the Frieze; that is
to say, if five portions are assigned to the Beam and as many equally to the Zophorus, the cornice
deservedly usurps six. And it exceeded this limit by so much the more, in that the discreet and
skilled craftsman had made a sloping licking-over above the margin determined for the Cyma of the
aforesaid cornice, half a foot remaining chamfered.

And this is not found to be observed in vain, because the lowest of the carved works set above are not
hidden by the coming-out, or projection, of the cornice. Although one may so much the more magnify the
part following above of the ornaments — as happens with the Zophorus, exceeding for this cause the
assigned Symmetry. Then above this first crowning there followed a perfect square, by this rule.

As much as the projection of the Zophorus was above the perpendicular of the columns, so much was that
one thrust out. Which, divided into two partitions, one part as it was found, so much thickness was
attributed to the topmost cornice. These two squares being constituted, one to a side: the remainder
therefore set between, at the perpendicular of the opening of the gate, divided into seven portions,
the middle one was reserved for a throne, or Niche, where the Nymph-like statue resided. Three then,
on this side and on that, were left to the flanking parts.

The coming-out of the projection of the upper cornice offers itself easily: making of the line of its
thickness a Four-square, divided by the Diagonal, the just rule of the projection is found.

Now taking together the whole figure of the twenty-four squares, the sesquialteral is found. Which
figure is O.P.Q.T. It is manifest that it contains in itself a Four-square, and a half. Such half,
equally divided into six portions by straight lines, there are found five lines between and six
partitions. Upon the fifth upper line, at its middle mark, is offered by rule the pinnacle of the
frontispiece, the lining sloping down from there above

the cut of the lateral extension of the cornice, where the fitting slope appeared. The edges of which,
or extremities, coupled themselves justly with the Cymatia of the projection of the crowning.

Finally the frontispiece, with exquisite correspondence sharing the lineament of the elegant cornice,
in its first order then usurped the flat of the projected square; and last, a part of dentilled
cornice, within which was contained the angular flat.

The aforesaid gate was most diligently wrought in a levelled polish of cut stone panelling, the waving
figures conforming themselves in the joining of the panels. With a pleasing fitness of the inserted
works, and the material bright and gracious.

On the one side and the other, separated by two paces from the compass of the gate, there stood still
unmoved two great and proud columns, buried up to their footing in the roughness of the ruin. From
which, removing the ruin as far as I could, I laid bare the bronze bases, uncovering them; and of like
material were the Capitals, excellently cast. And measuring for pleasure the thickness of one Base and
doubling it, it expressed the entire diameter of the lowest thickness of the column. By which
measuring I found its height more than eight-and-twenty cubits.

The two near the gate were of finest Porphyry and of gracious Ophite; the other two channelled, or
fluted, or grooved, and most excellently ready. Beyond these, then, on the left and the right hand,
stood others in orderly fashion, paired in company, with modest swelling, of hardest Laconian stone.

The half-diameter of the lowest circuit of the column made the thickness of the Base, which consisted
of Tori, of a roundel, or Scotia, or Trochilus, and a Plinth. That half being divided by three, the
Plinth usurped one for itself, its breadth one diameter and a half. The two partitions being divided
again into four, one took the topmost Torus. The three being distributed into twin parts, one took the
lowest Torus, and the other was afforded to the hollowed Trochilus, with the edges taking a seventh
part of it. Such measurement I found elegantly observed by the skilled craftsmen.

Above the ruled capitals of the aforesaid columns there extended an excellent Beam, or Architrave,
with the lowest band adorned with rounded whorls, or berries; and the second with an association
lengthwise of truncated spindles, with two whorls pressed down in a row set between the one and the
other. The third, with approved comeliness, was clothed with Cymas turned like little ears, in noble
foliage with stalk-work of most approved expression.

Above this sat the Zophorus of winding fronds, deeply carved among the spirals, or great turnings, and
various stalks and flowers with pleasing vine-work, in which many birds were nesting. Then above there
followed an order of exquisite Modillions, with

spacing between. Above which began the reversed stepping of a copious cornice. Beyond this broken
crowning, then, the greater part was seen demolished and shattered, with the trace, or imitation, of
paired and great windows, widowed of their ornaments — ill showing what the building had been when
defined and perfect.

Beneath the aforesaid beam ran down the top, or pinnacled summit, of the frontispiece of the preserved
gate. Where, between its slope and the lining of the beam, that space imitated the figure of a
stairway, which shows a triangle of unequal sides, or ribs.

Beneath the beam, in the space between the columns, there was sustained upon marvellous modillions,
with an artificial hollow between — in this figure described, as much as could embrace the greater
space — two roundels hollowed out, in imitation of a dish bound about at the lips with waving-work,
gullets and scotias; where in the topmost stepping, in the middle of the lineaments drawn about it,
there swelled a Torus, nobly clothed in oaken foliage, joined one beneath another, bound about with
grooved thongs, with fruits scattered.

Within which resided two venerable images, freed from the vase, that is to say from the hollow, from
the midriff upward. The breast part covered with a mantle over the left shoulder in an antique knot.
With shaggy beards and laurelled brows, with a bearing worthy and majestic.

In the square projection of the Zophorus above the columns written of, in front, was this carving. An
Eagle with wings spread, with clawed talons, rested upon a swelling little bundle of fronds and fruits
hanging in the middle. The slender extremities of which, on this side and on that, were held suspended,
bound about with straggling tendrils, of a working almost pierced through.

Therefore the conspicuous Gate, standing free in the flat of the levelling between the columns, of
marble jointly panelled, was situated with the highest approbation. For which cause, the required
showing of the more principal members of the said magnificent gate being somewhat fitted, it seems to
me opportune in what follows to explain its pleasing and most comely ornaments. Because for the
architect the *being* presents itself as harder than the *being well*. That is to say, that first it
belongs to him above all to dispose the solid, and to define in his mind (as I said above) the
universal fabric, rather than the ornaments, which are accessory to the principal.

Therefore to the first, the fertile skill of one alone is required. But to the second many handworkers,
or unlearned operatives — called by the Greeks Ergatai — necessarily come together. Who, as has been
said, are the instruments of the Architect.

POLIPHILO, HAVING MADE SUFFICIENT DEMONSTRATION OF THE SYMMETRY OF THE GREAT GATE, GOES ON TO DESCRIBE
EXCELLENTLY ITS MOST POLISHED AND MOST SKILFULLY WROUGHT ORNAMENT, AND HOW MARVELLOUSLY IT WAS
COMPOSED.

LET IT NOT VEX THAT NOBLE COMPANY who give themselves continually to pleasing love, that I have
lingered somewhat in what is narrated above — which perhaps to them is not in the least gracious,
being desirous, as they treat of it, to understand that thing in which (however bitter it be in
itself) they nourish themselves with a patient mind, placing their festive heart in it.

Whereupon, human affection being naturally variable, let it not for this cause be laid to their
charge: bread grateful to an unhurt palate is sometimes displeasing to a depraved one, but is rather
kindly welcomed by him to whose taste it is pleasing. For, having in some part made mention of the due
end of building — which is that excellent invention, to acquire by measure the solid body of the
edifice — thereafter, that being freely invented, the Architect reduces it by minute divisions;
neither more nor less than the Musician, having invented the intonation and the measured time in one
greatest note, then, proportioning it in minute Chromatics, neatly carries it back upon the solid.

By such likeness, after the invention, the chief rule peculiar to the Architect is the squaring. And
distributing this into the smallest parts, there is offered to him the harmony of the building and its
measured proportion, and to his principal the fitting corollaries.

For which cause, this gate being for excellence most beautiful by its admirable composition and
invention, and there being added to it so much especial elegance and with so amended a distribution
that no part accused itself as needing correction in the least cutting-back — I therefore now think it
worthy to describe its perfect completion.

On the right first there presents itself a pedestal, or column-foot, beneath the bases of the columns.
From which, a little cornice being drawn out above in due measure, and with its moderate swellings at
the base of the perfect square, it remained by rule broader than high — that is, four-cornered. Most
common expressions, and not native ones, I must use, because we are degenerate and cut off from that
treasure, so as rightly to set out

all the particularities of such a working. But with those who are unskilled in such craft we shall
keep our reckonings in reserve.

Therefore in this (as I so call it) Altar, deepened with gorge-mouldings covered with leaves, with a
modest stepping of fine cuttings — among which, of transparent Alabaster stone, the proportioned bands
remained untouched, going round by the extremity of the four-cornered front, equal-sided — there was
carved with the greatest diligence a man of an age passing beyond manhood, robust with rusticity, with
a thick beard of hair curled by hardness at the chin, its growth coming ill through the hard skin.

He sat upon a feigned rock, with a goat's skin, which, flayed at the hinder parts, he had girt about
him in a knot over his flanks; and the part of the neck, with the hair turned towards him, hung
between his knotted shins. Before him, in the middle of his swelling calves, was an Anvil, fixed in a
brawny piece of a truncated tree. Upon which, intent, he was forging a pair of glowing little wings,
holding the hammer raised and striking his work.

And there before him stood a most noble Matron, at whose delicate shoulders were set two wings of
feathered plumage. Who held a child, her son, naked, sitting with his little haunches upon the fleshy
thigh of his mother — the Mother Goddess holding him somewhat raised, with her bared foot set upon a
rock, held together with the seat of the hammering smith, feigned in a little hill of stone; with a
little furnace in a small cavern in which the coal-red fire burned.

And the Matron had her tresses composedly carried back over her broad brow, adorning her copious head
round about, so delicately expressed that I do not know by what reason those standing statues were not
stirred to her, who were likewise found at the smith's work.

There was moreover there an armed man of raging semblance, clothed in an antique aegis-breastplate,
with the fearful head of Medusa on the breast, and with other noble and exquisite breast-pieces; with
the baldric across the ample breast, and he held with his muscular arm a spear somewhat raised. And
with a crested helmet with its peak he had his head defended; the other arm not appearing, hindered by
the figures in front. There appeared also a young man, seen from the breast upward, clothed in thin
cloth, beyond the bowed head of the said smith.

The aforesaid history the craftsman had diligently carried upon a flat of coral-coloured stone, and
introduced within the waved bound of the Altar. Which colouring flooded through the translucent stone,
the coloured part being set only beneath the naked bodies and limbs, and in the hollow bounded round
about the figures. Like a rose, flesh-tinted,
every lineament of this column-foot was seen equally in the other, differing only in its history.

Likewise also, in the left column-foot, a naked man of manly age was carved, kindly in aspect, in
which he showed the greatest swiftness. He too sat upon a squared seat, adorned with most ancient
carving; shod with buskins, unfastened from the heel towards the calves. Thence sprang two winged caps,
one to each foot.

Where also that same Matron, naked, figured as a goddess — in whose narrow breast two little paps
budded, unmoved in their hardness and their roundness, with ample flanks, so conformably expressed with
the other that, sealed, they counterfeited one and the same form — offered that same boy, her son, to
this teaching man. Who, the little boy being already beside him, standing before him upon his little
feet, bent himself down and shrewdly showed him three arrows. By which act one easily conjectured that
he taught him by what art he should use them in his working. And the divine mother held the quiver
empty, and the bow likewise unstrung. At the feet of this master lay a viperous caduceus.

Here likewise was found the armed man, and a helmeted woman, who bore upon a spear a Trophy of a most
ancient breastplate hung up, and at the top a sphere with two wings; and between the one wing and the
other stood written thus: NOTHING IS FIRM. Clothed in a flying shift, with a showing of her breast
above.

The two ready Doric columns of Porphyry, of seven diameters, pressed upon each of these squares thus
explained; of a dark crimson colour with their little roundels lighter, confusedly scattered, shining
and polished. Channelled, with twenty-four Flutes apiece, between the most exact little cords. But of
the three parts, the lowest one was cabled.

The reason why they were so carved, hollowed and with the third cabled, I judged to be this: that this
most excellent fabric, or temple, must have been ritually dedicated to the one sex and the other —
that is, to a God and a Goddess; or to a mother and a son; or to a father and a wife; or to a father
and a daughter, and the like. And therefore the skilled ancient fathers attributed to the female sex
the greater part of hollowing, and to the male the cabling, because that slippery nature exceeds the
manly in wantonness.

The cause of all the fluted ones was for the temple of a Goddess, the flutes showing the wrinkled
womanly garment. Upon which they set the capital with the volutes hanging before, in token of the
twisted hair and womanly ornament. Those caryatids which have for capital a woman's head with curled
locks were expressed in the temple of that rebelling people; which, being afterwards subjugated again,
in token of inconstancy like women's, in the meaning
of the columns were so built for perpetual memory.

These choice and ready columns aforesaid the sustaining bases of bronze subdued, with the Tori, or
mouldings, of oaken fronds with the fruits expressed, closely girt about with a winding binding,
resting above upon the Plinth set beneath. The capitals set above, of the material of the bases, of
work fitting and requisite to all the harmony — such as Callimachus the Cunning Craftsman did not see
in the sprouted Acanthus from the Basket upon the buried Corinthian maiden, nor made to express his
comely ornament.

Covered by the curved Abaci, or bent lids, decorated with the lily in the middle. The vase of which
was excellently clothed with two orders of eight Acanthus leaves in the Roman and Corinthian manner.
Out of the said leaves came the lesser Helices, meeting in the middle of the vase, and produced the
lily most beautifully fitted into the curve of the Abacus. From which then the little stalks twisted
themselves beneath the projection of the Abacus. Such as Agrippa approvedly set in the Porch of the
wonderful Pantheon, attributed for its height one entire diameter of the base of the column, with
observable Symmetry in each of its parts and accessories.

Speaking now of the threshold of the gate: a huge green stone made it, degenerate with a seed-bed of
whitening, black and yellow markings, and of other various and imperfect mottlings, most hard. Above
this stood the straight Antae, free and shining in the aspect of the space between; as broad as the
breadth of the threshold set beneath, one pace, so broadly they stood; but the outward face was
notably carved. Without sign of hinges in the threshold, nor yet in the lintel; nor did there appear
any trace of the iron catches of the cramps holding the half-capitals of its stone.

Thence, then, arching the arch-beam, or half-circle, with the requisite lineaments and measured bands
of the beam — that is, little balls or berries, and with tenth-part spindles, as though threaded in a
row made equal, and dog's-ear mouldings, and with waving down-lying work antiquely curved, or
jagged, with the little stalks. The keystone of which, or clasp, or Wedge, worthy of admiration, and
of a subtle and daring feigning, and of elegant polish, offered itself thus most notable.

I gazed astonished, then, upon a stubborn and most black stone, at an Eagle almost wholly torn out of
the solid, with wings spread. Which had lovingly seized a noble and most delicate Boy by his little
garments. So shrewdly that the pointed and hooked talons, turning themselves aside, did not hurt the
soft flesh. And so, by gripping and drawing at the little folds, its clenched feet towards the swelling
and keeled

it left the little hanging child bared from the navel down. Where the tender little buttocks came down
between the feathered thighs of the winged one. This most shapely little boy, worthy of him who had
carried him off for himself, gave sign in his little face of dreading his case.

Both his little arms being opened, then, with his knobbed hands he had gripped himself tightly to the
rowing bone of the spread wings — that is to say, to the rowing part, which is that bone which,
connected with the body, adheres so as to move. And drawing his swelling little infant shins up above,
he had his little feet thrown across the widened tail, which most beautifully passed away beneath the
soffit of the arch.

That little boy was exactly and artificially made of the white vein of the Agate, or Onyx; and the
winged one of the Sard, which is the other vein coming together with it. At which most exquisite
expression I stood stupefied, considering how the elegant craftsman so perspicaciously imagined to
apply that stone most aptly to such an office and purpose.

So that I reasonably conjectured, by the feathers somewhat ruffled about the beak, and the beak
half-open with the playing tongue showing, that she openly accused herself of being wholly intent and
dissolved in desire. With her back she imitated the curve of the keystone, and with it she likewise
carried the arching back of the little boy.

The remaining Arch-beam then, disposed in the soffit in squared coffers excellently lined, held
hanging within them the rosettes sharply finished — as much as was the compass of the Antae, from the
binding of the capitals; above which binding it stretched beyond the antae, beneath the beginning of
the bend of the vault of the entry, or opening, of the gate.

In the triangles which the arch made, there was a shrine-bearing figure in each, of a most noble
carving, of that artifice which the common sort call Cameo. With the garments imitating the maidenly
little body, flying and yielding in part to the beautiful calves, breast and upper arms, with the hair
loose and unshod, holding out towards the keystone the Trophy of victory. Which most smoothly took up
the whole triangular flat of most black stone, to show the truth of the metals, and the Nymphs milky
and most white. Behind the columning was seen the white panelling of the best marble, fitted on.

Above the Beam sat the Zophorus, in the middle of which was a curved Tablet of gilded metal, with an
epigram of excellent Greek capitals of refined silver set into it, which said thus:

*To the gods Venus and her son Love: Bacchus and Ceres, out of their own substance, to the most
tender Mother.*

At the one and the other extremity of the bronze Tablet were two boys holding it, or winged little
spirits, perfectly formed, in such a manner that the diligent statuary of the famous burden-bearing
boys of the Ravenna Snail-stair never saw such an exemplar. Joining their swelling little hands to it,
they held it readily, naked, of the said metal. Aptly carried upon a flat of Cyanean stone, more to
the grace of its colouring than that which, compacted in little cakes, is forced to the vomiting-out
of the perfect azure; and it shone with a glassy lustre.

In the front of the Zophorus stretched above the porphyry columns were Spoils of Breastplates,
Corslets knotted of triple-threaded rings, Bucklers, Helmets, Bundles, Axes, Torches, Quivers, Darts
and many other engines of war — no less Airy than maritime and terrestrial — of most worthy making;
and thus at their Haunches they showed without doubt the victories, the power and the triumphs which
made high-thundering Jove resound, and mortals perish in sweetness.

Then in due order followed the wickedly fine Cornice, of such lineaments as decently concur with so
great an elegance of work. For otherwise, just as in the human body one quality discordant from
another brings on sickness — because fitness is not found in the friendship of the composition — and,
the accidents not being neatly distributed to their due place, deformity follows: so, neither more nor
less, is that fabric dissonant and infirm where due harmony and measured order are not found. Which
thing the modern unlearned confound, being ignorant of the placing distribution. Wherefore our most
wise master likens the building to a human body well proportioned in its sharing and decently clothed.

Beyond this cornice, with reversed stepping, four squarings presided: two standing above the order of
the fluted, or Caryatid, Columns, and two drawn in. In the middle division of the two remembered, there
sat a Nymph of excellent relief of brass, holding two torches: one quenched, turned towards the heavy
earth, and one lit, towards the Sun. The burning one in the right, and the other in the left hand.
On the right side, then, in the squaring, I saw the jealous Clymene, who

was turning into unmoving fronds. And Phoebus, grown stiff, indignant at it, weeping and pursuing; and
he, more fugitive, urging on the four swiftest runners of his winged four-horse chariot. Neither more
nor less than one pursued by a deadly enemy hastens his swift steps.

In the square above the order of the columns on the left, of unaccustomed carving, was contained the
history of how the disconsolate Cyparissus lifted his tender limbs high into the air, for the Hind
struck by his arrow; and how Apollo wept hard for it.

The third square, that which stood placed next above the resisting columns, offered such a most
beautiful carving: Leucothoe, impiously slain by her own father, changed her white and maidenly flesh
into tender bark and moving fronds and drooping twigs.

In the fourth squaring was shown the unwilling Daphne, in no way yielding her virgin flesh to the
burning desires of the long-haired Delian, sorrowfully transforming herself towards the warm heavens
into eternal greenness.

Now, in successive order, above the Cymatium — which of any lineament is called the topmost line — of
these histories described, there rose extended a dentilled cornice, and one of ovolos with the
thunderbolts, or little darts, set between the gape of one ovolo and another; and foliage, and the
tiles, with the whorls and Nicolo-stones and other Seals, and other choice workings expressed; and
modillions with the Astragals, without any defect; and last the Cyma foliated with Acanthus with a
most polished spacing between. Of which things so excellent a carving was afforded that, of works
sharply hollowed out, not the least mark of the gnawing Auger appeared.

Returning duly to the frontispiece, or pinnacle, in the disposition of which (as I have said before)
there are repeated in it all the cornices set beneath, in all the parts of the workings, answering to
the perpendiculars — the drip of the topmost cornice being set aside, denied to this member.

At present it falls to me to dispatch the triangular flat of the said temple-like part, in which,
not without admiring contemplation, there presents itself to be considered: as much as the extremities
of this inserted figure could contain, so much was fitted in it a crown of divers fronds and fruits
and stalks entwined, and diligently unfolded, of most green stone, drawn tight in four parts, in knots
of thongs plaited through the little bundles. Held by two Scyllas, half human and the lower part
fish-like, which with the arm above and the other below aptly embraced it. From the one and the other
of the lying angles above the cymatium of the cornice, they stretched out their sea-beast tails,
hampered by ready coils; and towards the end of the scaly tail

the fish-like fins. With maidenly faces, with their tresses partly twisted above the brow and the rest
womanishly dressed about the head, and part hanging in ringlets over the flat temples. From between the
shoulders then came the harpy-like wings, spread out and stretched towards the coils of the wrapped
tail. And about their monstrous flanks went the seal-like oars; where the scaling began, emptying
itself little by little towards the end of the tail, with the feet of a sea-calf turned against the
crown, fleeing the heavenly wrath.

Within the compass of the crown I beheld a shaggy and teeming she-goat suckling a little boy, who sat
beneath her, with his fleshy little Shins, the one thrust out and one drawn somewhat towards himself.
Holding himself with his little arms to the hanging and rough wool, and with his face intent upon the
swelling udders, sucking them dry.

And another of the Nymphs then, coaxing, bending down, held raised one foot of the goat with her left
hand; and with the other she held out to him the distended and heavy udders, to the sucking kiss of the
milk-drinking infant. Beneath which was read AMALTHEA. And a Nymph standing at the head of the beast
went dutifully about its neck with one arm, and with the other hand shrewdly bridled it by the horns.

A third stood besides in the middle, with foliage in one hand, and in the other holding a most ancient
Cup with exquisite little handles. At the feet of this one was inscribed MELISSA.

Two Nymphs then, between the one and the other of the three described above, danced nimbly leaping
with Corybantic instruments, each in Nymph-like habits expressly imitating the movement of the agitated
form. O how artificially they fulfilled their mystery of illustrious making! Chased work without fail
not of the stone-carver Polyclitus, nor of Phidias, nor of Lysippus; and to the pious Artemisia, Queen
of Caria besides, there were afforded, of such excellent mastery of the chisel, the relief-workers
Scopas, Bryaxis, Timotheus and Leochares and Theon. For this was most skilfully made beyond human
genius and any relief-work whatever.

Finally in the temple-like pinnacle, or frontispiece, beneath the order of the upper cornice, in the
flat of it there appeared in carving these two words in perfect Attic capitals: *Of aegis-bearing
Zeus.*

Of this conspicuous and most notable gate such a wonderful composition and excellent disposition was
to be seen. Of which, if its every measured proportion has not been particularly explained, the blame
must be laid upon regard for prolixity, and upon the lack of the proper words of description. And
because gnawing time had left this one alone untouched, therefore I did not approve of passing on
without having said and treated something especially of it.

It is manifest that the remainder of the aforesaid closure, on the one side and the other, was a great
display of stupendous building; and this was clearly understood from certain workings preserved
untouched here and there. As in the lower parts certain Dwarf columns designed to resist the
unbearable weight; others Corinthian with unnoticed swelling, pregnant with so moderate a polish, and
just as Symmetry required, and as the exigency of the heaviness and of the ornament wished — the
artificial reasoning being drawn as it were from human likeness, and shrewdly gained. As a man to whom
it belongs to sustain a heavy weight must have broad soles beneath robust legs, so in the measured
fabric the Dwarf columns are attributed to the weight-bearing, and thereafter, for the adorning, the
slender Corinthian and Ionic.

And according to the requirement of the harmony of the building, so all the parts stood with approved
elegance. With a decent sharing of the colouring of the marbles and a pleasing distinction, with a
gracious sharing towards the object: of Porphyry, of Ophite, Numidian, Alabaster, fire-flecked,
Laconian, and of white marble waved with veins, and dark-red degenerate with whitest markings. Others
of manifold colouring confusedly mixed. And from the circumference its rising was found by another rule
than from the diameter of the lower thickness.

I found also a rare form of Cushioned base, which above the Plinth had two trochili, separated by an
interposition of little necks and Astragals, with the topmost Torus.

And in divers parts there was a hiding by the hanging and thick ivy, creeping from the ground upward —
the wood whose cup divides Bacchus from Thetis — with its scattered fruitful Clusters of black berries,
and with green down, taking up here and there many places of the ancient building, together with many
other wall-shrubs. And in the cracks grew the lively little finger-fern; and elsewhere hung the
Navelwort, and Houseleek, to which its pleasing name belongs, hanging low in the eaves. And in other
breakages the Pellitory, and diuretic Chickweed, and Polypody, and Maidenhair, and the fringed
Spleenwort with its rusty back, and the jointed lesser Moonwort, and other House-leeks that love the
antiquity of walls and of stones, and the Hair-moss, and the green Olive-grove that dwells in ruins.
Whereupon many worthy works were clothed and covered with this and much other greenery.

And of the great and turned columns, one upon another, there was an inestimable collapse, so that they
appeared not columns but a confused heap of timber cast down to the ground. Among the ruin likewise
conspicuous relics of statues, with manifold acts: many naked, some with the garments wrinkled

or folded, clinging over the naked figure and repeating the covered limbs. Some resting upon the left
foot, and some upon the other, holding the heavy head perpendicular above the centre of the heel, and
then holding the other free and loosed of all weight, stretched forward. The foot distributed as a
sixth part of the height, that is, four cubits. Some still whole, standing upon their little Altar,
and some sitting in Thrones with modest readiness.

I saw innumerable Trophies, spoils of war, and infinite ornaments; and heads of oxen and of horses
disposed at due interval, and from their horns ropes of fronds with fruits, stalks and pods, and other
fruits hanging in their bulk, with little boys riding upon them in play.

For all which things it was rightly judged how copious the thought of that many-knowing Architect
showed itself, in care, in study and in industry. And with how much vigilance his fertile understanding
declared itself. And with how much pleasure he had laboriously set forth the effect of his purpose.
And how great was the Eurythmy, publishing the subtlety of the stone-cutter's art; and how much art
the carving showed in the stones — certainly with such facility that it seemed the material afforded
had been not marble, however hard, but soft clay and potter's earth. And with how great a closing the
stones were joined and composed, to the norm, the rule and the level.

This was the true art, which discovers our confident ignorance, and detestable presumption, and public
and most damaging error. This is that clear light which sweetly invites us to its contemplation, to
illuminate our darkened eyes. For no one, save he who struggling flees from it, remains blind with
open eyes. This is that which accuses wicked avarice, the ravening consumer of every virtue, the worm
continually gnawing the heart of him who is its captive; accursed obstacle and barrier to well-disposed
wits, mortal enemy of good architecture; execrable idol of the present age, so unworthily and
damagingly venerated. Deadly poison, that makes wretched whoever is hurt by you — how many magnificent
works are ruined and in part forbidden?

For which cause, being seized and taken with delight and unimaginable solace, and by that holy and
venerable antiquity, with such grace and admiration, I found myself with undetermined, unstable and
unfed gazings. Looking gladly here and there, and crowded with admiration, and encircled in my mind, I
examined, running over what the carved histories signified, gazing fixedly at it with a willing
pleasure. Intent with parted lips for a long stretch, none the less my greedy eyes and insatiable
appetite could not be satisfied with looking and looking again at those excellent and most ancient
workings.

Stripped therefore and sequestered of every other thought, only my beloved Polia came often to my
sticky memory, kept and most welcome. But for all this, with a sounding
I laid her somewhat ill aside. I persevered therefore in wonder at those most welcome antiquities.

POLIPHILO, HAVING ENTERED SOMEWHAT INTO THE DESCRIBED GATE, WITH GREAT PLEASURE STILL BEHELD THE
WONDERFUL ORNAMENT OF ITS ENTRANCE. AND WISHING AFTERWARDS TO TURN BACK, HE SAW THE MONSTROUS DRAGON;
AND HE, TERRIFIED BEYOND BELIEF, TOOK FLIGHT THROUGH UNDERGROUND PLACES. AT LAST, FINDING A MOST
LONGED-FOR WAY OUT, HE CAME INTO A PLEASANT PLACE.

A GREAT AND PRAISEWORTHY THING WITHOUT fail it would be to be able easily to narrate, and to set out
point by point, the incredible making and unimaginable composition of that vastest structure, and the
greatness of so much building, and of that most notable gate, conveniently situated in a high and
conspicuous place.

Whereupon the delight of contemplating exceeded my great admiration; for I judged that to Jove among
the gods no making whatever is hard, suspecting almost that by no craftsman and by no human knowledge
could so great a vastness be composed, and such most ample conceits expressed, and so much novelty
devised, and adorned with such elegance, and disposed with such singular symmetry, and perfectly
defined without supplement and correction — the illustrious and unimaginable display of that aforesaid
structure.

For which reason I should not doubt in the least that, if the natural historian had beheld or
understood this, he would have scorned Egypt, and the industry and genius of its craftsmen at which he
wondered — those who, distributed in distinct and various workshops, chose a part to be carved and
were assigned its length; and then with so much Symmetry all agreed with their own piece, and to the
composition of a huge colossus, as exactly as if it had been polished by one craftsman alone. And the
sagacious shrewdness of Satyrus the architect and of the other famous ones. And chiefly, for
Simandius, the wonderful work of the excellent Memnon, of three great statues of highest Jove carved
in one solid rock, of which one, seated, its feet or sole exceeded seven cubits. He would with reason
have made little of them.

He would likewise have given way here, that stupendous miracle of the statue of the magnanimous
Semiramis carved on Mount Bagistan, of seventeen stadia. And the writers, keeping silence too on the
insolence

of the Memphite Pyramids, would have written more diffusely of this. And neglecting the famous
Theatres and Amphitheatres and Baths, and Temples sacred and profane, and Aqueducts and Colossi — the
marvellous and wonder-filled Apollo brought over by Lucullus; and the Jove dedicated by Claudius
Caesar; and that of Lysippus at Tarentum; and the miracle of Chares of Lindos at Rhodes; and of
Xenodorus in Gaul and in Rome; and the colossal Serapis of nine cubits made incredibly of Emerald; and
the famous labyrinth of Egypt; and the solid statue of Hercules at Tyre — he would have passed them
over, and would most joyfully have fitted his eloquence to proclaiming this, written with the highest
praise as most wonderful above all; however inestimable a spectacle was afforded in the shrine of great
Jove by the Obelisk of forty cubits, compacted of four pieces, four cubits on one face and two on the
other.

Insatiably, then, considering now one and now another most beautiful and massive work, I said silently:
if the fragments of holy antiquity, and its breakages and ruin, and in a manner its very Chippings,
lead us into stupendous admiration and to so much delight in looking at them, what would its
completeness do?

And so I thought too within myself, reasonably: perhaps in the inner shrines is the venerable Altar of
the mysterious sacrifices and sacred flames, or else the statue of the Divine Venus, or her most holy
Aphrodisium, and that of her bow-bearing and arrow-shooting little son. And with devout veneration,
the right foot set upon the sacred threshold, there ran before me a fleeing and white Mouse.

At once, without other curious thought, with searching eyes I entered somewhat into the open space and
the lighted entry, and things worthy of eternal regard presented themselves to me. Here on the right
and left side the panelled wall was of most polished marbles. In the middle part of which levelling
was fitted a great roundness, enclosed in the circuit of a leafy jewel with excellent company of
carving. Which (like the other opposite it) was of the blackest stone, contemptuous of hard iron, of a
mirroring brightness.

Between which, passing (unaware of them), I was invaded by a sudden fear at my own image.
Nevertheless I was tempered again by an unlooked-for pleasure. Because in them there was clearly
offered the judgment of the histories notably painted in mosaic work. And on both the lower parts,
beneath the shining mirrors, were lengthwise seats of stone. The pavement clean and free of dust,
worked in new and gracious pottery-work. And so too the coloured soffit was free of the wicked
Spider's weaving, because there breathed there continually a most fresh air; the panelled walls joined
beneath the binding. Which binding, of most subtle conceit, extended from the capitals of the most
upright antae as far as the extremity of the said entry. As long as
by perspective I judged twelve paces.

Above which most polished binding the soffit began to arch, its vaulted bend conforming to that of the
gate. Of such a fertile and delightful conceit it offered itself, with such excellent carving, neatly
full of little water-monsters in the feigned water, and among the moderate wavelets half-men and
women, with spiralling little fish-tails. Upon these, near the back, some sat fitly; some of them
naked, embracing the monsters with mutual entwining. Some pipers, others with fantastical instruments.
Some drawn along, sitting in strange Chariots. Crowned by the ever-swimming Dolphins with the cold
flower of the water-lily; some clothed in its own leafage.

Some with manifold vessels of copious fruits, and with crowded horns of plenty. Others with little
bundles of sweet-flag, and of flowers of the Silvan's beard, struck at one another. Some were girt
with reeds. The other part, riding upon hippopotami, wrestled. And other divers and hateful beasts,
with tortoise-shell for shield. And here they gave themselves to wantonness, and here to various games
and feasts, with lively strivings and movements excellently carved and expressed. Completely, from the
one end and the other, they adorned it.

In the turning of the vault I saw a most diligent worm-like work of exquisite little glass tesserae,
with a gilded surface and of every most pleasing colouring. And first there presented itself a frieze
two feet broad, which, going about, adorned the enclosed extremities of all the vaulted space, from the
bindings recited upward, and along the length of the vault's pinnacle, with a companionable joining,
existing in lively colourings. Nor otherwise than as if they had been composed just then: with natural
foliage of emerald greenness, with the reverses of a Punic colour, with flowers of Cyan and of Phoenician
and of adulterate hue, with gracious entwinings and knottings.
In the space contained by these, I beheld this ancient history painted.

The young Europa swimming to Crete upon the counterfeited bull. And to her sons the edict of King
Agenor: to Cadmus, Phoenix and Cilix, that pursuing they should find their violated sister. And not
finding her, at the rising spring they strenuously slew the scaly Dragon. And thereafter, having taken
counsel, they determined by Apollo, with their companions, to build a city where the lowing Heifer
should stop. Whereupon that country to this day eternally keeps the name of the Lowing bellow. Cadmus
therefore built Athens; the other brother Phoenicia; the third Cilicia. Most excellently disposed, and
carried out in a drawn-out order, of feigning, of painting in natural colours as it required — the
acts, the places, and the fitting expression of the history — was this mosaic picture.

On the part opposite, in this same manner, I beheld the wanton Pasiphaë, kindled with infamous love,
and lying hid in the wooden engine

t:
and closed up; and the robust Bull wantoning upon the coupling he did not know. And then the Minotaur
of monstrous shape, shut up and imprisoned in the laborious and pathless labyrinth. Lastly the sagacious
Daedalus, fleeing from the prison-cloister, ingeniously making Wings for himself and for Icarus. Which
unhappy boy, not following his father's command and track, falling headlong into the wide sea, dying
gave his name to the Icarian waters; and afterwards the father, having kept himself unharmed, in the
temple of Apollo hung up the rowing engine framed of feathers, by a religious vow promised.

It happened that I gazed with parted lips most intently (my unstable and most swift eyelids not
moving), with my mind ravished, attending only to those most beautiful and so well disposed and
perfectly ordered and artificially painted and elegantly expressed histories, left inviolate by any
breakage — so tenacious was the seizing glue that the glass tesserae, pressed down page-wise and
perpetually cohering, stood to this hour unhurt, and not one removed from its placing. For that
excellent craftsman had gathered every absolute diligence to this excellent making.

And there, carrying myself foot before foot, pertinaciously examining with what direction of the
painter's art he had observed to place with pondered distribution the readiest figures upon their just
planes. And how the lines of the fabrics drew towards the object. And how from the eyes certain places
were as it were lost. And things imperfect brought little by little to the perfect, and so on the
contrary, granting his judgment to the eyes. With the exquisite by-works: waters, springs, mountains,
hills, little woods, animals. The colouring impaired with distance, and with the light opposed, and with
the neat reflections in the folds of the garments and in the other workings, not with little emulation
of shrewd nature. So wondering and absorbed that I was almost not present in myself.

In this manner I had come to the end of the entry, where the gracious histories ended, because beyond
was a most thick darkness that I did not dare to enter. But turning myself therefore to go back —
behold, without pause I heard through the broken ruins as it were a crashing of bones and of crackling
branches. I stood still, my so sweet solace suddenly interrupted and cut off.

And thereafter I heard still more plainly as it were a dragging, as of a great dead ox, through the
warty place and over the heaped and uneven ruins, always coming towards the gate with a nearer and
more consonant din; and I heard a very great hissing of an excessive serpent. I was stupefied. And my
voice being forbidden and my hair raised, I did not make myself safe by fleeing, and in that darkness
to rush on.

O unhappy me, and sad of fortune! Behold, of a sudden I see plainly, coming to the threshold of the
gate — not, as to Androcles, the limping lion in the cave, but a fearful and horrendous Dragon, its
three-forked

tongues vibrating, with its combed jaws of pointed and serried teeth grinding; with the bulk of its
scaly hide gliding and running over the pottery pavement; with its wings beating its rough back; with
its long tail of snaky slips it tightly gathered great restless knots.

Alas, a thing to terrify warlike and corsleted Mars, and to make tremble the terrible and evil-averting
Hercules with all his brawny and Molorchian Club; and to call back Theseus from his attempted
enterprise and rash beginning; and to terrify the giant Typhon more than the gods above were terrified
by him; and to make lose whatever shaggy, obstinate and impenetrable heart there ever was. Alas, a
thing to draw back heaven-bearing Atlas from his office — let alone a young man and small of soul,
finding himself alone among unknown places, unarmed and fearing peril.

And perceiving that it was smoke-vomiting, of foul breath, and deadly, as I rightly suspected —
mistrusting any escape whatever, and of saving myself from mortal peril, almost without breath, in my
little courage I devoutly invoked, trembling and terrified, every divine power.

And without delay, turning my shoulders and entering into the darkness, I committed myself to swift
flight, anxiously carrying my already hastened feet to flee. With the greatest nimbleness, unknowing,
penetrating swift-footed into the inner parts of that dark place, escaping through divers and oblique
turnings and windings of passages.

Where I firmly held that I had come into the inextricable fabric of the sagacious Daedalus, or of
Porsena, containing so many inexplicable goings and returnings with frequent doors to cheat the exit,
and to come back into those same errors; or into the chambered cave of the terrifying Cyclops, and into
the foul Cavern of thieving Cacus. So that, however much my eyes were somewhat accustomed to the
darkness, none the less by no means could I, wretched, discern anything.

But with my arms stretched out before my face, so as not to run butting into some pillar, I went, those
doing the office of my darkened eyes. As the Snail, bearer of its own governance, putting forth its
soft little horns and drawing them back, and feeling out the way and contracting them at obstacles. And
I likewise, groping, so as not to strike against those greatest supports of the mountain and Pyramid.
And turning towards the gate to see whether the cruel and fearful dragon came behind me, the light was
wholly spent.

I found myself, then, in the blind bowels and pathless passages of those shadowy caverns, and in
greater terror and mortal trouble than Mercury making himself an Ibis, and Apollo in Thrace, and Diana
in Chlomone a little bird, and Pan in his twofold shaping; and in greater than those of Oedipus, of
Cyrus, of Croesus and of Perseus; and in greater fright and destruction than the bear-shaped robber
Thrasyleon; and in greater straits than Psyche, and in more laborious perils than Lucius made an ass —
and when he heard the robbers' counsel of his own destruction, without any choice to be counselled,
truly ignorant and desperate.

At that point, made most fearful and anxious above all the fears, terrors and frights named, there came
besides the frequent flight of light-shunning owls about my head, to redouble the fearful straitness.
And sometimes, at their screech, without delay I believed myself to be among the pointed teeth of the
venomous Dragon, and held fast between its gripping jaws like a toothed saw. Without delay there
followed upon this a redoubling both of my perilous and grave terror and of the truth of my heart's
grief: there came into my mind the wolf I had seen, whether by chance it had been a pernicious portent
to me and a messenger of my wretched outcome.

Wandering and running here and there, like the corn-gathering ant that loses the scent of its track and
strays, with wakeful ears to perceive whether the horrendous monster had come upon me, sorrowful, with
the peril of its Lernaean and strong venom and its horrible sword and most foul devouring. And
therefore everything that offered itself to me in that first approach I suspected to be that very
thing.

And there, finding myself naked and deprived of every refuge in so mortal a strait and dissolute grief
— although naturally hateful death is in no way welcome, yet in this hour I esteemed it gracious. The

which I could will, but I could not avail not to will it. And constancy in awaiting it persuaded me,
because of that uncertain, unhappy and trembling life. Alas, that such a dissociation of spirit made me
reject its quality, unwilling, and justly to struggle against its evil coming. For I burned strongly in
thinking: alas, that without any effect of my immense love, so sweetly kindled, I must perish
unfruitful — although, if it had presented itself suddenly in the present case, I should have valued it
not at all.

But at once returning to my fixed and accustomed object, weeping for the loss of two things so much to
be desired — Polia, that is, and precious life — invoking her diligently, with a sighing and sobbing
voice sounding through that thick air enclosed beneath huge vaults, and in that hidden place, I said
within myself: if I die here so wretched and grieving, and altogether unconsoled, who shall be the
deserving successor to so great and so prized a gem? Who shall possess so inestimable and talented a
treasure? What serene sky shall regain so clear a light?

O most wretched Poliphilo, where are you going, most lost? Where do you direct your attempted flight?
Where do you still hope to see again any longed-for good? Behold, abruptly cast down and interrupted
are all your gracious pleasures built by sweet love in your entangled mind. Behold, in a moment cut off
and annihilated are all your loving and so lofty thoughts.

Alas, what unjust lot and malign star has led you so perniciously into these troublous darknesses, and
cruelly exposed and cast you down to copious and mortal languors, and destined you to perish by the
most savage voracity and sudden gluttony of this terrifying Dragon? That, alas, I should be thrown
whole into its foul and most filthy and dunged bowels to putrefy, and thence afterwards be cast out to
an end not to be thought of?

O lamentable and unaccustomed destruction; O pitiable ending of my life! Where are those eyes so
barren, sucked and drained and deprived of moisture, that they did not all melt into thickest falling
tears? But behold me dying, for I feel it at my shoulders. Who ever saw turned upon himself a more
atrocious and deformed savagery of fortune?

Behold unhappy and insolent death, and the supreme hour and accursed moment at hand, in this dark
gloom; and that my body and my human flesh should be the sating of this terrible beast! What ferocity?
What rage? What more monstrous misery could mortals suffer — that the sweet and friendly light should
be taken from the living, and the earth denied to the dead? O how much more ghastly a calamity and
enormous misery, so sorrowfully and so importunately desired, in abandoning my most welcome and most
perfect Polia. Farewell, farewell then, excellent light of virtue and of every true and real beauty,
farewell.

By such and so made an affliction and exaggerated disturbance, beyond all thought, my soul was bitterly
wrung and exasperated. Above all

I gave urgent effort to escaping the peril to be dreaded, and to saving my brief and scant contaminated
life — or else, by this violence without any remedy, sorrowfully gasping to die, and without further
delay; for I did not know, most confused, what to do with myself, wandering, fugitive and wayward
through uncertain places and pathless byways. And my legs now weakened and numb, and every bodily
power shattered and languishing, half dead, and altogether bewildered and as it were ghost-ridden.

Brought nevertheless to this tearful pass, having suppliantly invoked (my last refuge) the gods above
and almighty, and my good Genius, with a guiltless mind — they having perhaps in this miserable case,
by their perennial pity, some fortunate care of me — behold, I began to discover a little light coming.
Towards which, alas, with what alacrity swiftly making my way, I saw a hanging lamp burning eternally
before a devout Altar. Which, so far as I could then discern in a moment, was five feet high and twice
as broad, with three golden images sitting.

Here, disappointed by the condition of the light, I was struck with no little religious horror at those
venerable darknesses, in which little was seen, however much the illuminating lamp burned — because
light is an enemy to thick and bad air. And always with intent ears, and never empty of my familiar
terror; but somewhat the blackened statues appeared, and round about there offered themselves the vast
and uncertain openings and fearful Passages underground, or under the mountain, supported here and
there, and distributed in infinite places: many greatest four-square and six-square piers, and in other
places eight-sided props, scarcely discerned by the weak light, aptly set beneath in proportion to
bearing the excessive vastness of the pressing Pyramid above.

Here, praying a little while, without delay I made above all things towards unknown flight. Whereupon,
thus half dead, no sooner had I run past the most holy Altar than there appeared to me besides a little
of the desired light, which shone faintly as through a most subtle breathing-hole seen as a funnel. O
with what feasting and with what gladness of my exhilarated heart I beheld it! And hastening merrily
towards it without other thought — perhaps with greater nimbleness than Canistius and Philonides — no
sooner did I see it with such unbridled gladness and longing than I called back most gladly my
repudiation of that thankless and troublesome life; successively clearing my disturbed mind and
fluctuating spirit, and somewhat refreshed and as it were reassured; and my emptied heart, drained of
love, somewhat recalled, quickened again with resprouting love, and altogether filled; and every lost
and exiled thought fitted itself again to its former work. And now more fixed upon my lovable Polia,
binding me with renewed entanglements more closely,

it persuaded me with firm and flattering hope to obtain lovingly and gloriously in the future that
which, dying untimely, I judged I should sorrowfully lose. O how extremely it tormented me. Yet I did
not refuse any boiling and new-come accessory of love that should freshen itself, festering anew in my
long-suffering and occupied heart. And therefore, every dissuading obstacle being shaken off from it,
and every barrier removed, I gave it especially a fair opening and a wide and open entrance.

Being therefore somewhat consoled by the kindly light, and the spirits I had lost and renounced being
taken back into me, and my prostrate strength gently restored, my suspended and pathless journey and
flight urged me, striving straight on. For as I drew nearer to it I discerned it multiplying. To which
at last, the heavenly will accompanying me, and most beloved Polia vigorously reigning in my loving
breast, I came anxiously.

Where, blessing the gods undeservedly, and obsequious fortune, and my golden-haired Polia, I found a
wide way out; and thence hastily going forth, and urgently fleeing, waiting not at all. And my arms,
already stretched out to avoid striking against the thickest pillars, now most fittingly adapted
themselves as oars for flight. And thence, striving, Safe, I came into a most pleasant Site and region.

In which, still terrified by that horrible monster, I doubted of the wished-for sitting down and
settling myself, having it so impressed upon my mind that continually and without interval I thought I
felt it at my shoulders. And for such cause I could not so quickly dissolve or displace so great a
terror from there. Whereupon I justly judged, doubting, that it still pursued me. And I was moved also
by manifold persuasions to enter and go forward. First by the pleasantness of that most beautiful
place; then by my disordered mind urging me to flee at once. And chiefly, being always desirous to see
and find things perhaps not customary among mortals.

Equally such considerations provoked me by every means to enter, and to go on as far beyond as I could,
and to remove myself from the way out; where I might quietly calm myself in some place and clear my
mind, and put in oblivion the terror now past — there coming not unwelcome into my retaining memory
the appearance of the white Mouse in the entry of the gate. And this came as a very exhortative
awakening to hearten me, because it was always welcome in the auspices, and a propitious and good Omen.

Therefore it persuaded me opportunely to give effort to keeping myself for the kindness of fortune,
which sometimes may be to me a bountiful and long-haired minister of prosperous and favourable things.
And by this constrained and compelled, moving my sluggish journey a little more, and reined in by my
broken and

weakened legs, I made my way. But still trembling decently at not coming into such a place where my
entering by chance, and my hasty arrival in an unknown country, would not have been lawful, but a
wicked daring and presumption, much more than the entrance of the magnificent gate.

And so, with my breast continually beating and with a long-suffering mind, I said within myself: what
now persuades me to turn back? Is not fleeing and free escape easier here? And much better, I think, to
expose my doubted life in this light beneath the open sky, than cruelly to perish in the blind
darkness? Nor indeed should I know how to return to that opening and way out.

And in a moment, drawing from the depth of my sad heart groaning sighs, I turned over in my tenacious
remembrance how much pleasure and delight my senses had lost in an instant; for that working was full
of marvel and of stupefaction. Thinking again in what manner I was so ill deprived of it. Imagining to
myself the bronze Lions of the temple of that most wise Jew, which by frightening brought men into
oblivion.

Therefore, by such a likeness, I almost doubted that the dragon had done the same to me: that so many
elegant and marvellous makings and stupendous conceits, showing themselves not human, most worthy of
the telling, which I had diligently beheld, I must now let lightly flee from my dried memory; and that
by such an event I should not know how to narrate them in order.

I said: certainly this is not so, nor do I feel in myself any lethargic affliction. But I hold it all
placed most freshly in my understanding and my memory, kept safe, and painted indelibly. And truly that
huge beast was alive and not feigned, and so fearful, rarely seen such by mortals — alas, such as
Regulus did not see. And remembering it, my fallen hair rose again, and I hastened my nimble step.

Then, returning to myself in a moment, I said: here without doubt (as I shrewdly judge from the
kindness of the present site) there must dwell none but human folk. But rather perhaps divine spirits
and heroes are guardians here, and a lodging of Nymphs and of the ancient Gods. Therefore persuasive
appetite easily provoked my reined-in step, exhorting me to the journey begun. Whereupon I, as though
captured by persevering goads, with a fierce mind resolved to follow wherever playful fortune might
fall, though still wasting away.

Considering therefore that beautiful and pleasant country, and the fruitful fields and fertile
plains, and conjecturing the delight of them, I praised such an invitation most highly; and casting
behind me every trembling restraint of mournful fear, I entered somewhat. But first I invoked the
divine light, and the prospering Genii, that they should be present to guide me at this my entering,
and be Companions to my wandering Pilgrimage, and bestowers of their holy guidance.

POLIPHILO TELLS OF THE KINDNESS OF THE COUNTRY HE HAD FOUND AND ENTERED, IN WHICH, WANDERING, HE FOUND
AN EXQUISITE AND MOST NOTABLE FOUNTAIN; AND HOW HE SAW FIVE GRACEFUL DAMSELS COMING TOWARDS HIM, AND
HOW THEY, MUCH MARVELLING AT HIS COMING THERE, MERCIFULLY REASSURED HIM AND INVITED HIM TO SHARE THEIR
PLEASURES.

HAVING COME OUT OF THAT HORRENDOUS pit, and from those inner darknesses and that place almost of the
dead (for all that the holy and consecrated Aphrodisium was there), into the most desired light and
friendly air, and being come into this most welcome place, I turned back to look at where my going-out
had been. And where my life — a life I had never valued — I saw at that point troubled and in peril.

I looked upon a mountain of no great size with a moderate slope, all wooded with greenest and pliant
fronds: with acorn-bearing Oaks, Beeches, Ilexes, Turkey-oaks, Italian oaks, Cork-oaks, and the two
Holm-oaks — the one Smilax, or Holly, or Acilon. Then, towards the level, it was thick with
cornel-trees, with hazels, with sweet-smelling and flower-bearing privets, and with a fragrant
whitening flower; two-coloured Naxian, reddening in the north aspect and whitening in the south;
Hornbeams and Ashes, and the like in such aspect, with sprouting saplings.

Wrapped in greening and climbing Honeysuckle and in winding hops, they gave a cool and shadowy shade.
Beneath which was the Cyclamen, harmful to Lucina, and the jagged Polypody, and the Trientale
Hart's-tongue, or Spleenwort; and both the Hellebores named from the shepherd; and the three-leaved
tora, or triangularis; and the Groundsel, and many other shade-loving herbs, and Woodland trees, some
without and some with flowering — a place none the less broken and rough, and closely shut about with
trees.

The opening, then, by which I came out of those most hidden lairs, was somewhat high in the mountain,
all overgrown with shrubs. And so far as I could conjecture, it was built over against the other
mentioned before; and I understood that this too had been a wonderful working, a postern, and that
one ancient. But envious and rivalling antiquity, and the narrowness of the approach, and above all
the wall-shrubs of ivy and other branches, had made it a thicket — so that one scarcely discerned that
there was any way out or gape. A place only for going out, but showing the utmost difficulty for
returning. Then to me so much

the more, because I saw it all round about thickly leafed and hidden as by a thief. By which condition
one would scarcely know how to come back to it. Between the jaws of the little valley, with the rocks
stretched over it, dark continually with the vapours gathered there. Whence that gloomy light was
greater to me than the divine birth was to Delos.

Now, having left this leafy and stopped-up gate, going down by a certain slope, I came to a thick
Chestnut thicket at the foot of the mountain — a station, as I supposed, of Pan or Silvanus — with
moist pastures and pleasant shade. Passing beneath which with pleasure, I found a marble and most
ancient bridge of one very great and high arch. Upon which, on the several sides of the parapets, seats
were most conveniently built. Which, although they offered themselves fittingly to my weariness as I
came out, none the less I then valued them not at all, in my excited going forward.

In the middle of which parapets there rose somewhat, level with the top of the keystone of the arch
beneath, a Porphyry square, with an excellent cymatium of polished lineament — one on the one side, and
one of like form on the other, but of Ophite stone. On the right of my way I saw most noble Egyptian
hieroglyphs of this expression: an antique helmet crested with a dog's head; a bare ox's head with two
tree-branches bound to the horns with small fronds; and an ancient lamp. Which hieroglyphs — the
branches excepted, for I did not know whether they were of fir, or pine, or larch, or juniper, or the
like — I interpreted thus.

On the other side I beheld this elegant carving: a circle; an anchor, about whose shank a dolphin
wound itself. And these I interpreted most excellently thus: *Always make haste slowly.*

Beneath which ancient, solid and excellent bridge there gushed a broad vein of most limpid living
water, which, dividing itself, made two running streamlets, one to the right and the other to the
left. They ran through their fretted and gnawed channels, and between banks washed and cut, murmuring
most cold; the stony and shaded banks covered with trees. In which banks the straggling roots appeared
uncovered, and in them hung the Maidenhair, and the Adiantum, and the Ivy-leaved Toadflax, and the
tresses of other little woodland herbs that love the river banks.

Which wooded and cool grove was pleasant to look upon and desirable for its spaciousness, and joyful
with fronds, full of little woodland and mountain birds. Beyond the bridge it stretched somewhat
further towards a pleasant plain, everywhere sounding with sweet chattering. There leapt the restless
Squirrels and the sleepy Dormice, and it was inhabited by other harmless little animals.

In this manner, then, was shown this wooded district, shut about by the tree-bearing mountain, much to
be gazed at by the eyes; and the plain covered everywhere with a variety of herbs. And the most limpid
little rivers flowed murmuring down through the feet of the sloping mountains into the valley. Adorned
with the flowering and bitter Oleander, and with Periwinkles, and Coltsfoot, and Loosestrife; shaded by
tall black and white Poplars, and the riverside Alder and Manna-ash. And upon the mountains I saw the
tall single-stemmed Fir, and the weeping Larches, and Silver-firs, and other noble kinds of like
foliage.

And then directing my eyes to the adorned plain, anxiously passing by the aforesaid place, I beheld a
marble building appearing among the trees, and above the tender tree-tops its pinnacle. Whereupon,
made all cheerful, judging that I had at last found a habitation and some refuge, I came to it joyfully
without delay.

I found an eight-sided building with a wonderful and excellent fountain. Which also offered itself not
in vain as a sweet invitation to my thirst, so long held back and not till then satisfied and quenched.

This fabric, pinnacled with an eight-sided roof and covered with lead, had at one front a stone as
much higher as was one half of its square, of white and shining marble. Its breadth I judged to be six
feet. Of this noble stone were diligently made two fluted half-columns, with the bases supporting a
stretched-out Cyma with gorge and added dentils and little cords, with the capitals set beneath a

little Beam, Zophorus and Cornice. Above which there was added besides a quarter of the square,
condemned for the frontispiece. Every lineament bare of ornament, of the proper and single stone —
save that in the angular little roundel, or flat, of the frontispiece I saw a small band: two doves
drinking together at a little vase.

Then the whole space enclosed between the little columns, gorge-moulding and beam, hollow and
excavated, held an elegant Nymph carved within. And beneath the Cyma was the other quarter, which at
the footing waved with Tori, Torus-moulding and Scotias, and a Plinth.

Which most beautiful Nymph lay sleeping comfortably upon an outspread cloth. And beneath her head it
was beautifully stuffed and folded into a cushioned mound. And a part of the said cloth was then most
aptly brought to cover that which fittingly ought to stay hidden. Lying upon her right side, the arm
