beneath drawn back, with the loosed hand she idly propped her head beneath the cheek. And the other
arm, free and without office, stretched itself over the left loin, coming down open to the middle of
the fleshy thigh.

From the little buds — as of young girls — of her breasts there gushed a thread of most fresh water
from the right; and from the left it rose hot. The fall of both fell into a porphyry vessel, with two
receivers joined together in one solid piece, set six feet apart and distant from the Nymph, before
this fountain, upon a stone pavement fitly placed.

Between the one receiver and the other was a little channel set in, in which the waters met, their
edges cut in the middle of the one and the other receiver, where the waters made their meeting. Which
waters, mingled then, flowed away fallen into a water-furrow, or little rill. Whereupon the one being
tempered by the other, they made every greenness sprout; the hot one leaping so high that it did not
hurtfully hinder the other for him who set his lips to the right breast to suck and to drink, nor at
the crossing.

Now this most notable statue the craftsman expressed so exactly that I should truly doubt whether
Praxiteles had carved such a Venus — for which Nicomedes, king of the Cnidians, offered (so fame
flies) all the substance of his people. And so comelily beautiful did he express her that men, burning
in sacrilegious longing for her, violated the image. But so far as I could rightly value it, I judged
that such an image was never so perfectly feigned by chisel or graver; so that I almost reasonably
suspected that in this place she had been turned to stone from the living, and so petrified.

She held her lips somewhat parted and fitted for breathing, where one saw as it were down into the
hollowed and pierced throat. Then from the head the

tresses, pressed down upon the cloth and flooding over it, rivalled with their most subtle hairs the
wrinkled, or folded, form of the gathered cloth. The thighs were duly fleshy, with the plump knees
moderately drawn back somewhat towards her, showing their narrow little joints, provoking one to lay a
hand upon them and to handle and press them. And the rest of that most shapely body provoked whoever by
chance might have found her so.

Behind her head, then, was a leafy Strawberry-tree of unfalling leaves, copious with its soft and round
fruits, and with little birds that seemed to chatter and to be a cause of sweet sleep. At her feet stood
a Satyr, itching with wantonness and all stirred, standing on his goat's feet. With his muzzle joined
to a nose goat-like and snub; with the beard on his chin parted into two curlings of Goatish twists,
and so likewise at his shaggy flanks and in this same manner at his head, with hairy ears, and crowned
with fronds, with a face adulterated between goat and human. I judged that to his most acute genius the
stone-carver had most skilfully, and at his pleasure, had the workmanship of nature present in his Idea.

The said Satyr had violently seized the Arbutus tree by the branches with his left hand, and bending it
by his strength above the sleeping Nymph, showed that he made her a gracious shade. And with the other
arm he drew the end of a little curtain, which was knotted to the branches nearest the trunk. Between
the strawberry-tree and the Satyr sat two infant Satyrs: one with a vase in his hands, and the other
with his hands wrapped about by two coiling serpents.
*To the Mother of all things.*

For which cause I should not know how to determine whether the long and so keen thirst I had endured
the day before provoked me to drink, drawing me on, or the most beautiful awakening of the instrument.
The coldness of which gave me a sign that the stone lied.

Round about, then, this quiet place, and along the babbling rills, there flowered the Vervain,
Lilies-of-the-valley, and the flowering Loosestrife, and the sweet-smelling Sweet-flag, and Zedoary,
Celery and Water-dock, and many other prized water-herbs and noble flowers. And then the little channel

of the fountain's outlet entered, watering, into a break, or close, of no unequal height, of composed
rose-beds, orderly combed out, adorned in manifold ways with sweet-smelling roses. It watered,
outpouring itself, into a field of papyrus-like Plantains, or bananas, with very great leaves torn by
the blowing airs, with the crowded hanging cluster of their sweetest fruit. And it was filled besides
with other most pleasing orchards: there was also the Artichoke, welcome to Venus, and the greening
Colocasia with its shield-like leaves, and infinite sown plants.

And looking again upon the plain, I saw it everywhere most green, adorned and painted with a variety of
scattered flowers: the yellows of the buttercup, and of frog's-foot or ox-eye; and the peacock-blues of
the Satyrion, of the lesser Centaury, and of the garland Melilot; and the small ones of the Eyebright,
and the golden of the Shepherd's-needle, and the flowering little Turnips, and the azures of the Clary,
and of the cornfield Gladioli; and of Strawberries with flowers and fruits; and the small Yarrow with
its white little tufts, and the Sawwort, and Pancuculus, and infinite other most beautiful little
flowers.

Whereupon, lost in a wonderful pleasantness, I felt myself consoled. And here and there, with measured
and ordered distance and interval, with gracious spaces, composedly and to the level, were the
green-bearing Orange and lemon trees and Adam's-apple trees, with their branches levelled and hung one
pace from the ground, thick with fronds — such as the glassy colour appears, of a turbinate form, that
is, of a pinnacled length and rounded at the base — with an abundance of their flowers and fruits,
breathing a most sweet odour. By which my closed heart felt itself not sparingly refreshed to the
utmost (having perhaps been invaded by the pestilent stench and wasting snaky breath).

For which cause I stood long pondering, suspended and full of stupefaction, in what place I now found
myself, so delightful to my senses — having especially considered carefully that marvellous fountain,
the variety of herbs, the colouring of the flowers, the place planted with trees; the noble and most
convenient disposition of the site, the sweet and unresting song of the birds, the temperateness and
the most purged air. For all this I should have counted myself content, if I had found any inhabitant
there.

And the eagerness to go forward pressed me somewhat, the kindly place offering itself to me ever more
joyful — although the past terror had not yet altogether unstuck itself from my seizing memory, nor
been rooted out. And for this cause alone I stopped, doubtful, not knowing where and by what way to go
and set out.

Standing therefore in such suspension of mind, all stirred with thinking of the terrifying dragon, and
of having entered where I did not know — the hieroglyphs of the left side of the bridge suddenly
sprouting in my memory — I feared to rush into some adverse accident; and that such a monument, worthy
of golden carving, was not set in vain for those who
pass by: MAKE HASTE SLOWLY.

Behold, I hear suddenly behind me a great crashing and din, like the shaking of the bony wings of the
dragon; and behind me, alas, I heard a sounding of a Trumpet. At once, wretched and gasping, I turned
myself about, and I see on one side many trees of Egyptian Carob, with their ripened, very long fruits
hanging and shaking, which by the wind had somewhat struck one against another. Whereupon, coming
swiftly to myself, and falling into laughter at a case so befallen, I moved on.

For which cause I then religiously invoked the kindly gods Jugatinus, the goddess Collatina, and
Vallonia, that as I journeyed through their consecrated places they might show themselves propitious to
me. Seeing that I had almost feared a warlike army because of the trumpet's sound; but, considering, I
judged it to be of shepherds' trumpets of bark, whereupon I rather reassured myself than mistrusted
otherwise.

But after this there was no long delay before I hear coming, singing, a company (by their voices of
tender and flowering age) of damsels graceful (as I judged) and beautiful, sporting and taking their
solace among the flowering herbs and in the gracious cool shades, free of any retarding suspicion, and
journeying with great applause among the comely flowers. The incredible sweetness of their modulated
voice, carried by the temperate and dew-bearing airs, spread itself through that delightful place, and
was brought back with the sweetest sound of an accompanying lyre.

At which novelty, searching about and bending down beneath the low branches, I saw them coming towards
me with a gesturing step. With their maidenly heads gathered in most notable fillets of threads of gold,
wrapped and above bound and garlanded with flowering Myrtle and with manifold flowers. And over their
snowy brows the yellow and trembling forelocks curled like vine-tendrils. And then down over their most
white and comely shoulders flowed the long tresses, composed with nymph-like neatness and elegant art.

Clothed in a Carpathian habit of silk most adorned, and of various colouring and texture. There were
three tunics, the one shorter than the other and distinct. The lowest of shellfish purple; above
followed the silken one of most green colour woven through with gold. The topmost of finest cotton,
saffroned and crimped, girt with a golden collar beneath the bound of their round little breasts.

Their outstretched arms were clothed by the last tunic, and copiously covered by the cotton one, which
granted with the highest grace the colour beneath. And near their swelling little hands they were fitly
bound with little cords of fine silk, with little golden loops, of a pleasurable artifice. And some of
them had their little feet excellently laced with double soles, with manifold binding of threads of gold
and of purpling silk. Some shod then over stretched hose of scarlet and greening cloth, and some over
the naked, of soft and gracious shining leather, and others of chamois dyed in most beautiful
colourings, without accusing the toes.

With gilded borders, their shoes over the snowy ankles with a curved opening, bound tightly and
buckled with thongs passed through golden clasps, and otherwise commended with little loops of twisted
gold with exquisite knotting. And where the bound of the surrounding hems was, adorned with an
unimaginable cording, the round and ivory legs, driven by the moderate airs, often showed themselves
somewhat.

They then, becoming aware of me, stayed their Nymph-like step and stood, emptied of their sweet song,
suddenly invaded by this novelty of me newly come into that place. And marvelling to one another and
curious, silently searching me out, it appeared to them insolent and unaccustomed that in that famous
country a man foreign and strange should have arrived so by chance.

For which cause they stood for a little space among themselves, one to another with a secret
murmuring, and many times bending to look me over searchingly. As though I had been a phantom — alas, I
felt at that point all my bowels shaken, like leaves of Sweet-flag quivering in the impetuous winds. For
scarcely being reassured from the terror often spoken of, and judging at once and deservedly that they
had in them something beyond the human condition — knowing nothing else — I feared such a divine vision
as appeared to ashen Semele, deceived by the counterfeited form of Beroë of Epidaurus.

Alas, I began again to tremble, become more fearful than the frightened fawns seeing the tawny Lioness
roaring with hunger. Contending within myself whether I should kneel

to the ground, or turn about and draw back (because certainly they offered themselves to me as
merciful girls, and having something other than humanity, and of the heavenly), or persevere thus
constant and unmoved.

At last, having taken counsel with myself to make the venture and to risk whatever might follow — it
persuading me all the while that by no conjecture could there be found in these any inhumanity or
savagery, and above all that the innocent carries his protection with him — I stirred up my lukewarm
spirit, still reined in by a numbing shame, knowing myself to have come unworthily into this perhaps
holy place, and solacing assembly of most delicate and divine Nymphs.

And still it did not persuade me with a sincere and tranquil mind that I had entered and come there,
rashly perhaps into forbidden places and a prohibited country, and with wicked daring. Turning over
therefore such thoughts within myself — behold, one of these, more confident and bold, said: "Who are
you, then?"

Then, all confounded between my familiar fear and sudden shame, I did not know what to say nor what to
answer; and, my voice together with my spirit being forbidden me, I remained half alive, and like a
statue. But those virtuous girls, perceiving that in me was a real and human shape, but terrified and
fearful, all drew near, saying: "O young man, whoever you are here, our looks and presences should
never make you afraid here; therefore do not doubt in the least. For here no savagery whatever is
used, nor will you find displeasure in any way. Who are you, then? Speak, do not fear."

At this request, having somewhat taken back my voice, stirred by those alluring and nymph-like looks
and recalled by their sweet speaking, answering I said to them: "Divine Nymphs, I am the most
graceless and unhappy lover that ever could be found in the world. I love; and she whom I so ardently
love and heartily desire, I know not where she or I may be. And by the greatest and most mortal peril
that I could ever express, I have been led and come here."

And the piteous tears being already called to my eyes, and bowing to the earth and casting myself at
their maidenly feet, sighing I cried out, beseeching pity by the most high God. At once, all shaken in
their soft hearts with compassion and piteous sweetness, and moved almost likewise to little tears,
dutifully and striving with one another to draw me by the arms from the ground, they raised me up; and
with sweetest and most coaxing speech they said to me pleasantly:

"We think, poor little one — indeed it is so — that by the way you have entered here, wretch, few can
escape. But above all things praise highly the divine power and the kindness of your star, for you have
now escaped an extreme peril. But at present there is nothing more to fear that is disturbing, nor any
troublesome assault; for by this way you might perhaps easily find yourself blessed. Settle yourself
therefore, and be tranquil again, and comfort your mind. For here, as you plainly see, is a place of
pleasure and delight, and not of grief nor of any terror. Because the age is uniform, the site secure
and unchanging, time does not run, the joyful convenience, the gracious and companionable living

alluringly persuades us to it, and grants us to be perpetually at leisure. And this too you must
understand: that if one of us is pleasing, another shows herself more solacing still. And our delightful
and shared companionship cleaves together intensely with a perpetual glue. And one increases it; the
other leads to every extreme sweetness and most conveniently to solace."

And she added: "Here, in fine, is a wholesome Field, most wide in its bounds, various in herbs and
pleasant to the sight in its plants, fruitful of all crops. Fortified with famous hills. Filled with
all harmless animals, and conspicuous and most crowded with every pleasure. Copious of every fruit,
with a universal exuberance, and adorned with the purest springs."

Another said: "Hold all this fixed and firm, dear guest. This happy territory is more fertile than the
fruitful Mount Taurus on its northern aspect, of which wandering fame declares that the vine's cluster
is of two cubits, and that one fig-tree produces seventy measures of its fruit."

Then the third, festive, added: "This sacred shore exceeds the richness of the Hyperborean island lying
in the Indian Ocean; nor are the Lusitanian lands such, nor Talge on the Caspian mountain."

Continuing, the fourth said, affirming with more fervour: "The Egyptian abundance is empty in
comparison with ours, though it be called the public Granary of the world."

Lastly, one alluring in aspect to every headlong fall added with elegant pronouncing: "In this kindly
country there would be found no encumbrance of overflowing marshes vexing us with troublesome air, nor
any shutting-in by most rugged mountains, but by most adorned little hills. And on the outward side it
is strongly walled about with harsh and pathless precipices. And so, in this manner, every sadness being
eliminated, here is everything that can bring delight, and a refuge of the gods, with blessed security of
mind.

"Beyond all these things said, we are the followers of a renowned and distinguished queen, most
munificent and of most lavish generosity, called Eleuterylida, of wonderful clemency and most merciful;
who governs here with the highest and strongest wisdom, and rules with a most ample dominion, and
commands, fortunate and happy, with heaped-up glory. And it will greatly please her when we shall bring
you to her venerable presence and majestic sight. And if by chance the others, her fellow-servants and
courtiers, perceive it, they would come running here in troops to look upon what is rarely seen here.
Therefore drive from you and shut out every afflicting sadness, and compose your mind, taking your
comfort festively with us, and give yourself to solace and to pleasure, every trembling being driven
away."

POLIPHILO, HAVING BEEN MADE AT HOME AND MADE SAFE BY THE FIVE NYMPHS, WENT WITH THEM TO THE BATHS,
WHERE THERE WAS MUCH LAUGHTER AT THE JEST OF THE FOUNTAIN, AND ALSO AT THE ANOINTING. BEING AFTERWARDS
LED TO THE QUEEN

ELEUTERYLIDA, HE SAW ALONG THE WAY, AND AT THE PALACE, EXCELLENT THINGS, AND A CHOICE WORK OF A
FOUNTAIN.

BEING AFFABLY RECEIVED AND HIGHLY reassured by those merciful Nymphs, and altogether comforted by those
coaxing girls, and my fled spirits not a little refreshed — showing myself readily willing in everything
that I could judge welcome and pleasing to them — I set myself freely familiar and most devoted.

And because they had alabaster boxes of perfumed powder, and little cleansing vessels of gold and of
fine stones, and shining mirrors, and golden hair-partings in their delicate hands, and white folded
veils of silk, and bathing shifts, and offered me to be their carrier, they told me, refusing, that
their coming to this place was because they came to the bath. And immediately they added: "We wish you
to come with us. It is there before you, where a fountain pours. Did you not see it?"

I answered reverently: "Most comely Nymphs, if a thousand and various tongues were found in me, I should
not fitly know how to render the thanks I owe, and to thank so homely a kindness — for you have most
opportunely brought me to life again. Therefore not to accept such a gracious and Nymph-like invitation
would be reckoned rustic baseness. And for so much I should esteem myself happier being a servant with
you than ruling elsewhere; because, so far as I can conjecture, you are the dwellers and companions of
every delight and true good.

"You must know that I saw the marvellous fountain, and considered it with a shrewd sense; and I confess
and affirm it a work more illustrious than ever presented itself to my eyes. And I so occupied my
shrewd mind, allured, intently gazing upon it and drinking greedily, wholesomely quenching my heavy and
day-long thirst, that I went no further to explore."

One of them answered, saying placidly: "Give me your hand. Now you are safe and welcome. We are at
present five companions together, as you see; and I am called Aphea. And this one, who carries the
little boxes and the whitest linens, is named Osfressia. And this other, who is the bearer of the
shining mirror — our delight — Orassia is her name. This one who holds the sounding lyre is called
Achoë. This last, who bears this vessel of most precious liquor, has the name Geussia. And let us go
together to these temperate Baths, for pleasure and delight. Whereupon shortly you too (since your
propitious fortune has fallen here) will come with us

Afterwards we shall all return together, made glad, to the great palace of our distinguished Queen.
Who, most clement in all things and most munificent of a wide liberality, will most ably suggest and
dispose your intense loves and burning desires and lofty conceits. Take heart and comfort. Let us go."

With pleasurable acts, with maidenly gestures, with persuasive semblances, with girlish caresses, with
wanton glances, with sweet little words, they led me there, solacing and coaxing. Content with
everything present — save that my golden-haired Polia was not there for the fulfilment of the highest
happiness, and to be a sixth with these and make up the perfect number.

On the other hand I found myself discontented, that my habit was not conformable amid this delicious
company; but having made myself somewhat at home, I began affably to dance with them. And they laughed
sweetly, and I likewise with them; and at last we came to the place.

There I beheld a wonderful eight-sided building of baths. And at every single outer angle two piers
were paired; level with the floor began the base-courses girt about beneath them. Then the piers
followed, a third of their thickness drawn from the solid, with capitals set beneath the straight
beam; with a frieze above, going entirely round beneath a cornice. Which frieze was adorned with
choice carving: with several naked boys, excellently expressed, equally distant, with their hands
entangled in nooses holding swelling little bundles of leafy twigs bound together, girt with thongs.

Above the said cornice there then rose (with an elegant vaulting) an eight-sided little Dome, in
imitation of what was beneath. Which, from angle to angle, was pierced through with a marvellous
working by way of a thousand noble conceits, and stopped with little plates of pure crystal, which
from afar I judged to be lead.

The little wing was fixed above a pointed thing, the eight-sided form of the Dome being sectioned,
somewhat eminent; and there, immediately set above, was a Triangle, in whose topmost centre, fixed,
there rose a most firm shaft, into which was let another shaft, unstable and turning, free and playing;
to which was fitted a vane, which, driven by whatever wind blew, turned the tubed shaft with it, and a
ball at the top of a third of the one below.

Upon this a naked boy sat, treading with his right heel, holding the other leg hanging. The back of
whose head, as far as the mouth, was all hollowed in the form of a funnel, with the orifice bored
through to the mouth; to which, soldered, was joined a trumpet, held with one hand by the boy near the
soldering, and the other stretched towards the end of the trumpet, levelled in a line with the vane.
Every

thing of thinnest bronze cast perfectly, and most brightly gilded. Which Vane, and the Ball, and the
Boy — with the figure or face in the act of sounding, with the hollowed back of the head towards the
blowing of the wind — easily forced it; where, the air being breathable within, the trumpet trumpeted.

And therefore, the Egyptian carobs being shaken by the wind, likewise there too the wind made the
trumpet sound. For which cause I thought, laughing, that a man finding himself alone in an unknown
place and frightened is easily terrified by every little noise.

Now, in the face opposite the most beautiful Nymph of the fountain, I saw the entrance, with a most
polished door. All the artifice of that excellent Stone-carver who, I thought, had carved the sleeping
Nymph; in the frieze of which I saw this title in Greek characters: ASAMINTHOS. Such baths, then, the
amplitude of Tatius does not surpass.

Within, seats went round in four stone steps, girt with a continuous joining, all minutely inlaid with
jasper and Chalcedonies of every colouring. Two of the steps the tepid water covered, up to the margin,
or surface, of the third. In the angles there stood at each a free and rounded little Corinthian
column, of various colouring, with straggling waves of jasper — the more welcome, the more the artful
nature is wont to make it — with a decent base. And the capitals most excellently composed beneath a
beam; beyond which lay the Zophorus of naked little boys playing in the waters, with little
water-monsters, with wrestling and infant contests, with apt strivings of a readiness fitting to their
age, and lively movements and games; and it girt it round most beautifully with a crown set above.

Above the order and projection of the little columns there tended perpendicularly from each, to the
summit of the dome, a

torus with a moderate swelling of oaken fronds, one pressed above another page-wise, fringed and
curved, of greenest jasper, and branched about with gilded little beans; which, ascending, ran into
the vaulted heaven of the dome, coupling themselves into a rounding, within which a lion's head took
its place, with curled mane. It held biting in its jaws a ring, to which were commended hanging chains
of brass, excellently knotted, which held up a most polished vessel with a wide opening and little
hollowed, of the said most shining material, hung two cubits above the water.

The rest of the inner vault, apart from the stoppings of crystal, was all covered with a Cyanean
colouring of litharge, scattered and studded with gilded bosses, choicely shining.

Not far off there was in the earth a fissure, which continually vomited fiery matter; and taking of
this and stuffing the hollow of the vessel above, they laid on certain gums and scented woods, and made
an inestimable fumigation of a fragrance like the best perfumes. Then the twin leaves being closed,
pierced with metal and stopped with most limpid crystal, they gave a most joyful and manifoldly
coloured light. By this same piercing of open knots they clearly lit the fragrant baths, and the
fragrance was kept in, and the heat did not breathe out.

The levelled wall set between the one column and the other then showed a most black stone, of a
hardness rejecting metal, and shining. Enclosed by a surrounding band a quarter broad, of coral-like
jasper, adorned with a lineament of double gorges, or whorls. In the middle of such a wall, between the
one column and the other, resting there sat an elegant naked Nymph, with distinct resting and office,
of Gallatite stone of ivory brightness; firmly placed above upon fitting little altars, which, of round
lineament, composedly bound themselves in a circle with the bases of the columns. O how exquisitely
carved I beheld the said images, so that more than once my eyes allowed themselves to stray from the
true and real ones and to carry themselves to the feigned.

The paved little floor beneath the water was seen of various inlay of hard stones tessellated, in
marvellous drawings of divers colourings. Because the most limpid water — not sulphurous, but
sweet-smelling and temperately warm, without furnace or stoke-hole, and purged beyond all belief — was
no hindering medium between the object and the sense of sight. For the various little fishes, on the
fronts of the seats and of the floor, artificially expressed in mosaic in emulation of nature, appeared
to swim alive. Red mullets, or mullets; lampreys, and manifold others — the
nature not considered, but the comeliness of the painting.

The most black stones of the wall were cut through and diligently set again with a most notable
composition of interlacing, or bindings, of antique leaves and flowers, of shining Cytherean little
Shells, as most acceptable to the eyes as ever one could set forth.

Above the door, in a space of Gallactite stone, I saw a dolphin bending among the calm waves, and a
youth sitting upon it and sounding a lyre. Opposite, above the laughter-making fountain, likewise
another dolphin swimming, with Poseidon riding upon it and with his pointed trident. These little
histories were made exactly from the bounds of the same stone, and carried upon a most black flat.
Here I deservedly praised that illustrious architect, and no less the statuary.

On the other hand, the comely dignity of those shapely and pleasing girls exalted itself. For I did not
know how to compare, between the terror now past and this unthought-of and chance solace, the excess of
it; but without doubt I found myself in extreme delight and pleasure.

And there, having most joyfully entered into such a fragrance as could never sprout in Arabia, they
stripped upon the stone seats in place of a dressing-room, and laid aside their silken garments, their
blond tresses most beautifully wrapped beneath netted Fillets woven of threads of gold, and most
worthily bound. And without any regard they allowed their shapely and delicate persons, all naked, to
be seen freely and particularly discerned — honesty reserved — flesh without fail delicate, rosy, and
suffused with ripe snow.

Alas, I felt my stirred heart leaping to open itself and to be wholly taken up with a pleasurable
gladness; whereupon I esteemed myself happy then, only in beholding such delights. Because most
pertinaciously I could not withstand the most burning fires hurtfully assaulting and troubling me in my
furnace-like heart. And for this, sometimes for my better refuge, I did not dare to look so much at
those enkindling beauties heaped up in those divine little bodies.

And they, perceiving it, laughed at my simple gestures, taking girlish sport. And I for this stood with
a sincere and contented mind, at being pleasing and welcome to them. And sitting in the midst of such
burning, I bore no ordinary patience. But yet with tolerance I stood, bashful and forbearing, knowing
myself unequal to so fair and such a company. And being invited also, although struggling and having
excused myself, none the less I entered into the bath — like a crow among white doves; for which cause
I stood apart, blushing, with my eyes unsteady, searchingly allured by objects so excellent.

And there Osfressia, very witty and eloquent, said to me: "Tell me, young man, what is your name?" And
I answered her reverently: "Poliphilo, Lady." "It pleases me well," she said, "if the effect answers to
the name." And without delay she added: "And what is your dear beloved called?" I answered modestly:
"Polia." And she said: "Ah, I judged that your name signified 'much loving'; but what I now hear means
'the friend of Polia'." And at once she said: "If here

your Polia were found present, what would you do?" "That," I answered, "which befits her modesty, and
which should be worthy of your divine presences." "Tell me, Poliphilo, do you bear her a great love?"
"Above my own life," I said, sighing. "Beyond all delights and above all the riches of whatever
treasure most precious in the world, I bear that love pierced through and kept in my burning and
consumed heart." And she: "Where have you abandoned so beloved a thing?" "I do not understand it, and
where I myself now am I do not know." She said, smiling: "And if someone were to find her for you, what
finder's fee would you give? But be of glad heart, and give yourself to pleasure, for you shall find
your beloved Polia again." And with these most welcome and like little words, the most placid and
charming girls bathed themselves with much solace, and I with them.

At the space opposite the notable fountain of the sleeping Nymph outside, within the bath there was
another of statues, artfully made of the best metal, with a golden and mirroring brightness. These were
fixed above a marble hollowed in a square and drawn forward into a frontispiece, with two little
half-columns — that is, in a half-circle, one to each side — with the little beam, the little frieze
and the little cornice carved in the solid of the single stone. This excellent composition offered
itself as the residue of the whole work, wonderfully accomplished with choice art and invention.

In the cut hollow, or in the emptied space of the said stone, two perfect Nymphs stood, a little less
than the natural size, unclothed as far as their thighs, where the parting of the shift they wore over
gave way, somewhat flying with the movement of their office; and their arms likewise bared, save from
the elbow to the shoulders. And above the arm that held up the little boy the garment was raised and
thrown back. The little feet of which infant — the one in the hand of the one Nymph, the other in the
other's hand — they pressed; the faces of all three laughing. And with the other hand the Nymphs,
moving aside the little boy's fringes as far as his girdle or navel, uncovered him. And the child held
his little member with both his hands. Which, within the warm waters, made water of the freshest,
cooling them.

In this delicious and most excellent place I was, by such conditions, wholly dissolved in gladness and
content; but the chief pleasure of my senses was interrupted, only because among these contented ones,
and among such whiteness and dew condensed into hoar-frost, I saw myself as it were Egyptian and of a
swarthy hue.

One of these, then, named Achoe, affably said to me, smiling: "Our Poliphilo, take that vessel of
crystal and bring me here a little of that fresh water." Without delay and without further weighing of
it — save that I was gratifying her, and showing myself not only promptly obedient but even eager to
please her — I went at once. And no sooner had I set one foot upon a step to get to the falling water
than the little water-maker lifted his spout and drew across my hot face the coldest water, so that
almost in that instant I fell back upon my knees. At which so shrill and womanish a laughter rang
beneath the blunt dome that I too began (having come to myself) to laugh so hard that I felt myself
dying of it.
Afterwards I understood the deception of the artifice, most skilfully

devised: that setting any weight upon the lowest and unstable step, it moved downward, and drew upward
the childish instrument. Whereupon, the machine and its curious artifice being investigated with
careful examination, it pleased me greatly. And therefore in the little frieze this title was elegantly
inscribed in Attic characters: GELOIASTOS.

After much merry laughter, having bathed and all of us washed, with a thousand sweet, loving and
pleasant little words, and maidenly jests and caresses, we went out of the heated waters, climbing up
upon the dry steps with great dancing and festivity; where they anointed themselves with fragrant
perfumed unguents and were smeared with an ointment of nutmeg, and offered me too a little box, and
anointed me. Of which

such a soothing anointing and wholesome washing was very timely for me. Because, beyond its marvellous
sweetness, it proved chiefly profitable to my limbs, laid low in my past and so perilous a flight.

Afterwards, all being clothed — and they detained a good while longer in their nymphlike trimming,
combing and adorning — with great cheerful festivity they familiarly opened the vessels of the most
delicate confections, and comfortably tasted them, and I with them, the precious drink following after.
Then, sufficiently refreshed, and turning again to the mirrors with a scrupulous examination of the
adornment of their divine presences, and of the bright forehead shadowed with the little globes of
their hanging golden curls — and their damp hair wrapped in a clear covering — at last they said to me
joyfully:

"Poliphilo, let us go now with glad heart to our renowned and lofty Queen Eleuterylida, where you shall
feel a greater delight." And laughing they added: "Ha! the water did indeed strike you in the face."
And they renewed their sweet laughter without any measure, cheerfully making sport of me, nodding to
one another with a wanton blinking of the eyes and a sidelong, goatish look.

And thence, making a graceful departure and going in the midst of the festive girls, they began sweetly
to sing, rhythmically in the Phrygian mode, a droll metamorphosis. Namely, how a lover, wishing to
change himself by an ointment into a little bird, mistook the box, and was transformed into a rough
ass; concluding that some believe unguents to be for one effect, and afterwards they are for another.
By this I suspected that the point of it was aimed at me, from their looks turned mockingly towards me;
but at the time I thought nothing further of it.

Judging then, shrewdly, that that anointing had been for the relief of my weary limbs — behold, of a
sudden I began to be so stirred by a wanton itching and a goading desire, that I turned and twisted
wholly about. And those cunning ones laughed freely, knowing what had befallen me. So much did it
quicken that I felt myself every hour more sharply pricked. Whence I know not what bit, or what halter,
restrained me from falling upon them like a ravening and famished eagle that hurls itself out of the
air, rapacious and constant, upon a flock of partridges. Neither more nor less was I strongly goaded to
violence. And feeling so great an incitement grow every hour, it tormented me; and the more I burned,
bent beyond measure with desire, the more such fit and convenient objects offered themselves most
violently, stirred as I was by the increase of an almost deadly plague and of an unknown heat.

One, then, of these flaming Nymphs, Aphea by name, said to me in sport: "Poliphilo, what ails you? A
moment since you were jesting merrily, and now I see you altered and changed." I said to her: "Forgive
me, for I writhe more than

a withy band; I am undone — give me pardon — with a wanton ardour." At this they were all moved to
unbridled laughter, and said to me: "Ho! and if your longed-for Polia were here, what would you do
then?" "Alas," said I, "by that divinity to whom you submit and serve, I beseech you, add no more
torches, heap no more brands and resin upon my incredible burning, prick no further my kindled heart,
do not make me burst asunder, I pray you. For I am undone in no ordinary measure, and am utterly
consumed."

At this lamentable and mournful response of mine, straightway, their coral-red little mouths full of
laughing clamours strongly stirred, they came to such an excess that neither they nor I were able any
longer to walk for multiplying laughter. But falling down and rolling among the fragrant flowers and
upon the grassy ground, they were choked with unruly laughter; whence it was needful to slacken and
loosen a little the tight girdle across them. And lying thus half dead beneath the shady and leafy
trees, and in the spreading shade of the branches, they rested.

There, then, with a familiar boldness, I said to them: "O women full of fire, and mischievous to me, is
it thus you use me? See how a lawful occasion is offered me of breaking in and overwhelming you and of
doing you an excusable violence." And nodding towards them as though I would seize them, feigning a
boldness in doing what by no means I dared — they with fresh laughter called one another to help, and
fled, leaving their golden slippers and veils here and there, their fillets carried off by the cool
breezes; and their little vessels ran among the neglected flowers. And I running after. So much so that
truly I do not know that they did not swoon with it, and I as well, my powers laid low.

When, then, this comfortable make-game and this mocking sport had lasted a while, and my agitation thus
raised was fully satisfied, and the slippers and the other scattered things gathered up — near the
green and dewy banks of a running little stream, the sweet laughter being tempered and they most
tenderly pitying me, there by the trimmed banks of low and bending rushes and little willow, with the
osier swimming, and nearby plentiful in living water-simples, one of these, a well-mannered one called
Geusia, bending down, plucked up the Herculean water-lily, and a root of Arum, and Amella, which were
sprouting a little apart one from another; and laughing offered them to me, that I should choose which
of these pleased me and taste it for my deliverance. For which cause I refused the water-lily; I
condemned the little dragon-plant for its burning; I accepted the Amella. And this, being cleaned, she
persuaded me to taste. Whereupon it was no long space of time before, the slippery goad departing, the
intemperance was extinguished. Thus in this manner the carnal enticements being bridled,

the festive damsels solacing me, eloquent and witty, we came without noticing it into a famous place,
exceedingly pleasant.

Here, in fitting order and distance, was a way set with cypresses, straight and lofty, with their
angled and cracked cones, as thick with foliage as by their nature they could be, and composedly
placed. And the levelled ground covered on every side with the greenest periwinkle, abounding in its
little azure flowers. Which adorned way, broad with a due spaciousness, tended straight towards a green
enclosure; and to the opening of that the cypresses were distributed by the line, for a length of four
stadia.

Coming joyfully to that cloister, I found it equal-sided, of three walls, in the likeness of a straight
wall, as high as the lofty cypresses of the way. Which was all of choice citrons, oranges and lemons,
thickly heaped together with a most welcome foliage and knit with an artful cohesion; and I judged its
thickness to be six feet. With a door bent in the middle out of the tree-work itself, composedly
carried through with the diligent industry of the maker, as well as one could say or make it. Above,
in a fitting place, windows were set in order. So that on the surface no wood or stem whatever showed
itself, but only the pleasant and welcome green of the flowering fronds.

Among the fair, thick and living leaves it was most abundantly adorned with white blossom, breathing a
sweet orange scent; and to the desirous eyes ripe fruits and unripe offered themselves plentifully, in
the highest degree delectable. Then within the thickness I looked at the branches (not without wonder),
so compacted by such mastery that by them one climbed easily through the whole capacious composition.
Whence, by the propping of the knitted branches, those who climbed did not appear.

Entering, then, into this green and most welcome enclosure — to the eyes exceedingly worth looking at,
and to the understanding worthy of esteem — I saw that it was an elegant cloister facing a wonderful
and most ample palace, excellent in its symmetried architecture and very magnificent. Which rendered
the fourth wall of the leafy enclosure, of a length of sixty paces. And this circuit was a square open
court beneath the sky.

In the middle part of this most notable area I saw an excellent fountain of the clearest waters,
spouting on high almost to the top of the green enclosure through the narrowest little pipes, and
falling down into a wide basin, which was of the finest amethyst, its diameter containing three paces,
of a thickness of a quarter, dwindling towards the lips to an inch, of most excellent casting; and all
round about there appeared, in relief, most worthily expressed, water-monsters — as many as the
inventors of antiquity

were ever excellently able to feign in hard stone. A work of Daedalus, and notable for admiration. Nor
let Pausanias boast of having set up his bronze bowl at Hipparis.

It was aptly founded upon a distinguished shaft of jasper, of straggling mixtures, the one beautifully
adulterating the other, and cut across by translucent chalcedony of the colour of troubled sea-water,
brought to a most noble making. Raised of ewer-like vessels, one above another, with the parting of a
choice knot-work. Which stood upright, fixed in the centre of a rounded plinth of green ophite. Which
round was raised from the level pavement by a fifth part, with the surrounding porphyry, which was
curiously lined with well-polished little waves.

Round about the shaft, set beneath the basin, four harpies of gold with clawed and rapacious feet stood
upon the flat of the ophite. Which, with their hinder parts towards the shaft, the one directly
opposite the other, and with unfolded wings, held up beneath the violet lip, or basin, with maidenly
faces. Their locks flowing loose down over their shoulders from the neck. And with their heads not
reaching under the basin. With their serpent tails coiling into a globe, and passing at the end into
antique foliage. They made with the lowest ewer-vessel of the shaft a not ungrateful but a friendly
knotting and joining.

Within, at the middle navel of the vessel, above the order of the shaft beneath, there was raised
proportionately out of the amethyst vessel itself an oblong chalice turned upside down, lifted as much
as the vessel was hollowed, its middle standing clear of the surrounding lips of the basin. Above which
was raised an artful little altar, set beneath the three naked Graces. Of the finest gold, of a common
tallness, the one cleaving to the other. From the nipples of whose breasts the rising water dripped
finely, appearing like little rods of burnished and streaked silvered ash. And as though it had been
distilled through the whitest pumice of Tarragona.

And each of them held in her right hand an all-bearing horn of plenty, which rose somewhat above her
head. And then all three openings came elegantly together in one rounding, their mouths meeting equally
together. With fruits and various fronds hanging out of the rims, or lips, of the twisted horns,
abundantly filled.

Among the fruits and foliage six little pipes projected a little, set in order and flowing, from which
the water rose in the finest thread. And then the most skilful founder, so as not to hinder one elbow
with the other, had the statues hide with the left hand, as a sign of modesty, the part worthy of
covering.

Upon the lips of the gaping basin (whose circuit went about one foot wider than the ophite beneath it),
standing with heads raised above their viper feet, with a most seemly spacing

there sat six scaly little dragons of shining gold. By such a devised art that the water flowing from
the breasts fell directly into the emptied and open crown of the head of the said little dragons,
which, with wings spread wide and biting, likewise each of them threw back, or rather vomited out, that
water through a little pipe. Which then fell beyond the rounding of the ophite, and between a rounding
of porphyry, which stood equally more raised above the level of the area, or open pavement, than is
said above. Where, set between, there ran a little channel between the ophite and that porphyry
rounding, wide at its opening one foot and a half, and two whole feet deep. Which porphyry was three
feet in its flat surface, with a choice waving towards the pavement.

The remainder of the little dragons crept along the moderate hollowing of the basin, until they all
came together, their tail-ends transformed into antique foliage and into a most pleasant binding with
the little altar set beneath the three images, or rather their footstool, at a proportioned height.
Without any deforming encroachment upon the hollow of the precious basin.

So that, by the green meeting of the orange cloister, and by the shining of the bright material, and by
the purest waters, there was rendered a most welcome colouring, like a rainbow among hollowed clouds,
within the noble, proud and elegant vessel.

Then, in the swelling body of the basin, between the one little dragon and the other at an even space,
there stood out of that excellent casting heads of maned lions, with exquisite exactness, which,
vomiting, scattered through a devouring pipe the water dripping from the six little conduits set in the
most beautiful horns of plenty. Which water rose with so bridled a force that its fall came down among
the little dragons into the wide and sounding basin, with a most welcome ringing of the wide-open
vessel from the high fall of the said waters.

Of this most rare workmanship, then, chiefly built with so sharp a wit — such as was that uncommon
vessel, and the four most perfect harpies, and of what choice dignity was the little altar, where I saw
the three figures of most shining gold sitting, and with what artifice and polish it was ordered — I
should never know how to speak briefly and clearly, and still less am I fit to describe the whole. A
making not of human wit. But I may lawfully testify (calling the gods to witness) that never in our own
age was such a chased work, nor anything near its equal, devised more welcome or more worth beholding.

And thus astonished I considered besides those stubbornly hard stones of the support of the great
basin — that is, the shaft of ewer-vessels set one above another. With what ready ease, neither more
nor less than if the material had been of soft wax, were those drawn threadings made, and so

roughly carved between, and without the gnawing obstinacy of the hardest emery, such triglyphs so
excellently expressed. But with fit chisels and gravers of such a tempering as our modern craftsmen
know nothing of, shining with a choice brightness.

The whole space of the area, then, in the middle of which was raised this most notable artifice of the
famous and sumptuous fountain, had a stone pavement of squares of fine marbles of various colour and
shaping. In which, less than their measure, there were most beautifully fitted rounds of gracious
jasper, levelled with the utmost evenness, differing in their colouring. And the remaining corners were
beautifully satisfied with winding fronds and lilies.

Then the broad bands, or fillets, between the squares I beheld to be of the best tessellation of most
welcome coloured stones, with a minute cutting. In green leaves with crimson flowers, dark blue, purple
and grey-green, so much the better joined in a confederate way with an obstinate cohesion, the less I
should know how to express it — of an artful composition, and most bright with a choice shining, of
diligent polishing, a noble shaping. More lovely in colour than crystal of various tincture struck back
by the rays of the sun. Because the colours led about, with a most charming meeting, were reflected in
those burnished stones; no step betraying itself in the cut tesserae, lozenges, triangles and squares,
but with a most level directness, wholly equal.

By all which things I remained as it were dazzled in my senses and stupid, examining carefully within
myself the work, exceedingly notable, such as I was not used to seeing. And willingly I should have
wished to pause a little, and such dignity of workmanship would have needed a longer stay to
investigate, and to contemplate somewhat more diligently; but I could not, because it was fitting to
follow closely my eloquent companions and guides.

The aspect, then, of this sumptuous, magnificent and proud palace, and its approved situation or
placing, and the symmetry of its marvellous composition, at the first meeting won me to a chief
cheerfulness and comely grace; by the dignity of which making I was provoked to go on and contemplate
further. For which cause I deservedly judged that its most skilful builder was excellent above any
other that ever built. What framing, then, of beams and of rafters; what distributed disposition of
chambers and inner rooms and courts; what walls covered and crusted with precious panelling; what
wonderful order of ornament; what unfading colouring of pigment upon the walls; what rule of columns
and of spacing — and there, by this

let not the Praenestine way exalt itself for the Gordian building. And to this excellent colonnade let
its two hundred columns yield — Numidian, Claudian, Simiadic and Thistian, divided in equal number.
What marbles, what carvings, where I beheld the labours of Hercules in shining stone, marvellously cut
half free of the ground. Spoils, statues, inscriptions and trophies, wonderfully chased. What
gate-house, or vestibule; what royal portico. To this let Titus Caesar duly yield with his mirroring
and burnished Phoenician stones — such and so great that any feeble and mouldering wit would condemn
itself in wishing to tell of it.

There comes besides the dignity of the windows and of the notable door, and of the most noble podium,
the distinguished expression of the builder's art. No less excellent to see was the marvellous ceiling,
most beautifully coffered, with little coffers between the wavings, covered with foliage, set in square
and round. Adorned with exquisite lineaments, gilded of pure gold and of a dark blue colouring, and
elegantly painted. Let every other wonderful building be lost here.

Being now come to the opening of the notable door — behold, the way in was closed by a joyful and
marvellous curtain stretched across, all of golden thread, and rewoven and inwoven with silk, with two
most worthy images. The one of them was surrounded with every instrument fit for working; and one, with
her maidenly face raised, considered the heavens intently. The beauty of which not undeservedly warned
me off from thinking that any pencil (even the famous Apelles's) could reach it.

Here the eloquent and most beautiful and charming companions each joined her right hand kindly with
mine, wishing to lead me in, and receiving me they said: "Poliphilo, this is the order to be kept, by
which one must enter into the venerable presence and lofty majesty of our Queen. This chief and first
curtain it is granted to no one to enter without the receiving of a plain and watchful damsel
doorkeeper, called Cynosia." And she, hearing our coming, at once presented herself and courteously
drew aside the curtain. And we entered.

Here was an enclosed space, divided by another veiling of most noble artifice and composition, and
varied with every tincture. In which were signs, shapes, plants and animals of a singular reweaving. In
this place, at our coming, a woman likewise careful came immediately to us, named Indalomena. And,
frankly unfastening her curtain, we were led in.

Here too there was an equal space between the second and a third curtain, most excellently woven with
discourse and reason, and painted in fine work with endless bindings and holdfasts and with the most
ancient instruments for grappling and holding fast

with a bite. Without delay there placidly offered herself to us in this place a third matron, our
hostess and receiving us graciously. Whose name was Mnemosyne. She likewise, when we had been called
in, gave us free entry. And at last here my companions presented me before the venerable majesty of
Queen Eleuterylida.

*How great and notable was the majesty of the Queen, and the condition of her dwelling and its
wonderful furnishing, Poliphilo tells as best he can. And the kind and affable receiving of him. And
how she marvelled at him. And how wonderful and splendid was the banquet, exceeding the reach of human
knowledge, and the place where it was held (without comparison), he somewhat describes.*

Being come to the first doorkeeper, she saw me not without astonishment; and having greeted her
seemly and duly reverenced her, and being given by her a familiar invitation to enter and a courteous
welcome — and in like manner by the following curtain-keepers — I saw a lofty portico, as long as the
compass of the palace. Whose golden vaulting was painted with green foliage, with distinct flowers and
entwined fronds and flying birds, choicely embroidered in mosaic work. The cleanest paving, like that
outside in the enclosed court. The walls crusted with sumptuous stones artfully set in fine work.

At the last curtain that matron Mnemosyne very affectionately urged me to doubt of nothing, but to show
myself a strenuous follower of the Queen's royal urging and wholesome counsel, and a persevering doer
of it, because then the outcome would come out pleasant without fail. And entry being particularly
granted — behold, there presented themselves to my eyes things rather divine than human. A most
ambitious furnishing in a stupendous and spacious court, beyond the palace and adjoining it, opposite
the other, perfect in its square.

The most charming and precious pavement I saw set between a surrounding tessellation: a space of
sixty-four squares, of three feet the diameter of each. Of which the one shone with jasper of a coral
colour, and the other of the greenest, dropped with bloody drops, with an almost imperceptible cohesion
of the composition, like a

game of chess. The circuit then of an excellent embroidered border and enclosure, one whole pace its
breadth, of subtle devisings of stone cutwork, excellently compacted in the smallest shapes, like a
lovely painting of fine stones, cut evenly and framed to rule. The joinings not appearing; most
burnished and mirroring, and of so just a levelling by line and square that a round and spherical body
set upon it would have shown itself unsteady.

Beyond this, then, there ended a marvellous making of three paces of most noble knot-work of jaspers,
prasines, chalcedonies, agates and of other notable manners and kinds of fine stones. Along the walls
of the aforesaid area I considered certain most worthy seats of sandalwood, red and citron, most
diligently made, and covered over with the greenest velvet. Stuffed, or cushioned, with a moderate
downy convexity, or of a soft material that yielded most comfortably to the sitter; and the said silken
pile fixed along the rims of the benches with little golden nails with studded heads, upon a silver and
stretched braid, or flat little cord.

The splendid facing of the enclosing walls I beheld, all clothed with plates of purest and shining
gold, with chasings answering to it, and most fitting to that precious material. In the levelled and
most burnished flat, then, of the said plates — divided by certain little pilasters, or squares, of a
most fitting measure and correspondence — there appeared in the middle of each, clearly, round jewels
fitted in, moderately swelling in the form of the torus of a base, of a thickness suited to the
capacity of the space, covered over with fringed leaves pressed one against another. Girt about with
thongs, with the ends flowing, they perfectly adorned the jewel round about. Where there came in, most
aptly among the foliage in a fitting distribution, a fruitage of shining and various jewels, notably
shaped to various expressed lineaments.

In the remaining space, then, walled round with these swelling jewels, painted perfectly with beauty in
encaustic work, I beheld with great pleasure the seven planets with their inborn properties. The
remaining level, outside the roundness of the jewels, was wrought fiercely in endless and elegant
expressions of silversmith's work. With an adorned scattering of manifold and inestimable gems I saw it
wonderfully with its ornament.

At the left wall, or moulded partition, it was likewise. And with the spaces and jewels of the same
form of ornament and of the same number as the aforesaid — that is, in seven roundings — I contemplated
seven triumphs of those subject to the ruling planets, most skilfully made in the said painting. And on
the right side I saw likewise seven harmonies of them, and the passage of the soul, with its
qualitative receiving of the degrees of the circles, with an incredible history of the celestial
operations that come with it.

The fourth wall the palace made, with a distribution equal to those hinted at, save that the door took
up the middle space. The other six, with a ruled correspondence and harmony with the rest, in their
jewels (opposite the planets, and in a symmetried meeting) held the virtuous operations belonging under
those, expressed in the form of elegant Nymphs with the titles and signs of their effect.

The seventh, in the middle of the frontispiece, or gable, of the door, was placed directly over against
the seventh jewel, which held the planet Sun. Which was raised higher than the others by the placing of
the Queen's throne. For which cause every part most accurately answered — in material, in number, in
form to the line, and in every least part and placing most evenly and to the level; and thus mutually
the right side with the left, and here and there, agreed in a most exquisite meeting. Of which
surpassing place each wall was extended twenty-eight paces.

By such an elegant disposition this open court was made even, covered round about all in the most
perfect gold, a work wonderful and unspeakable.

The little pilasters, or half-squares, at a distance of four paces one from another, with a just
sevenfold partition (a number most welcome to nature), were of the finest and eastern lapis lazuli,
with a most joyful fullness of its colouring, adorned with a most charming scattering of minute sparks
of gold. The front of which, between the closing wavings, were marvellously carved with candelabra,
with a most notable company of fronds, horns of plenty, little monsters, heads maned with foliage,
figures ending in scrolls, birds, and horns, and little vessels of pomegranate flower, with
distinguished invention and thought, from the lowest footing to the topmost shaft, in a relief almost
torn free of its flat ground. The thickness of which was measured from its own rise. These, then, in a
sociable and most welcome assembly, made among the golden plates the interruption of the most seemly
spaces.

The capitals were of a making suited to the other workmanship. Above stretched the straight beam with
the chased lineaments required, with little cylinders, or rounds, the flattened whorls set between them
two by two. And following above it its adorned frieze. Which held alternately such expressions as
these: heads of oxen, with their horns knotted with fillets, flowing with hanging berries sewn on, with
two branches of myrtle, looped in the middle section with a flying selvage; and with dolphins, with
their gills leafed and likewise their fins, the outermost part passing into foliage; and at the whorl
certain little boys with their hands seizing the whorl, which ended in an antique flower. The dolphin's
head had a curve, one part of which turned back towards the little boy, and the other wound itself
towards a vessel with an open mouth,

ending in a stork's head, with the beak at the open mouth of a monster with its face turned back; and
there were certain vertebrae sewn on between the mouth and the beak. Which heads, leafed for their
hair, the one opposite the other, made the mouth of the said vessel full of leaves; from the rims of
which there hung a knotted cloth towards its lowest part, and the thin ends flowed down beneath the
knots, with every ornament of a making fit to such a place and material. And in the middle, above the
whorls, sat a face girt about in the manner of a little boy.

And with such and like lineaments the frieze extended itself in its adornment. Which a most seemly
cornice covered, composed of every polish of artifice. Above which, on the flat, perpendicular to the
projection set over it in the order of the squares, there were vessels shaped in the most ancient
manner, set at an ordered distance, a good three feet high and more, of chalcedony, some of agate, some
of a vermilion amethyst, and some of garnet and of jasper, alternated in colour, of various and notable
workmanship most subtly chased, their bodies chiefly adorned with little hollows twisted and straight.
And with masterly and excellent handles.

To the order and line of each jewel above the cornice there were aptly fixed square little beams seven
feet high, of shining gold, hollow within, with a further stretch of like little beams above them going
round the straight ones. And traversed crosswise in trellis-work with a ruled partition, they came
together seemly. Understanding that out of the vessels set in the corners of the walls the little beam
and the vine came out together. But out of the remaining vessels there rose alternately either a vine
or a bindweed of gold, various in kind. And lying over the crossed little beams, with a plentiful
stretch of scattering branches, entwining one with another mutually in an elegant

confederation, and with a most beautiful meeting, they covered over this whole court most aptly, with a
richest — nay, an inestimable — ceiling, and with a varied foliage made of splendid Scythian emerald,
most acceptable to the eyes, so that not such was the one in which Amenon was engraved. And the
sapphire and beryl flowers of every season, scattered abroad. And with the utmost disposition and
artifice, among the green fronds, other thick and precious gems variously shaped into fruits, with
feigned clusters heaped of little stones, hanging down, of a colouring answering to the natural
cluster.

All which most excellent things, of an incomparable, incredible and almost unthinkable cost, flashed
everywhere most precious, not only for the most noble and marvellous material, but likewise for the
great and most exquisite making. Weighing which marvellous thing with a most subtle examination, I
pondered upon the wandering extension of those most intricate branches, and proportioned in thickness.

So artful — by what art, and what rash daring, and what obstinate intent were they so aptly carried
through: whether by the workman's glue, or by soldering, or by hammering, or by the founder's art? By
these three conditions of working and forging metal it seemed to me impossible that a covering of such
a breadth and knitting should be so excellently made.

In the middle prospect over against our entry, upon a stepped and royal throne, adorned and filled with
manifold fitting-together of

burning gems and of marvellous making — such as was never that seat in the temple of Hercules at Tyre,
made of the stone Eusebes — the Queen herself dwelt, sitting with a venerable and imperial majesty.
Divine, and of a marvellous magnanimity in her aspect. Sumptuously clothed in cloth rewoven with
forced gold in the thread.

Her majestic head she held adorned with an ambitious ornament, of a silken and purple mitre, matronly
and royal, of a heap of uncommon and light and burnished pearls, which went round the wide forehead in
the fringe of the mitre. Which pressed down her blackest hair — shining more than Indian amber — that
descended with a comely difference, waving over her snowy temples. Then, from the back of the head, her
overflowing hair was parted into two tresses neatly plaited. The one here and the other there, they
passed above the little ears, and then met again in a wonderful agreement. At the top of the crown they
were bound in a knot, or tuft, of great and roundest pearls, such as the Indian promontory Perimula
does not bring forth.

And out of the knot flowed the remainder of the long and most abundant locks, covered by a most thin
veiling, with a golden parting-pin held by the said knot or tuft, which descended flying to her
delicate shoulders. In the middle of the mitre, at the parting above the crown, there stood out a most
precious little shape. And her rounded throat, suffused with a snowy whiteness, was encircled by an
inestimable necklace, with a pendant towards the fork of her milky breast, of an incomparable diamond
in a tablet of half-moon form, or oval, sparkling all over, monstrous in size, in a golden setting of
fine-wrought ornament.

Besides, from her ears there were most richly hung, exquisitely in the piercing, two inestimable
drops, of two great pure carbuncles, flashing without equal. She had also her feet shod in green silk,
and the little slippers with golden loops twisted at the straps, adorned with many jewels. They trod
upon a footstool, or rather a support, of a soft cushion swollen with a heap of down, of crimson
velvet, with a border going round of eastern pearls, such as are not to be found in Arabia in the
Persian gulf. With four hanging tufts at the four corners, covered with flashing gems, with their
little beards, or fringes, of twisted threads, and mingled hanging things of gold and of vermilion
silk.

On the right and left side, upon the sandalwood benches, the ladies of the court sat in a well-ordered
manner, with an honest and homely gravity, clothed in cloth of gold, with an incredible adornment of
dress, such as never was seen in the world's judgement. In the midst, then, sat this renowned and
sovereign Queen with pomp and the utmost state, and an unthinkable adornment. The borders led round her
ambitious garments were filled with most opulent jewels of alternating colour in such plenty that you
would say nature had hailed down there all the finest manners of shining gems, in a wanton array.

At so imperial and lofty a sight, then, worshipping and kneeling to the ground — without delay the
chamber-women and the ladies of the court all rose from their quiet sitting, provoked by such a novelty
and spectacle, marvelling exceedingly that I should have come to such a place. But much more did I feel
my sad heart open itself restlessly, anxiously thinking over things past and things present, beset and
full of a deep astonishment. Wholly suffused with a reverent fear and an honest bashfulness.

At which novelty the seated ladies called my companions to their ears, curious. And asking under their
breath who I might be, and my strange and unlooked-for case besides. And for this the drawn eyes of all
were fixed and directed intently upon me.

Finding myself, then, most humble before this most excellent and such a presence, I remained wholly
astounded, and as it were without breath and abashed. And being asked by her the course and manner of
my coming, and my entry into that place by my companions, they readily set the whole out and fully
recited it. Moved by this, the honeyed Queen made me rise, and having heard my name, began thus
affably to speak: "Poliphilo, be of good heart

but attend and tell me: how have you come in here safe? And how have you escaped the deadly and
horrible dragon? And how did you find a way out of those hateful shadows and blind caverns? I have
heard the whole of it distinctly and to the end. But I marvel in no ordinary measure, since few — nay,
fewest of all — are able to arrive here by such a road. Now, since your tangled fortune has brought you
to us unhurt, I judge it fitting that for no obstacle whatever should I deny you my kind favour, and
that I should host you freely, munificently, and with the greatest good will."

At this most liberal invitation and royal promise and welcome, as well as I then knew how, giving her
huge thanks with devout and honourable speech, briefly and succinctly I told her point by point of my
flight from the fearful monster. And thereafter with what laborious difficulty, hurrying, I came to
this most acceptable place. At which she marvelled greatly, and with her likewise the venerable ladies.
And how besides the five companions had found me terrified and wandering.

So to such distinguished magnificence I bent my mind eagerly with the utmost pleasure. Afterwards she,
smiling charmingly, said: "It shows itself a worthy thing that an ill beginning should sometimes fall
out to a happy issue and end. And before I lay upon you anything else to carry out at present of your
loving and settled purpose and warm desire, I will that, for the profitable easing of your modest
troubles, you too should sit down with this notable company at a banquet of friendship most freely
offered — since the favouring heavens have deservedly shown you our bountiful and pious hospitality,
and have brought you beneath our triumphant roof. And therefore, my Poliphilo, without any hesitation
set yourself there to sit comfortably. For you will most gladly see part of our most splendid ordering,
and the plentiful diversity of my more than royal delights, and the chief adornment of the elegant
service, and the household splendour, and the inestimable preciousness of my most ample riches, and the
wide effect of my beneficence."

Whereupon, at this sincere and holy command, her eloquent and kindly speech being finished, I humbly
made myself her bowing servant, and with a small boldness and slight daring, obeying at once, I set
myself to sit upon those delicious benches on the right side — still in my woollen gown, which yet held
the burrs, or little burdocks, stuck in it, and some clinging husks of goose-grass — in the midst of
the five companions, placed second, between Osfressia and Achoe, after the Queen. Six other
companions on the other side. So far apart one from another that they took up that length in an
orderly way. And in the lofty middle throne, come down upon the lower step, she sat in royal fashion,
and with an august dignity.

The crown above the throne, in encaustic painting, held a comely beardless image with flowing yellow
hair. With a little of the breast covered by a scant cloth, above the spread wings of an eagle, which
with head raised contemplated it fixedly. Which was wreathed with an azure diadem, adorned with seven
rays; and at the eagle's feet a branch here and a branch there of green and undying laurel, and such
signs, one to each side, were expressed. In the like manner I saw painted in every crown, that is, the
figure proper to its planet.

It fell out by chance that behind my shoulders was the jewel holding the history of wing-footed
Mercury; and, turning, I saw how his kindness was corrupted when he found himself in the malignant tail
of the venomous Scorpion. And straightening again I thought how, in a most abject habit, I found myself
among so many sumptuous garments — neither more nor less than that deadly beast, misshapen and vile
among the most noble signs of the zodiac.

Then they sat in an ordered way upon the magnificent benches. Which went round the whole circuit of the
walls. Now on the right side and the left of the court, as many as could aptly sit, the noble ladies
most richly adorned, and with unusual and elegant dressings of the head, with womanly devices, their
hair drawn back and plaited in distinct little knots, the fairest in the world. Some with the fair head
curled in Poppaean ringlets, justly parted and modestly waved above the rosy and shining foreheads and
the smooth temples. And others with hair (like obsidian, not of Latium, not of Spain, but of India) of
the deepest black, comelily adorned with the whitest pearls, and with clasps of incredible price
ornamented at their snowy shoulders.

They stood with so much reverence and attention that all at one time, when the servers at the tables
made their reverences kneeling, these did the same, rising from their pleasant seats. Each clothed in
shining gold, with marvellous weaving and workmanship. These did not eat at these tables.

Over against the triumphing Queen there answered the opening of the third curtain, which was a great
and distinguished door, not of marble, but of lovely and hardest eastern jasper. Made by art and by
ancient workmanship, very notable and worthy. On either side, here and there, of this

most excellent door, towards the ladies seated at the table, there stood the young musicians, seven to
a side, in most worthy and precious nymphlike dress. Who, at every changing or clearing of the banquet
table, varied their sounds and their instruments. And while the feast went on, others of these sang
sweetly with an angelic and Siren-like harmony.

Now in an instant there were set out tripods of ebony, and tables for the time, without tumult or
noise, but each server most ready for her appointed office, and eager and clear-sighted with an
affectionate effort, and wholly intent upon the service enjoined and laid upon her.

And here first of all, before the Queen, tripods of such a making were set fast. Upon a rounding of the
best jasper, distinguishedly lined. Above which were fixed three stems. The lowest part of which ended
upon the flat in a swift lion's paw of gold, engulfing the shafts with exquisite foliage, and clothed
round about with the most polished foliage. And in the middle of each was fitted a little boy's head,
held in the midst of two spread wings, from which there hung, from the one towards the other, a little
bundle of branches heaped together, swelling in the middle, filled with various fruits. Which shafts in
their topmost part had a projection most apt to bear up the round table before the Queen. This
framework was unchanging, but the sudden round tables varied. As the material of the vessels varied at
every change of table.

Then in the blink of an eye there was set upon this tripod a round table of gold, most level, three
feet in diameter and a thumb's breadth thick; and of this form and measure were all that followed. And
upon the ivory tables was spread a scented cloth of green silk, neatly stretched out, broad and long
almost down to the pavement, unravelled at the edge all round, with its own threads twisted and mingled
with threads of gold and silver, hanging beneath a band, or border, a sixth of a foot in its breadth,
subtly rewoven and richly furnished with pearls. Hung a hand's breadth clear of the pavement, evenly,
all round on every side. And of this workmanship all the cloths were
fringed at their edges and seemly adorned.

Next there followed a comely and nimble girl with a wide golden vessel heaped with flowers of violets —
amethyst-coloured, pale yellow and white, such as are fragrant in the new spring — which she most
readily scattered and strewed over all the tables (except the Queen's, which was always bare).

The sacred majesty of the Queen had put off the pompous royal mantle, such as Lollia Paulina of Rome
never saw, and remained in a most sumptuous figured garment of purple crimson pile, woven all over with
manifold birds and other little animals, fronds and flowers, of an ordered knot-work, and the work
somewhat swelling with the most illustrious pearls, with a very thin overgarment above. Tinged with a
little of a saffron silken colour, showing through, by its clear thinness, the covered work and the
crimson beneath. Which habit was in the highest degree graceful and comely and imperial.

Then there came two elegant girls. Who carried an artful fountain that poured continually, artfully
taking up again the water that it scattered; and it was of shining gold, founded in a basin of most
beautiful workmanship, and before all else they set it before the Queen. And no sooner was it presented
upon the golden table than together they made a graceful bow, bending likewise their adorned heads. And
kneeling within a thumb's breadth of reaching the burnished pavement. Like reverences, in an ordered
way and at one time, the attendant servers who waited made — following one another, and observing them
both before and after the offering of anything whatever, and at its removal.

Three other excellent young women followed after those. One with a golden ewer. And the other with a
basin, or hand-bowl, most shining. The third with a delicate towel of the whitest silk.

The divine Queen having washed her hands, she that bore the golden bowl received the washing, so that
it should not go back and be taken up again into the fountain. And she that carried the ewer poured in
as much scented water as was poured out, so that the fountain of wonderful devising should not empty
itself. The third lightly dried her hands.

The wide and spreading vessel of this fountain was artfully founded upon four little wheels, and they
carried it running along over the tables to wash most aptly

the hands of all who sat at meat. Which in the middle stood out beyond its own lips, set with studs of
