gems, seemly channelled, as was the hollow of the vessel round about, and with other expressions.

Upon this projecting part sat a most noble vessel, and above this another of a different kind, but both
joined by two little handles, with an exquisite polishing and elegant workmanship and most precious
ornament. For among the other inestimable jewels, in its cover passing into a flower, out of which
there rose a diamond shaped into a little pear, with its point fixed in the flower, shining all over,
of an unheard-of and unimaginable size. And by my sense of smell I judged the water to be of roses,
mixed with the juice of lemon rind and a little amber, or benzoin, in a skilful gradation, with a
welcome and sweet scenting.

In the middle of this stupendous space there was set out a wonderful vessel for perfuming, not only for
its noble and perfect material, which was pure and best gold, but for its notable and antique making;
with its support upon three rapacious feet of a foul harpy. Which, in foliage, gave a binding to that
triangular base, plentifully adorned with little histories, as such a metal demands.

Upon the outstretched corners of which three naked spirits stood, set in order, two cubits high, with
their little shoulders turned one towards another, near one to another. They trod upon the base,
resting at the corner with the right foot, and with the other hanging and free, towards the fixed foot
of the next boy. And each of them, both elbows raised, held a shaft in the form of a pomegranate
flower, slender at the bottom, and in the upper part opening into a little shell for every hand,
widened at the mouth and a little hollowed, with broad rims. Six there were in a due circuit, cleaving
one to another.

Between the shoulders of the winged boys, from the central point of the flat of the said triangular
base, there rose a shaft of distinguished expression of an antique candelabrum, which at its point held
its little shell, like those aforesaid, and of as great an opening as suited to fill the empty space
left in the middle between the six shells. Which shells the servers had

filled with kindled embers, and covered over then with ash; and above the ash there boiled a golden
flask for each shell. With a different liquor, or waters with a day's infusion of scented matter — as I
guessed, that each flask had its own distinct water, such as one might call rose-water, orange-water,
myrtle-water; of tender laurel fronds, of elder flowers and others well known, with a varied and
sociable scented matter. And these, boiling, breathed everywhere a most sweet and unknown fragrance.

In the presence of the most magnificent Queen there always waited three reverent and neat girls, with
the trimness of veiling garments of gold and silk woven in a wonderful manner. The colour graciously
changing to the eye, of the colouring of the table-cloths, so that as the cloths were changed, in the
same manner the nymphlike garments of the servers were varied as to colour; with a most charming
gathering of the drapery beneath their tight girdle, turning from their fleshy and snowy shoulders, and
drawn over the full breast moderately swelling. Shod with golden shoes with a moon-shaped opening over
the bare foot, all alike fastened with golden clasps. With flowing hair, blond and most abundant, and
falling to their calves. On the whitest forehead girt with little fillets of great and uniform pearls.

These three stood before her with a singular and devout reverence, very heedful and set to such an
office with a chief and ready service; who served at one table only. When afterwards the next change of
table came, all these stood upon their feet, made servants with their arms folded in the utmost
reverence. And thus in succession all the others observed it, and always as many again were renewed in
number.

Of the three servers to each guest: the one between the two offered the food; she on the right side
accompanied that food underneath with a little plate, so that nothing should fall elsewhere. The third,
on the left, elegantly wiped the lips with a most white napkin, fine and cleanest. At every act the
reverence was ready. The napkin was never used a second time for that office, but, thrown by the damsel
upon the pavement, was at once gathered up by those standing by and carried thence away. And as many
mouthfuls as were to be offered, so many scented and perfumed folded napkins they brought with them for
changing, silken, of wonderful woven workmanship.
To each of those at table, then, such an order of service they diligently

kept. For no guest at such a meal touched anything, but was fed in due time by the servers, save for
the cup.

At the first table, afterwards, all having washed at the aforesaid fountain of skilful artifice — by
the force of gathered, or enclosed, air the water rose and was taken up again. Which thing being so
exquisite, I thought that by twin pipes, here and there unequal, through a wall set between, pierced in
the middle, the vessel was divided within, and by its own impulse the forced water ascended; which,
having learnt by a subtle examination, was extremely pleasing to me.

After the washing of all, to the Queen first and thereafter to each in turn, the beauty-loving serving
girls gave a golden apple, distinguishedly pierced through, and enclosing a paste of a wonderful
scenting — for this cause, that the idle hands of each should be occupied with some act by the said
ball, and the senses in looking and smelling; and it was adorned with precious little stones.

Here, then, at every change of dishes, two damsel stewards drew most beautifully into the middle of the
royal court a stupendous store-carriage upon four running wheels, in its forward part in the form of a
boat, or skiff, the hinder remainder shaped into a triumphal car of the purest gold, wrought fiercely
with manifold Scyllas and little water-monsters, and many most exquisite expressions, and wonderfully
finished, with richest little stones in an elegant distribution and wonderful ornament, filled
seemlily throughout — the sparkling of which shone through all the space that could receive it, and
meeting in a flashing with the glowing of the other jewels set variously on every side, you would
freely say that Phoebus was there with his shining locks, with a Nymph sitting, whose face made her no
less lovely with her shining eyes. So that, for the continual brightness and splendour of so many
unspeakable workmanships, no addition could be found, nor any equivalent comparison, were it even the
Babylonian temple with its three golden statues.

Within which were amply prepared all sauces and seasonings needful for the whole requirement of the
varied table; it carried cloths, flowers, cups, napkins, vessels, little forks, drink, food and
seasonings. This waggon Nymph then readily distributed the preparation to those who cleared away.

The table being then taken down for the next change, everything above recited returned to the clearing
carriage. And when it had departed, the girls with the leading trumpets — such as were invented neither
by Piseus the Tyrrhenian, nor by

Maletus king of Etruria — and with them the flute-players immediately began to play; and in this
observed manner they did every time that the carriage went away. Playing while it returned; then they
ceased. And when the table was changed, these too varied their musical instruments; and when they
ceased, then the singers sang most sweetly, enough to put the Sirens to sleep, in the Aeolian mode,
with hautboys and double flutes, of which mode Dardanius of Troezen was not the inventor.

And in this ordered manner there were continually heard most welcome sounds, most charming harmonies
were listened to, delightful melody was felt, a most joyful scenting was drawn in, and a most splendid
fullness was received, tasting most sweetly. Everything, then, agreed mutually in dignity, in grace and
in delight, without any defect.

At this first and splendid table all the table utensils, or instruments, were of the finest gold, and
of this the round table before the Queen. And there was presented a cordial confection: as far as I was
able to conjecture accurately, it was a helpful and most excellent composition of shaved horn — that
is, of unicorn — with the two sandalwoods; pearls ground in burning water kindled at the fire, and
quenched in it down to the last cutting; manna, pine kernels and rose-water, musk, ground gold, very
preciously composed and weighed, and pressed into morsels with the finest sugar and starch. Of this she
gave two takings, at a moderate interval, and without drink, to each — a food to forbid every obstinate
fever, and to shut out any sad weariness.

This done, in an instant all things were taken up and removed, and the fragrant violets scattered on
the ground, and the table stripped bare. And no sooner was this so done than once again the table was
covered with sea-purple cloth, and likewise all the servers; and as at the first they covered it with
flowers of citron, orange and most fragrant lemon.

And here they presented, in vessels of beryl — and of this gem was the royal table (except the little
forks, which were of gold) — five little cakes, or fritters, of a saffron paste kneaded with hot
rose-water and sugar, and again sprinkled with a shower of the said finest musked water, frosted over
with the finest sugar. These little globes, of so sweet and varied a tasting, were diligently cooked
with this distinction: the first offering in oil of orange flowers; the second in oil of cloves; the
third in oil of jasmine flowers; the fourth in oil of the finest benzoin; the last in oil pressed of
musk and amber. Having tasted this delectable dish savourily and with an eager and greedy appetite,
they then presented a solemn cup of the stone named above,

with its cover, and above it besides a most thin silken veil rewoven in fine work, covered with silk
and gold, and thrown back over the shoulder of her that bore it, and hanging partly down her back. And
with this observance they presented all the little vessels for drinking and for seasoning, covered
over. Within which drinking-cup they had poured a most precious wine, whence without failing I plainly
suspected that the god himself, vintaging in the Elysian fields, had put his divinity into so sweet a
liquor. Let the Thasian wine yield here, then, and every precious thing that may be drunk.

Without delay, after the most welcome draught, this splendid table was taken down. And, the fragrant
flowers being scattered upon the shining pavement, a cloth was readily stretched out of purple silk
cloth; and they strewed over it flesh-coloured, or mallow-pink, roses, white, vermilion, musk,
damascene, four-petalled and Ghiebbedine, mingled.

And promptly the nine servers, clothed in the said cloth and colouring, set down before each of us six
cuttings of a blindly fattened head, moistened and sprinkled with its own poured fat and saffroned
rose-water, and mixed with orange juice, excellently roasted and then all gilded over, and with six
fitting slices of snowy Mnestorian bread. And thereafter with a seasoning of lemon juice tempered with
fine sugar, with pine seeds and with its liver ground, adding rose-water, musk and saffron and choice
cinnamon; and thus all the seasonings composed with a chief and exquisite gradation, shared out and
excellently seasoned. All the vessels were of topaz, and the round table.

This third frugal and magnificent table being, as above, unprepared, without delay the next was renewed
and covered with a silken cloth of satin of a bright yellow colour (and the servers clothed in the
same), and all flowered with fragrant flowers of lilies of the valley and of narcissus. Immediately
such a dish was set out: seven balls of partridge flesh with a sharp diligence, in broth, toasted, and
as many mouthfuls of eyed and milky bread. Seasoning: maple-sap, almonds ground with thrice-boiled
sugar, starch, citron sandalwood, musk and rose-water. Vessels of chrysolite, and the circular table.
Last they offered the most precious cup, and thus it was observed in those that followed.

The fourth rich table being removed, at the fifth the board was clothed again with cloth of purple
silk; and like was the nymphlike dress. Flowers dark, yellow, white and amethyst. For meat, eight
morsels of the flesh

of pheasant, most freely offered, roasted in its juices, and as many mouthfuls of light and whitest
bread; the sauce such: fresh yolks with little pine kernels, orange-water, pomegranate juice, sugar of
Colossae, and cinnamon. Vessels of emerald, and the table of the lofty Queen.

This solemn change being carried away, without any interval a cloth of violet silk was spread, and the
nymphlike garments likewise. For flowers, the three kinds of jasmine, crimson, yellow and white. For
food, nine mouthfuls from the breast of the ever-keeping peacock, moist in its broth and roasted in its
fat. A sauce greenest and somewhat sharp, with pistachios ground, Cyprian sugar, starch, musk, thyme,
wild thyme, white oregano, and pepper. Vessels of dark blue sapphire, and the royal table.

At this seventh sumptuous change they carried away the sumptuous board, all of the whitest ivory subtly
inlaid, and brought back another of precious aloe wood, excellently compacted with glue, and from one
end to the other hollowed with a wonderful devising into most noble knot-works of foliage, flowers,
vessels, little monsters and small birds, and filled in with a black paste of musk and amber in a
confederate mixture. This I rightly judged a most elegant and sumptuous thing, breathing a delightful
scent; the cloth whitest and fine, with a fine-wrought weaving of byssus of Carystus, and of such cloth
the adorned garments of the serving girls. Flowers of cyclamen, with all manners of gillyflowers
exceedingly fragrant. So that whoever might be able to consider so sweet and various a fragrance, with
its continual and new meeting most joyful to the sense, I do not dare to express.

An excellent confection in morsels: pulp of dates with pistachios, ground with rose-water, and island
sugar, musk, adulterated with precious ground gold, so much that all the takings appeared of gold;
three to each were given. The vessels of jacinth, and the circular table — a stone fitting to so
excellent an ordering of the divine board and its splendour, not subject to the Licinian law.

After the joyful and most welcome tasting of this marvellous confection, and the flowers rolled to the
ground, by a royal magnificence there was brought without delay a great golden basin full of kindled
embers, into which the cloth was thrown and the napkins of byssus; and so long a space they left them
in the fire that all was kindled and glowing, and thence drawn out and cooled, it was seen unhurt,
purified and cleanest, as before. And this too was a distinguished and unheard-of showing. Last of all
the tripods and the boards were readily taken down and carried thence away.
All which most excellent showings, the more carefully

I considered them, the more ignorant and astonished I stood; but certainly above all things I took an
extreme delight, with an intense admiration, seeing so many and so great and triumphing and most
lavish sumptuosities of incredible cost and splendour, that I judge it better to be silent than to say
too little of it — save that at the least price there yield here the Sicilian feasts, the ornaments of
Attalus, and the Corinthian vessels, and the delights of Cyprus, and the Salian suppers.

Nevertheless so supreme and excessive a cheerfulness and heartfelt delight, and the utmost (among such
delights) and extreme pleasure, was interrupted, intercepted and stained for me by one of these three
who at this change happened to serve before me: who had almost wholly the comely semblance and the
sweetest representing aspect of Polia, and in her stirring gestures, sly and most thievish glances.
This brought me no small increase of sweetness to the highest and chief sweetness of the filling and
rich seasonings and the most bountiful refreshment. But yet fittingly and carefully I drew back my
eyes, stirred and enticed as they were, from beholding so many most precious gems, everywhere and
universally shining with a flashing brightness, and such a diversity of unseen beauties and notable
adornments — and had as it were made them her bondmen, with an immoderate longing to behold the
answering of that highest beauty.

At last, in the order aforesaid, the tables being cleared, they made me a sign that I should not move
from my place, for the sweetmeats that followed and the richest and sweetest dainties.

And here first to the venerable and divine presence of the Queen, and thereafter to us, five shapely
servers, clothed in a garment of dark blue silk most beautifully woven with a golden thread, presented
themselves together at one time to each with a singular excellence. She in the middle of the others
held an uncommon little tree of cinnabar-red coral, such as would not be found in the Orkney isles, a
cubit high. Fixed with great care upon a little hill all of emerald. Which little hill lay upon the
mouth of an antique vase of the purest gold, almost in the likeness of a chalice, as high as the little
hill and the branching coral, full of marvellous artifice of foliage, not expressed in our age.

Between the slenderness of the foot and the bowl there was knotted with the greatest polish a little
apple of inestimable making; likewise the base and the cup were of distinguished relief-work of leaves,
little monsters and two-formed little Scyllas, as exquisitely expressed as ever chased work could be
wrought fiercely, with a proportioned circling. And the biting setting of the acorned little hill was
of incomparable jewels, and so throughout the base, where
it was most seemly and fitting. Placed there, they shone with a flashing light.

In the branches of which little tree there were artfully set certain open flowerets, shaped into a
five-petalled rose. Some of shining sapphire, and some of bright jacinth, or beryl. In five of these
flowers there were fitted within five little apples, as big as a sorb-apple and more, and of that same
painting, upon a pointed golden spike that stood out from the centre of the flower, so that they
feigned to have been produced there.

Which young girl, reverent and kneeling to the ground with her right knee, keeping the other raised,
held this notable coral fitly upon it. Which, besides the little branches taken up by the precious
flowers, had at the tips of the others monstrous pearls curiously fixed.

Another of these had the cup, with a precious liquor, such as proud Cleopatra did not give to the Roman
captain. The three others carried out the service lying upon them, as customary above. Plucking off,
then, one after another with the little golden fork those small fruits (unknown to me, and never seen),
and offering them to us, we tasted them most savourily. But the unthinkable sweetness of taste that I
felt was no otherwise than as if in the gracious matter, set apart, there were the entering in of the
longed-for form. And here were given back the round golden apples recited above.

Last of all there appeared a miraculous work, another perpetual fountain by a devised artifice of the
material named before. But of another most worthy shaping and figure, wonderfully wrought. Founded upon
a fixed axle, by which the turning wheels went round. Upon which axle there stood, made fast, an
unequal square three feet long,

and two feet wide, and raised a third of a foot. In the corner parts there sat upon each a harpy, with
both wings stretched out to the body of a vessel above, sitting over the levelled middle of this
square, best clothed at the edges with a little cornice of gorges and wavings and husks.

And on each of its faces, divided into three, the middle partition, hedged between with wavings, held
carved in half-relief a triumph of satyrs and of Nymphs with trophies and exquisite acts — except the
front and the hinder part, moderately curved, which, in the place of a squared lineament, held a
rounding waved within, in which was wonderfully carved a little sacrifice, with a most ancient altar in
the one and in the other with several figures and actions; and the remaining empty places nearby the
tails of the harpies, forked, and here and there most aptly turned into rolling fronds, distinguishedly
clothed over.

In the middle centre of the level of the said square, out of an antique foliage, there sprang a most
beautiful ancient vessel, its circuit not exceeding the compass of the square flat beneath it. And
this, with all the work that follows, with every proportioned inquiry both of the rise, the breadth and
the thickness, and with the most seemly lineaments of vessels, was most diligently filed and finished,
with a perfect and polished shaping.

Which, at its pressed-in mouth, brought forth a basin. The circuit of which exceeded the base vessel
beneath, adorned round about with little channels, and with a wide mouth and broad lips, such as no
chaser ever had power to work with the graving tool.

At the central point of which another vessel stood out, wonderful for its incredible making; in the
lower third of which were slices swelling on the outside, and then there girt it round an order of
various and inestimable gems set like navels, most brilliantly adorned with a mutual alternation of the
colouring. Above this was fitted a monstrous manly head. From which there went, here and there, its
covering in exquisite foliage, clothing it all over at the meeting with the head opposite, beautifully
adorning the free body of the vessel.

At the projection of the lip, perpendicular above the head, sat a ring, from which there hung, here and
there, a little bundle with heaped-up small branches of fronds and flowers and fruits, swelling in its
curve, with a well-polished knotting, both in the one ring and in the other.

Above the middle curve, beneath the projection of the lip, was fixed the head of a little old man with
his chin drawn back into foliage, biting a

little pipe through which flowed the water of the fountain, perpetual by artifice, into the basin
beneath.

In the opening, then, of this vessel there stood out a most precious little hill, marvellously heaped
of countless round gems pressed close one upon another, which with an unequal, or rough, shaping made
the stony little hill most charmingly, with the flashing of various lightnings of colour, with a
proportioned prominence.

At the top, or summit, of this little hill there grew a little tree of pomegranates, of trunk, or stem,
and of branches, and likewise this whole composition, of shining gold. The leaves set on of sparkling
emerald. The fruits, of their natural size, scattered here and there, with the golden rind widely
split, and in the place of the seeds there burned the brightest rubies, brightest beyond any touchstone
and of the thickness of a bean.

Then the ingenious maker of this inestimable work, being plentiful in his imagining, had marked off, in
the place of the pith, the seeds with the thinnest silver foil. Beyond this, and reasonably, he had
feigned certain other apples split open, but unripe in their seeding, where he had composed, with a
bold exquisiteness, thick pearls of eastern whiteness. Skilfully too he had feigned the pomegranate
flowers made of perfect coral in calyxes full of golden points.

Beyond this, out of the top of the pipe-like hollow stem there came a turning and free shaft, the lower
pivot of which was fixed in a socketed head, or rather made fast upon the middle of the axle. And it
rose up through the open and hollowed trunk.

Which shaft, firmly fixed, held up a notable vessel of topaz, of antique form, the lower body of which
was wide, girt with swelling slices; at the opening wonderfully with a little cornice, beneath which
was a little band enclosed by another set below it. In which binding, in four equal divisions, were
fitted four winged little heads of a boy with four dripping pipes at their lips. Then the remainder
narrowed to twice as much as the lower body, into a stopping above the mouth of an

inverted foliage. Above which was set another little vessel, almost circular, covered with a most
subtle foliage and little cornices and an artful mouth.

From the bottom of this there began a flowery tail of a dolphin, joined somewhat to the slenderness of
the vessel set beneath, and it descended with the head finned with fronds above the surrounding girdle,
where the boyish heads were fixed. And with a moderate hump, or bending, near the head and curving
towards the tail, it made most elegant handles. And all this sloping part showed, with an exquisite
polish, the expression of the best lineaments.

Such a topmost vessel, so placed, was so perfectly wrought that when the two-wheeled carriage was
moved, the shaft with the vessel joined to it turned round, spinning and pouring out the water from
within the tree; and when the wheels stood still, the turning ceased. And in this way I thought that
its spinning had its force from one of the wheels, which held another toothed one towards the turning
spindle, which had the sockets for the teeth, and moved the stem of the vessel. The wheels were half
covered by a winged work; there appeared, as it were, two spread wings, one here and the other there,
adorned with certain Scyllas.

This marvellous work, running before each of us, our hands being moistened and then our faces, all made
fragrant with an unthinkable scent, we rubbed our hands, so that never such nor so great a scent
offered itself to my senses. And in this manner the most apt girls bestowed it.

Bedewed, then, with such a sprinkling of the most fragrant water, the mistress's servers, with a
singular showing of kindness, offered a golden goblet, with which first the sovereign Queen, having
with a chief affability greeted us all, drank the sweetest nectar; and thereafter in order, one with
another, with reverent and gracious and mutual honourings, we solemnly drank. An excellent closing and
sealing of all the favours received and of the sweet tasting.

Last of all the sweet-smelling flowers were diligently swept up, and all gathered and all the leavings
carried thence away, the paving remaining bright and shining as the brightness of the most burnished
mirror, rivalling the aspects standing round about and the shining gems; and, each sitting in the place
appointed, the Nymph of the fountain departed.

Last of all the magnanimous and lofty Queen at once ordered an unheard-of dance, or ball, upon the
jasper squares, finished with an exact artifice, burnished and bright — such a thing as among mortals
was never seen nor devised.

*Poliphilo goes on to tell of an elegant dance after so great a banquet, which was a game. And how the
Queen committed him to two excellent maidens of hers. Who led him to behold delicious and great things,
and, talking with him, plainly instructed him upon certain doubts. At last they came to the three
doors. And how he stayed at the middle door, among the amorous Nymphs.*

So excessive and incomparable a glory and triumph, and unthinkable treasure, and frugal delights, and
the highest pomp, and solemn feast, and most splendid and sumptuous banquet of this most happy and most
opulent Queen having been recounted — if I have not distinctly and to the end worthily expressed her
chief dignity, let the curious little crowd not marvel at it; for anyone of sharp and ready wit, and
adorned and plentiful with a prodigal and most fertile tongue, could not satisfy this plainly, nor
altogether.

But much less I, who continually suffered, in every inward hiding-place of my burning heart, the
unceasing battle — however absent — of my lady Polia, the occupier and wasting plunderer of all my
powers. Beyond, the many marvels, unheard of in their excellence and diversity, things unaccustomed and
unlike, inestimable and not human; therefore dazzled and all alike weighed down in every sense of mine,
my excessive contemplation drawn apart by the notable variety, I should not know how to describe it
perfectly point by point, nor worthily to set it forth.

Who could think of the rich dress and exquisite ornament, and the most careful care; the perfect and
ambitious and trapped-out beauty without any defect; the highest wisdom, the eloquence of Aemilius, the
more than royal munificence. The distinguished ordering of the architecture, and the obstinate symmetry
of this building, perfect and complete; the nobility of the marble-worker's art. The setting straight of
the columns, the perfection of statues, the ornament of walls, the variation of stones, the royal
vestibule, the most ample peristyle, the artful pavements — who would believe with what luxury and

cost they were adorned and strewn with most precious coverings? The spacious and high inner hall, and
the most ambitious inner dining-rooms, bedchambers, closets, baths, library and picture-gallery, richly
and with a majestic adornment set out, and solemnly distributed.

Receiving-rooms capacious and wonderful in their art and incredible cost, with the choice praise of
their most distinguished maker, every partition and elegant agreement of the distinguished lineaments
deservedly approved. I beheld afterwards, with a singular pleasure, a coffered ceiling in the highest
degree skilfully adorned, stretched in an even flat, without peer or comparison; it made a proud
heaven, with set spacings of manifold shaping, with a drawn and levelled measure, hedging in the little
areas with a noble composition, with a ready prominence, which was duly adorned with the lineament of a
cornice, with little bands, gorges and egg-work, berries, or fruits of roses evenly threaded. And
leaves of acanthus licking along the corners of the square and oblong little areas, with exact roses
with a twinned order of foliage, the inner one smaller, with the required interval, all open, and the
curved parts, in a greater relief, everything clothed, or gilded, with the best and shining gold, and
with the finest and choicest dark blue colouring. With various other figurings of the ornament matching
the lineament — let the beamed roof of Salauces, king of the Colchians, yield here.

Then the voluptuous pleasantness of the ordered green places and orchards, and watered gardens, living
fountains, with little streams running in marble enclosures, held and hedged in with an incredible
making. Grass ever fresh with dew, and flower-bearing, and sweet summer airs and spring winds with the
various harmony of small birds. The pure serenity and unfailing temper of the sky, and the wholesomeness
of a freest and purest air; places neither low nor stony, nor swept by constant and frosty winds, nor
burnt by the unruly and scorching sun, but lit with an easy and kindly weather, and sincerely most
joyful with moderation and a middle measure; the fields fertile and untilled yet fruitful of every
good, sunny hills, leafy and cool little woods, pleasant with thick shade.

Afterwards the inestimable furnishing, the ready and manifold household and elegant service, the varied
youth with its growing age. The most welcome presence of the girls of the hall, of the court, of the
chamber, and of the royal household; the venerable and majestic sight of them, with a dress more lovely
and seemly and a distinguished ornament, and with an approved and most charming comeliness, as much as
ever anyone could feel or tell.

To such endless riches, then, supreme delights and immense treasure, let not the Hyrcanian pontiff
boast himself. Nor Darius, nor Croesus, nor any

human opulence and condition — behold, then, being in this part overcome, I can conveniently conclude
nothing else than that I stood senseless and out of my mind with astonishment; where I stayed with the
utmost pleasure, without weariness of the things present nor with any surfeit of them. But above all,
beyond what I have said, I was out of myself, turning over what fate had brought and destined me to
these blessed places.

But since I found myself thus, and in so great a heaping of glory, and a holy site, and a happy
country, and a blessed delight, and at the frugal and triumphing banquet — such as Clodius the
tragedian never made, subject neither to the Tapullan nor the Licinian law — refreshed with a moderate
fullness, and none the less by the royal promise of favouring my loving desire not vainly made secure,
I comforted myself, holding as nothing all that had until now befallen me and been set in my way; and
of everything I spoke well of Fortune, with a joyful gladness.

For which cause, the lofty Queen wishing to show, for a greater display beyond the things aforesaid,
the excess and the surpassing of the universe in all excellent and rarest magnificences — everyone
sitting in their places, after the miracle of the sumptuous banqueting, without any long delay she
ordered a game to be looked at, worthy not so much of the sight as of an eternal remembrance, which
also was an excellent dance, or ball, in such a course and manner.

Through the way of the curtains there entered thirty-two young girls, of whom sixteen were clothed in
cloth of gold (but eight of one uniform). Then one of those sixteen clothed in gold was dressed in
royal habit, and another in the dress of a Queen, with two keepers of the rock, or citadel; two silent
ones, or secretaries; and two knights. With an equal number, eight were clothed in cloth of silver, with
the same offices.

All these, according to their office, disposed themselves thus, placing themselves upon the squares of
the pavement: that is, sixteen clothed in gold on the one side, and sixteen in silver on the other,
opposite.

The musicians began to play with three instruments of daring invention, very concordant and sharing
together, with a most sweet consonance and tuned melody. At the measured time of the sound, upon their
squares, as the King commanded, the dancing and dolphin-like tumblers moved, and with the most seemly
turnings, honouring the King and the Queen, they climbed upon the next square, making an excellent
pause.

The King of the silver (the sound beginning again from the top) bade her that stood before the Queen
set herself over against her. She, going forward with those same reverent gestures, made her pause and
stood. In this ordered manner, according to the measuring of the musical time, thus they

changed place, or, staying always upon their square, danced while those driven forward, or taken,
departed — always at the King's bidding.

If the sound held one measure, those eight of one kind used that measure in passing to another square.
They could not go back, save deservedly for having climbed untouched upon the line of the squares where
the King had his seat; nor go straight forward, except by a diagonal line.

A secretary and a knight passed three squares in one measure: the secretary by a diagonal line, the
knight by two equal-sided straight ones and one turning off the line; and they could move to every
side. The keepers of the citadel could pass straight and freely over many squares. So that in one
measure they could run over three, four, or five squares, keeping the measure, and hastening their
step.

The King could climb upon whatever square was not blocked, or held by a garrison — indeed he may take
it; and that square is forbidden him where others may climb, and if the case be fitting he must yield,
with a warning going before. But the Queen upon every square of her own colour, where she first set her
seat. And it is well that she always follow her husband closely on every side.

Whenever the officers of the one or the other King found one of the other without keeping and garrison,
they made him prisoner, and both kissing one another, the vanquished went out.

In this manner they made a most famous game in a most elegant dance, dancing and merrily playing with
the measure of the sound, in such a way that the silver one remained the winner, with cheerfulness,
solace and applause. This solemn festival lasted, by its contests, flights and garrisons, for the space
of an hour, with such measured circlings, reverences and pauses, and modest stayings, that so great a
delight came over me that I not undeservedly thought myself carried up to the supreme delights of the
highest Olympus, and to a newest happiness.

The first game in dance being ended, all returned again to their appointed square. And in the same
manner as they had done at first, so the second time, having all alike returned in order to their
places, the players tightening the measure of the time, so the movements and gestures of the playing
dancers moved more busily — but keeping the measure with the sound, in so most apt a manner and with so
approved a gesturing and art that it was not fitting to say anything.

But the damsels were well skilled, with their plentiful tresses poured over their delicate shoulders,
hanging unsteadily and then leaping upon their backs according to the movement, bound at the head with
a little crown of fragrant violets. And when one was taken captive, they raised their arms and beat one
palm against the other. So that, playing and dancing thus, there remained
the winner a second time the first again.

In the third dance, all being ordered and set out in their places, the musicians tightened the measure
of the time still further, with the manner and tone of the stirring Phrygian — such a sounding as
Marsyas of Phrygia never knew how to find. The King clothed in gold made her that stood before the
Queen move upon the third square, going straight in her first passage.

For which cause there was at once seen a battle, a tournament, so delightful, with so ready and sudden
a vehemence; with bending down to the very ground, and then making a swift and twisting leap, and like
a turning tumbler, with two rollings in the air, the one opposite the other. And then without delay,
the right foot set to the ground, she turned round three times. And then at once with the other foot
she went round the contrary way; all this action they used up in one measure, so fittingly and with so
great an agility that nothing could go beyond it: with their deep bowings and ordered spinnings and
easy leaping, with comely gestures, as much as ever of such and like a thing was seen, nor ever could
be beheld, nor was ever attempted.

Nor was the one ever a hindrance to the other; but whoever was taken by the taker, the honeyed kiss
being given her in an instant, went out of the game; and the fewer that remained, the more one saw a
most charming skill in the deceiving of one by another. Such a worthy order and manner was kept by each
without defect, however briefly the measuring of the learned and excellent musicians hastened it — and
it stirred no less all those standing by to such movements, by the agreement of the consonant harmony
with the soul, being here chiefly and above all in the highest and concordant consent of the well-being
of their disposed bodies.

For this reason, of the power of Timotheus that most skilful musician, I warmly thought that he with
his song forced the army of the great Macedonian to take up arms again, and then, turning back the
voice and the tone, to leave their arms neglected and provoke them all to ceasing. Of this third game
she that was clothed in gold in royal form gloriously triumphed.

This most joyful festival being famously ended with an extreme gladness and the greatest solace, all
set themselves to sit. And here, being made to rise, and before the venerable seat of her divine
majesty I made a deep reverence, and seemly kneeling, she spoke to me thus: "Poliphilo, put now into
forgetfulness the past and befallen cases, and thence the wearisome thoughts, and the danger gone by,
for I am certain that at present you are fully restored. Since, then, you wish to go on undaunted in
the amorous flames of Polia, I judge it a fitting thing that for this recovery you should go to the
three doors, where the high Queen Telosia dwells; in which place

you will see, above each of those doors, its title and index noted and inscribed. Read it carefully;
but for the convenience of your guiding and defence I shall give you two of my witty and mistress-like
attendants, who, being practised in it, will lead you there most safely and will keep close by you. Go
therefore with glad heart, and with a happy outcome."

And at once, with royal largeness, drawing a golden ring from her ring-finger, with a stone anchitis:
"Take this," she said, "and you shall carry it gladly with you in memory of my friendly munificence."

At this exhortation and precious gift, being become as it were speechless, I certainly knew nothing
equivalent to say, nor how to give thanks. But she, kindly perceiving it, in a matronly way, and with a
native excellence and majestic gravity, turned to two distinguished and notable maidens, sitting near
her imperial throne; and to the one who sat commanding at the right side she said:

"Logistica, you shall be one of the two who go with our guest Poliphilo." And with a holy, religious
and venerable act she turned then to the left side, saying: "Thelemia, and you likewise shall go
together with him, and both give him to understand and to know clearly at which door he ought to stay.
Then, Poliphilo, they will present you to another Queen, very splendid and venerable. Who, if she shows
herself kind and bountiful to you, you shall be blessed; if the contrary, you shall be discontented.
Nevertheless in her face no one can grasp it, because sometimes she shows herself with a noble and
native courtesy and with a most charming pleasantness, and at other times of herself gloomy, malignant
and to be scorned, with an unsteady onset. She it is who ends everything. And for such a dark condition
she is not undeservedly named Queen Telosia; who dwells not in so proud and opulent a mansion as you
now plainly see me inhabit.

"I would have you know, however, that the highest Maker, nor ordered nature, could not give you a
greater treasure than to come to this my divine presence and wide munificence; wherefore artful nature
could not heap up greater riches than to obtain, and to win, my kindly favour, and to be a sharer in so
great a good. Whence, as you may exquisitely judge, no such treasure could ever be found in the world
in comparison with that which truly is found in me, a heavenly gift obtained by mortals.

"But Queen Telosia stays in a clouded place of hiding, and her dwelling has its approaches shut, since
she consents by no leave that men should discern how great and of what kind her beauty is; for it is
not lawful, nor permitted, that a divine beauty should appear to bodily eyes; and for such a reason the
effect of her outcome stands blind. But with a wonderful observance she transforms herself, changing
her skin and of many forms, unwilling to reveal herself unasked.

"And when the most ancient doors are opened to you, in each of them she will present herself before
your eyes as one to come; and yet you will not know her, unless moderating prudence somewhat sees her
in a riddle, and with an upright and sincere judgement, and rather considers her — because in habit and
in aspect she changes herself ambiguously. And by this two-headed watching, man is very often deceived
without remedy of what he expected.

"That, then, Poliphilo, which these two girls of mine, entrusted and committed to you, shall counsel
you by their suggesting — and at which door you ought to enter and to stay, and which of them shall
most please you — you may hear and listen to, and freely assent to it, by my most excellent and
gratuitous gift and the leave I grant, because these have some knowledge of that." And this said, she
made a sign to the two, Logistica and Thelemia, who without waiting made themselves humbly her
servants. And I then, in the act of speaking — not daring, nor knowing how, before so lofty a presence
— gave her thanks for her great munificence.

The two appointed companions took me festively with a homely readiness and maidenly gestures, the one
by the right hand and the other by the left; and leave being reverently obtained first chiefly from the
Queen, and then from all. Going out by the same curtains and door, still eager and unsatisfied, I
turned back to the notable door to gaze wholly at the artful palace, admirable in the builder's art and
finished, the subtlety of which work no valid devising of mortals could imitate. For I fittingly
thought that sagacious nature herself had here singularly feigned, for admiration, so many delights of
her imperceptible workmanship — most apt for convenience, for use, and for grace and glory, and firm
and constant for perpetuity, and lasting.

For which cause I should exceedingly gladly have stayed a little while; but a follower of the appointed
guides and my companions, I could not; true it is that in a swiftest stealing of a glance, in the
border, or frieze, of that door, I saw noted this inscription: HO TES PHYSEOS OLBOS. And as much as I
could draw with my readiest senses, so much most gratefully I received, taking in that passage an
extreme delight, as much as is incredible to say. O happy, then, whoever should be granted to be always
in such a place a citizen, or a dweller.

Having come into the enclosed area of the orange hedge, Thelemia says to me with a singular affability:
"Beyond the most excellent and marvellous things that you have beheld, Poliphilo, four more wonderful
things remain for you to see." And on the left side of the incomparable palace they led me into a most
notable garden of the greatest devising, of cost, of

time, and of the subtlest artifice. Which in its circuit and compass was as great as that where the
majestic residence stood; round about, cleaving to the walls, there stretched fitted garden-boxes, in
which, in place of greenery, every plant was of the purest glass — box-trees clipped (beyond what one
can imagine and believe) distinguishedly, with their stems of gold, such material being brought
thither. Between the one and the other of which there alternated a cypress, its height not exceeding
two paces, and of the box one. Filled then with a marvellous feigning of many-shaped simples, with a
most elegant following of nature, and with the most joyful and varied forms of flowers, with a distinct
and most welcome colouring.

The flat lip of the square opening of these little boxes, or raised beds, was corniced with gold, with
the subtlest lineaments, well polished and adorned; the faces of which, of glass plates gilded within,
and with a wonderful graving of a most curious history, stood out most beautifully, enclosed within
golden channels which held them bitingly, with the lowest socle raised a sixth of a foot.

The hedge going round the garden, at a nice distance, was with bellied columns of the said material,
clothed with flower-bearing bindweed, all in relief; and here and there there stood fluted squares of
gold, and from one to the other it arched, with the required beam, and frieze, and cornice, with a due
projection above the glass capital of the round column. The solid part of which beneath the arches was
feigned jasper with a manifold colouring, meeting and bright. Which arches were somewhat raised and
drawn up from the solid in proportion; the throats of the arches were stopped with rhombs of the purest
glass, a third of a foot their diameter, between twinned little channels likewise enclosed and hedged
about with a various encaustic painting most acceptable to the senses.

The whole area besides was strewn with little glass roundings and other most fitting figurings, to the
utmost grace, with a mutual consent and a steady cohesion, with a chief gemlike shining, without any
adulterating of foliage set beneath. Above the flowers there breathed a chief fragrance from an
anointing, they being smeared and made rosy.

Most skilfully here the sweet-spoken Logistica made some little narration, and, discoursing of nature,
praised the excellent making, and the nobility of the material and the art and the invention (such as
would not be found at Murano), and blaming its nature, she said: "Poliphilo, let us climb this most
excellent watch-tower, near the garden." And Thelemia remaining below, by a winding stair we climbed
cheerfully to the levelled upper part. Where she showed me, with a divine eloquence, a garden of a very
wide circuit, drawn out in the form of a various intricate labyrinth, and its circling passages not to
be walked,

but to be sailed. For in place of walkable roads there ran little streams of water. Which mysterious
place was of itself a wholesome and pleasant field, of happy soil and fruitful, various and filled with
every plenty of sweet fruits, and adorned with an overflowing of springs, and joyful with every
flowering greenness, poured out with every solace and with the greatest delight. And she said:

"I think, Poliphilo, that of this wondrous site you do not understand its appointed lot. Attend. He who
enters cannot go back. But, as you plainly see, those watch-towers set here and there stand seven
circuits apart one from another; and the extreme harm that falls to those who enter is this: that in
that central tower, in the open gap of its entry, a deadly dragon dwells, most devouring and invisible.
And this is most harmful on the one hand, and on the other quiet: not to be able to see it, and utterly
terrible not to be able to shun it. Which, both at the entry and in the going forward, wherever it
chances and is appointed to wish, devours those who have entered. And if between one tower and another
it does not kill them, they pass safely through the whole sevenfold circuit as far as the next tower.

"Those, then, who enter here by that first tower (look at the title written in Greek noting, and think
most carefully upon it: DOXA KOSMIKE HOS POMPHOLYX) go with the little boat with the current, and
without any care or labour the fruits and flowers fall into the skiff, and with the utmost pleasure and
sport they run through the seven windings as far as the second tower. And consider, Poliphilo, how
great the brightness of the air is in this beginning, growing to the middle tower, and thence little by
little, about the centre, darkening and growing gloomy and lightless.

"In that first tower there dwells eternally, presiding, a most pious matron and kindly giver, before
whom there stands most steadily a most ancient urn of lots and of dispensing, adorned with seven Greek
letters as you see thus: THESPION, packed with fated tokens; and to each of those who enter, most
charmingly and munificently she gives one of those, without respect of condition, but according as the
chance disposition falls out. These, being received, coming forth they begin to sail in the labyrinth,
the passages hedged with roses and fruit-bearing trees.

"The first long circuit of the seven windings being passed, from the Ram to the last fishy tail, coming
to the second tower, they find countless girls of divers condition, who ask of all the showing of their
tokens; and it being shown to them, they, most skilled, know the proper and disposed token, and
embracing him they receive him as a guest, and invite him with them to wander through the other seven
circuits; and according to his bent readiness, and with divers exercise, inseparably they lead them as
far as the third tower. In this place whoever will persevere with his companion, she never abandons nor
leaves him. Because there they find other more voluptuous damsels, and many cast off the

"first and cleave to these. So that, departing from that second tower to come to the third, they find
the waters somewhat contrary, and it takes the service of rowing. Having come and arrived at the third,
and thence making their departure towards the fourth, they find the water resisting more — however much
in these seven slanting courses a great and variable and inconstant delight is seen.

"Come to the fourth tower, they find other young women, wrestlers and fighters, and these, having
examined the first tokens, draw those friendly to their exercise. And those who have not their like
they let pass on with their own. And in these circuits they find the water still more against them,
where there is need of greater study and toilsome labour of rowing.

"Landing at the fifth tower, they find it mirroring, in which they contemplate how fair is their like;
and with this most joyful and most longed-for delight, keeping it in mind, they pass on with a more
laborious course. In this place is plainly discussed that saying, and golden: *the blessed have held to
the middle*. Not of line, not of place, but of time is this passage and bound, where with a sincere
examination the middle is discerned, and with whom happiness is coupled, or the blessedness of wit, or
of plenty. Which, not having with them, in what follows they are the less able to gain it.

"Taking leave from here, the waters through the circling windings begin to draw somewhat their swift
course towards the middle end, and with little rowing, or none, they are carried to the sixth. Here
they find elegant matrons, with unwedded and chaste looks, intent upon the divine worship; by the
divine aspect of whom the guests, taken with love of them, condemning the former and turning to a
loathing of it, hold with these a quiet commerce and a peaceful passage through the seven windings.

"These being passed, through those that follow, with a darkening of the air, with many discomforts and
a toilsome voyage, they weigh the crossing by much running. Because the more the winding of the
passages draws near in the figure to the centre, the shorter they are. And so much the more one runs,
fallen, with an ineffectual swiftness, and with slippery wanderings, into the whirlpool of the central
tower; and with the utmost affliction of soul for the remembrance of the fair places and the fellowship
left behind, and the more that they know they cannot return by turning the prow of their keel, because
continually at their stern are the prows of the others sailing. There comes to a greater pain the
frightful title above the entrance of the middle tower, in this Attic expression: THEON LYKOS
DYSALGETOS.

"And here, considering the displeasing title, they grieve at having entered such a labyrinthine
orchard, seeing that it holds in itself so many delights and yet lies under so wretched and unavoidable
a necessity." Then Logistica, smiling, inspired, added: "Poliphilo, in this devouring gap there sits a
severe beholder holding the scales, and a judge of those who enter, who with an even balance weighs and
scrupulously ponders their action. By which they might fare better, or worse,

"elsewhere. And because it would be long to tell all, let what is told be enough for now. Let us go
down to our companion Thelemia." Who, asking of our delay, Logistica answered her that it was not
enough only for our curious Poliphilo to see, but that I should also give him a knowledge of that
which, since the matter could not go further, he might at least understand and know by my
interpretation. And this said, Thelemia says:

"Let us go for a walk to the other garden, no less delightful and filled with delights: the glass one
adjoining the right wall of the proud, great and royal palace." And having entered there, I remained
wholly dazzled and exceedingly full of wonder to see a workmanship hard not so much of belief as of
telling. Which was of equal compass with the glass one, with a like disposition of raised beds, with
adorned lips of cornice-work and a golden socle, save for the workmanship and material of the enclosing
walls — for it was all made most excellently of silk: the box-trees and cypresses of silk, their stems
and branches of gold, not without a most apt sowing among them of gems; and the standing beds most
thickly filled with the simples that the mother of them envies, with a most joyful and most longed-for
flowering, with every exquisite colouring, fragrant, and like the other glass ones.

But the surrounding walls, of a wondrous workmanship and of incredible cost, were all of a covering of
pearl — that is, I saw all the faces covered with the brightest pearls, heaped and gathered into one,
and with a thick cohesion, joined together of a middling thickness; and above them most beautifully,
sprouting out of the boxes, a straggling and greenest ivy with its foliage somewhat raised from the
pearls and hanging, with its stems of gold most artfully creeping, with slender little roots wandering
among the pearls, with the utmost and most exquisite polish. And berries of jewels, knit to the
clusters, with an excellent division, headed by the golden squares, with a masterly and required
following of beam, frieze, and cornice of gold.

The faces of the beds rewoven in tapestry stitch with little histories of love and of hunting, in
threads of gold and silver and silk, feigned with so most fitting a painting that nothing could equal
it. The ground of the most level area was seen most welcome, of green silk pile, like a most notable
meadow; and in the middle of the area there stood a round enclosure, with a raised dome of little rods
of gold, distinguishedly covered with manifold flower-bearing rose-trees of the said workmanship.

So that I should almost say this making far more acceptable to the senses than the true one. Beneath
which roof, in the going-round form, were seats of ruddy jasper; and all the space between of a solid
rounding, as far as the ample circuit went, of yellow jasper, of various mixtures confusedly agreeing
and most charmingly adulterated in one. With
so great a shining that they rivalled every object set before them.

Sitting solaced here beneath it a while, the most witty Thelemia took the lyre that she carried with
her, and with a heavenly melody and unheard-of sweetness of sweet speech began to sing the origin of so
many delights and the rule of her Queen, and with what adornment her companion Logistica's sweet
fellowship was — I marvelling that Apollo did not come there to listen, so excessive was the harmony
she uttered. So that nothing else at present, however longed for, would I have valued at all.

The divine poem being said, at once the god-loving Logistica, taking me by the hand, led me forth from
that place, saying: "Poliphilo, I would have you know that things of the understanding are of a greater
delight to the intellect than things of sense are to the senses. For this, let us enter here, to
satisfy both the receiving faculties."

Who, with a most distinguished company, led me in near this garden to another, where I beheld an arched
colonnade of widely spaced arches, from the floor to the topmost bend five paces high and three in the
opening, all of brick, with a symmetried slope, or spread, in a continuous ring, all most beautifully
clothed and covered with green ivy, no least trace of the wall appearing; and there were a hundred
arches, and they closed in a flowering orchard.

Beneath each one of the arches, then, was set an altar of ruddy porphyry, excellently lined. And upon
each there sat a golden statue of a Nymph with a divine likeness, with varying dress, and the ornament
of the head, and of gesture, each of them reverent towards the middle centre of this garden.

In this middle centre there was mysteriously founded a base of translucent chalcedony in a cubic form.
And above this, within the square compass, there was placed a rounding two feet high, and of a diameter
of a pace and a half, of the ruddiest jasper. Above this then sat a triangle, by the measure of the
figure beneath, of a height of a pace and a half, of the blackest stone. The corners of which triangle
stretched to the edge of the plinth below it.

On the well-polished and free front of each there was fitted a most notable image, in aspect divine,
grave and venerable, with their feet upon the untouched part of the triangular figure of the rounding
pressed beneath, of a tall stature, as tall as the blackest stone, to which they clung with their
backs, with their arms stretched to the left and to the right towards the corners; they held a
horn of plenty packed full, fixed at the blunted, or cut-off, corners, the shortening of their fingers
made even, a foot and a sixth, of purest gold. The horns, thongs and statues shone forth, with their
hands wrapped in the wandering and straggling thongs. Flying along the flat of the stone. And in
nymphlike dress, a workmanship not human but divine. And therefore
let the tomb of Tarina, queen of the Sacae, yield here.

In the lowest figure, on each square side, in the flat face, were carved Greek letters — three, one,
two, and three, in this order: DYS A LO TOS. In the round one I beheld three hieroglyphic characters,
perpendicular, beneath the feet of each image. And first was stamped the form of the Sun. Then, beneath
the next, an antique rudder. Last there appeared a dish, with a flame within it.

Above the outstretched corners of the dark stone, looking, I saw an Egyptian monster of gold, lying
four-footed. One of which had a wholly human face. The other half human and half beast. The third
wholly beastly. With a fillet going round the brow, with two ribbons covering the ears, hanging down,
and likewise licking along the neck and breast. And one descending down the back; with the body of a
lioness, the face turned forward.

Upon the back of each, then, there pressed a massive golden triangular pyramid, up to its topmost cover
five lines of the lowest face, or of its diameter. On each front there was carved a circle of that
measure, and above the circle a Greek letter, OMICRON. On the next face a circle, and above it a
letter, OMEGA. On the third flat a circle, and above it a letter, NY.

Here Logistica, well taught, began to proclaim and to say: "By these figures the celestial harmony
stands. And take heed, Poliphilo, that these figures, with a perpetual affinity and conjunction, are
most distinguished antique monuments and Egyptian hieroglyphs, which, wishing to hint at it, say to
you: *To the divine and infinite Trinity of one essence.* The lowest figure is consecrated to the
divinity, because from unity it is

"brought forth, and on every side it is one, and of every figure it is the first steadying, and in
every base constant and abiding. The round one set above it is free of beginning and of ending. In the
encompassed flat of which those three lineaments are held, set directly before the face of each image,
attributed according to its property.

"The Sun, with a most joyful light, can do all things, and its nature is attributed to God. The second
is the rudder, which expresses the provident government of the universe, with infinite wisdom. The
third is the fiery vessel, and I feel of it a sharing of love. And though the three images are
distinct, yet they are one thing folded together, and singularly embraced, and everlastingly knit in
one, kindly communicating its good — as one may see by the horns of plenty at the elbows of the
figure."

And continuing her fate-telling, Logistica said further: "At the image of the Sun, mark this Greek
word: ADIEGETOS. At that of the rudder, look at that Greek noting: ADIACHORISTOS. At that of the fire
was carved: ADIEREUNETOS. By such effects, then, those three animals are set below, subject to the
golden obelisk lying above them, which are three great and famous opinions of such figures. And as the
human likeness effectually surpasses the others, so, neither more nor less, does the opinion.

"On the pyramid are three flat sides lined with three circles, each one signifying a time: past,
present, and to come. Understand that no other figure could hold those three circles unchanging save
that one. And none of mortals could perfectly discern nor see two sides of the said figure together,
save one wholly, which is the present. And therefore most wisely were those three characters stamped:
OON.

"For which cause, Poliphilo — not accusing me of being long-winded, but most ready to set you right in
such a telling — know that the first base figure is known only to itself, and to one so far as human
and translucent; but to us not in full clearness. Then he who is gifted with wit climbs above and
skilfully considers the colouring of the figure. Searching further, they climb to the third figure,
which by its colouring is dark and shut up in those three images of gold, and walled about.

"Last, climbing higher still, they consider a figure in a threefold aspect; and thence, the more they
climb contemplating towards the sharpest narrowing, and there, however well instructed, they have
nevertheless gained nothing else than that one sees *that it is*; but what it may be, they remain
ignorant, unavailing, and feeble."

Logistica having here excellently set out the most approved precepts with a most complete knowledge,
with a sagacious skill, plucked from the most abundant lap of divine nature, I began

without hesitation to feel a greater delight than in any other marvellous work graciously beheld with
my eyes — thinking upon the obelisk of so great a mystery, standing with an unspeakable evenness, and
whole in its firmness and perpetuity, solid and eternal, with an equality of likeness not to be
crumbled, and enduring incorruptible.

Where there breathed a most welcome breath of heaven, with unchanging airs, in this meadow flowering
round about, founded and abiding in a wide and circling space, with bending shrubs of every fruit,
sweet to the taste, and packed with every health, with a perpetual greenness, with the ordering of a
ruled arrangement for comeliness and charm and adornment, disposed and planted, brought wonderfully to
perfection by the chief study of nature, and unceasingly lit by the most precious gold.

Logistica being silent, then, both of them holding me by the hands, we went out festively through the
gap, or opening, of one of the arches, outside the girdle of the ivied enclosure; and going on from
there through the middle of that compass, Thelemia saying most joyfully: "Let us go now to the
appointed doors." So that, going forward through the pleasant region and country with a ready and
prepared advance, I beheld the sky purged of every darkening cloud, with sweet, witty and particular
discoursings.

I, being unsatisfied in understanding the whole of the inestimable riches, unconsiderable delights, and
unmatchable treasure (to which let Osiris yield, the builder of the two temples of gold, one to
heavenly Jove and the other to the royal) of the most sacred Queen, put to them this little question:

"Tell me, blessed young women, if my curious asking be welcome to you now. Among all the precious
little stones that I have been able to see clearly, I judged one of great worth and price — nay,
incomparable and most precious beyond esteeming. Much and far more was it than the jasper that had
stamped upon it the likeness of Nero in his breastplate. Nor such either was the flashing topaz of the
statue of Arsinoe, the Arabian queen. Nor was so great a cost laid out for the gem for which Nonius the
senator was proscribed, as for that shining and incomparable diamond, of so unseen a beauty and
thickness, that hung from the richest necklace above the snowy breast of our divine Queen. What carving
was that? For so great was its flashing, and being besides at a distance, I could not perfectly discern
it. So that this only remains, which holds me anxious and my mind in suspense to know."

Logistica, taking note of my honest question, answered at once, saying: "Know, Poliphilo, that in the
gem is carved the image of the highest Jove sitting crowned upon his throne. And beneath his majestic
and holy footstool are the ruined giants, who wished to climb up to his most high seat, level with the
height of his most ample sceptre. And he struck them with lightning. In his left hand he holds a

"little flame of fire. In the right a horn of plenty stuffed full of good, and he stands with his arms
spread. This is the whole of what is held in the most precious jewel."

Then I said: "What do those two very unsuited things mean that he holds in his divine hands?" Thelemia,
witty, answered: "By his infinite goodness the immortal Jupiter makes a show to earth-born men that
they may have at their wish that of the two hands which pleases them, freely to choose."

And without delay I added: "Since our pleasant talking has fallen here, most welcome companions — my
kindled desire to understand not being yet wholly fulfilled, and since my boldness did not displease
you — tell me this, I pray you. Before my horrible fright I saw, of a daring greatness and art, a stone
monster, which is an elephant. Entering, then, into its empty belly, I found two tombs, with writings
of an ambiguous meaning, about finding treasure: that I should scorn the body and carry away the head."

Logistica, without any other thinking, expounding it, answered cheerfully: "Poliphilo, I know fully
what you ask; I would however have you know that not without a great admiration of human wit, and with
an ardent study and incredible diligence, was that huge engine made, with a perplexity of the intellect
to understand its divine conceit. Take heed that above its front there hangs the ornament with that
double-headed writing, which in the mother and common tongue says: *labour and industry*. For in the
world, whoever living would have treasure, let him leave rotting idleness, signified by the great body,
and take the adorned head, which is that writing — and you shall have treasure by toiling with
industry."

No sooner were her soothing and effectual words ended than, being perfectly taught the whole, I gave
thanks for her affable kindness; yet, being still most eager to search out all that I had before
imperfectly grasped, and having made myself familiar with them, I made a third request: "Most wise
Nymph, in my coming out of the underground caverns I found an antique and elegant bridge. Which, on
both its parapets, in porphyry stone on the one side, and on the other of ophite, I saw certain
hieroglyphs carved. And of both I was the interpreter; but I remained ignorant only of the branches,
not knowing them, which were bound to the horns, and then why in porphyry stone, and not in the like of
the other side."
At once, without other pondering, she kindly answered me: "Of the branches, the one is

t:
"of fir, and the other of larch; the nature of which woods is such that the one does not easily hold
commerce with fire, and the other, laid under a weight when squared into a beam, does not bend. That
patience, then, is commended which is not easily kindled into anger, nor bends in adversity.

"The porphyry stone stands with a notable mystery for such an expression. For it is affirmed to be of
such a nature that not only does it not burn in the furnace, but it also makes the other stones
standing near it unburnable. Such does true patience show itself: that not only is it not kindled, but
it renders those that are kindled quenched. The stone of ophite has its property well known, fitting to
that saying.

"So that, Poliphilo, I commend you in this part, because you are eager for such inquiry; for to weigh
everything, and consider, and measure it, shows itself praiseworthy." Here I highly praised the wisdom
of the most eloquent lady, saying countless thanks.

And thus, with honest and most approved discourse, we came most festively to a most charming river.
Upon the banks of which I saw a gracious plane-grove, besides other greenest little trees, and water
shoots excellently set and placed, with lotuses set between. Where there crossed a proud stone bridge of
three arches, with its ends upon the banks above the firmest foundations, with the piers keeled at
their two fronts to hold the structure most firm, and with most noble parapets.

In which, at the middle curve of the wedge beneath the arch, here and there, there stood out, raised
and well polished, a porphyry square with a gable, holding a sunk carving of hieroglyphs. On the right
at our crossing I saw a matron bound with a serpent, sitting upon one haunch only, and with the other
leg in the act of rising; with the hand on the side she sat on she held a pair of wings, and in the
other, on the rising side, a tortoise. Opposite there was a circle, the centre of which two little
spirits held, turning their backs with their little breasts to the circumference.

Logistica said to me here too: "Poliphilo, these hieroglyphs I know you do not understand. But they are
much to the purpose for one who goes to the three doors. And therefore they are most fitly set here as
a monument for those passing by. The circle says: *the blessed have held to the middle*. The other:
*temper swiftness by sitting, and slowness by rising*. Now turn it over discussingly in your mind."

Which bridge was then of a moderate slope, showing the skilful inquiry, and the art and wit of its most
clear-sighted maker and inventor; and I praised in it the eternal solidity, which is not known to the
purblind moderns and false architects, without letters, measure or art, who paint it over, and covering
it with pictures and lineaments the building stands in every way ill-joined and misshapen. Which was
all of most comely Hymettian marble.

Having passed the bridge, we walked beneath through the cool shades, sweetly kept by the various
chattering of small birds. We came to a stony and rocky place, where lofty and steep mountains rose up.
And thence next to a broken and pathless and rugged mountain, all gnawed away and full of a bursting
roughness. High into the air, worn down to a spur, and bare of all greenness, and dry mountains round
about. And there were carved the three rough doors, rudely hollowed in the living rock, an antique
work, and beyond belief most ancient, in a great harshness of site.

Above each of which, in Ionic, Roman, Hebrew and Arabic characters, I saw the title that the divine
Queen Eleuterylida had foretold and prophesied to me that I should find.

After we had come there, the damsel companions immediately began to interpret clearly and to make plain
the titles to be noted; and knocking at the resounding right-hand valves, closed, of metal, stained
with a greenish rust, without delay they were opened.
pages.wcap: Figures at a Portal or Doorway

t:
And behold, there presented herself to us a woman far on in years, of an unwedded aspect, who came out
of a wattled little cottage with a smoky roof and smoked walls, by its small door (which had noted
above it PYLURANIA), coming with a modest matronliness; her little chapel set in a solitary place, and
in a shady cliff, crumbling with bare and friable stone; torn, squalid, lean, poor, with her eyes fixed
upon the ground; Theude her name.

And with her she had six companions and inseparable serving maids, meanly enough clothed and heavy. Of
whom one was named Parthenia. The second Edosia, and one Hypocolinia. The fourth Pinotidia. And next
was Tapinosa, and the last Ptochina. Which venerable matron, with her right arm bare, pointed to high
Olympus.

She dwelt at the entrance of a stony road, difficult to go along, hindered with thorns and briars. The
place appearing rough and displeasing, with the sky rainy and troubled, and darkened with a cloudy
gloom, and a most narrow path.

So that Logistica, taking note that at the first sight I shrank from such a thing, said to me, almost
sadly: "Poliphilo, this path is not known until the end." And thus of this venerable and holy woman
Thelemia, sharp-witted, quickly said to me: "O Poliphilo, the love of such a laborious woman is not for
you now." I, nodding shrewdly to Thelemia, we came forth from there. And the door being closed again,
they knocked at the left-hand one.

Behold, without any waiting it was opened, and we let in; and there came to us a matron with a golden
sword, with fierce eyes and ready in her look, brandishing her raised and shining blade in her hand. In
the middle of which there hung suspended a little crown of gold and a branch of palm laid across it;
with arms of Hercules and made for labour, with a magnanimous bearing, with a slender belly, small
mouth, strong shoulders; in her face with a showing of not being frightened by any hard and difficult
undertaking, but of a fierce and giant-like spirit. And her name was Eucleia, and she was venerably
attended by six noble young women, obedient. The name of the first Merimnasia; of the second, Epitide;
of the next, Ergasilea. The fourth was called Anectea. And the fifth was named Statia. The last was
called Olistea.

The place and site seemed to me to be very laborious. Perceiving this, Logistica readily began to sing
in the Dorian mode and tone, having taken the lyre from Thelemia's hand, and playing sweetly, to say:
"O Poliphilo, let it not weary you to strive manfully in this place. For, the labour being lifted away
and removed, the good remains." So vehement was her song that I was already consenting to dwell with
these young women, however much the habit of labour appeared there — when suddenly Thelemia, trim and
coaxing, and with a sweet semblance, said to me: "It seems to me a reasonable thing that before you
settle here, my dearest little Poliphilo, you should by all means see the third door as well."

I consenting, we went out from this one too; and the brazen valves being bolted, Thelemia struck at the
third and middle door, and the bar being removed, without delay it was opened. And being let in, there
came to meet us a notable lady, whose name was Philtronia. With wanton and unsteady glances, her most
joyful look at the first sight forced me to love her and drew me to it.

A dweller in a voluptuous place, its ground green with soft grass and clothed with flowers, abounding
in solace and pleasant idleness, flowing with springs of the clearest fountains and little streams,
running with a sounding gush, watered to the greatest pleasure; sunny fields, and the shades of the
leafy trees cool and fresh.

She likewise had with her six mistress-like and most shapely girls of her own age, and most charming in
their look, with a most welcome elegance and amorous ornaments, trapped out, seemly with an ambitious
beauty; of whom the name of the first was Rastonelia, the next was named Chortasina, the third Idonesa,
and the fourth was called Tryphelea. And the fifth was called Etiania; the last Adia.

Such and so made presences showed themselves exceedingly welcome and delightful to my intent eyes. For
this the sincere Logistica, seeing me readily disposing myself and already abruptly bent to the love of
her, and addicted in a servile manner, said with a sorrowful voice:

"O Poliphilo, the painted and feigned beauty of this woman is lying, insipid and savourless; for if you
would look discussingly upon her back you would grasp, with loathing, how much unseemliness lies
beneath, and how despicable and stomach-turning and abominable they are with their foulness, standing
high upon a great heap of filth. For that which flees is fleeting and vanishing, and the pleasure
passes, and shame with repentance, with vain hopes, with the briefest cheerfulness, with perpetual
weeping and anxious sighs, the toilsome life remains behind.

"O sweetness adulterated with misery, holding in itself so much bitterness, like the honey in Colchis
dripping from the leaves. O death most dreadful and foul, how you are clothed in a sweet poison; with
how many hazards and mortal perils and cares are you sought by blind lovers, unadvisedly and headlong.
