Present and before their eyes you stand, and the wretches do not see you. O of how many sorrows and
bitter pain and torment you are the bearer. O depraved, impious and execrable appetite; O detestable
madness; O senses defrauded — by you thus slipperily, with that same beastly pleasure, wretched mortals
are ruined. O sordid love. O most absurd frenzy. O disordered and empty desire, nesting and wounding in
the hearts you have touched with so many errors and torments. O wicked and deadly destruction of
manifold good. O huge monster, how easily and slyly you veil and cloud the eyes of your unhappy lovers?
O sad and ill-starred are they who make themselves birdlime with so many evils, in
so little, and poisonous, a pleasure, and pressed into a feigned good."

These and like words Logistica said, stirred with vehemence and with indignant wrinkles rising on her
brow; and, throwing the lyre to the ground, she broke it. Whereupon Thelemia, quick and undaunted by
such urging, laughingly made me a sign that I should not attend to Logistica. For which cause
Logistica, knowing my wicked leaning, kindled with disdain, turned her back and, sighing, hurrying and
running, went out.

And I remained with my conquering and dear Thelemia, who, coaxing and cheerful, said to me: "This is
that place, Poliphilo, where before long you will find without fail the thing most loved by you, which
is yours, which is the thing of the world of which your obstinate heart thinks and longs without
ceasing." So that, scrupulously running it over within myself, I found only that nothing else was
stamped upon my wretched heart, thinkable and most desired, save my sun-born Polia. By these
comfortable and most welcome and divine little words
I was gladdened and took an extreme comfort.

Thelemia, then, perceiving that such a matron with her company, and the place and its condition, were
to my pleasure and content, and her own kindness, kissing me like a dove and embracing me closely,
asked leave of me and departed.

And the metal valves being closed again, I remained shut in at once among those distinguished Nymphs,
who began most charmingly and wantonly to sport about me; and, hedged in by the voluptuous crowd of
them, to provoke me to enticing longings, alluring and persuasive.

Whence I felt a beginning of itching, their wanton looks fostering an increase of an amorous and
wounding fire. So that Phryne would perhaps have warmed the cold and superstitious Xenocrates with so
great an onset of love, and moved him and made him fall into luxury, nor would he have been called a
statue by her, if she had been one of these. With wanton faces, and forward breasts, coaxing eyes
sparkling and playful in their rosy brows.
pages.wcap: Garden Scene with Pergola and Nymph

t:
Most excellent forms, kindling dress, girlish movements, biting glances, a cleanest adornment. No part
feigned, but all perfected by nature, with an exquisite polish; nothing misshapen, but all a most
fitting harmony. Fair heads with the blondest tresses and sunlike hair, so many and so beautifully
folded together with little cords, or braids, of silk and twisted threads of gold, that they wholly
surpassed human work, wrapped about the head with a distinguished ordering and held with hair-pins; and
the forehead wooded with curling ringlets, hanging over with a wanton unsteadiness. And with elegant
garments of manifold invention for pleasure, all fragrant, musky, breathing an unknown scent.

Their speech of itself able to steal away and force any reluctance and hardness of whatever wild and
ill-disposed heart, and to corrupt all sanctity, to bind everything loose, and to fit every awkward
rusticity, and to crumble every flinty hardness. By which things my soul, being wholly inflamed with a
new longing, and already proscribed in the utmost burning of concupiscence, and every headlong and
slippery appetite of mine stirred to love and plunged in desire, suddenly I saw myself invaded and
infected with a fiery contagion, and made hot with such a kindling; and it growing within me, the
lovely damsels, without my noticing, left me alone, so kindled, in a most pleasant plain.

*An elegant Nymph comes to meet him in this place, where he was left alone and deserted by the wanton
girls. Poliphilo lovingly describes her beauty and her dress.*

My tender heart being excessively struck with amorous prickings, I do not know whether I raved, that I
stayed thus astonished at the manner in which so suddenly the most welcome company vanished and
disappeared from my eyes. So that, almost out of myself and as if carried off, raising my eyes a
little, behold, before me I see only an artful arbour of flowering jasmine, with a tall arching, painted
all over with its fragrant little flowers of the three colours mingled. Entering beneath this, heavily
anxious at the unlooked-for loss, and thinking again upon the various and great and stupendous things
gone by, and above all the high hope that I firmly held, according to the royal and fated promises, of
finding again my golden-haired Polia — alas, Polia,

I said, breathing; so that beneath that greenness there sounded the amorous sighs formed within my
kindled and treasuring heart.

And no sooner was I stirred in this agony and thus absorbed than, without noticing, I came to the end
of that flowery covering; and looking, there appeared to me a countless crowd of youth of both kinds
keeping high festival, with sounding voices and with the melodies of various instruments, with comely
and playful dancings and clappings, and with much and most joyful gladness, solacing themselves in
troops upon a most ample plain. So that, seized by this such and welcome novelty, sitting down full of
wonder, I stood in thought about going any further.

And behold, a Nymph, as it were notable and festive, parting from those with her burning torch in her
hand, was directing her maidenly steps towards me; whence, plainly seeing that she was a true and real
girl, I did not move, but gladly awaited her. And here, with girlish readiness and a modest approach,
and with a starry face, coming straight towards me and now drawing near, she came smiling, with such a
presence and comely

elegance as perhaps the amorous lady of Idalium did not show to warlike Mars, nor to her the shapely
shepherd Adonis, nor the delicate Ganymede to the highest and inflamed Jove, nor the most beautiful
Psyche to burning Cupid.

For which cause, if I had seen this one as a fourth among the three quarrelling goddesses, and had been
appointed judge by Jove above, as the Phrygian shepherd was in the shadowing woods of Mesaulon, without
doubt I should justly have judged her far more of an admirable form, and without equal more worthy of
the inscribed apple, and without any respect to the others. Whom at the first sight I suspected to be
certainly Polia; but the condition of the unaccustomed dress and place dissuaded me. And by this
lawful discerning, staying doubtful, I kept myself in a reverent suspense.

This sun-born Nymph, then, clothed her maidenly and divine little body in a most fine cloth of green
silk woven with a warp of gold (that most joyful colouring of the little feathers of a duck's neck)
mingled, over a white and crimped shift of cotton, covering her cleanest and most delicate flesh and
milky skin, such as the inventress Pamphila, daughter of Plates, first knew how to weave in the island
of Cos. Which shift graciously seemed to cover whitest and flesh-coloured roses.

But the gown above this, elegantly worn with the smallest little folds, or wrinkles, clinging, and
above the wide flanks girt most tightly with a little cord of gold, holding down the folds of the
thinnest cloth over the delicately swelling breast — above this first girdle the excess of the long
garment was drawn up, the fringed hem remaining evenly as far as her fleshy ankles.

Then this raised and tucked-up garment was fastened at the first golden cord with the sacred girdle of
holy Cytherea. Which gathered raising, curved about and elegantly composed, went round above the modest
waist, with a welcome swelling, and above the firm and quivering haunches; and the remainder of the
garment let down veiled the round and small belly with the finest wrinklings, unsteady at the breathing
of the soft breezes and by the movement of her body, falling as far as her milky hams.

Sometimes, by the tempered blowing of the little winds, the light garment being driven, it betrayed her
modest and neat shape, which made a ready scorn of it. So that I did not rashly suspect that she was
almost not of a seed-born composition. Then her outstretched arms, with her long hands, adorned with
fine and turned fingers, with longish, faintly reddened and

shining nails, such as were never dedicated to the like of Minerva of the flock. Which arms, through
the clearness of the sleeves, appeared little less than bare; and the coming-out of the one arm and the
other, near her white shoulders, was most beautifully encircled by a border woven of refined gold, and
plentifully adorned with shining jewels.

In this same manner were all the hems of the gown, with the tiniest little darts of gold leaf, hanging
unsteadily, most comelily dispensed in many places. Above the one side and the other the gown was
unsewn, or cut apart, and joined in three places by three little pins, which were three thickest pearls
braided with dark blue silk — such as Cleopatra did not have to dissolve in a draught; and with such an
order was that parting bound, showing her shift between the distance of one pearl and another.

About her straight and milk-white neck there went an artful thread of forced gold. Which parted upon
the nymphlike breast, narrowing then sharply to meet across it, woven in fine work, and plentifully
adorned with precious gems. Beneath this garment, as is said above, her thinnest crimped overdress
covered, of white silk of the smallest workmanship, which covered that precious flesh, like purpling
roses, in the parting of her spacious and delicious breast. To my eyes more welcome than the fresh
streams to the tired and hunted stag, more delightful than to Cynthia the fishing boat of Endymion, and
the sweet lyre to Orpheus.

The sleeves of which shift, fittingly wide, near the wrists of her bound hands, were girt in and drawn
by a little golden hem pinned with two thick pearls to each, of an eastern whiteness. Then, beyond all
these most welcome things, I gave stubborn attention, with stealing and busy glances, to gazing with
delight at the unruly little swellings, impatient beneath the pressing of the thinnest garment. Those,
then, I judged not unfittingly, that so great a dignity of notable work the maker had formed most
beautifully with every diligence for himself alone and for his own extreme delight, and had gathered
there every force of love.

Perhaps such were the four winged golden figures bound to the royal palace of Babylon, called the
tongue of the gods, not so forcible to reconcile spirits to the love of the King as I felt in these.
Alas, that they would scarcely have filled the hollow of a hand, with the fairest spacing that the
nature of life could feign.
At her whitest throat, whiter than Scythian snow, a necklace

precious girt her — not such as that of Caesar's hind; and I should doubt that such was even that of
the wicked Eriphyle, staining her, for the betraying of the hidden Amphiaraus. Which showed itself as a
threading of gems and of roundest pearls in this exquisite order.

In the pendant towards the fork of her whitening breast, in the middle between two great pearls, was
threaded a flashing ruby, most round; beyond the pearls on either side there followed two blazing
sapphires, and then again two eastern pearls. Beyond which, here and there, there followed two
lightning emeralds, and again two pearls, and then two most shining jacinths. All these gems of a
pill-like form, most just, and of the thickness of a berry, with an excellent and friendly parting.

Her most blonde head, with her hair spread out and loose, poured over her gracious neck, appeared
plentiful with curling and shining little locks, seen no otherwise than as the finest threads of gold,
unsteadily glowing. The parted hair of her crown, pressed down by a wreath of fragrant amethyst
violets, hanging a little above her festive forehead, made a delightful triangular parting, such as was
ever vowed to a Genius. And from beneath the little fillet there came out in an ordered way her
vine-tendrilled hair, part of it quivering and shadowing her fair temples, not hiding her smallest
ears, more beautiful than were ever dedicated to Memory.

Thence then the remainder of her yellow hair, spread out behind her sparkling neck, and hanging poured
from her round shoulders, restlessly stretching over her shapely back beyond the turning of her knees,
and moderately fanning itself in little waves — so that Juno's bird does not so lovelily spread its
eyed feathers; such hair Berenice did not vow for her Ptolemy in the temple of Venus, nor did Conon the
mathematician see such set in a triangle.

In her glad forehead too, beneath two fine, blackest, half-circled and parted brows (such as were
perhaps never seen in Ethiopia among the Abyssinians, nor had Juno ever such in her keeping), there
shone two festive and radiant eyes. Enough to pour Jove down in a rain of gold; ready with a clear
light, with the dark iris covered by the milky white; near which her purpling cheeks, with the round
and laughing dimples of two little hollows, comelily adorned with a choice grace. They breathed the
colour of fresh roses, gathered at the rising of Aurora. And then set in vessels of the cleanest
crystal of Cyprus, shining through no otherwise, with a reddening clearness: so, without fail, with such
brightness I judged them.

Likewise, beneath her straight nose, a most charming little valley followed, bordering on her small
mouth of a courteous shape; the little lips of which, not swollen but moist, and painted with a purple
tincture, covered the even ranks of her small and ivory teeth, not one standing out above another, but
set evenly in order. Among which Love unceasingly composed a breathable fragrance. For, thinking upon
it, I presumed that in those gracious lips there was nothing else than, for the milky teeth, shining
pearls, and for the fragrant breath, the warmest musk, and for the sweet voice, Thespis with her nine
daughters.

By all which things being exceedingly enticed, among my kindled feelings and my disordered and burning
appetite, there was straightway born a great sedition and a bitter contention, such as was not in the
presences told of before, nor among the most ample and various riches. For my various and thieving eyes
commended one part as far fairer than the others. But the appetite, carried off to another part of that
divine little body, argued and preferred that one to the rest.

And of this the whole ill beginning of so troubling and contentious a commotion were my unsated and
most troublesome eyes, which I felt sowing and stirring up so great and such a harmful quarrel in my
sad and wounded heart. By the stubbornness of which I then lost it altogether; and none the less
without them I could in nothing at all satisfy them. The raging appetite then extolled her most
delicious breast without equal. The eyes, consenting with delight, said: if only we could uncover it
all. So that those unsteady ones, thence violently lifted from her most comely face, matched every
extreme pleasure in it.

And here the appetite, strengthened and unfittingly forward, murmured: who would easily persuade me
that ever at any time there was a head so plentiful, with such native tresses and voluptuous ornament of
weaving, and of twisted hairs in a distinguished heaping, and with a joyful winding, adorning so fair
and so shining a brow. Such shavings of fir, always deserving to be in vine-curled circles.

That never such and so notable a Hesperia pleased Aesacus with her flowing hair, nor appeared to him;
with then two clearest and arrow-shooting eyes, like morning stars shining in a cleared sky — a brow
and head more beautifully adorned than ever the warlike Necho, adorned by the Acintani with shining
rays, saw; wounding me deeply in my heart like a dart let fly by an angry Cupid. So that, concluding, I
might almost dare to say that Delos, made steadfast, did not bring forth to mortals lights so gracious,
so bright, so

seemly as these fixed in that divine brow, most shining and amorous of this heavenly figment; and
therefore my sad heart, beset by so many quarrels, bore so great a disagreeing controversy of longing,
as if between them a frond of the standing laurel of the tomb of the king of Bibria had been placed in
the middle; nor did the strife ever cease unless it were cast away. And thus I thought that so great a
litigation would not cease unless from that heart so great a pleasure in her were taken away — which
could not be done.

And for such a reason the delightful and insatiable desire of the one and of the other could not firmly
agree; like a man sharpened with hunger and raging among manifold and various dishes, who, eager for
all, remains wholly content in his burning appetite with none, but infected with a ravenous hunger.

*The most beautiful Nymph, having come to Poliphilo, bearing a torch in her left hand, and with the
other free, invites him to go with her; and here Poliphilo, warmed more by the sweet love of the elegant
damsel, begins to feel his senses inflamed by it.*

Beholding present before me the real and intelligible object of a most excellent showing of so comely a
presence and divine aspect, and of a plentiful heap and universal gathering of unseen beauty and more
than human shapeliness, I reckoned small and slight for this, and unequal, all the inestimable delights
seen before, and riches and lofty magnificences, beside so great a worth as is hers.

O happy, then, is he who shall quietly possess such and so great a treasure of love. But not only a
happy possessor — truly most blessed I call him who, humbly submitting to all her desires and rule,
shall by any means be possessed and held by her. O highest Jove, behold the stamped trace of your
divine image, left in this most noble creature; whence, if Zeuxis had had her alone for his
contemplation, he would fittingly have chosen her as his one most apt exemplar, most praised above all
the girls of Agrigentum and of the whole round world, of the highest and absolute perfection.
Which shapely and heaven-dwelling Nymph, now

drawing near to me festively and cheerfully joyful, at once, her rarest beauties having been gazed at
somewhat from afar by my eyes, now contemplating them more openly from close by, I remained astonished
and carried away.

No sooner had her amorous aspect and most welcome presence slipped through the service of the eyes to
my inmost parts than remembering memory awoke, stirring the heart within. Presenting to it and offering
her who has made of it a plentiful workshop, and a quiver packed with her sharp arrows, and a familiar
and treasuring dwelling of her sweet likeness: it knew her again, and her who has at length used up my
tender years in her warm, first and strongest loves. For I felt it, now leaping out of place, and
without delay beating steadily upon my hurt breast like a hoarse drum.

And although in her comely and most acceptable aspect, and by her blonde tresses, and in her tendrilled
brow with its crisp and quivering locks playing above, there appeared to me that golden-haired Polia
extremely loved — and for whom my life has never for a moment been able to move itself out of the
burning flames, nor, tossed as it is, to be tempered — nevertheless the proud and unaccustomed nymphlike
dress, and the unknown place, made me remain greatly in suspense over it, doubting and of two minds.

Who, with the snowy arm of her left side, resting upon her breast white as snow, carried a kindled and
shining torch, standing a little above her gilded head, holding the slenderest end of it with a
clenching fist; and shrewdly offering her free arm, whiter than ever was that of Pelops. In which
appeared the fine cephalic and the basilic vein, like sandalwood lines drawn upon the cleanest papyrus.
And with her delicate right hand, taking mine in a well-ordered way, with a wide and splendid brow, and
with her laughing mouth fragrant of cinnamon and her dimpled cheeks, and with her most adorned coaxing
speech, she pleasantly said:

"O Poliphilo, come safely with me, and do not hesitate at all." I then felt my spirits astonished,
marvelling how she knew my name. And all my inward parts, laid low, encircled by a burning amorous
flame, and my voice taken from me, shut in between fear and a reverent bashfulness. And thus,
unawares, I knew not what I might worthily answer her to that, nor how otherwise to reverence the divine
young girl, save that I readily offered her my unworthy and unfitting hand.

And having put it in hers, I felt her press it between warm snow and milky curd. And it seemed to me —
nay, so it was — that I was touching and handling something other than a thing of human condition.
Whence, after I had done so, I remained wholly stirred and shaken and suspicious, not understanding
things unvisited by mortals. Nor yet what ought to follow from it, with my common ragged dress and with
my foolish and vulgar manners, judging myself misshapen beside her, unfit and unlike such a fellowship,
and that it was unlawful for a mortal and earth-born man to enjoy such delights.

For which cause, my face blushing, filled all with a bashful wonder, and grieving somewhat at my own
lowness, I made myself her follower.

At last, though not with my whole and wholly recovered mind, I began to bring back my frightened and
troubled spirits, persuading myself that I was deservedly at a most blessed outcome, beside such a
beautiful and divine object, and in such a place. Whose excellent aspect would have had force enough to
draw and carry the lost souls out of the eternal flames, and to bring the bodies not yet joined in
their tombs back to their partner; and Bacchus would have neglected the famous drunkenness of Gauranum,
Faustianum and Falernum, and

Pucinum, or Pictanum, to have a perpetual sight of her. And following behind her with my beating heart
(restless with love), more shaken than the little bird sisura, and in no other manner than the timid
sheep carried off by the ravening wolf by the bitten throat.

Here, fervently touched with pleasant ardours, they began little by little to grow and to warm the cold
fear, and to fit the altered heat by disposition to a sincere love. And being already almost overcome
and vanquished in no ordinary measure by the kindling and inward appetite, thinking silently within
myself, I argued in various ways: O most happy above any lover whoever should be joined and made a
sharer in the love of this woman, if not wholly, at least in some part.

Then, blaming my own wicked desires, I set against them, saying: O, it would scarcely be given me to
believe that such Nymphs would deign to be with unequal and earthly men, unlike them in all things. But
without hesitating: this one is worthy of the close embraces of the gods above, and of drawing them,
stripped of their divine forms, changed and disguised, down from the high heavens to her delightful
love.

On the other side I comforted myself, that, offering her my loving soul (having no other worthier
gift), however divine she be, perhaps she will not despise it. As Artaxerxes, king of the Persians,
bent down to the water presented in the hands to drink. And for this, with lukewarm sighs, I felt the
inmost parts of my invaded breast stirred and greatly moved. Which willingly fitted itself to such a
service, and prepared itself to be kindled more easily than a dry reed-bed to the blowing east winds,
the small spark being set to it, which at the beginning begins to catch impetuously, multiplying, and
then all takes fire.

By this likeness I most abundantly felt the growth of a pleasant and familiar little flame spreading in
the prepared subject, in such a way that her amorous glances were by now to me deadly and mortal
strokes, as the flashing thunder splits the strong oaks with a sudden onset, breaking out. And I no
longer dared to look at her shining eyes, for whenever I looked at her (forced by the incredible beauty
of her most welcome aspect), and if by chance her radiant eyes had met mutually with mine, for some
little while all things seemed to me doubled, before the wavering blinking of my eyes and their former
light were restored.

By reason of all these things, plundered and spoiled and wholly conquered, I was then disposed to take
in my fist some fresh little herbs and, offering them to her, to say as a suppliant: *I yield*. Seeing
that already in my mind I silently confirmed it, and had granted her free entry and a wide opening of
my appointed soul. At once, upon this, my warm breast humbly

having opened itself like the red and ripe fruit of the pomegranate, widening at its first splitting
and then cracking wholly open. And having received into itself the accustomed and familiar (though
somewhat interrupted) burnings, at once the used and worn hearth knew its own heat and fire again,
piercing my burnable and practised inward parts, with that maidenly aspect adorned exceedingly with an
unthinkable elegance.

For already at the first cooking of the first amorous burnings, brought most sweetly into my mind (but
like the horse in Troy, complete and stuffed with ambushes), it gave the beginning eternally to an
unknown and implacable battle, remaining deeply fixed in my tenacious and most simple heart. Which,
easily seduced by a most sweet semblance, without delay and unadvisedly did not tarry to split itself
open, and to set wide windows to the amorous approaches and kindlings, and to be lit again by
disposition at the pleasant fires, and aptly to put itself under so great a burden.

So that already in me a familiar stirring grew stronger at the busy and inward ardours. To which I
reckoned her at present a worthier and fitter help than to the hollow little ships sailing in the swift
and tossing waves of the measured sea in ill weather is Tiphys with his tiller and most convenient
guiding, and the star of Castor. More welcome still than that of Mylitta to the beaten Adonis. And to
Aphrodite that of Peristera, her obedient Nymph. And more acceptable than the dittany of Ida, brought
by the daughter of Dione, with its purple flower, to the wound of pious Aeneas.

And feeling my breast already shaken with inward roughnesses, and silently filled again and closely
packed, and my straying thoughts gathered into it, and thinking with a busy love, the wound no longer
to be healed widened and grew. And my little spirits being drawn back into me little by little, I
almost dared to assure myself of showing her, and expressing, my intense burnings and amorous
thoughts. Then, wholly lost in a blind desire — for which cause I could no longer refuse the invading
approaches, nor resist the burning boilings — I cried out with a stirred and full voice and said:

"O delicate and divine damsel, whoever you are, use less strong torches to burn me and to consume my
sad heart. By now it burns all over with an unceasing and goading fire, and I feel a pointed and
sharpest and flaming dart pierce and go through the middle of my soul."

And saying thus, meaning to uncover the hidden fire and to lessen a little the sharpness I suffered —
excessively growing worse from this raging and terrible inflaming (of love) remaining hidden — yet
patiently I stayed; and in such a way all these fervid and heavy stirrings, and rash thoughts, and
wanton and violent appetites, I turned back, seeing myself with my

soiled gown. Which still held the hooks of the biting burrs fixed in it from the wood; and as the
peacock, looking again at its foul and vilest feet, lays down its rounded tail, so, neither more nor
less, I put down the goadings of every pleasure, breaking off my stubborn desires and vain thoughts,
considering how unsuited they were to so divine an object.

For this cause I was strongly disposed with all my strength to conquer and shut in my loose and
wandering appetite, and my wavering mind, and to overcome my immodest will, judging by now that it
could not be otherwise than so.

At last, thinking upon it in the secret of my kindled heart, I began to think that without fail I could
match my present and continual pain to that of wicked Tantalus, to whose dry and thirsting mouth the
cold and purest waters offer themselves, tasteable and joyful, and to whose raging appetite the sweet
fruits present themselves most welcomely up to his gaping mouth — and he remains at last unfed and
fasting of the one and of the other.

Alas for me: in no other manner was a most comely Nymph, notable in form, of a flowering age, adorned
more than can be said with angelic manners and famous for a chief honesty, presented most kindly before
my eyes — the sight of whom exceeded every exquisite and delightful human content; and I at her side,
she full of everything that avails solacingly to love and provokes to longing, and drawing the
intellect away from every other working, heaping it in herself alone — and yet it did not succour my
panting and delighting desire.

Now, since by such a way the burning longings were not put out, as much as I could I quieted my
languishing heart, inflamed beyond measure, by slackening it with an amorous and solacing hope. And
with this reasoning: that no coal is ever found so far quenched that, being near a kindled one, it does
not likewise, by the fitting disposition, take fire. But my unbridled eyes, more than at any hour,
inflamed that heart, defenceless and unarmed against any power, with a more uncommon desire for her
chief and divine beauties. Ever more beautiful, more elegant, more comely, more to be longed for, and
extremely apt and excellent to love, showing herself plainly with a marvellous increase of sweet
pleasure.

Then I thought sincerely: if by chance the highest gods perceive that I desire and wickedly long for
and presume upon forbidden delights — perhaps in this holy place, and of such a person, reasonably
forbidden — might it not easily befall me, as a profane man, as it did to many others who have
shamelessly offended: the cold and unbroken angers justly used upon bold and most confident Ixion? And
in like manner

the Thracian would not have found the deep seats of Neptune either, if he, rash man, had not first
adulterated pure and savoury Bacchus by mixing him with liquid Tethys, and had not unworthily thrust
himself into divine estates. And Galanthis, the royal handmaid, that liar to Lucina, would not carry
her offspring in her mouth, if she had not deceived her.

Whence perhaps this divine Nymph is reserved for her Genius, or for some other lofty hero, and I,
unworthily attempting such a sacrilege, might deservedly stir him to indignation against me.

Weighing such a reason in good time, then, I thought that those who lightly make themselves secure also
lightly perish, and that for such men deceit and failure are not hard to come by. And that among the
bold (as it is wont to be said) all deceiving and mocking Fortune does not stand. And besides this, it
is hard to search out another's heart. For which cause, as Callisto, feeling with shame her swollen
belly grow heavy, withdrew herself from the presence of chaste Diana, so, stirred by shame, I drew
myself back from such an impulse, bridling my delighting and unseemly desires.

But steadily, with a lynx's eye, and unceasingly, I examined with the utmost pleasure and with a
wonderful affection the most beautiful Nymph, disposing myself wholly to her most welcome love, with an
unfailing, obstinate and most settled mind.

*Polia, still unknown to her lover Poliphilo, graciously and wittily makes him secure. Who, by her
wondrous beauties, gives himself to love in his mind; and both of them drawing near to the triumphs, he
saw countless young men and girls keeping festival with much delight.*

Cupid the archer being strongly and most aptly set in my captive heart as a presiding tyrant, and
having bound me strongly with the solidest chains of love, I felt him prick hurtfully, and the raw and
urgent bite force me violently, being already put under the privilege of his hard but pleasant laws.
And filled with a doubtful delight, sighing beyond measure, I melted and wasted away. The excellent
Nymph, with a most splendid adornment, without delay coaxing, and with her

purple and honey-speaking mouth, and with forceful and drawing little words, made me secure, and
banished from my mind and put away all frightened thoughts, cheering me with her Olympian aspect, and
cooling with her bright speech my already rekindled soul; and with an amorous and wanton glance and
with a gracious laugh she said:

"Poliphilo, I would have you know that true and virtuous love has no respect for outward things; and
therefore your dress neither diminishes nor lessens your spirit, perhaps magnanimous and gentle, and
deservedly worthy to behold these marvellous and holy places and realms, and the wondrous triumphs. For
which cause do not let any fear at all take up your mind, but look carefully at what realms those
crowned by holy Venus possess — those who have manfully striven, and persevering, serving at her
amorous altars and sacred fires, have lawfully gained her most ready favour."

And now, ending her shrewd and sweet talk, we both moved our steps, neither hurried nor yet slow, but
at a modest pace; and, discussing it within myself, I considered, saying:

O most valiant Perseus, for this woman you would have fought more strenuously with the horrible
monster, to win her sweetest love, than for your Andromeda. And then:

O Jason, if the lawful marriage of this woman had been set before you — with far greater peril (I swear
by Jove) than was that of winning the golden fleece — I reasonably judge that, setting that aside, you
would have contended fiercely for this one, judging her above all the jewels and precious treasures of
the spacious world, and above even those of the richest Queen Eleuterylida, most precious, and of a
greater worth and incomparable price.

Every hour and continually she appeared more shapely, more comely in aspect, with a cleanest adornment.
Nor does plentiful gold show itself so welcome to Hippodamia, and to the ravening and anxious
misers. Nor does the entrance of a quiet and safe harbour so offer itself to sailors, nor a cable or a
mooring-post for their fastening when they are shaken in the winter storms. Nor was the falling rain so
longed-for and timely at the pyre of Croesus, as the delicious Nymph offered herself, most acceptable
to love. More joyful and dearer to me than the bloody battles to raging Mars; than to Dionysus the
mysteries of great Crete.

And than to unshorn Apollo the chattering lyre. More welcome still than the fruitful clods, and the
thick ears of corn, and the sacred first-fruits and the Thesmophoria to Demeter.

And going further with her most festively through the grassy and flowering plain, tressed with green
hair, sometimes my searching and

curious eyes I turned most attentively to her delicate little feet, shod in vermilion leather, to whose
little swellings the shoe clung, stretched delightfully; and sometimes her ready and whitest legs,
the silken garment moved a little by the soft breezes, flying above her maidenly limbs, uncovered
themselves with a shapely and exquisite showing. And these, with a sincere judgement, I affirmed to be
tinted with the finest scarlet, such as was ever gathered in the Peloponnese, among the whitest milk,
and set and curdled together with fragrant musk.

By all which most delightful things, chained in the difficult and inextricable knots of a vehement
love, more unloosable than the Herculean knot, and more than that which Alexander the Great undid with
the sword; and most amorously netted in the most tangled nets; and my enslaved heart in most ardent and
troublesome thoughts and most fervent desires, mailed, gripping me wherever I turned, feeling more
prickings and more little nails in that loving heart than faithful Regulus in Africa, carried within
the nailed barrel.

So that with nothing else did I cool my grieving spirits from the amorous burning, and from the most
exquisite torments sharpened, which burned in my thundering breast, save by swallowing my busy sobs,
gaping like a hunted fawn.

Being then plunged headlong into frequent anxieties, and seeing myself wholly carried away to a most
violent love of this woman, I said from myself to myself:

O Poliphilo, how can you leave the love once inseparably kindled in your honeyed Polia, for any other?
And here, wanting with all my strength to untie myself from this biting noose, which drew me more
sharply than the claws of the gripping crab, it was not a work that could be done. Whence nothing else
did I feel that more troublesomely ensnared my tormented soul in affection for this one than the true
likeness of every bodily thread of hers, the comely semblance, and the excellent gestures of my sweetest
Polia.

But above all this there offered itself to me a most cruel torment: how could I ever give up my most
acceptable Polia? And at once, the warm tears called up in my moist eyes, it seemed to me despicable
and very hard to renew my wasted heart, and to bring in a new and unknown lord, and impiously to
banish its ancient one.

Then, comforting myself, I said: perhaps this is she, according to the divine oracle and the high and
true promise of Queen Eleuterylida, but she does not reveal it; for, if I do not err, this one
infallibly seems so to me. And this amorous and running thought being made, and this persuading
presupposition, and being gone out of every other desire, I only pondered, with my heart and with my
mind returning to the notable Nymph. By the great love of whom, closely

taken and in no ordinary measure constrained, I dared with an unaccustomed wonder to gaze steadily upon
so unvisited a making. And my eyes, aptly plentiful of the nymphlike and incomparable beauties, made
themselves most absorbing whirlwinds; and after they had been so warmly stirred to drink up the highest
sweetness of so kind and notable a presence, they took an eternal strength to hold gathered together
with them, at such a delightful service, all my other captive senses solacingly agreeing — so that from
her alone, and from nowhere else, I should seek such cooling and delight, chiefly for my burning
flames.

Thus, then, by a sharpening love painfully hurt and afflicted, wavering, we came at length to the right
part of the spacious field.

The Nymph beloved of Venus stood still, and stayed there, and I with her. Where, looking with an almost
half-power of sight — because it could not be wholly moved away from its amorous object — by the
kindness of the pleasant region, I saw drawing near the numerous chorus of a thronging crowd, festive
and dancing, of most delicate and splendid young men and youths, with unshorn hair exulting, with the
tresses of their ringed locks twisted without any pains, amorously crowned and combed with garlands and
little circlets of manifold flowers, and of vermilion roses, and of leafy myrtle, and of purple
amaranth mingled with melilot.

And with these an extreme multitude of most beautiful girls. More delicate and fair than would be found
in Sparta. And the one sex and the other clothed in a proud covering, not of Milesian wool, but rather
in richest garments of silk, and some of waving watered silk, not subject to the Oppian laws; some of a
changeable shot colour, belying the true colouring. Some of purple chosen from the murex, and some of
finest linen, such as is not produced in Egypt, white and crimped, and cloth crossed with saffron, most
subtly woven. And of countless other colourings. Some of sky-blue, others of crimson, many of green and
scarlet, of sandarac and of dark blue dyeing, with sumptuous delights; many of a saffron tincture, such
as Corycus does not bring forth, nor Centuripe, exceedingly gracious to the sight, threaded with a
golden filament. With a choice adornment of shining gems at the outermost hems about the ankles, held
by the purest gold. Some were mingled among them with sacred fillets and of a divine and pontifical
worship. Some with a hunting dress.

And most of these distinguished Nymphs had their blonde hair gathered together, with exquisite little
twists in three parts, and knotted with a delightful weaving. Others spread their unsteady and restless
tresses loosely, poured behind their milky necks. Some with their most abundant hair wrapped in the
thinnest veils, their glad brow left graciously shadowed with twisted hair. And so, without labour,
mistress nature gave them no ordinary grace.

And with fillets woven of threads of gold with a border of sparkling pearls; and others had adorned
their haired heads with richest and delightful bands. And at their straight throats the most sumptuous
necklaces, and precious collars, and armlets, and clasps; and their small ears most beautifully hung
with various jewels. And the dignity of the hair with a clean and notable adornment, the brow encircled
with a threading of great and roundest pearls. All which most excellent things, together with their
most elegant persons, would easily have altered any rustic, fierce, obstinate and inhuman heart.

Then they showed delightfully their whitening breasts, uncovered as far as the round little swellings.
Then the maidenly little body upon straight legs, with small feet. And some bare upon antique sandals,
held with little cords of gold between the great toe and the middle one, and near the least, and about
the full heel; and thence they came together neatly upon the top of the foot in an artful lacing. Some
tightly shod, and with little golden hooks and loops. Some with soled buskins of purple and of other
joyful colours, such as Caius Caligula never first wore. Others with fitted high boots girt above their
white and fleshy calves; and some with little slippers, with masterly little loops of gold and of silk;
many with the ancient Sicyonian shoes, and some with choice silken pumps and with golden clasps most
seemly set with gems.

And besides, at their neat heads, their free brows bound about with flying veils of a spider's making;
and with their biting and festive eyes, brighter than shining stars in the purest sky, beneath their
fine and circled brows. And the small nose between their apple-round cheeks, reddened like those apples
in autumn, duly with their laughing little hollows, or dimples. And their front teeth and eye-teeth,
with the others set in order, small, of the colour of refined silver, between their moist lips like the
finest coral.

Many likewise with sounding instruments, such as would never be found in Ausonia, nor even in the hand
of Orpheus, keeping high festival through the flowering meadows and the most level plain with sweetest
sounds, and with the sweetest voices and exulting songs, and with a multiplied glory, making one with
another amorous

battles, with solacing and most joyful acts and caresses, festively going round four most precious and
divine triumphs, the like of which were never seen by mortal glances, with a sincere and most delightful
applause.

*Poliphilo in this place aforesaid saw the four triumphing six-horse cars, all of various stones and of
most precious jewels. With the mingled multitude of blessed young people, greatly worshipping in praise
of the highest Jove.*

Reasonably, I judge it in no way difficult for the gods above to do; nay, any effect whatever readily
shows itself easily to be done at their will, and in every place, and above everything created. For
which cause they are duly called almighty. Perhaps whoever shall sometimes hear told the marvellous and
stupendous — nay, divine — works, might marvel exceedingly. For art, the rival, strives as much as it
can to imitate natural things. But divine things, without doubt, cannot aptly be feigned or copied by
any created wit and intellect without their help and inspiration. So for such a reason no one ought to
let himself be taken up by any doubt, but quietly taking note let him set in his mind that to the gods
above every making unaccustomed to us is possible — such as I saw thus.
*The description of the first triumph.*

The first of the four wondrous and divine triumphs had its four swift wheels of finest stone of the
greenest Scythian emerald, sparkling with atoms of a coppery colour. The rest, then, of the car I
beheld, astonished, made all of tablets not of Arabian nor of Cyprian, but of iron-sparkling Indian
diamond, defying the hard emery and the steel, victorious over active fire, its scorner and stubborn
foe, but quiet and tameable to the warm blood of a goat, welcome to the magic arts. Which slabs,
divinely worked with a sunken carving in relief, were carved and wonderfully set and enclosed in the
cleanest gold.

In the right-hand tablet I beheld expressed a noble and royal Nymph with many of her own age in a
meadow, crowning the victorious bulls with manifold garlands of flowers. And one clinging to her, made
very particularly familiar with her.

The left-hand tablet held that same trusting Nymph, who had climbed upon the meek and white bull. And
he carried her, timid, across the swelling sea.

On the front face I saw Cupid, with a countless crowd of both kinds of people wounded, marvelling that
he should draw his bow towards high Olympus. On the hinder face I beheld Mars before the throne of
great Jove, complaining that his son had torn his impenetrable breastplate. And the kindly lord showed
him his own wounded breast. And in the other hand, his arm stretched out, he held written: NO ONE.

This figure of a car was four-cornered, of two perfect squares in length, of six feet, three high and
as much wide, with the required cornice above and beneath the plinth; and from here upward, a foot and
a half, there was a flat two feet and a half wide, five and a half long, with a slope towards the
cornice, all scaled with most precious stones, with an alternating meeting and order of colouring.

And at the four corners were fitted horns of plenty turned about, with their mouths upturned, above the
corner projection of the cornice, packed with many fruits and flowers of thick and manifold gems,
sprouting among the varied foliage of gold. Which horns I saw clothed with a distinguished showing of
leaves of the horned poppy, and with twisted hollows, and with their slenderness wound at the end of
the flat. Which broke off into a fringed antique leaf, that most beautifully ran over the back of the
elegant horn of the said material.

At each corner, from the plinth towards the cornice, at the projection there was made fast a harpy's
foot, with a moderate curving, and with an excellent turning here and there into acanthus foliage.

The wheels were covered within the car, half of them appearing; and the plinth — that is, the outermost
part of that engine — in the forward part, near the harpy feet, rising somewhat and neatly narrowing,
turned into a snail-like scroll. In which the nooses, or holdfasts for drawing, were fittingly
committed. And where the axle was fixed and turned, fitted to that plinth there hung a pointed piece,
of as great a breadth at the joining of the plinth as was twice the distance from the turning hub to
the top. And here there began exquisitely two foliages, which, dividing, ran down beneath the plinth;
in the middle of the space between which there stood out, moderately, a five-petalled rose, in the
middle of which that pole turned upon the axle.

Now upon the flat aforesaid there lay a fateful, whitest and kindly bull, adorned with many flowers, and
with the pomp of an ox for sacrifice. Upon him sat a royal maiden with her wide shoulders, with her
long and bare arms, as if frightened, holding and embracing his hanging dewlaps. Clothed most
exquisitely in a fine cloth of green silk and gold, of a marvellous weaving, in nymphlike dress, with
the ends of a veil tucked up at her ankles, filling like a sail, not without a plenty of various jewels
for adornment, with a crown of gold pressing down a most elegant and golden head of hair, neat and
shining.

Such a triumph was drawn by six wanton centaurs, sons of the falling seed of bold Ixion. With flat
little chains of gold exquisitely looped at their strong and horse-like flanks, the rings knotting one
with another close together, and held in golden clasps and joinings, and then running in the fitted
rings, all six drawing evenly. Nor did Erichthonius find a like manner in the joining of fierce horses
to his flying four-horse cars.

Each was ridden by a notable Nymph, sitting with their shoulders turned one to another, three with
their notable faces turned to the right, and three to the left, with musical instruments sharing
together in a heavenly harmony; with most abundant and yellow hair spread down over their white necks,
their heads adorned with garlands of all fruits; the two nearest the triumph clothed in dark blue silk,
of that bright and choice colouring of the little feathers in a peacock's neck.

The two in the middle in flashing crimson. And the first, going before, of satin cloth of a green
emerald colouring. Not without the nymphlike additions and adornments, singing with their rounded
little mouths, and playing with so great a sweetness of melody as to keep the soul unfed and ever
living.

The centaurs were crowned with mistletoe. In their hands, the one at the lower part, and embracing it
with the other, the two nearest the car carried vessels of antique shape, of topaz of Arabia, with its
flashing golden colour, welcome to Lucina, and at which the waves grow quiet. Slender at their bottoms,
and in the middle growing little by little to an immoderate body, and thence rising to their mouths, of
two feet in height, without handles, of a wonderful artifice. Out of which there leapt a clouding smoke,
scattering a fragrance beyond all esteeming. Those that followed blew golden trumpets, with a hanging
cloth of fine silk, interwoven with gold, with

a threefold binding at the trumpet's pipe; the other two with the most ancient horn-blowers, each in
concord, and with the instruments of the riding Nymphs.

Beneath which triumphal six-horse team was the axle at the middle, in which the spokes of the wheels
were fixed, of a pomegranate-flower lineament, narrowing then at the pointed lips with a little apple
at the circumference. Which pole was of finest and weighty gold, refusing the gnawing rust and the
burning fire, the deadly poison of virtue and of peace. It was exceedingly kept by those who held
festival, leaping around with measured and sudden turnings, with the most solemn clappings, with their
garments girt with little flying bands; and those seated upon the drawing centaurs praised amorously,
with consonant voices and with sung verses and with an extreme exultation, the holy cause and the
divine mystery.

The following triumph was no less marvellous than the first. For it had its four turning wheels
entirely, and the spokes, and the hub, of dark agate, lovelily straggled with white little veins. Nor
certainly did King Pyrrhus carry such a one, with the nine Muses and Apollo in the midst playing,
stamped there by nature.

The axle and the form of it like the first, but the tablets were of dark blue eastern sapphire,
sprinkled with little sparks of gold, most welcome to magic, and by far most acceptable to Cupid in his
left hand.

In the right-hand tablet I beheld carved a notable matron who had given birth to two eggs, set in a
royal bed of a marvellous palace, with the midwives astonished, and many other matrons and Nymphs
standing by; out of one of which there came a little flame, and out of the other egg two most notable
stars.

In the other slab, the curious parents, ignorant of the new prodigy, devoutly asked in Apollo's temple
of the divine image, by an oracle, the cause and the outcome. To whom the kindly godhead answered thus
perplexingly: *the one is pleasing to the sea; the other is pleasing to the sea.* By such an ambiguous
answer they were kept safe by their pious parents.

On the front face there was seen a most beautiful boy Cupid, raised into the upper air, and with the
cutting point of a golden arrow violently painting in the starry heaven various figures of animals
four-footed, creeping and flying; and on the earth men stood marvelling at so great an effect from one
frail little arrow. On the hinder one, great Jupiter set a skilful shepherd in his own place as judge,
being stirred by him next to

a most charming sleeping spring. Where he gave judgement upon three naked and most shapely goddesses.
Who, seduced by busy Cupid, granted the apple to his most witty mother.

This triumphal car six white elephants, yoked two by two, drew — such as would not be found in the land
of Agisymba, nor among the Gandari; nor were such subdued to the African triumph of great Pompey, nor
were such set to draw the triumph of Father Liber when India was conquered. With their trunks armed with
ivory and deadly tusks, and with a sweet trumpeting, they drew fittingly, with traces of finest silk of
a dark blue tincture, most beautifully twisted with threads of gold and of silver mingled, in tightest
knots woven four-square like ears of corn, such as are seen on Mount Gargano; with golden breastplates
filled with a multitude of most flashing and differing gems, with golden rings fitted, in which the
binding of all six ran.

Six most tender girls rode likewise in the manner of the first, with other unlike instruments,
excellently sharing in one sound; and all that the others did, these did in like manner. Two clothed in
crimson, two in a shining yellow, that inner colour of the flower of the crowfoot, and two in violet
purple.

The drawing elephants were covered with a covering of gold fringed with thick pearls, and pompously
adorned with other gems. And their necks encircled with round and thick jewels; and above their wide
foreheads there hung an unsteady little apple of marvellous pearls, with a long little beard of various
silk and golden threads, unsteady at every movement.

Upon this proud and triumphal carriage I saw a whitest swan, in the amorous embraces of a renowned
Nymph, daughter of Theseus, of an incredible beauty formed; and kissing her with his divine beak, his
wings let down, he covered the uncovered parts of the noble lady; and with divine and delightful
pleasures they stood, both joined together most joyfully; and the divine swan set between her delicate
and snowy thighs.

Who sat comfortably upon two cushions of cloth of gold, exquisitely stuffed with soft down, with all
the sumptuous and adorning accessories fitting. And she clothed in a fine nymphlike gown, of whitest
silk woven with a warp of gold, shining, with an elegant ornament of precious stones in the fitting
places. Without lack of anything whatever that comelily comes together for the increase of delight.
Exceedingly notable and delightful to those who looked. With all the parts that were described at the
first, of praise and applause.

The third heavenly triumph followed, with four turning wheels of Ethiopian chrysolite, flaming with
little sparks of gold — through which, being pierced, the bristle of a little ass puts malignant demons
to flight; welcome to the left hand — with all that is said above of wheels.

Then its slabs, set round about in the manner told above, were of green heliotrope of Cyprus, with
power over the heavenly lights, hiding the one who carries it and giving the gift of divining, spotted
with little bloody drops.

The right-hand tablet offered this history carved. A man notable for royal majesty prayed in a sacred
temple to the divine image, for what should follow from his most shapely daughter. The father, hearing
of his own casting out of the kingdom by her, and that she should not be got with child by any man,
made a fortified building of a lofty tower, and had her shut in it with a solemn guard. In which,
sitting idle, with an excessive solace she saw drops of gold distil into her maiden lap.

In the other tablet was stamped a noble young man. Who with the utmost religion received the protection
of a crystal shield; and he, valiant, with the curved and cutting falchion beheaded a terrifying woman,
and proudly carried the severed head in sign of victory. From whose blood there was born a winged
horse, which, flying to the peak of a mountain, made a mysterious fountain rise with its hoof.

On the front face there was seen the powerful Cupid, who, shooting with his golden arrow towards the
starry heavens, made drops of gold rain down amorously. And an endless crowd of every condition,
wounded, stood all astonished at it. Opposite, I saw Venus in anger, having with an armed man loosed
her son, whom she had caught by the wings in a fated net, taking her revenge,

and wished to pluck him, having already her fist full of his flying little feathers; and the boy
weeping, one with winged sandals, sent by lofty Jove sitting upon a throne, freed him unhurt from his
mother's hands. And then offered him thus to him. And helping Jupiter said to him, carved
distinguishedly in the Attic tongue over against the divine mouth: *you are to me both sweet and
bitter.* And he covered him beneath his heavenly cloak.

This was pompously drawn by six most fierce unicorns, with a horned stag-like forehead, reverent to
cold Diana. Which were bound at their strong and horse-like breasts in an ornament of gold plentiful
with most precious jewels, with twisted little cords of silver thread and of yellow silk artfully
knotting one with another, making the neatest knots, with the excellent accessories of those described
before.

Six young girls sat above, in the manner and pomp of the others, and in dress interwoven with gold, of
finest dark blue silk, woven with various flowers and foliage; all six with marvellous and most ancient
wind instruments in concord, and expressed with incredible breath.

Upon the flat of it, in the middle, there lay a precious seat of green jasper, excellent in silver,
serviceable at childbirth, and a medicine for the chaste. Which was six-cornered in its foot, rising
fittingly slender beneath a plate-like little shell. The lower part of which, as far as its middle, was
laboriously furrowed. And then plain and curved as far as beneath the braided lip. The hollow of which
was shallow, for the ease of the sitter, with notable lineaments in the cutting.

Upon this there sat readily a most adorned Nymph and most beautiful, in a garment of gold interwoven
with dark blue silk, in a fine dress of girlish neatness adorned with manifold gems. She showed her
affectionate delight in gazing at a plenty of heavenly gold in her lap. With the solemn honours and
joyful applause like the others, she sat with her abundant hair poured over her back, crowned with a
golden diadem and with many-formed little stones.

The fourth triumph four wheels carried, of iron-like Arcadian asbestos, once kindled refusing to be put
out. The rest of the four-square tabling, in the manner aforesaid, was of flashing carbuncle of
Troglodytis, not fearing the thick darkness, with most polished chasings, long to speak of distinctly.
But such workmanship ought to be considered in what place, and by what maker, it was wrought.

The right-hand face, then, showed excellently this history. A venerable matron with child. To whom the
highest Jupiter appeared divinely (as he is wont with the goddess Juno) with thunders and lightnings,
so that, kindled, she was burnt to ashes; and out of the burnt body they drew a most noble and divine
infant.

In the other I beheld that same helping Jupiter offering that same infant to a heavenly man with winged
sandals and bearing a herald's staff. And he then committed him in a cave to many Nymphs to be nursed.

In the front square I saw Cupid, a great plenty of both sexes marvelling as they were shot, that with
his hurtful little arrow shot into the high heaven he should draw Jove in his divinity to the
contemplation of a mortal girl. Opposite, behind, the greatest Jupiter was seen sitting as judge in a
tribunal, and Cupid limping, called into judgement against his kindly mother, making sorrowful

complaints — seeing that by her doing he had extremely wounded himself with love of a most beautiful
damsel. And that by a spark from a lamp his divine little leg had been burnt. The most beautiful Nymph
being present too, accused, with the lamp in her hands. And to Cupid, laughing, Jupiter said: *bear the
spark, you who set fire to heaven and to all.*

This single line was carved in our own letters upon a tablet before the face of the venerable godhead.
The rest as those described.

This mysterious triumph six spotted tigers of Hyrcania drew, with markings of a shining tawny, and
swiftest in their speed, most beautifully bound with the pliant shoot of a fruitful vine, full of tender
fronds, with their winding tendrils, adorned with vermilion clusters. Drawing with a tempered movement.

Above which, in the middle of the flat, there was set a base of gold, of a lowest diameter of one foot
and three palms, and of nearly the same height. One part at the lowest rounded course, and a half at
the wave, or upturned moulding and braid. The rest was distributed to the pulley moulding, and to the
inverted wave with the accessory braids, or rules and little cords.

The flat of this was hollow in the middle in a circle. Into which hollowing there descended the tails
of four eagles, founded upon the levelled surface of the base. Which were of precious crimson aetites of
Persia. And these stood with their backs one opposite the other. Having their clawed golden talons
fixed and treading upon the said base. And each with both wings raised and touching.

Upon these, at the elbow, was founded this wondrous vessel of most bright Ethiopian jacinth, an enemy
to the chisel, a gracious companion. Which vessel was crusted with emerald, with manifold other little
veins of gems, an incredible thing. In height it was two feet and a half. Almost of a rounded form. The
diameter of its thickness stood at a foot and a half, and the circumference was three diameters. Which
vessel, made fast from the bottom upon the wings, rose a third, and then there was a border going round
the last

thickness of a palm. From which border, to the beginning of an ewer-shaped vessel that was held in one
with this same, a palm; in all, as far as here, it is a foot and a half.

Above this measure there grew a form of the vessel aforesaid, raised a foot, and began to widen for a
palm and a half. Which half was given to the exquisite border of wound fronds and flowers, almost all
torn free of that jacinth. The diameter two quarters and a half. Beneath this little border there stood
out round about certain slices of a modest rise and a tempered keeling, somewhat thick at the top, and
narrowing away at the bottom.

Then it rose most beautifully to the mouth two quarters and a half. Distinguishedly hollowed with
twisted little hollows. The mouth of a little shell with wide rims, beneath the body with an elegant
moulding, and at the grasp of the vessel with turned gorges, waves and rounds. Of such lineaments were
the borders set both below and above.

At the border of the ewer below, within the said enclosure, there were held two cut half-rings, pressed
down by their figure, set crosswise opposite with their hooked ends one to the other. Which were held in
the biting jaws of two lizards, or little dragons. And the little dragons, left perfectly of a vein of
emerald, the rest crusted away, lay with four lizard-like feet upon the ridge of the lower vessel;
which ridge, between the ewer and the lower vessel, had a rise of a quarter. And from its lofty
narrowing, descending, it ended with a lineament of an inverted moulding at the encircled rim of the
body, where the surrounding border was.

Which sloping ridge was most diligently scaled of the jacinth. Only the little dragons left of the
emerald vein, with their serpent bellies held above the scaling, and so the four little feet. Which
little dragons, one at each side, at the cut end of the fall of the said ridge, above the cut of the
little cornice, made with their turning tails a round and ready coil towards the spine. And then they
made another like it below. These coils were for the handles. The lower whirl, where it was joined with
the vessel, cut into two parts, one here and the other there, passed into a marvellous foliage. And at
the right and left side they entered half a foot with an elegant polish into the border. Which fronds
were seen almost wholly in relief; and the ground, that is the solid flat lying beneath the body, was
of the jacinth. The whole circumference of the body was taken up by these leafy tails, or rather a
girding band of two feet.

It remains to speak of the space that stands a foot and a half to each side. The body of the vessel
from the girding downward I judged a stupendous work, and rather divine; I beheld the said vessel
covered all over with an exact vine of carving. Of which the stems, or shoots, with vine-leaves, with
little tendrils and ringed shoots, of a vein fitted to the devising, of topaz. Such as would not be
found in the island Ophiodes.
The foliage of finest emerald, the clusters of amethyst. O how

most joyful it showed itself to the sight, and graciously to be contemplated by the intellect. The
solid ground from which this exact workmanship was set apart shone of the jacinth, more burnished and
rounded than would have been brought about on the lathe. Only beneath the leaves was a slight remainder
left, which held the foliage to the jacinth beneath, all open and separated from the ground by almost a
thumb's breadth. The curved leaves, with all the accessory lineaments skilfully polished, with a rash
rivalry of nature, and no less at all the fruits, vine-leaves and wandering shoots. To this wondrous
making let not the cups of the divine Alcimedon be matched. Nor yet the cup of Alcon. Which vessel was
filled with fine and holy ash.

Let us return to the surrounding girdle of the most precious vessel, or bordered band. In the empty
space left between the tails, I saw two histories worthy of the greatest admiration in such carving.

On the front face of that vessel I beheld, excellently cut, high-thundering Jove. He held in his right
hand a cutting golden sword of a vein of Ethiopian chrysolite, shining. In the other a flashing
thunderbolt of a ruby vein. And he with a threatening aspect of a vein of galactite, crowned with
sparkling stars like the thunderbolt. Standing upon a sacred altar of sapphire.

In whose divine and dreadful majesty I looked upon a festive chorus of seven Nymphs, white in their
dress, showing that they sang religiously, with a worshipping applause. Who then were transformed into
green trees of an emerald clearness, filled with shining dark blue flowerets. And they bowed devoutly to
the highest godhead. Not that all the Nymphs were changed into fronds, but the last being wholly turned
into a little tree, and her feet into little roots; and the next with her feet gone; and the third from
the girdle upward, with the beginning of her arms; and each of the rest thereafter. But at the top of
their maidenly heads they showed the metamorphosis that was to follow upon them all in turn.

On the other side, in relief, there appeared a festive and joyful godhead, with the semblance of a
slippery girl, crowned with two long and coiled serpents,

the one white and the other black, knotted with a lively coiling. He stood set delightfully beneath a
fruitful vine. Upon whose arbour there climbed, with laughing faces, certain most beautiful naked little
spirits. And thence they plucked the hanging and heavy ripe clusters; some shrewdly offered them to
this divine godhead in baskets. And he, perceiving it, placidly received them. Some lay on the green
ground on their backs, provoked to a sweet sleep by the juice of the grape. Others busily did the work
of the vintaging autumn. Others idly sang, sounding their stretched drums.

Which expressions, according to the requirement of the colourings, had their veins so naturally
accessory and fitting to the maker's determined devising of the precious stone; and in these little
images, however small, nevertheless no defect at all showed itself, even in the least parts. But every
part was seen distinctly perfect.

Out of the vessel aforesaid there sprouted a leafy vine of gold with curled vine-leaves, fruitfully
adorned with little clusters, with crimson grains of Indian amethyst, and the foliage of the holy green
selenite of Persia, not subject to the movements of the moon, and placid to Cupid. Keeping its bearer
safe; and it roofed the six-horse team.

At each corner of the flat of the triumphal car there shone widely, set there, a most skilfully made
candelabrum, founded upon three little horned feet, of branching coral, excellent for country folk.
Lightnings. Whirlwinds. And driving off tempests, and kindly to its bearer, and an amulet. Such a like
was not found by Perseus beneath the Gorgon's head, nor such in the Red Sea, nor such in the Persian,
nor such the Drepanic.

Then in one of them the whole shaft was of sky-blue Lusitanian thunderstone, unfriendly to tempests,
and chiefly friendly to Diana, with a tempered body, and a narrowing of longish pomegranate-shapes and
knots. With a notable display, adorned with fine-wrought work, of a height of two feet. The other stood
of finest

Dionysian stone, with spots reddening in its blackness, smelling when ground of the god. The third of
best Median stone, sown with a dusky golden colour, with a nectar-like taste. The last of precious
nebris, dedicated to the god, in whose choice black colour white and green met mingled together. In the
little shell of which a pyramidal little flame of unquenchable fire burned continually.

By which brightness I could not steadily behold the choice workmanship and reliefs, by the reflection of
the flickering light, and by the flashing of the most precious little stones.

About which divine triumph, with much and solemn devotion and the greatest pomp and religion, countless
Maenad Nymphs with their hair loose and scattered. Some naked, with nymphlike mantles flowing from
their shoulders, and some in fawnskins — that is, clothed in a pelt varied with the colour of a young
deer — without the other sex, cymbal-players and flute-players, held the sacred rites, crying out with
shouts, and dances, as at the three-yearly feasts, with thyrsi of fronds of cone-bearing trees, and
girt and crowned with vine fronds twisted over the bare body, running and leaping.

There followed immediately the triumph old Silenus riding his little ass; then, immediately behind this
rider, they festively led a shaggy goat adorned with the pomp of sacrifice. And one of his followers
carried a wicker fan, with disordered laughter and frantic gestures. With this most ancient and holy
rite they gloriously extolled this fourth triumph; and with a reverent discourse, crying out
confusedly with a loud voice to Bacchus, there followed, keeping festival, the Mimallones, satyrs,
bacchantes, Lenae, Thyiads, Naiads, Tityri and Nymphs.

*The Nymph eloquently declares to Poliphilo the multitude of the loving young men, and of the divine
amorous girls: who they were and how they were loved by the gods; and he saw the choirs of the divine
poets singing.*

No one of so unwearied an eloquence would ever aptly fit himself to come out and escape from setting
forth the divine secrets plentifully and fully. Nor could he expressly tell, and with words sufficiently
express, with how divine a pomp, unceasing triumphs, unfailing glory, festive gladness and happy
dancing, these four unvisited six-horse cars of memorable show were surrounded.

Besides the renowned young men and the thronging troop of countless and most joyful Nymphs — more
prudent and grave and shrewd than the tenderness of their years — with their most acceptable lovers of
downy and beardless cheeks. In some the first shining down crept over their cheeks; they kept festival
cheerfully and deliciously. Many having their torches kindled and burning. Some I saw bearing shrines.
Others with straight spears adorned with ancient spoils. And some excellently ordered

and composed with various trophies, went before, both kinds gladly, the mysterious triumphs, with high
shouts of joy sounding up into the air. Some with the trumpeting instruments, various in form and in
breath, trumpets drawn out and whole, and with sounding pipes. Some singing with heavenly notes, and
with unspeakable delights and eternal solaces, exceeding all that human wit could imagine at its
utmost, going round the everlasting triumphs in glory, circling through the flowering and blessed land
and happy country, and the spring fields, a place most holy, dedicated to the blessed.

Not hindered nor taken up by any growing shrub. But all the flowery ground was one level meadow of
fragrant herbs and flower-bearing with flowers, endless of every colouring, and most beautiful of
manifold form, and sweetest of scent, as much as could ever be said. Which did not fear the burning
invasions of Phoebus, since he does not run in this most pleasant place with his swiftest horses to the
last west. But the air always purest, and every hour unveiled of clouding vapours, but eternally a
clear and unchanging day; and the earth continually grass-bearing, springlike and fragrant with
flowers, like a gracious and choice painting, standing always unhurt with its dewy freshness, and with
its colour without the interdict of time.

Here the four kinds of violet, cowslip, melilot, anemones, cornflowers, nigella, cyclamen, crowfoot,
columbine, lily of the valley and amaranth, cassidony, spikenard, Celtic nard, ambrosia, amaranth, wild
mint, citron and clove basil, and the other smallest ones; and many other fragrant and flower-bearing
herbs; all the kinds of gillyflower and the smallest Persian rose-trees, fruitful with fragrant little
roses, and hundred-leaved, and of all colourings. And countless others, with all the fragrant and
notable herbs, without any human labour excellently distributed for beauty by excellent nature herself,
and untilled they stood, with their flowering greenness never falling, and with an unfailing
pleasantness and delight. And to the utmost gratifying of the senses.

Here, then, among the notable and seemly girls, with an approved comeliness, I saw Callisto of Arcadia,
daughter of Lycaon, with the unrecognized Diana; Antiope of Lesbos with the honoured satyr, daughter of
Nycteus, from whom were born Amphion the musician and Zethus the countryman; Issa, daughter of
Macareus, with the dear shepherd. And Antichia, daughter of Accus. And the young Canace. And also her
born of Athasius. And Asteria, born of the Titan Coeus. And likewise Alcmena, gladly playing with her
counterfeited husband.

Then in turn I looked upon delightful Aegina, taking the highest pleasure both in the bright river and
in the divine fire. Her too born of Fullus, and her of Menemphus, festive with the feigned father. And
the other of Diodes with her lap filled with most beautiful flowers, and reverent to the twisting
serpent. And the seemly girl no longer grieving at the horns sprouted on her. And Astyoche

and Antigone, daughter of Laomedon, solacing themselves delightfully with the flying feathers. And
Curisice, inventress of the first four-horse cars. The Garamantian Nymph dancing, held by the tip of
her finger on the bright banks of the Bagradas, washing her delicate little feet from the footed crab.

Then I saw in flight a fleeing quail, and a hook-clawed eagle following. Thence too Erigone I saw, who
had her sparkling breast packed with savoury grapes. And the daughter of King Collus pleased with a
strong bull. And the wife of Eripeus gracious with her changed husband. And her born of Alpus quietly
delighting in a shaggy and woolly ram. And the maiden Melantho with the swimming beast. And Philyra,
daughter of ancient Ocean, with the father of Chiron.

Afterwards I saw law-giving Ceres, her brow bound with yellow ears of corn, embraced in a delightful
pleasure with the scaly serpent. And the most shapely Nymph Lara of the Tiber delighting with the
slayer of Argus. And the fair Nymph Juturna. And many others, long to tell of.

Now, with an excessive delight, while ignorant and astonished I carefully contemplated with an applied
mind the heavenly troop and the divine triumphs hedged about with such dances, and the delicious fields
— what they were was wholly unknown to me, save that they were amorous mysteries — the divine Nymph, my
faithful companion and guide, taking note of my dullness, with an excellent face and adorned and
sweetest little words (I not asking her) providently said:

"My Poliphilo, do you see that one?" (showing me who in the fleeting age they had been). "By high Jove
she was ardently loved. And likewise that other beloved one. And this was such a one, and those
godheads were taken with her sweet love." And in this manner besides making known to me her noble and
royal lineage. And the name I did not know she affably, all solacing, told me, pointing.

Then she showed me a venerable crowd of young girls. To whom three holy matrons stood before with
divine bearing, going ahead of so great a delight. Adding (changed somewhat in her angelic face), she
said lovingly: "My Poliphilo, I would have you understand that no earth-born creature could enter here
without a torch kindled — either by ardent love and with the utmost labour, such as you see me carry
burning now, or by the safe company of those three matrons." And sighing from her heart she said: "The
present torch it will behove me, for your love, to quench at the holy temple (as you shall see),
offering it."

Such and so made a discourse pierced my inflamed heart, so most acceptable was it to me and delightful
when she called me thus: "My Poliphilo." Because I was made wholly suspicious that without fail she was
Polia. For which cause I felt myself, from head to foot, inwardly altered and refreshed with the
highest sweetness, and my beaten heart flee to her alone. And of this vehement effect

my face and my low little sighs accused me. And she, skilfully perceiving it, breaking off this strange
and new happening, began placidly to say, coaxing me:

"O how many would most gladly wish that they could look a little upon what you now see clearly. And
therefore lift up your mind to high things, and look diligently, Poliphilo, at how many other noble and
renowned Nymphs show themselves deservedly companioned with their amorous young men, reverent and
generous." Who, with amorous and sweet-sounding notes and measured verses, praising them and their
unwearied lovers, and unceasingly keeping festival, alternating with an extreme delight, and extolling
the triumphs above, together and with the air full of the manifold and most welcome chattering of
various little birds.

In the first song, then, and glad dance, to the lofty praise of the first car in its rejoicing, the
most holy Muses sang, with their divine lyre-player going before. Then there followed the heavenly
triumph an elegant damsel of Parthenope, calling herself by the name of Leria, with her brow crowned
