with undying laurel. Attending upon a most beautiful girl, Melanthia, embraced with her divine father of
chief beauties. Whose garments and voice showed a proud Greek. Upon whom the great Macedonian always
laid his heavy head in sleeping. She carried a shining lamp, which freely shared its light with the
companions following, sweeter than the others in voice and song.

And here the distinguished Nymph showed me most ancient Iphianassa; and then the ancient father of
desire, stirred with his beloved daughters into a sweetest music, joined with these a plentiful and
most easy Lycoris. And a matron singing between two Theban brothers, and with the fair Silvia. All
these and others went before the first triumphing car, singing sweetly with heavenly lyres and
sweet-sounding instruments, and dancing most readily, with brightness and magnificence.

At the second glory of triumph the notable Nemesis with Corinna of Lesbos, Delia and Neaera, with many
others more amorous and more wanton than the rest, gave high-sounding and immortal praise, with Crocale
of Sicily.

At the third pomp of triumph likewise the smooth Nymph, showing them to me, said: "Do you see those?"
Quintilia and Cynthia Nauta, with many others, spread their delightful verses of melody. "Look also at
the maiden Violantilla with her dove, and the other weeping for the sparrow."

To the praises of the fourth triumphal car there went before the noble Lyde, Chloe of Lydia, and
Neobule, with the comely Phyllis and with the fair Lyce; and Tiburtus and Pyrrha with a sounding lyre
rejoiced delightfully. Now after this fourth triumph there followed among the Maenads a notable damsel
who, singing with her beloved Phaon, longed for horns for the beauty of her head. Last of all, after
them all, she showed me a most honest matron of white
garment, and another clothed in an undying green colour, who also sang behind all the singers.

Thus, then, most joyfully they went circling round through the whole flowery and most pleasant plain.
Some crowned with laurel, and some with myrtle, and with manifold garlands and varied adornment; with
most solemn prayers, with a religious discourse, divine and triumphal, without term and ending, without
weariness and without labour, with the utmost fullness of every delight, gloriously rejoicing, and
mutually enjoying the divine sights; and the most happy realms, and the holy country, without
interruption they quietly possess, most blessed.

*The Nymph, having fittingly declared to her Poliphilo the triumphal mysteries and the divine love,
invites him to go on further from there, where with the utmost delight he saw countless other Nymphs
with their most welcome lovers, delighting themselves in a thousand solaces among the flowers, and
through the cool shades and clear streams and clearest fountains; and how Poliphilo, strongly stirred
by love, raged there. But tempering himself with hope, he was quieted, gazing upon the sweet face of
his fair Nymph.*

Not only would he reckon himself happy, but he would be blessed above any other, to whom by a special
favour it should continually be granted to see the divine pomps, the heavenly triumphs, and the glorious
sports, and the kindly places, and such goddesses and demi-goddesses and adorned Nymphs, of incredible
beauty and ornament. And to have a particular fellowship with them, and to look upon them unceasingly.

But above all to have beside him, as an equal companion, so renowned a Nymph of chief beauty, with an
exquisite nymphlike and divine adornment, a guide and a sincere leader. And this I judged no small and
scanty part of blessedness. Having really beheld these things, I stayed a great while in thought, and
gladdened beyond esteeming, and marvelling beyond measure.
Afterwards the

tender and delicious damsel my guide, coaxing, said to me: "Poliphilo, let us go further now." And
departing thence at once, opposite the coolest fountains and shaded streams, we took a solacing
journey. Where the flowing little rivers, from the living and rising fountains, went round the
flower-bearing fields in a ring, running with crystal waters in gracious wavelets.

In which cleanest waters there gazed ardently at himself the purple and flowering son of the Nymph
Liriope, out of his tender leaves; and the river-loving and crimson water-mint; and here and there the
flowering iris set out. And all the fair banks full of other fair and most notable flowers, sprouting
among the greenest and most joyful grass.

Which blessed place was of an ample and widest circuit, ringed with shrubby little mountains of a
moderate height, plentiful with green laurel, with fruit-bearing arbutus, and with tufted and loftiest
pines and firs, with white and temperate myrtle; and round about the clearest little channels with a
gravelly and sandy bed, and in some places the ground was of tawny sand; there lived the watery and
three-leaved dryope, in which the sloping water flowed with a soft murmur.

Here, then, was a great plenty of delicate and divine Nymphs, soft in years, with the fragrant flower of
modesty, beautiful beyond belief, with their beardless lovers, perpetual dwellers and citizens of this
most worthy place.

Of which Nymphs some, comelily, with their forward faces solacing themselves in the brightest waters,
had gathered up most beautifully their finest garments of silk, shining with a various and welcome
tincture, and, those being gathered at their snowy arms, they showed the elegant form of their full
flanks beneath the living little folds. And their whitest legs revealed, and their round calves shown
as far as their fleshy knees. And the running purest waters bathed them near their round ankles.

Which then, reflecting the excessive whiteness of their bright and shining limbs, and their neat
faces, among the little waves not leaping up, and their heavenly faces — as in a shining and most
burnished mirror likewise, where the current was not great — the waters, feigning, showed them; and
their little feet broke the met waters, and the opposing ripples, with an oncoming bursting and a
sounding meeting, invading them.

Some, solacing themselves, ran girt through the waters with the swimming and tame web-footed swans. And
then, drawing up the water with their hollowed hands, they scattered it laughing one at another. Some,
out of the flowing streams, standing upon the soft herbs, busily wove jewels of the fragrant and
variously coloured flowers. Which they familiarly offered to their most welcome lovers, and afterwards
lovingly did not deny the accessory succulent and

savoury kisses; nay, readily kissing closely, more shut and biting than the suckers of the octopus's
arms, and more than the shellfish clinging bitingly to the Illyrian rocks and to the sea flats, with
moist and quivering little tongues fed with fragrant musk, playfully they touched lips mutually
between their laughing and moistened lips. And on their whitest throats some made with their small
teeth marks that did not hurt.

Others had set themselves upon the green grass and the coloured flowers, at a welcome sitting near the
adorned banks, not tangled with little reeds, but adorned with various flowers. In which the melting
waters, clearer than the Axius in Mygdonia, sounded, breaking at the feet of the crimson oleander; and
beneath the shadowing trees they were combed one with another, like the viper locks of Medusa, and more
than the tangled dodder, in delightful embraces, and gripping more closely together than the creeping
ivy to the ancient elms and to the most aged buildings.

And to their reverent lovers not fierce, not refusing, but purely with a companionable love kindly and
affable, and yielding themselves to their desires, consenting with their bare and full breasts. Which
gave themselves to the eyes beyond measure welcome, with loving gestures more delightful and gracious
than flowing tears to cruel and pitiless Cupid. And much more than the cool little streams to the
grassy meadows, and the morning dew. And more than the longed-for form to matter.

Some sang fitly amorous verses, with tired voices taken up with little sighs in their inflamed breasts,
full of sweet accents, able to make sweetly enamoured the fierce hearts of stone, and to tame the
harshness of the pathless Caucasus. And to hinder all that the lyre of Orpheus did, and the accursed
face of Medusa. And to call back any horrible monster, pleasant and to be handled. And to quiet the
continual goad of raging Scylla.

Some lay idly set in the chaste laps of the seated girls, and told the pleasant jests of high Jove; and
they, sharp-witted, went about their curled hair with garlands of savoury flowers, and of fragrant
little herbs, and crowned them with the utmost solace.

Likewise some of them were lovingly and feignedly refused, pretending to flee what both one and the
other intently desired. And here, following, they ran one after the other with their little mouths open,
full of laughing and womanly cries, with their blondest tresses poured down over their milky shoulders,
veiling them, shining like a threading of gold, pressed by garlands of green myrtle. And some had them
knotted elegantly with nymphlike care, with flying veils. Some with hair-fillets woven of a golden
plaiting, adorned with gems.
Then, drawing somewhat together, they

bent down, and, the fair flowers being plucked and their little swelling hands filled, with amorous
semblances they scattered them upon their comely faces, solacing and sporting themselves with much
delight.

Others courteously, opening the closely fastened bosoms of their gowns, adding flowers to flowers, put
within them the roses stripped of their petals, the sucking kiss following after. And at one time they
struck each other with a hand that did not hurt, without weal or bruise, giving each other slaps sweetly
upon their dimpled cheeks, faintly reddened as shining Phoebus shows himself in the wheels of the cool
dawn, with the newest and most unthought-of battles that ever Love knew how to feign.

All festive and cheerful, and all provoked to delights. With girlish gestures and movements and a
maidenly simplicity, tangled in a sincere love without offence to honoured virtue. Free and exempt from
any sad encounter, and from the rivalry of skin-changing fortune.

Beneath the tempered shades let down by the weeping sisters of wicked Phaethon, and by the undying
Daphne, and by tufted pines, with fine and pointed fronds, and by the tree dyed again with the burning
blood of the unhappy Babylonians, and by the straight cypresses and the greenest orange and cedar
trees, and by other most notable and most leafy trees, most fruitful of flowers and fruits, with an
eternal greenness, most beautiful beyond esteeming and fragrant. Which, set in order upon the gracious
banks and dispensed through the plain, at a moderate distance and interval, took up the grassy earth,
full and clothed with the green periwinkle with its sky-blue flowers.

Alas, then, what heart would be so cold and frozen that it should not be excitedly kindled, seeing
present before it such real and delightful offices of an even and answering love? So I reasonably
suspected that even Diana the huntress would wholly and easily have been set on fire. And the icy
Helice pursued by her.

For which cause I should almost have dared to utter a foolishness: that the spirits below suffer no
other torment than the envy they have of these. Who without end live happily in delights and triumph,
with the utmost pleasure, with no weariness of things present nor any surfeit of them.

Whence more than once my heart, kindled through my eyes with an extreme sweetness, and greatly burning,
my amorous soul went out as far as my hesitating mouth. And keeping my mind fixed upon those delightful
pleasures, and the soft kisses, and the abundant rewards of winged Cupid, looking on with a curious
gaze, it certainly seemed to me in that space to feel of that kindled soul that this was its passing,
and that it was sweetly departing to the last and utmost bounds of blessedness.

And in this manner I found myself wavering beyond all measure, lifeless and astonished, so that I
almost thought myself drugged. There offering itself to my tenacious memory the unguents of the
mischievous

Circe, the powerful herbs of Medea, the hurtful songs of Byrrhena, and the grave-verses of Pamphile. So
that I lawfully doubted whether bodily eyes could see beyond humanity, and whether there could be there
a most lowly, ignoble and heavy body, where the immortal blessed rest.

After I was drawn out of these long and anxious thoughts and fantastic imaginings, remembering
exquisitely all the wondrous, holy and divine things seen by me until now nakedly and openly, at last I
knew that they were not deceiving illusions, nor false magics, but truly things imperfectly grasped.

Looking intently, then, with these thoughts, the most excellent Nymph at my side and so close by,
wounded my sad heart unceasingly, dying as I was, with her eyes packed with amorous and busy darts. By
which she at once stirred up every wandering and straying thought of mine, and, all of them gathered
and hardened into that one fixed object, she called back my deadened soul vigorously to renew itself in
its first fires.

Which suffered bitterly for not daring to ask whether she were my divine and most desired Polia. Seeing
that she had before given me a somewhat ambiguous and suspected knowledge; and doubting deservedly
(since my rude and untilled speech would not have been fitting at all) that I should shamelessly offend
her, my warm voice having come many times to my silent lips, for such a reason I pressed it down.

But whatever it was, being beset by a marvellous astonishment (like deceived Sosia by the counterfeited
son of Atlas), I found myself greatly in suspense; above all, examining the heavenly workings with
subtle glances and heartfelt weighings, invaded by an ardent desire — so that beyond measure I longed
thus, saying within myself:

Here I would gladly be reckoned a perpetual citizen; and if it could be, no toilsome trouble could seem
heavy to me, no threatening peril would frighten me. However deceitful fortune should set itself
against me, I would then, without further thinking, lay out my dear and precious life entire. Not
refusing to take up the laborious and heavy choice of the two doors shown to the son of Amphitryon, and
to use up my sweet youth and my pleasant years through the mortal perils of the raging sea, and through
the fearful places of Sicily, with greater and highest labours and terror than were borne by wandering
Ulysses, being in the darkened and pathless cave of the horrible Cyclops Polyphemus, son of Neptune, and
by the transformations of the company of Calypso; and not to spare my gracious life for any thing
whatever, and to bear a harder and longer servitude than the loving Hebrew shepherd bore, and a more
dreadful one than that of Androdus the slave — because there every labour is shut out where love burns
— and to set myself to the

proving of the loving Milanion and Hylaeus, and for the fair Atalanta. And to strive in no other manner
than the sinewy and strong Hercules, wrestling manfully for his beloved Deianira against the monstrous
Achelous, conquered him; and I in no other way, to win so many delights, and to enter for long into the
holy and most fruitful places, disposed with every delight and pleasure.

And above all to win the precious love, and to gain the long-desired good will of this woman: fairer
beyond comparison than Cassiopeia, more shapely than Castiamira — alas for me, who carries my dying and
my life in her will. And if by chance I appear unworthy of such fellowship and amorous commerce, at
least that it might be eternally granted me by a special gift and privilege and favour to gaze upon
her steadily and intently.

And then, speaking to myself, I said: O Poliphilo, if the burdensome and troublesome heaviness of this
amorous weight should by chance frighten you, the sweetness of the fruit invites you, a lover of labour,
to any sad toil; and if the toilsome perils frighten you, yet the hope of the patronage and help of such
a Nymph ought to make you fierce and persuade you.

Then, my varied wavering having departed from here without delay, I said: O gods above and greatest,
and you sovereign goddesses, powerful over mortals — if this is that most acceptable Polia whom at
present I see, whom without interruption I have carried and keep most preciously stamped in my burnt and
tenacious heart, cleaving with an everlasting glue, from the first years of love until now, I am content
with everything, and beyond her I ask nothing else; but only this I beseech as a suppliant: bind her
likewise to my fervent loves, and that she, with that same burning fire in which I so hardly feed
myself for her and burn consuming, may burn equally, and both of us mailed together; or else loose me
alone.

For which cause I can no longer feign and pretend the bitterness, to hide the strengthened burning. I
am forever dying while living, and living I feel no life; I am cheerful while grieving, and I do not
grieve, and I go on suffering; I consume myself, feeding in the flame, and the overflowing flame grows;
and burning like gold in the strong crucible I find myself solid ice.

Alas, wretched me: this so heavy love troubles me more than heavy Inarime troubles Typhon; it scatters
me more than the ravening vultures the coiled entrails of Tityus; it tangles me more than the
labyrinth's winding; it disquiets me more than the storm-bearing winds the quieted sea; it presses me
more than the biting hounds pressed Actaeon in flight, and more than horrible death troubles sweet
living, it troubles my spirits.

And my tormented heart is more hurtfully gnawed by her biting eyes than the crocodile's entrails are
eaten by the ichneumon. And beyond belief it is so taken up by them with unceasing strokes, as upon an
anvil, more than the Ceraunian mountains often struck by the heavenly thunderbolts. And so much the
more that I cannot, with all the power of my wit,

ponder and understand in what part of the world I find myself. Unless over against and stubbornly
facing a sweet fire of this demi-goddess, which consumes me without bodily hurt.

Whose abundant and yellow hair is to me a knotted snare stretched and set about my hedged heart; her
wide and smooth brow, whitening like lilies, twists me like a rod bound in a garland; the arrow-shooting
glances of her life hang me up, sweet awakenings to afflict me; her rosy cheeks invite me sweetly to
sharpen my pain; her cinnamon mouth makes me long for a sweet torment.

Then her delicious breast, white as winter snow on the northern mountains (which, being in itself an
extreme sweetness), is to me a bitter and hurtful scourge. And her more than human semblances, and her
comely person, drawing my appetite to an imagined delight, cruelly waste me.

And against all these insulting martyrdoms, and against this so perilous a contest, and against impious
and treacherous Cupid, with all these insulting parts of that smooth little body, my provoked heart
vigorously throwing itself in as a strenuous wrestler — nevertheless it could never resist, but, like
Milo beside her, I find myself torn apart, every strength put to sleep, nor can I turn aside from
there, as if I had entered incautiously into the Babylonian marsh.

So the only worthy and fulfilling present remedy and fitting medicine that would offer itself, however
much I felt myself accepted, with all these harshest and intolerable pains of mine, would be that this
goddess should be Polia — she who has secretly set me on fire and burns me without delay, and burns me
all over with the flames of hard Cupid, neither more nor less than Minerva kindled the figure of
Prometheus, the burning fire snatched with a light reed from the running wheels of shining Phoebus.

O Tityus, I should ill persuade myself that my torment were less than yours, while the sword-like
vultures split your warm breast, and thence, without staying, your living heart, torn out and smoking,
and seizing it with their taloned feet, and cruelly tearing it limb from limb with their hooked beaks,
they devour it; and in a little while afterwards, it being restored, they return swiftly to that same
butchery. And the sorrowful carnage begins again from the top.

Likewise, my inflamed breast being opened, two most thieving eyes without pity harshly scatter and tear
my loving heart, and, tearing it, bitingly devour it. Then it is not long in time before her festive and
most joyful aspect heals it again, as if it felt no hurt; and after a little instant, beginning again,
they return to its stricken wounds.

Alas for me. Then, having said this to myself secretly, I began wretchedly to weep, and, sighing, to
call up abundantly the familiar tears to my weeping eyes, and to find the way to long for most hateful
death. And for some space, thus fiercely goaded by an excessive and deadly love, which sorrowfully
stirred me beyond all bound, and with a

burning heat with piteous sighs tormented me. Now, disordered with such anguish, many times I set this
purpose in my mind: to cry out with the highest wailings and say: O more than most beautiful Nymph, my
goddess, and chief and only hope, be moved to pity now, and helping me succour me, for at present I find
myself at the point of dying.

But at once, dismayed, judging this deceitful, I rejected it as a false and light thought; and in an
instant, moved by a raging and roaring spirit, confounding myself, I said: Why do you waver,
Poliphilo? To die for love's sake is praiseworthy. And yet would it ever be, by my sad and malignant
ill-luck, that my sorrowful happening, and my heavy kindlings, and my noble love of such a Nymph should
be recited in the hollowed earth? And then that the fine and pliant reeds should sprout, which,
sounding, should afterwards make plain my growing and hurtful loves?

Not shutting out such wickedness of my wandering thoughts, I said rightly: Perhaps this woman, as she
shows, is a venerable goddess; and therefore talking Syrinx of Arcadia, in the reedy and marshy seats of
the river Ladon, would not have been given, shaken, to the goading and forward east winds, and to the
tumultuous and frost-bearing north wind, and to the blowing and cloud-bearing south, and to the
troubled and rain-bringing wind, if her untimely and unseemly speech in the presence of the goddesses
had been fitting. And answering Echo, by such a likeness, would not have been made into a last voice, if
she had spoken seemly.

And therefore, the gods being of themselves most pious, such contempt and negligent daring makes them
severe avengers. For which cause the companions of slow and searching Ulysses would deservedly have been
kept safe without the mortal peril of shipwreck, if they had not shamelessly and wickedly stolen the
fated herd of Apollo, watched over by the Nymphs Phaethusa and her sister Lampetie. And Orion likewise
would not have known the horrible vengeance, if he had not rashly set himself against cold and chaste
Diana. And the son of burning Phoebus was rashly struck by lightning from highest Olympus, and bound
eternally in the Stygian waves, for using the peony herbs.

If, then, I should show by any sign any unseemliness towards this divine Nymph, might not the like, and
worse, easily befall me? At last I came out of so great a stirring of my quarrelling mind.

Taking, then, the highest delight, I grew calm; and looking at her adorned elegance and contemplating
the comely form of this noble and distinguished Nymph, I wholly comforted myself. Who held plentifully
in herself all that can perfectly delight in love, and all that can be sweetly loved, dispensing so
great a sweetness widely from her festive eyes that, the troubling and unbridled thoughts being driven
out of my disquieted

mind, I tempered it somewhat. And I turned back my sounding sighs, and with flattering hope (O amorous
food of lovers, and often enough joined with a tearful drink) I wheeled my stirred thoughts by another
biting bridle, with so much considered and made pleasure, gazing with an extreme delight upon that most
welcome and native body, upon those rosy cheeks, upon those bright and shining limbs, solacing myself.
By which singular things I kindly comforted and softened my raging desires, redeemed from the furious
angers of too great an ardour, and from the amorous fire so near that they were readily taking light.

*The Nymph leads the loving Poliphilo through other fair places, where he saw countless Nymphs keeping
solemn festival, and cheerfully keeping the feast about a sacred altar with the triumph of Vertumnus
and Pomona. Then they came to a marvellous temple, which he in part describes, and its builder's art.
And how in the said temple, at the warning of the priestess, the Nymph with much ceremony put out her
torch, showing herself to Poliphilo to be his Polia. And afterwards, having entered with the
sacrificing priestess into the holy shrine, before the divine altar she called upon the three Graces.*

I could no longer contend against the heavenly and violent armour; and, the most elegant Nymph having
lovingly gained an irrevocable lordship over wretched me, further on with her (I following her measured
steps), driving me as her equal, she led me towards a spacious shore. Which bordered upon the
flower-bearing and hilly valley, where the adorned little mountains ended at this shore, and the
vine-bearing hills, with their ways shut, enclosing round about this golden country, full of incredible
delight.

Which were of wooded groves of a notable thickness, as though the little trees had been pleasantly set
in order: the yew of Corsica and of Arcady, the fruitless and resinous wild pine, tall pines, straight
firs, careless of bending and stubborn under a weight, the burnable spruce, the spongy larch, airy
torch-pines, and lovers of the hills, kept and tended by festive Oreads. Here we both,

through the green and flowery plain, I hedged about with amorous fire, the notable Nymph guiding as my
leader — I and she went among the loftiest cypress, among the spreading beeches, among the fruitful and
green oaks, abundant with new fruits in their cups, loved and welcome to high-thundering Jove; and hard
oaks with rough bark, and the pricking junipers that love eternity, and brittle hazels, and the ash for
spear-shafts, and the berried laurel, and shady holm-oaks, and knotty hornbeams, and lime trees,
disquieted by the cool breath of the soft west wind spreading through the tender little branches, with
a kindly driving.

All which trees were not of a thick planting, but dispensed at the required distance, and all duly
distributed in a fitting place and aspect, greatly delightful to the eyes, and springlike with leaves.
The country-born Nymphs frequented there, and the wandering dryads, their nimble little bodies girt
with soft and twistable fronds, and their leaping hair above their wide brows; together with the horned
fauns crowned with the hollow reed, and with pithy fennel-stalk, and girt with sharp pine, with the
leaping wanton and swift satyrs, keeping solemnly the faun-feasts, come out of this pleasant and
venerable precinct, with more tender, green and new fronds than that grove of the goddess Feronia put
forth when the dwellers wished, because of the fire, to carry away her image.

We entered, then, where there were measured square spaces hedged about with the bounds of wide,
straight, four-way roads, a pace high, of dog-thorn, or thorny grape, and of ground juniper, and most
thickly bound to a wall-like level of most even box, enclosing the squares of the flowering and dewy
meadows.

In the order of the said hedges I beheld planted symmetrically the lofty victorious palms, with their
fruitful clusters of dates hanging out of their sheaths: some black, some crimson, many yellow, such as
would not be found in dewy Egypt. And perhaps the Dabulan of the tent-dwelling Arabs is not so choice,
and perhaps Jericho does not bring forth such. Which stood alternating with the greenest citrons and
oranges, hawthorn-medlars, pistachios, pomegranates, quinces, tree-myrtles, and medlars, and
service-trees, and many other noble fruit trees, most adorned with fruitfulness, in the fields as if
newly come into the spring.

Here upon the greenness of the flowering meadows, and in the cool shades, in a gathered multitude, I saw
a great troop of unaccustomed and rarely seen people of both kinds, glad together, clothed rustically in
skins, some of the fawn with white spots, dappled and painted, and others of lynxes and of leopards,
others in the leaves of burdock, some of butterbur, and of taro, of mallow, and of the greater
coltsfoot, and of other fronds with various flowers and fruits upon the bare flesh, with buskins of
sorrel leaves, and garlanded with flowers, keeping festival

with a religious dancing, clapping and rejoicing — such as were the hamadryad Nymphs, and, at the
fragrant flowers, the Hymenides, greening again, leaping joyfully before and on every side of the
flowery Vertumnus, bound at the brow with purple and honey-coloured roses, with his lap full of fragrant
and most notable flowers, lovers of the season of the woolly Ram; sitting in triumph upon a most ancient
car, drawn by four horned fauns bound with garlands of new fronds; with his beloved and most beautiful
wife Pomona crowned with fruits, with the flowing ornament of her blondest hair, sitting as his equal,
and at whose feet lay a baked-clay water-clock, holding in her hands a packed horn of plenty of flowers
and ripened fruits with foliage mingled.

Going before the car, near the drawing fauns, two shapely Nymphs bore the standards: one carrying a
spear-trophy of mattocks, two-pronged forks, hoes and little sickles, with a tablet hanging before it
with this title:

*To those who till me I offer the soundest health of body, and steady strength, and the chaste
delights of the table, and a blessed security of mind.*

And the other carried a trophy of certain buds and green shoots joined together, and country
instruments; leaping with an ancient rite and applause, solemnly circling, and going round a sacred
four-cornered altar in the middle of the tufted and flower-bearing meadow, watered by the clearest
springs, religiously set up. Which, with all the exquisite lineaments of a most excellent making, was
distinguishedly carved in white and shining marble.

On each front of which there stood out an incredible relief of an elegant image, almost wholly free of
the ground. The first was a most beautiful goddess with flying tresses girt with roses and other
flowers, with a most thin overgarment rivalling the comely limbs beneath; with her right hand she
devoutly scattered flowers and roses upon a little sacrifice, a little flame leaping out of an antique
three-footed pot; and in the other she held a little branch of fragrant and berried myrtle. Beside her
there stood a winged and most beautiful little boy, laughing, with his wounding tokens, and two doves
likewise. Beneath the feet of which figure was inscribed: *sacred to the flowering spring*.

On the next side, I saw, of wondrous carving, a Damsel, virginal in aspect, indicating a matronal
majesty in the figment, with the utmost praise of the artificer. Crowned with corn-ears, with an
elegant downflow of hair and nymphal habit, holding in the right a stuffed plenty of ripe grain,
and in the other holding three stalks with bearded ears, and at the feet a bound little bundle of
ears lying, with this subscription:
> **FLAVAE MESSI · S.** — "To the golden harvest. Sacred."

On the third face was a Divine simulacrum, nude, with the aspect — with wondrous manner and art
expressed — of an infant crowned with clusters of grapes, all laughing with lasciviousness; a
vine-branch clustered with grapes he held in the left, and in the other a full plenty of grapes,
out of the lips with the fronds and tendrils pendent; at the feet of which stood a wool-bearing
he-goat, with this writing carved:
> **MUSTULENTO AUTUMNO · S.** — "To the must-laden autumn. Sacred."

The last part had a regal image of conspicuous carving, ruddy in aspect and rigid, holding in the
left a sceptre, gazing toward the sky — in the dark, turbulent and stormy air — and with the other
touching the hail-clouds. Behind, likewise, the rainy and cloud-bearing air. Clad in a pelt-
covering over the nude, shod with antique sandals, and subscribed with this title:
> **HYEMI AEOLIAE · S.** — "To Aeolian winter. Sacred."

t:
For this noble figment the outstanding artificer had shrewdly chosen the marble, which — beyond its
whiteness — was veined (in the requisite place) with black, to express the tenebrous, unlit and
nebulous air, with falling hail. Upon the flat of the said venerable Altar, rigidly rigorous, stood
forth the rude simulacrum of the garden-guardian (Priapus), with all his decent and appropriated
insignia. Which mysterious Altar a cupola'd little canopy covered, affirmed and sustained upon four
poles fixed in the ground. Which poles were diligently invested with fruited and flowered foliage,
and the top all covered with manifold flowers; and between each pole, at the rim of the opening, or
gap, of the canopy, hung, fixed, a burning lamp; and, in circuit, ornately, gold foils, by the
fresh and spring-bearing breezes inconstantly vexed, and sounding with metallic little rattles.

At which simulacrum, with the utmost religion and ancient rural and pastoral rite, certain little
flasks, or glass ampullae, with the foaming gore of the immolated Ass, and with warm milk, and
scintillating unmixed Wine, scattering, they broke; and with fruits, flowers, fronds, feast, and
jewels they libated. Now, behind this glorious Triumph, they conducted, with antique and sylvan
ceremony, the little old Janus ensnared, of ropes and tresses twisted of manifold flowers, singing
songs rurally — Talassian, Hymeneal, and Fescennine — and rustic instruments, with supreme joy and
glory, celebratedly exulting, and with solemn applause dancing, and female voices high-sounding.
For which thing, no less pleasure and delight, with stupor, did such solemn rites and celebrated
feasts here invade me, than the admiration of the preceding triumphs.

Then, from here, both of us somewhat progressed, with inexcogitable solace, and proceeding further,
I beheld again, at the clear and fresh founts of the gracious and grassy meadows and shady groves,
the cascade-Napaeae dancing, and the pleasant Naiads playing, and the marine Nereids singing —
clad, some, in the skin of the sea-calf (not harmed by the wrath of supreme Jove), with great bark-
vessels of *estur* in hand stuffed with fruits and flowers, gathered from the gravelly shores, and
with diverse solaces idly making festival. Many were, in their hands, bearers of green Thyrses,
which at the summit were compacted of orange-flowers, with soft fronds, and of Egyptian roses,
yellow and Persian, and of Narcissus-flowers, with handfuls of crimson flowers, and odorous of
*amuletum*; with sylvan Pan the Arcadian, and the demigod sylvan hill-dwellers, and the Dryads, and
many others, and Zephyr with his beloved Chloris — to whom he had conceded the power over the
beautiful flowers — and many active and singing Shepherds, in their songs expert to contend, and
armed with their crooks, praised together, jubilating and applauding, with serious games and jests,
with most-ancient instruments of straw and of reed, and with trumpeting Tibiae of bark, of *scytala*
form, of a strange sound, the amorous and omnipotent Jove — festively glorifying — and the holy
country-life, and making most-devout the Floralian feasts.

For which thing, how much voluptuous pleasure I felt, I leave to judge to whoever in his cogitation
could feign it. Therefore, copiously stuffed with incredible joy, with my most-pleasing companion,
traversing, we continued our happy itinerary and amorous walk. Whence, some time, the eyes from
their sweet prison and binding — and almost proscription — somewhat removing, Lo! looking above the
tender and greenest tops of the wanton trees, I saw a lofty Pterygium (winged pinnacle), above,
appearing to me of a round fastigium (gable), esteeming it to be little distant from the whispering
shore, toward which she, facetious, was leading me. And in which the gliding and sloping little
rivers, that circled the valley, terminated; and from the feet of the most-ornate hills and little
mountains — part grassy, part wooded — ran, with most-swift water, in clearest little channels with
a grassy and sandy bed, one leaping down to a side. And then again, beyond the said Pinnacle, I saw a
superb and eminent cupola, appearing to me covered with livid lead. Which at the summit had a cyma in
octagonal form with columns, and above another cupola, and then eight quadrangular piers, covered by
a single top, in balustered figure, upon which stood forth a stylus with a most-round Triangle fixed,
especially splendent with golden brightness. Whence very pleasingly offered itself to me such a
showing, by which I was not —

t:
— mediocrely moved by ardent desire, to behold that more nearly and perfectly, suspecting reasonably
there to be a great and antique structure; insomuch that, for this, I almost wished to pray my benign
Guide that she conduct me to it — although toward the place we were all the while traversing. But
within myself, castigating such desire, I said: "Alas, I dare not obtain that thing for which, with a
thorny goad and with sedulous vehement impulse, I am solicited — and especially that thing so warmly
desired, which I firmly judge that, obtaining it, I could make myself content above whatever lover.
Therefore, repressing and suffocating, and vainly damning such inconsiderate conceit, not demanding
henceforth of so long a torment help, with the diurnal pasture of heartfelt sighs — why, then, ought
I to ask of this, to me not so opportune (a thing)? Alas, active heart, shared and not wholly mine —
how willingly dost thou follow the rapacious hawk of thy living?" — which, wrapping itself in these
wanton snares and fecund cogitations, caused, exciting in the inflamed breast, a continual palpitating,
as the tear-weeping Pheasant, down from the fronds, impelled to flight by the cruel Falcon, its sad
heart beats it.

And so, by these such amorous corollaries frequently agitated, proceeding somewhat beyond our moderate
pace, with my Venerable Nymph, eloquently confabulating, and of the marvellous things clearly seen by
divine grace affably conferring, with mellifluous eloquence, we arrived finally, a little distant from
the re-beaten shore, washed by the pleasant waves of the restless sea. In this place of most-pleasant
site, we found, of the building-art, a most-ornate, most-excellently-made and antique temple, of
antiquarian workmanship and of the greatest cost, sumptuously skilfully-made, and consecrated to the
physizoic (life-giving) Venus.

This sacred Temple, then, by architectonic art constructed round, and within the quadrangular figure
in the evened Area shrewdly worked out — and as much as the diametral line found, so much did it render
its height; and in the circle contained in the area, a squaring is noted. From one side of which, upon
the diametral line toward the circumference, such space (was) divided into five partitions, and toward
the centre a sixth supplied. From which, having then circled another circular figure, the learned
Architect had raised this egregious structure and superb building — as to the principal parts, with the
commodulation, dimension, and of all the compass and content he had been able (to make) — and the
thickness of the walls and of the exterior Piers, and between one circuit and the other (that is,
between the principal band and the columnation, or Peristyle), the free vaulting. From the centre to
the circumference, then, in ten radii, or partitions, the lines deduced, where —

— cut the circular interstice, he ordained ten arches, resting upon serpentine columns; and, opposite
the solid support, between one encompassing arch and the other, of a facial breadth of two feet, of the
inner circular band, there resided promptly a hewn and polished Corinthian column, of a height as much
as the Ionic of nine diameters (excepting the capitals), of burnished Porphyry — which carried, with the
bronze capital, to the straight architrave, carried round with the frieze and cornice, led up to the
solid of the fastigium of the inflected architrave, or Arch.

Which architrave, frieze, and cornice, at the order of the live (stone), or of the firm, of the
Corinthian, stood forth with as much projection as the perpendicular line of the aforesaid Porphyry
asked — with base and capitals of fine metal caustically gilt and translucent, with elegant *enthesis*,
or swelling. This order, then, of projection was regularly observed throughout all the Porphyry
(columns), balanced and paired, which had to overstand the requisite little wall of the columnation. But
the illustrious Architect, to give the Area a freer expedition, made the intercolumniation passable.

Whence the inflected architraves, with their horns, rested upon the Ophite (serpentine) columns, turned
and lathe-round, illustrable with friction, the due little slab, or plinth, set upon the capital to give
it a solid footing, and not aerial, through the lids insinuated of the said capitals. And under the base
was reserved a half-altar which had to be the little wall, upon which half-altars the bases of all the
Ophite (columns) firmly resided.

The Corinthian (columns) footed upon a sub-column, or truly a sub-base, of the form of a half-Tube, here
and there, with the half-Altars becomingly joined. Which was worked out from two squarings found from the
diameter of the lowest thickness of the Corinthian; there remained a *sesquialter* (one-and-a-half) for
the rest, to little-waves, Tori, Gulets, Knots, and Cymas, or the like lineaments, above and below,
conveniently dispensed, decently conjoined, with the free bases assigned above.

Each Arch stood elegantly decorated of its keystone, with little boys, and alternately of little barks
with flowered foliage. And every triangle (spandrel) specularly shone with a round jasper of varied
colour, its setting egregiously circled, of little-waved foliage translucently gilt.

In the pier of the Arches, opposite, behind the Corinthian, a third of a fluted quadrangular (pilaster)
stood forth, with the base upon the pavement, standing in the face of another (in the band under the
arch that divided the vaults, fixed) wholly similar. The interval of these, from the one to the other,
the radii drawn to the circumstance made, set upon the line of the outermost Piers. Upon the semi-
capitals of which went round a circum-ligation of gracious workmanship.

The half-Tubes and half-Altars were of bright Alabaster, with curving ropes, or bundles, of manifold
fronds and fruits — of *lacterii* (spurges), of medlars, and stalks of Poppy, growing heavy in their
middle descent, of wavering shoots ensnared, suspended and knotted in certain rings comelily adorned.

Under that circum-ligation a little above narrated, between one and the other striated half-quadrangular
(pilaster), in the primary wall was a quadrangular window of one square and a half, as is required in
antiquarian temples. The opening, or lighting, of which artfully occupied a mirror-like, or diaphanous,
plate of *sogobrina* stone, not fearing old age. Whence, in sum, eight windows there were — because one
part the door of the temple occupied, and, directly opposite the Pronaos in front, another part (the
door, with the golden valves, of the rear chapel, or the sacred Adytum, the description of which will,
in another place, be more fittingly treated).

Over against the above-recited quadrangular columns, fixed in the first mural circuit, the piers
projected outside, worked out from the wall of as much thickness as that of the wall — to which their
breadth the lines of the radii of the division, from the centre to the circumference, gave. Which
breadth divided: one portion was for the breadth of the pilaster; the other portion, again deduced into
a twin partition (one here and one there, the other attributed to the collateral Pier), were for an
arching in the solid of the wall, or vaulted, between one pilaster and the other. Of which Piers the
projection, or outlet, divided by a third, usurped the prominence of the vault from the plane of the
scarped wall; and the two thirds the Piers stood forth, in a solid arched wall-and-Piers. This exquisite
observance the elegant Architects praised, so as not to give the wall a rude thickness so great that the
windows should accuse themselves obtuse (deep-set), with conspicuous respect of the rude and superfluous
solid; and for exterior adornment, which vaults in a ring turned themselves, conjoined most-excellently
one to the other with the same thickness, with due binding, from the Piers, carried round upon the wall,
throughout beautifully girt. Not otherwise, between one and the other contrasting arch, opportunely it
stood.

In this intervalled void, between one Pillar and the other — or between the jaws of these arches just-
said — upon the left mural plane, excavated was the window. Which vault, as much as it was distant from
the Pier, so much it circled under the first outer cornice, encompassing the first roof. Ten Piers, or
bones, of the building there were, and as many arches in the solid, with the exterior wall — excepting
the face where, set fast, resided the chapel (sacello).

The said cornice, embracing the round sacello, joined it with the temple. Beyond this binding ascended
its roof, which was a blind cupola, distinct and free of the greater one by itself.

Let us return, then, now, to the interstitial binding above the circum-columnation, or Peristyle — of
the straight architrave, fascia and cornice, stretched perpendicularly above the Porphyry columns —
where there were born, for each stretch of the binding, little half-columns of quadrature, striated, of
egregious Ophite. Upon the semi-capital of which went round a cornice of conspicuous lineament, from
which the convex of the lofty cupola began its beginning above.

Between one and the other of the half-quadrangular (pilasters) just described, I saw a proportioned
window, timely situated, and of a plate of Bononia (Bologna) of Gaul, opaque, constituted in a field
gilt, of artful Mosaic. Which spaces, with commensurate distribution and equal partition, I beheld most-
admiredly depicted, of wormwork tessellation: the property of each Month of the year, with its effect;
and above, the Zodiac occurring, with the Sun operating; and, to that of the Moon, the phases — and she
is called, among the monthly (states), the new little crescent, the halved, and the pre-swollen (full) —
and her circuit, by which the months are included. And the windings of the investigating Sun, the
solstices and the winter-turns, circling; and of night and of day the vicissitude; and the quadrifarious
commotion of the seasons; and the nature of the fixed and wandering stars, with their efficacy. I
suspected that such art was here ordained by the most-noble mathematician Petosiris, or by Necepso. The
inspection of which things (was) enough to draw the inspector, with excessive solace, to a choice and
wondrous speculation — not without egregious spectacle, and elegant fiction, and comely distribution of
figures, with defined painting of colouring and shadings, by which the commodulation of the bodies and
requisite lights, to complacency representing themselves with most-worthy expression of the effects, with
laudable and joyous show to the senses of the soul. A work, without doubt, worthy of pondering, as much
as ever one could contemplate. Then, in one division, the content of the meaning of the aforesaid works,
of antiquarian letters, was elegantly inscribed. The spaces interposed between the half-quadrangulars
were hedged round with bands, carved of comely workmanship.

The remaining walls of the temple, with manifold and various-form Emblemature, were laboriously
incrusted of precious marbles — as best the much-knowing Architect, imagining, could often apply to so
great a magnificence of structure; nor, perhaps, was such made for Ammon. Above the order of the
Corinthians, of most-perfect sculpture, the eloquent Apollo resided, lyring. And above each of the
others, in circuit, upon a fit Altar, of the whole entire, a Muse of *pilates* stone — at the opportune
gestures and office, with the utmost praise of the Statuary most-exquisitely carved — set above the
aforesaid, above, of the encompassing binding.

The huge cupola showed the greatest token, rather of divine operation than of human ostentation. But if
human, not without stupor and accusation of the ambition of so much attempted of the founder's-art by
human wit — for, considering so great a vastness, in one sole and solid casting and pour of metal (as I
judged), I remained most-highly marvelling and hallucinated, damning it almost to impossibility.
Nonetheless, this such Bronze-work was all of Vine springing out of most-beautiful vases, of the bronze
material, standing at the perpendicular and order of the columnation — diffusing the branches, vine-
shoots, or twigs, and Tendrils, dizzily entangling themselves, with most-pleasing conjugation, in
observance of the formation of the convex of the said cupola, one with the other with decent density;
with leaves, clusters, little infants climbing and plucking, little Birds fluttering, Lizards creeping,
in emulation of nature, most-excellently worked out, and all the rest passable (open).

The described works (were) so directly conducted, that, proportioned, in the area they artfully appeared
as much as the natural. Of most-perfect gold, all shiningly gilt. The openings — that is, the void of the
foliation, fruits, and animals — most-fittingly presented themselves stopped with crystalline plates, of
diverse colouring tinged, like translucent gems.

To the congruity of the structure opportune is the integrity of the harmony; for every girdable inner
binding demands the outer girdle. The external piers continued the *areobate* footing, with the three
uneven steps, binding all the base of the temple — as much librated from the area as the inner pavement
was raised — above the *areobates*, or *stylobates*, or Scabelli, in place of a Base: an ornament, with
Tori, Alvei, Fasciae, Gulets, and quarter-circles circling round, and again round the sacello becomingly
circled. Its lowest projection received (worn) from the human foot; and above, the Pilasters. Which, in
the interstice, were pierced through, or tubed, and perforated — that is, the guttering, or compluvium of
the precipitate waters, through the Tubes let down to the ground, were —

— engulfed, of excellent jointing, one conjoined in the tongued (socket) of the other. For in open-air
buildings, stairs, compluvium, or gutters, ought not to be placed: first, for the peril of the slip;
second, he who makes water next to his own feet destroys, and befouls his footwear. Therefore such
inconvenience ought to be fled. The uncovered guttering, by inundating water, excavates the area — and
more enormously, if a resistance of subjacent stone opposes — so that the water climbs so much the more
to the footing and walls, as it defends itself from the drops, from the resulting drips.

Not without grave injury, damage and loss (and, by the ventilating impetus, the water pours through the
walls, rendering them then putrid and earthy, and through the windows leaking, exhausted and vanished
every rendering): by the sprinkling of which, there grows in the joints herbage — cotyledon, or cymbalaria,
maidenhair, digitello, pellitory, and polypody — and, ready to produce little shrubs and wild figs, a mural
ruin, with populous and reviving fibres, or roots, rendering the walls inconstant and rift.

Let us return. The band of the first wall derived its height to the level of the summit, of the thickness
of the inflected Architraves, or Arches, above the columnation, and those of the vaulting, from the wall,
opposite the Corinthian column. Above the surface of which wall — that is, of the binding of the circum-led
cornice — was a little channel excavated. Near the lip of which, toward the temple, terminated the scaled
slope of the bronze and gilt roof. The topmost of which summit, above the curved (dome), evenly began,
opposite the sublime line of the cornice, of the Frieze and inner Architrave. In the said little channel,
above the wall, in the flat of the cornice excavated, the waters that by rain ran down the sloped roof were
poured into the receivers of the Piers. And by this way the rivulets of the conceived rain guttered,
precipitating to the bottom; and by hidden pipes, or subterranean passages, flowed into the Cistern. Which
had a Devourer (overflow-drain), by which the superfluous of the waters went out, and sufficiently for the
sacred things remained.

— showed as much descent, or slope, as that of the scaled and gilt roof-covering — such as was not that of
the Capitol gilt by Catulus, nor such scaling had the Pantheon. In this manner, between the opening of the
wall under the cupola, and between this adjunct of Pilaster (founded, level, upon the external mural
circuit), was born an arch, gapingly open, contrasting, with the lineament of an Architrave. The horns of
which footed on both the sides of the wall and of the Pilaster, upon the capital of a half-quadrangular
(pilaster) intruded in the wall (excepting the facing third of the inner Ophite), and the other in the
adjunct of the Pilaster. The face of which adjunct of Pilaster, in front, was a Niche, or Solium; and
before this Solium, or Niche, perpendicularly above the flat of the Pilaster, was situated, for each, a
most-noble statue, with manifold acts. On the right and left side of which adjunct was seen such sculpture
as on the front of the Pilaster beneath. The last surface of the thickness of the exterior arch was even
with the flat of the topmost Pilaster.

The slip (of the dome), then, from the girdle began, upon which beginning the cupola usurped from without,
and fell upon the Pier, with all that lineament binding itself, that was in the girdle circled under the
cupola; and under this slip the arch made resistance. Which girdle was a denticulate and echinate, or
ovolo, crowning, with the drip-course rolled, or channelled, with the cinquefoils between the whorls
circum-led, perfect with the occurring lineaments.

In the plane of the surface of this binding, or crowning, lay the beginning of the cupola; in the
projection of which was an excavated trough, into which the waters of the cupola derived, running; and
down by the channelled slips they belchingly engulfed themselves into the Pilasters.

Above the slippery (curve) of the cupola, terminating at the Pilaster — that is, at its cyma, or flat — a
bark, or little cartouche, covering, made two contrary volutes: the one accosting the cupola supine, and
the other, near the Pier, resupine, making the volutes with a snail-line. In the inflections of the volume
were born pods, or cases (pregnant of their birth), bean-like, or lupine-like. Which bark was covered with
gracious scales. And above the resupine convolvulus crept, falling upon the scaled undulation, a leaf of
Cynara (artichoke). Which cochlear (spiral) wrapper easily, by the norm of the compass, fittingly wraps
itself — fixing the stable (foot) and turning the semicircle; then placing the stable (foot) between the
led semicircle and the point, opening the compass, and coupling the unstable (foot) with the extreme of the
semicircle, and turning, and so opening, and moving the point — that —
pages.wcap: Section and Ground-plan of Rotunda Temple

t: — the just figure is conducted.

Newly, above the topmost flat of each Pilaster, of wondrous make, was set a candelabrum of illustrious
brass (orichalc), the orifice of which was dilated into a shell-form, in which, unceasingly, of
unconsumable material, an inextinguishable fire burned — which neither by winds nor by rain could be
extinguished. Which marvellous candelabra, of a proportioned and matching tallness, were seen, fittingly
handled (with handles).

From the one and the other handle of which, marvellously, a festoon hung, ensnared and un-knotted in
many parts, retaining itself with most-subtle artifice, of fronds, and flowers, and diversified fruits,
with due pregnancy curving in the middle, and thonged, and passably (openly) excavated. Upon the little-
basket-like binding of the thongs, on the middle Tube, brooded a lively and inane (hollow) Eagle,
grasped-fast, with wings outspread, in the area to the sight showing conspicuously the perfection of the
natural — of the material of the candelabra, with a ballast weight set under, all hollow and cast of most-
subtle surface. Foliage, hollow fruits, and florets, and the other works, subtly reduced. The soffit of
the inner curved-vault, between the columnation and the outer wall, of wormwork, of gilt tessellation
with graphic (design) of most-explicated art, with concurrent colouring, was depicted.

Of the height treating: it is not completable to have only concluded this universal rule — that a round
temple raises itself as much as is its diameter. But it concurs, regularly, to find the height of the
binding above the peristyle (that is, of the topmost line of the cornice): for, the line deduced from the
centre to the circumference of the first circuit, so much presents that height. Then, all the diameter
divided into six divisions, four of those rectified will likewise give the last surface of the upper
binding.

The rule of the descent of the roof ought not to be neglected: one takes the intercapace from wall to
wall, where the ridge-slip ought to be placed, and reduced into two perfect squarings as much as they can
come; and, the diagonal extended, cutting the line, discriminating the two squares — thence, beautifully,
the slope is exacted.

Universally, the Symmetry of this wondrous fabric, by the outstanding Architect elegantly disposed, with
consentaneous bindings, inner and outer, congruous. Much more diffusely the regulation could, to all
conveniences, to the corollaries of the solid, be manifested — and, by those figures of the area, to find
the Height of walls, which here stood straight, as best one could do without obliquity, or straightness,
and —

pages.note: This leaf is a full-page woodcut — the illustration of the Temple of Venus Physizoa. The source transcription holds only the gathering-signature "n iii" at its foot; there is no body text to translate. The image renders the rotunda whose architecture pp. 197–204 describe: the domed round temple on its stepped base, the vine-wrought cupola, the eternal-fire candelabra, and the peristyle.

t:
— its thickness, and whatever least particle and line, and even the cuttings, without error. O unhappy
times and our age — how, by the moderns (using a convenient vocable), is so beautiful and worthy an
invention ignored! For which thing let no one imagine that Architraves, Friezes, Cornices, Bases,
Capitals, Columns, half-Columns, Pavement, Incrustations, Bands, Boarding, and all the Compagination,
Dimension, Partition, should accuse themselves without token of the shrewd and outstanding wits of the
ancients and the elders, exquisitely excogitated and digested. And of Marbles the egregious *xesturgy*
(polishing-art), such as neither the foam of burnt tin renders, nor yet the burnt ceruse.

In the centre of the said Temple stood forth a well-head orifice of a fatal Cistern, with a most-prompt
Chorus of Nymphs in circuit, of prominent carving — in default only of the spirit (i.e. lacking only
breath) — of Alabaster, most-excellently expressed, as best with the chisel one could carve, with their
flying habits and veils.

In the middle part of the closure of the inner summit of the lofty cupola went round a jewel of dense
fronds, of the aforenarrated metallic vines, which in the depth of this heaven ended so perfectly, one
tightly entwined with the other, as best one could imagine. Which fittingly admitted (left) so much
circulation (opening) as showed above, the opening of the inverted ewer-vase. Which circum-led space,
supplying, most-beautifully occupied the viperine head of the furious Medusa, artfully cast of the
material of the cupola — which, among the balled-up serpents, the vociferating mouth and handle-like and
wrinkled brow, stood in the centre, perpendicularly above the Cistern. And out of the extremes of the
mouth came a little conduit, from which, fixed, a most-excellent knotwork perpendicularly descended,
suspended above the well-head orifice.

This knotwork, all of perfect gold, at the lower extremity ended in a ring, which another retained, set
fast to a slenderness of the bottom of an inverted little conch (that is, the opening downward, and the
bottom, sima-moulded, above), thinning, tapering to the ring; and in the resupine lip, of a circuit of a
cubit in diameter, it had set fast four little rings, or clasps, in which four hooks harped (gripped),
from which, ensnared, four little chains hung. And these too, holding, seized a circular plate in the
flat, evenly suspended. Upon the upper circumference of this margin, in incision, brooded four monster-
made girls, with loosed hair, with the forehead wreathed of choice —

— work, cast. And each of these (girls), discriminating itself at the thigh, and the fleshy hips
dissenting, turned those then into antiquarian fronds, with Acanthine foliage; meeting one with the other,
they joined themselves; then toward their flanks, or sides, the voluble ones seized them with a tight fist,
with the harpy-like wings outstretched, toward the little chain — which, behind their shoulder-blades, were
knotted. In the order where the sinuous and jagged fronds of the one and the other girl met, was fixed, at
the back, a hooked Grapple. Which shoots, meeting at their back, joined themselves; and out of the middle of
the binding, above, came certain seeded, half-cracked ears (of grain). And beneath the binding, three little
follicles, four bindings, and four grapples.

From those little scorpions hung another four little chains, which, suspended, retained the marvellous lamp,
of spherical figure and of a cubit's compass.

In the flat of the aforesaid rotundity, in the middle, it was circularly open; and then, by diameter, level,
from one damsel to the other, gaped four round openings, less than two palms in circuit. In these four
little mouths hung four hollow spheres, which, with their own lips, or rims, with an exterior reflex into
themselves, in their opening, and retained in those mouths — so, with artifice, diligently expressed, that
almost all their rotundity was free, appearing wholly pendent below. Which little lamps were excavated of
precious stone, an incomparable work: one of Balas-ruby; the other of Sapphire; the third of Emerald; the
last of Topaz.

The greater lamp, as above is said, was spherical, of most-clean crystal — nor at the lathe would such
justice have been usurped — subtly carved, a work of great exquisiteness, and incredible make. Which, toward
the orifice, had four little handles, justly distributed —

— in four locations, by which, concatenated, hung the mouth (vessel), open of a half-arm; and in this
mouth was let in another urn-like vase, or of cucurbit (gourd) form, likewise of purest crystal.

Which so regularly, let in, hung, that in the centre the light of the lamp burned. Then all the body of
the greater lamp was full of burning water, five times reiterated at the distilling. For which the effect
made me suspect (a marvel), because all the spherical body simulated burning, by the wick being placed at
the middle point. And by this, the sight could not ably fix itself upon it — as, ill, upon the Sun — the
material being of wondrous perspicuity and of subtle make.

No less the unconsumable liquor was most-limpid in the cucurbit bottom, by this demonstration. And likewise
of such liquor the four upper (lamps) burned. Where reflected the vague colourings of the precious stones,
in the greater lamp, and the greater in those, with inconstant splendour vacillating throughout all the
Sacred Temple. And by the mirror-sheen of the most-terse marbles — such an Iris the Sun, after the rain,
does not paint in the air. But above all, a marvellous thing this represented itself to the sight: for the
sculptor-artificer had perspicuously excavated, in circuit, upon the corpulence of the crystalline lamp, of
*cataglyph* (relief-hollowed), or coffered, work, a most-prompt battle of little infants riding upon the
knotty and swift Dolphins, with the tails inspiring themselves (curling), with manifold and dissimilar
effects and infantile efforts — not otherwise than if nature had feigned it; and they appeared not
excavated, but of raised work, and so-made expressed, that the intent of my eyes, away from so delectable an
object, from the accompanying Nymph, they violated (drew off).
— violated. And the vacillation of the light seemed to give motion to the sculpture.

Finally, for the absolution of this marvellous structure of Temple, it remains to say briefly that it was
compacted of quadrates of Augustan stone in part, and part of the above-narrated marble, in perfect
jointing, without iron and timber, with more subtle investigation of sculpture than ever in our century
could be done, nor imagined — nor such did they construct for Apis, the Samnitic-Egyptian God.

Under the bases of the little Pilasters, or quadrangulars — which was the lowest and continuous binding, in
the first band, or wall; and the upper girdle likewise, with the encompassing capitals — went round, in the
most-even pavement, a strip, or band, of finest Porphyry, as much as was the projection of its square, and
contiguous, almost without dispute, another of Ophite. Under the sub-base of the columns was circled, as
much as its thickness, a strip of Porphyry, with two collateral of hardest serpentine, with the order of
the Peristyle in circumduction. The like was seen of the orifice of the cistern, girt in the pavement — a
strip of Porphyry and another of Ophite.

The remainder of the much-admired pavement, between the well-orifice and the peristyle, was of marvellous
emblemature, of little-minutiae, of little tessellation of fine stones circling themselves, elegantly
included, deduced in partition: ten roundels, a foot in diameter, of their colour and species, the one to
the line of the other. There were two of reddening Jasper, most-pleasingly suffused with various spots; two
of Litharmenon, of little sparks of gold, more minute, disseminated of rutilant atoms; two of green Jasper,
variegated with chalcedonic veins, with reddening and yellow spots; two of Agate, confusedly undulated of
milky threads; two, lastly, of most-limpid Chalcedony. And, by the narrowness of the lines toward the
cistern, likewise the circular figures decreased.

Under the vaulting were, in the floor, an *Asaroton* of wormwork emblems — foliage, animals, and flowers,
tessellated of most-minute little bodies, of stone-cuttings diligently tessellated, depicted, and most-
evenly rubbed smooth, or sculptured. Which art Zenodorus had not, in paving at Pergamon; nor such was the
*lithostroton* at Praeneste, in the shrine of Fortune.

Let us return to the cyma, or Pinnacle, of the magnificent cupola — of the same metallic material, refinedly
gilt, above the heaven of the —

— stupendous cupola, eight fluted and *somphe* (spongy), or hollow, columns egregiously rose, with a
noble footing, drawn apart by an interjected and encompassing fenestration, with little arches between
one and the other, upon the collateral piers overstanding. Above which, with an exigent harmony,
*sesquialter* (3:2) of the height, of composite and lineament, were circum-led the Architrave, Frieze,
and Cornice, with the projections level with the subjacent columns. A scaled cupola resided. Above the
projections, level with the substitute columns, resident, for each I saw a simulacrum of a wind, with
elegant expression of its nature — winged, with the wings outspread, and stretched at the shoulders — on
an unstable Peron, or stylus, artfully fixed to turn; and, at whatever blowing wind, all eight *Petasi*
(wind-hats) investigated, circling, involving themselves — the face they turned toward that opposite to
the blast.

In the aforesaid summit of the just-narrated cupola, again eight little Pilasters, with the height of two
squares, rose straight, with an ewer-vase, with the opening inverted, above them. The ascent, then, of the
whole, with exquisite commensuration, and with an object mathematically proportioned to the inspectors.

Upon the bottom of the ewer-vase (so I interpret it, for its form), roundabout, most-beautifully scored of
melon-scoring, was impressed a stalk of the proper metal, which began from the breadth of the bottom,
moderately slender ascending. And by as much as was found the middle of the vase, the stylus, ascended,
sustained a huge hollow triangle, together with the stylus artfully cast. In the summit of which gaped a
round opening; and in the low, corpulent (part), in four locations, it was bored — conjecturing, I
pondered, the shrewd device of the provident artificer for this: that water let in by rain, or conceived
frost, should not occupy it from its office, and to avoid the weight. Through the upper Opening of the said
sphere, free of the lips, the said stylus, or spindle, passed, sharpened at the tip. From the outlet
upward it was as much as from the bottom of the vase to the sphere.

In this fastigium a bronze moon was fixed, eight-day (crescent), as much as she shows, with the horns to
the sky. In the gulf, or sinus, of which sat an Eagle with outspread wings. Under the moon, on the stylus,
were four solid and firm grapples, in which four little chains of the aforesaid metal were retained, and
with the whole bronze-work cast — to indicate, of the founder-statuary —

— statuary, the large fertility of his wit. Whence one could easily judge that such subtlety the shrewd
founder investigated: to found, or cast, an entire little chain without soldering — making a fit mould,
quadripartitely cut, in the centre made a pervious hole, into which is let the first ring, and then, the
formed parts applying themselves into one — infinitely, one derived from the other, lightly it will be
cast.

The said little chains, upon the middle corpulence of the bronze sphere evenly deriving, each in the
extreme, ensnared with itself, retained an airy (bronze) *Chodon* (bell). Which bells, from their middle
toward their low (rim), had comb-like fissures, within which a little ball of fine steel resulted, to
render enclosed the tinkling sound. These bells were, at exigent proportion, agitated by the blowing winds;
upon the corpulence of the hollow sphere they beat, and rendered their tinkle sharp, harmonised, with mixed
booms of the metallic triangle — a grateful and sweet and great sound, curiously excogitated and thoughtfully
found; and perhaps beyond the sound which, at the summit of the Temple of Jerusalem, the pendent chains with
the bronze vases (made), putting the birds to flight.

Lastly, to conclude, remains a rule for understanding all the dimension of the most-celebrated temple. The
wall where were the eight windows — its thickness was one and a half feet; as much the scarped (part), or
that part which turned itself; that same, the outlet of the —

— Pilasters, which, beyond the cornice, usurp the square of all this thickness, on every side — that is,
three feet.

The door, then, of this holy and stupendous temple offered itself antepagmented (framed), of Doric form
and workmanship, all of finest Jasper. And in the fascia of its sublime (lintel), of Greek majuscule
antiquarian letters of pure gold fixed, this saying stood inscribed:
> **ΚΥΛΟΠΕΡΑ** (KYLOPERA) [?the reading and sense are uncertain; the letters are given as transcribed]

The gilded valves, with most-polished ornament of metal, of which door they were, and of most-beautiful
and pervious (open-work) workmanship — so much the more beautiful, as less could their like be made — of
illustrious brightness, closed with an exterior bolt. Which the Conductress Nymph did not dare to remove,
unless first the Divine Priestess of the said venerable and sacred Temple, with the other frenzied long-
haired and most-comely virgins (which in all were seven), religiously unbolted it. These sacred virgins
most-integrally there ministered, most-officious, in the sacred things, to the Priestess-Sage of the
sacrifices; and to her alone to concede the ingress most-deservedly pertained. Whence the sacred virgins,
having benignly respected us, domestically blandishing, accepted us. And, from my faithful conductress
Nymph the cause of her and of my advent heard, to us all — easy and gracious, with large (open) faces —
with them they made us ascend, by seven porphyry stone steps, to the egregious door, bound with the
encompassing footing of a magnificent and elegant propylaeum.

There we found a noble pause, or little area, of a square of blackest and indomitable stone (such as would
not be found in the Euganean fatherland), even and lucidly rubbed smooth, hedged in most-beautiful
emblemature. Before the holy threshold of the dedicated valves, all inter-excavated (intaglio'd), and in
the excavations intersecting little barks of Cytherean conch, of the most-beautiful intersected lineaments
that ever to human eyes most-pleasantly could present themselves. In this place, all affirming themselves,
and both of us, the sacred Priestess began then to make a prayer. Then, in reverence, the Nymph and I
inclined ourselves. What she said to herself, I certainly ignored — because, my head somewhat bent, without
delay the most-ready and exploratory eyes, to the unseen whiteness and polish of the most-vague feet of the
accompanying Nymph, I carried back. Where, again, a little portion of the glittering right calf was
uncovered; for, moderately, by her act moving, the most-tenuous lappet gave way, removed, laying bare the
whitest whiteness of the snow-making —
— and bristling Boreas.

And then, incontinently, an enucleated admiration succoured in the warm memory: that, it being natural
that whiteness disgregates (scatters) the visual power, this (whiteness), with so much delectation, drew
and congregated all the seeing into itself — not only not harming it, but, to the utmost solace and
extreme pleasure, that so precious object, viscidly retaining it bound to itself, and taken, occupied it.
Whence, the Sacred Woman's devout prayers to the Gods Forculus and Limentinus, and to the Goddess Cardea,
being sincerely finished, and (all) righting themselves, the beautiful Nymph (I alone persisting, with
eyes fixed on her voluptuous operation) — nor for all that would I ever have moved myself, had not the
most-subtle cloth returned to re-cover the divine delights.

Then, suddenly, by the libation-woman the Bolt removed, those twin valves — not with a strident noise, not
a grave rumble, but an acute and grateful murmur, reflecting through the vaulted temple — hissed sweetly.
And, animadverting this, I recognised (it), by seeing under the extreme part of the ponderous valves, of
the one and the other, a voluble and turned little Cylinder, which, by the axle fixed in the valve, upon a
terse and evened plate of hardest Ophite inverting itself, and by the friction, made a most-acceptable
tinkling.

Beyond this, reasonably I was stupefied that the valves, each by its very self, without any impulse, opened
themselves. Whence, then, all having entered, of a sudden — without looking elsewhere, there affirming
myself — wishing to investigate whether the said valves, so timely and moderately, by a counterweight were
drawn, or by some other instrument: whence I beheld a divine device. For in that part where, one with the
other, the valves met in the tongued closure, from the inner part, was a plate of fine steel soldered upon
the metal, most-terse.

There were then, marvellously, two little Axles of a third (foot) in breadth, of best Indian Magnet (to
which the Diamond does not dissent — of Callistone the lover, to human eyes outstanding, by the *scordeon*
made mortal (weakened)) — singularly opportune to navigators — which showed, of their fit colour, cerulean,
smooth and illustrious, fixed most-polishedly in the thickness of the opening of the marble wall (that is,
in the jambs, contiguous to the antae of the artful door). Then, in this manner, by the violence of the
rapacity of the Magnet, the steel plates were violated (drawn); and consequently, by themselves, the valves,
with temperate slowness, unbolted themselves. An excellent and most-exact work — not only to see, but beyond
measure of subtle device. What improbity (audacity) of an artificer's investigation!
pages.wcap: Procession of Seven Virgins to Altar

t:
In a tablet of Magnet, to the right of the ingress, was carved, of exquisite antiquarian Latin letters,
that celebrated Virgilian saying:
> **TRAHIT SUA QUEMQUE VOLUPTAS** — "Each is drawn by his own pleasure." *(Virgil, Eclogue II.65)*
On the left, the tablet I saw, of most-ancient Greek majuscules, elegantly inscribed:
> **ΠΑΝ ΔΕΙ ΠΟΙΕΙΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΤΗΝ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΦΥΣΙΝ** — in Latin, "Each ought to do according to his own nature."

Raising then the eyes, curiously stimulated, to the magnificence of so great a Temple, and to the vastness
of the noteworthy and sky-reaching cupola, with the other most-exact parts — of ambition, and of outstanding
artifice, of divine device, and of superb workmanship, and wondrous lineaments, of stupendous ostentation,
seasoned most-marvellously. And much more marvellous I judged the incredible beauty of the divine Nymph,
which enticed my inspecting eyes, and held all my soul — insomuch that from the right disquisition of
whatever considerable part of it (the temple) I might move, and she alone, drawing, coarcted (me) to
contemplate her with stupor and marvel. Give pardon, then, reader, if I have not perscribed every fitting
particular.

And so, then, the sacred Priestess entering the Temple, with the ingenuous and outstanding Nymph, and I
pertinacious following her, and with all the other sacred Damsels — with their most-rich hair falling, most-
ornate, over the milky necks, dressed in most-choice purple, and above, worn back, the most-tenuous cotton
(robes) shorter, or curt, than the first garment — to the fateful orifice of the mysterious cistern, devout
and festive, they conducted us.

Into which, as was said, no other water entered save that which, through the perforated Pilasters, from the
water-channels and compluvia of the fastigiate Temple, freely, without harm to the structure, poured itself
in. The high priestess there made a nod to the virgins, and they went into an Adytum sacristy; we three
alone remained.

And lo, with the utmost veneration, maturely, one carried, with registered procession, the ritual book,
duly invested with velvet of Cyan silk, of most-round pearls-in-union, in the form of a flying little
dove nobly of padded re-weaving, with little gold handles — each of them (the virgins) marked with
Pancarpies (all-fruit garlands) on the comely head. Another brought two most-subtle little veils,
lily-decked, and two purple Tutuli (fillet-caps). The third had the holy brine in a golden vase. The
