fourth held the *secespita* (sacrificial knife) with an oblong ivory handle, round and solid, joined at
the pommel with silver and gold, and nailed with Cyprian copper; and, as well, a *praefericulum* (ritual
jug). The fifth was bearer of a hyacinthine *lepista* (bowl), most-eyeing (beautiful), full of fountain
water. The sixth bore a golden Mitre, with richest Lemnisci (ribbons) pendent, throughout ornated
copiously with precious and most-refulgent gems. All these, a little priestess, candle-bearer, preceded,
with a Candle never yet kindled, of candid, most-purged, and virgin material. These delicate virgins,
taught to do the sacred and divine things, and scrupulous at the ministries — more expert than the
Etruscan discipline — and, at the sacrosanct sacrifices, with ancient institute apt and most-observant,
to the pontifical Priestess, with obstinate religion reverent, presented themselves.

And there, with the utmost devotion, and with ancient rite, the sage seeress first accepted a Tutulus, and
bound the hair; then set over it the superb Mitre; and in the middle of the precious Mitre, tightened above
the most-tenuous little veil, covering the holy head.

The other Tutulus, with the other little veil, she gave to the Nymph. And she, without delay, having ornated
the blonde head with the Tutulus, set over it the veil. Both the veils were bound in the crisping (of the
hair), and conjoined, with a stupendous jewel — of most-shining and full-of-colour Sapphire, the one
consigned to the Nymph; but that of the Priestess, of *Ananchitides* (a divination-stone).

Vested, then, devoutly, over the orifice of the mysterial Cistern, without delay she made me approach there;
whence, having accepted a golden little key, with religious observance she unsealed the bolted Well. Where the
sacrificer, consigning to that Virgin who had carried the Mitre the candid candle, took, venerating, the
Ritual book; and, having opened it, put herself before the high Prophetess. Who began, low, in the Etruscan
tongue, somewhat to read. Then, scrupulously, she took the sanctified Brine, and, with many sacerdotal
signings, with the right hand into the thundering Cistern she poured it. Then she made, from the ardent torch
(of which the Nymph was bearer), the pure candle be kindled.

This done, she made the ardent torch be turned, with the little flame downward, into the middle of the
orifice; and, interrogating the Nymph, said these words: "Daughter, what petition and desire is thine?" She
answered: "Holy Priestess, grace, for this one, I ask — that together we may come to the amorous realm of the
Divine Mother, and drink of this holy fount." And to me likewise she said: "And thou, my son, what askest
thou?" Humbly I answered: "I, most-sacred Lady, not only the efficacious grace of the supernal mother
supplicate, but above all — that she, whom, doubtful, I esteem to be my most-desired Polia, I beseech that by
her, more ambiguous, in so great an amorous torment I be not thus retained." The divine Priestess said to me:
"Apprehend, son, then, now, that kindled torch, from her pure hands, and, holding it thus, with me three times
sincerely, in this manner, thou shalt say:

> 'Just as the water shall extinguish this burnable torch, in the same manner, the fire of love re-kindle her
> stone-made and gelid heart.'"

With the holy rite, and with those proper words which the Hierophant said to me, saying — at whatever
terminated and finish, all the expert priestess-virgins, with venerable ministry, this responsory said: "**So
be it.**" At the last time, the ardent torch, into the frigid Cistern, she made me, with reverence, immerse.

Not so soon did I do this holy command, than she, taking the precious hyacinthine *lepista*, and with a
little cord of gold and of crimson and green silk (deputed to such office), infusing it into the cisternal
water, drew out of the blessed water, and, with religion, offered it to the Nymph alone. And she, with prompt
devotion, drank it. Immediately then the hieratic Priestess, with the golden little key, diligently re-shut
the covering of the Cistern; and, somewhat reading over the holy and efficacious prayers and exorcisms, she
enjoined the Nymph to say, three times, these words toward me:

> "May the divine Cytherea hear thee, to thy vow; and, propitiated in me, may she nourish her son."
> Responsory from the virgins: "**So be it.**"

The said ceremonies religiously terminated, the Nymph, in that instant, reverent, at the sandalled feet of
purple re-woven with gold, ornated with manifold gems, of the Priestess, having prostrated herself — of a
sudden she made her rise up, and gave her a holy kiss. And to me then the Nymph, boldly turned, with her comely
presence placid, full of pious semblances, with a sigh come warmly from the base of the inflamed heart, thus
said to me:

"Most-desired and my most-cordial Poliphilo — thy ardent and excessive desire, and thy sedulous and
pertinacious love, from the chaste college has wholly stolen me, and has constrained me to extinguish my
torch. And for this, henceforth — although thou reasonably didst suspect that I was she, notwithstanding that
—

— until here I had not revealed myself to thee — nonetheless, no small fire has it been to me, to keep it
occult and concealed, and thus so long suppressed. But be that as it may, I am, without doubt, that Polia of
thine whom thou so lovest. Congruous, therefore, it presents itself, that so worthy and so-made a love be not
immune from vicissitude, and from equivalent reciprocation and requital. For which thing, behold me, to thy
inflaming desires, all most-ready! Behold, that I feel the ignited fire, from most-fervent love, throughout
all of me to grow up, and to scintillate! Behold me, the end of thy bitter and frequent sighs! Behold me,
most-delightful Poliphilo, a salubrious and present remedy to thy grave and molesting sorrows! Behold me, to
thy amorous and acerb pains a consort principal, and of the whole partaker! Behold me, with my profuse tears,
to quench thy cordial burning, and, for thee, to die, prompt and most-surrendered!"

And, for the Pledge (*arra*) of all this — "Take (me)!" — (embracing me, straining me) she gave me,
lip-to-lip, a little-biting and sipping kiss, full of divine juice; and, provoked by singular sweetness, from
the starry eyes some few little pearls in the form of little tears (fell); insomuch that, by her blandishing
speech, and by the salivous and most-pleasing kiss, from head to feet all inflamed I was altered, melting
myself into sweetest and amorous tears, and wholly lost myself. And likewise the sacrificing Priestess, with
the others standing by — moved by singular sweetness — could not contain themselves from little tears and
sweet little sighs.
pages.wcap: Two Virgins Offering Swans and Doves

t:
Which thing the infecund and fasting tongue would not know how to gather, nor so many fit words to beg,
that I could condignly express even a little of what the enkindled heart made of it, in so sweetest a flame
as, in every part, o'erwove it. I remained, then, like one fallen of the Epilepsy. Ultimately, these
amorous and holy gestures and ceremonial rites — in so singular and choice a sweetness and incredible
delight, by love, expedited — I found myself almost in an unthought experience of dying content.

The Hierophant said: "Let us proceed, Polia, then, to the completory of the inner sacrifices of our
sacral undertaking." Now toward the round and blind Sacello — situated directly opposite the door of the
magnificent temple, and with it artfully joined and contiguous — all, composedly, went. Fabricated of
antiquarian and unwonted make, and noble material.

Which was all of stone, diligently re-squared to the form, of precious **Phengite** marvellously built,
with a cupola'd and round roof, of a single and solid rock of the said stone. Such was not, of such
marvel, the Sacello of the isle of Chennim in Egypt, nor that of the celebrated Sacred (place) of Ravenna.
Which stone, of such miraculous nature, that — not being windowed, but all obtuse (closed), and having only
the golden valves — throughout, clearly, it was illuminated (a secret absorbed by it, hidden from our
cognition, from its parent (the sun)); and therefore thus is it denominated. In this interval, two of those
virgins, unburdened, and by precept gone, carried, with sincere veneration: one, a pair of whitest male
Swans, grateful in the auspices, and a most-ancient little urn with sea-water; and the other, a pair of
candid Turtledoves, by the feet bound together with crimson silk, upon a wicker basket full of vermilion
roses and oyster-shells — and, near the golden valves, upon a sacred and quadrangular *anclabris* (offering-
table) disposed, devout and venerating, let them repose.

And there, the golden valves unsealed, together they entered. But I affirmed myself upon the holy and
reverend threshold. And with vigilant eyes, immovably fixed on the most-beloved object, respecting, I saw the
admonitress bidding that my Polia — true *myropolis* (perfume-seller/sweet one) — should genuflect upon the
sumptuous pavement, and, with sincere devotion, prostrate herself.

Which pavement was marvellous, all of gems, stony, orbitally composed, with subtle make, with manifold and
elegant knotting politely distinct — a work bonily tessellated, disposed in greening leaves, and flowers, and
little birds, and other animals, according as opportune was the grateful colour of the precious stones,
splendid, shining, with perfect evening — from which, doubled, it re-showed those who had entered.

Upon this, then, my little-bold Polia, having religiously denuded the milky knees, with the utmost elegance
genuflected — more beautiful than ever Mercy saw (knees) dedicated to herself. For which thing I stood
suspensefully attentive, with silent lips. And, so as not to interrupt the holy offerings, and contaminate the
propitiations, and interrupt the solemn prayers, and the mysterious ministry, and perturb the altar-
ceremonies, the wicked sighs, by valid love inflamed, I duly incarcerated.

Now, before a sanctified Altar — in the middle of the little sanctuary laboriously situated, of divine flame
lucent — genuflected, humbly, she stood.
pages.wcap: The Altar in the Temple of Venus

t:
The demonstration of which Altar, succinctly saying, I beheld a conspicuous device of unwonted make. The
lowest of the said, upon the stepped and marble footing, was a round little slab. Upon which undulated an
auricular foliage, most with polish jagged, and choicely cauliculate, ending its point at a little cord, or
knot, or fillet, contained upon the little slab. And likewise, at the birth of the encompassing foliage,
sat above another little cord; and between this and another was pressed a *trochlea* (pulley-moulding)
moderately channelled, and then a little cornice. Upon the bracket, or plane, of the said Trochlea, over-
stood another regulated rotundity; then, somewhat gulleted, it contracted itself toward the flat and
unencumbered surface. In the middle part of which stood forth a striated stylus, more stretched in the lower
part, upon the flat, with a proportioned base. The diameter, then, of the inner rotundity of this stylus
divided: one partition was consigned to the encompassing projection; the upper head had two portions, with
turned gulets, and the lowest also duly reserved.

The aforesaid stalk covered an inverted flat rotundity, turning in projection as much as the extreme outlet
of the lips of the subjacent Trochlea, ornated in the upper part, in the extreme circuit, in a sloped
demonstration, with a Sima of noteworthy foliage, from an egregious little cornice most-polishedly being
born. In the circled content, then, of which little cornice, beautifully occupied the opening of an elegant
flower, in balustered lineament fashioned, with the calyxed lips over the flat lambent, and quadripartite
into most-pleasant acanthine foliage, gaping. Under which, in the jagged discrepancy, subsided another
leaf, artfully carved. Upon the point of which, after the due lineaments, egregiously rounded a knot of
exquisite expression. To which, fixed, set, dilatedly stood forth an antiquarian platter of purest gold,
with the lips broadish, and a little lacunate (hollowed). In the flat rim of the lips, alternately, stood
forth incomparable Diamonds and Carbuncles, with outstanding pyramidal fashioning, in the circuit
marvellously disposed, of incredible thickness. Let yield here the *Scyphus* of most-strong Hercules, the
*Cantharus* of pleasant Bacchus, and the *Carchesium* dedicated to immortal Jove.
pages.wcap: Temple Ceremony: Miracle of the Roses

t:
At the margin of the soffit of the inverted flat, in the rim, evenly distant, were contained four most-
beautiful handles, deriving, and solid with the Trochlea; their volutes were under the inverted flat, and
ended above the Trochlea, with the cochleate whirl, spreading with the slope of the little slab. Then,
moderately, they inverted themselves toward the soffit, at a grateful up-curve, submitting themselves to it
with the whirl resupine, and the other supine.

This marvellous sculptile was all of one solid of finest jasper, of manifold mixture of colouring most-
admiredly coming together, and in whatever part with incredible and most-exquisite lineaments. A work, most-
certainly, not worked out by force of chisel, or scalpel, but with unknown artifice marvellously expressed.

From the marble and stepped footing, up to the beginning of the stylus exclusive, it was raised a cubit; the
stalk as much; the remainder, up to the golden platter, a foot and a half. Thence, above, a quadrant: from
one upper volute to the other spread gold threads, through the middle of which were threaded, in longish
berries, coruscating balas-rubies, bored, and of most-refulgent Sapphires, and of scintillating Diamonds,
and of springing Emeralds, with gracious and amicable colour-alternation strung, with inestimable and
monstrous pearls — such that, without doubt, such a gift Octavian did not make to Capitoline Jove.

In the inversion of the lips of the golden platter, quadrifariously, perpendicularly, hung orbiculate gems,
and pierced, through which, pervious, let in, a gold thread, threaded, they were retained, suspended, and
bound to a clasp, free in the grapples — larger than a hazelnut, seven to a thread. At the extreme of the
thread, interdicted (finished) by an elegant little floret, with the little spirals of varied silken thread,
gold, and silver, intermixed. Again, from one clasp to the other likewise knotted, gold threads, gemmed,
spread in the aforesaid manner —

— and order, but of number nine, in the middle with gracious inflection curving. The platter, within and
without, with a half-explication of most-excellent expression of little boys, little monsters, flowers, and
foliage, copiously decorated; and the whole presented itself most-admired and marvellous artifice.

Before, then, the aforewritten and most-sacred Altar, of incredible cost and artifice, of a sudden the intent
little priestess, admonished, opposite the sacrificing Polia, with the ritual book open, venerating,
presented herself. And all (the Priestess excepted), in that manner, upon the stony, sumptuous and bright
floor, bowing, genuflected. And in this celebrated and solemn *eusebia* (piety), with voices devout, and
tremulous supplicating, I heard, with such an oration, the three divine Graces invoked, reading:

> "O joyful **Aglaia**; O verdant **Thalia**; O delectable **Euphrosyne** — Charites (Graces) divine of the
> high and high-thundering Jove, and of Eurynome most-beloved daughters, and of the amorous goddess most-
> observant handmaids and unceasing servants. From the waves of the Acidalian fount of Orchomenus in Boeotia,
> or from the blessed seat and assistants at the side of the venerated Throne of Apollo, benignly conjoined,
> depart (hither). And, as divine Graces, to my devout prayers piously succour, propitious — that, in his
> (her) divine sight and venerable majesty, it may please (her) these my religious dedications, and my pure
> and votive sacrifices, and the poured supplications, with maternal affect moved, to hear."

Finished the holy and sincere oration, all, singing, made the responsory: "So be it." For which thing, having
I, with most-devout auscultation, venerating, heard, and the holy oration clearly understood, with the utmost
sincerity of heart I stood attentive, and, into myself all that revoked, with scrupulous diligence, and with
exploring eye, immovable, such mysteries I considered. And likewise I, genuflected, observed the expertise of
the antiquarian and sacral ceremonies of the divine Priestess, excessively commending, above all, with what
elegance of promptitude Polia adapted herself to such and so great a *mystagogy* (initiation). Most-intent,
nonetheless, upon that which of it ought to follow.

I cannot in the least let myself be persuaded that such rites, ceremonies, sacrifices were found out by Numa
Pompilius, nor at Caere of Tuscany, nor ever in Etruria, nor by the holy Jew; nor with so much religious
observance and order did the Memphitic Seers sacrifice and burn-offerings to Apis in Egypt, immersing the
golden patera in the Nile; nor yet with so most-religious a veneration, in the city of Rhamnus of Euboea, was
Rhamnusia (Nemesis) worshipped; nor was Jupiter Anxur worshipped with such superstition; nor those who, at
Feronia inspired, found such rites — walking without harm upon the kindled coals. Nor so entranced were the
Edonian Clodones, nor the Mimallones, aspired by the numen, as in the present they were entranced.
Deservedly I judge (beyond that which I have openly beheld) that, by the things prepared and superstitiously
disposed, (a marvel) ought to succeed. For, of the hair, the golden Polia Nymph — of such-made office worthy,
in the sacred things imbued and initiated — no sooner saw the nod of the sacristan monitress, than, from the
most-clean pavement, without voice, delay, or noise (no other one moving), most-promptly, religiously, she
rose. Whence, by the sacred monitress, to a wondrous hyacinthine little urn, set apart in the sacello, she
was conducted — such as, of such artifice, Mentor never knew to make.

And I, most-attentive, regarding her, in all acts scrutinously observed. And in aspect now I saw her such as
the most-lucid Phoebus, with the new day, colouring, paints the fresh aurora. And there, ceremoniously, with
prompt and untouched hands, an odorous liquor she drew out; and her milky and vermilioned face, breathing
purpling roses, with the delicate moistened hands, all shrewdly, she irrigated. Whence, thus devoutly
purified, with more sincerity than perhaps had the virgin Aemilia — before the step of the most-holy Altar,
where stood a wondrous golden candelabrum (which was of most-exact and much-admired expression, and elegantly
circum-ornated and knobbed with thick gems; in its summit stood forth, exigently, a round opening of a little
shell, or a platter, less than an arm's embrace) —

In this, then, was placed the sweetest sperm of the huge whales (ambergris); odoriferous musk; the crystalline
and fugitive Camphor; odorous Ladanum of great Crete; *Thymiama* and Mastic; both the Storaxes; the almond-
scented Benzoin; the ponderable Aloewood; *blatte-bisantie*, or Indian nails (onycha); and the happy germens of
Arabia. Which all precious things were, with distributed weight, most-excellently graded. To which the
solicitous Polia, and with —

— exquisite diligence, venerating, admonished, set the ardent candle. Then, when these aromatics she had
kindled, without other thinking she extinguished the candle, and set it apart.

In which smoky little flame, and of incomparable fragrance shining, having placed there a little branch of
arid myrtle, she kindled (it); and of a sudden, upon the sacrificial Altar (whence she had taken it),
returning it kindled, all the other little branches placed upon the said altar she set afire. Whence,
intent and affectionately taught, into this fire she threw the pair of candid turtledoves — first
diligently plucked, and upon the sacred *anclabris* table throat-cut, un-backed with the *secespita*, and
together bound with gold threads, and knotted, and with purpling silk — having, with the utmost veneration,
the warm gore reserved in the *praefericulum*. Thrown, then, the immolated turtledoves into the odoriferous
flame and burning, the seeress, precentor of the rubricated rites, began to sing, and psalm, and, following,
all alternating. But before the fore-dancing Priestess, two of those, with Lydian Tibiae, preceded, most-
sweetly sounding, with the Lydian mode and tone (such as Amphion could not find out); and then Polia and the
others, one following the other, each holding in hand a branch of odorous and flowered Myrtle. Dancing in
chorus, then, with time, step, and continence, with even uniform distance, and leaping with solemn and
religious *thiasi*, with intoned voice concordant to the sonority, produced forth from the virginal breasts,
reflexed with incredible symphony under the obtuse cupola, around the incensed Altar, thus rhythmically
saying:
> "O holy fire of odour: thaw the ice of every heart; placate Venus with love, and grant us her ardour."

In this mysterious manner singing, and tibia-sounding, with most-elegant chorus, orbitally they gyred, while
the sacrifice burned. And, extinguishing thus, the little flame smoked. I think that those odours were to
suffocate the stench of the roasted flesh, beyond the (main) purpose. Then, no sooner was it extinguished,
than of a sudden, to the pavement, all silently (the Priestess excepted) they prostrated themselves. For
which thing it was not long time, that I openly, out of the holy smoke, saw a most-beautiful little spirit,
oracular, and of form other than human, as beautiful as, with shrewd discourse and investigation, one could
imagine. And at the divine shoulder-blades a pair of arched little wings it had, with an unseen and unwonted
light — which, not without some lesion of my eyes regarding it, most-avidly, the lost heart truly felt. With
so vehement an impetus, more than the thunderbolt created of water —

— of fire, cloud, and of fulminating wind. Whence, the sacrificer, aware of me, made a gesture that I not
frighten myself, and with a token that I keep silent.

Which pretty boy, in the little swelling hands, bore a myrtle crownlet; and in the other, a little arrow of
ardent, scintillating fire. And on the summit of the divine head, downed with little gold threads, went round
a most-precious crown of most-splendid diamonds. Circum-fluttering three times the incensed and smoking Altar,
at the last, uncoerced, he resolved himself, and so dissolved himself in the manner of nebulous smokes in the
air; and from the eyes, infuscated by so much shining refulgence, he took himself, and vanished
incontinently.

Which mystic and divine things, in that guise marvelling, and such-made a portent having I, trembling, seen —
some space in the soul considering — I remained thought-heavy, full of devout horror. And after a little, the
intrepid monitress made all the virgins rise up; and, taking a golden little rod in the purified hands,
ordained that my most-choice Polia — from the ritual book open before her, held by the little priestess,
reading, and according to the rubrical orders — should take of the remaining ashes from the cremated
sacrifice. Which, with singular veneration taken up, in a golden sieve prepared for such ministry, upon the
venerable step of the dedicated Altar, sifting, most-aptly she riddled, with so shrewd a promptitude as if
another had ever, most-devoted, operated (it). Where the most-erudite monitress, the other fingers of the
left hand contracted, made her extend the ring-finger; and in the holy ash she expressed certain characters,
with most-exact diligence, such as, in the pontifical ritual volume exemplar, marvelling, limpidly she painted.

That the most-diligent Polia had done this — the sage monitress made Polia, and all the others, again upon the
precious pavement humbly genuflect; and, most-accurately upon the ritual index marvelling looking, likewise she
too, with the golden little rod, superstitiously, in that same ash, signed some mysterious figures.

For which thing I, stupefied and totally alienated, and made all timid — insomuch that on my head not a hair
remained that was not raised — with the soul much suspended, doubting, thought-heavily, in this solemn and
sacred propitiation, that my ingenuous Polia was not stolen away (like Iphigenia), and some other animal, or
damsel, put in — and of losing, in a moment, all my desired good: whence the heart smitten, and into itself
concluding all the little spirits, without vital vigour almost I found myself. Nay, so strongly it shook me,
as the mobile reeds, wind-blown by the impetuous and wanton breezes; and more tremulous than the wooden
shavings, and with the mind vibrating, more than the thin sedges in the marshes, by forceful winds —

— impulse, vibrate. But, be it as it might, the ever-vigilant eyes from my sacrificing Polia I never
dislocated, but, with suspectful admiration, pertinaciously observed, noting what most-aptly she did, and
together the high Priestess.

Who, the ritual seized, with many signings, and with innate sanctimony, exorcised all those things that to
pious love might be impediment and noxious. And a branch of sanctified rue — presented to her by one of those
ministers, dipped in the Hyacinthine little urn, in the liquor with which Polia had made fluid her comely
face throughout — she asperged all, and all (the virgins), and me. The holy aspersion performed, and then
collected the other myrtle branches and this of rue, one of the ministers admonished, the golden little key
received from the Priestess, she devoutly opened the well of the cistern. And within, the aforesaid little
branches, and the little feathers of the immolated turtledoves, she immersed, holding the well open and
waiting. Beyond this, she those holy ashes, somewhat reading over most-holy execration, sanctified again.
And with obstinate ceremony, those charactered ashes, with a little brush of odorous hyssop (with gold
threads and murex silk bound into a little clump), she gathered up. And, having put them in a palm-sized
little box, with solemn religion, she preceding, and Polia with the others venerating following, to the lip
of the sacred cistern (opened), in order they came.

Which little box, the Nymphs singing measured hymns with decent offering and censing, within she immersed;
and then, buried, re-shut the cisternal mouth. Having she this immersion sincerely made, with that procession
and order they returned into the marvellous sacello. Where the divine Altar three times with the *molucra*-rod
she struck, with many arcane words and conjuration. Making demonstration that, to the pavement, again all
should prostrate themselves — she standing on foot, and with the pontifical (book) open, the little priestess
before her genuflected most-devout — with low voice, pausingly, thus praying, in our tongue she said:

"O most-holy and inspired **Erothea**, pious mother, and illustrious, unceasing and valid patroness of the
ardent and holy loves, and of the amorous fires, and of the sweetest conjugations untiring helper. If, to
thy divine numen, from her the invoked graces have arrived — by which grateful and accepted be her excessive
ardours, and her already-vowed heart — render thyself pious and yielding to her poured prayers, full of
affectionate and religious espousals and instant entreaty. And remember the exhortatory and divine
persuasions of Neptune to furious Vulcan, by thee sedulously made, when, from the Mulciberian (Vulcan's)
nets, bound with amorous Mars, thou wast loosed unharmed; and to thy supernal clemency it pleased thus to
hear me. And, propitious, grant to fulfil the determined vow and fiery desire of these two.

"Wherefore, by thy blind and winged son — she being, in this her tender and florid age, apt to thy holy and
laudable service, and to thy sacred ministries disposed, separated from the colds of Diana — to thy amorous
and divine fires (conserving nature), with the utmost and integral devotion, she wholly prepares herself. And
already, by that wounding son, her soul pierced through, and out of the chaste breast her soft heart uprooted,
she feeling (it) — he not refusing, but patient, and meekly inclining himself — that (heart) —

— with singular religion and approved devotion, into the divine fire of thy most-sacred Altar thrown, and with
special sincerity dedicated, without remission, inflaming, she offered it. And now, feeling the amorous
heaviness that protrudes and presses in her burnt heart, for the atrocious love of this her young man, easy and
pertinacious, and with unchanged soul she disposes herself — worthily adapting herself to thy delectable and
honourable ardours — and so much the more fervid, as the more thy divinity, entreated, will lend her favour.

"Therefore, both being most-desirous coveters of consequuting thy merits, and of feeling the holy graces, and
of seeing thy most-holy numen — O **Amathuntean** genetrix — for both, I, in the present, pray, orate, and
supplicate, and, adoring, beseech: in this her good and sincere piety, that they may navigate and cross over
(by means of thy most-potent son) to thy delicious, triumphal and glorious realm. And, by me, mediatress and
most-observant religious of thy mysteries, fulfil the urgent and stimulating desires, and extinguish the
subtly-rising incitements, and grant (them) to come to the ordained end of thy venerable sacrament.

"Be moved now, most-pious **Autophies** (self-born) Goddess, and untiring Mother of mortals, benign
Preserver; and hear the most-devout entreaties, as were heard the intent orations of Aeacus, of Pygmalion, and
of Hippomenes, humbly offered before these thy divine Altars; and reach forth, and lend thyself favourable and
gratifying in succouring them — with that innate pity which affectionately thou didst show to the boy-shepherd
(Adonis) beaten by jealous Mars; and by that divine blood which then, in a rosy flower, thou didst scatter.

"Whence, if our merits and beseechings, in the sight of thy high majesty, were less worthy: grant, and make,
that thy amorous clemency, with the holy flames, to our feeble effect mercifully supply. Inasmuch as they,
inseparably, with firmness of soul, with singular promptitude of heart, and with un-dissolvable resolves, have
warmly vowed themselves, and strictly bound (themselves), with special obedience, to succumb, and with sedulous
service, to thy venerable and most-sacred laws, and from those never in the least to discrepate — in which,
already many days now, the young man, corroborated, continuing, has been an impavid and strenuous Athlete, and
in this same (service) she scrupulously professes, with wondrous hope of thy divine and efficacious patronage,
and, all refuge imploring. Interceding, then, I beseech, supplicating, thy high sanctity and sublime power,
that thou, munificent, repay the desired effects. O **Cyprogenia**, by those amorous burnings which it pleased
thee to inflame thee with, with beloved Mars; and by thy furious husband; and by thy struggling son — which
—
— eternally live with thee in the supernal delights and glorious triumphs."
To this end, all the sacred virgins, with high voice, responded: "**So be it.**"

From the holy orations and pious intervention the holy lips were no sooner occluded, than the praying
Priestess — of the sacred (things) most-expert — took of the odorous roses prepared, and many little barks of
little conches, or marine oysters, and, with the most-clean hands filled, those ceremoniously, above the
altar, in circuit of the fire-holder, she scattered; and, placing (some) in a bark of oyster, of the sea-water
of the little Urn she asperged all the divine Altar.

Then, upon the *anclabris* table, the two swans, throat-cut with the *secespita*, immolating — the blood, with
that of the incensed turtledoves, in the golden *Praefericulum*, with devout ceremonies and affectionate
deprecation, the virgins singing measured Odes, and she low-voiced reading — she committed that the bloodless
and slaughtered swans be cremated in holocaust in the sacristy, in a place disposed for such a deed; and that
the ash, collected in a box, in an opening under the Altar, be thrown.

Taking, then, she thence the sacred *Praefericulum*, with both the bloods, before the consecrated Altar, upon
the terse and most-luculent pavement, the sacrificing Expiatress, having dipped, with great reverence, her
forefinger in the purpling blood, many arcane characters diligently signed; and, Polia called, the —
— like she made her do, the virgins continuing in the sweetest song of the most-pleasing Odes.

This done and performed, the notable libation-woman washed her hands with keen diligence, and Polia likewise,
of the sacred blood — because no other contact was licit — the little priestess pouring the most-purely
expiated water, with the golden ewer, and receiving the consecrated washing in the golden *simpulum*.

Polia then, admonished by the most-expert Priestess, with a virgin sponge, those sanguine characters most-
tersely wiped up; and, in the washing of the purified hands, compressing it (the sponge), she washed it, most-
diligent.

Then the Monitress — all with the face turned to the pavement — that washing, tremulous, and with venerable
ministry, devoutly, upon the fire-holder poured. Whence, of a sudden, a smoke leapt to the convex heaven of
the cupola, little by little ascending — incontinently, when she had thus done, and to the ground prone
prostrated herself. Lo, a little instant — suddenly I felt move, and the grave earth quake under the round
knees, with an unthinkable din in the air; and in the Temple, with a horrendous roaring, thundering — not
otherwise than if, from the high heaven, into the measureless deep, a great mass were suddenly felt to fall —
and the strident hinges of the golden valves gave a rumble in the vaulted Temple, as, in a sinuous cavern, the
broken thunder should inwardly thunder.

Whence, full and surrounded by marvellous terror, and fearfully agitated, I invoked, silent, whatever divine
subsidy and pity. And, scarce somewhat opening the frightened eyes, I looked to the smoking Altar. Out of
which, purest smoke I saw miraculously issue, germinating, and successively multiplying itself into a
verdant **rose-bush** — which, with multiplied little branches, a great part of the sacred sacello copiously
occupied, to the raised altitude of the cupola, with a numerosity of vermilion and rubricating roses
together, and with many round fruits, of wondrous odour fragrant, of colouring candid-and-vermilioned; which
offered themselves more pleasing to the taste than, by chance, are not those which, to the famished mouth of
Tantalus, present themselves. More beautiful were they not, those desired by Eurystheus (the Hesperides'
apples).

Upon this rosy bush, then, appeared three white little doves, with some little birds gregariously fluttering
in the branches; and, festive, they leapt, colluding, and most-sweetly sang. And, by such a portent, the
numen presented — in that guise occulted — of the most-holy Mother, rightly I suspected.

For which thing, the sacrificing Priestess having risen, with matronal decorum — and Polia too, with special
beauty (more than ever to my eyes she appeared gracious), and in her sweet aspect laughing — both, reassuring
me, invited me into the sacrosanct sacello to enter; and, within, calling me before, venerating, of the divine
Altar, between the Priestess and Polia genuflecting me, the Priestess, with veteran ceremony, three of the
miraculous fruits extirpated: the one for herself reserved; of the two, to me one, and to Polia the other,
offering. Those, with revoked religion, and the utmost integrity of heart, together, all three, we tasted.

Now, no sooner did I taste the miraculous and sweetest little apple, than without delay I felt in me refresh
and renew the rude and gross intellect, and the anxious and mourning heart all recreate itself, anointed in
amorous joy — neither more nor less than one who, overwhelmed in the deep sea, and to the bottom immersed with
shut lips, without draught of breath, from above returns, most-avidly taking the fresh and most-pleasant airs,
and vivifies himself. For which thing, incontinently, in me more amorous flames began to burn; and with a more
sweet torment of new qualities of love it appeared to me to be transmuted. And therefore I began evidently to
know, and effectually to feel, what the Venerean graces are, and of how much efficacy they present themselves
to the earth-born, and how great a reward joyously they attain, who — through the delightful realms, intrepidly
soldiering, and in the amorous, pertinacious battles — arrive at them. Ultimately, after the devout and sacred
refection of the fatal fruits, taken without hesitation, that divine germ (bush), vanishing from the eyes,
disappeared. The libant Priestess went out of the holy sacello, and Polia paired with her, and I, and all.

With such and so-made order, terminated and defined the mystic sacrifices, and libations, and immolations, and
the divine cult — both, having deposed the sacred vestments, and stripped off, with choice veneration, all
those mysterious and pontifical instruments, with domestic and templar obsequies, in the sacristy reverently
they re-deposited.

And there, weighingly, the high Priestess, with special majesty, thus familiarly said to us: "My children, now
by me expiated and blessed, to your amorous undertaking and voyage go. I pray, again, that the divine mother
show herself auspicious and affable, and to your amorous conceits, intents, and cases, be pitiful, favourable,
and propitious. And, in the present, encloister the profound and frequent sighs; the lamentings postpone and
leave; put to flight every mourning. For already, by my instance, this present hour will be to you salutary and
favourable. Then, to these my salubrious admonitions and profitable commands let your soul attend, so that she,
with her pious and sweet affect, grant you happy success."

After the sacred monitress with bland speech had said (this), we — immortal thanks saying — from all reverently
took leave, with sweetest and mutual salutes, indicating (by) the wet face that our departure almost troubled
them. Nonetheless, bidding farewell, out of the magnificent and superb temple we went; and, my
*chrysocari* (golden-graced) Polia admonished of our way and itinerary, finally we departed.

O comitation so long desired, so most-pleasing, and happy, and prosperous exit of the transacted sadnesses! Now
my heart, breathed-upon with internal sweetness, and the noxious fire perfused with celestial dew, no longer
wavers me — but firmly and evidently this is my so most-desired Polia. My tutelary goddess. The genius of my
heart. To whom, well-deserving, due gratulation I owe, of so great her service to the divine mother, and of so
great a showing of love in this most-pleasant comitation. These and like words low-voiced saying, Polia, in that
instant aware of my depressed speech, regarded me with two festive eyes kindled with love — more clear than most-
lucid stars, without the horned Cynthia, in the serene sky coruscating; not otherwise than as the ignited steel
upon the anvil, malleated, scintillates, so, in my smitten breast, those (eyes) frequently scintillated. And, in
speaking, comely, with angelic accents, with the purpling mouth (hiding-place of every fragrance, apothecary of
oriental pearls, most-rich seminary of enucleated and sweet little words), timely, soothing, she delineated
(dissolved) all my mental inquietude. A speech, without doubt, to make pleasant the terrific aspect of Medusa,
and to mitigate the horrendous atrocity of the inflamed Mars, and to despoil him of his bloody armours; to steal
the most-beautiful Ganymede from the hooked talons of the supreme bird; and, from tenderness, to burst and
minutely cleave into tiniest fragments the hardest marbles, and whetstones, and crags, and roughest rocks, and
abrupt (cliffs) of Persia, and of the pathless and cloudy Mount Atlas in the Ocean-part; and, quieting, to tame,
or make gentle, the most-savage beasts of Libya; and to vivify every dusty and ashen dead. Thus she said:
"Poliphilo most-delightful" (having taken my hand), "now let us go to the roaring —

— shore; for I hope — nay, so certain and most-firm I hold it — that we, joyous, will come where our ardent
heart desires. And for this cause, from the laws of Diana obnoxious (bound), yielding, I have extinguished the
torch. The solemn sacrifices, and supplications, immolation, and burnt-offering being made, and, praying, I have
poured out the humble prayers, and tasted the miraculous fruits — so that, expiated, clean and purified, and
worthy, we may see the divine presences, which to the unclean sight of mortal men are not conceded."

Whence the notable Polia, likewise, and I, of immense sweetness upheld, and in sincere love corroborated —
(she) with me these arcane conceits mellifluously conferring, and paired and adherent to her walking — to a
most-ancient building we came, alacritously joyful, festive, and gladsome. About which was a religious grove.

Which was built up above the sea-sounding and (wave-)washed shore, by the refluent sea. And there, again, was
left a great vastness of walls, or partitions, and of structures of white marble, and a fragmented and battered
mole of a harbour nearby. In the fractures of which, and left joints, the salt-loving and littoral *crithmum*
(samphire) germinated; and in some places I saw the littoral *cakile*, and much *kali* (glasswort), and the
odorous marine wormwood; and, by the sandy embankment, *eryngo*, and purslane, and marine rocket, and very many
other celebrated simples — the *caratia*, and *myrsinites*, and like shore-dwelling herbs — from which harbour,
by many uneven steps, one ascended to the suggestum of the propylaeum of the temple. Which building, by voracious
time and by putrid antiquity, and by negligence, to the humid earth collapsed, here and there demolished, had
left without capitals the shaft, or decapitated trunk, of some huge columns of Persian stone of red grain; some,
with mutual alternation of Mygdonian marble; some had the contracture (fluting) broken — the *hypothesis*
(base), nor the *hypotrachelion*, nor Astragal was seen; some, again, I beheld of bronze, of marvellous art
(such as were not in the Gaditan temple) — but every thing under the open sky, of decay and old age offended.

My frugal and well-mannered Polia here said to me: "Poliphilo my sweetest, behold what worthy monument of the
great things, to posterity thus, in such supine ruin, and in so great a heap of stone-breakages, rough and
humpy, left. Already, in the primaeval (past), it was an egregious and marvellous temple, about which already
most-solemnly they held market, and huge multitudes of mortals thereto, every year, convened, making spectacles;
and, for its elegant structure and for the observed sacrifices, diffusely famous, most-religiously by the earth-
born celebrated. But, because at present abolished is, and ignored, its dignity — thus, as thou seest it lie,
disrupted and ruined, expressly destitute — it is denominated the **Polyandrion** temple. In which, Poliphilo, my
little-heart, are many little tomb-pits, where were buried the pulverable bodies of those who, badly, for wicked,
unlucky, and lugubrious love, to obscure death, miserable, ceded. To the infernal Pluto dedicated; and, by
returning years, at the Ides of May, with ancient and solemn ceremonies —

— all those who, to affable love indulging, gave heed — both men and women. In this place, to the celebrated
funeral and solemn panegyrics, from diverse regions and provinces, neighbouring and remote places, mourning,
they convened — beseeching and sacrificing to the numen of three-bodied Pluto, that they (the dead) should not
have stumbled to so great an impiety as to be conscious (causes) of their own and untimely death. Therefore
they immolated the dusky victims, or blackish sheep not yet known by the male, upon a flagrant bronze Altar —
the males to the god, and the females to the goddess — and, making the *lectisternia* for a triple night. That
flame and fire then, with the scattering of a multitude of roses, and with *arferia* (offering), they
extinguished — as, in this place, a great rose-garden of whatever kind, still left, openly thou seest. Which,
then, to gather them was a nefarious thing; but the priests commuted (permitted) them.

The incense-sacrifice finished, the infuled pontiff — on the breast ornated with a marvellous and mysterious
golden fibulation, with the adornment of a precious stone *Synochitis* — somewhat of the holy ash, to each,
with a little golden *simpulum*, then with much devotion gave. The ash accepted, in crowds they went out of the
temple, with observed veneration, to the rushy shores of the near sea (as thou seest). And, in a reed the
sacred ash placed, out into the deep they blew it, with religious superstition, with high-sounding voice, and
inelegantly exclaiming, and with feminine ululations confusedly intermixed, and saying: "Thus perish whoever
shall be the cause and conscious (author) of his lover's death."

Then, when in such manner they had scattered the ash into the sea, the reed thrown, having spat three times into
the said sea, three times saying "Fu, fu, fu," they returned, festive, with other roses — those, throughout all
the temple, disseminating, and especially upon the sepulchres (with funereal weeping), which, in order, in the
temple were situated — singing lugubrious sepulchral and tearful songs, sounding with sacrificial and kite-like
tibiae.

Newly, they set, each with their fellow-countrymen, in a circle upon the pavement, the tables and the viands, and
whatever edible by those brought, in one communicating exposed, with the Salian feast-fare. And there, with holy
rite, they made the *silicernium* (funeral feast); the superfluous then, the Manes being called, at the sepulchral
altars they left; and, beyond this anniversary, they held the secular games.

— diverse places (each) hung the borne cypress-branch. Which branches, fixed here and there, with superstition
observed, stood until the future anniversary. And, the year returned, all those dried fronds — the sacristan
libation-men gathering them — the sacrifice they kindled. Finally, after all this most-festively performed, and
with the utmost observance the funeral offices celebrated, with suppliant prayer, with religion and ceremonies of
the gods (whatever evil genius put to flight), the high priest **Curio** first, and then, saying the last words:
"*Ilicet*" ("It is permitted to go") — everyone, licitly and festive, could return to their own dwelling, and,
glad, betake themselves homeward.

With this such order, my magniloquent Polia — eloquently having, and with bland little words, so much observance
worthy of most-laudable commendation, integrally expounding, narrated (it), and me compendiously instituted — to
the spacious and sandy shore, of pleasant surges rushing, washed (rolled-back), where was the destroyed and
deserted temple, we came.

In this place, then, upon the fresh and flower-bearing little herbs, we gladly exposed ourselves to sit. Thus
staying, insatiable, with the face-beholding eyes I subtly contemplated, in one sole perfect and untouched
little body, so much congruity, and accumulation of beauty — an object, without doubt, refusing (that I) should
not see a more gracious thing beyond, (with) my eyes, nor of so much content — where, of new and re-sprouting
conceits, my ardent heart, with tacit joy refreshing, and somewhat the vulgar and common sillinesses deposed, I
considered a more intelligible effect; and, together, the most-serene sky, the salubrious and most-mild air, the
delightful site, the delicious fatherland, the ornate verdures, the pleasant and temperate hills ornated with
opaque little groves, the clement weather and pure airs, and the comely and pleasant place — dignified by the
rivers flowing down, irriguous, through the wooded valley, near the curved hills, to the right and left part
softly running, to the near sea precipitating; a most-salubrious field, and of most-pleasant grass, filled with
manifold trees, canorous of the concert of little birds. Let yield here, then, the Thessalian river and field
(Tempe). And there, together thus sitting, among the springing and redolent flowers and roses, in this celestial
effigy, with so much delight the gaping eyes, occupied, fixedly I held; and to so beautiful and rare a make, and
divine image, with all the senses, gazing, most-devoted and applied — and, in me, more pleasant, resulting the
heated vexing impulses, in which the soul, from sweetness liquefied, insane I stood, and all anxious, projected
all and curious to consider, marvelling, by what mode and reason that purpling liquor — at the touch of the
precious flesh of the little swelling wrist of the hand, remaining most-pure milk, for some little space — to its
place returned not. No less, with what artifice, in this most-comely body, the mistress nature had particularly
dispensed, and stuffingly disseminated, all the Arabic fragrance; and how, again, industriously, in her starry
forehead, of gold threads becomingly vine-tendrilled, she had fixed the most-beautiful part of the sky, or the
shining Heraclean (star).

Then, to the comely and slender feet the sight converting, I beheld on them the vermilion shoes violently drawn
on, and, over the ivory instep, moon-wise mouthed and sinuated with a *phytontea* (plant-like) opening, with
little gold rings, and with little cords of cyan silk ensnared, and tightly re-bound — most-apt instruments to
intercalate (bind) the life, and excessively to torment the more the inflamed heart. Then, straightway, the
lascivious regard returned to the straight throat, berried in a circle with oriental pearls — not understanding,
of the one and the other whiteness, the true distinction — of a sudden descended to the glittering breast, and
delightful bosom, where sprouted two round little apples, resistant to the garment, and obstinately repugnant;
nor such, without fail, in the orchard of the Hesperides, did Hercules furtively gather; nor such does Pomona ever
see in her orchard, as these — most-white in the rosy breast, standing immovable, fixed, whiter than the flocked
and lucid snow —

— in the season of Orion at setting, under the *pissatile* (?) body of the placid monster of Pan. Among which
(beauties), voluptuously, I beheld a delicious little valley, where was the delicate sepulchre of my soul — such
as Mausolus had not, with all his having, collocated. Being, then, I, for this, content — and the lacerated
heart conscious that the eyes, distracting it into whatever of those most-elegant parts, dispensed it moribund —
nonetheless I could not, for this, so much bridle the amorous and inflamed sighs, and so covertly castigate
(them), that I did not concede them their simulated sound to express itself.

By this such-made accident, immediately she too, provoked by the contagious love, and stirred, the lewd regards
most-placidly (special envy to the Sun) into me converted; and throughout I felt an irritating fire, itchingly
diffusing itself, into the lowest and interstitial parts, and even through all the capillary little veins,
seminarily to scatter itself. Whence, in her illustrious and notable features continually to contemplate, a
mellifluous sweetness, and solace, sweetly I heaped up. And there, some time, collided by disordered and
insatiable appetite, and by fiery and importunate stimulus gravely oppressed, with piteous words, full of
suasive and vehement prayer, secretly imploring, I appetited within me the desired kisses, sipping and fluid,
and sweetest, with vibrating (like a viper) and succulent little tongue — imagining to feel the extreme
sweetness of the savoury and little mouth (breathing-hole of odorous air, and mossy spirit, and freshest
breath) — and, feigning to enter into the hidden treasure of Venus, and there, mercurially, to steal the most-
precious jewels of parent nature.

Whence — alas, sighing — by that divine mother surrounded I found myself, and by the flame-bearing son circum-
walled, and by so most-beautiful a figure invaded, all henceforth morbid and infected by such notable
circumstances ornated and comely, and by the golden-fleeced head enticed (that whatever hair offered itself to
me a constricting snare, and chain), and beset by these torturing knots, and by the plenitude of such pleasant
pastures, and of amorous sweetness viscously baited — I could not, with whatever shrewd effort, resist the
accessory and invading ardours, and irritating thoughts; and, in me, the arrow-bearing love, having forced
itself, wholly disposed me — so insupportable a burning (patience overcome) to extinguish — and, spurned every
repugnant reason and mature counsel, in the solitary places, with Herculean audacity, to make assault, and the
divine and untouched Nymph, unbridled, to fore-attempt. But first, with sighing and precatory voice, of pity
impetrable, thus to say:

"Alas, divine-born Polia — in the present, for thee to die, eternal praise I esteem; and death more tolerable
and soft, and more glorious, with these thy delicate and swelling hands, would be to me the last end and demise.
For, the soul circumfused by so many tormenting ardours, ever more savagely quickening themselves, it, languid,
scorching, without intermission and pity they burn — so that never is left me to take a quiet hour, nor peace."

For which thing — by this way wishing to this incentive and frequent stimulus to put a finish — lo, that, of
other most-savage fires, my scarred heart, all from the beginning, to burn candently I felt. "Alas, how wilt
thou do here, Poliphilo? Somewhat cogitate of the violence done to Deianira, and to the chaste Roman
(Lucretia) — badly and unhappily turned out — and of many others. Consider that the omnipotent gods of earthly
loves have received resistance — let alone a lacerated and most-abject man. Revoke into memory that all long
time accrues to him who can wait; and that the fierce lions, again, by continued days, are made gentle, and
each other sylvan and cross animal; and the grain-bearing ant, again, by assiduous journey — however most-tiny —
in the hard flint imprints its trodden (path): let alone that a divine form, hidden in a most-human little body,
ought to take in itself the vestige of fervent love."

And thus, observed, reprobating, I confuted (refuted) so great a harm — the vexing passion taming — hoping to
attain the amorous fruits, and coveted effects, and triumphant contest. In memory questioning the holy orations,
and sacrifices, and libations, and the extinction of the torch — in which divine offices herself, and her
Poliphilo, she had intently and especially commemorated with commendatory entreaties — for so much I thought, by
suffering, a more efficacious reward and requital, and the implored (thing) to attain, than that, with perilous
improbity, to profit my most-bitter languors, and lose thence every hope.

The Nymph Polia, aware of the versicolour (changing) of my face, and its varying — more than the illustrious
*Tripolion*, or *Teucrion*, that three times a day changes the colour of its flower — and seeing me altered, and
solicited certainly by the intimate love (so many warm and frequent sighs), pitifully, with her adulating
regards, timely tempered and delineated (dissolved) the impetuous movements and irruent agitation. And so, and
not otherwise, my soul burning, in these continual flames, and burnable asperity, love stimulated me patiently to
hope — that, as the Arabian phoenix, in the aromatic twigs, in the aspect of the ardent Sun kindled, from the
arid ashes hopes to renew itself.

Above all the excogitated and exquisite torments of love not mediocrely beset seeing myself — and to the pre-
chosen and salubrious and present remedy, and my heart-healer, being near — stupefied I marvelled that,
against every natural order, she more morbidly infected me. And whatever her outstanding act, ornate eloquence,
biting regard, from so opportune a health, finding myself near, abdicated me (drove me off); whence ever more
multiplied an exhortable suasion, of wishing, to the provoking commodity (a grateful little gift to ravishers),
not to present myself ungrateful and pusillanimous. Fremishing like a furious and snarling dog, the pursued
beast having reached, in the alpine leaps: so I, neither more nor less, a furious coveter, the very desired prey
here reached, wholly to satisfy myself. Accustomed now to an assiduous and familiar death of love, I did not,
for this, repute the atrocity a passion, that thence might be ensued. And therefore every inconvenience, however
most-damaging, licit it suaded me. Whence my *eutrapela* (witty) Polia, shrewd of the improbe condition of
blind Love, and aware — to mortify so importunate a burning, and somewhat to syncopate it, and, as my singular
preserver, succouring — thus benignly says to me:

"Poliphilo, of all mine most-beloved, I am never unaware that antique works supremely please thee to see. So,
conveniently thou canst, in this interval, while we await lord Cupid, go licitly to see these deserted temples,
collapsed by devouring and obsolete old age — or by fire assumed, or by many years shaken — to thy solace to
behold, and the noble fragments left, of veneration most-worthy, to speculate. And I, in this place sitting,
content, will await thee, watchful, awaiting our lord to come, who must ferry us to the holy and coveted
maternal realm."

Then I, greatly most-avid — with the other most-commendable works seen — also these, most-accurately and
multividuously to contemplate, rose from the happy session, from under the tempered shades of laurel, and of
myrtle, and among tallish cypresses (then, about the place, the honeysuckle painting its odorous flowers, where
a voluble flowering jasmine, with soft shade, opaquely covered us, disseminating over us copiously its whitest
flowers, at that time most-sweetly odorous). Absorbed, without other cogitating, from beside Polia, by those
devious embankments of fastigiate and vast heap and ruin — in the greater part occupied with ground-ivy, and
*terrambula*, and implicated with thorns — solicitous I came. Where, ponderingly, I conjectured this to have
been a magnificent and marvellous temple, of choice and superb structure, according as the proven and
illustrious Nymph had shrewdly vaticinated to me. There, then, it appeared that, in a ring around the round
temple, were —
pages.wcap: Hieroglyphic Devices and Julius Caesar Medallion

t:
— tribunes disposed; because still left were some semi-integral, or semi-ruined, parts, and great fragments of
gates, with sinuous beams, and horns of vaulting, and tall columns of varied species — some Numidian, and some
Hymettian and Laconian, among the above-named — and other most-comely sorts, pure and unencumbered of lineament.
By the disposition of which tribunes, thus openly I judged, that in those were located the sepulchres.

In this place, before all things, at the rear part of this archaic temple, I beheld a great and lofty **obelisk**
of reddening stone. And in the base quadrate, I saw, in one face, these hieroglyphs carved.

First, in a circular figure, a balance (*trutina*), between which was a platter; in the triangular (spaces),
between the balance and the circle of the platter, on one side was a dog, and on the other a serpent. Under which
lay an antiquarian little ark; and from this, raised straight, was a drawn sword, with the point above exceeding
the balance-scale; and there a regal crown was inserted. Which thus I interpreted.

Then, under this, in another quadrangular figure, I saw: an eye; two ears of wheat, transversely bound; an
antiquarian *acinaces* (scimitar); then two wheat-threshers, transversed, between a cycle (circle) and heaped
(?); a world (globe) and a rudder; then was a most-ancient vase, out of which sprang a frond of olive berried
with fruit; there followed a *pansa* (full) platter; two Ibises; six —

— coins in a ring; a sacello with an open door, with an Altar in the middle. Newly, there were two
perpendiculars. Which figures, in Latin, thus I interpreted:

> **DIVO IULIO CAESARI SEMP. AUG. TOTIUS ORB. GUBERNAT. OB ANIMI CLEMENT. ET LIBERALITATEM AEGYPTII COMMUNI
> AERE S. EREXERE.**
>
> "To the divine Julius Caesar, ever Augustus, governor of the whole world, for his soul's clemency and
> liberality, the Egyptians, with common bronze (funds), erected (this) as sacred."

Likewise, on whatever face of the recounted base quadrate — like the first circled figure, such another
presented itself, in line and order of the first. On the right plane, then, I beheld again these elegant
hieroglyphs. First, a **viperous caduceus**. At the lower part of the rod of which, here and there, I saw **an
ant that grew into an elephant**; toward the upper (part), equally, **two elephants decreased into ants**.
Between these, in the very middle, was a **vase with fire**, and on the other side a **little shell with water**.
Thus I interpreted them:

> **PACE AC CONCORDIA PARVAE RES CRESCUNT, DISCORDIA MAXIMAE DECRESCUNT.**
>
> "By peace and concord small things grow; by discord the greatest decrease."

Over against this was the other circulation (panel). Within which I beheld such designs of egregious expression:
one anchor, again, in the diametral place, transverse; upon which sat an eagle with wings outspread, and in the
anchor's little shaft was intricated a bond (knot). Under these lineaments a soldier, sitting among some warlike
instruments, speculating, feared a serpent. Of this I made such interpretation.

With extreme voluptuousness contemplating these most-noble conceits, in such figuring expressed, I beheld also
the fourth, over against the first circle. I saw a triumphal Trophy in the lower part of the lance, of which two
in-transversed palms; and, item, to it knotted, two bounteous cornucopias raised themselves. In the middle, on
one side was an eye, and on the other a comet-star. This said (thus).

For the magnificence of which **obelisk**, I thought that such was not carried down to Thebes, nor in the Circus
Maximus erected. Then, into the front part returning, I found all disrupted the propylaeum; and at the ingress of
the destroyed door, lying, I saw a fragment of a frieze-architrave, and part of the cornice in one solid; in that
frieze, inscribed, I saw, of elegant writing of majuscules, this saying:
pages.wcap: Cupola Above Entrance to the Crypt

t:
> **D · M · S ·**
> **CADAVERIBUS AMORE FURENTIUM**
> **MISERABUNDIS POLYANDRION**
>
> "To the Gods of the Dead (*Dis Manibus Sacrum*). The Polyandrion, for the wretched corpses of those raging
> with love."

This noble and much-admired fragment, in one solid frust (chunk) — and a little portion of its fastigium, or
frontispiece — still retained itself egregiously delineated. In the triangular plane of which, two figments I saw
carved, and not entire: a decapitated bird (I judged it to be of an Owl), and an antique lamp, all of perfect
alabaster. Thus I interpreted them:
> **VITAE LETHIFER NUNTIUS** — "The death-bringing messenger of life."

Come then into the middle part of the temple, somewhat immune and unoccupied of rubble I found it. Where, again,
the consuming time, to one illustrious work of note — all of rubicund porphyry — had only pardoned. Which was
sexangular (hexagonal), with the bases upon a solid stone of Ophite, of the same figure, fixed in the pavement;
and six little columns, distant one from the other six feet, with the Epistyle, Frieze, and Cornice, without any
lineament and sign, but simply terse and pure. Which were, on the exterior, imitating the (hexagonal) form; but
the interstices in a circled figure. Where, upon the flat of the cornice, was born a cupola of a single and solid
rock, marvellous artifice; which thinned at the summit, where a pervious funnel, streaked and mirror-like, covered
a subterranean vacuity, illuminated by a circular opening of egregious grating, impeded (closed) of metal casting.
Which noteworthy ciborium, of the utmost polish, thus I found.

Through which grating, looking, it appeared to me to see, below, a certain squaring. For which thing, kindled with
curious cupidity of being able to descend to this part, rummaging among those fractures, and minutiae, and ruins,
searching out some passage — lo, that in a marble pier, comminuted (broken) all to about two paces, invested with
an obstinate and flex-footed ivy (by which I found almost all occupied the opening of a little door): into which,
by too scrutinous desire seduced, without other pondering, and inconsiderately, I entered. Where, by a blind,
sloping little stair descending, at the first ingress there appeared to me horrend lurking-places and unlit gloom;
but, a little after, the eyes somewhat accustomed, to discern I began, and I saw a great and ample subterranean
place, vaulted in the round, and, by the humid, ill-resounding. On dwarf columns it was upheld and sustained.
Six of them were subjected, at the perpendicular of the overstructures of the cupola, with the arches including as
much place of opening as the contained compass of the six upper (columns). From which dwarf (columns), then, all
this place vaulted itself, candid of marble, of polished squaring cemented, and almost not discerning the joints.
In which was much *aphronitum*, or *baurach* (natron/saltpetre) deputed. There I found the sectile paving, most-
beautifully expressed, levelled and flat, but befouled by a frequency of night-owls.

Between the dwarf (columns) was founded, on the floor, a bi-square Altar, all of orichalc (brass), six feet long,
and with the socle and little cornice half (that) high. Which was hollow, tomb-wise, like a sepulchre. But in the
opening, from the surface downward a sextant, I saw a grating, or a grate, of the proper material, cast together.
On one face I saw a little window — I thought, by this, the sacrificers ministered the fire to holocaust the
victim, and thence drew the holy ash; and again I cogitated that, upon that grate, they set (things) to incense,
or to burn the animal — the soffit of the opening also appearing smoky. There, juridically, I conjectured, that
the —

— smoke of the sacrifices, ascending, sublimed itself through the passage of the porphyry cupola, and exhaled
outside. And, by chance, I suspected that the *tholos*, or middle summit of the temple, was open, by the Egyptian
rite, and (that) of the holy smoke the reek, or burning, without molesting the temple, went out. On the other
side of the aforesaid Altar I found, of Roman letters exquisitely excavated, this title (I thought of the altar
found by Valesius at Tarentum):

> **INFERNO PLUTONI TRICORPORI**
> **ET CARAE UXORI PROSERPINAE**
> **TRICIPITIQUE CERBERO**
>
> "To infernal Pluto three-bodied, and to his dear wife Proserpina, and to three-headed Cerberus."

In the circling of this earthy, or subterranean, place, other work I saw not, save fixed seats of the proper
material. All these things, with great and unmeasured pleasure, and singular devotion, diligently beheld, I
returned above; where, marvelling at the integrity of this notable work of the ciborium, within myself I
confirmed the suspicion that the heaven (roof) of the temple was open — for the ruin, in circuit, was heaped up,
and this part I found immune. Now, there inspecting, I moved the eyes, and saw a tribune somewhat entire. Of a
sudden, with the eyes accompanying the feet, to it, hasting, I went. In the heaven (vault) of which an artful
painting was there left, with incredible effort and efficiency of the artificer, of colorific work of mosaic
subtly expressed.

There, cavern-wise, was painted a vault infuscated of thick gloom, showing a huge and sad, and frightful cavern,
all carious, like a many-holed or fistulous pumice; which, on the left side toward the middle part, near a most-
rough, pathless, ferruginous and craggy rock, terminated. In which was seen a gap of concavity in front; and in
the face, toward its ending, distant from a tufaceous stony mountain, scrupulous and chasmy — this, in the same
manner incaverned opposite, and pervious. In the middle height, between the one and the other, passed a bipartite
bridge of iron, candent (white-hot) to the middle, and then it appeared most-frigid —

— metal. Beyond these pendent and rotten rocks, by that division between the one and the other, it showed within
to be all a burning place of fire, full of ignited and flying sparks running, and white embers falling (like most-
dense atoms in the solar rays), crackling through the flames, feigned shrewdly; and an ignited boiling lake; and
many steam-vents, by the rocks, appearing.

On the front part, a dark and clay-muddy, glacial and most-rigid lake, showing itself. And on the right side,
again, was a craggy and rough and murex-like mountain, of sulphurous colour; through which, in diverse little
gaps, it vomited foul and caliginous smoke — as of matter repugnant to the ingress of the active fire — and
immediately gushing a suppurated ignited matter; which vomition gave the appearance of crackling, or making a pop,
like a concreted vapour compelled to exhale diffusely, and then, in the fistulous passages, the belch to return;
and that demonstration which one place did not make, the other place supplied to indicate. In this was a scabrous
rupture, cavernously in-caverned, with crude, grave and Avernal shades. In which fissure was fixed **Taenarus**,
with a bronze door, roughly worked out in this burnt and pumiceous rock. And there, under these cavernous
curvings and crags, three-throated **Cerberus**, sleepless, sitting — of blackest and humid coat, headed with
frightful serpents, of horrend and terrible aspect — with grave breath, those metal valves, unlulled, exploring,
with un-winking vigilance, in perpetual light the pupils keeping-watch.

In this horrend and cuspidate shore, and most-wretched site of the freezing and stench-bearing lake, stood the
raging **Tisiphone**, ferocious and cruel, with the viperine hair, upon the poor and most-wretched souls
implacably furious. Which fell in droves into the eternally most-rigid lake, down from the iron bridge; and,
rolling through the freezing waves, hastening to flee the painful and death-bearing cold, came to the most-frigid
shore. And, gone out, unhappy and fugitive, from the Tartarean fury, over a most-difficult, laborious and rugged
bank, to the left hand, they fled headlong, with the jaws open, and with the brows depressed, and with the
reddening and tearful eyes indicating clamours, stridor of jaws, and with dolorous weepings and woes. Which,
oppressed, and by horror one against the other impelled, and treading each other down, into the most-frigid Avernus
and deep, rushing, precipitated themselves. And those that escaped the precipice, in the scabrous cavern met the
other horrible fury, **Megaera**, and (she) prohibited that they should not precipitate themselves into the flying
flames; and, compelled, upon the incendious bridge they climbed. Such a painful order I judged to be on the other
part, because the mournful **Alecto** — sister of the two named, daughters of Acheron and of black Night — she too
was obstacle, and furially impeded, that the souls deputed to the everlasting flames should not overwhelm
themselves in the freezing lake; but, frightened by the horrend fury, they climbed, they too, with the others
meeting, the accursed bridge. And thus —
pages.wcap: Mosaic of Hell on Crypt Ceiling

t:
— it appeared to me, that the souls that were damned to the ardent burning, into the ice desired to migrate; and
those that were adjudicated to the most-torpid lake — much more frigid than the Stygian marsh — excessively desired
to enter, refreshing themselves, into the maledict and heat-bearing flames. But, forced to climb the fallacious
crossing (the candescent pass), by fatal disposition it divided itself in such manner, that the souls proscribed to
the inextinguishable fire fell again into their eternally constituted place. By the like, those that attempted to
evade the inevitable cold, refuged, were, from the bridge, re-submerged into the most-freezing deep. By virtue then
of the divine justice, the transit returned to its pristine being.

Without interval, other dolorous souls attempted this same, successively, with vain and impotent wish, and by no
means could they attain the desired effect. Those most-wretched souls, then, that hastened without quiet to flee,
by furious horror and rabies agitated — the incendious flames — could not, by relieving, come and refresh themselves
in the ice. And those likewise, that gave assiduous heed to fleeing the hardest cold, and entering into the ardent
flames, frustrated of the greatest desire, could not. And this, to those, was inescapable, and a pain unceasing —
ever more desirous, losing every hope. Which so much the more ardent avidity increased, as, upon the bridge, the one
and the other felt — those (of the fire) the reflex of its cold, and those (frozen) the heat — the one with the
other meeting at its term (the bridge's midpoint). And this, in the affect, was the greatest quickening of pain and
of torment. For which thing, with so obstinate an art of colouring, and of simulated gestures and expressed
efforts, I saw such a painting skilfully-made, and exquisitely perfect, as ever could be made and shown. And the
title, indicating, was inscribed: that, in the burning flames, were condemned the souls that, for too much fire of
love, killed their very selves; and, in the horrid ice, were immersed those who, rigid and chilly to Love and
refusing, had obstinately shown themselves.

Finally, with such disposition I beheld this odious, frightful and to-be-avoided Barathrum (pit), that where the
lakes met — that is, the frigorific with the most-ardent — by the contrariety they must make, with eternal
controversy, a terrible thundering; because then, meeting, both immersed themselves in an abrupt precipice, effused
into a dark, vast and most-deep passage and immense abyss. Where the profundity was so artfully feigned by the
artificer, that, by the colouring, those demonstrations feigned (themselves) to be true, and (one seemed) to see a
most-absorbing vortex, with wondrous emulation of the colourings, and of lineal symmetry of prospect, and of the
figures the elegance, and copious invention, and artful designation, and with incredible sharpness — such that
Parrhasius of Ephesus, notable painter, could never first glory himself of a like device.

Then, whoever accurately considered such an expression could easily conjecture (it) to be thus; because the maker,
most-rich of shrewdness, and of outstanding cogitation, had here exquisitely feigned the souls to a corporeal
expression — which shades cannot appear save (as) concreted air, and condensed in that effigy, by which the effect
is comprehended. And therefore many souls, stopping their ears; others (covering their eyes with the little palms)
dared not look into the terrific and gulfy abyss, full of frightful, terrible and various monsters; others, pale,
to express the torpid cold, straining their arms to the breast; some, to demonstrate the ardour, blew out smoky
breath; others, to indicate the mourning sadness and dolorous pain, the fingers of the hands joined comb-wise, wept.
Whence, upon the limited bridge, in the diagonal compacture, meeting in droves, the one and the other of the first
butted (against each other), and could not proceed, by the treading-down of those following. Then the bridge, by
fatal everlasting order, separating itself, rejecting its own, into its own place returned; and re-joined, again,
others unceasingly attempted, successively, that (bridge) —

— climbing. Whence the dolorous souls, desperate, wishing the horrific death much more than they abhorred the
frightful places and horrend furies, (wished) that same odious death, vainly affected (desired). Which unhappy and
stench-bearing Erebus was so conducted and polished, that even to the inspectors no slight fright it induced.

In this place I saw a **square Altar**, on the face, or front, of which, of perfect majuscules, this title I found
inscribed:

> **ARA DEUM INFER(NORUM).**
> **VIATOR, HIC CAESAM LAODIAM PUBLIAM INSPICE, EO**
> **QUOD AETATEM SUAM FRAUDAVERAT ABNUERATQ(UE),**
> **CONTRA PUELLAR(UM) RITUM, IUSSA AMORIS,**
> **SEMET EXSPES GLAD(IO) INTERF(ECIT).**
>
> "Altar of the infernal gods. Traveller, behold here Laodia Publia, slain — because she had defrauded her own
> (youthful) age, and had refused, against the custom of maidens, the commands of Love; and, hopeless, killed
> herself with the sword."

Much gladdened, from here departing, among the ruins I found a noble stone of square marble, on one side broken, but
the greater part reserved: on one front, among the undulations, in the middle, in the manner of two little
quadrangles with the arch, was inward-carved; and here and there a tallish ovoid figure — the one had **D** and a
head of a mask (larva), and the other an **M** and another head — the cyma somewhat fastigiate, but decapitate, where,
fixed, an ancient bronze vase stood forth, without lid, gaping (I thought in it the ashes were stored), with this
inscription (the rest of the lineaments immune):

> **· D ·        · M ·**
> **ANNIRAE**
> **PUCILLAE**
> **PUELLAE**
> **INCOMP(ARABILI)**
> **DIDUS (?)**
> **AEMULATRICI**
> **MOESTISS(IMI)**
> **PARENTES · P(OSUERUNT) ·**
>
> "To the shades (*Dis Manibus*). To Annira Pucilla, incomparable girl, [a?] rival of Dido(?), the most-mournful
> parents placed (this)."

Next to this, lying on the floor, I saw also this elegant epitaph, on a porphyry tablet — by which to have been a
superb sepulchre I conjectured, because at both sides it appeared continuous by fracture, and not thus a simple
tablet, but this part stood pure of lineaments, immune, with the lettering left. About which germinated the hybrid
nasturtium.

> **· D ·        · M ·**
> **GLADIATORI MEO AMORE,**
> **CUIUS EXTREME PERUSTA,**
> **IN MORT(IS) LANGUOREM DECUB(UI);**
> **AT EIUS CRUORE, HEU ME**
> **MISERAM, IMPIATA CONVALUI. D(IVO?)**
> **FAUST(O) AUG(USTO)**
> **PIE MONUMENT(UM) RELINQUENS,**
> **UT Q(UOT)ANN(IS) SANG(UINE) TURTUR(UM)**
> **INTER SACRIFICAND(UM) ARC(ANAE) RELIG(IONIS)**
> **HANC INTINGI, E XLIX ACCEN(SIS)**
> **FACUL(IS), ET COLLACHRYMULANTES**
> **PUELLAE SOLVERENTUR,**
> **LUCTUMQ(UE) FUNERAL(EM), OB TANTI**
> **INDICIUM DOLORIS, DEVELLAT(IS)**
> **CRINIB(US) PROMISSIS, RUSSARENT**
> **PECTORA FACIEMQ(UE) DIEM**
> **INTEGRUM; PROPITIATIS**
> **MAN(IBUS) CIRCA SEPULCRUM**
> **SATAGERENT ANNUALITER**
> **PERPETUO**
> **REPETUND(UM).**
> **EX T(ESTAMENTO) F(IERI) I(USSIT).**
>
> "To the shades. To my gladiator, by my love — for whom, burned to the utmost, I lay down in death's languor; but
> by his blood (alas, wretched me!), unpurified, I recovered. Leaving a pious monument [to divine Faustus
> Augustus?], that yearly, with the blood of turtledoves amid the sacrifice of the arcane religion, this [torch] be
> dipped, with forty-nine kindled torches; and that the weeping girls be loosed (in mourning), and, for the token
