> of so great grief, funeral lamentation — with hair torn and let flowing — redden their breasts and face a whole
> day; and, the shades propitiated, they busy themselves about the sepulchre yearly, in perpetuity to be repeated.
> By her testament she ordered it made." *(Several abbreviations are conjecturally expanded.)*

Then, when I had these two epitaphs accurately perused, and most-pleasingly seen, solicitous, inquiring, turning
the eyes — lo, that I see a **historiated sepulchre**. To which, without tarrying, I went. On the anterior part of
which, fixed, was a little altar, together with such (figures) expressed. Upon the flat of it, of wondrous
artifice, was set a head of a sylvan goat, held by one of the horns by a little old man, with the head of hair, in
the old manner, tormented (dressed), confused; who was clad, over the nude, in a pall thrown back over the right
shoulder, coming under from the left, returning over the right, and at the back pendent; near, he was clothed in
goat-skin — one (skin) in front and the other behind at the back, over the shoulders, the feet of both skins
knotted, and the others hanging between the thighs with the rough hair turned to the flesh; and girt with a torque,
or fillet, made of *tanus*, or black vine, with its leaves.

> **HAVE**
> **LERIA,**
> **OMNIUM**
> **AMANTISS(IMA),**
> **VALE.**
>
> "Hail, Leria, most-loving of all — farewell."

Who (the old satyr), with the tumefied cheeks, sounded two rural Tibiae, and (was) propped upon a knotty trunk of
*Dendrocissus* (tree-ivy), all hollow of old age, with pervious cracks and rami discordant, rare of leaves, with the
hair (foliage) unkempt and un-fronded. Between these two leapt a nude boy. On the other side was one who, upon the
robust shoulders, bearing a leaky *Armillum* (wine-jar) with the orifice inverted, over the horned head scattered the
unmixed wine. Beside him was a matron, with the hair let down, dishevelled — and she, and the porter of the wine-jar,
nude — and tearful, holding a torch with the kindled part downward. Between these two appeared a little Satyr-boy, who
in the hands squeezed a serpent much involved. There followed then a rustic old woman, basket-bearing, clad over the
nude in a flying cloth, girt over the flanks; on the inelegant head, over the bald (crown), she had a *cesticillus*
(pad); and above she bore a wicker *cista* full of fruits and of fronds, and in the other hand held a vase of oblong
clayey orifice. These figures most-excellently were carved, and roughly (in high relief). On the little altar thus was
inscribed. Excited most-highly by so much comeliness of monuments, questing, to me a most-elegant Roman epitaph,
inscribed on a stone, offered such a most-pleasant dialogue, and with such ornaments:

> **· D ·        · M ·**
>
> **VIATOR, HUC PROPIUS FERTO**
> **OCULOS; DEINDE VERBA MECUM**
> **FACITO. — "FUI SINE AMORE VIVA;**
> **AMANS, HEU, MORIOR."**
> **— DIC, QUAESO, AMABO: REM ME(AM?)**
> **HUIC POLYANDRIO DEDI, MORTUAM**
> **OB AMORIS INCENDIUM**
> **PUERI FLORENTIS AETATE**
> **FORMOSISS(IMI). — "QUID INSANIS? AT AMANS VIVEBAS."**
> **— PROFECTO: CUM NOXIE**
> **AMARE COEPERAM ADULESCENS,**
> **SPRETO AMORIS MUNERE, ABNUIT;**
> **CONTABUI, MORTE RAPTA,**
> **HIC SUM. — "QUID TIBI POSSUM?"**
> **— NEVIAM ROMANAM, CRUDELIS**
> **PROCULI AMORE**
> **DEFUNCTAM MISERE,**
> **TOTAM PER URBEM**
> **ORBEMQ(UE) DICITO.**
> **HOC SATIS. VALE.**
>
> "To the shades. — *Traveller, bring your eyes closer here; then make words with me.* — 'I lived without love;
> loving, alas, I die.' — *Say, I pray, I beg: my [body] I gave to this Polyandrion, dead by the fire of love for a
> boy in the flower of his age, most beautiful.* — 'Why art thou mad? Yet thou wast living, in love.' — *Truly: when,
> a young woman, I had begun (to my) harm to love, the gift of love spurned, he refused; I wasted away, snatched by
> death, here I am.* — 'What can I do for thee?' — *Nevia the Roman, wretchedly dead of love for cruel Proculus,
> through the whole city and world proclaim. This is enough. Farewell.'*"

Leaving this, which with the utmost gladness I saw, I entered into a **tribune, broken and disrupted**. Where, again,
part of an egregious painting of most-lively mosaic I found. In which I saw a **Matron, prostrate upon a kindled pyre,
and raging upon her very self, killing herself**. And there, no other than feet, womanly shod, appeared — some part
with the calves, and little covered with drapes. All the rest was, by the unsated and voracious time, consumed, and by
antiquity, and by winds, and rains, and ardent Sun destroyed. In this same place the Ark (tomb) was comminuted, and the
greater fragment was this, reversed, which, righting it, I found with such writing. Next to this, lying on the floor, of
alabaster stone, I found an antiquarian **vase**, high more than a pace and a half, with one of the handles broken, and
part broken in its body; up to the opening, part superseated a half-cube, or *Taxillus* (die), high one foot, or —

— four palms. On which, on one face, at the front of the fracture, was inscribed; and likewise, where it was
broken, by the token of some letters part fragmented and entire, part remained. Then, in the subjacent body, from
the circling girdle toward the bottom (in which were fixed the handles), on the front of the fracture, was this
outstanding writing.

Leaving these broken monuments, to a destroyed **tribune** I came, in which somewhat a fragment of mosaic was
comprehended. Where, painted, I beheld a **man afflicting a damsel; and a shipwreck; and a youth, upon his back
carrying a girl, swimming to a deserted shore; and part was seen of a lion; and those two, in a little boat,
rowing** — the following (part) destroyed. And again this part was in many places lacerated: I could not wholly
understand the history. But in the marble-incrusted wall was interset a bronze tablet, with Greek majuscules; such
an epigram it had inscribed — which, in the idiom (Greek), to so much pity provoked me, reading so pitiable a case,
that of tears I could not (refrain), damning the guilty (party). Which, as best I could, thus (I rendered) in
Latin:

> **HEUS VIATOR** — *(the epitaph of Leontia and Lollius; Poliphilo's Latin rendering of the Greek)*
>
> "Ho, traveller! Interpose thy hands a little (in prayer), being adjured; and, reading, much-groaning, give kisses
> to the metal, adding: 'Ah, cruel monster of Fortune! They ought to have lived.'
>
> "Leontia, a girl, the chief beloved of Lollius, a freeborn youth — when the intemperance of love pressed (her),
> afflicted with paternal torments, she fled away. Lollius follows; but, amid embracing, taken by pirates, they sell
> them to a certain trafficker. Both captive, they board a ship. When, by night, Lollius suspected Leontia to be
> carried off from him, seizing a sword, he butchers all the sailors. The ship, the sea's savagery arisen, dashed on
> the rocks near land, sinks. They climb a rock. By the impulse of hunger, seizing Leontia, I set her on my shoulders.
> 'Favour, be near, O father Neptune,' saying, 'us and our fortune I commit to thee.' Then, with a dolphin-like effort,
> with my arms I cut the little waves. But Leontia, amid the swimming, speaks: 'Am I a trouble to thee, my life?'
> 'Lighter than a water-skater, Leontia, little heart.' And, oft asking, 'Hast thou strength, my hope, my little
> soul?' 'I say (yes).' Those (words) thou rousest. Soon, embracing (my) neck, she sweetly kisses her bearer, solaces,
> exhorts, gives spirit to the diver. I exult. To the shore at last we come, safe. Unhoped-for, a roaring lion attacks.
> We embrace each other. The lion spares the dying. Terrified by the chance, a little boat cast up on the shore
> together with a rowing-oar, we fugitives board. Each in turn, singing, we row. A day and a night — and a third —
> wandering. Only the sky itself, on every side, lies open. By lethal hunger we are tormented; and, wasting with long
> fasting, we rush into embraces. Leontia saying, 'I pray thee, dost thou perish of hunger?' 'It is enough to be with
> thee, Lollius — I am fed.' But she, sighing: 'My Lollius, dost thou fail?' 'Not at all,' I say, 'in love, but in
> body.' With only vibrating and mutual tongues we fed ourselves sweetly; and, more tightly, with gaping mouths, sweet
> kisses cast, ivy-like we embraced. Both, without turning (breath), we die. By the surges — not (even) raging —
> hither, by the breeze, we are carried; and, wretched, in the estuary-air, bound in those very embraces, among the
> Plutonic shades here we are laid. And whom the piratical rapacity did not retain, nor the leonine maw devour, and
> the sea's immensity refused to take — the narrowness of this little urn here holds them both. This unhappiness I
> wished thee to know. Farewell."
pages.wcap: Epitaphs: Greek Urn and D.M. Lyndia

t:
From here departing, more avidly lustrating through the heaped ruins, I found another **tetragonal altar**, which on
its flat had a base without plinth — that is, a gula (cyma), then a little fascia, and then a torus. Beyond this it
was levelled. On which levelling sat a plinth, or little slab, that from angle to angle made a sinuous (curve), as
one of its square figure incurving little by little; the projection of which angles did not exceed the circumference
of the torus, or torus, subjacent. Upon which abacus-plinth lay a circular (base) of a vase; the circumstance of
which did not pass the outlet of the angles of the subjacent plinth. Which vase dilated itself, in the opening, as
much as was the extreme of the lowest of the underlying gula of the base. The rim, or lip, of which — keeping its
thickness — tended (in) an inflection, into itself inverting. On the altar I saw such an epigram:

> **INFER(IS) D(IIS) DEAB(US)Q(UE).**
> **C. VIBIUS ADULESCENS,**
> **INTEMPERATO AMORE**
> **PERCITUS PUTILLIAE**
> **SEX(TI) PUELLAE GRATISS(IMAE),**
> **QUOD ALTERI ULTRO**
> **TRADITA (EST), NON SUSTINENS,**
> **CRUENTO GLADIO**
> **SIBIMET MORTEM**
> **CONSCIVIT. VIX(IT) ANN(OS)**
> **XIX, M(ENSES) II, D(IES) IX; HORAS**
> **SCIT NEMO.**
>
> "To the infernal gods and goddesses. Gaius Vibius, a youth, stirred by intemperate love for Putillia, most-pleasing
> girl of Sextus — because she was willingly given over to another, not enduring it, with a bloody sword took death
> upon himself. He lived 19 years, 2 months, 9 days; the hours, no one knows."

Thence departing, I found a noble fragment of best porphyry, with two equine heads carved, from which came out an
intricate binding — two branches of myrtle, in-transversed and pendent, retaining. In the middle of the transverse
they were knotted with a tight shoot of wondrous make. Between the one and the other (horse-)bone, over the myrtle
fronds, I saw, of most-beautiful Ionic majuscules, such writing (the rest of the writing, with the stone, destroyed).

> **ΤΟΜΟΚΟΥΡΕΙ / ΔΑΡΚΙΑ / ΑΡΤΕΜΕΙΣ / ΛΟΝ…ΧΟ** (TOMOKOUREI · DARKIA · ARTEMEIS · LON…CHO)
> *(A Greek inscription, fragmentary; the reading is uncertain.)*

Excited most-highly by so much comeliness of monuments, searching, to me an epigram somewhat perplexed, candid in
marble, I found — only the inscribed part of a little altar remaining; the rest, broken, lay on the ground:

> **· D ·        · M ·**
> **LYNDIA, THASIUS,**
> **PUELLA,  PUER.**
> **HIC SUM. SINE (TE)**
> **VIVERE NOLUI,**
> **MORI MALUI.**
> **AT, SI NORIS,**
> **SAT EST.**
> **· VALE ·**
>
> "To the shades. Lyndia, a girl; Thasius, a boy. Here I am. Without (thee) I would not live; to die I preferred. But,
> if thou (now) knowest — it is enough. Farewell."

With the greatest delectation and pleasure beholding these noteworthy fragments — avid, still more, searching, to find
other new (things) — thence, then, like an animal questing the ever-more-pleasing pasture, transferring myself through
the embankments of ruins, of huge chunks of columns, and some entire. Of which, wishing to know the proportion, one I
measured, extended on the ground, and from the socle to the contracture (fluting) I found, of its shaft, the tallness
seven diameters of its lowest thickness. There, near, offered itself to me a most-ancient sepulchre, without any
writing, in which, by a fracture, looking in, I saw only the funeral vestments and footwear, petrified. I conjectured
reasonably (it) of the sarcophagus-stone (of such effect) of the Troad of Asia — suspecting (it) of the cadaver of
Darius.

And nearby I saw a noble sepulchre of porphyry, exquisitely carved among sylvan little shrubs, of which offered itself
to me to read an elegant epitaph; and it had the cover in the form of an egregious little temple, scaled scale-wise —
one part of the said, over the ark, remaining, and the other lay cast down on the floor, and inscribed with such an
outstanding title.

> **· D ·        · M ·**
> **P(UBLIA) CORNELIA ANNIA, NE IN DESOLATA ORBITATE**
> **SUPERVIVEREM MISERA, VIVAM ME ULTRO IN**
> **HANC ARCAM CUM VIRO DEF(UNCTO), INCOMPAR(ABILI) AMORE**
> **DIL(ECTO), DAMNAT(A) DEDO; CUM QUO VIX(I) ANN(OS) XX**
> **SINE ULLA CO(NTROVERSIA). LIB(ERIS) LIBERTAE(SQ)UE NO(STRIS UT) QUOT-**
> **ANN(IS) SUP(ER) ARCAM NO(STRAM) PLUTONI ET UXORI PRO-**
> **SERPIN(AE) M(ANIBUS)QUE OMNIB(US) SACRIFICENT, ROSISQ(UE)**
> **EXORNENT; DERELIQ(UO) IBI EPULENTUR. DO(MUS) D(IVAE) P(ARENTIS)**
> **M(ONUMENTUM). D(EDIT) A(NNIA). EX (SESTERTIIS) LLSX ATQ(UE) T(ESTAMENTO) FACIUNDUM DELEGA(VIT).**
> **VALE, VITA.**
>
> "To the shades. Publia Cornelia Annia — that I might not, in desolate bereavement, survive, wretched, alive — of my own
> will give myself, condemned (to death), into this coffin with my dead husband, loved with incomparable love; with whom
> I lived twenty years without any controversy (quarrel). (I charge) our children and freedmen that yearly, over our
> coffin, they sacrifice to Pluto and to his wife Proserpina and to all the shades, and adorn it with roses; with the
> remainder let them feast there. Annia gave this monument of the divine parent (?); from (a sum of) sesterces she
> ordered it, and by testament, to be made. Farewell, life."

Below again (from here departing), under a corymb-bearing and wandering ivy, pendent from a decayed course of wall, very
dense of frond, a noteworthy *zygastrion* (chest) sat, of a stone like ivory, until then in the greater part still terse
and bright. Within which, curiously looking, through a fissure, or chink, of the flat cover, I saw **two entire cadavers
reserved** (preserved). For which thing rightly I judged this sepulchre (to be) of *chemites* stone. On the front of
which I saw these **Egyptian hieroglyphs** carved; and within, again, many glass ampullae, and many earthenware
(vessels), and some little statues in the archaic Egyptian manner, and an antiquarian lamp of metal artfully made — and
in the soffit of the covering, pendent, that one little chain, ensnared, retaining (it), suspended, burned; and, near the
head of the buried, were two little crowns, which I judged golden, but by time and by the lamp-smoke infuscated. Such was
the interpretation:

> **DIIS MANIBUS.**
> **MORS, VITAE CONTRARIA ET VELOCISSIMA, CUNCTA CALCAT, SUPPEDITAT, RAPIT, CONSUMIT, DISSOLVIT. MELLIFLUE DUOS,**
> **MUTUO SE STRICTIM ET ARDENTER AMANTES, HIC EXTINCTOS, CONIUNXIT.**
>
> "To the shades. Death — contrary to life, and most swift — treads on all things, tramples, seizes, consumes, dissolves.
> Mellifluously (sweetly) it has here joined two, who mutually, tightly and ardently loved each other, (now) extinguished."

Gladdened, with incredible solace, by so much variety of antiquarian and magnificent works, still, without doubt, my soul
increased (in wishing), insatiably, more lustrating, to investigate other novelties. Whence, even if before, tearful, the
Greek epitaph of the two miserable lovers dead of starvation (Leontia and Lollius) had excited me — much more, again, there
presented itself to me a much-admired but pitiable monument, of two other most-unhappy lovers, standing in a great stone,
with such lineament expressed: a square, by the diagonal raised (set lozenge-wise), contained in itself two little
pilasters, with a little cornice and a half-hemicycle above; between which, from the angles of the little arch, hung a
tablet, on which, reading, I saw such a pitiable epigram.

> **O LECTOR INFOELIX** — *(the epitaph of Lopidia and Chrysanthes)*
>
> "O unhappy reader, be present at this monument while it calls thee — and then, afterward, it asks that thou read
> into what human pleasure falls. Here is the ash of two lovers, who, long since, mutually burning insolently with
> itching love, by the wicked, unbridled impulse of pleasure, met in a deserted place among ruined rocks, where by
> chance also stood the broken walls of sacred buildings and rough ruins. There we both were ardently urged to pay
> Venus the desired gifts. Lying back, I, Lopidia, saw a snake, slipped down from on high, threatening. 'Ho! cease
> from what thou hast begun,' I say; 'my Chrysanthes, rise, flee — lo, a serpent about to devour us!' — as I watch it
> hurling itself from the wall. Soon he, terrified, looking up: 'O my Lopidia,' he says, 'I beg thee, go thy way, flee
> thou the road, let me attack the dying dragon.' Scarcely had I risen — alas, sad, wretched me! — when I saw my
> Chrysanthes, my life, entangled to destruction and tightly circled in the snake's coil, now anxiously breathing.
> And suddenly it wounds the throat of my Chrysanthes with biting teeth; then I behold my Chrysanthes being
> suffocated. 'Ah, ah, I perish, unhappy! I feel my Chrysanthes dying!' At once, furious, I rush at the serpent, and,
> a club seized, I hasten to strike; but the serpent twists its wrangling neck, nor by force could I drive off the
> entwined one. Striking at last, incautiously missing, I killed my Chrysanthes, most unhappy. Alas, I am undone!
> What have I done? What shall I do? Shall the serpent and I, so wretched, survive? By no means! But with Herculean
> daring — nay, with a ghostly, snarling fury — with that same club, the blow turned, upon the fallen corpse I strike
> the coiled beast, and kill it. What then, a girl, was I to do — lost and dead? My Chrysanthes and the beast,
> witnesses of my crime, thrown over my shoulders, I carry into the city, watering them again and again with sighs,
> heart-grief and tears. I climb a certain platform in the public forum, and, sighing, I make the matter known. In a
> crowd the citizens run together to the cruel and hateful spectacle; they pity the entangled chance, accuse Fortune,
> damn Venus. I attest my crime, I invoke the infernal powers: 'Therefore,' saying, 'receive me to pay the penalty
> together with my Chrysanthes; now let me transfer all the guilt upon myself.' Then, desperate, in the public sight
> of all, a sword seized, I transfix my breast, and gave my most-wretched self to be buried here, in an eternal tomb,
> with his corpse. Farewell."

Having read the compassionate case of the unfortunate lovers of this most-outstanding epigram — from here, again
supremely content, departing, not many paces making — there occurred to me a noble tablet of tetragonal marble, with
somewhat of fastigium (pediment), with two little columns, one to a side; of design immune and unencumbered. And, to
the compass of all the quadrangle, was, as if uprooted (in relief), a foliate crown, or jewel, diligently conducted;
in which I read such an inscription. Which stone lay cast down on the earth, but with the workmanship supine (face up).
Which elegant varieties not a little pleasure, in my soul, joyously accumulated.

More ardently invaded (I) found myself to the investigation of the most-worthy antiquarian works. There presented
itself to me a disrupted **tribune**, with the right wall reserved, in which I saw, with excessive voluptuousness, a
**porphyry sepulchre**, of most-worthy device, and of most-excellent workmanship, and of marvellous cost, and of
incredible artifice of sculpture. Which stood — at the extreme sides raised by two quadrangular little columns (a
third of them worked out, with regulated flutings, upon a footing with the base collocated) — and, perpendicularly
subjacent, was a little altar, with three elegant mourning Nymphs, toward the middle turned, weeping together. By the
like, on the other side, semi-detached from the solid, not without the corollary and requisite lineaments. Above both
the capitals the epistyle, ornate, extended itself. Then, with volutes of most-comely fronds and flowers —

— invested, the Frieze resided above, located, covered with a becoming little cornice. Between the one and the other
quadrangular (column), somewhat, a *solium*, or niche, with regulated excavation of fluting, stood forth, level with
the plane, between those quadrangulars. The projection of which made, on the one and the other side of its opening, a
little pilaster, with capitals and base; upon which rose an inflected architrave — so detached from the levelled, or
plane, that there remained, in the interior part (that is, at the lips of the solium), a little tongue (ledge). Level
with the capitals, a wavy binding girt the solium, and above (it) the half-cupola.

Which little pilasters egregiously were ornated of sculpture. Under the little pilasters lay a projecting tallish
little altar, with the ornaments of the overstanding little pilasters. Between the one and the other projection of the
said little altars, or sub-column, I saw a **Greek inscription**, by which I knew this to be the monument of the pious
**Queen of Caria** (Artemisia). Thus it said:
> **ΑΡΤΕΜΙΣΙΔΟΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΔΟΣ ΣΠΟΔΩΝ** (ARTEMISIDOS BASILIDOS SPODON) — "The ashes of Queen Artemisia."
With socles, and little crowns, and cymas, and gulets, most-excellently the whole girt and companionable.

On the lower plane of the niche was a plinth of the narrated material, in aspect most-beautifully adorned with
sculpture, upon the flat of which stood fixed four equal-placed lion's claws of gilt metal; which pressed (bore) an
antiquarian little ark, with lineaments of notable expression. Upon the cover was a bench (throne), to the compass of
the covering, feigned covered with silken cloth, with an encompassing fringe.

Sat upon (it) a **Matron-Queen**, with regal cultivation, and majestic vestment, on the breast fibulated over a fitted
garment; which, from the collar down through the breast, and transversely in the girding, went round a little fascia,
and, over the belly, dilated in the form of a *tetraphyllon* (four-leaf), that is, in a figure of four hemicycles; in
which, of Greek majuscules, was thus annotated:
> **ΜΑΥΣΩΛΕΙΟΝ ΑΤΙΜΗΤΟΝ** (MAUSOLEION ATIMETON) — "The priceless Mausoleum."

With the right (hand) she held a **chalice to the mouth, drinking**; and in the other she held a little rod, or
sceptre; with the poured (loose) hair, over the head wreathed with a somewhat-fastigiate crown, tapering to another
crownlet at the nape; from which, becomingly and combed, descended the hair.

Upon the keystone of the arched architrave stood forth an oval figure, flattened, of a height up to under the
projection of the Sima of the cornice; in which I beheld impressed a face of regal majesty, crowned, with prolix beard
and twisted hair. I judged it to be the true simulacrum of the husband (**Mausolus**). Retained, here and there, by two
nude winged little spirits, seated upon the extreme circling of the arched architrave; which, with the other hands
free, the little arm extended, a bronze little cord —

— held pendent, incurved (the bronze cord the winged spirits held). Through which had passed some balusters. And
from the retaining hand, perpendicularly, they held suspended a copper thread, festooned and beaded, all excellently
gilt.

Upon the flat of the crown, somewhat inclined, ascended a plinth, with manifold ornaments. In its flat, in the
middle front, resided a rounding of metal, which, enclosed, had a **blackest stone, also mirror-like**, in which I
saw such writing, of Greek majuscules:
> **ΕΡΩΤΟΣ ΚΑΤΟΠΤΡΟΝ** (EROTOS KATOPTRON) — "The mirror of Love."

The encompassing lip, of metal, a palm in evened breadth, was comelily bossed. On its upper circle stood straight a
perfect **nude image, of gilt metal**, with the right holding a little spear, and in the other an antiquarian
*clypeus* (shield) of egregious lineament carved; on the one and the other side of this rounding — one here and the
other there, with the back propped, sitting upon the flat — two winged boys, toward the projections, held a kindled
torch.

On the slope of the aforenarrated plinth, likewise sitting back-to-back, were two nude and winged infants, upon the
flat of the crown; with the hands in view they retained an apple, and with the inner arms seized a most-ancient
bronze **candelabrum**, most-lucent, gilt, in the form of a vase, by a dolphin handle — which handles were two up-
curved, biting dolphins at a knot, and, with the tail, derived, hooked, over the body of the vase, thinning to the
shell-shaped gap, with two other knots toward the orifice; which, somewhat in circular dilatation, upon the lip, in
order, had fixed four sharp pins, and in the middle one, that exceeded the others, with the foot-stalk between the
shins of the boys.

All this sculpture, founded, sat upon a square Ophite (base) rising from the pavement, nude of lineament, except that
in the middle, carved, I saw a **maritime, or naval, trophy** (I thought, in monument of the victory attained, the
fleet of the Rhodians vanquished): a rostrum, or part of the beaked prow, of a most-ancient ship; in the middle of
which stood forth a trunk, in the branches of which was invested a military cuirass, and, by the brachial outlet, the
branches extended, truncated of tips; to one of the said, hung by the ring, was a shield; on the other, a naval
instrument; under the cuirass, transversely, on the trunk, hung an anchor and a rudder; upon the top of the trunk,
where the collar came out, a crested helmet was most-beautifully set. All which things it is not to be believed were,
without symmetry and greatest artifice, exquisitely, with all the requisite lineaments, expressed, and most-
excellently polished — worthy of noteworthiness and eternal memory. The commensuration of which, whoever knows the
proportion of the *sesquialter* (3:2) will easily conduct it perfect. I suspected that by one (workshop) the sculptors
of the Mausoleum and this (were) perfected.

> **ΕΡΩΤΟΣ ΚΑΤΟΠΤΡΟΝ** (EROTOS KATOPTRON) — "The mirror of Love."
> **ΑΡΤΕΜΙΣΙΔΟΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΔΟΣ ΣΠΟΔΩΝ** (ARTEMISIDOS BASILIDOS SPODON) — "The ashes of Queen Artemisia."

This leaf carries only a printer's asterisk-ornament — a decorative section-break following the Artemisia-tomb woodcut (p. 267). There is no body text to translate.

t:
> **ASPICE, VIATOR** — *(the epitaph of Sertullius and Rancilia)*
>
> "Behold, traveller, (the ashes) of Quintus Sertullius and of my sweet betrothed, the maiden daughter of Gaius
> Rancilia, together; and then afterward read what licentious Fate does. In our very flowering age, when the sharper
> force of love rushed upon us, mutually captured — at length, with father-in-law and mother-in-law consenting — in
> solemn wedding we are joined. But, O unhappy fate! On the first night, when, by the law of importunate pleasure to
> be discharged, we were compelled to extinguish the torch and render our vows to the shades of Venus — alas, in the
> very act, the marital house, collapsing, oppressed us both, most joyful, embraced, with the final sweetness. O
> deadly Sister (Fate)! Nor do I know what I had done (to deserve it). Consider: our longer hour was not then in the
> fates. Dear parents, bewail not our wretched and ghost-marked funerals with mourning nor tears, lest you make them
> more unhappy. But you — live your years longer than ours, best reader, and live your own. (Farewell.)"

Not far distant from this — somewhat moved to little sighs by the preceding unhappy case read — I found another
noteworthy and most-worthy monument, with two fluted little columns, one to a side, semicircle-worked out of the solid
rock, of whitest marble, with little bases and capitals, little architrave, little frieze, little cornices, and little
fastigium; in the three-sided (pediment) of which two whitening turtledoves drank together in a little vase. In the
content between the fluted (columns), of low relief carved, was an arched soffit, evenly distributed into little
coffered squares, where, in each, a cinquefoil occupied, by the optic norm (in perspective), the linings diminishing
with the content (depth). Under which an artful ark somewhat stood forth, fixed with two little doors — in one of
which entered —

> **· D · DITI ET PROSER(PINAE) · S ·**
> **· V · F ·**
> **TREBIAE Q(UINTAE),**
> **L(UCII) S(EX?) TREBII FILIAE.**
>
> "Sacred to Dis and Proserpina. (This) monument of love and of piety Aulus Fibustius, her husband, (raised) — with
> whom, with the utmost longing, delightfully she lived one month, three days. She, my wife, most-loving to me, most-
> unhappy, left me tears and eternal mourning. Perturbed by an extreme jealousy — when she suspected that I had lain
> with another woman — her sweetest love converted into fury, with the iron (sword), through the middle of the breast
> driven, she killed herself. Alas, wife — why this? My dear consort, thou oughtest to have removed from thy lover not
> only the deed, but even the suspicion. Farewell freely. But I, uncertain, unhappy and trembling, my life loosed
> (undone), rest.
>
> — THE INEVITABLE STATE OF NATURE THE STEPMOTHER.
> — THE BENIGN EDICT OF NATURE THE MOTHER."

From here, with most-joyful solace, departing — with curious desire most-eager to behold new things — hastening to
a semi-integral tribune, I beheld some exquisite relics of mosaic painting, wormwork-made. In this place I found no
sepulchre; but in the glasswork painting, still, **Proserpina, with Cyane and with the Sirens, gathering flowers near
the burning mountain of Etna**, was perfectly discerned. Where **Pluto, unsealing the fire-rooted crater of the
flame-breathing mountain, voluptuously ravished her to his love**; and Cyane, for not being able to succour her,
piteously weeping. There I found huge stones of the putrescent wall gaping, and grassy through the cracks with aster
and pellitory; which was also entangled and destroyed, as by a wedge fixed of a big root of an aged wild-fig, whose
roots, springing everywhere, creeping, had destroyed the tessellations, and, the coition of the joints deserted,
rendered great looseness of the walls.

Whence I only beheld part of a little river, (that) seemed a vestige of human form transmuted into it (Cyane), of
incredible art feigned, and marvellously expressed — such the like as once, in the shrine of Minerva on the Capitol,
in the tablet was seen the rape of the said (Proserpina), painted by Nicomachus. Where, with the mind applied to such
pleasant regard being — lo, at my back I hear the fall of some tessellations; and, finding myself solitary, in a
deserted and silent place, suddenly somewhat frightened, and, turning back, looking, I saw a gecko, or wall-lizard,
that had been the cause of such ruin.

Therefore no little displeasure invaded me, for not being able to see the whole work integrally, it being in the
greater part demolished. Considering, then, the violent manner in which Proserpina was suddenly seized, a sudden and
sad thought, in the loving heart, fiercely struck me, saying: "Alas, wretched, impudent and unhappy me! O importunate
investigation, and unbridled curiosity of past things, and of broken stones inquiring — to what am I devolved? If, by
my ill misfortune, my most-beautiful Polia were seized from me, and, by neglect of so great a present thing — above
all the treasures of the world most-pleasing — were driven off from me!" And, in a moment, a more bitter blow
transfixed the sad heart, presenting already in the confused mind the piteous and lamentable case: that the fugitive
of the burning fatherland (Aeneas) incautiously lost his beloved Creusa. And much more excessively it disturbed me,
invading, such a terror, remembering that, on the sandy and solitary shores, drawn away from my presence, my most-
loving Polia sat alone.

And that thus, to her, the trident-bearing Neptune might not violently do (as to Medusa)! Alas, at this point I
certainly experienced what is the affliction of spirit, and the quality of true lovers — extremely more trembling,
terrified, and stupefied, and finding myself in greater anguish, and into more miserable trepidation deduced, than
when I saw myself almost a putrescible little morsel among the gaping and horrend jaws of the venefic dragon, at the
next-door demise. With so much terror that I could judge (myself), through the priest and the removed simulacrum of
the Pellenean temple, to have every serenity struck from the mind, re-cruding every hour, the more, the formidable
grief in the fluctuating heart.

For which thing, impelled by the coquent cares and urgent anguishes, without any delay, most-swiftly brazen-footed —
leaving so noble an undertaking, and illustrious inquisition, and laudable lustration, and virtuous solace — suddenly,
then, through those windings and infested bushes, and rough shrubs, and through the place made narrow of stones and of
thorns, and through those prolapses of marbles, and formless heap of rudiments and fragments, uneven, scrupulous, and
among caustic nettles and pathless ruins, I hasten, with hostile course, by rough ways and innumerable stumbling-
blocks, with prompt velocity — not esteeming the laceration of my ragged toga, here and there held by thorny fronds,
and all full of burs and down, and thistle-tufts, and goat's-beard, and sowthistle, in some part entangled by the
rapacious seeds of hound's-tongue — firmly holding to have arrived at the newest troubles, and formidable perils, and
ultimate and deadly privation of all my hoped good, to my sweetest and most-precious Polia: not wholly alive, but half-
dead, like an asthmatic drawing the breath (not by other way than if the grave odour of the Babylonian gulf I had
drawn), with the eyes wet with tearful dew, near her, having prostrated myself, spasming, with incredible heart-grief
and swooning, scarce I arrived.

And she, with the soft soul moved, with serene forehead, and propitiated and soothing face — thus lurid and afflicted,
with assiduous pulse in my dolorous breast, with bloodless pallor trembling — miserating, grieving, with amorous pity,
marvelled at it; raising me, pretty, into her sweet embraces; and, with a genuine sweetness, and with a most-tenuous
saffron veil, my dirty face, dewy in most-rich sweat, with amorous obsequy lightly rubbed, dried me — both most-
officious and, with blandishment, sponging me. Whence, the cause and accident of so much bitter and troublous anguish
eagerly inquiring, and most-benignly blandishing me —

— with those persuasive and suasible little words, and soothing eloquence, with elocutive fluency, that opportunely
served to recreate me, and to vivify a body deformed in death, I somewhat, and satisfyingly, relieved, returned; and,
in me, little by little, the prostrate virtues quickening, and, laid up, in her venerable lap lying — every sad terror
(gone) — I narrated to her, sighing and groaning, the suspicious cause. She pleasantly smiled, and, amorously, with
prompt little kisses kissing me, with egregious shrewdness assured me, saying that soon she awaited the holy God of
love, Cupid; and therefore, blandishing, exhorted me that I ought patiently to give heed to pleasure — because
suffering, most often, is the cause of most-noble effects.

Consoling me, then, my beauty Polia — on this pact, paired with her residing — the semi-fled life refreshed me;
the boxwood pallor converted into its (natural) colouring, and the trembling invasion changed, I evaded into generous
magnanimity. But like a cineous cadaver, or dusty putrefied body, near my divine Polia, that (was) not integrally, and
to the (full) number, re-vivified. And therefore the habituated eyes returned to their accustomed gain and peculiar
pasture, tenaciously fixed on her.

Lo, that she, the calm Polia, with outstanding gestures and modest movements, and with celestial semblance, and
festive face, and with paternal customs, with adorned beauty — worthy and illustrious of everlasting sight, and
venerable beholding, of wit, form, (and) modesty egregiously endowed — composedly, without delay and any tarrying,
rose from the pleasant seat under the frondy little canopy; and, with reverent leave and inclination, duly venerating,
and without any motion, with singular reverence, devout, she stood kneeling, with the face suffused with vermilion,
more than the ruddying Claudian apples.

For which thing I — of such cause and act ignorant and unaware, because the eyes, unceasingly to contemplate her
immense beauties retained and sedulously occupied, I knew not, revoking, to dislocate, nor to remove them, and thence
fittingly to decline them — I did the like (suddenly to her accosted): I genuflected on the ground.

And lo, that (I not adverting) opposite us, the divine **Cupid** — with naked and uncovered body, comely and pretty
boy, in a swimming and swift little boat presented himself, with his unveiled eyes navigating to the whispering
shores where we sat awaiting; and, to the ancient (by age-emulating time worn) mole with the stern arriving, by no
means —

— my eyes, for the disproportion, suffered not, in the celestial form, firmly (unless the eyelids pressed) to collimate
(fix upon): so much rutilant splendour that puerile and divine aspect breathed, that by this it reasonably persuaded me
rather not to be among the mortals, but, without any failing, truly to be among the divine heroes — beholding a
heavenly spiritual (being) informed corporeal, and to the material eyes unwontedly and rarely sensible showing itself,
and objecting (before me). Whence, in extreme stupor, the dejected soul contemplated his head over-gilt with little
crisp and most-tenuous hairs, with two great and illuminating eyes of special majesty, frightful — the light of which,
beyond the vacillation, mortified my feeble sight. Then the round and swelling cheeks, suffused with purpling roses,
with all the other parts so beautiful, that I would deservedly repute the greatest felicity (for) him who only should
think it thoroughly, let alone (him) expressing it. And, as a winged god, at his holy shoulder-blades two wings stood
forth, fixed, of little gold feathers, of rosy-peacock colour, and cyan, and of mallow colour, and glittering,
agglutinated.

Persevering, my patroness and god-like Polia, and I, genuflected, we stood, thus, while the flying God began to speak;
whom I recognised by conjecture, marvelling — and (he), of so great a workmanship of Polia the wondrous rarity
admiring, and the magnitude of so many virtues and beauties stupendous (I thinking, verisimilarly, that to his most-
beautiful Psyche, in his soul, not without concupiscence, (as) more comely, more outstanding, and of more eminent
excellence he preferred her). And there, with speech of celestial afflation, a voice formed — (a voice) to recompaginate
every dissolved thing, to reawaken unharmed the sleeping cadavers in the humid earth, and out of the eternal sepulchres,
and even from the initial matter; and to bridle the edacity of the insatiable Vulcan (fire), and to make the horrid
waves lay down their turbid swelling, and to mitigate the unquiet alluvion of the intemperate sea, to make silent the
groaning shores, and to quiet the foaming and gnawed rocks; to incite whatever hollow (heart) to holy Venus, and to her
pleasant service — thus he made his persuasive little words:

"Polia Nymph, and thou Poliphilo — in the amorous obsequies and sincere cult of our venerable genetrix, intent
cultivators, and, in my flaming fires, intrepid, religious effects (doers): in her divine sight are your purely-vowed
sacrifices, your sedulous interventions, arrived, and your most-devout prayers, and dedicated service, and chaste
obligations. For this, your ardent desires merit, and efficaciously will be resolved (fulfilled), according as, praying,
you have obtained. Put then, with thy —

— individual companion, with secure safeguard, into my little boat. For to go to the maternal realm, and destined
island, none avails, unless I, as its proper navarch and ferryman, transport it (thither)" — and, with divine
reasonings, facetiously he invites her to enter.

Polia then, not tarrying, and unlazy, festive, my hand alacritously re-taken, rose, silent, but all prompt; and, with
elegant acrimony (keenness), with profound veneration and venial (reverent) bendings — she and I, having climbed upon
the fateful little boat, and, in the poop, set to a commodious sitting, and I paired with her without delay — those
divine Nymphs composedly, from the up-jutting shore, as much as one drawing of the hand, rowed.

The little boat was an *exeres* — that is, a little vessel not leaky, but fixed with a rowing-apparatus of six oars —
with a marvellous exterior daub: not of *palimpissa* (pitch), nor blackened with *zopissa* (ship-pitch), but with a
precious liquamen composite of almond-scented benzoin, ladanum, musk, amber, *zilibeth* (civet), and with twin storax,
and, with ordered distribution of quantity, with a most-noble mixture throughout anointed, and, of excellent artifice,
compaginated, and interwoven of white sandalwood, and citrine odoriferous, and of grave and non-carious aloewood,
exuding a wondrous and never-so-felt fragrance, over-smeared; fixed with little gold nails, which, in their bosses, or
their nipple-headed caps, shone with wondrous artifice, encloistered, most-precious gems. The gratings and the thwarts
were of blood-red sandalwood. Beyond measure they rendered the heart exhilarant.

Which wondrous and unwonted little boat, six most-apt and supremely-disposed and lordly maidens rowed. The oars, with
the blades, were of illustrious and snowy ivory, not with radish (bleached), but genuine, pre-shining; and the rowlocks
of gold, and the (oar-)thongs of commixed and twisted silk. These maidens were dressed most-richly, of most-limpid
cloth, to the swift and modest breezes inconstant and flying-prone; impeded by the re-blowing (of the wind), with
voluptuous ostentation of the members of the sub-adhering form, the flower of their little age it showed — with the head
becomingly wrapped of abundant most-blond tresses; some with rich hair, lucid, more black than Indian ebony. And how
pleasing it presented itself to see two opposite (types) accosted: the flesh beyond measure snowy, of the face, shoulders
and breast, surrounded most-richly by blackest hair, disposed in spirals and textures, wantonly bound of little silver
cords, with knotting and snares so pleasant, and most-grateful to the senses, as ever any voluptuous thing could appear
— to revoke them (the eyes) to itself from every other noteworthy sight, and enthralled, distracted — over the nape
constrained (bound up) with oriental pearls, to which let yield that which —

— Julius (Caesar) bought for his dear Servilia. And some had, of roses and of other conspicuous flower-wreaths
entangled, the little-crisp hair, tendril-wise shadowing the lucid forehead; with sumptuous collars of turbinate stones,
of various and companionable colouring, most-precious, encompassing the milky and straight throat. Then, tightly, they
were girt, transversely, under, close-by, the hard little breasts — an obstinate obstacle to succumb to the thin
breast-garment — which, however violated (constrained), nonetheless, to their dwelling somewhat quaking, proterve
(saucily) returned. Which breast-garment, in the circuit of the collar, had an adornment of over-thread of gold,
interwoven, in the greatest polish of expression, of constrained threads, with the rims of ordered and pellet-like
pearls; and along the length of this hedge, composedly outspread, shone most-precious gems.

To replicate aptly I would not know that which to me was licentiously conceded, and (I) made partaker, to speculate —
every thing, scatteringly, in the soul revolving, with amorous device, embracing (it), in the memory repeating, in the
mind representing a sweet enjoyment, and sweetly, of so much beauty, a soft pleasure verisimilarly I usurped. Two, then,
of these — **Aselgia** and **Neolea** — were of lascivious adornment, preciously clad, Attalically, of *chamochaino*
cloth wefted with golden weft, and of a warp of cyan silk, such as King Attalus in Asia could not find. Two others,
likewise — **Chlidonia** and **Olvolia** — had the voluptuous Babylonian dress of precious *thalassium* (sea-purple),
with varied texture. The last, **Adea** and **Cypria**, were invested of most-noble *melledarum*, with wormwork and airy
stitching, with most-minute and pervious slashes, manifoldly jagged, in the ground set under with gold foil at the
extreme fringes. And at the joint of the arms was, broadly, an outlet of the proper garment, whence came out the ivory
arms, bared, for ostentation of another whiteness than the milky coagulation, with all the requisite ornaments and
nymphal additions. The fresh and wanton breeze then, according to its motion, now the form of the round, untouched and
hard belly, reflowing, disclosed; and the noteworthy pubis; now the fleshy thighs; some time the trembling buttocks.
Then, on the longish little (feet), the footwear, by force (with a shoe-horn conducted) brought back — such were of cyan
silk, and of greening and Punic colouring, exquisitely tanned; on the vertex of the foot, with a sinuate opening,
moon-shaped, most-polishedly fenced round, with rims and gold buckles politely strapped, and with crepidae and gilt
soccoli; and some with silken little cords, gold-pointed, and alternately, by some, suppressed —

— golden circlets, threaded, strained (them, the shoe-cords). And with others, manifoldly adorned, of wanton and virginal
shrewdness, invented to gratify the senses with laborious voluptuousness. All these things, of special dignity, so
gracious and much-admired offered themselves to our amorous mystery, as, to the ardent flames, the fatness (fuel); and to
Vulcan, the sulphurable matter; and, of the Tartarean pit, the vigilant custody to three-throated Cerberus; and to Megaera
and her sisters, the mortal fright; and the florid youth to amorous Cupid; and to the mother (Venus), the commodious
lurking-places.

Separated, then, from the sandy shore, these divine boat-nymphs beautifully reined the ivory oars in the flat grating, by
the gyrons (oar-loops); and each, with the most-shapely faces toward the nude lord (standing on the prow), with majestic
reverence, joyously turned themselves — and their whitening backs to us. My genius, and Polia, with most-luculent
confabulation, said to me: "My Poliphilo (every other thing postposed and refused), most-beloved — I wish that thou
understand and know, that these six present little maidens are the readiest handmaids of that lord, and opportunely
ministering to his pleasant service."

Sitting, then, these solacing, comely and outstanding little Nymphs upon the sandalwood thwarts, paired, turned toward the
divine lord, and to us the delicate back — the divine helmsman, the smooth wings distended, explicating, having called
with odoriferous breath to himself the sweet zephyr, wind-blowing rendered the holy feathers (more than the ardent
carbuncle to the pre-shining torches, coruscating lightnings), and, the plumate wings filled with flower-bearing air, we
began to abandon the garrulous shores, and to navigate upon the deep and spacious sea, with grateful calm tranquil. And,
of great and fearful veneration, and of singular sweetness and alacrity, my amorous and contumacious heart being stuffed,
and all shakeable, distinctly with my genius I cogitated: what heart so inhuman could ever be found — or one of such
hardness, so vivid and so vigorous, however more rough than the bark of the palm to imagine — that, to such-made beautiful
and concupiscible presences, and divine objects, to all gentleness most-tender and most-soft, and mortified, invalid, and
most-lenient, of a sudden would not have shown itself?

And what imprisoned and extinguished concupiscence — glacial and depraved appetite — that would not here have vigorously
unbroken the tenacious cloisters and biting snares, and most-aptly restored itself to the comely, most-beautiful and
amorous spectacles, and would not have turned itself into flame-bearing Etna? And what Diana would have spurned so benign
fires — (fires) to contaminate the chaste Hippolytus, and make lascivious the most-modest Orithyia? But what must those
have felt, who wholly were apt, near, and uniformly disposed (to love)? I found myself like the little fish born in
boiling water — thence extracted, and in other waters set to boil, it never cooks (again). Beyond, then, stupidly I
beheld that divine little spirit, and, in his over-gilt feathers, some restless little plumules, tender and delicate,
such as are on the immature wings of the young hawk not yet flying from the nest, and, at the dewy winds, tremulous
resulting. O how gracious, and how most-pleasant to the senses, the little golden-crimson feathers presented themselves!
Which golden colour, in some feathers, refulged, and (some) of phoenician colouring; some of glaucous colour, and of
emerald tincture, and of mallow colouring, and of cyan, and (some), more than the icteric little bird, yellow — in a
golden colour most-admiredly coming together, and, with harmonic dispensation, most-decorously, through the divine
wings.

For which thing, all the jewels of fecund nature, distributed there, participatingly, to coruscate, I easily judged —
because they irradiated like mobile and most-tenuous foils of most-pure gold, suspended in the breeze, and, in the clear
sun, wind-blowing, comelily painting the waters of the most-placid colours; then torn (reflected) by the unstable and
crisping little waves, in a great emulating gyre. I beheld also the incomparable beauty of the divine composite of Polia,
from hour to hour ever more delicious and shapely presenting herself. Then I beheld also the most-purged and serene air,
the moderate and placid weather, and the saline cerulean waters — like perspicuous crystal, most-limpid, seen even to the
most-open shallows — and, here and there, many wooded rocks; and, ornated of vernal verdure, the scattered (Sporad)
little isles, thick of leafy greening shrubs, and most-pleasantly shady; and many vague places, from the senses, afar,
lost themselves; and in the flattened (waters), like spots, they appeared. Likewise the frondiferous trees over-shadowed
the littoral little banks, and the greenish reflex, then, in the most-nitid and mirror-like waters, as the proper (thing),
was discerned.

Proceeding, then, our solacing and triumphant navigation — where presided the empire and divine monarchy of potent Love;
where resided that lord who, in extreme sweetness, renders himself austere, and, in austerity, feigns himself so sweetly
sweet, and, in sweetness, so bitter, and, in bitterness, presents himself so pleasant. O happy, therefore, whoever,
navigating, should feel his feathered wings prosperous and favourable! Finding myself, then, thus, between two so pleasing
lords — the one inflamed me, the other consumed me — lo, that the marine gods: **Nereus** with the most-pleasing **Chloris**,
—

— with the daughters Ino and Melicertes, upon the non-foaming waves, making festival, came, upon their bigae (chariots),
adoring the divine boy. And there the wave-born **Melanthus, or Posidonius (Neptune)**, with the cerulean beard, hispid,
with the pungent and tri-cusped trident (fuscina), towed by great seals (*phocae*); and the cerulean and piping **Tritons**
with the sonorous conches trumpeting — so that through the ether the clangour, bellowing, resounded, leaping — with a
throng of Nymphs, the Dircean and the **Nereids**, seated upon the most-swift and curved **dolphins** (at the aquiline
breath everlasting, conveyors of Arion, friends of the same name), and the sea-monster (*pistrix*), and the monstrous
**Cephisus**.

And with this same order came the ancient father (**Oceanus**) with his consort **Tethys**, and with **Erato, Ephyra, and
Phillyra, Hippo and Prino**, the daughters, festive, presented themselves; and then the daughter of Nereus, with the
grieving **Aesacus** (of the mournful voice, clad in anthracite colour, or dusky garment, in mourning for his dear Epiriphe,
bitten by the venomous serpent); and **Halcyone**, plaintive of her beloved and awaited Ceyx, flying, made festival; and
**Proteus**, drawn by the hippocampi; and **Glaucus** the fisher, with his beloved **Scylla**; and the other fish-monsters —
many horse-fish (hippopsarii) and man-fish (anthropopsarii) — with unthinkable applause, with flux and reflux, and the
fragour of the facing and hoary waters, submerging themselves, and thence bursting up; and, with honorary veneration, with
solemn honorifics, with huge stridours, most-choice wave-wanderers, of monster-making and fishy effigy. And, again, a
multitude of shore-dwelling little birds, and whitest swans — some swimming, and some flying through the air, and, with the
extreme (highest) voice, singing sweet concerts, resounded. Praise and glory, unanimous, they gave, as to the omnipotent
gods (their) subjects, gratulation most-celebratedly discharging; making, too, jocosely, great fragours with the movements
of the waters, agilely, with the breathing gills, and little wings, and rowing fins, leaping and salient, and with grateful
din whistled softly. For which thing, I, incredibly delighted (at) so much variety of aquatic gods, and Nymphs, and
monsters, before by me never seen, with so much venerating dance and honorific exhibited to the divine boy, marvelling
stood stupefied. For no less than ever a triumphator I judged myself, than whoever in Rome triumphing; and then, for its
being to me by the gods so benignly and so well communicated, more happy I esteemed myself than the fortunate Polycrates.

It befell now, that, my heart being already domesticated in a solacing fire, with plenitude of delightsome pleasure, and
contiguous to my delicious and divine Polia — beyond all the memorable spectacles, I tasted a refreshing odour, breathing
from the utmost cleanliness and delicious daintiness; fallen into the greatest stupor, with my genius, within me, I said:
"Behold, that which I —

— coveted, I have now victoriously attained; and openly I see it; and that salutary help, so long wished-for, embraced,
I hold — with no less gratification and voluptuous solace than the splendent Cynthia, solacing, with her beloved Endymion
(scrutator of the shallow waters), the supernal realms relinquished, in the wobbling, light and piscatory little skiff,
near the Lamian rocks. Nor could even Paris glory so much of the litigious judgement (of the apple), nor of the smuggled-
away Ledaean (Helen), sailing with swollen sails at the blowing south-wind. Nor Jason, of the malefic and deceived Medea.
Nor Theseus, of the Minoan prey (Ariadne). Nor the Roman Captain (Antony), of the ambitious Egyptian (Cleopatra). Nor
could the granddaughters of tall Atlas glory equally of their grandsire, sustaining, with most-robust shoulders, the
starry sky. Nor the painter Apelles, of the amorous gift the Great Alexander made him (Campaspe). Nor is the *spicilegium*
(gleaning) so most-accepted to golden Ceres, as I (glory) of having beside me my divine Polia — the comeliness of whom
would have hastened slow Saturn, and stopped most-swift Phoebus, and stabilised the caduceus-bearing Cyllenian (Mercury),
and set aflame frigid Diana, and (would have) even had the gods officious (in her service).

Navigating, then, with the light and sweet appulse of the outstanding breezes, I, with scrutinising and perspicacious and
inconstant regard — intently, not being able to affirm (fix on), now the one, now the other speculating — but of this I
could not discern, nor delimit, the disparity of the two (Cupid and Polia), save (in) the divinity. And there, strongly by
an inexcogitable sweetness compelled, to both I freely repudiated (surrendered) my soul: commending it to the power of one
(Cupid), who fittingly could condone to it his amorous salvation; and to the will of the notable Polia, that she too
benignly should lend her consent. But yet, undoubtedly, I esteemed, confident and reliant, that to such majestic presence
and venerable aspect no other effect and exit could breathe than ardent love, and that she now could no more flee her
triumphal boat, nor retreat; and much more I hoped for the sequel of my extreme desire, by the saying of the amorous
hieroglyphs of the fluttering standard (*Amor vincit omnia*) of this glorious little boat of the divine and most-potent
Cupid — where, exulting to be conducted into such dignification, most-blessed, and glorying to be adorned with so excellent
a companion and amorous reciprocation (that Apollo cannot so glory of the ornament of his quiver and cithara of Peneian
fronds, nor Polycrates of the recovery of his ring, nor the Great Alexander of the attained victories and elevated trophies)
as I judged myself glorious, finding myself in so great a triumph. Nonetheless, beyond belief marvelling, by what mode, or
instinct, in that divine little body was so active and forceful a fire fruitfully placed — which the universe inflames —

— and burns; transcends, penetrating the most-solid heavens, and thence, without any diminution, the profundity of the
abyss — a fire of marvellous nature, which neither the liquefying Tethys, nor the ancient father Oceanus, nor the trident-
bearing Neptune could ever resist. What fire is it? — that the mortals, in it, with supreme sweetness dying, nourish
themselves, and live.

Still greater a miracle I beheld, cast into stupor: how, in that flocked snow of Polia's delicious breast, it burned
without contrast, and purpling roses germinated? I cogitated affectionately how it burned, too, in those whitest lilies,
replete and superfluent of juicy and milky humour? I felt myself not even able to discuss how it inflamed so sharply in
those glittering roses, sprouting among the wintry frosts of rigid Capricorn? I found myself likewise ignorant in what
manner the breathable Eulus (breeze), in the festive eyes of the fair Polia, with so much impulse of soliciting,
provoked that fire so inflammable — (a fire) that the leonine rays (of the Sun) of the Gaditan fleet, to burn that of King
Theron, proceeded not with so much burning as, from her eyes, burnable, into my heart irradiated — unknowing, more, and out
of my mind, by what manner Pyragmon and the companions (Vulcan's smiths) had fabricated, in them (her eyes), their so
thick and domestic workshop, to fulgurate. But above all things this exceeded — that I, by no shrewd way, could investigate:
with what virtue, wasting, collided, mortified, and wholly prostrated to so many wicked insults and frequent battles,
struggling, I repugned? — with the lightning heart captive and tightly rebound, surrounded by hostile pleasure, and
circumvallated by kindled and gracious flames; which (against their own name), unable to conflagrate that pricking bramble-
patch and that most-rough, imbricated thistle-bed (my resistance), were, in my heart, angularly implicated, and, by those
most-placid eyes (faithful dispensers of the holy treasure of the great Cupid), diffusely disseminated.

"O sweetest winged one" (turned to that god, I then said), "how sweetly thou nestlest in my soul!" "O most-pleasant" (then,
to the star-bearing eyes of Polia, I said), "O sweetest executioners — how, of my sad heart, have ye known to compose and
gird so full and crammed a quiver to the divine flanks of Love? Nonetheless, ever more gracious I wish you, and warmly
desire — much more, and without comparison, than the auricled (ass-eared) Lucius desired, in so many noxious troubles and
supreme and mortal labours, the vermilion roses; and more grateful and opportune than, to the unhappy Psyche, the succour of
the grain-bearing ant, and the reedy warning, and the eagle's aid, and the innocuous little prick of Cupid's arrow." For all
which things, I could not, however, revoke the ardent soul out of the delicate arms and voluptuous embraces of my
beautiful-haired Polia — because my insatiable conceits had there firmly, and eternally, imprisoned and proscribed it —

— and she, with this high lord, this continual prey, navigating, divided and imparted. Therefore this
alone I esteemed extreme sweetness of delight — to which, in presence, the blessed celebrity and triumph
invited me.

> POLIPHILO NARRATES THAT THE NYMPHS, HAVING RESTED THE OARS, BEGAN SWEETLY TO SING. AND POLIA,
> SINGING IN COMPARISON (in answer), FELT A GREAT SWEETNESS OF LOVE.

With the utmost auspicious, superb and great pomp, insolent triumph, with unthinkable joy and voluptuous
gratification — with stimulating darts savagely fixed in the scarred heart, at the amorous eyes of Polia,
and at the arrow-frequency of Cupid, an opposing and most-firm target — with an amplified heart, more
furnace-like burning, ever more avid to augment the ardour, through the solicitous ministry of the
insatiable and impatient eyes (to which reasonably I pardoned it, considering the cause that made them so
cupidinous, and supremely applied to it, and sedulously intent): like the simulacrum of Apis, which
toward the sun ever turns, gazing — so, and not otherwise, were my eyes directed upon her, who was a
conspicuous and exciting object, from that much-admired irradiating face, in the world proscribed of
equivalent beauty, and by every means interdicted.

But more noxious, and much more iniquitous and vexing slaughter, did the furtive and wandering thoughts
experience of this valorous lord — best of such matter the shrewd quaestors, and of the gain the most-apt
artificers, to fabricate and compose, of fire and of flames, so sweet a torment, so venerable an idol, so
shapely a simulacrum, so outstanding a form, in the workshop of the imaginative faculty, and solacingly
to feign. Oh, how much — molesting, and refusing all temperament, declining to succumb — did these
unbridled and public cut-throats of my repose and quiet show themselves, and insatiable and raging of the
unseen beauty of my golden-haired Polia; sometimes sweet, and sometimes bitter, sometimes glad, and more
often sad; many times desirable, and often to be fled, they accused themselves. What most-valid forces,
then, could have imprisoned the incontinent senses — reluctant, to dissent; and dissenting, to repugn;
and repugning, to drive off; and driving off, to spurn —
