— whatever hedge and enclosure, throughout that pleasant meadow diffusely flower-bearing of the singular
and choice delights of Polia (like a murmuring bee), most-richly, unwearied, they gathered — so much
sweetness, and sweetest delight, diffusing it through the oppressed viscera. Where the amplest serpent-
flames, without relaxation insulting, violently invaded. For which thing I did not judge it worthy, nor
convenient, that the amorous and carbuncled heart, vigorously exercised in these such works, and
sustaining them, should be moved to remove it, and by molestation to debilitate it. But rather, most-
modestly, I ought, tolerating, to support it — which so willingly, for my affable content, it had
laboriously contracted.

Now, in the fateful ship's-command, without sternpost and rudder navigating, we the first-sailors, and
upon this unpremeditated vessel, where all the mysteries of love breathed — which had for its poop the
prow, and for its prow the poop, with the most-worthy and exquisite artifice, accommodated to Cupid by his
mother — than which never an apt and most-richly eloquent tongue of round oratory could, expounding,
express, and expressing recollect, and distinctly recollecting recount.

In the very middle of which — that is, in the mast-step — was raised a golden spear, with a triumphal and
imperatorial standard, of thin silken cloth, of cyan dye; in which, of little gems of the opportune
colouring, with whitest pearls, were polishedly, picturewise, re-woven, on both faces, with manifold
foliage, with the utmost most-comely adornment, three hieroglyphs: an antique little vase, in the mouth-
gap of which burned a little flame; and then was the world; joined together with a little branch of osier,
at the soft breaths of the spring-bearing and obsequious zephyr wind-blown, flutteringly volant, and
choicely inconstant. The interpretation of which I made thus:
> **AMOR VINCIT OMNIA** — "Love conquers all."

The divine Steersman I, with reverent and decent regards, willingly willing him, with every possible
effort to contemplate — the disproportionate object, my feeble sight fittingly did not suffer. But,
conniving with my cheeks (half-closing my eyes), in this manner somewhat the divine boy I manifoldly
comprehended. Sometimes he appeared to me of twin aspect; sometimes of triple; and yet, sometimes, he
showed himself with infinite effigies. Who, with Polia, made our itinerary happy, blessed, and glorious.
And by this way the amorous and prow-standing Cupid, fanning the sacred feathers of his perpetual wings —
in which Canens, lover of Picus, solaced herself — shone more than refined gold, of various and most-
pleasant colouring, rotating in a circle above the little waves. More beautiful and more pleasing than
the crystalline triangular column of Euclid demonstrates, approximated to the eyes.

Now the nautical Nymphs gave beginning — with a most-sweet note, and with a heavenly intonation, from the
human wholly deviated, and beyond belief, with reasoned song-craft — to sing, and to trill a most-sweet
concord, with consonant voice and melody. Insomuch that rightly I doubted I should shatter from excessive
sweetness, because almost from its place removed I felt the resulting and wounded heart, and of sweetness
it seemed to me, reasonably, that it should exile itself through my lips. And they, following, with
vibrating little tongues, in the sonorous palate broke, crisping, doubling, and tripling into one the
briefest little chromatics, or tailed notelets — and, first intercepted, two by two; then three and three;
then by four; last, all six — the rosy little lips, tremulous, moderately opening them, and graciously
joining them, they proffered the modulating spirits, with mosaic proportion, with mellifluous voice, in
the warm heart syncopated, and with weary utterance of love. A voice sighing to the places, most-sweetly
throating — enough to put into oblivion the natural need, and to neglect it — with stringed instruments
they sang the sweetnesses and qualities of love: the facetious thefts of supernal Jove, the solacing
warmths of most-holy Erothea (Venus), the lasciviousnesses of festive Bacchus, the fecundities of the
foster-mother and golden Ceres, the savoury fruits of Hymenaeus — with versifying manner expressing, and
rhythmically proffering, *melos emmetron* (metred song).

For which thing, with a straying mind, most-firmly I held that such was not that sweet-sounding one which
Eurydice, borne in the winged three-team to the infernal (regions), and —

— from the most-shady seats, from the eternal flames freed (Eurydice). Nor yet, with such a sound, did
Hermes lull to sleep the eyed shepherd (Argus). Such (a sound), through the most-purged air scattering
itself, breathed out of the precious and coral little lips; and through the white throat one saw the
vocal spirits passing, with modulated sweetness diffusing itself. For that was celestial flesh, and a
divine composite transparent — like crystalline, most-frigid, and refined camphor, tinged with crimson.

Whence Phoebus would have stayed from coming to bedew the wolf-light dawn with his coruscating rays, and
would have forgotten to paint, and to make the colours for the flowers, and to renew a gracious day for
the mortals. And by this, without doubt, the bow-bearing Diana would have forgotten the curved bows and
the flying arrows, and the sedulous huntings, and the dense woods; and, warming the gelid fount, she
would not have spurned the presence of the incautious hunter, and would not have turned the horned stag,
to the biting dogs lacerable (i.e. she would have spared Actaeon). And the all-wandering Selene would
have withdrawn from illustrating with her splendour the supernal heavens and the shadowed earth. And the
frightful Proserpina, in her mournful realm, would not have racked the doleful subjects, had a like tone
reached her ears. And the solacing Bacchus would have made resistance to the slippery lasciviousnesses,
and would have neglected the Ogygian hills, Elis, Naxos, Chios, and Mount Massicus, and Mareotis, and
would have made little of the must-sweet delights of the vintaging Autumn. And the fostering Ceres would
have kept the ears of corn ever in green, postponing the abundant realms of Ausonia, nor would have
exchanged the fat and four-grained ears with Chaonia. And the cloud-thundering bird (Jove's eagle), out
of the hooked curvature of its inverted talons, would not have felt the ravished Phrygian cup-bearer
(Ganymede) flee away — so most-sweetly the Nymphs sang, and concordantly sounded, and each of them, with
my Polia singing along, dispensed celestial melodies to the open ears.

By which the black and multiform and lucubratory Cerberus would have been lulled; nor would he have kept
watch, with unmoving eyes, the metallic valves of Taenarum. And then the raging Tisiphone, with the
monster-bearing sisters, to the wretched souls would have shown themselves most-placid and benign. Nor
ever were Parthenope, with her sisters Leucosia and Ligeia — daughters of Achelous and of Calliope —
singing at the Capri isles near Pelorus, heard with so much harmony, of voice, mode, Lyre, and pierceable
tibia; whence the soul, incendiarily inflamed, removed from its place by the happy songs, and sounds,
effigies, beauties, retinue, and majesty, I could not redeem, nor make it my own. But, most-tightly
bound, it commended its estate into the delicate arms, and in the whitening bosom of Polia, a perpetual
and surrendered hostage, obliged it. Which then, cogitating, by delectable paths and voluptuous conduits,
arrived at the arcane delights. And thence, with all my excited virtues drawn into myself, I could resume
nothing else but a solacing imaginative, and glorious.

By which, of over-rich pondering, the anxious mind, with a refreshment of spirit, fed itself; and with
little curious regards, and lewd appetites, the manifest and perfect shapelinesses (and rarely such a
habit of appearance) of Polia most-avidly I beheld, refusing every other thing worth watching, avertible
of protection. But singularly, then, most-pleasing to me was her glittering breast, wondrously painted
with purpling roses, and with milky lilies, in their first opening — in the tearful dawn, without
obstacle to my eyes, a most-placid spectacle, openly conceded, and without an impeding medium, but
sufficiently coloured — to that most-admired object which was her face, so enticing and marvellously
beautiful, graceful, and perspicuous, that such does not appear, with its ornament Hippe, in the pure sky;
with little tendril-curls above, and the rosy forehead and flat temples trembling, which, with the utmost
adornment, down the snowy neck and whitening shoulders flowed. The wanton and spring-bearing breeze
choicely re-blew them. As much as ever the most-high Jupiter can imagine, to confer on the nature of it,
and benignly to produce and skilfully-make — nor ever could Apelles have painted a like one, and much less
Aristides, who feigned human souls with his little brush.

Of which sight I could not sate myself — neither more nor less than the murmuring bees do not sate
themselves of the odorous thyme and *amellus*, and the wanton she-goats of the flowering *cytisus*, and of
the tender fronds. And with willing soul, and with incredible pleasure, I would have unlocked my most-
amorous heart, judging it no way grievous — and tessellated (it) — that she, thence, having seen it,
should have received by proof the token of what are the qualities that, loving, one endures. As to Caesar
the stigmatised Antipater (showed his scars), and as my soul was promptly seduced by her sweet little face
and notable figure, and reduced into servile surrender — not otherwise making pervious my breast,
lacerating, fenestrated, than the most-pious Egyptian Pelican, dwelling in the solitude of the turbid and
headless Nile, to its raging chicks, for hunger, with piercing and cruel beak splits and shatters itself,
disembowelling the pitiful and maternal heart. Which, not to Dionysus, but only to her, perpetually is
most-dedicated, excitable; and, diffusing itself, flowed in me the insane and Lernaean loves, and the
fiery desires; and the incitative thoughts it feigned in the consenting heart, composing, to consume me,
and to destroy my very self, an ardent and most-burning flame, by me wholly conceived. And with greater
miracle the lethal and death-bearing dart, innocuously transfixed, poised itself in my wounded heart, than
the pendent lethal dart in Ephesus, without a noose, in the temple of Diana. The soul therefore
interdicted, to vivify me fully availed not.

Therefore, for such-made cause mortified, beyond measure ardent — if not her delectable regards, refreshing
me, recreated me, and the amorous nods —

— comforted me, and the low and sweet little words vivified me. She soliciting me affectionately, that I
should give heed to the sweet songs of such egregious and divine singers, and to enjoy so many marvellous
things with the senses — interrupting the fixed regard upon her, and all my cordial intent. Beyond all
that one can opine, more pleasing was my most-beautiful Polia to my fervescent burnings, than, by chance,
so pleasing and expected would not have presented themselves the rapid waves of Xanthus and of Simois to
the Ilian flames (that burned Troy). Nor so pleasing showed itself the honoured gift of the head of the
bristly Boar, from Meleager to Atalanta. Nor to the beloved Alcmena the fair gift from the benign Jove.
Nor so pleasing and opportune offered itself to Hannibal, in the waters, the elephant — as Polia, most-
pleasing to my every delight and content.

Constant, then, to the begun work, between sweetest voluptuousness and odious delay, I persevered — neither
more nor less than the ponderous gold persists to the utmost cement, and to the most-subtle liquors. I
turned me then to the divine boy. "O flame-bearing Cupid," murmuring I said, "you, some time, my lord, with
the most-beautiful Psyche, wounded your very self, and with your own cruel arrows, up to the newest line of
ardour — as the mortals — she supremely loving, and it pleased you to love her above all girls. And much it
grieved you, the guileful counsel of the envious and fallacious sisters, and upon the cloudy cypress
against her, with long-lasting lament racked, you made irate, lamentable complaints, upbraiding her. Use
and exercise, therefore, toward me, pity; and consider, expert, the fragile quality of the cupidinous
lovers; and temper somewhat your burning torches, and modify your noxious arms, and slacken your death-
bringing bow — for of love I am all racked.

"For which I reasonably argue: that if, in your very self, savage and pitiless, you wounded yourself — what
equability of soul persuades that I should not fear that, without pity, toward me, more harsh and unbridled
and most-savage, you would not show yourself?" And so, exasperated, concitatedly I dared; and with diverse
petitions, and prayers, and fabricated complaints, and feigned satisfactions, I somewhat softened the
strong invasion, and the frequent impulse of the wicked and eyeless love. But for all this my enkindled
heart was not condignly reconciled, nor really satisfied to my disjointed appetite. And that which then I
prayed him: only that he put an end, at least, to my tormenting and long-lasting hoping, with the molesting
expectation of a prison-like issue.

For, however much the coveted future be much more sweet of avidity than the acquired past delight, yet
every hostile love contends toward the expected end. Therefore, abridge, with sudden abolition, the timely
hope. My lord, this ungrateful and displeasing deferring — more than to the pure eyes the smoky Cloud, and
to the teeth the stupefying sourness, and than the —

— being slow with help to the coveter — because to a concupiscent soul it is a grave torment, the odious
day-postponing, and the prolonging of the desired end. Accusing then also, and pregnant nature reasonably
— that she shrewdly had all things, and most-excellently, conciliated, save that she had left uncompacted
the appetite with the power. Then returning into myself, strongly marvelling. For I could not perfectly
know where so much prepared and durable material (like unconsumable Etna) he found, and a fire-place
copious of so much fire, within my nursling and burnable heart. At the end, only to guard vigilantly the
choice and most-noble adorned, composed, and ornate object, and to exhaust, with my hidden ears, the
sweetest consonances with heavenly intonation — from which, receiving ineffable diversion, I tasted, to
the senses, a quickening and extreme delight.

Now, in this inexperienced manner, over the placid and levelled little waves of the un-furrowed deep, our
speeding six-oar ran like a light water-skater; and the most-comely rowers, most-festively jubilating,
sang in the Iasian mode; and the divine Polia, again, without the others, alone — from those minimally
dissonant, but comparable — Lydian-wise sang. Not the plaints of raging Tragedy, nor in the cackling
Satire, nor in the deceitful Comedy, nor in the tearful Elegies; but with a most-adorned poem, and with
elegant little words, the supreme sweetnesses of the holy and fostering Erycina (Venus) they composedly
proffered, and the delectable fallacies of the assisting son (Cupid) they eloquently sang. And Polia,
affable and comely, of cultivated adornment, polished and elegant, congratulating — the thanksgivings of
the obtained graces (provoking to admiration) she sang, with such vehemence and sweet-sound as, of blind
Demodocus, at the hearing of the wise Ulysses, with wailing cithara, did not attain. Which most-pleasing
companion — feeling herself no less delighted, partaker — speaking jocosely, and blandishing, tempting
me: how did the instant things appear to me? Naming to me, of whatever rowing Nymph, the proper name; and
with sweet persuasion she affirmed to me that **perseverance alone wears the victor's diadem**. And in
this unbridled avidity wholly slipped down, and most-cast-forth, most-pleasantly we navigated, and
prosperous we arrived at the delicious island Cythera.
pages.wcap: The Bark of the God of Love

t:
**Having come most joyfully to the longed-for place, whose worthy loveliness
Poliphilo affirms, fittingly describing its plants, herbs, birds and dwellers.
But first the form of the little boat, and how, at the descent of the lord Cupid,
many gift-bearing nymphs opportunely presented themselves to meet him.**

The divine boy making sail with his spread wings — not from the wineskin of
Ulysses, but urged by the obsequious and dew-bearing breezes, daughters of
Astraeus and of rosy Aurora, of one unanimous consent — Polia and I, finding
ourselves kindled and headlong with eagerness to reach the destined end, with the
greatest delight of love that ever human sense could feel, nor foreconceive, nor
much less divulge. Which, however excessive it was intimately in the heart, was
nonetheless the more readily quickened by the deific presence, and by those most
witty rowing nymphs, and by the sweetest singing, and by the mysterious form of
the solid and unshaken little boat — a fit instrument organised of love — and by
the precious material, and by the sweetness and pleasantness of the place; and
much more by the near flame that Polia, with rare excellence, exuberantly breathed
into my burnable heart. For her amorous and most refulgent eyes, gliding
lightning-like through mine to my inmost heart, seditiously stirred up a most
bitter conflagration; by which, heated through and prostrately wounded, frequent
sobs gushed forth — not otherwise than the cook pours out over the burning and
excessive fire through the lips. Just so, neither more nor less, the boiling gasps
compelled from my fervent heart abundantly boiled up, showing themselves
resounding; and the importunate fires I fittingly mitigated with the sole beauty
of my lovely Polia, my guide. But how it was, I most abundantly experienced such
pleasure that I was wholly absorbed and consumed — more than ever my most decent
tongue could adapt itself to such expression.

Finally, most joyful, glad and triumphant, to the island extremely desired, with
our proud and oar-wandering ship of six banks — not ballasted, but light — which
was compacted of a form thus.

Of a fourfold partition, two were used up in the poop and in the prow, thus alike
in lineament or form, the one as the other. The two other partitions were
dispensed in the remaining hollow body; and —

— one gunwale and the other, between prow and poop, began and ran with a bent
slope. This falling-away sloped a quarter, and thence little by little, level, the
rest lengthened out to the opposite end. These bent curvatures stood two feet high
from the decking. And in one and the other the three thwarts were fixed
transversely, raised a foot and a half from the decking. The keel then was clothed
with plates of gold, and so the bent ribs, from one end and the other rising
belly-wise. At the last tapering — called the dolphin — bent round in its shaped
likeness, it hooked, rendering a graceful volute; in the rounding of which shone
an ornament of thick and most precious gems. From the winding of which, toward the
flat of the poop and of the prow, little by little it stemmed into a stalk,
turning into an antique foliage, amplified upon the flat with a natural and
exquisite shaping of the finest gold, sparsely serpentining, with exact little
stalks and tendril-lacings, or incisions, and fringings, most elegantly expressed
lapping over the flats. From which scroll likewise there proceeded most
beautifully, descending inlaid from the pointed summit of the flat, following the
shaping of the gunwales — that is, the rail, or lip, where the tholes were fixed —
a marvellous frieze, a palm's breadth wide, all of gold and gemmed, of incredible
cost, egregiously girding it with a marvellous and friendly distribution and
placing of the gems; and all the wooden composite so diligently, and with
exceptional polish, with the planks joined plated fashion without the caulker's
art, and without any wedging, appearing an even-matched joinery, as of one whole
solid. And over the coating of the fragrant and blackest pitch, gleaming and
mirror-like, and with a gold trituration, throughout most admirably designed in a
Syrian lineament, with all the other circumstances above fittingly described. Thus
it was.

With these amorous triumphs, and the euphonious voices of the sailor-girls, and
beyond by the sea-deities, the serene air was filled, and the cerulean deep, with
confused clamours, and a multitude resounding — the waves, and feasts, and dances,
and especial gesticulation and festive gladness, and devout veneration — as,
gliding to the most pleasant place, we put in. So kindly and most gratifying, so
delightful and beautiful, offering itself to the senses with singular tree-set
ornament, as ever the most excellent and voluptuous thing could be beheld with the
eyes. For every fertile tongue would accuse itself of poverty of expression; and
by such a likeness the things commemorated before would be too unbecoming and
abusive a comparison to this. For beyond estimation it was a most solacing place,
and of delights — all planted and adorned as a kitchen-garden and herb-garden, and
a fertile orchard, and a pleasant pleasure-ground, and a gracious tree-plot, and a
most delightful shrubbery. Which was a place not of trackless and disused
mountains, every roughness done away, but flattened and even right up to the
circling steps toward the marvellous theatre at its heart. The trees were of most
sweet odour, most fertile of yield, of the widest spread of branches. A garden of
incomparable delight, affluent, of the largest fruitfulness, of most delightful
flowers, and stored, free of impediments, and of ambushes all adorned, of flowing
fountains and fresh rivulets. The sky not rigid, but temperate, most wide, clear
and bright; not of the horrid shades of infernal places; immune from variable and
inconstant weather that might offend with the ambushes of tainted winds harassing,
nor with troublesome and wintry frosts; nor the swelter of an importunate sun, nor
an invaded and torrid place of the dryness of heat; nor scorched with horrid
freezing. But all springlike and salubrious — such as the air is not to the
Egyptians who look to Libya — of long health and salubrity, and destined for
eternity. A place planted with green things, of admirable density of leafy trees,
of most gratifying show, with most lovely presentation of greenery; and everywhere
through the liquid air an incredible breathing of flowery fragrance, with all the
grassy ground steeped in fresh dew, and flowering meadows; and beyond the imagining
of every pleasure, teeming with natural goods — with coloured fruits among the
perennial green foliage, in stable cohesion and consent, with paths marked out
among the plants, and arched over with manifold roses. Let the watered and
tree-set field of Themiscyra yield place here.

Wherefore I judge it more than arduous, and reckon it difficult, to wish — even
with keen wit — to narrate it. But as much as my grasping, retentive, yet arid
memory, set upon its praise, shall recall to me, so much briefly I will adapt
myself to write.

This holy place, dedicated to nature — witty to mortals, and pitiable — nursling
of the gods and their station, and lodging of the blessed spirits, encircled (as I
could rightly conjecture) three miliaria; and on every side an interflowing of
salt —

— most limpid waters. Which was not heaped of tufa crags, gnawed by the obstinacy
of the surging and foaming waves, full of cracks like rough Plotae; nor of shallow
shores broken and eaten by the wave's harassing injury, nor by the clinging salt;
nor was it composed of proud Niobe's rock, nor do her most sharp and hard children
appear there. But all minerally of the most polished material — not brittle, nor
friable, nor turning to mud, but translucent, whole and undefiled, like keen and
artificial crystal.

Where with careful diligence I explored the little pebbly shores wiped clean by a
kindly wash, of scattered gems of varied form and colouring, shining. There too,
dispersedly, appeared an abundance of the fragrant issue of the monstrous whales,
carried in by the fruitful tides. A most adorned island, then, of most gratifying
and new and perennial covering of springlike greenery, admirable everywhere over
the flat.

But first, upon the bare shore-banks close by, I beheld the coeval and tall
cypresses with their close-set and cracked cones, persevering, and durable for
weighty roofs — timbers not savoury to the gnawing woodworm — and the spacing
between cypresses of three paces, one separated from the other. This regular
order, turned round in a ring, was observed throughout the whole outer circle of
the island. Then, in a circle, there went round a most delightful and flowery
myrtle-grove, loving the talkative shores; which stands votive and dedicated to the
divine mother of the amorous fires. Compacted and most densely reduced and shaped
in the manner of a walled fence, a pace and a half tall, enclosing within it the
trunk-stocks of the straightest cypresses, the beginning of its foliage rising two
feet from the levelled top, or flat, of the myrtle-grove. Thus this greenery,
so made, walled about the shore-banks, with fitting passages left and distributed
at the seemly places. Which fence showed the least wood, but, protected by the
delightful and flowery foliage — no top exceeding another, no leaf — kept its
summit and its circling shorn with exceptional evenness.

Within this walled-about myrtle and green hedge (which might be, from it toward the
centre of the island, about a semitertio of a mile), I saw, by the drawing of lines
from the centre to the shore-circumference, in equal partition twenty, each of the
immensity of a stadium, with a fifth part added — imitating the outer enclosure of
the myrtle. In each division was a little grove of diverse meadows variously
grassed, and of tree-plot the like; distributed specifically according to the
required aspect of the kindly sky. Let Dodona's wood yield here. Which divisions,
in a ten-angled figure, fittingly interposing a line for each interval, multiply
into twenty. Which figure, made in a simple circle, and making section mutually of
two diameters, gave also the central point. One half-diameter of these —

— which you will, divide by an equal half, with a prick. And from this point draw
obliquely a straight line, toward the topmost summit of the half-diameter; and at
this topmost point, upon this aforesaid line, mark off from the half-diameter as
much as is a quarter part of a whole diameter. Then extend a line from the centre,
cutting over the mark to the circumference: this will be the division of the
ten-angled figure.

These twenty divisions were, by most noble fences, diversely latticed with fitting
and convenient marble openwork, two inches thick, between the measured placing of
most polished little pilasters, of whitening marble, and the rest most lustrously
reddening; clothed with a varied delight of creeping plants, one shut off and
separated from another. In the middle of the fence there opened, level, in each,
a gate — seven feet in the opening, nine high up to the arching of its topmost
curve. Which latticings were of such rhombs, and little squares, and such
degenerate from the quadrangle, and by other most beautiful devices. Along these
serpentined the periclymenon; others the jasmine; some of bindweed; some of hops;
and some of black bryony, or black vine; others of convolvulus, with the
lily-like half-azure bells; some all white; some of momordica — so each was varied.
Some of Jove's flammula; of smilax, which for love of beautiful Crocus made itself
Autophoros, adorned with a white fragrant lily-flower, with a thorny and
ivy-like leaf; of bittersweet; of the little vine, with the three-cornered
bladder-campion, its seed spotted with whiteness; and of many others which,
serpentining on high, are unknown to me by name.

In the first partition the grove was a daphnon, or laurel-grove, of manifold
laurels: here I saw the Delphic, the Cyprian, the Mustax with its greatest and
whitening leaf, and the wild, the Cinos, and the Royal or Bacchalian, the Taxa,
the Spadonic, and Chamaedaphne — such as never on Mount Parnassus, most admired
and most pleasing to Apollo, most noble gift sent to the Romans. Nor did such
laurel-bearing earth kiss Brutus, most pleasing to Tiberius; nor did Drusilla see
such, borne by the white hen; nor were such born of the augur's command, planted
in the villa of the Caesars, triumphal ornament — chiefly the Sterile. I saw also
the Daphnoides, or Pelasgian, or Euthalos, fragrant with frankincense; nor did
Peneus's daughter make such a perpetual green of so much beauty, with whose leaves
Apollo was wont to adorn both his lyre and his quiver. Let the airy Sicilian
mountains yield here, both as to their sweetest springs and as to their
loveliness — however the most beautiful son of Mercury delighted himself there with
Diana — which are not prescribed by the wrath of most high Jove, offering
themselves so pleasing to cover the bald head of Caesar, mixed with many Comari in
the most pleasant soil.

I beheld also another little grove, in which, with even placing, was a most
pleasing oak-wood of tender leaves. And here I saw the broad-leaved, and the
common oak, and the robur, and the *hemeris* producing the medicinal *canchry*,
and the *haliphloios* with its salt bark, with plenty of Italian oaks, and Turkey
oaks, and cork-oaks, and beeches, and holm-oak — or smilax, or holly — here leafy
with leaves that do not fall, tended by the Querquetulan nymphs.

In another fence there followed, in equal order, another most gratifying little
wood of fragrant wild cypresses, savin, romidascalo, or junipers, led topiary-wise
into manifold figured devices, with minute and pricking leaves — the willing
consort of the divine mother, preservable — and loftiest cedars of manifold use,
weeping cedar-oil, of foliage like the cypress, of which at Ephesus stood the
statue of Diana, in the most noble temples most highly prized for its eternal
hardness; the aged Carie, and refusing the gnawing moth; fruitful to its great
Crete, beautiful in Africa, and fragrant in Assyria; with a lovely interspersing
of *vrate*, or savin, of perennial greenery, harmful to Lucina, shaped, and
likewise variable.

Afterwards I saw also a tall and leafy pine-wood of pine-nuts: here the Tarentine,
or wild pine, and the urban, and the bitter stone-pine, or Apine, and the
pinaster, and the Zapina, and the weeping Resina, artfully distributed.

Again, in another cloister, there stood a most copious box-grove, planted in round
and square marble tubs, among fragrant and flowering little pot-herbs — such as the
like would not be found on the Macedonian mountain Cytorus — most dense, with a
lovely tapering to a point, diminishing in just measure and degree, and thinning
with a graceful gradation, not without commerce of many other most admirable
devices most beautifully reduced. But one marvellous work exceeded all these. For
of this kind of little tree I saw all the labours of tall Hercules industriously
and with antique shaping composed [in topiary], not without manifold representation
of innumerable other feignings of diverse animals, always green, with leaves that
do not fall, regularly placed, and with a proportioned and congruent interval
distributed through the grassy and flowery meadow.

Likewise there was another neatly planted with manifold trees. And here the hard
cornel, with its blood-red fruits, and some of white fruit; and there was the most
bitter yew, pleasing and most apt to the lethal instruments of Cupid. Afterwards,
mixed together, I saw the elm, lindens, and the finest *phylire*, chaste-tree,
hornbeams, and ashes, and the flowering spear of Romulus, and many medlars, and
rough service-trees.
There offered itself also one of straight-stemmed and lofty firs, however —

— they show themselves fugitive from the ample sea, and its site is mountainous;
nonetheless, here tall and reaching to heaven, set among them in order, the spongy
and agaric larches, or *larigni*, that refuse the fire — and others like these,
disposed with fitting and gracious placing.

Most notable, following, offered itself another, where was the walnut, first called
*diuglans*: here with no hostile shade; and the peach, and the basilica, or
*molusca*, and the Tarentine, not without the social company of hazels. Let Avella
yield here, and Praeneste, and the Pontic nuts. Consorting also with these was the
impatient Phyllis grown to a tree — she who gave the name *phylla* to the leaves,
first called *petala*. She offered herself flowering, as at the coming of loitering
Demophoon summoned; and the Greek nut, and the almond, and the Thasian.

Not without utmost pleasure I beheld also a little wood of chestnuts, with the
fruit armed in a pricking bristly husk, such as first the Sardians found — whereby,
by the Greek word, they were called Sardian acorns; to which afterwards the divine
Tiberius gave the name Balanus. I sincerely thought that to these the *parthenia*
rightly yielded, and the Tarentine of easiest shelling, and the more easily
balanite, and rounder. These surpass both the pure Salarian and the praised
Corelian, and the quick-boiling, and the Tarentine and Neapolitan; where too was
the broom, or myrica, or Aspalathus.

There were then here also little woods of most noble quinces, or cydonians, and a
carob-grove such as Cyprus does not produce the like; and of slow palms there
offered itself a dense palm-grove of most useful fronds with knife-like point,
resistant and not to be bent at its summit, laden most thickly with its pulpy
fruit — not squalid and small like the Libyan, nor like the sweet dates the inner
Syria produces, but far more excellent in magnitude too, and in sweetness, than
Arabia and Babylon yield. There was also a most lovely one of most noble
pomegranates of all the kinds — sweet, sharp, mixed, acid, and vinous — to which
are not to be compared the Egyptian, nor the Samian, nor the Cretan, nor the
Cyprian, both the seedless and the red-tufted and the white-tufted, most fecund of
fruits and blossoms.

Afterwards I saw a most gratifying little wood of lotus, or nettle-tree, Syrian
bean, *ciceraso*, or *melli*, or *celtis*, with a far sweeter yield than the
Syrtic and Nasamonian — here in all Africa surpassed, it stands. Nor was there
lacking one of Christ's-thorn with reddening fruit, a rival to wine in sweetness.
Let Cyrenaica yield here, and inner Africa, and that too which is born about the
shrine of Hammon; and one of both the mulberries — the one expresses in its fruit
the mournful love, the other affords nourishment to our delights —

I beheld also one of most teeming olive, and a fig-grove of all the kinds with
copious yield. And a most delightful poplar-wood, and likewise one of
*hippomelides* with the Egyptian pods, with the weeping *metopon* — such as, at the
oracle of Ammon, dripping gum-ammoniac, would not be found.

Which little trees were of most elegant and most artful distribution and order —
which the aspect of the sky there did not want, but without repugnance of nature
everything stood best placed. Whereby that ingenious nature there manifestly
avowed all the delights which, scattered through the universe, she had shrewdly
produced. Here heaped together, and with especial study, one may conjecture all to
be created. The ground too was grassy and flowery and with springing and shaded
fountains, of glassy water most clear, moist with waters sweeter than the fountain
of Salmacis. And there they suffered neither the frost-bearing Bear nor the
cloud-born South Wind, but the air most salubrious, most purged, and most pure,
and by far most lucid, freely pervious to the eyes, most light and even, and
invariable, with great loveliness and a temperate sunniness of place and sky, that
never suffers turbulent alteration; but dissipated, and every cloud driven off,
that liquid sky shows itself, the bold winds shut out — the crackling east winds,
the whistling north, and the malignity and asperity, with great crash, of the
raging storm, and every iniquity of weather — not subject to the tumultuous changes
of waters nor to the cold Balance. But everything may be regarded lustrous, and the
desirable light, glad and pullulating in the station of the woolly Ram drying his
fleece in the illuminating and Herculean Phoebus, with no falling but a perpetual
green, celebrated by the manifold song of birds — as, flitting in the air, the
little crested lark, and together the singing nightingale, made all the air resound
with singing.

At the outermost boundary of this semitertio of a mile, all distributed into little
woods toward the centre — because a circumference of circular figure is of as much
measure as are three of its diameters, and so much the more that in eleven
partitions, one diameter deducted, there are two portions; therefore the diameter
of this voluptuous island stood at one mile, with two of the eleven partitions
added — there went round an excellent enclosure, of a height of eight paces and of
a foot's thickness, so densely leafy that the least stem did not appear, with paired
pervious windows, and, in order at the fitting places and passages, arching open
gates, made and compactly conducted of orange, lemon and citron trees, with lustrous
greenery in the mature leaves, and of new fronds, of the first and mature fruits,
and of the most fragrant flowers dispersedly adorned — so much the more pleasing and
admirable to the aspect, as it is most rarely wont to be granted to human eyes to see
an equivalent work.

In this pleasant and delightful enclosure, between the greenest myrtle-grove and
this flowery orange fence encircling, innumerable and mingled animals, shut in,
roamed loosely — however nature, unlike, repugned — harmless and tame. They wandered
there in mutual friendship. And first the goat-born satyrs with their pendent and
twisted little horns; the two-horned fauns, with the other sex. Then the half-wild
stags, and the rock-seeking roes, and the timid does, the spotted fawns, the leaping
kids; the long-eared hares; the timid rabbits; the cat-kind, white and yellow
weasels, and the lying *gallante*; restless squirrels, and drowsy dormice; the
fierce unicorns, and *tragopan* and *tragelaphus* [goat-stag]; every leonine kind
without any fierceness, but playful; the long-necked giraffes, swift gazelles; and
infinite other animals, intent on the solaces of nature.

Beyond this cloister, then, toward the centre, I found the magnificence of an
excellent orchard, or delightful pleasure-ground — such as never could humans, not
only order, but, I persuade myself, so much as think. It is easy, then, that the
second workers act according to the first worker. And I too consent to this, that
no wit so fecund is found that could singly avail worthily to publish somewhat, by
report, of so many most excellent works of this sacred place. Let the hanging
gardens built by King Syrus yield here. Wherefore I rightly judged that by no
other, but only by a divine artificer, was so most exquisite a conception, for the
contemplation of the fostering goddess of nature, produced to such order and effect
most becomingly.

Which most admirable garden, stretched toward the centre, of 166 paces and a half,
divided into meadows. Which division stood by passages straight to the centre, and
circularly transverse, five paces wide. The primary meadows, in the first line of
their squaring toward the enclosure, with the lateral ones, were 50 paces. But the
fourth line, toward the centre, decremented; and from this line took its dimension
the first line of the second meadow, and in the same manner the third meadow was
squared. Because the force of the lines tending to the centre caused the narrowing,
and the straitness of these meadows and of the streets; and therefore the squaring
was deformed, the transverse ones remaining in their integrity.

Which streets were pergola'd, and in each ridge was a little dome upon four Ionic
columns, the shaft or their tallness being of nine diameters of their lowest
thickness. And here and there of the passages, or streets, were tomb-shaped
platforms of finest marbles, with most becoming lineaments. And every four
diameters stood one of the aforesaid columns. Such columniation, and
intercolumniation, was observed throughout.

Out of the little chests, or platforms, beneath the socle of the solid columns,
sprouted rose-bushes, their height not exceeding a pace. Which between one column
and the other made a delightful fence; to each column, on this side and on that,
perpendicularly raised, in the middle of the inner column adhered, most straight, a
rod of rose-bush. Which — beyond the most noble architrave extended over the said
columniation, of red stone like most gleaming coral — without other support the
rose-bushes made the topiary bend. The summit of the said pergola, with the little
chests, columns, and straight beam, stood five paces in height. From which summit
the little domes began to round, or swell, in bubble-form; these alone covered with
yellow roses. The pergolas along their length were roofed with all kinds of white
roses, and the transverse ones with vermilion roses of every condition, with
perennial fronds and flowering in the utmost multitude, and a breathing of
fragrance; and out of the little chests sprouted every generation of flowers and of
aromatic herbs.

The first surrounding pergola continued with the cloister of the orange-grove,
which had a window of the opening of the arch terminating at the cloister of the
pergola, directed toward the centre, less open from the ground up by one pace,
equal to the intercolumnar fence.

Each meadow had four gates, in the middle of the enclosing columniation, the
little chests left pervious. Which gates, through all the meadows, uniformly
corresponded to one another, level.

In the middle of the olive-set and flower-bearing meadows, an elegant work of
excellent distribution and especial polish, I saw. First, in the first meadows, I
beheld a most celebrated fabric of a gushing fountain, set beneath a little watch-
tower of box greenery of shrewd device. Which was found uniform throughout the
whole primary order, and in the circuit of the meadows, in this manner.

In the middle of each, with equal distribution, three steps, turned in a rounding,
were built up. Of the topmost, in the levelled surface, the diameter was two paces
and a half, with a peristyle of eight little columns raised above, with the little
bases in the circling round of the upper step, and with the capitals. Which usurped
seven diameters in their tallness (Doric, of the lowest thickness) and bellied
arches from one to the other. Above the arches went round the beam, fascia and
cornice. At the perpendicular of the underset little columns, for each, was
superstructed an antique vase. By diameter of its dilated bulk three feet, with the
round bottom pointed, and thence little by little dilating, it came to the middle
prominence, adorned with an exquisite little girdle. And thence from the rim the
moderate slope ascended to the orifice, with lips of great polish about the gap of
its opening; and thence to the rim a foot and a half, the rest down to the —

— its foot, three feet high, and the foot half a foot, with little channels, or
runnels, twistingly, with a most slender beginning, moderately amplifying toward
the rim, with two twisted handles, both at the lips and, above the outer slope,
oppositely coiled — not without emulation of the lathe. Out of the mouths sprouted
straight stocks of leafy box, of the thickness of the underset little columns, the
belly removed, with little arches from one stock to the other. The triangles
[?eyed — pierced?].

Then, sloping stretched on high, as much as the stocks, from the opening of the
vase to its little head, with hairs [thin shoots] that grew in an even line going
round the upright over the stocks — among which hairs, from their beginning the
separation somewhat dilated, ascending curved they migrated, thinning the
discrepancy toward the lineament of this part, which above narrowed, with divided
loosening, between the one and the other above inflexed; at the base of each
sloped hair, so named, an outstretched branch made a hooking, in the curve of
which hung a pommel [ball]. Then bending back, raised toward the top of the hairs,
with a ready gaping curve, at the summit it held a free jewel, or circle. Beyond
this recounted arrangement, on high there continued six straight stocks, and tall
two-thirds as much as the haired part, with little windowed arches; then a little
cupola swelled. Above which swelling rose a squared thing, half-and-one pace of an
oval, and a four-parted pervious opening; and from the base of the angles issued an
outstretched branch, hooked upward. Upon the inverted hooking sat, for each, a
flying eagle in the act, with its beak in prospect. The top of this square peaked
itself, and upon the point sustained a cone-shaped, or globular, deformation. From
the vases upward, it was all of the greenery, close and cohering, of the box set in
the vases, artfully heaped and best conducted with density, and justly clipped
tithe-close and shorn — so that truly, to the eyes, a thing more lovely than such
topiary artifice and material could not be accommodated.

In the middle intersit of the levelled, most solid inlay of the peristyle was a
fountain, founded within a rounding somewhat shell-like hollowed, from the centre
of which rose an inverted baluster, two feet. Above sat a platter, the gap of its
opening having by diameter four feet; in the very middle of which, three straddling
tails of three golden hydras, through the bottom outlandishly three-forked, then
tightly intertwining in a most beautiful knot, divided by the belly one from the
other in a bag-like form, with an arching discrepancy, and in their throats
snake-wise knotted, with the head three-forked apart, vomiting the most fragrant
water into the shell — equally sustained upright, two feet, a vase of ovate figure.
Of which, in the part above the surface, were fixed eight little gold pipes, from
which a most slender thread of water leapt forth. And through the gaps or intervals
of the box columns it issued, dewily moistening the whole meadow. The interstice of
which watch-tower was clear and pervious. The stone-work was all of finest jasper,
reddening and lustrous, adulterated drop-wise with infinite spots of manifold
colouring, with elegant and exquisite carving at the fitting places.

Now in each corner of the quadrangled meadow, with a proportioned distance from the
little chests, was disposed a platform of four steps, in square form. The first
step, most solid, in front appeared two feet; in the flat, or mouth, a side of a
foot and a half; and they were hollow platforms. Then followed the other above, in
graded order, tall as the open breadth of the first; and so the third, and so the
fourth. In the first, fragrant herb germinated; so in the following. Here, then,
were crisp and tiniest basils, citron-scented and chervils, which did not overpass
the middle front of the step, the fronds kept even; the like stood uniform
throughout. The other had fragrant and small thyme, gracious to the honey-making
bees. In the third, the small and bitter *glyciacon*, or nectary, or southernwood,
such as the Sicilian does not offer. In the topmost, Celtic spikenard, of pleasing
odour.

This arrangement, in all four platforms placed at the corners of this first
meadow, showed itself all clothed with flowering *chamaedaphne*. The opening of the
topmost step was a foot in diameter, and in each was planted a most noble and
fecund fruit-tree, led uniformly topiary-wise. And first they were apple-trees: in
one corner I saw most fragrant Appian apples; in the other, Claudian apples; in the
third, Paradise apples; in the fourth, the little Decian apples. But in each meadow
of this first order the species of the said fruit varied. Trees here fecund with
apple-bearing offspring, the fragrance diffusing everywhere — with such beauty of
colour, and producing such sweetness of taste, as the tree of Hercules of Gades did
not produce, nor such trees as Juno commanded to be grafted in her gardens; whereby
they might be called *pomarii aphyracori* [orchards of golden apples].

The topiary shaping, and the circled thickness, was of a crown, with the winding
toward the watch-tower. The parapets, or fences, of this stepped platform stood of
most beautiful mirror-jasper, oversown with golden sparks, and mingled with yellow
mottling, and with cyan veins serpentining, and reddish ones running, and confusedly
dappled with a chalcedonic waving, squared off with most gratifying little wave-
lines.

Beyond, then, from this described first order of greenery toward the island's
centre — in the second order, in the middle of the area, in place of the watch-
tower — I beheld a most admirable device of box, in artful topiary. A stone ark set
of precious chalcedony of the colour of soapy water, with most becoming lineaments,
its height three feet and in length three paces, destined to the line of the
transverse streets. From the one and the other end, less a foot, was set a box in
the form of an antique vase, both two equal and uniformly egregiously conducted,
with the little foot, bulk and orifice, raised a pace, without handles. Upon their
mouths a giant three paces tall, on this side and that trod with the foot, with legs
apart. Clothed in a rounding down to the cap of the knees, girt, with the arms
spread on high, and to human stature the neck, head, breast, shaped with exacting
harmony. He was helmeted; with his arms he sustained two towers, one per hand, four
feet wide, six tall, with the base —

— two-stepped, with little windows, porticoes, and battlements, or crenellation.
Out of one and the other tower issued, with a little stock, a pommel — as much in
roundness as the content above the tower. In the upper part of the one and the
other pommel, in the middle, issued the trunks, which, coupling with equal
partition, conjoined inflexed, like an arch of masonry raised in the arched summit,
as much as the height of one tower. Next to the slanted trunk — that is, at the
beginning of its exit from the pommel — rose another slender and straight stock,
holding a cone-shaped pommel, smaller than the underset. The lower rounding of
which answered to the summit of the arch. Beneath which summit, in the middle of
the convex, fixed supine, was another pommel; like one of the stocks, raised from
the said pommel, in the middle bend of the summit a trunk half a foot grew, which
sustained a shell somewhat hollowed, and sprinkled from its orifice, a little less
than the content of the arch. Out of which platter rose as much of a stalk again as
the underset of the shell, which subsided into a form of lily with supine lips
about. Out of which lily — that is, basket — grew a box raised in eight suppressed
pommels, gradually diminishing toward the top, somewhat separated one from another;
all the work from the arch upward being of six feet, the aforesaid box excepted. No
indication showed itself in all this excellent topiary of woodwork, except the
straight stocks; but all was covered with most propped foliage and most evenly
shorn, with diligence and art clipped.

Between one and the other vase, in the chest, was seen a box without a stock, in
onion-form [?cepacea], a pace wide, two feet and a half tall. In the middle of which was led a
pear-tree, raised four feet, with the pointed top. Above the tapering it held a flat
circular figure, its diameter four feet. In the middle of this lens-like round
sprang forth a little stock holding an egg-shaped form, tall as the pear beneath.

In the corners also of the present, and second, meadow toward the centre, as in the
first were constituted the chests of four steps, with all the regulation, dimension,
and placing that the other platforms of the first meadow have — except of the stone,
which was of blackest amber, or *ambrum*. Never did the Phaethontides beside
Eridanus pour out such in their weeping, nor would such be found in the Electrid
isles, nor does the temple of Ammon produce such — of mirror-smoothness, drawing the
straw when rubbed. Which chests were figured circular.

In the lowest germinated the fragrant cassia; in the next grew odoriferous nard. In
the third was Mint, the nymph, betokening the fierce hatred of Proserpina. In the
fourth grew the unlucky royal Amaracus, extinguished amid his own odour — and such
Cyprus does not produce.

In the upper middle likewise, planted, sat a fruit-tree for each. But dissimilar in
fruit, and in topiary form, to the first. For [?…] they were four, of a spherical
figure most beautifully; they produced kinds of pears — one, musk pears; the other,
Crustumian; the third, [?…] and succulent Syrian; the last, tenderest little
*curmunduli*. [?…] in this secondary order of meadows, the others [?…] varied the
species of the fruit, with [?…] colour, with most gratifying odour, and with [?…]
taste. The ground alone clothed with fragrant and tiniest [?…], and the platforms
of [?…] simples.

Following in order, the description also of the third meadow toward the centre,
which in its middle had a chest of round content, raised three feet, by diameter
two paces the opening, with the accessory lineaments. Out of it exalted itself an
artificed box, of the following topiary composite. The chest was of finest
litharge.

The stock a foot and a half; above sat an onion-shaping, somewhat exceeding the
round of the chest — which was hollow, and open at the top by diameter a pace and a
half. Above the lips of which opening a columniation of six greening stocks turned
with little arches, four feet high. Then a metal-shaped summit, or shaped into a
chalice-foot, ascended; on the summit of which lay a most exact pommel, three feet
in its thickness.

Upon the lowest end of the domed summit, at the perpendicular of each stock, there
coiled the tail of a serpent, with the belly bent and the spine arching, as much as
was the projection of the onion-bulk; adhering with its neck to the pommel existing
above, with the head outstretched and jaws open, and through most hidden pipe-like
passages it leapt, pouring most fragrant water from the mouth, with the feet
extended toward the head, with the wings spread — six in number.

Out of the top of the pommel sprang three branches, three-forkedly divided, and
raised two feet bending. Each of which, then, at its summit sustained a little
rounded altar, or a little tube, with exquisite diligence attributed above the
little coronet, and below the fitting throats, with most even clipping. The height
without the lineaments three feet. Above the flat sat an antique water-jar, four-
handled, raised three feet. From each of which singly grew a box with two steps of
box rounding. The lower exceeded in circuit the bulk of the underset water-jar,
raised from the orifice above the stock one foot; the other, upper, stood off from
this somewhat lessened, as much again. Beyond this raised, as much again, was a
pommel of the vase's compass. Out of which, at equal height, one standing opposite
the other with a triangular separation, rose for each a most straight stock — one
conjoined with another by three semicircular arches, the bend of which tended from
the distance of one stock to the other; but to the horns, or feet, of the arches was
adjoined a stock for —

— elegance of its springing. Between this arched trigon, with lovely consent of
form, was made a tortoise-shell summit, or shade-canopy; the uprights of the stocks
did not rise higher than the summit of the ceiling, but all three by rule met in one
height, sustaining a lily-like chalice. Out of which, raised, sat a turbinate, or
globular thing, with the slender part downward, or the volute turned down. The
gracious loveliness of these most delightful devices offered itself to the sight so
most acceptable, as the bodies and figuration of most admirable greenery, so justly
exact, as one could best compose them, and inform them of such material for topiary,
and compact them in such lineaments.

In this said meadow of every mingled flowering herb — far more than a feigned
picture — again in the corners the platforms, with the described regulation, were
three-cornered. But of chrysolectrum of yellow gold, such as is not gathered by the
virgin Hesperides, with a most sweet rubbing of the citron odour, more than the
translucent and clear one gathered in Citros, an isle of Germany, renders; nor are
such the tears of the Meleagrides. There germinated, in the lowest chest, the most
sweet *saliunca*; in the upper was mountain *polion*; in the third were labdanum and
cistus; in the topmost the fragrant *ambrosia*.

The fruit-bearing trees of hemispherical form in the convex, which in this third
order did not exceed one another, but of convenient stature, and of varied species,
and of manifold fruit. Here were pistachios, tamarinds, all manners of myrobalans,
and *hippomelides*, and of all Damascene plums, of many other most delicate fruits.
Besides those which [?…] are peculiar to us, of diversified species, of [?…] and
form, and of sweetness of [?…] unknown, and [?…].

Which fruits and flowers redounded, with leaves that do not fall, offering
themselves to the beholding senses with the utmost delight. Which, moreover, did
not contend with oblique, wayward and intricate branches, but were neatly clasped
in diverse forms. Not subject to the lunar changes, nor subjected to the paling of
Phoebus, but ever bound, with tender and juicy greenery, unchangeably, and in one
same state, and product, endured, and a fecund yield.

And by this condition likewise the flowers and the fragrant little herbs endured;
from which, throughout, an unexperienced fragrance, most acceptable, was diffusedly
spread. The rose-bushes then showed themselves with the more grace, the more diverse
and, to me, unvisited the kinds. Here flowered copiously the Damascene, Praenestine,
five-petalled, Campanian, Milesian, Reddening, Pestan, Trachivian, and Alabandan,
and of all noble and most praised kinds — which, with their most sweet odour, and
most delightful colour, and most gratifying flower, among the greening fronds,
perennially preservable persisted. Nor sooner did one fall than another succeeded.

The chests were expressed with most cunning art. The striations of which mirror-wise
emulated to have in themselves both the air, and fronds, and flowers, and foliage
dispensing.

Beneath the topiary works and pergolas, the paved streets were of a more excellent
paving of make than ever any accessory could be in human wit and thought.

Beyond the aforementioned equally three-parted meadows, a most magnificent
determination, of an excellent and admirable eustyle bellied peristyle, most
beautifully enclosing, circled in circumference, walling about. The little wall of
which circling columniation was constructed of most noble and orderly and
daedally-perplexed latticework, interspersed with the little altars, preserving the
solid beneath the bases, fittingly plated with —

— the socle and cymatium, undulate and gulleted correspondingly. The
intercolumniation had the spaces at the intervals of two columns and a quarter part;
and where the ways derived to the peristyle, there, as much as its found breadth
was, so much was constituted, or caused, within the peristyle the loosening — which
the continuous surrounding discontinued. And there a most noble gate was wrought. The
low-bent arch of which footed with its horns upon a column on this side and that, as
much as its shaft and placing conjoined uniform with the others; but in thickness
they dissented, being symmetried to the superstructure. Beyond the incurved beam sat
the summit, or frontispiece, with all the correlative ornaments most polishedly
carved. Above the surrounding columns there stretched continuously in a ring the
architrave, frieze and cornice, with marvellous devices and befitting lineation.
Which, with marvellous tomb-like work, hollowed and stuffed with earth, stood forth;
out of which every sort of most admirable flowers germinated. And at the
perpendicular of the underset columns were planted topiary box and junipers. Thus
upon the collateral ones, in a preservable order without indication of stock, was a
most round pommel of box; and upon the other, so alternating, above a foot of stock
rose the juniper with four pressed pommels gradually decrementing, and the flowers
interposed.

This marvellous peristyle had the little walls, and the supra-columniation, all of
most noble alabaster, diaphanous and lustrous, without rubbing and polishing of
Theban earth, nor with pumice. But the columns varied in colour, because those that
stood in a facing place in one place were of translucent chalcedony, and the
collateral ones, above the —

— little wall, shone with greenest stone *hexacontalithos* of manifold colouring. The
other two, on this side and that, were of lustrous *hieracites* with most gratifying
blackness. Then the other two of whitening *galactites*. The two next, in order, of
*chrysoprase*. The last of gleaming *atizoe* of silvery brightness, and pleasing
odour.

And thus they alternated inlay-wise, with incredible delight of beholding. Which had
their entasis so artfully, as if they had been turned exact on the lathe — with such
art as Theodorus and Tholus, architects in his workshop of the turning-lathe, did not
find for turning columns. A work certainly sumptuous, proud, precious, and elegant.

The Ionic columns with their capitals, with the echini within the lanceolate — which,
clothed with a bark-like enwrapping, shone with bases of finest gold, such as the
gold-bearing Tagus does not produce in Hesperia, nor Padus in Latium, nor Hebrus in
Thrace, nor Pactolus in Asia, nor Ganges in India. The frieze was adorned with antique
foliage convolved on itself, egregiously carved. And the lattices hedged between the
little altars were of finest electrum — such as was not that of which, in the form of
a breast, in the isle of Lindos in the temple of Minerva, was dedicated by Helen.

Upon the flat of the little wall, for each interval between one column and the other,
was set an ancient vase of fitting work to the rest recounted, with most cunning
polish, varied of stone and of colour — of *sphragis*, of *colorites*, of chalcedony,
of *coaspites*, of agate, and of many other precious and most gratifying stones — in
its burnish simulating any object most cunningly, most polished and expressed, with
lineaments I thought not human. Out of which were seen most admirable simples and
plantlets, heaped in varied topiary shaping. Here marjoram, the aromatic and crisp
*sentonica*, southernwood, myrtles, and others than which no more delightful object
could be offered to the content of the eyes.

From the aforesaid peristyle to the banks, right up to a river, the nearest ground
was occupied, grassy, with dewy grass. Here, with gracious dispensation, was the
flowering *xiphion*, lavenders, marjorams, fleabane, white marjoram, Mint the nymph —
who received the beautiful gift from Pluto — and there flowered also the tears of
Helen, called *helenion*, salubrious to the face, and of the holy Mother
Conciliatrix; and innumerable other most celebrated plantlets, aromatic, and of most
acceptable fragrance; and the whitening, and cerulean hyacinths, and purple — such as
in Gaul is not produced.
