t:
Now among the flower-bearing and tender little fronds, innumerable birds adorned with
excellent plumage, of small and middling stature, and various little birds and
fowls, flitting unstably here and there, wandering, now up, now down, leaping with
delightful chatter, the sweet sonority of their song resounding everywhere — which
would have had virtue to provoke any woodland and inept heart to pleasure, joy and
solace, making festival with their little wings and feathers. Here the plaintive
nightingale, Daedalion weeping the death of Lycaon's daughter; the spotted blackbirds,
and the singing crested lark, or *galerita*, and the *terraneola*, sparrow, or lark;
the solitary sparrows; the most eloquent parrot, of manifold clothing — green, white,
yellow, crimson, and yellow with green; the singular (but not here) and marvellous
Phoenix; most white turtle-doves; Picus, husband of Pomona, betokening the swollen
angers of Circe; Aedon, tearful for her beloved husband Itylus; Asterie with feet
shod in rose; and the two magpies, Procne the roof-dweller; and pious Antigone, too
beautiful, without a tongue; Itys, doleful and funereal table; the gluttonous
*icteris*; Tereus the rock-dweller, keeping the royal pomp in his feathers, seeking
*pou pou, pu, pu* in his song, and in his head a bearer, marked with the military
crest; and, by Syrinx, the drowsy shepherd; and the birds of Palamedes, and the teal,
and the wanton partridge and *porphyrio*; Periclymenus, whose form Jupiter freely used
for his loves; and the *sygolis*, or *melancoryphos*, or blackcap, changeable in
autumn; likewise the robin, or redstart, and innumerable others of a lengthy telling.

> SHORE · ENCLOSURE OF MYRTLE · ENCLOSURE OF THE GROVE · PERISTYLE
> BOSCO, 20 paces · PAVING, 14 paces · THEATRE, 25 paces
> FIRST MEADOWS, 58 paces · SECOND, 48 · THIRD, 38
> SEMITERTIO, 166½ paces · ENCLOSURE OF THE ORANGE-GROVE · RIVER
> ONE THIRD, 333 paces

For more evident demonstration: the circuit of this delightful and most pleasant
island, by measurement round, stood at three miles. The figure of which gave, for
its diameter, one mile. Which, divided in three parts — one third contained 333
paces, one foot, and two palms and somewhat more — from the outer lip of the shore-
banks up to the orange-cloister occupied the measure of one semitertio, 166 paces
and 10 palms. From this boundary began the meadows, tending toward the centre,
another semitertio as much. Thus, one whole third being suitably distributed, there
remains one semitertio to dispense up to the very middle, 166 paces and 10 palms.
From the aforesaid peristyle, somewhat of space was granted, remaining for the
contraction of the aforesaid meadows, to avoid the straitness of the squarings —
which did not have their boundary up to the completion of the third; and this
shrewdly happened, to proportion somewhat the last square by the lines drawn to the
point. Which space, intercalated between the river and the peristyle, all —
pages.note: The plan-woodcut on this page is labelled, from the shore inward:

t:
— graciously covered, offered itself of most gratifying grassiness, as is
sufficiently described and narrated before.

The boundary of the recounted space ended in flowering banks of a most limpid
river, more so than Argyrondes in Aetolia, and more than Thessalian Peneus. The
banks of which were of precious greenest Spartan stone, like the Tiberian Augustan,
planked platewise, and the whole river hedged about between these marble limits.
Which banks were not entangled, nor occupied by *siler*, nor by willow-beds, nor by
osiers, nor by little reed — but the most purged and silvery waters, let in, hedged
them. The surface of which appeared, with celebrated and manifold flowers, most
delightful and beautiful. Which springing and flowing river, by passages and pipes
underground, in diverse and constituted places gushed out in order; and then, by
aqueducts of finest stone swiftly running, watered this solacing and happy site
everywhere evenly with a pleasant murmur.

The waters then pouring headlong into the neighbouring sea. And in this manner the
most clear river, exhausting its increment through the distributed devouring
outlets, did not overabound, but persisted at a perennial evening-out and content.
Which was in breadth twelve paces. The springing veins of which exceeded any
celebrated fountain, and even Cabille of Mesopotamia, more excellent. Nor did the
Virgin Castalia make such a one of hers. As these rendered the waters sweet,
fragrant, musky, and pure, sixteen palms deep — for of so most sweet a source the
fountain of Hercules in Gades did not so abundantly flow. Which were purified,
limpid and subtle in such a manner that they did not occupy the medium between the
sense and the object, nor make it disproportionate; but everything in the open
bottom throughout, as it subsided, was seen perfect. And with mirror-emulation they
rendered whole the things presented. The bottom was flattened of golden sand, full
of fine pebble-stones of manifold most shining colouring.

The greening, leafy and moist banks of which were most adorned with flowering
narcissi, and the emetic bulb, or water-loving sea-onion. Nor were lacking the
hyacinth and the lilies of the valley, and corn *xiphion*, and Illyrian. Here were
copious the marsh-marigold, and the horsetail, or mare's-tail, and the lion's. Infinite
violets — Tusculan, marine, Callatian, autumnal — and the balm-mint, or *cimiadon*, or
*trachiotis*, and other most noble riverside shoots. With innumerable little river-
birds. Here the halcyon of cerulean feathers, and other sudden little water-fowl.
Here the gluttonous and swimming swans, pleasing in the auspices, with the last song
of the meandering waters.

Upon the aforesaid most admirable banks, on one side and the other, were inlay-wise
distributed bitter-oranges, citrons and lemons. From trunk to stock the interval
three paces. Which stocks, a pace high from the ground, began to spread their
branches, meeting one with another, and most excellently entangling, rendered an
arch, from earth to the topmost bend three paces.

The remaining branches then, from one bank to the other over the river, opposite one
another, with artful conjoining and social embrace, vaulting and enveloped, pleasantly
shaded — in a most excellent pergola-work. The surrounding of which, with leafy
density elegantly heaped, with the show of an even shearing, or clipping, one frond
not exceeding another save with utmost grace and loveliness, rendering most placid
shade, and, by the sweet breath of Favonius, tremulous and fanning, full of
nourishment, that made its greenery lustrous, as in the first sprouting they showed
themselves — with the whitening little flowers, and pendent fruits, fit hiding-places
of the plaintive Philomela, ever most sweetly lamenting, singing, perfectly without
echo, by the daughter Glaucopis of high and lightning Jove made clean and most
purged, resounding. Which pergola-work, from the topmost convex down to the raised
water, stood seven paces. Oh, with what allurement and sweetest suggestion to its
contemplation it easily drew the wandering eyes! For in that river ran certain
skiffs and little boats of golden material, delightfully covered, with many long-
haired girls, fair-tressed and Alphesiboean, wreathed with fragrant and various
flowers, rowing — in limpid and crisp and saffron shifts, or smocks, everywhere
edged with gold, over the nymphish nude, clothed and girt with a wanton adornment,
not impeding the sight to offer voluptuously the rosy flesh covered; nay, by the
spring breezes voluptuously impelled and pressed upon the admirable women, it
excellently revealed the delightful little form and any other part according to its
motion, with the whitest and half-appled breasts unclosed to the rounding of the
little nipples with the greatest and voluptuous grace, elegantly girded with gemmed
gold Phrygian bands — with many youths of every warlike nation, gesticulating,
brawling, rushing among themselves in play, laughing at the naval fight, contending
persistently against those attacking them; intently keen on the spoils, they
overturned their skirts and carried them off; the girls remained despoiled and
stripped in the waters without favour, nor made resistance against their harm, but
festively solaced themselves. These being then left, mocking among themselves, made
new fights one with another, submerging the seized little boats; and so the submerged
gave work to the rams in the water of —

— to recover and renew the playful battle, with festive and pleasing solace, with
the gracious cheeks laughing girlishly, mingled, and sharp cries leaping and
gesticulating.

Moreover the water was copious with manifold fishes, of form beautiful, and various,
and outstanding, with their scaling of golden and grey-green colour; nature,
reluctant, opposed nothing here, so that they were secure and did not flee timid.
Some of such bigness that, as bearers, they conveniently bore the girls, mounted,
to the solacing battle — embracing with their snowy calves and comely little feet
the scaled and yielding bodies, which without any fishy stink swam softly, and here
and there twisting, and willing to do the women's bidding, one drawing the other.
Heaped together were the white swans, with the voice sent forth with the tears poured
out for beloved Phaethon; and otters and beavers, with other water-animals, all most
joyously beneath the topiary covering made festival to voluptuous delight, without
other pondering — so that nothing arose to cause molestation to their pleasure and
solace, nor anything displeasing to oppose it — a silent desire sprouting again in
my soul. In this happy place I would willingly still, with my goddess Polia, wish to
dwell eternally. But then, every other roving desire extinguished and repudiated,
without delay I fell back to my most firm intent, in the unique love of my most
beloved Polia. Nonetheless I judged this without doubt a thing super-excellent, and
super-delightful, above any delight, above every sweetness of pleasure.

Likewise, in the first circular and wooded enclosure of the groves, creatures of the
one and the other sex, ever within that same hedge, dwelt with those animals
appointed to pleasure. In the greening meadows within the peristyle, by another
turning, I saw innumerable youths and outstanding girls, intent on solaces, on
sounds, and songs, on dances, and delightful conversations, and pure and sincere
embraces, given over to adornment and personal cultivation, to compose muse-songs,
and to various works the studious and devoted damsels — where I judged virtue to be
more affected than any other lascivious pleasure.

Beyond then this most clear and delightful river, with a continuous circling, was a
grassy meadow as great as that which stretches from the peristyle to the river. This
river was passable by symmetrical bridges, built with wondrous and exquisite skill,
delineated of most excellent marble, alternately one of porphyry and the other of
serpentine, shining with splendid brightness, preserving the lineament of the roads
tending toward the middle navel of that mysterious island, verdant with every
fecundity of delights.

After the aforesaid meadow began seven steps, level and pedal in front, circling
continuous; in height they climbed seven feet, and in breadth —

— as much, of marble work, one of red streaked *triglia*, and one of blackish stone,
blacker than the chisel could withstand, and of greater hardness than the most
illustrious Paduan of its own nature — without the rubbing of a cylinder, or with fine
powder and soot; excluding the rule of the sextant or the *dodrans* thickness, nor
with a foot-and-a-half's setback, nor two feet, but as is recounted above, and by such
measuring all the rest.

Upon the topmost step of the blackest stone stood forward an encompassing and elegant
little colonnade of *pycnostyle* spacing, its continuity interrupted, or intervalled,
by the rule of the breadth of the bridges, which observe that of the roads. These
excellent bridges were duly roofed by the immaculate pergola over the river; and
although the roads tended directly to the centre, the steps were not on that account
cut through from their whole circling. Then, as just said, above the ascent of the
steps there was, of the little columns, as much opening as the width of the paths
afforded. But the royal way tending straight to the gate of the wondrous circus,
opportunely excluded from the narrowing of the lines toward the centre, stood alone,
even, and uniform in its breadth, and its rise over the steps sloped most conveniently
walkable; and so in this place the stairs were necessarily found discontinuous.

Which pycnostyle, with its doubled little columns, the plinths of the bases — of
which, by an ant-like distribution, one made mutual contact with another at the angles
by a diagonal line, set into the straight faces with successive coupling — between
every two, one of alternated colouring of most shining outstanding jasper, and between
every seven, one square of red, capped with a translucent gilt-bronze sphere; and the
others likewise, bound and girt with a little architrave, frieze, and cornice of the
material and colour of the square one, with most decent lineaments. Above the little
columns' capitals, the interspaces were of chalcedony, six in number, one between two
of green jasper spotted with manifold flecks, with due and companionable distance.

Upon which most pleasant pycnostyle I saw, wantonly running about and pausing,
innumerable peacocks — whitening, red, and some fanned with their own colour, and
others with their much-admired feathers let down — and there, intermixed here and
there, all the species of parrots, with no mediocre adornment and delightful show upon
the said work.

The fronts of the steps were seen carved wonderfully with noble and Assyrian
knotwork; and for its greater relief, the intercarving was gracefully stuffed full of
material, in the red ones azure, and in the black ones with a whitening filling.

From this much-admired colonnade up to the following steps, it was levelled into a
circling marble path, six feet in breadth. Where immediately began another seven steps
to climb, with the aforesaid work, measure, and material, and colouring — and all this
was kept entire in what follows.

Upon the topmost was a box-like excavation, four feet in opening. The hollow of which
was sufficiently deep, and so in those that follow. In which grew a hedge of box, of a
glassy sheen, most pleasingly greening. And, level with the bridges and roads, I beheld
a tower of the said greenery, raised nine feet, and five wide, with an open door
gaping three feet, and six high, and so the following ones.

This first hedge, of three feet's thickness, and six high — and so those that follow —
was seen of densest foliage, and was so disposed of the feathering of its own
tree-growth. Between one tower and the other I saw excellently made a triumph, with
horses drawing a chariot, and preceding the one who triumphs certain sword-bearing
soldiers, and with triumphal spears artfully compacted, varying most beautifully the
works. In another space between towers stood forth a naval Enyo. Between two other
towers, a fleet-battle on land. Between two others, a hunt, and antique fables of love.
With most diligent relief, and most exquisite fashioning. Such an order going round,
varying in its sequences.

Within this first rampart, after an encompassing path — like the lower one, between the
colonnade and the steps, of marvellous tessellation, which offered itself to great
admiration, and an excessively delightful artifice, without doubt to weary all human
sight and sense. Which, at first aspect, I readily judged to be *charaine* carpets laid
out and spread flat upon the level, with all manners of colouring, which for such a
show it fittingly served to express — in the manner of a gracious painting, conducted
into more varied and manifold groupings and figures and signs, with the fit diversity
of colourings, of little pot-herbs, to the required distinction of the feigned work.
Some full of colour, others of dark colouring, some middling; some clearer and gayer,
some leek-green, others of a pale verdure, some less so, and of a somewhat reddish
colouring, with a most pleasant reconciling. The principal figures, containing in
themselves manifold designs, were: between two rhombs, a circle; and a rhomboid
between two circles, alternating continuously in a ring — except in that part where the
ways were providently left to intercalate. Which paths always passed between two
uniform figures.

Which fashionings stood hedged in a circular lineament, imitating (as is said) the
island's figure. And first they were surrounded by the encompassing path next to the
box-cloister, joined mosaic-wise with the straight ones tending to the centre. These
roads were paved: the middle part, of seven partitions, took three for itself, of
blackest hard and mirror-like stone — of such-made blackness that a touchstone in the
river Oxus would not be found; and here and there, joined immediately, was one
partition of milky stone, of such whiteness as the compounded milk-glass of Murano —
most obstinate and translucent — was never seen; the outermost were two other portions,
one here and one there, of finest stone reddest more than streaked coral; and among the
black were most excellently driven the tessellations. This comely disposition,
observed, is continued through all the following ones, of the following cloisters.

Between the recounted roads, hedged round in the intervals, were the aforewritten
figures. Within the rhomboids, circles. Within the circles, rhombs. Then various
figures interwoven, of most fecund and gracious contrivance. In the navel of the round
ones, planted, rose up a tall cypress. In the middle of the rhombs, a most straight and
tufted pine. Likewise in the circling friezes between the boundaries of the roads, at
the one and the other extreme — with the moderate distribution of various works, and
figures egg-shaped and half-round — at the mid-point rose up greenest *vrathe* (savin),
corresponding through the intervening cypress and pine, and with the summit even, and
of uniform bigness. Of branches thick and of cypress-order, used by the divine mother
to hide the calumny. Then, in the fit places, the much-admired flowers were skilfully
imparted, of whatever colour dispensed, with most elegant harmony and redolent
fragrance.

Of the one and the other sex, in these most beautiful and most pleasant greeneries,
intervalled, they applied themselves solely, devoted to the work of fostering nature,
and content with cultivation, labouring at the conservation of such garden-works. Nor
did the most just king of the Phaeacians, Alcinous, show such diligence about the
custody of his kitchen-gardens as here was observed — with wondrous and sedulous —

— study, every thing applied in pairs, appearing born in its destined place.
Illumined by the marbles with distinct splendour, and so the circlings that follow.

THE SECOND kitchen-garden cloister follows immediately after the just-recited work.
At the edge of which, in order, the other seven steps toward the centre began. Upon
the last was compacted a varied close of tree-colouring, most highly to be admired,
with towers, or watch-turrets, most excellently heaped up of orange-trees; and, flanking
the door, were planted in order two jambs — that is, between the wall of the tower and
the opening, or door-leaves, those rising out beyond the top of the tower mutually
joined themselves into one, lifted three feet above the tower's summit. Then the thick
foliage began, fashioning itself into a moderate cypress. And so, in circuit through
all, of two paces its height. The between-tower hedge varied in colour, and in
tree-kind: between two it was woven of juniper. Between two others, of mastic. Then of
arbutus, of privet, of *dendrolibanum* (rosemary-tree), of dog-thorn, of olive, of
laurel. Ever in one fashion in its fresh green foliage. Reiterating, after the last, the
first successively — most beautiful of topiary work, free of any tow-stuffed show, with
never-perishing fronds.

Where, between two towers, upon the level, in the middle a wondrous pinnacle stood out.
For, in the intervals of the wall-hedge, sprang up plants of box, with exquisite
artifice led into symmetrical crescent-horns, to the completing of the between-tower
space, with its hollow, or upturned gap, fashioned with singular diligence. In the
middle, between the two horns, rose a juniper, step by step declining in tiers, up to
the top attenuating, as if they had been turned whirling on the lathe, and the pricking
little fronds made even. The thickest set in the middle gap. Between the horn-work
ascended, upright, a stalk, mounting a foot and a half, where a box-sphere rounded
itself, most justly proportioned.

Within this close, between the boundaries of the ways, were kitchen-garden squares of
wondrous make, dissimilar in the plotting of the herb-work, alternating to the
completing of all this admirable circuit.

The first quadrangle, marked off from the other by the roads — by which the illegitimate
squares came out — was a knotwork of the square lineament, fashioned by little bundles,
with the greatest polish, three palms wide. The first band in the middle passed off
into a circle, and from the two angles the bands met again at the rounding, one above
the other. Which ring knotted within itself another band, divided from the first,
inclusive, four feet. And that part —

— of the circle that was uppermost was subjected to the other band, and so now one, now
the other, alternating under and over. And this second squaring, at its angle, ringed
itself, occupying from angle to angle, ever alternately keeping the band-lineament, now
uppermost, now undermost, to the regulation of the knots.

The first rings widened out within the second square, making a circling rotundation to
the capacity of that square. Then there was caused another square, equidistant from the
second as that second from the first; and this likewise ringed its angle toward the
angle of the second, upon the diagonal line, entangling itself with the rounding,
climbing and passing under. Within this newest square a figure went rhomb-wise. The
angles of which, with tight volutes, knotted the middle of the band of the last inner
quadrangle.

In the triangular space between the rhomb and the square interval, upon the diagonal
lines, as a filling, was a free circle. Within the rhomb was a circle, unknotted to the
capacity of the rhombic figure. In the middle of which circle was an eight-petalled
rose. In the centre of which was set an empty altar, rounded, of stone of tawny Numidian
(marble), with three head-bones of oxen; and between the one and the other, of daring
carving, hung little bundles of fronds and fruits, swelling in the middle, with wandering
thongs bound in knots about the heads, and girding the bundles, with choice lineament —
at the socle and the abacus, with most beautiful cyma-moulding, and other adorning
ornaments. Out of which altar grew a savin, in compact cypress-form, the opening of the
altar stuffed with manifold chervil.

The kitchen-garden expression of the picture of the preceding square — thus was the
colouring distributed. And first, the first band was most densely of marjoram. The
second of southernwood. The third of ground-pine. The rhomb of mountain thyme. The
rounding contained in the rhomb, of germander. The rose, of amethystine violets. In the
circuit of the rose, and outside its bound, were sweet-scented violets, densely
flowering. The four circles within the last square, in the triangles made by the rhomb
and enclosed by the square, were of *melanthium*, that is *gith* (love-in-a-mist),
within yellow violets. All the hedging in these triangles, of cyclamen. The circles
between the first and second square were filled with rue. The circles of the third, with
flowering primrose. In the first bound, between the first and second square, were plotted
acanthus-leafings, one opposed between two, of mountain *polium*, bordered with maidenhair.
In the centre of the circles set upon the diagonals, for each, was raised about a foot and
a half a sphere, with an even law kept in all — of height and spherical girth and placing —
excepting the four caused by the interposed square at the diagonal angles. In which, at the
centre, rose up three-cubit stalks of purple and mallow-coloured hollyhock, many-leaved and
five-leaved, with a large flowering yield. In the first, *santonica* (wormwood). In the
second, rosemary-tree. In those fashioned by the circular figure contained with the outer
and first square band, at the centre were spheres of hyssop. From the encompassing roads,
both the straight ones to the centre and the transverse ones near the green hedge, and near
the steps the excluded — such was the squaring, and of the rest.

The other companion square of this close, of most pleasant and comely and wondrous work,
and device, and marvellous kitchen-garden distribution, and most noble knotwork,
distinguished in the colouring of various simples. Next to the marble limits of the
encompassing roads, in the square — fashioned by the interval left from those — a band went
round, a foot and a *dodrans* wide. From which, conjoined, departed all the bands, uniform,
to the composition of the work of this square, marked off from the other by the interposed
road. There were nine squares, equidistant, to the compass of the principal square. Which,
from every angle to angle, coupled one with another, with a mid-section, one band with
another meeting justly; and such a lineament filled the square, ending and coinciding with
the outermost band. By which plotting, between these squares an octagon was caused, the
squares including one another. Between the angles of the squares, equally formed, was
another square, set with its sides toward the said angles. Upon each meeting-section, in —

— a rhombic demonstration knotted, with its angles too, and these — both, and the
transverse, and perpendicularly conjoined — and by such mutual commerce, and likewise
these, another octagon within the first they prettily formed, companionably encloistering
the nine squares.

Wherefore all these figurations, joining one with another, under and over and alternating,
rendered graciously an elegant knotwork of manifold figuring. All this square completely
figuring. Which fashionings were lined by plates fixed in the ground, of whitest marble, a
half-*dodrans* their surface thickness, and here and there walling round the simples. Within
which stony enclosure, between the bounds, the little herb-varieties, most evened and thickly,
germinated together to the perfect expression of the figuring; and all this likewise observed
throughout every such composite artfully stood. A show, by Jove, conspicuous, and to the
senses supremely most pleasant.

The pictorial kitchen-garden distribution stood thus: every free square enclosure was
clothed with flowering cyclamen. Its bands, of *myrsinites* (butcher's-broom). The band-bounds
of the others, knotted with the meeting-section, were herbaceous of mountain *polium*. The
four little squares of the crossed section, joined within the square, were all covered with
thyme. The octagons walling round the free squares, with the requisite allotment of little
herbs, stood thus greening: one of *laurentia*. One of tarragon. The third of yarrow. The
fourth of groundsel. The fifth of *diosmo* (buckthorn). The sixth of *terrambula*. The seventh
of *baccar* (sowbread). The eighth of marjoram-gentle. The ninth of maidenhair. These two
recounted squares, alternately in a ring, filled up this close most admirably.
But for the completing of the preceding squares, there remains to tell of this just-described —

— in the middle square a porphyry altar resided, at the angles of which, near the little
cornice, stood forth four horned wethers' heads, snail-wise and smoothly carved. From which
hung down incurving little bundles, with all the accessories recited of the round one. Upon
which lay an antique amphora-vase, with four handles equally divided, of finest sardonyx most
beautifully conjoined with its familiar agate, expressed with wondrous artifice. Out of which
came forth a most-polished box, with its lower sphere, or rounding, of one pace its diameter. On
the top of which were four stalks, equally a foot apart and distinct, and each a proportioned
sphere; upon each a peacock, with its tail let down, resided, with its head in a salver upon a
middle stalk exceeding the four spheres. Out of the salver ascended a stalk again, with four
branches, and each sustained a sphere. In the middle, raised, the stalk held another sphere. Upon
which grew an egg-shaped circle, spreading two branches to a side, and each had a sphere, and the
like at its top. Such a disposition was ordinarily observed in every vase, uniform — the place, the
box, altar, vase, lineaments.

NEXT follows, and the other seven steps. Upon the height it encompassed, in the manner of a wall,
of greenest myrtle, with towers — like the others fashioned, with cypresses, and with all the rest,
with a fleet-like feathering most excellently heaped up. Within this cloister likewise were two
squares, alternated of kitchen-garden figuring, with such a plotting. There were two quadrangles
banded with symmetrical knotwork, and with the enclosing circle, in the manner of the quadrangle
first described. In which circling, egregiously painted, was seen an **Eagle** with outspread wings,
comprehending the circular space. In place of the acanthine foliage, there were majuscule (capital
letters); and first, at the left side, between the two bands, in the space excluded by the circles:
in the first were two, **AL**. In the other excluded, four, **ESMA**. Toward the hedge, in the first
space between the circles, three, **GNA**. And in the following, four, **DICA** —

Consequently toward the road, in the same manner and placing, four, **TAOP**. In the
other, three, **TIM**. In the outermost, toward the steps, with the aforesaid order and
kept to the writing, two, **IO**. In the next, two, **VI**.

> *(The letters planted in the beds spell, around the eagle:)*
> **ALES MAGNA DICATA OPTIM. IOVI**
> — "A great bird, dedicated to Jupiter the Best."

The bands, circles, and the interstitial rounding, of rue densely pressed. The eagle, of
thyme; what is excluded by the surrounding bounds, of mountain *polium*. The letters, of
marjoram, walled round with *iva* (ground-pine). The filling of the circles was: of one,
flowering violet-blue; one, of yellow; the third, of white, with a great yield of its
florets, never falling, but perennially flowering. And the pot-herbs continuously, with
uniform evening, greening — forbidden to proceed to the destiny of fecund nature. From the
triangle caused by the rounding and by the angles of the inner bands, was for each a little
circle of the herbaceous colouring of those enclosing; the excluded, of butcher's-broom. In
the centre of which were planted four spherical spheres of most-compressed and most-evened
myrtle, with a two-foot stalk, and of the rest.

The other quadrangle — bands, circle, as is now recounted. In the circling were two birds:
on the one part an Eagle, and on the other, facing, a Pheasant, with beak straight to beak.
Upon the lips of a vase they footed. Which had a scrap of a foot-stalk, and from the back
the wings of both raised. Between the volutes of the bands, on the eagle's part, in the
first and lower space, were formed three letters, **SUP**. In the other, three, **ERN**. In
the upper part, in the first space, three, **AE·A**. In the following, three, **LIT**. On
the pheasant's side, in the upper space, three, **IS·B**. In the one below, three, **ENI**.
Between the two lowest bands, in the first space, three, **GNI**. In the following, three,
**TAS**.

> *(The letters of the second roundel spell, between the eagle and the pheasant:)*
> **SUPERNAE ALITIS BENIGNITAS**
> — "The benignity of the celestial bird."

Within the circuit, inwardly, beyond the bounds of the figuring, all was of mountain
*polium*; the pheasant of *laurentia*; the eagle of groundsel; the vase of asarabacca. In the
gap between the encompassing lips, of butcher's-broom. The outer bands, with all their course,
of periwinkle. The other band, of *trinità* (heartsease). The circles in the intruded angles,
of marjoram-gentle. What is excluded and intruded of these, of *digitello*. The letters, of
thyme; the spaces, of maidenhair. The fields of the round band-work, of *santonica*. In the
centres of the circles, between the triangles, was a sphere — two of sweet-smelling southernwood
and two of lavender, raised a foot and a half upon its stalk. In the rest, alternately, a sphere
of savin and one of juniper, three feet. All the herbs with most comely thickness, and freshest
verdure, and most pleasant look. A wondrous work of exquisiteness, of pleasantness, and delight.
Irrigated by narrowest little pipes, orderly distributed, vomiting a most tenuous and droplet-like
sprinkling.

FOLLOWINGLY, with the kept rule, ascended other seven steps, upon the topmost of which a
much-admired railing encompassed the whole, of red and most illustrious jasper, with elegant
open-work, agreeing concordantly to most pleasing patterns, of a sextant's thickness. This
railed hedge, and the following, was without any opening, but continuous; and here ended the
roads tending straight to the island-centre — but it stood passable only in the triumphal road,
and so the following.

In this voluptuous cloister I beheld a grove, conspicuously shady of density, of most-celebrated
shrubbery. Here were the two female terebinths, tenacious to old age, of choice and blackish
splendour, of pleasant odour; bdellium with oaken foliage; the *malus medica* (citron), perennially
apple-bearing. Precious ebony, the pepper-tree, clove, nutmeg, the threefold sandalwood, cinnamon,
the most-praised silphion — which would not be found in the vale of Jericho, or in Egypt at
Matarea. Here the whitening costus, which the isle of Patale does not produce. And the shrub nard,
with its ears bearded, most praised of spike and of leaf. And the aloewood, of unspeakable
sweetness, which the headless Nile does not carry down; and storax, and stacte. And —

— the incense-tree, and the myrtle, which does not germinate in Sabaea, and infinite other
little trees and aromatic shrubs, with a most-evened soil, covered everywhere with asarabacca,
which is not in Pontus, nor in Phrygia, nor in Illyricum, rivalling the nard. Which most
delightful place was the station and gathering of the newest and most beautiful little birds
that were ever set before human eyes, seen or known — intent on the work of love, sudden, with
most pleasing chatter, singing among the modest density of the branches of the most lively and
never-falling verdure. Which blessed and happy, most pleasant and leafy grove — the bursting
waters, by little channels and running rivulets from the liquid, clearest and sacred founts, ran
with a drowsy murmur. And there, beneath the fresh and interwoven little shades, and at the soft
reflection among the new little fronds, the manifold and sharp chatter running on, innumerable and
illustrious Nymphs, with the other sex, were hiding — at a discreet pleasure apart from the
others — and singing, with antique instruments, fugitive from sweet Cupid, and intent on the most
opaque shades and rustic doings. They were dressed shapelessly in silken habits, subtle and crisp
and pleated, of half-saffron tincture, and the greater crowd of sweet-scented and marigold and
galbanum-yellow, and some of colossine colour, with little sandals and nymphish footwear.

Now all the dwellers of these voluptuous places, feeling the triumphant advent of the arrow-shooting
lord, without delay suddenly, festively venerating, presented themselves to meet him — the newest
excepted. Then to their peculiar solace and continual delight they returned.

Lastly, beyond the recorded little grove, without any intercalation, and the other newest gradation
of seven steps following, with the observed norm, had upon the high step a much-admired close of a
little colonnade, like the first after the aforesaid river, of artifice and material. And there was
walled round a sectile, spacious, unencumbered and levelled area, with wondrous invention of
tessellated emblem-work, and with knotworks of little circles, triangles, small squares, and conoid
figures, and almond-shaped, and half-round, and rhomboid and scalene, most beautifully fashioned into
manifold designs coinciding, and with mirror-like illumination, and with egregious distinction of
various and choice colouring.

Finally, the middle third of the mile, from the river to the centre, was in such measurement
mosaic-wise distributed. Which semitertio, then, stood (as aforesaid) at 166 paces and a half.
Wherefore to the river are given 12 paces; to the meadow beyond the river, 10. All the steps
occupied, lengthwise, 8 paces and 2 feet, and in universal height as much. The little path, 6 feet.
The first garden, 33 paces; the second, 27; the third, 23. The grove, 25. The area encompassing the
theatre, 16. The theatre, from its middle to the centre, contained 16 paces. Of the island's
commensuration, enough.

> HAVING COME OUT FROM THE LITTLE BOAT, TO MEET THEM INFINITE NYMPHS CAME,
> SUPERBLY ARRAYED WITH TROPHIES. POLIPHILO NARRATES ALSO THE MYSTERIOUS
> MANNER IN WHICH THEY OFFERED THE DIVINE INSIGNIA TO CUPID, AND WITH WHAT
> HONORARY PROCESSION, HE BEING SET TO SIT UPON THE TRIUMPHAL VEHICLE; AND
> POLIA AND POLIPHILO, BOTH BOUND, FOLLOWING BEHIND, WITH GREATEST TRIUMPH
> CAME TO THE GATE OF THE MARVELLOUS AMPHITHEATRE — WHICH, BOTH WITHOUT AND
> WITHIN, HE FULLY DESCRIBES.

Sweetly, with a mild breeze breathing zephyr, the comely and golden little wings
of the divine boy softly vibrating, and by his tranquil spirit conveyed, we came to
the ebbing shore. Many and infinite gift-bearing demigoddesses, and notable Nymphs,
of conspicuous beauty, came out with us from the fateful little boat. Straightway, to
meet the divine and winged boy, with a chosen troop, with great apparatus of
ornaments, and of pomps, and sumptuous vestments, with a splendour and cultivation
more than regal, with a most exquisite adornment, especially and solemnly venerating,
of tender and most flourishing little age — most delightfully in pyrrhic dance, with
virginal allurements, and heavenly and illustrious aspect, humbly, and with most
decent attendance, obsequious, all bounteously offered themselves.

And before them all, the sacrificing shrine-bearers, the tower-bearers, and the
jubilant fore-dancers went preceding, with trophies of military ornaments arranged on
gilt spears: with the cuirass of furious Pyroeis; with the other conquered armours;
and with the bow, hanging crosswise, retaining the cuirass; and with the barbed quiver
and the axe bound to the extremities of the bow; and, beneath the cuirass, the
spread-out net; with, set below, the face of a little winged boy, and a twin one; and
an apple affixed to the face, transfixed through the middle by the spear; and at the
summit, the starry helmet.

t:
Another was bearing yet another trophy. On the point was a little band of laurel;
beneath it, a pair of wings of blackest eagle, outspread; and then, set below, lay the
face of a most noble boy. There followed, and then, crosswise, two thunderbolts bound
together with little bundles of gold and woven silk, flying; and, likewise bound
crosswise to the spear, a sceptre, holding suspended a superb robe.

A bearer, too, was another, of a trophy: of a helmet, with a buffalo's head; and beneath
it an antique cuirass, with two shields knotted at each brachial outlet; between which
two little bands, one to a side, hung pendent, holding the Cleonean skin, with the
knobbed and gland-knotted, sinewy club.

Next in sequence, one raised a trophy with special polish. On a point passed off the
topmost spear-shaft; descending below it, a covering over a rounding half a sextant
thick, resupine in the manner of a plate, in the middle of which was carved a circled
formula. Which a small vase-stalk suppressed. Then a tablet with this majuscule writing
subjacent:

> **QUIS EVADET?**
> — "Who shall escape?"

To this an apple was set below, and next another rounding, like the upper but smaller.
Walled round by a rim, and superimposed upon a solid, or massy, little dish. From which,
continued, descended a longish baluster, and then a little basin.

Likewise another Nymph carried a spear. On the pointed end was an egg-shaped figure, with
a bossed little rim in a circle, and in the middle a sapphire rounding, imitating the
figure, an inch thick; set under it, a small board, thus with the title:

> **NEMO**
> — "No one."

And between two wings the spear, somewhat balustered, passed through. At the bottom a
little dish followed, as is recounted above.

Consequent was another most noble trophy, borne aloft. On the high spear-shaft a sphere
stood forth upon a *pyrronium*, between an inflected lunar-crescent of two little wings,
subtly leafed with gold foil, one leaf pressed page-wise upon the other.

The remainder of which, forced into a circling, rendered a crown held by a little band,
through the middle of which the spear, slightly balustered, passed perpendicularly. Under
the crown a little basin, with the bottom of an ewer-vase descending upon the oarage of
two conjoined wings. Then an egg-shaped figure, with a byssus-boss coruscating in the
navel. Fixed under this was a sphere, scored melon-wise, with flying little bundles
opportunely bound in.

Many others, of prolix telling: the standard-shafts of which — some of ebony, others of
red, citrine and white sandalwood, and of whitest ivory, and gilt, and covered with
silver, and of other precious woods. Every thing skilfully fashioned of most tenuous gold,
silver, and of polished material, and formed of green silk, and of every other gracious
colouring, with pleasant flowering. Multiply adorned with gems in the fit places, every
thing harmoniously destined and conspicuously applied, with pendent vertebrae —

— or little whorls of precious stones, pierced, through which was drawn a golden filament;
and every thing requisitely depicted with most pleasant colouring, and shining with a
scintillating illumination. And the gesticulating dancers gloved with gloves of needle-
texture, in manifold little knots and florets of gold and silver thread, and of silk of
various colouring artfully interwoven, with a purse-like closure in a jewelled *phrygium*
(embroidered band) at the rosy and fleshy arms, with little gold cords beautifully mingled,
elegantly heaped, of various colouring of elegant silk.

Before all these trophy-bearers ran an outstretched and displayed one: the standard-bearing
of the little boat's conveyance ran ahead with prompt bearing. And immediately, in
imitation, followed another, with a triumphal *celibar* (standard), which at the top had a
winged Cupid, unveiled, in the act of drawing with the bow, treading upon an apple; at the
top, inflected, a jewel of laurel-foliage of foil. Which was upon an inverted bottom of an
ewer-vase. And there it was ensnared: the little bands, licking above the interval of the
jewel, burst out flying. Within the content of the circle was a tablet, through the
thickness of which the spear bored, and through a sphere superimposed on the tablet in the
middle of the outer part; and so in its lowest part another, subjacent, penetrated. Likewise
in the abacus-work, on both the left and right side, a little spear-shaft jutted somewhat,
passed through the jewel, and stood forth outside. From the one and the other jutting pendant
were two little cords twisted of gold and silk, threaded through berries of precious stones.
Under the reverse of the jewel, an ewer-vase with its bottom uppermost pressed on; and its
orifice, in a balustered opening, bit an egg-shaped figure, with lineaments imitating the
form. With two little apples above the circumference, one to a side, in the middle of the
diameter; at the bottom another sphere. Lastly a golden little knot, with varied texture,
fluttering. On the tablet, on the one and the other face, was, in Greek majuscules, this
title:

> **ΔΟΡΥΚΤΗΤΟΙ** (DORYKTETOI)
> — "The spear-won" (captives taken by the spear).

And many others, trapped-out with much polish of various flowers, fronds, and little
fruits, not without the company of gold and silver foil, and infected with every colouring
encaustically, with infinite ornaments and exquisite elegance of polish — proceeding most
joyously, with many other insignia and victory-marks, and with trophy-ornaments of exuviae
and spoils and plunder, conquered by the potent and divine arrow-shooting boy, preceding
with moderate distance of triumphal procession, and with much applause and divine revel-rout,
and with sounds and guttural jubilees of the quiver-bearers.

Then, first, there presented herself his goddess-wife Psyche, in a queenly robe, with a
villous underlay, and shining with crimson gold, of gold texture triple-twilled and wefted,
clad in lucent silk — such as Hermaria and Malicha of Hesperia do not produce. And, in
sequence, the companions in silken robes of discreet and versicolour dye, sumptuously and
genially clad, with superb habits, unwonted and new, most opulently jewelled — such as our
nature interdicts the human wit to make, step-motherly — with crisp pleats wrinkling over
the delicate and most-clean little bodies, and over the virginal hips, at the soft impulse of
the fresh, restless breezes.

Some with adhering breastplates of scaled gold-work, with comely and companionable adornment
of most-lucent gems. And others had set their fitted garments over the whitest breasts,
whiter than the winter frosts of Capricorn, with adornment and delight at the first swelling
of the untamed little breasts — like little rounded apples, upright-nippled, with a half-cluster
put forth and affixed — and above them, up to the breast-band, in a cyanean depilate colour,
a sumptuous *phrygium* wound spiralling, stuffed with oriental pearls, somewhat swelling,
occupying bounteously the whole diaphragm, or all that part above the girdle, of artful
volutes, of egregious foliage, such as was never invented in Phrygia by the Phrygian
embroiderers. And in a Phoenician (crimson) colour, that spiralling somewhat of springing —

— of little emeralds in pellets stood forth. And in leek-green colour, of ardent rubies in
berries. And on the saffron robes, of shining sapphires in whorls; and in purple, or bright
crimson colour, of most-lucent pyramidal diamonds. In amethystine tincture, or Punic (red),
of just and whitest pearls.

And thus there were, and again with this dispensation, other conspicuous and most-vivid
colourings — such as mallow, *thyreus*, murex-purple, sandarac, iron-grey, and pomegranate-
flower. Which silken garments were some shorn, others villous, and some in triple and
quadruple little gradations of pile, with work in most-pleasing figures of flowers and little
animals excellently woven. Others with silken cloth of silk warp and weft of gold and silver
in every colouring and figuring, interwoven with the utmost disquisition of art. Some with
zoned vestments alternately — now a gold, now a cyan, then green, and consequent silver — and
with the remaining colourings distributed amicably and correlatively, not without comely
texture, and voluptuous show. Some had oyster-purple investitures, and twice-dipped Tyrian;
and others the saffron-mantles, such as were never in Scythia made, of the arboreal down
(cotton), diversely segmented and variegated. Others, with a thin cotton pall, shadowed the
noteworthy belly, closely adhering.

Accessorily, on their tufted heads, ornamental nymphish fillets, gemmed with wondrous
congruity, wormwise worked in most-exquisite little nets of choice invention; and with ribbons
with golden filament squared in rhombic figure and reticulated, and covered with golden tiaras
— so that the twisted and doubled threads were distinct one from another, with a triple
association, one gold twist standing forth above two silken, with exquisite little knotting
where they met. Among which the circular and resplendent gems were variously sewn in order,
according as the variety of the garments is told. Others, a golden diadem divinely binding the
head.

In the little rhombs whitened (and likewise in all) roses made of six thick pearls-in-union,
of which, standing forth in the middle in conoid form, resplended a thick jewel of the
allotment that went round by the embroidered fillet. Also from the part that hedged over the
spacious forehead with royal ornament, where the parting of the richest hair divided itself,
with the comely trace of low little waves. Others elegantly had woven to the head their golden
locks, with a genial little cluster —

— some with twisted little knots, with a tight swelling prettily arranged, the shapely nape
gathered nymph-wise into a little clump, and bound again with little cords of silk and gold,
twisted. Others had the most-tenuous hair over the flat temples most ornately woven in. And
some then held part of the festive forehead comely-occupied with hair curled, twisted and
crisped, like illustrious golden threads, and with narrow tendril-like curls circling round;
and, for some, the fore-blowing little locks covered the rosy forehead, and, at the moderate
breezes delightfully inconstant, lay decorously about the head and neck. And behind, too,
through the middle of the most-beautiful ears, the outermost part of the embroidered fillet,
of even rubies coruscating, and among them, with egregious coupling of diamonds and of
springing emeralds and most-cyan sapphires, hung manifold little darts of gold and silver
foil, unstable, scintillating, stretched beneath the tresses, with a threading of oriental
pearls. The rest, thence, of the copious and abundant hair, fluctuating with the vaguest
little waves, measured from the most-delicate shoulders down past the round calves, above and
down from the firm and freshest buttocks, most profusely wandering, ran.

Some, wantonly, the cleanest hair let down from the ornate nape, and hanging from the occiput,
with even discrepancy from a golden binding, dividing here and there over the milky neck. Then
beautifully, and with choice polish, sinuated and balled up into an egregious whirl, they
elegantly met at the topmost crown, thinned to a point, where a most-precious tuft of pearls,
to the highest voluptuousness, bound both the braidings; and beneath, the little breezes
masterfully conducted, passed over the flat temples, and arrived, with even thinning, at their
seat and voluptuous meeting.

For some the hair was reddish, with much-admired wrappings girdling round the head with an
amicable springing floret. Some golden, more than leafy orpiment of outstanding lustre, and of
colour, with a decorous whirl composed tendril-wise to the nymphish and voluptuous adornment,
with a pretty adjunction of various and precious little stones, and to the expression of
extreme delight; some blackish, more than the anthracite plumes of Aesacus, in comely volume
shining, covered with limpid golden veils, and above the parting, held with hairpins, with a
conspicuous and gracious flight, with manifold curled knots, with much resplendence, with art
and artifice that exceeded every wanton study and nymphal voluptuousness — combedly combed,
and most-decorously composed. Little snares baited with the retaining, biting, and noxious
birdlime of amorous hearts. With whorls of inestimable value hung at the pierced ears, and
with most-precious necklaces and segments torqued and girt the straight and snowy throat, with
wicked collars sumptuously begemmed, with more excellent research of adornment, and in
decorating so much womanly affectation as could never subtly be excogitated.

Beyond this, some, with most-purple buskins on the little feet, with gold ankle-pieces, shod
themselves trimly. Which terminated upon the white pulp of the calves, where a genteel
re-woven band of a *policaria*'s breadth went round, wondrously adorned with precious stones,
with little laces of gold and silk. Some, barefoot, bore the vermilion silk sandals with
voluptuous vanity. Many were shod with soccoli of golden leather, closely chased with many
elegant figures. Very many wore crepidae of rosy leather, edged with gold. Some exquisitely
shod with polished, crescent-shaped footwear, or with a recurved opening, and of thonged soles,
with more new and marvellous ligatures, laces and thongs than could ever be told, of blue-grey
silk and of golden filament, with the vaguest and most-pleasing interlacings knotting round the
fleshy heel — more than one could devise in the mind — and from the narrow sole the little snare,
prettily entangled in a knot, of Armenian texture, came out, impeded, holding the great toe. And
thence toward the least (toe) it passed off, whiter than bone-lime. Then, climbing over the
little swelling insteps, most-beautifully they conjoined, with a little tongue let down from the
surrounding binding of the heel, over the top of the ivory foot, adorned with wormwork of gold
and of lucent gems.

Some, of silken satin cloth, with figures heaped by such artifice, with varied colouring
voluptuously shod, distinct from that of the superb and nymphish garb. Concluded comely with
gold buckles, with hooked clasp, and ensnared. Over the exquisite crepidae, the little swelling
insteps pressed by the elegant little gold-eyeleted straps, and the pearled instep-covers, and
with little knots of coloured silk and of gold with the ends of burnished silver fixed, were
decently interwoven, retained, with so beautiful an adornment as to blind and put out the eyes
of the unbridled bulls. Oh, what polish, beauty and brightness; what perspicacious ornament;
what unwonted works! With what keen diligence was seen the thoughtfully-found artifice of
giving to the beholders sweet and incentive pleasure, and a little death.

In the dressing, likewise, they were arrayed, beyond the superb and delightful invention, as
comely as the happy place condignly demanded, with artful fringes and slashes, or breaks, with
subtle intercutting of versicolour, and most-decorously with wondrous wormwork stitching. And
from the tight girdle downward, in front, hung in order the golden little tags of wormwork
labour. Some, in place of the little pears (tags), had chains of pearls of hazelnut thickness. At
the bottom, with a fastigiate length of alabaster figure; and likewise in place of the golden
tags, was a woven strip, or golden band, of a sextant's breadth, of wormwork. From its sinuous
bosom to the encompassing fringe, coupling among the minute —

— slashes distributed. And such as the little pear-shaped pearls had turbinate gems with
the flattened squarings, and with the rounded ones, with most-pleasant commerce and elegant
consent of their colour and fashioning, variously dispensed, and with the utmost comely
congruity. Some, too, I beheld with a superb and divine cultivation, with notable and
egregious and most-sumptuous and incredible adornment, and of incomparable preciousness.
Which, over the flanks, were clad in sinuate silken cuirasses of amethystine bright satin;
and thence, behind, to the last vertebra and to the thigh, hanging with moderate curving, of
padded antique foliage, and covered with middling pearls. The whorls of which, with little
knots ending above the little breasts, and above the navel, defined themselves in white. In
which were little roses of most-precious stones, and other marvellous devices, encloistered
in gold, and choicely adorned with encaustic work, and wormwork-polished. The lips of which
cuirasses, of a wondrously wild train of golden texture, the embroidered bands continuously
went round; and at the lower extreme, alternately, thickest pearls and little pears, with
inconstant motion, hung playfully.

Thence then a green silken investiture, with golden weft, descended, and reached down to the
knees. Beneath this, down past the ankles, another was let fall, of crimson wefted with gold.
Which, with frequent little pleating, were fringed, of a half-inch's breadth, with a doubled
order at the extremes of thick pearls. And in the field of the first embroidered band,
inestimable rhomboids of gems occupied. Among which, with distributive colouring, the circular
ones interposed shone, artfully assigned in a golden field. Beyond the outermost lips were
merlons serratedly formed, and in every angle of which a rounded little stone hung. And at the
bottom, among the merlons, unstably, gold darts fluttering. From which embroidered band gold
threads knotted in rhombic form descended, and were retained by a pellet-gem. In each,
therefore, of the interposed sections was a gem, through which crosswise a trained gold thread
passed. Above the just-said gem, in the border of the band, set fast, sat a circular one like
the collateral in form and thickness, with little gold barbs pendent; on the said crosswise
thread, in the very middle of the rhombic figure, a marvellous egg-shaped little stone was let
in. And in the middle of the sides, likewise threaded, was a pellet-gem, each with straight
distribution and elegant order, and of the colouring varied, evenly meeting. All the lower
angles of the said figure, intercalated, in one there hung an inestimable square precious
little tablet, under which, and from which, suspended, hung a berried little stone. Between one
and —

— the other appended gemmed board was an oblong, or egg-shape, all of wondrous thickness. The
embroidered band of the second (nymph), between the pearls in half-round form, were little
tablets of a thumb's length and half that breadth, intervalled between two circular ones, and
then between two square ones, with other additions of little stones, comelily set fast in the
voids, and of little ornaments to delight and grace most excellently inserted — to stupefy
nature herself — with continual most-lucent flashings coruscating, and most-pleasant in the
convenience of their colouring; with most-beautiful sleeves, and superb arm-pieces with an
adorned breast-work; and at the brachial outlet and at the collar, of such recounted embroidered
bands, and ornaments, most-beautifully they went round.

The arms were bipartitely covered, from the outlet to the elbow; and from the elbow to the grasp
of the hand was the little sleeve, of all-golden texture, woven with choice low-relief work,
walled round by a little embroidered band of nymphal study diligently invented, prettily laced at
the elbow-division, with gold cords, or with little twisted cordlets. In the divisions was an
elegant outlet of a copious little cluster, with a curved little folding of the snowy cotton
chemise, most-tenuous and shining, bound in the decent part, with silken little snares doubled
into armlets, or let into flattened gold circlets, and pointed with pure gold, with pendent
little knots, with exquisite virginal (art). For there desire, and the thing coveted, with the
knowing and the power, reconciled itself with the will. So much, by Jove, to the amorous eyes was
it most-pleasant, that one would truly desire nothing else but to be able perpetually to gaze —
and Nymphs so comely, and of such shapeliness and delight, outstanding, with their bright-eyed
aspects so sumptuous, and wantonly comely, and so, with snowy garments of the utmost polish,
pre-shining.

With such provocation that to bitter death a man would offer himself, of his own accord and
willing. O contagious artifice! O alluring ministry, O assaulting siege-engines — which any heart,
however sound, most safe, valid and quiet, and free, and resisting, you easily infect, suddenly
subvert and depopulate, without delay prostrate, without respite perturb, totally subjugate, and
without struggle drag away. To lay low, scatteringly, all moderate, incredible and stubborn
continence. These are those true and infallible satellites of laborious Love, with an amplifiable
number of most-monstrous executioners, ambushing the immune, remote and disjoined reflections, and
excluding those inclined to such subjection from being able by any means, nor with a daring spirit,
to prevail — and, by the presented, inevitable and drawing sweetness, with so shrewd and diligent
study ensnaring, and with subtle wit invented so most-exquisite a working, and to so beautiful and
most-shapely a work by fecund nature herself, an artifice found for destroying, and a choice
adjunct and accessory of torment. Alas — which reasonably ought to be feigned, and used, for marble
statues, and not for human and fragile hearts. For even that noble and divine sex, despoiled and
denuded, supremely torments and infects the imperilled, let alone with this voluptuous addition of
pernicious snares devised. But this alone accrues: that they do not consider it enough to perish of
love naturally, without adding so much increased increment of excogitated modes, to conduct the
wretched and soft lovers to the death of heart-grief more easily, and continually to excite little
sparks extremely incendiary, to quicken the amorous and fervid little flames to consumption —
divine objects, to refill and confound the warm breast with bubbling little sighs, and to ferment
the heart to love. Now I would not know how duly to express by what means so great a foundation of
love, stable and sincere, firmly placed in Polia, felt itself somewhat shaken by these inevitable
and ready ambushes and impetuous violences. Alas, then, within myself I silently repeated: O my
dear little beautiful Polia, guard your won prey! For a great peril is the passage through so many
piratical fallacies, and manifest cut-throats, and little ambushing plunderers — which, against
all sincere rectitude, are for their amorous offence commended and laudably approved, and by the
sad, offended ones so much the more desired, and reverently the more sought, and the more sweetly
loved.

Now, on her most-joyous forehead, under two half-circles like threads of subtle silk, and blackest
brows more than shining amber, two arrow-shooting eyes festively shone, more than the most-
irradiating stars resplendent in the most-limpid sky. And in her aspect more beautiful than
incarnate and fresh roses; and the cheeks not rouged, but with a most-pleasing and genuine redness,
than which —

— apples of Decius (?) in the wine-bearing autumn, reddening, and more lucid than the whitest
ivory rubbed smooth, where the Sun showed itself more clear, perhaps, than such a Titan appeared
to the Achaemenians (Persians), or to the Egyptians Osiris, or Isis, or Serapis with the
*calathus*, or the three-headed simulacrum, or Mithra in the sacred cave to the Persians — such
did the delightful and divine Nymphs expose themselves, at the advent of their lord: conspicuous
with venerable semblances, mannered and well-mannered with adorned gestures, most-admired with
unvisited beauty, and choice with outstanding gracefulness, illustrious and comely with elegant
honesty, and adorned and most-comely with entire boldness.

At this point, deservedly, with a venerable band flying, and with frequent retinue following, the
most-beautiful Psyche, full of gratitude, revering her dearest Husband, all easy and blandishing
received him; and with the utmost veneration set on his head a most-precious little crown, such as
was not the votive one of Hiero. And two of the Nymphs, honourably accompanying her — Imeria the
one — placidly received Polia; and the other, Erototimoris, most facetious, took me by the hand.
Then, distinctly following, many others, most joyous, three and three, with solemn procession, and
order, and most-honorific pomp, and decent veneration, and with nymphal genuflection, came in
motion, revering.

And first came **Toxodora** (Bow-giver), who cunningly offered him the sinuous and wound-dealing
bow, which was rigorously extended. She was in the middle of two others: **Ennia** the one, who in
her little swelling hands bore a chiselled little amphora-vase of most-coloured sapphire, with most-
pleasant resplendence, with a broadish orifice mosaic-wise carved. From which a little slope of
manifold flowering, expressed with the greatest polish, descended moderately to the dilated
corpulence; and above the beginning of the tapering, receding from the turned body toward the
orifice, the little handles adhering, most-diligently fashioned in a viper-effigy. They bit the
gullet-moulded rim elegantly. Then the girt-round swelling body, on the outside carved with wondrous
little images, and most-politely fixed; and where the body began to pass off into the narrowness of
the slender and oblong bottom, it was of —

— little channels obliquing, excavated with moderate rivulets in-channelled, ending upon a little
knot, with a temperate swelling to the shrewd device, with a subjected little foot, stuffed with
most-beautiful and manifold flowers, disseminating them. And her consort **Phileda** (Love-of-
pleasure) gathered up in her lap those which Ennia, solacingly scattering, disseminated.

Likewise, between two other most-adorned little Nymphs, came forward **Velode**; she festively
presented to her lord a marvellous quiver, superb of artifice and of egregious invention, with two
most-swift arrows — one with the shaft of pure silver, and the other with the pointed shaft of
black, heavy, cold and inauspicious lead. That with this he might gird his tender and divine flank,
or his shoulders, with the flying weapons. And her companions **Omonia** (Concord) and **Diapraxe**
(Accomplishment), with two balls, joyfully played, one to the other alternating. But of shining
gold was Omonia's, and of fragile crystal her Diapraxe had; and when one of them caught up the gold
one, she sent back the crystalline, with a shrewd avoidance of their meeting together.

To these, then, in order, the others followed: the most-beautiful and reverent **Typhlote**
(Blindness), with religious and deserved honours and dignification — she offered, bowing, a most-
tenuous veil, that with it he should band and cover his unveiled eyes. She had with her two wanton
damsels, of immodest semblance. Of which one, named **Asynecha** (Heedlessness), turning now to the
right side, now to the left, inconstant; and **Ardelia Comazista** (Busy-Reveller) danced. And like
Thymele the histrionic, leaping, a jester, and a notable *lamia*.

And the other, **Aschemosyne** (Shamelessness), among all the clothed ones naked, undaunted and
salacious, presented herself — neither more nor less than if she had drunk from the fount of
Salmacis. And in her left hand she held a sphere formed of golden plates, with its centre. And with
her right she would not consent to let her long hair, taken up, extend over the fleshy and quivering
buttocks, with unashamed petulance, like a wanton huckstress — but indicating a most-obscene
Tribade insolence, with an extolling of her inconstant, blue-grey eyes, and with a lustful act, like
a bold Gaditanian (Cadiz dancing-girl), gesticulating with too much lasciviousness, ineptly, and
more than the most-filthy Hostius had in himself, gazing in his hollow mirrors.

Newly, three other unpremeditating matrons presented themselves: **Teleste** (Initiatrix) the first,
clad in ardent purple, with her loosed and abundant hair, and on the fillet-bound forehead little
curls hanging in front — she, elegant, gave to her god a kindled torch. And a companion, **Vrachivia**
the bearer, gave of an emerald —
pages.wcap: Precious Stone Vase with Fiery Sparks

t:
— little urn, most-excellently expressed, and of antique artifice, and of an audacity insolent for
human workmanship. Its orifice had contorted striations, which striae, or rivulets, ending
moderately in the middle amplitude of the vase, with most-even distribution somewhat dilated. Then
the comely girt-work descended toward the round bottom, the corpulence little by little thinning,
clothed with an inestimable making of celery-leaf foliage, standing forth from the solid with
egregious separation; and, continued from the lips of the orifice toward the down-slope, twisting
themselves into exquisite foliage, two little handles they rendered, with wondrous relief, and with
a little foot.

Out of which broadish orifice, flying and crackling, with a most-pleasing pop, sparks leapt out,
running lucent through the air; which then, extinguished, fell as ashen sparks.

The other companion, **Capnolina** (Smoke-girl), bore a little goatish, or earthen, vase, with a
narrow orifice, raised somewhat high and thinning at the bottom; and above its dilation, under the
handles, it had circularly, with even distance, thirteen most-measured Greek letters diligently
impressed:

> **ΠΑΝΤΑ ΒΑΙΑ ΒΙΟΥ** (PANTA BAIA BIOU)
> — "All the things of life are little [trifling / short-lived]."

With many other ornaments and obliquing little channels. Which, from the letters toward the orifice,
was polished-smooth. Out of which, and through the vent-holes, leapt forth a misty and sweet-smelling
smoke, resolving into nothing through the air.

> *(The inscription on the smoking vase, continued:)*
> **PANTA** [BAIA BIOU]

Received finally the offered mysterious and fateful love-tokens and fitting insignia, the divine
boy set himself to sit upon a golden and antique car, or triumphal vehicle, there prepared — all
of golden plates, an embroidered band a *dodrans* wide going round all the fringes. In which,
sun-like, shone encloistered ostentatious gems of bigness and unthinkable price, and of
imperceptible artifice and rarest invention, divinely disposed, and orderly destined. With two
vehicular wheels having the circumference of gold, and the spokes proceeding from the central
axle, in which the pole lay; and, fixed in the middle, they were fashioned longish, in balustered
figment, of precious stones various of fulgurant colouring.

Sitting, then, he — without protraction of time — both taken and captured were we, Polia and I, by
the outstanding Nymphs **Plexaura** and **Ganoma**, at the imperial nod of the triumphing, dominant
little boy; and, both our arms thrown back behind, and our hands bound at the back, like captives
Polia and I were ensnared and bound, connected and re-netted with tresses and little wreaths of
roses and various flowering. And behind the pompous and divined car of the prize-bearer and greatest
triumphator we were drawn, softly and willingly, by **Synesia** (Understanding), a most-outstanding
Nymph.

For which thing I began almost to tremble. But because the Nymphs, with my world-key Polia, laughed
facetiously, of a sudden I was reassured. There followed immediately after us the curious Psyche.
And behind her were following the girl-damsels who, venerating, had made offering. Which Psyche was
bordered, or clad over, with a matronal and most-ambitious mantle, or chlamys, of gold — such as
Silophontes did not give to Darius, nor could Numa, first king and inventor, use such-made. Over the
right shoulder, foldedly cast, and eyeleted in pressed gold circlets, where among thick carbuncles
most-purged and touchstone-tried, and coruscating with splendour, she held encloistered a diamond an
inch-and-a-half long lengthwise and flattened, and a thumb in breadth, and of iron-like scintillation,
full of wondrous stupor, with inestimable adornment standing forth — such that of so great a price
was not the gift given by Gyges to —

— Pythian Apollo. In which — not by the noble Pyrgoteles, but rather divinely — was Cupid most-
excellently carved, cruelly lancing himself, and incautious Psyche handling him with the arrow, with
a lethal puncture; where the loosed arm bore the flying and vehement golden arrow, or her firebrand;
and in the other hand, elegantly cast back with gracious folding over the left shoulder, the chlamys
reversed and stuffed with a golden and most-tenuous pile, bearing a hyacinthine lamp of antique
workmanship and of perspicuous effigy, kindled, scintillating. Which most-sumptuous chlamys was most-
opulently fringed with marvellous precious stones, over a most-exquisite and pleated amice of
springing silk and wefted with purest gold, girt under the little swelling breast, with divine and
delightful make.

Towing, then, this superb vehicle of triumphant Love drew two scaly serpents, **skinks**, beyond
their nature great in this place, for this amorous office and mystery and conveyance valid and
vigorous, inflamed with three-forked and quadruped vibrations; with their necks stretched out,
becomingly entwining their scaly breasts with marvellous knotwork of thongs and retainers interwoven
of gold train, with little swelling bosses standing forth, of various and excellent gold chasing
alternated with gems, most-excellently, with irradiating coruscation, buckled in gold buckles and
most-choice clasps they passed through; and thickly adorned with thick little stones, at the drawing
not swiftly, but with a temperament of triumphal procession.

This divine triumph all the triumphal Nymphs preceded, as before is described: the shrine-bearers,
then the trophy-bearers, then the torch-bearers, the torches banded with little bundles of gold; next
the light-bearers with golden lamps, brands, and tapers of whitening and purest material, luminous
with clear candour. Continuing, followed the scent-bearers (Osmiferae) and Sweet-smellers (Euosmiae),
with golden scent-vessels of unseen make, and with golden censers, or incense-caskets, scattering
wondrous fragrance beyond that which the happy place diffusedly breathed everywhere. Some with little
golden vases, with the narrowest outlet, sprinkling a most-odorous inconstant liquor drop by drop,
bedewing all. Very many others, with a heavenly order, held in their longish hands sounding
instruments: sweet symphonies, pierceable pipes, tibiae, sounded with sweet measures; and twisted gold
horns, most-preciously gemmed. Some together, with sweetest consent, harmonically, in the Lydian mode,
singing, with angelic utterance, and a voice rendering no familiar sound, and reiterating the comely
songs. Some others with the tinkling Cymbals. Others with rattling and raucous Drums, suspended from
the left hand —
pages.wcap: Terminal Figure with Three Male Heads

t:
— and, with little cords of gold and silk twisted, hanging at the fleshy arms near the grasp of the
hand. And then, with their turned and longish fingers, solicitously they forbade, and in time
yielded, upon the pierced tibia, leaping — not such as was found by Mercury — the whistling voice
which, among the most-purple lips, received composedly the sonorous breath. With gracious swelling,
apple-rounding the coloured little cheeks. And then, with the little right hand, the drawn and
stretched skin they beat with little beaters of whitest ivory, with measured and mosaic
participation, with a soft and grateful murmur and raucousness, resounding in concord with the
tibia's whistle.

Some with twin tibiae — to the invention of which let Marsyas yield, and the Phrygians likewise.
Some lyring with garrulous lyres, and some citharising with citharas, exciting upon the trained
brazen strings, with tender and delicate fingers, or with plectra, the brazen sound, striking it
together; and again with other most-noble and marvellous and organed instruments, with golden and
rattling sistra clattering with a sharp tinkle; and with steel triangles, with playful rings
tinkling, soft and sharp, at the sweet stroke; and others conformably with hooked little horns,
diffused an unheard harmony, with a crackling trumpet fore-singing.

Wreathed with diadems of jewels, flowering with a spring-crown, among the varied flowers gold foil
becomingly intercalated — chiefly of amethystine violets, and of sky-blue flowers, and of purpling
amaranth, and everlasting, and of cyclamen, and with little wreaths of melilot, with yellow and
white violets, measuredly composed, and mixedly inserted, and of other coronary florets, and with
whitening pearls and other gems, accessorily their ornate locks girdled round and woven in. And
some, most-elegant, of beautiful voice, dispensed so much soothing harmony, communicating it to the
hearers, as perhaps Apollo — nay, without hesitating — playing the lyre to the Heliconian Muses does
not render, nor offer. Nor such and so great a sweetness of sound did the Tyrrhenian sailors hear;
nor did Arion, with so much sound, upon the dolphin his conveyer, make the crossing to Taenarum. Which
women musicians were not in one place, but disposed in ordered procession, and processional division
at their requisite and constituted place, to great extolling and triumphal glory and victorine
praise, in redundant troops.

Through which divine things, I firmly persuade myself, every fecund and eloquent tongue would prove
vain, striving to express a particle of the sweetest sounds, of the sweetest canticles, of the solemn
and playful dances and feasts, of the divine Nymphs and notable girls, of their singular and
incomparable beauties. Of the excellent and illustrious and most-elegant adornment — enough to
interrupt and amputate gracious life, and to dissipate and distract every hard and obstinate heart —
rejoicing with various and triumphal insignia, and with alacrity —

— gesticulation advancing; and of so sumptuous and superb a triumph, and of so many delights and
pleasantnesses, and immense amplitude of precious riches and greatest opulences — rather divine
than of nature — to my eyes, by the Cytherean grace and cupidine privilege, openly to see, and
clearly and really to behold, especially indulged.

In the last place, immediately, in front, next to the drawing serpents, two aegipans and wanton
satyrs, with goatish beards, with goat-feet and cloven, proceeded. Which lewd ones, joyous, with
little wreaths of flowering *satyrion*, and of flowers of *helenium* and of *cynosorchis* (orchid),
pressing down the unkempt hair over the wrinkled forehead, crowned. Each bore a monster, rudely cut
in wood, and gilt, effigied human, clothed: from the three-heads to the diaphragm only; the rest, in
a square, tapering to the lower part, passed off into a basal gullet-moulding, with a little slab,
with an antique foliage at the arm-site, with an apple at the breast. And in the middle of the
square, in the broadest part, appeared the ithyphallic sign.

Before whom, immediately, preceded a polished Nymph, on whose snowy face the porphyry cheeks
reddened, with the ivy-crowned forehead of corymbs, clad in a segmented pall, quivered here and
there by the soft zephyr-breaths, the lappets of the reflexed bosom; she bore a golden little vase,
rounded in the manner of a nipple, from which, by the narrowest channel, sprinkling milk, she
libated.

Likewise, again, two Nymphs preceding, wreathed the one of leaves of the female Mercury-plant, and
the other of male *Hermopoane*, were bearers: the one, of a whole gilt little boy in the right hand,
and in the other another, mutilated of the head, little arms, and neck. The other, with special
honour and obstinate superstition, bore the simulacrum venerated by the Egyptians, of Serapis. Which
was a head of a lion; to the right jutted a fawning dog's head; and to the left, a head of a rapacious
wolf. Which effigy was all contained and surrounded in a coil of a dragon, emitting fore-sharpened
rays; which dragon, with the head, derived to the right part of the simulacrum, most-excellently
