gilt.

Whence, with mosaic distance, and with long and solemn progress, was accompanied the triumphant boy;
and both, Polia and I, bound with flowering little wreaths and rosy withes, festive. The Nymphs, of
facetious nature, most benignly active, gratifying us, made alluring amorous blandishments, with
festive faces and genuine hilarity, and soothing amorous solace.

Finally, with this triumphal and mysterious discourse, and with the quiver-bearing pomps and amorous
enticements, among fragrant flowers successively proceeding — the standard-bearing of the notable
victory preceding, with the fore-singings of the most-joyous nymphal youth, with flowing gait and
fore-dances, and with coruscating torches pre-shining, and with clear light pre-glittering, they went
before — and among fragrant pot-herbs, sweet-smelling and living trees, odoriferous fruits, odorous
air and clement and most-liquid sky. The road hedged, planted with every kind of shrubbery, and in
every part covered with little herbs, and with green grass. Not lacking, step by step, the roses, and
the plenty of flowers — every thing fragrant, and a place happy, blessed, delightful, and most-
pleasant. And with so great and divine a following of the miscellaneous throng of Nymphs, with
peculiar pomp, with religious progress — nay, triumphal — the one accompanied the other, with stature
and determined distance, advancing under the rose-pergola of every manner, with new and spring fronds
and leaves. Which, with sweet noises, whistled softly.

And there all the ground was fertilely overwhelmed and covered with strewn leaves of roses, and of
orange-flower, of amethystine violets, and matronal yellow ones, and of white bells, and of purpling
*pulliphure*, and of flowers of jasmine, of lilies, and other conspicuous and most-odorous florets. And
singularly was disseminated the seed of the single-stalked marsh-mallow, and little branches of
flowering myrtle — upon the most-even paving, of most-lucent marbles in infinite works tessellately
compacted. Many bore thyrses of manifold flowering heaped together; others, with branches of olive;
some, of laurel; many, of myrtle, and of other celebrated trees, with intrepid little birds familiarly
perching upon them, singing with canorous chatter and sweet concerts, with the —

— singing Nymphs, hymns and canticles, and with sweetest measures psalming, everywhere resounded;
with celestial applause most-joyously making festival, with hilarious ceremonies and with delicate and
virginal dance, busily; and some with pyrrhic leaping; and, with high-sounding praise extolling the
divine Genetrix and her potent little son, with festive spectacles, with greatest triumph and superb
pomp, little by little we came to a proscenium, where was a conspicuous, and most-excellently made, and
most-cunning gate, gaping — of material and of workmanship of a most-marvellous amphitheatre, sublimely
built of fabric, full of artifice of ornaments and art never so seen, neither in Atella nor in any
other famous place; most-exquisitely wrought and perfectly absolute, of long narration explicable, and
almost not conceivable. Which one might call not human, but rather divine, operation, and greatest
ostentation of structure.

ARRIVED, then, with most-solemn gladness, and incredible joy, and solacing delight, by the triumphal
way — with distributed sprinkling, here and there, through certain narrowest golden little pipes,
irroring the processionaries with most-odorous little waters, and all the triumphing throng dewily
suffused — at the gate of the entry, I beheld that it was of stupendous artifice. Which was constructed
of oriental *litharmenon* (a golden marble), in which infinite sparks, like scattered filings, were
discerned, of fulgurant gold. And of this pure metal were —

— of the exact columns the bases, the capitals; the architrave, frieze, cornice, and pediment,
threshold and antae, and every other working, of the recounted material was seen — refusing the hard
and tenacious steel, and spurning it, the toreutic (relief-work) antiquely varied, gracious, elegant
and most-admired in expression, and a structure beyond measure magnificent. Which I think not makeable
by earth-dwellers, save with the utmost expense and long-suffering, grave and lasting labour, and with
no mediocre wit, care and industry, and diligence — that to such a marvel it should be perfected and
skilfully-wrought. In the closure of the whole arch it was of ophite stone, and the collateral columns
both porphyry. Then the others varying — one ophite, and the other porphyry. The middle ones,
superstanding upon the porphyry, both ophite; and the overstanding quadrangular middle ones of
porphyry; and then, contrarying one to the other, and so by the contrary change were capitals, bases
and little altars.

Before which, one to a side, was a most-precious vase: one of sapphire, the other of emerald, of
greatest and obstinate artifice most-excellently and daedally made. I thought of the vases set at the
entrance of the temple of Jove in Athens.

At this described marvellous gate, from the triumphal and winged vehicle, the lord Archer descended.
The amphitheatre was of incredible, unvisited and unheard structure. For the elegant footing, and the
mosaic joints —

— or bindings, and the symmetrical colonnade in a circle. Beams, friezes, and cornices, all
exclusively, were of cast bronze, encaustically over-gilt with fulgurant gold. The rest, all of
diaphanous alabaster, and of shining brightness; and the antae with the arches, or inflected beams.
Nor such a work did M. Scaurus make in his aedileship.

Which, on the outermost part, had two equal orders of passable arches, intercalated between the
columns; one order superposed on the other, of hemicycle, its inflexion with the addition. And
between the openings of which, in the solid, broadly and perpendicularly, stood forth set half-
columns, striated, with their lower third fluted with little knots, or fillets. Some, with even
alternation and distribution, filled with figures and little images, such as in Ephesus were never
seen. Set under the bases of which, becoming little altars lay, and with the requisite lineament. At
the angles of which, set fast, hung two bones of a ram's head, one here and the other there, with the
wrinkled horns spiralled, or with twisted whirl; through which came out certain shoots knotted
together — a leafy jewel with pressed foliage, and retaining and ensnaring prominent fruits, in the
content of the square undulation of the little altar. Within the compass of the jewel, egregiously
carved, was a satyric little sacrifice: with a little altar set under a tripod, with an antique
boiling cook-pot, and two nude Nymphs, one to a side, with a little pipe blowing on the fire; and,
next to the altar, two little boys, one to a side, with a little vase apiece. Likewise two lascivious
Satyrs, with a token of vociferating, with a fist tightly raised toward the Nymphs, with snaky
entanglement. Which (Nymphs), with the free arm, gripped those of the satyrs — who, with the hand of
the other arm, stopped the orifice of a leaky vase, forbidding the touch — and, inclined, with the
other held the little pipe, intent and unmoving at its office. Some other columns of this same form,
with the two-thirds of twisted fluting, and the lowest one altared, as is said, changed, doubled in
lineament. Such had, among swelling ropes of fronds and fruits incurving, playful little boys. Some,
manifold trophies, sculptures egregiously made; many had carved heaps of spoils. Others, occupied
with set figures of applauding goddesses, and little boys, and copies of victories, and titles, and
other most-congruous ornaments.

Above the topmost shafts sat the choice capitals of the recounted columns, with artful abaci, or
lids, under the projections; beneath which subsided the most-polished greater helices (volutes), the
trabeate binding, and of frieze and crowning, circling round, with the projections of the live (stone)
congruently to the perpendicular of the columns.

Between one projection and the other, in the order of the door, in the middle part of the frieze, stood
artfully expressed a most-noble device and invention: of a most-ancient vase, stuffed, having the
orifice of antique and prependent fronds. And here and there lay a horned bull, prostrate, with its
feet stretched toward the vase, and with the head raised; and a nude one riding it, with the right hand
lifted and gripping manifold little rods, indicating he will strike; with the other embracing the
dewlapped neck. Next to which a nude girl sat, dorsally, with the arm toward the solid embracing the
nude one over the paunch, and with the other, snatched, held a veiling cloth above the filleted head;
impeded, it came out under her seat, over the embracing arm. In prospect, a satyr, the bull's horn
grasped with the inner hand, and with the other, turned with his back to the bull, raised toward the
woman, held a balled-up serpent. Within, another satyr, with one hand retained to the other horn, with
the other snatched by the thongs a pendent gravidity of heaped fronds, reversed above the lowest of the
vase's body, defined itself; then, with moderate incurving, to meet, in the —
pages.wcap: The Amphitheatre in Island of Venus

t:
— hand of the other satyr. The posterior part of the bulls, migrating toward the projections,
transformed itself into most-noble spirals of antique fronds. In this same manner, varying, the frieze
was comelily carved and decorated.

Beyond this first binding followed, ascending in order, a similar order of columns, in every thing
conformable, and in no part discrepant. And although the building-art appetites that superposed columns
ought to be shorter by a quarter than those set below — of which the perpendicular came, without the
altar-work, above the centre of the columns beneath, with the sequence, and the third (order) a fifth
(shorter) — nonetheless in this elegant and symmetrical building this was not observed, but of one
height, the overstanding with the underlying. The third quadrangular ones obeyed in the third order.
These superseated columns had also the encompassing binding, like the subjacent. Beyond this girdle,
the quadrangular ones, or little pilasters, furrowed, rose. And between one and the other, a third of it
emerging from the solid, in the evened intercapace gaped a window — not quadrangular in the temple-
manner, but as is requisite in profane buildings, obliqued, or arched.

Supremely, in a turned orb above the square columns, the royal cornice, without projections, with every
ornament and most-requisite lineament, and with the special due drip-moulding in it, with every harmonic
proportion, went round. Beyond the said, raised, circled a clean and unencumbered band, a pace and a half
high.

All this celebrated, illustrious, superb, and supremely-approved building, of finest Indian alabaster, of
glassy sheen, artfully constructed, most-excellently decorated, and egregiously perfected — without any
smearing of lime-paste, or cement, but with stable cohesion and contracted consent, perfect. Which pre-
shining material was not disdained by staining smoke, nor paling by the anointment of oil smeared on, nor
muddied by the infusion of vermilion wine, but in every part unliable, without any infection, kept in its
superb, luculent brightness.
The Area contained, by diameter, 32 paces. The thickness of the composite (the built ring), 8 paces.

The partition of the encompassing colonnade was quadrifariously divided over the circumference. Between
one and the other interjected partition stood, with even discrimination, eight divisions, where the
columns were constituted and set. From which the solid proceeded toward the centre; and, both by the
straight and by circuit, transverse in a ring, stood commensurately the columnar supports; between one
and another, partitely, the gaps of the openings, corresponding linearly, passable, and inter-void, and
artfully vaulted the porticoes, or fornices — the lines narrowing with wondrous convenience, the straight
and the circling transverse, the altitude reserved, and every rule accessory to the harmony. The
pavement floor was egregiously sectile, of marvellous invention and of conspicuous art —

— so the upper as the lower, of most-beautiful stones, of varied colouring most-excellently, and with
most-even cohesion, feigning one integrity, with mirror-like striation and most-comely polish,
noteworthy. The soffits, with elegant work, the shrewd and beautiful-crafting architect had induced with
histories of most-admired mosaic, most-highly adorned with most-elegant pigmentation. Which histories
were all the effects done by Cupid. Thus, in this marvellous building, I diligently considered the
expressed skill, and the acute and great solertia of the artificer, the outstanding art of the maker, and
the force of the wit of the comely Tessellator, explicated. To which structure let yield the marvellous
Ephesian Temple, the Roman Colosseum, and the Veronese Theatre, and every other — because the Columns,
Capitals, Bases, Cornices, Incrustations, Pavements, Statues, Figures, and every other accessory, not
without magnificence and divine operation, wondrously composed, and coordinated, and perfectly castigated,
and most-excellently consummated, with the utmost admiration, most-admired, stood. Let yield here the
superb fame and admiration of the images of Divine Augustus, and of the four Elephants dedicated in the
temple of Concord. Nor to this can be equalled the magnificent image of Menelaus, and every other
stupendous marvel.

Out, then, of this marvellous entrance, or middle and Royal gate, all those officious Nymphs remained
excluded. And the divine lord, and his most-pleasing Psyche, and we together — with those two who bound us
— most-joyously, and with extreme voluptuousness, entered. Here in this entry-way only were not the
loosened spaces, but walled, and hedged, and closedly boarded of the noble stone before insinuated. Thence
we came, by under the vault, to another facing little door, the summit of which was conterminous, under an
evening of a little pergola, which shall be told.

There arrived, being out of the interstitial opening of the vaulted entry, and into the levelled Area of
the Theatre — most-highly worthy of admiration — entering, I, at the first aspect, saw a miracle greatly
and grandly stupendous. For all the pavement of the space of the middle Area of the enclosed cavea of the
Theatre, paved, I saw of a solid and integral Obsidian stone, of extreme blackness, and of indomitable
hardness, polished and so lustrous, that I — abstracted upon it, at the first placing of my right foot —
in that instant, into an Abyss inconsiderately (and I, all occupied with love and sweetness, truly
moribund), feared to precipitate. But the facing resistance suddenly restored to me the shaken and
terrified spirits, with the hurt of the deceived foot. In which stone clearly was seen, and perfectly
discerned — as in a placid and calm sea the limpidity —

— of the profound sky. And likewise all the things existing there in the ring reflected, much more than
a most-clean mirror, and so the overstanding ones.

In the middle of which Area, at the centre, was the most-holy and delicious fount of the divine Genetrix
and mistress of that Love, most-artificially constituted. Of which most-sacred fount, before I speak of
it, I shall first treat of the unheard disposition and most-happy theatral interposition — which,
setting aside every doubt, was composed above the grasp of our imagining, and miraculously defined, in
the form (as I have said) of a Theatre.

The gradation of which began from the area of the most-lucid stone. Not solid, nor massy steps, but
inane — that is, hollow — four, with the stepped ascent, one above the other, like the gradation of the
benches. In the height of the seat, six palms; and in the breadth, two feet and a half, or in the
opening. Which were, in their encompassing circuit, surrounded by boxes stuffed with diverse flowers,
which did not exceed the middle of the following little box. The fourth and supreme step levelled its
opening, with the lips, to an interposed little walkway, five feet wide. Which, encircling, was covered
by a little pergola, a pace and a half high.

Beyond then the summit of the inflexure of such pergola, the other order of as many steps followed in
order. The first, lower, began so much higher in the band, or wall, encompassingly at the inner part,
that the sublime incurvature of the pergola did not occupy the seeing of the front of that first step.
Such symmetry was directly observable in the subsequent. Then the fourth gradation of this second order,
and so of the third — like the first — was of walkway, and of pergola, and of uniform commensuration.

The boarded walls, or the sides of the said pergolas in circuit, were of blackish stone of mirror
sheen. The first wall of the lower pergola was boarded of *spartopolia* stone; the second of
*hieratites*; the third, supreme, of *cepionis*. The sheen of which, under the pergolas, simulated an
opening of the serene air, that shone within it, and not a closure.
— was discerned, by a line directly deduced over the angles of the steps.

The wall which the last pergola girded, set fast, was so much raised that the arching of that pergola did
not, to those inspecting in the Area, wholly obstruct the seeing. Within which wall was a trough, or
channel, inter-void, capaciously fabricated — both at the bottom and at the opening a pace and a half,
inclusive, its capacity — with the estimated band, clean and spaced, above the fenestral order.

Of all this discoursed fabric, the interior girdle — that is, the hollow steps — stood made of best
jasper, ponderous, continuous, and oriental, and perhaps Cyprian, of confused colouring, with wavering
little waves most-diverse. The lips of which boxes, and the socle, were most-beautifully fringed, in
continuous circuit, of pure refined Gold, in little waves and gullet-mouldings; and over the cohesions
of the just division of the tablets, with a working transcending human thought, and most-exact
expression, and utmost effort. Here must perish the luxury of the golden vases of Bassus, and that of
Antony; let yield also the glory of Nero, who gilded the Pompeian Theatre. Let Gorgias of Leontini be
put to sleep with his (golden) statue. Nor ever was such (gold) dug up, so outstanding, by the
Scythians, from the ants and Griffins.

The topmost trough, or box, led in a channel and filled and stuffed with earth, had planted cypresses,
two and two, one next (but untouching) to the other, the pairing three paces distant. Which, with even
form and justly, with a fitting rule interlacing mutually their summits and fore-joined together, with
egregious conjugation inflected themselves — with such-made connexion that they appeared one and the
same. That is, the point of the fourth (cypress) with the fourth. The two then of the middle: that on the
right coupled with the fourth on the right order; and the left, by the like, joined itself with the
fourth on the left side, alternating, one below and one above, knotting themselves, so much the better as
could not be told. Between one and the other of the inflected, or the leaning-together, of the collateral
cypresses, resided a densest Box, of spheres in order, diminishing with even decrement, fastigiate — that
is, decimated into manifold rounding — so excellently shorn (as with little shears) that not one leaf
showed itself to offend its order. And between the neighbouring and curved cypresses, rose a straightest
stalk of Juniper, in a most-just sphere, topiaried with spring foliage, which adorned the empty triangle
of the cypress-arches. The remainder of the terrace-top abundantly germinated various and exquisite
aromatic little pot-herbs, copious of their odoriferous flowers, as appears designed at the top of the
Theatre.

The first, then, lower pergola, was covered of odoriferous myrtle and full of flower, laboriously compacted
of little gold rods above, in arched curvature, led round to the cornice, upon the little arches of the
golden columnlets. Which resided above, with the little bases, on the surface of the inner lip of the fourth
box, led round with most-exquisite chasing.

The levelled ground under the first pergola — not so much to stupefy the intellect, as to un-sense the
sense. It was, then, all paved, in a ring, of odorous ladanum, with a graded mixture of Amber, Musk, Storax,
and Benzoin, condensed in a dusky colouring. In which most-fragrant mixture were then, elegantly, whitest
pearls fixed, like tessellation, reduced into a circumvolved embroidered band of antique foliage, with
olive-fructification; and within the loops the flowers, or within their calyxes little animals and little
birds — a divine and incomparable working, and pressable by divine feet — pavemented as never Zenodorus
availed to find.

The covering of the second levelling of the flatness under the pergola, of manifold roses opulently
disseminated, and with the accessories of the first, was of a paste of Coral, which in the grinding had kept
its redness. And in this fulgurated, comelily depicted, a marvellous embroidery of most-ancient fronds of
finest emeralds, and the flowers of most-even sapphires.

The third walkway, likewise of minute and flowering myrtle was the pergola, of a most-precious composite of
lapis lazuli ground small, ponderous, with its cyan colour somewhat adulterating toward green, marvellously
flagged. In which, with excellent glue, were commixed fragments, or minutiae massed, or cuttings, of all the
jewels universally that fostering nature has known to produce; and with points of gold most-beautifully, in
an evening to the level, most-terse, pre-shining, pavemented. Think how much voluptuousness, how much
pleasure, and solace, and allurement of so many delights, it incredibly conferred on the human senses — that
to the blessed spirits it offered itself marvellous.

These pergolas, on the front anterior, the little gold columns with their little arches sustained, which,
like a peristyle disposed in a ring, most-beautifully continued. But the triangular inter-void between one
arch and the other, grey, or obtuse, was of Chalcedonies, of Agates, of Jasper, and of other precious
stones, flatly tabled, without any lineament, most-pre-shining. And the inner part of the pergola, not
arched, but of a line lengthwise straight, sat fixed in the wall, above a —

— encompassing cornice, with frieze and little architrave, with wondrous and most-absolute expression,
with the subjacent brackets facing the capitals of the little columns, set fast.

There, beneath, restlessly, choral dances they led, and continually many most-joyous Nymphs — ever
mosaic-wise — in the middle of the arch of the columns, with elegant continence, found themselves, and,
toward the fount, with measured time, inclining themselves, all reverent. Then, after the reverent
inclination, all together, departing from that middle, migrated to the other, with successive
continuance. The two extreme choruses gyred against the middle chorus, with most-tempered leaps and
elegant revolution, ever in the middle of the arch. With superb sound, concordantly, of four ductile
golden trumpets, and four sweetest *epiphonia*, *antiphonia*, *messophona*, and *chamaephona* (upper-,
counter-, middle-, and ground-toned instruments), turned of red, citrine and white sandalwood, and of
blackest Ebony, not without manifold ornaments of gold and of gems. With a sonority most-sweetly
united-in-tone, and with briefest utterances, one explicated symphony, in this supremely-delightful and
most-happy enclosure, becomingly reflecting together — and the choristers, not with a broken tumult,
jubilated. Where was perceived a wondrous variety of voice, and an inexperienced equability of
proportion, and sweetness, and harmony, which extremely delighted my mind, and, rapt, held it soothing.

The middle Nymphs, nude, with their whitening and most-shapely bodies, proceeded. The others, most-
exquisitely comely, with much-admired adornment of their divine little bodies, clad in byssus robes and
veiling shifts, with virginal gestures and motions, and with girlish delight. As many again, in the
wall, specularly feigning, the blackest stone.

In prospect, then, of the door of our entrance, corresponded a stair of seven steps, of the stone of the
boxes. By which one ascended to the plane of the first pergola; and, over against the stair, under the
pergola, was built into the wall a slender door. Through which, then, one could — by interstitial stairs,
and passages, and goings — wander and go, through the fornices and vaults, and conveniently through all
the building. And under the other pergolas too, level with the first, were likewise little doors of gold,
most-excellently chased, valved. The first order, or lowest, of the lower steps was halved in its
continuous going-round by the door of the entry, and by the recounted stair. The first step, or lower
box, above the Area, between the stair and the door, stuffed with earth, was germinous with Ianthine, or
amethystine, violets, eternally —

— flowering, and so in the other. In the second order the boxes abounded with whitest violets. In the
third order were xanthe, or yellow, violets. In the fourth flowered narcissus, such as would not be found
in the mountains of Lycia, with more flower-yield than herbage.

Beyond the first pergola, in the first circularly-continuous box, germinated the cyclamen, with the
reverse of the leaves vermilion, of an ivy colour, with its inverted flower most-richly appearing, most-
odorous. The second step was flowering with cyan corn-flower. In the third copiously flowered most-purple
chervils, densely leaved. In the newest, densest melilots.

In the third order, beyond the second pergola, grew, in the first step, the grey-green and most-beautiful
flowers of the herb *tora*. In the second, reddening Anemones. In the third, sweet-scented chervils, five-
leaved and many-leaved. The topmost, into ten partitions equally divided, every partition with harmonised
allotment, was of various and much-admired flowers. The first contained the primrose. The second,
everlasting (*heliochrysum*). The third, amaranth. The fourth, the matronal russet violet. The fifth,
Ianthine *passerina*. The sixth, the *opula*, or white bell. The seventh, yellow *pulliphura*. The eighth,
lily-of-the-valley, of whitening floret, with the little inverted *calathi* (bells) hanging most-odorous on
the little branches. In the ninth, manifold lilies — the heavenly, and white iris, and hyacinth, and yellow
and reddening ones. In the newest, the flowered Columbine, germinating azure, white and russet flowers.

This delightful and choice disposition of the much-admired flowers succumbed here to no temporal change,
nor order — nor such as in Memphis — but, ever irrigated and fresh, in one vernal being, and never
deciduous, existing.

For which thing, contemplating such majesty of place, with so much grace astonishing, with this elegance
ordered and allotted, and most-pleasant harmony of variation of the flowering colour — such as, in the dewy
dawn, they present themselves fresh — with all the discoursed miracles, astonished and lifeless I wholly
remained. My internal and external senses occupied, and surrounded with ineffable voluptuousness and
delight — beyond the excessive love, which all the while in my lanced heart strongly burned, and the
unceasing siege of the incomparable beauties of my most-comely Polia, my delight — insomuch that I did not
know in what being I was. Finally, into this most-happy place, and most-blessed site, introduced — of a
sudden the two Nymphs who bound us, there, again, unloosed us from the entangled little wreaths. And the
venerable Psyche, most-honorifically, to her beloved Husband, laughing, restored the little golden arrow.

*(the last line of the preceding chapter)* …by which we were brought before the
holy and sacred Cytherean fountain.

Which fountain, at the very middle of this more-than-human building, was
divinely constructed and set out in this manner.

Of that blackest stone which alone, and entire, made the whole paving — that is,
the floor of the area — there rose at its centre a little wall a foot high,
brought to an excellent polish and furnished with every fitting ornament,
heptagonal on the outside and round within. It had its running cymatium and
socle, its small plinths and its wave-mouldings, wrought and set in due order
beneath the bases; and over the middle point of each angle there was built up a
column swelling in the shaft — that is, bellied — seven of them in all, turned
with the utmost exquisiteness. Two of these stood answering one another,
equally, opposite the entrance, in full view of where we knelt face down.

One of these lathe-turned columns, on the right hand, shone blue with the finest
sapphire; and on the left one glowed spring-green with an emerald of a colour so
surpassing, and more brilliant, than the stones set for eyes in the lion on the
tomb of Hermias the prince. Nor was such a one given by Ptolemy to Lucullus; nor
was that of so great price which the King of Babylon presented to the King of
Egypt; nor were those of the obelisk in the Temple of Jove of such estimation;
nor was the statue in the temple of Hercules at Tyre so great a marvel, as this
one showed itself to be.

Next to this followed a column of turquoise stone, most beautifully coloured a
lovely cerulean, endowed graciously with its virtue; and though it was an opaque
stone, it was nonetheless most brilliant, and shone back like a mirror.

Touching the sapphire column there stood another precious one, opaque also, of a
most delightful colour like melilot, and with a lustre like the translucent
flower of the buttercup. Adjoining this was one of jasper of a glassy colour, and
the other of topaz flashing with a golden colour. The seventh, alone and
singularly, was hexagonal, of the most limpid Indian beryl with an oily sheen,
giving back whatever stood before it reversed.

And this one answered to the midpoint between the first two — because every
figure of an odd number of angles has one angle facing the middle of the interval
between two others. So then: the circle drawn about its half-diameter, an
equilateral triangle set up within it, and then a line from the centre, and in
the middle of that line —

— drawn upon the adjacent circumference: such is the sevenfold division of the
said circular figure.

In the middle of the shaft of the seventh, the beryl column, on the inner face,
there was marvellously carved out of that same stone — as though wrenched free
of the sculpture — a little Hermaphrodite child, held in a socket. The three
shining columns of the right-hand order had likewise, each of them, an infant
boy caught in a kind of receptacle; and so too on the shaft of each of the
precious columns of the left there hung, set into it, the female sex. And this,
by a mystical artifice, was expressed naturally at the middle of the columns,
with such a scintillation of polish as neither the biting of whetstone nor emery
with licking Tripoli chalk can give.

The bases, the capitals, the Phrygian architrave and the cornice stood out in
the purest gold. The arches, and all the solid between one column and the next,
were of the wrought stone of one of the columns of the surrounding order — that
is, of sapphire toward the emerald, and of emerald toward the turquoise — and so
on in sequence, the whole arcade was marvellously constructed.

At the angles of the crown, above the true central perpendicular of each column
beneath, there stood a small altar, and rising from it projected the image of a
planet with its proper attribute, its size exactly a third of the column below
it, symmetrically, and of the purest gold. On the front face, at the right, sat
scythe-bearing Saturn, and at the left the night-shining Cynthia; and beginning
from the first and going round in order they ended at Selene. Beneath these, in
the frieze running round, chased with the most exquisite artifice, were to be
seen the twelve signs of the zodiac, with their governing impressions and
characters, expressed in outstanding carving.

The crown then of this most marvellous fountain, and its roofing, blazed with an
extraordinary cupola of the finest crystal, veinless, utterly pure and
transparent. Xenocrates saw none such; none like it was found in Cyprus, nor
produced in Asia, nor in Germany — without rust or roughness, without a clouded
speck, no core of salt, nor any hairline flaw to be seen. Nor did Nero shatter
such a one. But pure, surpassing, and unalloyed, it was girdled with a raised
work, in a fitting and even binding of foliage issuing from certain little
monsters, with small boys wonderfully interwoven playing among them; and it was
of excellent bulk and convexity.

At the tapering of its topmost peak was fixed a miraculous show: in a golden and
most cunningly wrought [?setting], a carbuncle flashing lightning on every side,
egg-shaped, and of the thickness of an ostrich's.
On the faces of the little wall of that darkest stone, upon which —

— the ready columns were raised, there were cut, perfectly excavated, letters of
the most ancient Greek, the shaft being three-quarters of a foot. In the hollows
of these there shone, laid in, words of refined silver. On the front face only
two letters were to be seen, intersected with companion emblems of gold and
elegantly polished; and then following, on the other faces, three and three,
they said this:

> ΩΣΠΕΡ ΣΠΙΝΘΗΡ ΚΗΛΗΘΜΟΣ
>
> *as a spark, so enchantment*

Each face was three feet, and from the golden bases up to the architrave the
height stood at seven feet. Of the artifice of this thing, marvellous and most
highly finished, I judge that its dignity will be more fittingly preserved by my
keeping silent than by my discoursing of it poorly and meagrely.

There, between the sapphire and the emerald column, hung on bent rings with
knotted loops the most beautiful little veiling curtain that fertile nature could
ever have devised to produce as a thing more pleasing to the gods — so beautiful
a weaving, and of such a material, that I should never know how to describe it;
but of a sandalwood colouring, woven with the loveliest flowering, and with four
Greek letters of gold subtly embroidered over it, **ΥΜΗΝ**, stretched out most
becomingly and heavenward. Let the marvellous curtain the Samians sent to Delphi
rightly yield place here. This appeared to my Polia as a most precious treasure,
and gracious; and it was this that veiled and hid the majestic and divine
presence of the venerable mother.

And so, both of us — Polia and I — kneeling face down upon our bending knees, the
divine lord Cupid gave the golden arrow to the nymph Synesia, and shrewdly made
her a sign that she should offer it to Polia, and that Polia with that fearful
arrow should rend and split the most noble curtain. But Polia, as though grieved
at the command for such a cutting and breaking, however subject she was to that
divine authority, seemed unpractised, and refused to consent. The lord in that
same moment, smiling, charged the nymph Synesia that she should hand it to the
nymph Philedia, and that she should then present it to me; and that what the
honeyed and most upright Polia did not dare to do, I — [?spellbound], and most
greedy to look upon the most holy mother — should carry out.

Whereupon no sooner had I taken hold of the divine instrument than, ringed about
with a blind flame and not refusing, but rather with an urgent and headlong
passion, I struck the little curtain. And as it split I saw that Polia was almost
saddened by it; and the emerald column, cracking, seemed as though it must
shatter entirely.

And behold, all at once I plainly see the divine form in the salt fountain,
brought forth out of that venerable majesty from which all beauty deliciously
flowed. Nor sooner had that unlooked-for sight —

— that divine sight breathed upon my eyes and passed into them, but both of us,
roused by an extreme sweetness and driven and harried by a new pleasure so long
desired, remained together in a devout fear, almost in ecstasy.

And finding myself so, I began with some reason to be afraid, misdoubting the
vision that the son of Aristaeus had in the vale of Gargaphie; and in a moment it
put both wonder and terror into me.

In the midst, the divine Venus stood naked in the clear and most limpid little
waters, up to her ample and divine flanks — waters which gave back the Cytherean
body neither thickened nor doubled nor broken nor foreshortened, but wholly and
simply, so that it was perfectly discerned in them just as it was. And round
about, at the lowest level, there rose a foaming that gave off a fragrance of
musk. With such divinity was that body transparent, with such particular clarity
did that majesty and venerable aspect present itself, as a precious and
coruscating carbuncle flashes in the rays of the sun — with features and a
marvellous composition neither seen nor ever imagined among human kind.

She had — oh, with what loveliness — her golden hair pleasantly and delicately
dressed, neatly curled and crisped above the milky whitening brow with wandering
and restless whorls, which were hindered from spreading out like vine-tendrils;
and from her rosy shoulders they were becomingly kept from falling free by the
most beautiful little waves. The face rosy and snowing. The eyes starry and
luminous, with an amorous and most holy regard. The honeyed cheeks purpled. The
small narrow mouth most purple, of coral — the dwelling and the little estate of
every fragrant bud. The breast more than snowy and treasured up, with two small
swelling paps that resisted every inclination. The body most ivory and smooth.
Divine semblances. Ambrosial — breathing, rather, a spirit of musk.

Her hair then, most beautiful, like the finest golden threads trailing, lay upon
the purest waters, not sinking, but scattered in a gyre and floating out very
long: in that show the rivals of long-haired Phoebus in the clear Olympus,
radiating illuminating rays. And above the twisted little locks, over part of the
loveliest brow, with a dense growth and an airy heaping, they shone out before
her and covered her as with a little shade, down to the small ears. From these
hung two ostentatious pearls, such as the divided Union did not hang for her in
the Pantheon at Rome; nor did the island of Taprobane ever produce their like for
conspicuous whiteness. And a circlet went about her, or rather a plaited band of
vermilion-whitening and pleasant roses, springlike interwoven, and it flashed
with little gems.

And within the inner circuit of the most sacred fountain, clear of the join of
the sumptuous steps, flowering, purple Adonis sprang up among its kindred
leaves, purpling, kept just clear of the water; and on the left side likewise
*thelygonon* flowered with its pale grape-clusters, and on the right
*arsenogonon* — most admirable herbs, and always in flower. And in a circle
about the goddess certain small white doves fluttered, dutifully and decorously
ministering: dipping their golden bills in the most spotless waters, they
mysteriously bedewed the little Cytherean body, and the droplets showed on her
translucent flesh as nothing other than orient pearls set there. Close by stood
the nymph Peristeria, promptly and even boldly ready, attending with a whole
mind upon the services of Venus.

Likewise outside the fountain, upon the stone floor where Peristeria stood, at
the right side, three other divine girls stood naked in this manner,
inseparably embraced: two of them, Eurydomene and Eurymone, showing their
maiden faces toward us; the third, Eurymeduse, turned with her whitest
shoulders to us, her hidden hips veiled by the long outpouring of her most
golden hair. These were the gracious daughters and handmaids, prompt to the
effect of the goddess mother. And she held, lastly, in her divine hands an
opened oyster-shell packed with fresh spring roses, and in the other a burning
torch.

Now from the topmost step, upon which the columns stood, six little steps more
went down to the lip of the fountain, of dark agate; and the flat floor beneath
the water was wave-worked with the loveliest and most graceful milky veining,
variously spiralling — as delightful an object as could ever be set before the
senses. The fountain's water reached to the edge of the fourth step; the others
stood clear of it.

And above the upper step there sat at his ease a wanton figure in the shape of
a man, the god Nyctelius, whose look was that of a pert and striking girl, most
witty, the breast bared by the parting of his garment. His horned head was
bound with a vine-band of writhen tendrils, adorned with savoury grape-
clusters. He leaned upon two most swift tigers.

And on the left in the same manner sat, at her ease, a most beautiful and
nourishing matron, her broad and curled brow wreathed with a blond garland of
wheat-ears. That renowned lady rested upon two scaled serpents. And each of the
two held a spherical ball of some thin and yielding stuff in their laps; and
with these, at measured intervals, through a cunning and fateful nippled
opening, they dripped into the fountain, drop by drop, a most sweet, foaming
and potent liquor. Which diligently —

— they took care to dip their little rosy feet in the salt fountain; and of
their ready little toes one stood out beyond the rest, the one nearest the
great toe. Then the others, step by step, with graceful measure, sloped down
toward the rounded ankle, diminishing in good order toward the outer edge.

By this divine arrangement, then, the most holy majesty of the goddess sat
voluptuously in the very middle of the fountain; and the part of the divine
body that stood among the waters showed neither more nor less than a ray or
splendour of the sun shining through the most polished crystal.

Kneeling there and devoutly persevering, my mind wavered, gazing beyond all
measure and to excess, unable to look fixedly upon the divine spirit breathing
everywhere. And no less thoughtfully I turned over the cause — by what sweetness
of fortune and faith, by what means and merit, such mysteries were granted me
to see clearly, and with my eyes unfit for such an object. But I judged it to be
only the free will of the immortal gods, and the kind consent and faithful
prayer of Polia. Above all things it displeased me that among so many celestial
and divine persons I alone stood there contemptible and foreign, in worn and
threadbare clothes, unlike them in every way, most abject and most poor; and I
would then most gladly have had some means of covering my deformity — as
Erichthonius had, to hide his viper feet. And so, stupefied in my mind with
incredible wonder, I praised the divine benignity to the utmost, that it had
allowed an earth-born man openly to contemplate the works of the gods and the
treasure of fermenting nature.

Whereupon those illustrious nymphs, who beneath the pergolas rejoiced with their
applause and songs and sweet harmony for the prey that winged and rash Cupid —
keener-sighted than Lynceus and eye-covered Argus — was vigorously ready with
his weapons to take in triumph: after a little hour had been spent by the mother
goddess, and the celestial sounds and songs were broken off a while into
silence, to both of us, with divine eloquence and soothing charm, in a gentle
address, that most holy mouth uttered such sweet-speaking words — words shrewd
and beyond doubt able to lull to sleep the wakeful guardian of the fatal
treasure of Colchis, to call back to a kindly shape Aglauros the daughter of
Cecrops, to restore Daphnis of Ida to human form and to the grateful flock, and
to recall Cadmus and Hermione from the hissing voice and the scaled body — to
Polia thus saying:
Lovely Polia, my worshipper, your holy libations, your assiduous observances —

your religious ministrations propitiating me, have made you worthy of our
sweetest and most fruitful graces. And for your sincere, suppliant and unspotted
offerings and solemn ceremonies, commended to my appeasing, and with a devoted
heart and observant novitiate praying, I am willing to incline myself, kind and
favouring and munificently bountiful, your preserver — and that your own
companion Poliphilo, standing here glowing with your love, be likewise numbered
among the true and happy lovers; and cleansed here of the plebeian and vulgar
filth, and if by chance he was chastened of any foul defilement, let him be
purified, expiated, sprinkled with my dew; and let him be unceasingly devoted to
you, and prompt and assiduous to your gentle desires, and let him refuse nothing
of your will. And loving one another equally, of your own accord and with wholest
consent, you shall both serve my amorous fires and increase them; and for the
rest of your life, protected under my keeping, you shall live blessed and
glorious and exulting.

Now, so that so great a love of yours may have a happy outcome, Poliphilo, I will
give and consign to you four illustrious little maidens, and dower you with their
adorned virtues, well suited to your excellent spirit and generous love; and with
them be you a keeper more steadfast than firm Picus toward his Canens, and a
worshipper of Polia.

And without delay, calling to her from the pergolas the excellent nymph Enosina,
she said to her: take with you the girl, matchless Monori, and watchful Phrontis
and her silent sister Critoa, and be inseparable companions of this our athlete
and loving servant of Polia. And by my fated command be the cause that both of
them are of equal and mutual affection. And without pause she drew from within
the oyster-shell two rings, each with a precious violet gem set turning in it,
and gave one to Polia and the other to me, with most eloquent command that we
should endure forever adorned with such a divine gift, and should keep her edict
deep and always hidden, with a serene brow and a kindly, soothing face.

And turning in a moment, to you, Polia, she said: likewise I present four other
noble and most accomplished maidens into your unceasing company, who shall make
you worthy and elegantly honour you in this most celebrated love of yours.

Calling them too from that place, at leisure from their songs and sounds, she
charged Adiacorista with the three noble sisters, Pistinia, Sophrosyne and
Edosia, saying: now let these not leave her for the least while without you, so
that she, loving her Poliphilo by equal law, may live bound in a Herculean knot,
adorned with the most accomplished and most beautiful love that ever in her —

— famous age she might feel herself, and worthy of memory; indulging her genius
and never defrauding it. Offering herself a yoked sacrifice with sincere and pure
faith toward him, and steadying what would falter, anxiously and carefully and
kindly to receive him, and gratefully, with the most tenacious bond, to embrace
him.

All these divine nymphs, at the command of the sovereign goddess and without
delay, each began lovingly to kiss with open kisses the one committed and
entrusted to her, in close embraces, with many nymphish blandishments and
attractive endearments; and promiscuously eager, and often pressingly embracing
and kissing us, with due and fitting inclination assenting to the divine Mother,
they began assiduously and with especial courtesy to serve the charge committed
to them.

And to the most prompt little son — the holy little words scarcely uttered and
the divine discourse hardly finished — he, with native licence, bold and pitiless
and severe, with the flying golden arrow (not the Gortynian, and drawn not from
the Ityraean bow but the divine one), no sooner had the string's [?loosing] driven
it out with the force of the taut cord than it struck, carried through the middle
of my unwitting heart, and suddenly pierced it; and then, so quickly, dyed with
gore, smoking from the hot blood issuing out of the arrow-wound — a wound not to
be healed by the Cretan dittany shrub — without delay it transfixed also the
heart of my red-haired Polia, and in her throbbing breast, stained with her own
unspotted soul, he took the wounding and bloodied arrow up again, and at once,
washing it in the maternal fountain, laid it back.

Ah me, that straightway I began to feel in the innermost and deepest bowels the
honeyed burning of an exuberant little flame, spread and sown far and wide, and
occupying all of me; and clouded over with amorous ardours I trembled, and my
eyes were darkened. And without pause my kindled breast, opening to itself, drew
her to it more harpy-like and more bitingly than the snaky hair of the polyp,
than the whirlwind swallowing water; and the precious love and the divine and
never-to-be-blotted image of Polia being let in — with its noble, chaste and
sweetest conditions, informing the prepared and lovingly disposed subject where
it remained eternally ruling, that heavenly and unwashable likeness most firmly
imprinted and most beautiful — I remained like dry and parched straw kindled in a
sudden and violent fire, and like the torches of burnable pine, not a hair's
particle preserved that the amorous flame did not penetrate. And it almost seemed
to me that I was fittingly changed into another form, with great wavering and
faintness of the intellect, unable to comprehend it except by that likeness of
Hermaphroditus embracing Salmacis in the living, fresh spring, when he, in the
mingled sex —

— is seen to transform into a single form. Neither more nor less than unhappy
Byblis, feeling her own tears become for her a liquid fountain of the Naiad
nymphs. Dwelling then already in the sweetest flames, no longer alive than dead,
without a living pulse — and by an unimpeded passage, out of the height of
sweetness, I freely let my little spirit exhale, thinking I had been seized by
epilepsy, falling with buckled knee.

The most merciful goddess, suddenly, with her cupped divine palm — having set
down the oyster-shell and closing the spaces of her longish fingers — divinely
drew up the salt waters and, moistening, sprinkled them over us. Not as
indignant Diana rained upon the unlucky hunter, tearing him to a beast for the
dogs, but on the contrary, unhesitating, sprinkling to transmute — gratifying and
embracing the sacred nymphs. And no sooner had she kindly done it, and I was
sprinkled and anointed with the sea-dew, than in me at once the clarified spirits
were stirred and grew more intelligible; and without waiting my burnt and
consumed members reverted to their former state, and I felt myself, without
fail, renewed with worthy qualities. I knew truly that I was renewed in a like
manner to Aeson, nor did my return to myself seem otherwise than when
twice-living Hippolytus was called back to the longed-for light, by Diana's great
prayer, with the herb *glycyside*, to desirable life. And the assigned nymphs
affectionately stripped from me the plebeian robes, and dutifully clothed me anew
in a white and somewhat elegant garment. And being made tranquilly secure of our
amorous and strengthened state, and most delightfully refreshed, consoled, and
moved and anointed with sudden joy and gladness, at once they made us kiss with
new-wine kisses, and with the vibration of the tongue sweetly to kiss and closely
to embrace. And in like manner both of us, the joyful and festive nymphs, in
their sacred college receiving us to the new novitiate and office of fruitful
nature, all sweetly and charmingly kissed.

Whereupon the mother goddess, with most elegant address and placid discourse, and
propitious with a majestic gaze, reasoning, and with divine breath dispensing a
genial balsam — things unlawful to publish, and to vulgar men not to be told —
labouring long to establish and to ferment our kindled loves, and to unite our
hearts as one under her fruitful and sweet laws for a long age, made us
great-souled in stable and equal love. And therefore, ever devoted to offering
and munificently conferring favour and defence against every chance perturbation,
she largely and freely promised; and in such discourse, most gentle, most
charmingly conferring her grace.
It came to pass, then, that a manly soldier, divine in aspect, down the —

— steps, out of the recesses beneath the first pergola, valiantly making for the
sacred fountain, with a majestic and vehement face, and breasted and stout-
hearted with formidable ferocity, brawny and tall with broad shoulders, with the
lights of his eyes keen and terrible, but of a venerable dignity. Sumptuously and
proudly and divinely adorned, with a most cunningly wrought silver-gleaming
shield such as Brontes and his companions did not make for the exiled Trojan; his
head covered with a shining helmet wreathed with olive flowers, with a
prominent crest and a noble golden apex above the cone; clad in a golden
cuirass, such as the divine Julius did not bring from Britain nor dedicate to his
mother in her temple; nor did the excellent craftsman Didymaon ever make such a
one; with a pendent baldric, or cross-belt, girt about him, with a most sumptuous
golden scimitar knotted to it; with all the most beautiful military accoutrements,
most robustly holding a scourge in his hand, and attended by his growling
Lycaon.

Come now at last to the delightful and delicious fountain, he showed himself
eager to lay down his armour and, disarmed, to go in to the beloved goddess. And
there he and she embraced one another intricately, not with human blandishments
and endearments but with divine gestures and affection, in knotting embraces.
Whereupon the nymphs, perceiving this, with humble and reverent speech obtained
leave, and I too, and my lively Polia doing the like, in what manner we then
could, having spoken our thanks to the immortal graces, departed. There remained,
then, only the divine Mother with her son, and with those continually standing
about the fountain, and the armed one newly come, cast down to divine and
solacing delights — all the attendants withdrawn.

**By the coming of the armed one just recounted, Poliphilo tells how they went
out of the theatre with all the company, and with the other nymphs came to a
sacred fountain; where the nymphs tell of the sepulchre of Adonis, and how the
goddess yearly assembled there to fulfil the holy ceremonies; and, ceasing from
the dance and song, they urged Polia that she should tell her origin and her
falling in love.**

Adorned with new qualities, with my excellent Polia and with our companions,
departing thence from the sacred fountain, we returned out likewise by that same
gate and entrance by which we had come in, where all the nymphs of the sweet
sounds and singing awaited. Who came festively together with us; whereupon I,
stuffed with fruitful love in my kindled and enlarged breast, with every
accessory sweetness, shut out my past sorrows, every troublesome contrary
extinguished, every doubtful thought curbed, no longer now hesitating over Polia,
but as to the sole Augusta of my soul. Sylvia of my heart, and the Ptolemaïs of
my life. Arsacid of my senses, and Myrrha of my love, and of all of me the
mistress and revered Empress — festive and glad, humbly and most devotedly, I
contentedly succumb, with a more intense, sincere and honourable love than pious
Aeneas bore to his dear, beautiful and divine mistress. Having now at last won
her precious love and willing heart, in this amorous contest an Aristaeus.

It came to pass that the merry little throng of nymphs returned to their former
solaces and pleasures, with the celestial harmonies and angelic concord, with
girlish games and solacing jests, and showing themselves briskly full of laughter
at our obtained and consummated desires, gently giving themselves around us in a
sporting round. And through the holy island, by the paths or streets marked out
among the plants of the fruit-bearing orchards, which were green with perennial
and spring —

— foliage, walled about with box like little walls, and with myrtle and juniper,
ten paces long-wise, alternating, and hanging steeply the other way. Beyond, then,
these described enclosures were exceeded by two paces of elegant latticework of
marble, a sixth of a foot [thick?], with a symmetrical square columniation
suitably distributed and placed, with every excellent requisite. These had their
openings figured as roses and rhombs, and with a lovely allotment of a reddening
colour like bright cinnabar. Through which, vine-like, wound rose-bushes of
manifold colouring and foliage.

Through these aforesaid places, both holding hands, they began to lead, pleasantly
urging Polia that — in the manner in which for them and for her there were little
flowering wreaths pressed round like blond crowns — she likewise should gather up
the scattered flowers for me, and lovingly compose, threading them, a jewel. And
there, with great solace and excess of pleasure, some of the divine nymphs,
attending the gathering, placidly inclined themselves with my much-loved Polia,
and helped. Who without pause, easily compelled by the amorous rules, with her
ready and most apt hands, with quickened delight began composedly to weave the
circular *Polycarpia* of the various fragrant little flowers; and, uprooting from
her copious head the golden and very long hairs — glittering like the finest
spun thread of pure gold, which, stretched out in a long series flowing down her
chaste back, waved beautifully — she busily set about binding the gathered heaped
flowers. And with such pleasure and sport of sweet flame, most glad and
untiring, we dallied. Now through flowery meadows, now through greenest little
woods, hedged with irrigating channels and trembling brooks; now through the
sweet shades of the tree-set walks covered with flowering periwinkle, with the
crown of topiary work — and the fame of the place and the clemency of the sky,
without the trouble of showers and heat, drawing us on with a voluptuous
invitation, provoking and alluring — joyfully we came to a most limpid and sacred
fountain flowing from a broad spring. Not with mossy, hairy-mossed, maidenhair-
and-spleenwort banks, but its banks were hedged about and adorned with borders of
Macedonian marble, not red, but of itself lustrous and veined, decorated with the
shade of riverside shoots, with manifold offspring of flower of various and
pleasant fragrance, and their freshest and dewy fragrant leaves disposed.

From which a most pleasing little rivulet carried off the liquid flowing waters,
trickling, hastening beneath the leaf-bearing manna-ashes with a soft and gentle
murmur, running away. And in this pleasant place, from an immortal laurel the —

— temperate shades breathed, mingled with reddening cornel-cherries copious with
their fruit, and with a fresh-sprouting cone-shaped little cypress-grove, and a
lofty palm-grove, and a poplar, and a resinous and cone-bearing pine-grove — set
in order with composed distance and mutual arrangement, and distributed in a
circle about this fated fountain, and adorned and decorated with a clothing of
flower and leaf — covered the shaggy ground with soft and finest little pot-herbs,
like a carpet of fresh shade. Beneath which planting of straightest trunks, clear
of a single obstructing branch, the free air of the neighbouring parts could be
beautifully seen through.

To which sacred fountain, holy, shaped as a hexagon and twelve paces in its
surrounding measure, the inner tree-set enclosure stood off from the containing
edge of the fountain — that is, from the marble borders — by four paces; and in
circumference, thirty-six paces. It was all of orange, lemon and citron trees,
affording a pleasant and most placid enclosure, or cloister; offering to the
eyes it granted a most admirable show, of thick density, of festive leaves and
fragrant flowers — a most pleasing picture, russet, or vermilion mortified in
yellow, of the ripened fruits, and excellently shining with a thick offspring,
one tree to another, composedly matched in an alternating marriage, uniform, full
of every singing bird — chiefly of nightingales, of thrushes, and of solitary
blackbirds, with delightful expressions, urged to the sweet warble by the amorous
impulse of the spring season.

And there, at the round trunks of the trees just recounted, a lattice-fence
artfully hedged them, raised a foot high, surrounding in a circle, of manifold-
devised open interlacing, of red erythraean wood, of sandalwood; in which were
excellently woven and intertwined rose-bushes of the hundred-petalled kind,
little Greek autumn ones, and small crowns of purpling flower straying twined
along the lattice; with leaves not to fall, of unthinkable fragrance, of most
admirable freshness.

Here, by a little postern of the same aforesaid work, we religiously entered. In
sight of the entrance to the fountain there was a little pergola adjoining, as
wide as one face of the fountain, angle to angle, and raised as much — one pace to
the perpendicular, and one to the assigned bend. Twelve feet long, roofed with
most noble rose-bushes teeming with vermilion flower, with their most delightful
fragrance, carried fittingly upon little rods of gleaming gold; with the bright
stone floor, or tessellated and inlaid pavement wrought vermiculate of precious
little stones. And close to the sides of the pergola stood seats of jasper —
pages.wcap: Fountain of Venus: Sarcophagus of Adonis

t:
— material, and of fitting most elegant lineaments marked out, seven-twelfths and
a half-as in the seat, upon the flat.

The tessellated pavement was laid level over all the enclosed ground. Which was
on every side green without any bareness, and all tressed with tiniest fragrant
thyme, of which a single leaf did not stand above another, with a gratifying
denseness clothing right up to the banks of the fountain, springlike, with an
even shearing.

Here beneath I beheld a venerable work, which these divine nymphs and we devoutly
reverenced. A marvellous sepulchre, full of mystery, stood there appointed: five
feet in length, and in breadth as much raised — ten inches — excluding the socle,
with the little cornice, which was a quincunx; which tomb the nymphs said to be of
the hunter Adonis, slain in that place by the tusked boar. And in this place
likewise the holy Venus, coming naked out of this fountain, tore in those
rose-bushes her divine calf, to succour him who had been beaten by jealous Mars,
with a woeful and indignant face, and with anguish of soul.

This little history was seen perfectly carved on one long side of the sepulchre;
and the son Cupid then gathering the purple blood into an oyster-shell — adding
that that divine gore was laid up in that sepulchre, placed with the ash, with
every holy rite. Whereupon on the front of our entrance to the sepulchre it was
hollowed out in a circle to the size of the square, and then stopped up with the
precious stone jacinth, of a transparent vermilion colour, with great coruscation
of flaming splendour, burning unsteadily by the light set opposite, so that I
could scarcely fix my eyes on it for the wavering.

On the other long side of the sepulchre I saw likewise Adonis, carved with some
shepherd-hunters, among some little shrubs, with dogs and the dead boar, and he
slain by it; and Venus falling sorrowfully weeping into the pitiful embraces of
three half-swooning nymphs, clothed in finest cloth, weeping together with the
goddess; and the son, with a little bundle of roses, I saw wiping the maternal
eyes, tearful with flowing tears.

There, between the one sex and the other, in a garland of myrtle, I saw thus
inscribed: **IMPURA SUAVITAS**. In like manner on the other little history, in
Greek, was thus expressed: **ΑΔΩΝΙΑ**. So exquisitely feigned in sculpture did all
these things present themselves, that I was moved to a sweetness of pity.
The square opposite that of the light derived perpendicularly —

— above the fountain. In which was aptly fixed a golden serpent, feigned to creep
out from a hidden cleft of rock, which, with coiled windings of a fitting
thickness, vomited abundantly into the sonorous fountain the clearest water. So
that by this mastery the meaning craftsman had cast the serpent in a globed coil,
to curb the force of the water — which, by a free and straight pipe, would have
scattered beyond the limits of the fountain.

Upon the flat of the aforesaid sepulchre the divine Mother sat, carved as a woman
in childbed — not without utmost astonishment — of a precious three-coloured
sardonyx stone, upon an antique seat, her seat not exceeding the sardine vein; but
with incredible invention and artifice the whole little Cytherean body was of the
milky vein of the onyx, as though unclothed, because only a veiling was left of
the red vein concealing the secret of nature, veiling part of one thigh, and the
rest descending over the flat, passing then up over —
pages.wcap: Poliphilus and Polia at Fountain of Venus

t:
— the left nipple, resisting it. And from the shoulders, turned to the water,
hanging down, it showed — imitating with marvellous sculpture, nonetheless, the
holy members — she embracing and giving suck to Cupid, indicating with the image
the maternal affection, with a gracious colouring of the cheeks of both from the
reddening vein, with her right little hand [?patting]. O most beautiful work,
miraculous to contemplate, wanting only the vital spirit. With the parted brow,
the ringleted hairs over the smooth temples, and at the back of the head gathered
composedly with a little knotted band; the loosed part thence extended down to
the seat, tendril-like. And exactly sculpted the little tresses, with the openwork
whorls egregiously expressed by the labour of the drill, preserved of the
translucent shining sardine vein — such as, of happy Polycrates, enclosed in the
golden horn, was not dedicated by Augustus in the shrine of Concord. The left
little foot she held drawn back to the seat, and the other stretched to the
outer edge or rim of the flat. Which holy foot the nymphs, bowed and fallen
kneeling, and we, kissed with utmost religion. Beneath which little foot, in the
little cornice, there remained a small band of lineament clear; and on this, in
little letters of our own, I saw annotated this distich:

> Non lac saeve puer, lachrymas sed sugis amaras,
>    Reddendas matri, carique Adonis amore.
>
> *Not milk, cruel boy, but bitter tears you suck,*
> *to be given back to your mother, for love of dear Adonis.*

Having done and duly performed this honorary and devout ceremony, we went out of
the sacred little pergola. The illustrious nymphs with affable eloquence said to
us: Know that the present place is mysterious, and most celebrated with the
greatest veneration; and every year, anniversarily, on the day before the Kalends
of May, the divine Mother comes here with her beloved son in a divine pomp of
lustration, and with her all we her subjects, of our own accord at her command,
with observed attendance and with proud solemnity, assemble. Come here, then,
with sweet tears and little sighs, she commands us that all the roses of the
pergola — and the lattices too be stripped of them — and over the alabaster
sepulchre, with high-sounding invocation, ritually to strew them, and heapingly to
cover it. Then in the said order and process she first departs. On the following
calendar day the despoiled rose-bushes reflower to the same number of glowing
roses.
And on the Ides another time the goddess, returning in the former manner —

— she says that devoutly the heap of roses is removed from the sepulchre, and
within the fountain, with divine applause, all scattered; and, thrown into the
emissary rivulet, thence they are carried away.

After the divine Lady, as is her custom, has washed herself in the fountain and
come out of it, again in commemoration and amorous memorial of the dear and
beloved Adonis, beaten by Mars, with moist eyes she throws herself embracing over
the sepulchre, weeping, her rosy cheeks bedewed with flowing tears; and all we,
with a lamentable piping, piteously weep, because on such a day the divine calf —
of the little foot we kissed — was pricked by the thorns of these roses. And
therefore on that same day the cover of the holy repository is solemnly unsealed
by her and revealed, and with venerable ceremony all we, glad and exulting and
singing — the son having received it, carries the oyster-shell with the divine
gore, and she, the priestess and newest bearer of the bundle of roses unwilted of
their greenness, with serene grace, most festive.

No sooner is the precious liquor drawn out than at once all the whitest roses, as
at present they appear, are re-dyed in purple colour. And in such order, three
times pompously lustrating this fountain, and she alone weeping, her eyes wet,
wipes them with the handful of roses; at the third circling, the sacred things
laid back in their place, all that most celebrated day is solemnly dispensed to
pleasures alone, to dances, sounds and songs, most dedicated. And on such a day
her grace is easily obtained.

Opposite the sepulchre, at the fountain, there were five steps of the bordering
stone, sloping down to the flat bottom — not rough, not gravelly, but of precious
and vermiculate inlaid paving. The channel of the emissary rivulet flowed on,
underground, beyond the lattices, carrying the succeeding water.

The maiden nymphs having domestically and eloquently narrated so memorable and so
curious a mystery, began again to sound, and rhythmically, most sweetly and with
the greatest pleasure, to sing the recounted little histories and the past
happenings. And dancing in a circle about the fountain for a long while, then all
kneeling and seated and interlaced, in such most acceptable pleasantness and most
delightful greenery — I then, particularly stripped and freed of every holding-
back respect, in that unwonted fragrance of my dainty Polia, which still breathed
from her most elegant and cleanly self, and being all perfumed with a recent
exhalation of that fragrant sweetness of her delicate garments dewing balsam — I
placed myself amorously and freely in her lap, eagerly kissing both her milky
hands and that snowy breast, ivory and lustrous shining; and then mutually — not
ungrateful but voluptuously vying — being in her sight, such impulses of love
approved themselves. Whereupon the singers, set out over the most pleasing
greenery —

— and their melodious instruments, and the singers, the mellifluous voices held
back in their delicious breasts, fell silent.

Whereupon, thus briskly and voluptuously at leisure, with nymphish converse for a
little while, they showed themselves much desirous to learn our state and
condition. And one among the others, named Polyorimene, most witty and pleasing,
said: O Polia, our consort and partner fellow-servant of the goddess we
cultivate, the loveliness of your elegant aspect and your conspicuous and notable
form, and your noble and illustrious virtues and excellent well-mannered mind,
and your especial and incomparable beauty, make us not undeservedly eager to
learn the cause of your happy loves, and the original beginning of your excellent
and generous lineage — which we judge to be notable and sublime and of illustrious
origin. For we have gathered you to be of probity, of wit, and not meanly learned
in letters; distinguished in shrewdness, with especial grace in your virgin
gestures, of exceptional form; of surpassing beauty, with most sweet loveliness,
and most excellent in modesty, and worthy in the highest degree of honour.
Because your most admirable countenance and heavenly likeness, extremely beautiful
and genial, is not wholly earthly, but rather appears in every way, by open
token, to have more of the divine. Therefore tell us — grateful, indeed most
grateful — of the troublesome torments and the impudent disdains, through discord
and unequal disposition, and how at times you feigned yourself deaf, not to hear
the anxious prayers of importunate and passionate lovers; and how, the two not
continually seeing one another, the sad and desiring heart feeds only on a
consoling persuasion, proceeding from composed imagination and delightful
figments, such as they would wish and most greatly desire, vainly satisfying
themselves with sweet little sighs and feigned solace and pleasure. And in such
commendable leisure, intent on the act, our quiet and solacing sitting will not
grow wearisome.

When the nymph, with most gentle courtesy, had finished her kind persuasion and
most acceptable reminder, my golden-haired Polia, ready and most mild, rising with
her festive and most witty images or semblances, and with cheeks flushing and rosy
little lips suffused with an honest and reverent blush, made ready to satisfy in
every way — of a nature prompt to every virtue — and to give effect to the honest
petition. Not, however, that she could first conceal it, or hold it in at all,
that she did not inwardly sigh a little; which sweetest little sigh penetrated,
reflecting, into the depth of mine — nay, of her — heart, by the uniform accord,
as happens to two equally shared and concordant war-trumpets. And each, gazed
upon with a divine gaze, intrepidly, with those playful and flashing eyes fit to
shatter (ah me) adamant into a thousand little fragments — with pious and humble
voice, and with most elegant gestures becomingly revered by every one, she
returned to her solacing seat upon the thyme-grown ground, following the begun
work, seated. With fitting —

— pronunciation, having first made a little pause, thus most polishedly she set
herself, and clearly committed herself to narrate.

> POLIPHILO BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK OF HIS HYPNEROTOMACHIA, IN WHICH POLIA AND HE, CONVERSING, NARRATE BY TURNS
> IN WHAT MANNER AND BY WHAT VARIOUS CHANCE THEIR FALLING-IN-LOVE (CAME ABOUT).
>
> HERE THE DIVINE POLIA NARRATES HER NOBLE AND ANCIENT ORIGIN; AND HOW, BY HER PREDECESSORS, TREVISO WAS BUILT;
> AND OF THE LELIAN GENS (SHE) DESCENDED; AND BY WHAT MODE, UNAWARE AND IGNORANT, HER BELOVED POLIPHILO
> IMPROPERLY FELL IN LOVE WITH HER.

My feeble voice, O gracious and divine Nymphs, will come to your benign audience as discordant and inelegant as
the terrific raucousness of the diving Aesacus to the sweet song of the plaintive Philomela. Nonetheless, wishing
I, with all my slender efforts of the intellect, and with my scanty sufficiency, to satisfy your pleasant petitions,
I shall not desist from (my) power. Which (petitions) — every hesitation set aside — they, more than would elsewhere
be congruous, worthily merit a more copious river of eloquence, with far more rounded elegance and more adorned
polish of pronouncement than in me, by any pact, is found, to attain their gracious affect. But to you, celibate
Nymphs, and to me somewhat — however confusedly and inelegantly stammering — I shall, in some little portion, have
gratified much (enough), when, willing and devout to your desires and demand, I shall present myself rather with a
soul not mediocrely prompt, humble seeming, than with enucleated, terse and comely eloquence pleasing. The ancient,
then, and most-antique genealogy, and lineage, and my fatal love, garrulously I shall begin to weave. Whence,
already being in your venerable conventual sight, and seeing myself sterile and fasting of eloquence — and (before)
so outstanding and divine a company of you, O Nymphs, sedulous handmaids of kindled Cupid, and in so benign and
delightful and sacred a site, of sincere airs and flower-bearing breaths breathed-upon — I, fittingly compelled to
assume a venerable daring, and a tranquil fear of speaking. Then, before all, give pardon, O most-beautiful and most-
blessed Nymphs, to this my babbling, and to the female and earth-born and pusillanimous efforts, if it happen that,
in some part, I incautiously —
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
— in my professed haranguing transgress. O sacrosanct fount, in which mysteriously is the disposition of the arcana
and of the treasure of the celestial genetrix, full of assiduous sanctimony and pacate religion — and which, at
present, upon thy flowering banks seats, with so much consolation, and so notable, the demigoddesses; and in which
the most-excellent and contemplable part of her most-beautiful body specularly (in mirror) thou feignest to have —
for which thing thou art most-highly, of obstinate reverence, to be worshipped: for so much, never let (it be) that,
whatever of you I behold, all veiling my piteous eyes, they be not converted into flowing tears — approaching, in my
tranquil mind, to commove (the memory of) the lacerated Dirce, the weeping Byblis, the envied Galatea, the fugitive
Arethusa, and the dolorous Egeria — I return not wholly free of my spirits. Then, with what affect of soul, and what
study, and with what vows is the inelegant tongue invited to such narration? For my first original stock was unhappy,
inasmuch as of it was (one) who, by divine will, justly, into springing fountains and liquid rivers transformed
himself. O deplorable metamorphosis! O unfortunate case, and badly luckless, and miserably grievous! O indissoluble
series of the fates! O inevitable and perpetual order! In such a case, precipitate and adverse, shall I be able to
narrate thee without grave sighs, and dolorous voice, and imperfect, sobbed words — and without irrigation of tears
upon the dry cheeks? As the wandering Ulysses, reciting the miserable ruins of Troy to Alcinous, King of the
Phaeacians, wept — and (why) does it not break my breast, of cordial sighs, in this most-holy place of felicity,
(where such are) denied and interdicted of provocation? And in which place, reasonably, the eyes of tears, and the
breast of sighs, sterilise themselves — and, to so blessed and gratifying an audience, remote and alien — and
especially in this most-sweet and dearest victory, of my most-appreciated Poliphilo.

Marvel not, then, auspicious, most-comely and heaven-dwelling Nymphs, if I, incontinently — both for my feeble
parentage and progeny, and for my first falling-in-love, difficult — some time, sobbing, should interrupt my prolix
sermon; worthy, nonetheless, of tarrying, and of a considered and attentive audit. For, undoubtedly, two marvellous
things you will comprehend: one, first, an unwonted and unheard cruelty and inhuman — nay, swinish ferocity, and
feminine atrocity, beyond belief — arrived at such a happy and amorous exit as, at present, openly you see it. The
other, the greatest and unthinkable love of the whole world, having such a beginning and exordium.

Divine and Cytherean Nymphs: in the time when the verdant and fecund palm, sprung miraculous and prodigious out of
the woollen fillet, in the Vestal flames, from the forehead of Ilia Silvia, over-shadowed, triumphant, the spacious
earth and the immense sea — the Lelian family, most-noble, was amplified into great —

— state and dignification of magistracy, for its things most-excellently done, and its manifold victories strenuously
attained. Nor to you is hidden the reason that magnanimous men, and whatever virtuous action, in the ancient and
imperial city, were condignly stipended (rewarded).

One, then, of this ancient and honoured lineage, descended, named **Lelio Syliro** — by the holy Senate (long is the
most-potent reason) sent as Consul, and designated, into the region and March **Taurisana**, so named from the high
mountain (Tarvisium/Treviso). Thither, again, coming to people (it) — where presided a magnificent and opulent and
