most-sumptuous lord and high-dwelling regulus, parent of an only daughter, named **Tito Butanechio** — who gave his
outstanding daughter in solemn and just and untouched wedlock. Marrying, then (by *confarreatio*), alacritously, with
this (girl) endowed of prudence, and a notable maiden of egregious character and matronal gravity — beyond the
conspicuous beauties, and the affluent plenty of the goods of fortune — she, ingenuous and generous, of manifold
virtue and preclear learning, and most-comely, nurtured bounteously in regal delights and paternal good-manners,
called **Trivisia, Calardia, Pia** (her mother named **Rhoa Pia**). She, amply dowered of patrimony by her father, was
given a great part of the tenth region, Venetia — a level fatherland, hedged by lofty and conspicuous peaks of imminent,
notable mountains, of founts, streams, and down-fallings of rivers; wooded, and of harmless animals abundant.

Celebrated, then, most-magnificently — the Herculean knot dissolved — the legitimate Hymeneals; and religiously invoked
holy Cinxia, fulfilling the matrimonial laws, favouring the divine Zygia Lucina — they had most-noble seed, and copious
birth, taking up (bearing) more sons, male and female, alternately. Of which the first-born was **Lelio Maurio**,
surnamed from the dusky colour; the second, **Lelio Halcyoneo**; the third, **L. Tipula**; the fourth, **L. Narbonio**;
the fifth, **L. Musilistre**. In the daughters, nature — seconding the superior virtues — conferred so much beauty and
comeliness, that never, by human conceit, would they be reputed conceived (of mortals). The first was named **Murgania**,
and one **Quintia**; the third, **Septimia**; the fourth, **Alimbrica**; the fifth, **Astorgia**; the sixth, **Melmia**.
Whence, briefly saying, the parents, unmindful of the fecund benefit of the presider over birth (the goddess), and
glorying of the elegant offspring, deemed them born of their own virtue. Alas — who ever the fatal difficulty, and the
inconstant, fallacious and mobile fortune, expedited and unharmed can evade? For to them it befell, by the demerit of so
great a divine gift — not otherwise than to Atalanta and Hippomenes — and, beyond this, comparing themselves improbably
to our Lady Mother, the Cyprian (Venus), genetrix of our arrow-bearing Lord, and, of beauty and dignification,
preferring themselves. O evil and nefarious deed, and temerarious daring! Wherefore, then, when the years of her
infancy began to exceed (grow), the plebeians, and the vulgar, rude and ignoble, and uncultivated people, not otherwise
than thus —

— judged that Murgania was Venus herself. Whence, in the suburban places, they constructed a Sacello, in which she,
lurking, at appointed times, ceremoniously showed herself, feigned (as the goddess); and with annual and suppliant
vows, superstitiously, the popular concourse worshipped (her). Thence was born such a name, among the peoples, even
to this day: **Fada Murgania** (the Fay Morgana); and the place still keeps the memorial name **Murganio**.

For which unjust and enormous thing, and cruel human impiety — audacious, avaricious, ambitious, superb, and
nefarious — the gods (who do not suffer mortal offences unpunished, nor permit any insolence to grow up), irascible
that the earth-born should wish, usurping, illicitly to assimilate themselves to the supernal gods — (and to compare
with) the most-holy mother of our tremendous lord (to whom now most-deservedly we serve) — showed themselves a raging
avenger (not otherwise than Juno to Antigone, and the indignant Eriboea to Isis): the impious temple thunder-blasted,
the royal house lightning-struck, reduced to coal, not far distant hence, where by chance she then found herself,
remained an eternal name, **Casa Carbona**; and Murgania (turned) into founts, with all those who in that place found
themselves, converted. And so likewise **Quintia** and **Septimia**, sisters fleeing not far from Murgania, and they
transformed into welling founts. And **Alimbrica**, made ash, not distant from the said, by the terrific lightnings of
the great indigene and lightning-hurling Jove; and all the palace and royal mansion, in that place also built for
pleasure, all converted into coals; and the place was called **Carbuncularia** — thence it leaps forth into a little
river. And **Astorgia**, fugitive, weeping the miserable cases, she too into a little river runs down into her father.
And likewise **Melmia** — their perpetual name they gave to those places, licking in waves, embracing the sweet father
**Lelio Siliro**. And he, transmuted into liquefying matter, augmented by the dear daughters, makes a celebrated river,
of most-purged welling waters, which still in that most-pleasant region, flowing, most-fresh is seen: from his truncated
name, **Sile**, it is named. And his consort (**Calardia**), thunder-struck, weeping the miserable and horrend cases,
transmuted herself into a notable fount, from her surname called the **fountain Calardia**, near the beloved father
**Tito Butanichio**, made into a liquefying river, weeping the hard and cruel lot, mingled with those of his line. And
her mother **Rhoa**, between her husband and her most-beloved brother **Caliano**, flowing, derive into the sweetest
son, Sile.

Nor was any, even of the males, unpunished by the celestial ire and just vengeance. For the second-born, **Lelio
Musilistre**, made into a rivulet of his name, embraces the father, inundating the Altinate peoples. And the other two
younger brothers — innocent, unweaned, teething — the divine retribution somewhat more temperate, they too experienced
metamorphosis: one into a little bird of his name, **Alcyoneo** (clad with regal and incorruptible plumes), and the
other, younger, into the **Tipula** animal (water-strider). Which, dwellers of the father, not immersing themselves,
ever with him stand, fluvial.

Being, then, from this feeble and pitiable case, the only survivor escaped — the first-born **Lelio Mauro** — who, being
in his boyhood invited by his kinsmen, the lords of the Altinates, to a solemn anniversary funeral (outside the Manian
gate, where it was named "ad Manes," in which place were buried the cadavers of the whole city, and still, the vocable
corrupted, kept, one says "alli Mani"): the pompous obsequies made, with most-ancient rites and patrician custom, he
remained with some youths at leisure. It befell that, finding themselves at the maritime places, near the watch-tower,
or shrine, of the port of Altino, named **Turricella** (from which, at present, is called the noble town **Turricello**,
there founded) — in that his puberty, then, by invading **Pirates** they were captured. Whence he was, by lot, into the
ancient Bruttian people conducted, into a famous city, which at present is called **Teramo**. Who, adopted for his
ingenuous character by a noble and magnificent man, **Theodoro**, grew up patricianly; and, after sufficient learning,
to the military exercises, assiduous, strenuously gave heed. Whereupon, being come to the virile age, and, in progress
of time, for his things most-excellently done — and, with a soul strong, exalted, generous, robust — most-constantly
various victories attained, and all the military honours discharged (like Bellerophon exalted from Heurie): for this
reason, no more **Lelio Maurio**, but, for the egregious condition and outstanding effects, was named **Calo Maurio** —
to extinguish, with the choice virtues, the ill-omened name.

For all which things, from the most-holy Roman Senate, with military prefecture, with the *paludamentum* (general's
cloak) designated, he came, deputed to dwell — by chance — where he was born, and whence he was descended, keeping his
fatherland secure and guarded from the barbaric invasions. Which place, of shade and air most-pleasing, and of rivers
and founts pleasant, chosen, was named by him **Calo Mario** — so that, by the benefit of the site, more promptly, amid
the molesting assiduity of the infesting foe, he might some time avail to delight himself, where was the verdant area,
clad of herbs and of flowers.

There, then, when he was made *poliucho* (city-protector) — round about, in serviceable memory, and of his dearest
mother, an eternal monument — a noble and great city of municipal people (named from the hill **Taurisana**), and of
literal and military study, and of site most-rich and pleasant, and of most-ancient cult, and of sanctity and religion
a most-true hostess, upon the hastening and swift Father **Sile** — and, given it the name of the Pious Mother
**Trivisia** — whence, even to this day, the maternal name it retains (**Treviso**).

Which, with auspicious increment, a long time, with affluence, with togate peace, and social federations of the
neighbours, with life led, pacate, he, happily dominating, possessed; and, of him, the successors —

— hereditarily, for many years. But the various and inconstant case, and order of fallacious fortune, and infidel time,
under diverse tyrants occupied — finally, under the most-just empire of the holy and fierce **Marine Lion** (Venice),
aided by the best and greatest Jove made human — being become happy: I, of the surviving lineal and ancient Lelian
family the nursling and progeny, was (born). And, put upon me the outstanding name of the **chaste Roman** (Lucretia),
who, for the son of the proud Tarquin, slew herself — nurtured patricianly, with many delights, I came to the flower of
my age, in the year of the human redemption after the four hundred and thousand, in the sixty-second (**1462**).

I stood, as to the wandering little adolescent-girls is customary, at the window, or the podium, of my palace, with my
most-blond hair — girlish delights — over the candid shoulders disposed, and from the ambrosial nape pendent, like gold
threads rutilant, at the rays of Phoebus, sunning, drying themselves; glorying, most-accurately, combing (them), I
combed them. Thence, by chance, then passing, **Poliphilo**. Whence I dare to say that so beautiful, to Perseus, did not
appear those (locks) of Andromeda, nor those of Photis to Lucius. Thus he, with intent and biting regards aware, without
measure, and with increment of love, suddenly took fire; and his tender and apt heart, without respect, opened, and
through the middle shattered (as a rough Oak, by the lightning-hurling Jove struck, splits), at the first and pure
regard. And Cupid, unloosed and unlazy, with his burning multipliable flames intromitting himself — suddenly, without
any defence and resistance, kindled and captured (him): like a simple little bird, in imbricate snares, for little bait;
and the little fish, hooking the hook, incurs — placidly he yielded. And, of my graceful and comely aspect a desirous
inspector made, warmly he appetited; which, many times, I, in the mirror clearly regarding, doubted lest that which to
Narcissus befell might, to me, the like, happen (as, at present, in my aspect you see it patently). Nor for this ought
(it) to be simulated (charged) to me as boastfulness — because it befits: as to feign and simulate the false is a vice,
no less to conceal the true. Then, of the new and primary fires founded in his breast, an amorous torment — then, of me
an affectionate lover. Whence, already taken in such an amorous decoy, to have some condign attainment of such Love,
every single day, from my palace he took a sedulous journey; at the high and empty windows regarding, he could not
fulfil the sword-like desire of re-seeing me, at least one time. And for such cause, having, with so much anguish, many
days and nights, paces, vigils, songs and sounds, with little words formed of sighs, with urgent solicitude, vainly
squandered — only he, pain and tedium of his tiresome and molesting living, desperate —

— attained, and continual sadness, and, the soul with embittered ache unceasingly to afflict. Wherefore, henceforth, no
shrewdness and vigilant solicitude availed, that he might see me. And if it befell (and this rarely), yet he comprehended
not the least sign, nor token, in me, of love, nor of consenting dissimulation, such as in hard flint would not appear.
And, although my frigid heart was not alien (unfeeling), nonetheless, most-admired Nymphs, it was matter remote to the
disposition of the amorous fires — my mind holding itself totally indisposed and inept; to me was presented no cognition,
then, of the supreme and amorous affliction that Poliphilo, from vehement love cruelly consuming himself, suffered.

> POLIA, STRUCK BY A PESTILENT DISEASE, VOWED HERSELF TO DIANA; AND, CONSECRATING HERSELF, BY CHANCE POLIPHILO SAW HER
> IN THE TEMPLE. WHERE, ONE DAY AFTER, HE FOUND HER ALONE, PRAYING; TO WHOM, HE NARRATING THE GRIEVOUS PAIN AND THE
> MARTYRDOM THAT, LOVING HER, HE SUSTAINED, AND CALLING FOR MITIGATION — SHE, PERSISTING UNMERCIFUL, SAW HIM SWOON TO
> DEATH; WHENCE, LIKE A MALEFACTRESS, THENCE SHE TOOK SWIFT FLIGHT.

Universally, in those days, a great slaughter of the mortality of humans, and of whatever age, promiscuous — there
being, through the infected air, corrupted by a contagious and internecine pestilent disease, an extreme multitude
dying. And, atrocious terror and fright already come upon the diseased earth, and the men, of terrific mortal (fear)
concussed, finding themselves — each, solicitously, out of their cities, taking flight, to the suburban and rural places
fled. Whereupon, a horrible extermination of people being, it was almost suspected that the fetid Austrine (south)
breaths, from dewy Egypt, had not brought it — when, by superfluous increment of the turbid Nile, in the fields it
generated manifold animals, which then, putrefied, stinking, in its decrement, infected the air; or, that the sacrificer
of Argos had not yet lost the oxen to sacrifice to Juno; and there befall that which came to Aegina; and then Aeacus's
fair desire; and the projection made on Mount Parnassus by Deucalion and Pyrrha. Whence, by my feeble and malign lot, of
a **gland (bubo) in the pudic groin** I felt myself struck — it pleasing, by chance, the highest Gods, for my better
success (outcome). And, the pestilent inguinal invasure being multiplied, gravely it fatigued me.
pages.note: Chapter argument — Chapter XXVI:

t:
For which thing, deserted by all, and relinquished, I was — save by my piteous and best Nurse, who remained to aid, and
to see was the last sigh and exit of my spirit. And already, often, implicated by the grave disease — incomposite words,
and frequent laments and little groans, variously raving and vacillating, I returned to myself. And there, better than I
could and knew, sincerely, from the Divine **Diana** succour I invoked. Wherefore, then, to me of other Numina was no
notice, nor any cult, save that Goddess. And with multiplied prayers, with the tremulous voice purely exorating, I
prayed: to her holy and gelid chastities, tormented by grave sickness, promissory, suppliant, I vowed myself, and,
religiously, to serve ever her sacred temples, with tenacious chastity, if she, pitying me, freed me from the mortal
contagion and disease — with firm and persevering purpose in my mind. And with so much the better hope, as I remembered
the benign favour that the said Goddess to **Iphigenia** lent, while Agamemnon, by Apolline admonition, wished to immolate
her in sacrifice; and, the piteous parents hard weeping, moved by this and pitying, she interposed a fume-bearing cloud,
reserving Iphigenia; (and) the hind was found (in her place). Then, by such-made similitude, I, almost secure, her holy
aid and defence hoped. And therefore there was no dilation of time, that I was cured, and, miraculously convalescing, the
pristine health restored.

For so much, to the high and spontaneous promises, and solemn obligations bound, to the execution I intently exposed
myself, and, sedulous, my professed vows to fulfil — with no lesser purpose to conserve myself inviolate than the Matrons
in the Thesmophoria, sleeping on the strewn leaves of the Agnus tree (chaste-tree); nor with lesser devotion and religion
than Cleobis and Biton had. And, admitted into the holy temple, and into the consortial convent and society of many other
virgin girls received (who to that chaste and pure Goddess served), I began, I too, sedulously, with them, to visit and
humbly the Dianal Altars to venerate. Whence, the most-beautiful part, almost, of my most-flowering girlhood and pleasant
age, consuming in the chaste colds — it intervened that **Poliphilo**, our fervid and insolently enamoured (one), all this
intervalled time (which was a year and more), the wretch ever stood discontent, and in heart-grief. After that, more (of)
my aspect, and the blond hair, by any pact he could not re-see; and, having become distanced from my cold heart, and more
divided than Abila from Calpe (the Pillars of Hercules); and, from my sterile breast, of love scraped out, and totally
diluted, and from my reminiscence obliterated, never came he into my mind — neither more nor less; nay, not so obliterated
were, from the walls of the temple of the Good Goddess, the written and painted male animals, and the ingress of whatever
living (male) excluded, than out of my —

— heart deleted and wiped was every cogitation of that Poliphilo — as if I still had drunk the waters of Lethe, son of
Phlegethon; nor less as if I were ringed with the ring of the good Hebrew (Solomon), as the amorous Ethiopian-woman
oblivious. But he — who, acerbly, of blind fire was, and of stimulating love wounded, and, of the Cupidine lancination,
the breast lancinous — (I understand not how his own intellect could imagine it, or that his favourable fortune benignly
lent him the tufted forehead (opportunity), that he, dolorously consuming himself, and in asperity of love wasting himself,
and, in him, the savage Cupid intemperately domesticating himself) — found me, on the day of my sacred dedication, with
some other little maidens consecrating myself. At which solemnity it is customary for the wanton and juvenile throng
avidly to convene at the sacred spectacles. And, of me clearly aware, totally he lost himself. Then he, for this,
affectionately hoped to have found (a) present and opportune remedy for his inflamed heart — yet ignorant what he ought
to do, save to behold and re-behold, with most-intent gazes, the most-pleasing head, with the adornment of the blond
tresses; in which adornment he had supremely, solidly, collocated and fabricated all his pleasant and delightsome pleasure,
and happy and determined content, and fixed thought.

But because, from then backward — that (having) bound myself, with votive heart, to the espoused vows — by (any) man ever,
or most-rarely, more I let myself be seen; but covertly, and the veiled face over-covered, with most-occult recess and
access to the holy temple, and almost unknown, for a long tract of time, I gave heed to keep myself unconspicuous.
Poliphilo, wretched lover, who prized not gracious life more than frightful death — computing the day as a year, for the
long delay of not being able to re-see me — all anxious and perplexed, but with constant, pertinacious soul, so-little
astutely, and with provident and sleepless disquisition and diligence (like a man bound, thrust into a horrend prison-
house, solely intent, most-vigilant, on the breaking-out to flee; and like a sick man, desirous of health, intent on the
escape) — he knew so corneredly to investigate, exploring (and perhaps, by the flying Love, directed to so watchful a
vigil), that in the temple, one day, where alone I remained to pray — he, blinded of excessive love, and orbed
(blindfolded) by fiery desire (like an animal without discourse, that ponders not the end of its suasive appetite) —
moribund, approached. Whence, no sooner before me did I see him, than promptly, contaminated, my indisposed heart — like
frigid Diamond, which, by burning, alters not, rigid, froze itself — became more freezing than the Porphyry stone; and,
with soul unmild and ferocious, spurned and stupefied every pity, into great hatred against him I converted my soul.
Perhaps more —

— atrocious and inhuman than that of Eteocles and Polynices — who, most-inimical, mutually killing themselves with
reciprocal wounds, and, in the ardent pyre their cadavers thrown, by no pact could be cremated together until they were
separated, with open token, in death itself, of the unbroken hatred — and more cruel than Hypsipyle; nor did Orestes have
so much savagery toward Clytemnestra. And he, me piteously regarding, re-regarding, half-dead I, without fail, saw him,
and his flesh, with erubescent (blushing) pain, to pale, and from the extremities the natural heat to flee, and strongly
by a mortal accident to be invaded. And as much as, now, he availed — with the few little spirits finding himself, and
with debility and laxity, and with the face discoloured — to me, with a low and tremulous, and sole-remaining, little
voice, he said such tenuous words, not without weeping, and a sighing consort to the melting tears:

"Alas, Polia, fair-haired Nymph! My goddess! My heart! My life! And sweetest trainer (*lanista*) of my soul! Have pity on
me — if, in thy divine nature, and in thy singular beauty, lives that virtue to which my soul (as to the sole, chosen,
chief and primary lord in the age), not refusing, but festively offering itself, inclined, yielding. Now move thyself,
placable, benign, and mitigating, succouring my grave martyrdoms. For I evidently know that, if to those, now, opportunely
propitiated, thou succour not, every hope truncated, wholly I see myself perish, for not being able so many my sad pains
incessantly to tolerate. And, for a newest refuge of this, at present, to die will be better to me than troublously, and
without thy love, to live. And so, rather, I gladly expose myself to perish, than, without thy most-desired affection, so
miserably to live the noxious life — because a swift demise is better than to die long. And if, by chance, some Numen with
inexorable savagery presses me, at least licit will it be for me to die for thee, if licit is not to me the sweet living —
because, thy angelic and venerated presence being removed from my eyes, and lifted and departed that veracious, unique and
solacing delight which, of it, I avidly and unsated took — what more most-damaging evil, and more deadly than this, could
one ever feel? And therefore, to these my rough and insupportable languors, no more did I hope to be able to attain
opportune remedy, save when the benign heavens should concede me to re-see thee — because otherwise, of my tedious life,
rough ruins I saw, invading, threatening. And for so much, like a damned man awaiting the inevitable capital blow, almost
grieves not (any more), I gave and consigned my miserable life into the hand of the terrific Sisters (Fates); distempered,
and more furious some time, by rabid and stimulating love, than were Atys and Pentheus attained by the sisters and by the
wretched Agave — because I saw myself relinquished, like Achaemenides left by Ulysses between Scylla and Charybdis."

"And so much did the urgent ardours, re-boiling in the intimate of my heart, exacerbate me — having no other good to hope
and desire, save thee alone, Polia, chief and most-valiant medicine. And I was unknowing of thee, deprived of thee,
relinquished by thee. And the more I excogitated of the ungrateful absence of the outstanding form, and of the celestial
beauty, and most-comely face, and of the elegant heap of thy choice virtues — so much the more increased in me pain and
bitterness, not being able to enjoy them. For which things — O wretched little lover me — with so much impetus,
inconsulate and precipitant, I accepted these horrend injuries and fallacious blandishments and subtle allurements of
love, veiling and sub-covering the bitterness, and most-unquiet agitation, that thence, some time (nay, most of the time),
invasively, must ensue. And therefore, purely having, and with so much tolerance, voluntarily, for thee, my Lady Polia
sweetest, these its most-rough ambushes received, they have made me then unjustly to remain (alas, sad me!) so great an
interval of time without re-seeing thee, all my good, all my hope, all my consolation, thee solacing prison-house of my
heart — and without the spectacle of the choice and venerable adornment of this thy most-beautiful head, without the
intuition of this so gracious aspect, and notable and wondrous simulacrum. As the Arbonensian lake of Africa, the Sun
absenting itself, the waters of which fervidly boil, and, in its presence at midday, freezing, cool themselves — so I, in
thy absentation, Polia, my most-irradiating Sun, all adust, infervescing, like liquable wax, melted myself, liquefying;
and now, in thy Solar presence, of horror I freeze. Whence ponder somewhat, Polia, my delight and my protection, that so
long a tract of time in supreme anguish, and formidable perils of my living, I have found myself — which living, for thy
love and perpetual service, willing I reserved, at greater peril than the blond and mature crops in the spacious acres
remain (at peril of the crackling lightnings, and coruscating thunders, and falling rains, and blowing gusts); and, in
similitude of the serpent and cross Ivy, embracing the old poplar, thence extirpated and torn — not, by itself, then,
able to climb — falling to the humid earth, lies soft and debile, and clinging, remains; and like the scandent vine,
without its footing and prop upheld, and without the grateful Elm, prostrate, leans. So, and not otherwise, without thee,
my most-firm column, and protection, pillar and most-constant post — to which I had, amorously, inflexibly, and with
obstinate purpose, propped my life — thy absentation, then, is cause that I, prolapsed to dying, so relinquished find
myself."

"For which thing, so much had my furor amplified itself, that it permitted not the least (space) to feel the grave grief;
nay, more stingingly agitated and pricked by solicitous Love, it made me fiercer, more validly, to greater tolerance.
Nonetheless, I feigned manifold and various things in my soul, simulating prosperously (things) to come; many subsidies,
solaces and supplies, verisimilar, I composed with myself, and things of wondrous magnificence of love I largely promised
to my very self — and all I find fallacious hopes, and inane cogitations. Whence, thy choice and so enticing presence
divorced (from me), and from these sad eyes abstracted, I gave the primordium of a beginning of marrow-deep destroying
the basal underpropping of my life, and of beating (O me, most-bitterly!) the pulsing breast, sighing, thundering, with
frequent little sobs panting; and like an inane reed, or little reed-pipe, of its soul (which in thee alone lies and
lives), I found myself. And most of the time contristated, not knowing what, of this, I ought to do, I wept, tearing;
and, within myself groaning, thee, enemy of my every quiet good, I inculpated; thee, cause of all these errors and
troubles, I accused; thee, of my ardent loves the deserter, thee, sweet foe of my health, I calumniated; and, almost
out of my mind and maniac, compelled, against thee provoking the cupidine ire — as, to an atrocious and most-cruel one,
her most-holy torches (Love's) protervely spurning, and sole cause of my damages, I esteem (thee)."

Having patiently heard such a reasoning against me, up to this point, ignorant of like things — interrupting both his
molesting and displeasing and ungrateful speech, and my prayers (devotions) — without not only answering him, but even,
in the face not looking at him, indignant, blushing, suddenly I rose. And thence, having left him, made-little (of him),
as vain words, I fled, deriding him. But, the successor day come, judging that he would not persevere in the previous
day's invasion to molest me, no more, confident, I came into the said place to pray. Lo, that I — regarding him, with a
leaden and sad face, in the same manner aggressing to perturb me — thus likewise, sighing, timely he said:

"Alas, Polia most-beautiful — nay, conspicuous exemplar of whatever beauty — move thyself, mild, henceforth, and pious,
to so many my languishing pains, which, without intercalation, both day and night, and incessant, afflict me, and to
thee to come constrain me. And thy indecent, embittered heart, in so great hardness, one little bit soften; and,
repugning, insurd not thyself to my just desires, caused by the love that thy not-mortal beauties have diffused, all
through me, dolorous. And, again, extricate and loose the most-implicated bonds of thy tenacious mind. And reduce thee,
and dispose thee, merciful, to restore, conserving, with equivalent affection, this little of the fluctuating and
perilous living of mine — consuming itself of nocturnal tears, and annihilating itself of diurnal languors. And for so
much, do not wish, I pray thee, to vilify thy not-human condition by atrocity, showing thyself against (one) who so
sweetly, ardently, thee loves, thee desires, thee venerating worships. Because, being ingenuous, excessively beautiful,
and, of every virtue and elegance, most-comely endowed and —

"— outstandingly dowered, and of most-flowering age, and to the amorous mysteries most-accepted: then obscure not so many
most-ample gifts, by the benign nature (given), with improbe pertinacity and impious obstinacy — denied to this sweet,
ductile and soft sex — as, yesterday, without reason, against me, unhappy, thou showedst thyself guilty. O me, alas,
Polia, chief mistress of my heart — if thou didst feel one minimal little portion (of it), and if to feel this were cruel
and illicit, at least, my little heart, imagine feeling it, conjecturing (that) these plaintive and lamentable words
proceed from nowhere else than from the intimate torment of the amorous and mortally-struck heart, with a more lethal
wound than Philoctetes. By which so dolorously I suffer, for this biting affect — so continual a pain in me tribulously
corroding, more than the gnawing Moth to woollen garments, and more than the thirsting caterpillar in the liquor of the
pale fronds of Minerva (the olive), and more than the rodent woodworm in the cut beam under the hirsute Ram (spring), and
more than blight to the trees and carious stalks, and more than the biting *terma* in swine-flesh, and more than saffron
rust to hard steel, and more than the foam that impetuously demolishes the rocky banks. And it is to me more infesting
than Antaeus in Libya, and, at the town Lixus of the promontory Ampelusa (or Tingis), with a direr battle than the Cranes
to the Pygmies. And in this recounted manner, the years of my celibate adolescence I fruitlessly dissipate; and so, by
cruel love kindled in me, diurnally I torment myself — finding myself in worse state and condition than the insensible
creatures: like the verdant plantlets under the torrid Sun, burnt in the fierce Lion (July), and when Sirius is in the
mouth of the ardent Dog — which then, in the moist night, by the matutinal dew irrigated, refresh themselves, and, by the
dewy sprinkling, return vivified, as if the previous day's lesion they had not felt. Alas, wretched lover me — for thy
love, Polia, hear! — continually at evening I kindle; at twilight I all inflame; burning, in the dead of night I ardue;
in the depth I consume myself; and at cockcrow, like a cinerous thing, I feel myself. But what does then thy sad little
Poliphilo, O my most-desired Polia? Likewise, for thy love, so embittered in me — at morning, in sighing weepings I
commove myself; and at daybreak, in those all suffused, freezingly frozen I find myself; in the coruscating aurora, my
sterile and stepmother fortune I curse; and my ardent love, caused by the most-elegant and shapely Nymph of the world,
gratulating, I bless. At the fresh morning, again to kindle myself I begin; all inflamed I find myself, the new day
refreshing itself; at midday, languishing, to die I feel myself, without a mirror (glimpse) of any aid of my adverse
love, and without any consolation in so great a greatness of ardour. What constancy, then, would be found, and robust
body, that in so many and such tortures could, enduring, evade? But, without doubt, were it not, my beautiful and sweet
little soul, that, only of thee imagining, I feign, and in myself falsely-make, a soft delight —"

"— and a pleasant figment, already, dislocated, my soul would freely have departed — such as, at present, at that point
disposed, I feel it advancing. And by such a mode I prove the shattered heart somewhat to restore itself, and a little to
respire. Of a sudden, then, I see myself totally frustrated, and left inane and void of every subsidy and help. And so,
orbicularly, in the aforesaid agitations relapsing, pass and flee my days, this exasperated life dolorously living. O me,
often, with industrious and sagacious cogitation, I would wish to withdraw myself from so molesting a weight, and from
this urgent burden and pressing yoke, and from so sweet a pondering of thee, and from this deadly subjection to free
myself, attempting. Alas, then, more irate and more indignant, Cupid encapistrates (halters) me in evil errors, and,
against the attempted flight more vigilant, and more entangling me, enveloping, impedes me from fleeing. O most-beautiful
above all outstanding Nymphs — would it please the gods (that), henceforth, by thee, rather, odious death were given me,
than that, at present, in so exasperated a bitterness, thou shouldst not hear these my amorous and just petitions, with
affectionate entreaty, and prolix laments, produced by the subministering occasion, already, more than one (day),
within the cremated heart conceived and heaped up. Wherefore, Polia, most-worthy of veneration, beautiful thing and
eternal glory and preclear praise — for thy love, to die I persuade myself, and by the unfitting ferocity of Cupid —
whom I may juridically pardon, if, in this mania, reproaching him, I should curse his cruel and malefic power, which has
so strongly, to the tyrannic arbitrament of its urgent and fallacious laws, subjected and taken me, and, having captived
me in so strong a flame, retrograde-flying, in such a manner has despoiled and deserted me of every help, and of every
quiescence destituted. Then, in a moment, repenting, those imprecations and the curse I revoke, terrified, fearing, alas,
lest he, in me, more impiously provoke himself to anger, and then more fecund a pain to my heart, and doloration, ferment;
and lest he kindle the more my delight and ardent desire of thy conspicuous elegance and gracefulness; and, on the other
part, (fearing) thee intractable, and less pious, as at present I suspect. And when this, O me, I premeditate,
considering intrinsically the yesterday's impiety — without doubt, derived, it seems to me to be between the mouth (with
the attrition of sounding and foamy teeth) of the Calydonian Boar, and between horrid Python, and between the leonine
spear (jaw), which, my flesh lacerating, they devour. And it seems to me to hear, sadly, murmur the infernal souls, and
all the infernal furies, and the frightful **Proserpina**, serpent-tressed, and three-headed **Cerberus**, and internal
**Pluto**, and **Acheron**, the wretched Tartarean ferryman, at the tremendous *scaphidium* (skiff), to invite me to
navigate the Stygian waves of Lethe and Cocytus, to the trembling judgement of **Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, and Dis**.
But, beyond all these abominable things, one more pestiferous accessory, in the mind, offends me: that I fear to be, as
yesterday, today too, repudiated by thee. Alas — what —"

"— worse? In truth, nothing. And so I all terrify myself, and all lose myself, every hope cut off. And sometimes I
reassure myself, saying: in me is not found the false boasting of Ixion, nor that of Anchises; nor the insolence of
Salmoneus; nor the sacrileges of Brennus and of Dionysius of Syracuse; nor the impudence of Echo; nor the improbe
loquacity of Syrinx; nor the temerarious audacity of the Pierides; nor the stupid confidence of the weaver Arachne; nor
the cruelty of the daughters of Danaus. Then why does Cupid, against me, so guilty (of nothing) and so dire, so most-
savagely, openly show himself? Why so much deception to the tender and credulous lovers — to offer itself with so much
simulated sweetness, with so much fallacy of mortiferous venom and pestiferous confection smeared upon the ruin? — I,
wretched, not understanding of the malign fate and deadly lot, its exit and destruction imminent to my scanty life; and
to what disaster Fortune intends me, I know not, nor can know, nor foresee — with what calamity, with what troubles, with
what mourning and grief I am implicated, and to eternal weeping proscribed — if thou, my chief hope, succour me not, in
the present anguishes devolved and prolapsed. Whence, considering this effect of love, disproportionate to that cause, I
cannot, by any pact, come into the cognition of it. For this love appeared to me a sweet thing, but the effect that I
feel is supremely bitter. I understand not, then, what thing is this monstrous love — save that I come into conjecture
that thou, Polia, consentest to my tormentous anguishes; nor, however, in thy angelic face do I see any token of pity and
clemency. And for this only, the exasperated soul, by disdain, to flee I feel; nor more can I sustain it, because I lose
the frozen spirits, virtue and health. Alas, then, unhappy lover without peer, troubled — O, above whatever lover, most-
calamitous — I, before me, see the dark death prepared, threatening; of the aspect of which terrified, consternated and
oppressed — for thee, sole hope of my living (that so to be it persuaded me). O fallacious! O iniquitous! O perfidious!
— thou hast conducted me to this most-bitter point. Alas, Polia! Alas, my Polia — what should I more do? What other
refuge, nor succour, can I attempt? To what side can I turn me? Alas, Polia, aid me — for, to my very self, unhappy,
without thee I cannot lend help! For which thing I feel myself perish!" And, the miserable voice raised, with the
springing tears, wretched, the last words terminated, **prostrate on the ground, he died**.

Now, in this sole extreme power — that a man, all the other members and senses lost (most-piteous Nymphs), only the
talkative tongue valorous remains — he made long laments, much better than that which I now can replicate, with so much
bitterness of heart, piteously weeping — much more than the weeping of the wretched Ariadne, which the son of celestial
Jove (Bacchus) commoved. And, the supreme word said, for me — suddenly — I all felt —
pages.wcap: Polia in Temple of Diana; Poliphilus Prostrate

t:
— to diffuse an obstinate frigidity, and, made rigid against him, and impious, and to his suppliant prayers deaf — with
displeasing and torve aspect, and wrinkled forehead, regarding him. **Harder than Daphne. More wicked than Medea. More
iniquitous than Atreus and Thyestes. More dire than Theseus. More fugitive than Narcissus. Much more harsh than
Anaxarete to her cruel Iphis.** And there, tribulating, and bitterly grieving, with the eyes stilling greatest tears, and
with sounding sighs, against my savagery and ferine hardness passionately, querulously lamenting — and against my
obstinate silence, (begging) only to say him one responsive little word — but, to whatever his entreaty, my ears deaf and
stopped I held. Whence, of this, in me there was not the least vestige of pity, my pertinacious will captived in my dire
and stony breast, harder than the flint of that sacred sepulchre — no otherwise than as if I of the river of the Cytonians
had drunk. Then, aware of this, every hope lost, and the natural forces consumed — not being able, henceforth, any more to
resist, nor to obviate the neighbouring death — regarding, in his face, great grief increasing, a pallor and squalor
appeared; with the eyes fixed on the ground, showing now a filtered fastidium and tedium of looking at the amicable light;
and the macilent cheeks, already wet with liquid rivulets of weepings, I saw him sink to the ground; and, prostrate — muted
the throbbing sighs, with the groaning voice — the submerged eyes shut, **beside me he died.**

For which thing — not moved a little from my fierce purpose, presentially seeing him expired, no other sign of compassion
for him having, save to give heed, cautiously, to flee, and to leave him to whatever might befall him — but, boldly taking
him (O immanity, more than ferine!) by his cold feet, illicitly wicked, into a corner of the temple (by me nefariously
impiated and polluted), I, with all my power, drawing (him), left (him); and, relinquished without other funeral-anointing,
I sought secretly to flee. Whence, much around me looking, with the eyes I wandered; nor seeing, nor hearing anyone, out
of the Holy Basilica I escaped; by devious streets, with great fatigue of soul, distressed, I contrived thence to depart
afar — and, promptly and swift (perhaps more than Hippa), to my palace, as a conscious malefactress, to return.
pages.wcap: Polia Drags Prostrate Poliphilus from Sanctuary

t:
> POLIA SOMEWHAT EPILOGUES HER IMMANITY (INHUMANITY); AND (TELLS) THAT, FLEEING, SHE WAS CAUGHT UP BY A WHIRLWIND, AND,
> WITHOUT NOTICING, CARRIED INTO A FOREST — WHERE SHE SAW MADE A BUTCHERY OF TWO DAMSELS; TERRIFIED BY THIS, IN THAT
> MANNER SHE RETURNED TO HER PLACE. THEN, SLEEPING, THERE APPEARED TO HER TO BE RAVISHED BY TWO EXECUTIONERS. TERRIFIED
> THEREBY, MOVING FROM SLEEP, SHE ROUSED THE NURSE AND HERSELF; WHO GAVE HER USEFUL COUNSEL UPON THIS OCCASION.

Deservedly, Polia, being come to this pass, could not moderate herself, nor contain herself, that somewhat piteously she
should not sigh. And, more times speaking, the tears drawn into the amorous eyes, and the rosy cheeks somewhat flowing,
she commoved, provoking likewise the circumstanding Nymphs to compassion of the dolorous lover Poliphilo — that thus
sadly, by vehement love and excessive grief, he should have perished — (and) they drew, from the deep of the tender heart,
amorous sighs. And, upon me the placid and humid eyes benignly converting, almost as guilty they damned Polia. But, for
so much, being more avid to understand the end of such an unjust occasion, and, a little pause made, they solicited that
she should follow her gracious speaking. And there Polia, mannerly, having taken the most-subtle sudary (kerchief) that
from the candid shoulders hung, the moist eyes wiped, and the most-purple cheeks dried; and, the warm sighs interdicted,
and the sweet voice affirmed, with matronal gestures, in this manner following, said:

"Most-blessed Nymphs, hear a great savagery — that I know not what soul, mild and pious, would not now, against me,
injuriously, alter itself. The divine retribution, then, where was it hidden? — that, by my malevolent obstinacy and hard
pertinacity, my beloved Poliphilo died unworthily. O celestial vengeance, why wast thou then tardied to delay? — that,
rightly, against my iniquitous and perfid soul, in that point, thou oughtest not to have lulled thyself. But, indeed, it
stood not, then, much time, that I manifestly saw prepared the enkindled ires of the offended Goddess, and of her arrow-
shooting son — unless I expiated my rude iniquity, and, candescing (kindling) the most-frigid and rigid heart, that most-
holy Numen had not devoutly placated, and out of my pertinacious purpose, of the false suasions and vain thoughts, and my
mind of fallacious and subtle opinion, opportunely —
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t: "— had not retracted (me).

"Then, only taking covert flight — my heart being still hardish, persevering, and, then, intractable; the mind
insuperable; the will harsh and savage, more cruel than Phineus, and than Harpalyce — most-freezingly my breast having
glaciated, more than the hard crystal of the northern Alps, and more rigid than *gagates* (jet) conserving the eggs of the
Eagle — as if I had mirrored myself in the frightful mirror of Medusa. Which (heart) was, of love, inhospitable, and, of
pity, spurning. For he (Poliphilo), with querulous wailings and precatory, most-sad voices, and with a frequency of more
piteous tears than the Hyades wept, and with a sweeter mode and more anguished and lamentable voice to commove me using
than Britannicus proffered, singing his infelicities to the people — humbly, desiring, praying, aid and mercy in so many
his assiduous languors and tearful woes, with every effort to retract me, and, from the harsh and hard and atrocious
inclination, to seduce me, propitiating, insisting — but I, inexorable of his torments, with (his) sweetest supplications,
and cordial execrations, and amorous prayers, and, uncontaminated of any his anguish enduring, spurned and refused every
humanity, and, repugning any consent — there was no mode nor way that he, in that ill-omened day, could, one little bit,
that rigid and Tigrean breast tame, nor commove — much more than would befit — inadulable and accursed; in which Love, by
no mode, could adhere, nor approximate itself. Spurned and stupefied his power (so diversely applicable to human hearts,
lording it), like wax — however sticky, impelled and compressed onto the wet rock — avails not (to fix itself). O too
formidable and acerb case, by which I terrified me not, moved me less; and I, of all women the most-savage, no stimulus,
any token of grief and pity excited; from the eyes no tear expressed, any groan provoked; by no mode availed any sigh, in
the dire breast, to compose, nor to find; in which I could not the reins of the incarcerated pity break. Whence Phoebus,
almost already wishing the waves of extreme Hesperia, with the following Vesper, to find (setting) — postponing (leaving)
Poliphilo extinct, as I suspected — to the refuge (home) I intended, conscious and guilty butcher of his amorous heart.

"For which thing, not too-far a tract from the recounted shrine, hastening finding myself, with most-sinister auspices, and
the girlish paces accelerating, swift — lo, that suddenly, unaware, by a windy whirl caught up, and turbinately
circumvolved, without other harm and any lesion, into an agrestic Grove — a shrubbery, and shady wood, of tall and vast
trees planted, and forested, of horrid thorns a thicket, much impeded and pathless — in —

"— a moment I was, through the air, deported and set down. And there, then, with the beating heart, beyond belief
frightened of so sudden a case, and so unhoped — I began to feel that which yet I wished: 'Woe! woe!' most-strongly to
exclaim, with feminine ululations, and feeble voice, and fearful laments, as much as they availed — such as the Noble
Ravennate heard and saw (in Boccaccio's tale of Nastagio).

"Where, without delay, I saw, disorderedly coming, two doleful and luckless girls — here and there, and often stumbling
(the utmost provocation of pity) — to an ignited (fiery) vehicle constrained, and, with chains candent (white-hot) of
strong steel, to the yoke ensnared; which, hard-straining the tender and whitest and downy flesh, scorched (it). And
dishevelled, nude, with the arms bound at the back, miserably they wept, the mandibles stridulous, and, upon the fiery
chains, the melting tears frizzled. Incessantly stimulated by a flame-bearing, and without measure furious and implacable,
boy — who, winged, above the ardent vehicle sat, with his aspect formidable (more indignant and horrible was not the
terrible Gorgonean head to Phineus and his companions) — with a beast-like rage and fury, and with a nervy (sinewy) and
incendious scourge, ferociously he beat (them), without pity stimulating the ensnared girls; and with a greater vengeance
than Zethus and Amphion against Dirce the stepmother."

"Which (girls), errant and ignorant, most-intent on flight, through devious and pathless places, and through dense thorns
forced to go, and by the lacerating and mortal friction, and by the ardour of the fiery chariot, many times, exorbitant,
scrabbling through the shrubs — from head to feet lacerated, and, of blood, the shattered members rained, and the torn
flesh; and the vermilion and fuming blood copiously to scatter itself through the barbed briars, and through the earth, I
saw. And disorderedly, through the thick and pointed brambles, by furious rage driven, now here, now there, badly the
ardent and ponderous chariot they drew — which still cruelly burned the soft and delicate little flesh; which not only
were cooked, but, like a burnt hide, cracked. And so, with 'wah!' and cries, miserably afflicting themselves, in high
clamours and weepings, and miserable ululations, they exclaimed, turned into a greater fury than Orestes. Whence the
scabrous and most-wooded place all resounded of the piteous accents; and, henceforth, the mandibles restraining
themselves, and the tired and consumed voice made raucous, no more availed the dolorous, lifeless ones to endure. Then, a
little hour after, many most-cruel animals joined them. And the executioner and unmild boy, after long and cruent
butchery and immanity of the ill-fated and wretched adolescent-girls — like one cruent and exercised in such butcheries —
of the ardent vehicle suddenly descended; with a *soliferrum* (all-iron javelin) and cutting *rhomphaea* (broadsword),
(the girls) loosed from the molesting yoke and grievous drawing, through the middle of their pulsing heart, he — despoiled
of any pardon and miseration, with rigid and uncontaminated severity — suddenly transfixed (them)."
pages.wcap: Dream of Polia: Cupid Punishes Two Women

t:
"And, at the present striking, there came many hunting dogs, bristle-haired, famished, with fervid barkings and dissonant,
intoning (such as the Albanian King did not give in gift to the Great Alexander); and rabid Lions, and roaring; and
raging wolves; and, in the air, rapacious Eagles, and fasting Kites; and hissing Vultures — to the warm blood and
nefarious feast they presented themselves. And the boy — from him every humanity removed — the stricken girls (their last
weeping and voice proffered) beating-down, into two partitions cut (them); and, unsealed their female breast, the living
heart he drew out, and that to the fierce fowls threw, and the fuming viscera to the savage Eagles; and the rest of the
pallid bodies, quartered, to the rabid animals cast. And there he watched the spear-like Lions, devouring, assaulting, and
gluttonously avid, into the human flesh their toothed jaws to put, and to un-nerve; and, with the taloned claws, to
split, and, lacerating, to fragment; and, in the purple blood, dyeing their tawny manes, to make (them) cruent; and to
make, ultimately, a terrific *laniena* (shambles) and tearing of the divulsed and dissipated members of the two damsels,
of tender and soft age compelled, immature, their extreme spirits to breathe out. Ah, cruel spectacle! Alas, horrend mode
of burial!

"O me — being (consider, piteous Nymphs) frightened at the aspect of so much evil and cruent immanity — I found myself, of
every counsel, indigent and naked, and greatly terrorised, and beyond belief affrighted; I stood lurking and hidden among
a biting thicket, enveloped with thorny sloe-bushes, and dog-roses, and of pricking wild-pear, and, with valid prickles,
the harsh Christ's-thorn (paliurus). And under this brushy density, and nemoral shade, thus standing over-covered, I
doubted, and, without measure most-terrified by such-made a vision — putting myself in a greater fright than the horrible
simulacrum of Clytemnestra to the matricide Orestes, armed with serpents and with ardent fire — fearing lest the untamed
and smell-tracking beasts, in the secret and thick wood, (against me) sole and unarmed, and, of sex and of age, fragile
and simple, and without hope of aid, should not, on me, make a similar laceration. And within myself I said, tremulous:
'Alas — should I ever be, like Iphigenia, hither by winds reported, among the most-cruel Tauric strangers, to be made a
victim? Alas — what Caucasus, what Hyrcania, what interior Libya, or Agisymba, so immense, so sanguinary beasts nourished,
that could be equalled to so incredible a cruelty?'"

"'Alas, this exceeded — without measure, wretched me — of all the beasts the atrocity and rage, that the most-savage
animals the lying prey, piecemeal disserping, excarnified (tore the flesh from).' O spectacle of incredible acerbity, and
of cruelty notable! O unheard and unwonted calamity — a scene horrend to watch, of considered (thing) miserable, to feel
formidable and frightful, and, of pondered (thought), spurnable and to-be-fled! O sad me, and wretched, grieving —
whither, without hope, to these mortal perils, am I thus come? Alas, afflicted and unconsoled me — what things are these,
maledict and furiable, that I really and openly see?

"For which thing, invaded by mortal fright, doubting the statuted and decreed death to be approached to me, I began then
dolorously to weep, with copious frequency of tears, and frequent and suppressed sighs, and non-sonorous groans —
awaiting lest, to me too, a similar dilaceration be made; with drawn gaze observing, lest the irate and atrocious Boy,
with the hostile arms, and with savaging severity, connive not (perceive) me to be there, lurking. Then to the glittering
and chaste breast of mine the tearful eyes somewhat I inclined — which I believed henceforth converted and liquefied into
irrigating tears. With anxious words, vacillating, interrupted by sobbed panting in the breast, tumid of frequent groans,
contending to break the encloistered sighs, with the debilitated voice and impeded tongue, tacitly I said:
"'O day unlucky and funereal! O day formidable and horrend — for all my life, to mourning and —'"

"'— most-bitter weeping consecrating. Alas, dolorous and unhappy — in what calamity am I implicated and entangled, in what
state I find myself, I avail not to explicate! Who ever saw the subtle fortune with so malign and atrocious an aspect? —
that in such a manner (O holy Lady Diana, whom I serve) these my female and virginal flesh must be impiously slaughtered
and consumed, and the flower of my pleasant age, in this bushy and sylvestrous grove, perish; and, with so much torment
and savagery, the sweet life end?'"

Henceforth I felt the feminine virtues withdrawn, the dear little spirit to flee from its place; and, thence almost
removed, at this pass — alas, alas, bitterly weeping, with most-rich rivulets of tears (a peculiar humour, without fail,
fecund and ready) irrigating the face, and the breast made-wet — the hands, desperate, in the blond hair I put, with
hatred of my adornment, and, the tresses scattered, I wept, and the most-beautiful face, with the hostile nails reddening,
I defiled. And, beyond measure tribulating and afflicting myself, this increment to my grave grief accrued: not to be
able to exhaust the anguished laments and groans, and, in so afflicting and lost a lot, and in so many tormentable pains,
not being able to unseal the cloister of my grief, in the heart impatient more to contain itself. And much more, that
there was no mode I might avail to investigate this most-turbulent case — and that, unadvertent, with an innocuous
conveyance deported, fearful and trembling, weeping, I found myself unharmed, and, without more hoping, in that same
place, whence I was seized and carried off.

O me, heaven-dwelling Nymphs, cogitate how alacritous and content I found myself — let no intellect present itself to
explicate — and my mind alienated from the compassionable case (which I held of little (account)) of the wretched
Poliphilo, lifeless. Because, from the vexed memory wiped and scraped, in itself it kept him not; but only to the devoured
girls, and impiously killed, and most-harshly agonised, held occupied and implicated my mind, and to so most-iniquitous a
butchery. Finding no prohibition to the sobbing and frequent sighs, nor an apt mode to settle the anguished mind — with
ill difficulty the flowing tears sequestered — at length I returned, no more alive than dead, to the desired and secure
mansion, the befallen immanity tacitly re-kindling in the heart, repeatable.

And ardent Phoebus beginning the round back of his swift and flying (steeds) Pyroïs and Aethon to Hesperia to show, and
the golden hairs in the saffron splendour re-dyeing, the serene sky beginning ornately to paint with irradiating stars,
and, to the long and diurnal fatigues, already —

— whatever animal the sweet and sleep-bearing quiescence desired. With such similitude, having I all that frightful day
in gravest pains consumed, and of sighing weepings all dispensed it — supremely afflicting myself (what fatal cause could
it be, that so unwonted and unused, and impious, an immanity, to the ill-fated girls, made, it made me see; and, beyond
this, with what sudden mode, from my fleeing journey I was impeded, and through the air reported) — all these things, with
solicitous and sighing sobs, straitly considering (alas, afflicted!): O most-happy Nymphs, hear — unless anguish, and
weepings, and an ambiguous and dolorous living for the future, a portent to me it were, and a fatal decree, I judged. And,
stupefied by this, from stimulating fear I intended, and, by various and turbid cogitations, to conjecture — I could not,
by any way, investigate the occult cause. Conscious of this, tacitly, all that unhappy and ill-omened day, groaning,
fastidiously consuming it, I passed — in which I would rather have found the pale Corydon (i.e. death) than to have run
into so many unvisited sadnesses.

And there, surrounded by acerb dolorations, and copiously by most-molesting pains oppressed, robbed of any security, and
not daring, for the nocturnal fallacies, to sleep alone — and, through the dark and ambrosial night, I called to me the
dear and revered (in place of a parent) my Nurse, in whom, deposited, reposed, and collocated I had, every my confidence
and hope; because, alone, I, in the past, with my chaste Goddess Diana, had been.

Now, both — the hour being arrived that the whitening Cynthia had left the Lamian Rocks and the condense woods, and put
an end to the solacing huntings — finally (the bedchamber closed and hedged), we went together to the nocturnal
quiescence. And there, the pulsing breast, that still with unquiet beatings frequently beat — scarce, in itself, gathered
the frightened and bewildered little spirits, and, with supreme fatigues and efforts, the large course of the round and
dripping tears re-shut, somewhat interdicted — I began, badly and with difficulty (frequently, by frightful
interruptions, awakened), to sleep.

And, in the deep and first, soporous and soft sleep immersed, the loosened and shattered little body, suffused, slept in
the tacit night. Lo, with great and strepent impetus, it seemed to me (as if under the head Eumetes's stone were placed)
that the bolts were removed, and the bars seized, and, by breakers-through, the locks broken, and violently laid-open the
closed little doors and barred thresholds of my chamber, and to enter —

— temerariously, with concitated and swift step arriving, two horrible **executioners** — with inflated and tumid cheeks,
with rude cultivation, with gestures rustically atrocious and rough; much, in their aspect, unbridled and displeasing,
with frightful and torve eyes (more than those of the mortiferous Basilisk), gross and round, unstably standing, in-
cavernated under the hirsute and grottoed brows, which were thickly bristly, hard, and of long hairs, like Silenus's.
They had two great moustaches, with the lips pendent, tumid, crisping, and gross, mortified of their colour; with great
molar teeth, unequal, and ferruginous and rotten, like the ancient iron, destitute of the gums and abandoned, and of the
lips (which protected them not); with a gaping mouth, tusked like a toothed Boar, foaming in the hunt, and of a stench
sordid, with the aspect maniac and deformed; of a dusky, or rain-stained, colour, full of pocks and furrowed. Of their
goat-haired hair — which, unctuous and unkempt, blackest, half-grey, sordid, and, like the bark of an ancient elm, rough,
appeared — and their callous hands, great, bloodied, and their besmeared and putrid fingers foully taloned. Which, on me,
wretched girl, savagely they appeared to wish to use, with crisping and wrinkled forehead, maledict and blasphemed, the
eyebrows drawn down, with turgid face. Who, on the robust shoulders, still two twisted ropes bore; and under their girding
were transverse the lictorial instruments (little axes). Clad in Cynyphian (goat-cloth) over the nude — such as I
suspected of the habit of bloody headsmen and most-polluted men. And there, with atrocious and terrific voice to bark, as
the boom (of oxen) to bellow in the hollow caverns I heard — with superb and arrogant speaking and obstinate soul,
haranguing, saying:

"'Now come, come, proud and nefarious one! Come, come, rebel, and, to the empire of the immortal Gods, adversary enemy —
come, come, mad girl, repugnant and negligent of her own pleasingness! Ha, wretchling, wretchling — that now the condign
and divine vengeance of thee, cruel, shall be made, guilty woman, and (with) great tearing! As, yesterday morning, thou
sawest of two other (girls, like thee) wicked adolescents, of their members lacerated — and as, a little instant hence,
on thee the like to be made thou shalt see.'"

O me, wretched, thus most-terrified by the reproaches with railing proffered — most-mild Nymphs, cogitate of what
temperament, then, my terrified soul found itself, seeing, into my chamber, unwonted and so most-immense and truculent
satellites entered — the advent of which I esteemed much more frightful, and much more displeased me, than, to the
sacrificing Pelias, the advent of the son of Tyro the Nymph (Jason) with the unshod foot; for, scarce the rude and
terrific words austerely said, more they frightened me than those of the —

— unfortunate Polydorus to Aeneas the Pious. And with greater agony than Andromeda at the shore finding myself, and with
greater terror than Aristomenes seeing Panthia and Meroe (over him). Incontinently, on me stretching the malefic and
sinewy arms, sacrilegious and profane, with the hands sanguinary and filthy, and polluted and besmeared — by my blond
hair, dishonouring, snarling, dishevelling me, they began impiously to draw (me), without any clemency (which, in them,
not the least was prompt). More fright and terror they put in me than, to the chaste Lucretia, Sextus Tarquinius, with the
unsheathed sword in hand, the opprobrious death threatening. Whence, without spirit, beyond belief bewildered, at one hour
marvel and fear struck into me the dire and sanguinary men — insomuch that, evacuated and emptied each vein, to the
dolorous and mourning heart (the blood) concurred. Made more timid than a doe, and more fearful than the long-eared and
timorous hare (that, among the dense shrubs and rushy tufts lurking, hears, round about it, the barkings of the savaging
and fierce dogs) — for which thing, without delay, torrentially I began, with high 'wah!', to weep, and, dishevelled by
them, 'O me! O me!' to cry. And, wishing to resist the incendious dragging, I, as much as I availed — their arms seized,
slackening — forced myself, and, with the hurt and all-debilitated forces, strove to mitigate the violent drawing of the
furious men (harder than Sciron, son of Neptune, and harsher than Phineus, and than Polydectes of Seriphos). And, by no
prayer and supplication, would they cease, but intended, thereby, to draw me from my already-wet bed. But, 'O me! O me!'
— for God's (sake), mercy and succour and supplies calling — and with the naked feet, and with both the hands, resisting.
And they, more violent, rabidly angered, threatening, offending my smell, with great displeasure, of an emetic putor
which, moving, exhaled from the offscouring of their rancid and putulent flesh, extraneous and insupportable, that,
nauseous, evaporated — with an odious aspect, with the streaked forehead, funereally terrifying me.

At last, enduring, anguished and by mourning afflicted, in this long contrast and altercation wearied, and in bitter
weepings strongly perturbed and lifeless — and, perhaps agitating myself, and turning myself over my uncontaminated
little bed — so much that my piteous **Nurse**, who soporously slept, feeling, by chance, my somnolent movements, and
ill-understood stammerings, awoke; and, expergefacted, roused me from the furial sleep and unquiet nocturne. Without
delay, into her arms she embraced me, removing me from my assiduous (torment), and exciting me: "Polia, my beautiful
daughter — Polia, my dearest little soul — Polia, my life, and my little blood," saying, "what things are these that
thou feelest?" Suddenly removed from my eyes the dolorous, maledict, and unhappy sleep, and the fearful vision —

— I awoke, saying nothing, save, most-sadly sighing, to say: "Alas, alas me! Wah, wah me!" — finding myself all
concussed, and full of grave languors. And my shattered and contaminated breast, more, with a frequented and importunate
palpitation, was struck by the lively and terrified heart, than the solicitous Vulcan, fabricating the tremendous
lightnings of the thundering and fulminating Jove, strikes (the anvil). And, of irrigating tears, I had already
made-wet the candid linens; and the most-subtle chemise, adhering to the girlish little belly, moist, was, of my hair,
inelegant (disordered); with the soul afflicted, in dolorous torment and lamentous, by a mortiferous thought
circumvented and invaded. Nor could I, thereby, by any way, use my juvenile and scanty forces; but, abandoned and
intermitted by the mortified members, wholly prostrated, of great lassitude, more dead than alive, and almost bedridden
— then, not judging life gracious, imbecile and destitute, and deplored.

And then, somewhat after — when the benign Nurse of mine, with many blandishments adulating, and sweet entreaties, and
female suasions (seeing me in these such-made anguishes), sweetly persuaded me to relief, and to receive comfort and
consolation — (asking) what it might be (she ignorant), and, in that point, most-highly desirous, and most-eager to
understand what I felt, and, with anxious care, questing, and what so great a mania wished to say:

And, holding me in her senile embraces and arms, she likewise grieved of my ill, and un-understood accident; and, with
me bitterly weeping, after long and caressing blandishments, and my protracted anguishes and affliction — the soul,
somewhat, pusillanimously, in me revoked — with more fright tremulous than was that of supreme Jove (when that highest
father, for the Giants, personated himself in a hirsute Ram) — the horrend vision, badly, and with sighs syncopating, I
narrated to her, babbling; and the fortuitous case of the day before, and that, from the violated Temple returning, it
befell, seriously I told her — **except that, of the undue and importunate death of Poliphilo, as I suspected, not the
least I spoke to her; but well (I told her) that I had shown myself, to Love, insipid and foolish (blitea)**. No sooner,
then, had I recounted this, than she — ponderingly, and with senile expertise — the cause suspected; piously
refreshing, with many suasive blandishments, my mind, somewhat settled and a little tranquillised, she remade;
proffering herself, of all my grave and molesting languors, to be the true remedy-maker, if I, to her weighed and
salutiferous admonitions yielding, should present myself observant. And there, lifted of every other thought, and, of
extraneous cogitation, loosed — chiefly and solely, to her faithful and polished counsels a most-following imitatrix,
and, with wondrous effect, most-mild, disciplinable, I offer myself, if she —

"— only, out of so anguished, afflicted, and prodigious a peril, will draw my mind, and the successive life, out of so
much mourning and grief."

> POLIA RECOUNTS BY WHAT MODE THE SAGACIOUS NURSE, BY VARIOUS EXAMPLES AND PARADIGMS, ADMONISHED HER TO AVOID (THE
> GODS') IRE, AND TO EVADE THE THREATS OF THE GODS; AND HOW A WOMAN, DESPERATE FOR INTEMPERATE LOVE, KILLED HERSELF.
> COUNSELLING (POLIA), WITHOUT TARRYING, TO GO TO THE PRIESTESS OF THE HOLY TEMPLE OF THE LADY VENUS, (AS TO) WHAT SHE
> OUGHT, UPON THIS, TO DO — (WHO) WILL BENIGNLY LEND HER FIT AND EFFICACIOUS INSTRUCTION.

Not without supreme fatigue and expended labour, divine and outstanding Nymphs, can one draw a disposed and inclined
soul back from a purpose — most of all (a purpose) made difficult by obstinacy, and by time habituated, and the more
while, from it, one takes some delightful diversion and recompense. And to wish to adapt it to the contrary, and revert
it wholly alienated (from the former), by a fallacious estimation, most-most-difficult it shows itself. And, marvelling
at this, one is not (moved) in the least, if the sense, some time depraved, distorted, and corrupted, is wont to make
things of sweet matter appear ungrateful, unsweet, spurnable, and bitter. And less marvellous it offers itself, most-
outstanding Nymphs, if whiteness, to the sick, impure, and blear eyes, appearing blackish, offends; if things rutilant,
of a livid coating, and the (things) glittering of candour and of splendour shining, spotted, sprinkled with rust,
covered with caligo, suffused with cuttlefish-vomit, and infuscated with atrament (ink), are damned — without doubt, not
by defect of the object, but by the sensual disease. So, and not otherwise, I: since, to the colds of chaste Diana, my
soul and my mind being firmly habituated and professed, and religated and proscribed — grave, then, and much difficult
rendered itself the ingress of ardent Love, acceptable.

To which (Love), as to a cruel enemy, to resist (inexpert of its sweetness), I had opposed a pertinacious, contradictory,
and repugnant Nausea. And, wishing then, probably intent, into the gelid heart the new love to induce, it necessitated,
industriously, to seclude the repugning contradictors. Now the sagacious and versute Nurse, most-intent to wish that hard
and massed —
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
— gelid (ice) diverting, to impigliate (grasp), that in me for long time had habitually been confected and hardened — as
she, shrewd, with pure and sincere judgement, judged, grieving that the divine threats, effectively, she saw not (fulfilled)
— thus, adulating, to remove them, pre-choosing providently, cunningly she said to me:

"We have found — nay, it is even wont to be said — Polia, my sweet little daughter, and my mirror: he who takes counsel
could never, by himself alone, perish. Then, ruminating, cogitate well, lest, with some simple obstinacy, thou hast
inconsiderately offended the supernal (gods). Wherefore, how much acerb and full of torment their wrath has been against
those who have not revered their power, and have been rebellious — it is not to be doubted, that (wrath) to have been the
greatest, and so much the greater, the more it is retarded, to the frightful and inevitable vengeance. Therefore, by a
stultified and inconsulate levity, and by a superstitious and inconsiderate opinion, of some of you young girls — for so
much, it is not to marvel, if to you, some time, the fearful Heaven-dwellers, irately and vindictively, present themselves.
Whence rightly we know the harsh ires visited and used against Ajax Oileus, as contumacious, and to the severe Gods
maledict — and therefore, by celestial lightning, miserably he perished. Likewise, again, the famished companions of
Ulysses perished. And he (Diana) who, for the entreaties of the huntress Diana, revoked Hippolytus from obscure death to
the light of the fostering day. And so many, by this way, have mortally perished, by negligence and little fear of the
divine retributions threatening. The most-impudent **Propoetides**, who despised the holy Venus, into hardest stones were
badly transmuted. And the weaver, the Lydian maiden (**Arachne**), was transformed by Minerva into a spider. And, for
disobedience, again, the shapely **Psyche**, into so many troubles and intolerable labours, perniciously found herself.
No less, too, many other noble girls — to their vowed lovers rural and ferine cruelty using — the supernal vengeance,
upon their malevolent hardness, bitterly, by diverse and terrific cases, an inexorable avenger has shown itself. Beyond
this, it is to be greatly revoked into the mind: how cruel, how unmild, how impious, how violent, how potent in his
Tyranny, the son of the Divine Mother is — so much truly, that, by true and undoubted experience, we have liquidly found
(however hidden it be) that not only the mortal men, but even the divine breasts, he has, vigorously, without any respect
and miseration, acerbly inflaming, wounded. Did not the rain-bringer and sky-clearer **Jupiter**, with difficulty, from his
amorous —"

"— and ardent torches, avail to avoid himself, nor evade unharmed — (Love) having made him personate himself, for the love
of many damsels; and, by that same Cupid, then, the delightful conjoinings he attained? Now let us intermit the other Gods,
and convert our speaking to the furious and belligerent **Mars** — who, continually bearing the impenetrable Lorica, and
hard and fatal armatures, could not, one little bit, prevail against that Archer Cupid, nor protect himself, nor from his
robust breast drive (him) off, nor reluct, and less defend himself from the amorous wounds, nor to the pointed arrows
resist. Then, my little daughter Polia, my little heart — great is his power! And therefore, if he to the supernal, most-
omnipotent (gods) has not pardoned, how believest thou that he does with the terrestrial? — and especially to those who,
for his service, are disposed and apt; and much more to those who, debile, fragile and unarmed, dare, rebelling, vainly to
repugn? — against which continent ones, that flee him, much more irascible, active and laborious, he opposes himself, with
manifold and troublous invasion, and frightful damages. And if he, of his very self, pardoned not, to fall in love with the
beautiful Psyche, how, to others, will he be innocuous?

"Do we not openly know that, in his marvellous quiver, he contains **two dissimilar arrows**? The one figured of fulgorous
gold; the other, of livid and ill-omened lead. The first, of forced and vehement love, most-violently the hearts to
irritant loving kindles; the other, on the contrary, intolerable superbity, and a rabid and prompt hatred exciting,
provokes, and displeasing cruelty. Of which two exercising — that of the amorous burning — the Sycophant **Phoebus**
(Apollo), striking, direly and extremely he smote; and the (women) beloved by him, with the leaden arrow, he wounded —
because he (Apollo), the all-seeing, manifesting, revealed (Venus's adultery with Mars), and, temerarious, wished to
impede the holy loves of the divine Venus. Whence he (Apollo) long grieved of it, in repudiations and denials and ill-
terminating effects; and the like, to all who, subject, under him find themselves — and to none was he (Love) prosperous.

"Whereupon, the more ardent the affected girls (are), the more displeasing they render themselves, atrocious, austere, and,
of him, refusing and fugitive; and this same, to his lineage and progeny. And for so much, many, of every condition, fell
into such reciprocation and vengeance, for wishing inconsiderately to resist him, and his swift darts lightly to contemn.
And therefore, in this acerb night, by dire and truculent image, he has shown it (to thee). Hear, then, my daughter, and
take the digested, sane, and useful counsel: never wish to oppose thyself to that which thou canst not resist, with
equality of power, nor to contrast; nor that which cannot otherwise be, not to flee (i.e. do not flee the inevitable). And,
even, to the weighed and mature counsels, refuse not. For, being of body most-comely and most-whole, and of soul shrewd,
and of tongue —"

"— eloquent, of rarest and memorable beauty, with the face of outstanding and elegant filament by the Greatest Maker
created — thou oughtest somewhat, and most-accurately, to consider, that almost one could preconise (proclaim) him to have,
in thee, celestial beauty singularly shown: a composite without peer. And, beyond all the preclear and incredible beauties
that in thee especially he placed, of two amorous and splendid eyes thy choice and comely forehead he adorned — (such)
that, so adorned, would not appear (even) of the nine stars, with the three more lucent, the crown of Ariadne in the limpid
sky... (nor the) forehead of Taurus of the Hyad sisters. For which most-worthy things, perhaps the Lady Venus, to her holy
Altars, with an arcane summons wills thee; and so much beauty, of a notable polish, is not to be lost, without her amorous
fires, like the fruit-losing willow. Wherefore thy graceful aspect indicates, rather, to be worthy of her warm services,
than of the gelid and unfruitful Diana. Then, perhaps, for this, the divine disposition and fate, of thy girlhood pious
care having, by nocturnal revelation, the prodigious tokens of the Gods, cautious render thee. For easily it could befall
thee, as to many others has intervened — because to the Gods enemies they present themselves, who the outstanding office of
nature (love and generation), in this life, neglect. And for so much, take, briefly, such an example:

"I, already, my dear little daughter, in our city knew an adolescent-girl (it is not many years), most-beautiful — like
thee, generous, and endowed of choice famousness, and of preclear progeny and delicious lineage born and descended, and of
manifold virtue comely; delicate, and, in whatever her work, most-apt and refined, and busy, of exquisite cultivation, and,
to the womanly polish, studious and cultivated, and, with the increment of fortune, in riches and delights grown-up. Whence,
finding herself in the florid age, which to the highest Gods is wont to be grateful — by many suitor-youths frequently she
was requested. But, especially, among whom, one — a peer of elegance, and coequal of gentility, and of virtue outstanding,
and of soul generous, adolescent — with much petition desired her. Whence, after great and large espousals, and importunate
prayers, she never, by any mode, would consent. And, persevering in such ambitious levity, boastful, the florid years, and
the most-potent and beautiful part of the verdant youth — O me, Polia — brief and scanty she consumed, not pondering that
there is no more amiable and coupled thing than the similitude of love of the matched age. And, sole remaining in that
depraved diversion of soul, in the cold and unpartnered beds — finally, beyond the twenty-eight years finding herself, Cupid
(who is not unmindful of injuries done him) —"

"— irate and implacable, resumed his curved and dolorific bow, and, noxiously, through the middle of the superb breast,
wounded that sylvan and contumacious heart, with a pointed golden dart penetrating to the extreme line; and, the limit
being transgressed, and in her bosom, burning, nestling itself, the most-valid Love, with the blind fires, fervidly began
to re-kindle; and the wound so profound, perilous, atrocious, and various, that, drawn (healed) into a scar salubriously,
it could not (be). And, by the stimulating ardours amorously forced, and under the unwonted bite and bridle, and sedulous
pricking, impatiently vexed, she began, all languishing, to perish — desiring, then, the sweet petitions that the noble
adolescent vainly made — and, to his aspect, no more he appears (i.e. he was gone). And already Love, his convenient
