violences licitly using, immodest, in her, beyond thinking, and urging, quickened. And, having made of her re-struck heart
a furnace-like fire — not so much the most-beautiful and elegant youth, but, by her ill misfortune, made venereous, of
whatever condition anyone had been (had she, of special grace, been able to have him), to her ardent and voluptuous desires
and itching concupiscences, without respect, she would have appreciated (him) most-opportune. I judge that, had an Egyptian,
or an Ethiopian, and an exploded (base) man offered himself, she would not have refused him to her demands — let alone (any)
of our patricians.

"Ultimately, the ingenuous Matron — excessively amorously languishing, and, in the acerbities of the reinforced flames,
exaggerated, and by the enticing ardours stimulated, and of itching appetites, and intemperate lasciviousness, incredibly
agitated, and by so much importunate libido irritated (as if in Didyma born) — and the intolerable pressure not sustaining,
in bed, most-sad, sick and infirm, she fell. Whence, like Antiochus, son of Seleucus, of his stepmother beyond measure
enamoured, and by an immortal languor invaded, (who) was detected, by the pulsing touch (of the pulse), by Erasistratus the
physician, to be languishing of love for the stepmother — by such a way, by the shrewd and expert physician clearly
understood that the woman lay languid, of measureless love maniacally suffering; consulting upon it, the stepfather and her
mother, that death might not supervene, found the opportune remedy: to marry her. So that it stood not long time, that there
was found for her a patrician man, of good condition of kindred, and rich — but old, and of precipitate age, and occiduous
senectitude, more than he (being shaven) showed; come almost to the doubtful age; and somewhat the cheeks were pendent, the
eyes ulcerated, the hands tremulous, the breath fetid, the head hiding (because there appeared the back of a scabby dog), and
the habit (of body), in the breast, all drooping; only, anxious, holding the soul to rapacious avarice most-devoted, and, to
the inexplicable Cupidity, supremely intent. And being come —"

"— (I suspect the dark, funereal, and deadly pre-announcer was the night-wandering, ill-omened, immense and improbe
Ascalaphus (screech-owl)) — the unhappy Hymen; and pompously celebrated (as is bounteously wont) the tight commerce of
matrimony. And, come the desired night, that the yearning woman so long had concupiscently expected — firmly judging (it) to
be the hour of extinguishing the fiery and venereal appetites, not considering what the husband might be: for she, at that
point, blindly excited of libido, of unbridled desire enveloped, only pressed to the fruit of the delectable conjugio; and,
beyond measure of itching appetiting, and to the libido most-abandoned — the frigid and impotent old man adhering, and set
in the debile arms — inflamed beyond the fit by incontinent and biting concupiscence to sub-enter (be roused), Cupid
irritant, sedulous in amplifying the fire (more than the bellows to the little fire exciting) — she consequuted no other (by
her ill misfortune) save that, by the foaming old man, her comely face and purple mouth, from the salivous lips, was spat
upon and slobbered, as if a snail, running over it, had lined it. Nor with blandishments, nor with venereal and petulant
gesticulation, and caresses, nor endearments, could she ever heat, commove, nor irritate the impotent and sterile, queasy
old man to be roused — the breath of whom seemed an aura of a putrid cloaca, and of a fetulent quagmire. His gaping mouth
held the pallid lips, gapped and crisping, and with a discordant voice; and almost toothless — in the upper palate had
remained but two rotten big-teeth, and cavernous, like Pumice stone; and below, four others, two to a side, quaking, and, in
their site, unstable. The beard hard, like the hairs of a long-eared ass, like pricking briars, abundant and whitening. The
vermilion eyes moist and tearful. The nose *silo* (flat), in its hollows bushy, and gaping, and mucous, and snaily, and ever
snoring — so that all that night it seemed he bellowed with a most-windy wine-skin (bellows). The face foul, and the head
whitening of *morphea* (leprosy); and the cheeks warty; and, over the eyes, the brows turgid. The throat, with hispid skin
like a marsh-tortoise's, deformed and goitred. And the trembling hands, without any vigour. The rest of the body putrid,
morbid, and invalid, and, of its tardigrade, decrepit. And, in moving, the garments exhaled a putor of fetid urine.

"For which thing (my daughter, attend, and lend thy memory to this audition), the most-lascivious woman, of her voluptuous
appetitions totally frustrated, could never (all the scortatory efforts, and of illustrious harlotry, discharged) excite the
prostrated members of the enormous and unvigorated senectitude. Now it befalls that, for a long time, she, by the malevolent
and tedious old man — idle, inert, desidious and craven, more jealous than the barbarian decurion — not being able to
receive, nor consequute, other save beatings (converted into infinite Jealousy), and railing, and garrulous cries, and cold
and languid sloth, and fastidious tedium —"

"— and deceived of her unbridled desire, she recognised, in herself returned, her unhappy lot, ashamed of her ill
obstinacy. And hard, not so much of the fastidious and nauseated old man and the unfruitful copula, but of the passed-
over and neglected, irrecoverable time, uselessly dispensed, from her infancy up to that hour, supremely grieving —
which she never knew (how), henceforth, that she no more hoped, by any mode and price, to be able to re-have it, nor
re-acquire, with the greatest doloration she contristated herself. And, beyond this, to her ill, was a mortal accessory,
thinking of the other happy and content married-women, and, frequently coming to mind, imagining, of those that lay in
the sweetest embraces of their most-desired lovers, and of the amorous and delectable solaces, and of their consummated
appetites and desires — as she judged, the wanton nature stimulating, and the wicked and scelerate love. She, in herself
finally re-taken, and in ardent envy bursting, and, in the mind sedulously repeating the intolerable and tedious
superbity of the odious old man, and of the dolorous, unconsoled life having grown weary — she set to scratch and claw
the face, and the breast, with the little palms, savaging, to beat; every hope truncated, dissolved into inundating
tears. And the facile eyes, into weepings more bitter than Egeria's converted; no thing grateful, none appetible, every
thing untasteable, save the improbe death — and to desire the accelerated end that Iphis made. Whence, of here, was born
a rabid furor, of her very self a lovesick and most-cruel executioner concrete; she took, secretly, one black day (the
husband of this unaware), a cutting and knifed iron; and, like a conscious malefactress, impotent of her desires, and
every confidence broken, of herself a mortal enemy made — consenting to the furious conceit — she used a horrend and
frightful vengeance: and, crowned with funereal smilax and with fronds of *ostrya* (hornbeam), through the middle of the
sad heart, impiously (the infernal and mournful Furies invoked) — O unheard crime! — all transfixed the noxious iron.

"O wretched and afflicted me — if, in this my little age (which may the supernal (gods) preserve me from), such a
misfortune, as of thee, could befall, for some similar offence, I would die before the time, of grief, and, of sadness,
accelerating the supreme cloister of my life. O me — who would sufficiently avail, then, to this horrid, most-unhappy
and urgent tempest, and miserable demise of the recounted woman — and my calamity, in kind, in amplitude, in weight, and
asperity, ably, then, assimilating, to compare? What (encounters) of shades, of Lemures, of Manes, of Larvae; what
nocturnal apparitions; what of Demons frights, ever more noxious and horrible, could incur upon me — if these dolorous
eyes should see some sinister of thine, and damage? Then, Polia, my daughter, and my sweetest hope: attend, with the
soul erect and united, the inevitable ire of the Gods — either timely, or with tardiness, wont infallibly to make like
vengeance — such as, for her displeasingness, came to Castalia, from Apollo; and, by this same mode, the shapely Medusa —"

"— who, with so much direness of soul displeasing to the young suitors, and reluctant, then, for her ferine hardness, by
the supernal Gods, the blond hairs (were) made horrible and sinuous vipers; the amorous throng, thenceforth, terrified,
from the snaky head, in flight converted themselves; and she, more rabidly agitated, desiring, affected them — whence she
could not re-have them. And so, making little of the celestial dispositions, and ordained causes (which make, in the
opportune, due, and destined time, the young to fall in love), the mad girls, in this most-appreciated age which thou
(art), no more considering, make to such mysteries a bad resistance, injuring the heavens and the benign nature.
Wherefore it is not to marvel a little, if so miserably, some time, they perish.

"O me, most-beautiful Polia, my most-precious daughter — the time of our life is more to be esteemed, and supremely
appreciated, more than the amplest treasures of Darius, and the riches of Croesus, and the felicity of Polycrates, and
above every thing of the world. And this our life, of little age, more perpetually and swiftly is a-running, and more
fugitive flees, than do the rapid Horses of Phoebus; and more it empties itself out than the most-tenuous evanescent
Bubble. For all this, we ought joyously to adapt the sweet years to facetious Love — opportune, and matured coming.
Because then, into the incommodious old age coming, still shrewdly we wish to feign the youth passed; and for so much we
give heed, intently, to extirpate from the hoary head the white hairs, and to infuscate and draw them to blackness, with
lye of litharge, and quicklime, or with barks of walnut — and to wish, by art, longly to feign and conserve that which the
natural denies: to illustrate the skin, and, painting it, to extend (smooth) it, and to conserve the shrivelled flesh
swelling and fresh. And, beyond measure, we are gnawn, mordantly, in the heart, of continual and unceasing pain, sighing
and weeping the transacted time, delicious, amorous, and solacing; and of the despising of that repudiated age, and of the
rare, much-desired regard, by the refuged youths interdicted — because the age asks parity of similitude. And,
commemorating the lifted (lost) loves and the amiable sweetnesses, and avidly desiring to live more than in the time of
the florid youth (which is not known, then, by remoteness from the end — but, the privation approaching, for this urges the
appetite of living), if possible it were, the years of Nestor, and of Priam, and the years of the Sibyl.

"Then, Polia, my dear little treasure — for as much as thou appreciatest the present life and little florid age, gracious —
O me, take heed, lest, for such a cause, in thee Cupid pre-demonstrate, and, by such a vision and show, presage the
tumefied, and already conceived, ires, perhaps, against thee. Whence, perhaps, to the supernal Gods thou believest, with
superstitious and vain —"

"— opinion to supplicate thee (the gods) and please (them). Cautiously animadvert that, to thee, there come not, as to the
repudiated **Hebe** — who, to supreme Jove and the other Gods less cautiously ministering, fell, and, the light vestments
removed, the obscene and pudent parts discovered (whence her soul intended not to offend, but yet, of this, irate Jupiter,
she removed from the cup-bearer's office, and Ganymede was substituted). Dislocate, then, distracting, thy cold purposes,
if in thee any remain; and go suddenly into the shrine of the most-holy Venus, solitary of arbitrament, and find the
sacrificing Priestess (who, to the divine sacrifices, is the chief admonitress and Index); and recount that which thou
knowest cause of such menace, and openly confess to her thy contumacy, and reveal that which, perhaps, to occult it would
be more cause of thy loss and noxious ill than to manifest it. And she, benignly, without tardiness, will give thee
opportune counsel, and necessary favour, and salutiferous instructions — whereby thou canst succeed, and evade, the
doubtful and suspect affliction, and (escape) so great a trouble, and flee the divine and irrefrenable ires, if any, by thy
inconsiderate rebellion and improbe contempt, were prepared."

> POLIA, TERRIFIED OF THE DIVINE IRE, BY THE EXAMPLES OF THE PRUDENT NURSE, DISPOSEDLY BEGAN TO FALL IN LOVE, AND WENT TO
> THE TEMPLE WHERE POLIPHILO LAY DEAD; AND, WEEPING AND SHEDDING TEARS AND EMBRACING, SHE RESUSCITATES HIM. AND HOW THE
> NYMPHS OF DIANA DROVE THEM OUT; AND SHE NARRATES THE VISIONS THAT, IN HER CHAMBER, POLIA SAW. THEN, GOING TO THE TEMPLE
> OF VENUS, SHE FOUND THE AMOROUS POLIPHILO.

Judging (herself) to have sufficiently persuaded — the expert, veteran, my Nurse, with the utmost prudence and sharpness, to
suspect of the nocturnal presage — to her cordial admonitions and shrewd counsels, and to her discoursing, she put a term.
And already the sky had the nubilous caligo dissipated, and put to flight the atrous cloud of night; and the air of the new
day depicted, the golden Sun surging, and having somewhat the matutinal dews from the herbing meadows dried — I, opportunely
admonished, my soul mourning for the fearful and grave re-ponderings, began intimately to sigh; and —
pages.note: Chapter argument — Chapter XXIX:

t:
— she, having gone out of the chamber, I remained alone. And there, scrupulously, I re-cogitated, ruminating, the useful
sayings, the warm and weighed admonitions, the manifest and terrible examples — most-excellently having touched that part
which, me contumacious and savage rebel, rightly damned, and, by the celestial ires, keenly to be punished. Whence, those
(ires) I, terrified, desiring, to my power, avoiding, to flee, and free from this scruple to evade — there came to my mind
(ignorant by what celestial care led) the lover **Poliphilo**, whom I knew that, by my impious ferocity, in the sacred
Temple, bitterly, of his gracious life he despoiled himself.

**Love**, then, artful, in this first motion finding somewhat of a little entry of ingress — together with kindled little
sighs, little by little began to penetrate the interdicted place; and, with its first sweet little torches, in the hard and
torpid heart, quietly nestling itself, collocated itself. And already, feeling a pleasant little flame to run and dilate
itself through the cordial parts, and even to the intimate base of my inexpert heart, and to nourish itself, from the
consent beginning — an incentive and sweet desire, to enter, vigorous and intrepid, under the amorous laws of the solacing
Cupid; and no more to wish to present myself an obstacle, nor extraneous, to the amorous darts.

And being now, with prompt deliberation — I thought, ambiguous, of various encounters and dispositions of the various lot,
and manifold ends, interposed, only for this sweet Love; and the industrious and tenacious little memory, for this, in my
mind, up-boiled, the fearful vengeances of Juno representing, which strongly terrified me. Considering, then, of the
dolorous **Phyllis**, when she, for the blind love of the tardy Demophoon, saw her delicate flesh expressly cover with hard
bark and turn woody. And the incontinent and enkindled **Dido** I see simulacred in my mind, who, with the funereal gift of
the son of Anchises (Aeneas), blinded and turned in fury, killed herself. And of the lying **Stheneboea**, for the illustrious
adolescent Bellerophon, to perish. Then accedes **Scylla**, daughter of Nisus, King of the Megarians, with a ferocious soul
impelled by immoderate love of the King of Crete (Minos), shearing the golden hair of her paternal head — she consequuted no
other, wretched, effect than badly to perish. And likewise, of those two ingenuous Egyptians (Lopidia?), I see naught but
the obscure death of their ardent affect. And **Echo**, for the unfruitful son of Cephisus (Narcissus) — what befell her? O
sad and dolorous me — the undue love of **Byblis**, and of the tearful **Dryope**; and the unjust appetence of the weeping
**Myrrha**, which she had of Cinyras. **Nyctimene**, daughter of Nycteus, she, with a scelerate love of the paternal
conjoining ardescent, saw herself then (turned) into a nocturnal bird (owl), enemy of the precious light, and fugitive. Also
the warm **Menthe**, for the father of Proserpina (Pluto), into an aromatic pot-herb was mutated. And of the —

— infauste virgin **Smilax**, who found herself (turned into) a flower-bearer (bindweed), for the beloved Crocus. I see, too,
the tears of the unfortunate **Canens**, interspersed along the pleasant banks of the Tiber. I cogitate, frequently, of the
one suppressed (crushed) by Polyphemus, by the Molossian rock (Acis). And, lastly, how much burning, and cruel slaughter, was
for the smuggled-away **Helen**. O dolorous and grieving me — could it be that I, unaccustomed to such exercises, should
enter, thus unarmed and debile, unknowing and inexpert, and, in such an Agon (contest), fighting, contend? Are not these my
pudent and untouched flesh religiously vowed to that Diana? And therefore, Polia, leave and obstruct this first rudiment of
love, and these new insults, and new expedition, and frightful enterprise; and to whom (Diana) thou art professed, requite
(remember). And in what Tyrocinium (novice-service) thou art bound. And there, almost demented, vacillating, fearful, doubting
of worse than the mordant dogs of Actaeon (that so rabidly discerpted their Lord), and, for the miserable case of Callisto,
still much more I began, unbecomingly, to trepidate — like, by impetuous winds, the suspended texture of the wanton Arachne,
quaking; and like the barbed rushes, agitated by the intemperate breezes, hiss.

And, within myself replicating all these things — nor sooner had I such an imaginary repudiation pondered, than within the
tremulous and rude heart a tepid and unthought little flame I felt proceed, with a gradual, glowing increment, and with a
sweet little palpitation, and a divine little impulse, through all diffusely dispensing itself, and successively altering me
— fecundly to scatter an internecine anguish, of new love frequently sobbed, and, without delay and intercalated pause, with
an amplish diffusion (as, through the most-robust body of the sacrificing Hercules, the Lernaean venom of the blood of the
Centaur Nessus resolved itself). And there, ex-inopinato (unexpectedly), suddenly, newly, another new percussion — the
solicitous and sedulous Cupid, impelling, adding — my vacillating and cross mind, drawing back from the up-boiling and inane
thoughts, and frivolous opinion, and vain frustration, artfully deviated; and from those totally succeeded (freed), with all
my soul already suborned of amorous suggestions, to the swooned Poliphilo I returned — him willingly desiring in his first
essence (alive), beyond measure dolorous of his death. And after many, various, oblique, ambiguous, and molesting
cogitations, and ambivalent terrors, I exposed myself, daring and yielding, to go to re-see him — and to wish, dead, to
behold him whom, with infest malignity, I would not see alive. Alas me — already this solicitude not mediocrely anguished my
soul, considering probably (wretched me) that him, tenderly loving me, I reputed an enemy and a mortal foe. And, by every
mode, to understand what, then, had befallen him. But, afflicted me — how much did the most-cruel Anaxarete (and I, impious,
like her) terrify me, going the —
pages.wcap: Poliphilus Dead; Polia Kneels in Grief

t:
— unfortunate Iphis, to see (him), it should not befall me. Almost from the purpose it drew me back; but, vanquished and
prostrated by the blind and new stimuli, and by obstinate love compelled, no acceding fright had any force — nay, by the
increment of love, spurned, to the improbity of my inflamed Peletronian (fierce) desire; and thus profoundly wounded, sole,
immediately soliciting the incited paces to accelerate, to the sacred Basilica I arrived.

Into which, after I, with the utmost avidity, had entered — not as was my pristine custom, to the holy Altars religiously to
present myself, but, without other saying nor doing, to the place where, scelerate corpse-bearer (Vespillona), I had dragged
Poliphilo, I went. And there, with a tearful face, I found him — with the constricted cheeks, truly lying dead, colder and
more congealed than a hard marble; and thus he had been, the transacted night, bloodless, wan and pallid — whence, of fear
and pity, I paled.

At this pass, most-celebrated Nymphs, bitterly afflicted, mournful and dolorous, the eyes, of tearful miseration,
abundantly filled themselves; and torrentially I wept, my low laments syncopating with sounding sighs — desirous, to such a
condition, to be consort. And, like the unconsoled **Laodamia**, moribund, lying-down upon the dead Protesilaus, I prostrated
myself, I too, upon the gelid body; and, most-tightly embracing him, I said:

"O most-cruel, terrifying and immature Death — of every good the devourer, and of every sadness the inevitable
truncation — lazy not, wish not to delay, at present, to unite me with this one, who, for me (of all the women of the world
the most-impious, and, of importunate impudence, malefactress), innocent and guiltless has migrated from this desirable
light. This one, who loved me excessively, sole his singular and destined good reputed (me). O me, iniquitous and fierce,
beyond every other savagery most-unmild, malign and guilty — more than the most-cruel Phaedra against the innocent
Hippolytus. Who, now, denies to give me the last demise of this most-turbulent and odious life? O accursed first light,
that to my eyes graciously appeared! O maledict vital airs — why do you last so little (why not end)? O odious spirit, at
present bridled — why findest thou not, now, exit and opening? ... O maledict eyes, that, alive, this one you would not see —
you make me, at present, behold him extinct! O tremendous lightnings of high Jove... where remain you extinct — not to
incarbuncle me, and, into little dust and ash deservedly, condignly, to reduce (me)?"

"— O me, dolorous case! O guilty fortune of mine — what more can I (do), save equally to die? Who, then, of us two, is
found the more miserable and unhappy — O my amorous Poliphilo, dead; or I, in so much inconsolable life, surviving? Come,
then, all you pitiless and horrible Furies — as, to Orestes, so, upon my soul, fittingly use the supreme savagery. For, by
my malign and perverse cause, the wretched Poliphilo — and only for me (O bitch, and perfid, barbarous, unworthy, and
immeritous) loving (me) — and, for so great a maleficence, hostile, the wretch is dead."

And already, having my eyes made a lake of weepings, sedulous tears flowing, and all of him, and me, fluid of falling and
interpolated droplets — and by the same mode that the most-faithful and courageous **Argia** made upon the weeping cadaver
of her beloved Polynices — and, somewhat having put the hand upon his cold breast, I felt in it a scanty and deafened
pulse re-boil. And, more and more closely embracing him, there re-warmed, excited, his fugitive spirits; and the lively
heart, upon itself, the —

— so most-desired flesh feeling (in which his soul, quickening, nourished itself), he awoke, sighing, and re-opened the
occluded eyelids. And I, suddenly most-avid, panting at his unhoped reiteration (renewal) — having received the debilitated
and abandoned arms — piously, and with sweetest and amorous little tears, with sobbing handling him, and hand-leading him,
and often kissing him, presenting to him, I showed him my — nay, his — whitening and apple-bearing breast openly, with a
most-humane aspect; and, with enticing eyes, he, without variance of an hour, revived, into my chaste and delicate arms, as
if a lesion he had not suffered; and, somewhat re-assuming the contaminated vigour, as, then, he availed, with tremulous
voice and little sighs, meekly said:
"Polia, my sweet Lady — why so wrongfully dost thou make me (suffer)?"

Of a sudden — O me, most-celebrated Nymphs — I felt, almost of amorous and piteous sweetness, and excessive alacrity, the
heart, through the middle, much more to be dilacerated; because that blood which, for grief and too-much fright, had, in
itself, been constricted, for too-much and unwonted gladness, to loosen the veins I felt it, exhausted; and, all absorbed
and astonished, I ignored what to say to myself — save that I, to the still-pallid lips, with loosed audacity, offered him,
blandishing, a lascivious and must-sweet kiss; both of us sealed, and constricted, in amorous embraces, like, in the
Hermetic Caduceus, the intricately convolved serpents, and like the involved staff of the divine Physician (Asclepius).

Whence, no sooner had he completely re-assumed and refreshed the pristine virtues — in my bosom and in my arms — and
somewhat re-purpled the cheeks, than the Pontiff (Priestess) of the Sacred Temple, with a tumultuary throng of the
obsequent little priestesses and ministers of the holy service (perhaps, my anguishings and tearful lamentations, and the
high and improbe sighs, in the thundering Temple, having heard), came there toward us; and, animadverting (arrived) of the
illicit operations, interdicted in that holy and unpolluted place, gravely offended, with her other ministers, of ire
extumescent — some with rods, and others with branches of young-oak, at us reproving, and gravely threatening, and
beating — dissociated our sweet embracing, perturbing it.

For which thing, then, immodestly I doubted lest to me should befall that which, to the terrific Medusa, the irascent
furor of Minerva befell — when she, in her clean Temple, Neptune amorously knew (lay with). And that which likewise
befell Hippomenes, and the avaricious and swift Atalanta — who, for illicit conjoining, converted themselves into Lions.
And, again, the fury of the Proetides, by Juno. And scarce, out of their hands — unless with laborious greatness we had
fled — and —

— fleeing me out of the sacratory Temple, and, of her chaste consortium and co-service, me, as a rebel and prevaricatress,
abdicating (expelling); and, with notable contumely, privately they banished (me). Whence, dishevelled, and my twisted
tresses loosed, and with grave reproaches and turpid exprobation, by one of them (who, before, was a most-familiar fellow-
servant in the sacred institutes, called **Algerea**), I was seized. But I, then — excited all my infirm forces and debile
efforts — in her hands leaving the most-subtle veils, scarce I took flight; but not without manifold flagellations, by
injury, upon my delicate shoulders, (they) soliciting to exclude me from the Temple.

And there, both of us fugitive, and from the Dianal shrine exiled and propelled, together, alacritously — not magnifying
such an *hyperoria* (banishment), nor the preterite languors, nor the opprobriums, nor railings (for the enkindled love
super-abounded), nor did all that the sacred worshippers did, in the least, embitter me — finally we came, adherent to the
city. Where, amorously (after long confabulations of the piteous lots), I obtained then an ungrateful leave, with many
sweetest kisses and amorous strainings, with firm and faithful espousal mutually, one to the other, and with much and
festive gladness. Poliphilo, extremely content, went to his journey; and I tended to the desired home-going.

And thus I, of love ardently sub-agitated, with moderate pace, and with the soul acting manifold cupidine operations, at
the contiguous regress at last of the desired palace returned — but of another quality, immuted. And there, hilarious and
most-pleasant, into the conscious and peculiar bedchamber entering, I saw no more the image of the Goddess Diana offer
itself; and, in the imaginative (faculty), it began to vacate. And, introduced the benign effigy of my sweetest Poliphilo,
solely, chiefly, of him I pondered, and, in every corner of my heart fixed, dominant, efficaciously I felt him. Whence
proceeded such an effect:

I, being sole, and my mind consociated, and in amorous captivity partaker finding itself — could cogitate no other, of
this, than of the most-desired Poliphilo. For so much, to my sedentary and accustomed exercises devoted — breathing (upon
me) the inciter Cupid — I set myself, of crimson silk, to form a little Heart, wormwork-sewn, with expression such as, in
that my heart, artfully Love depicted; the border of the circumference of which adorning with lucent pearls; and in the
middle of which, then, with his beautiful and most-pleasing (name), and my sealed and consigned name. This is the first
Greek figures (letters) (asked by him), joined, of millet-pearls, and expressed — so much the more perfectly, as Love,
present impeller, ruled me. And also I made a little torque (chaplet) of gold threads, and of green silk —

— with my longest hairs, plucked, in sign of perfect and fervid love; and that, at his neck, pendent, he should bear it, I
sent it to him.

For which thing, Love being, with lasting firmitude, in my abstemious and inviolate breast, with a stronger flame each hour
fermenting — and solely to the new wounds keeping the mind occupiedly encloistered, and to the gracious Poliphilo indissolubly
bound (of whom he, already my lord, above all elected, and unique successor of my enamoured heart, and with a perennial little
knot and eternal establishment most-tightly ensnared) — and to the sweet cogitations all disposing myself, and the lost delights
to reintegrate, to the recent amorous (one): for the love of whom, henceforth, excluding every rigidity, and postposing every
austerity, and (having) humanated sweetly every ferine and displeasing soul, and converted into a little furnace the rigid
breast, of incensed love, and re-mutated the sylvan and atrocious customs into most-mild dispositions — and, from timid,
magnanimous; and, from cold, fervid; and, from bashful, an incautious lover, transmuted; and immuted the disdainful hatreds
into inseparable loves and long-lived affects; and the momentary and vague mind made immutable; and, of the thing inexpert
(love), supremely desirous I found myself — and all, of extreme love, in solacing gratifications resolved, I felt myself.

And the most-laborious Cupid, from hour to hour successively, to heap a blindfold and blind desire of pleasure, I experienced;
and a congeries of little arrows, contending, penetrating the soul with the utmost voluptuousness, I sustained — sprung from
the most-beloved Poliphilo, from continually thinking of whom my soul could not sequester itself, because, there intruded, it
comprehended incredible delightment. By these such accidents already inclined, and in the extreme laws of love avidly
immersed — with the vigilant, and devouring, and rapacious imaginative — I operated, with him absent, that which, presentially,
I could not, nor knew (how).

But, in my Cubicle sole sitting, circumvallated of unwonted enkindlings — lo, that I see, suddenly and unthought, come out of
the open windows, with great vehemence, and impetuous strepitus and terror, a **Vehicle all of Crystalline ice**, drawn by two
candid and horned stags, haltered with little chains of livid lead; upon which sat an irate Goddess (**Diana**), crowned with a
little chaplet of Agnus-willow, with an un-corded bow, and with the inane (empty) quiver, to me demonstrating a terrifying
aspect, and, of furor incandescent, of wishing to use cruel vengeance. Suddenly, behind this, another followed — that
(other) fleeing, all of coruscating fire, drawn by two candid Swans, ensnared with little cords of gold — upon which
triumphed a potent and Divine Matron (**Venus**), with the starry forehead, wreathed of roses; and with her she had a feathered
little boy (**Cupid**), with —

— the unveiled eyes, having a flaming torch, putting to flight the cold and torpid Goddess (Diana), who, at me,
odiously, menaced. And so-far, into the air, (Venus/Cupid) persecuted the freezing car, that, by the fervour of the
other (chariot) all liquable, emptying itself out, both dissolved and disappeared.

After that, thus expressly, with amorous daring, I had seen (this) — I found all my bosom, and the floor of my cubicle,
with scattered odorous roses, and with little branches of verdant and flowering Myrtle almost covered — whence, excluded
every fear, and having taken a licit security (only for this, that the boy appeared, with supplies, to patronise my
cause, and to defend, from me, the perturbed avengeress (Diana), and, like my lord, for me most-safely, most-
invincibly, fought) — whereupon, being conducted to such-made a pass of exterminate (boundless) love, by stimulating
desire compelled, I proposed, with soul determined and firm, to proceed after such delightful work, and sweet
expedition, and voluptuous office.

But, before every thing — postponed whatever other importunate cause, and wholly deposed and lifted — I deliberated the
sincere and counsellory decree of the faithful Nurse, by every mode and with effect, to complete; and to go, without
fail (Cupid stimulating), to the venerable Altars of the divine mother — for, at present, it appeared to me to
discover and reveal the occulted burning, so fervidly mordant, and which, like an imbricate thistle of rapacious and
hooked prickles, all my heart carminated (combed/tore). And no more —

— to be lazy, delaying, to provide for the resulting and impatient flames; and to recompense the expense of the time lost,
and uselessly and unfruitfully dispensed. And, already come the hour so-much desired, that eternally this my soul, under
another's will, should alienate itself (as the *cesticillus*, or head-pad, under modifying the weight) — and entering,
with the utmost avidity, into the most-holy threshold, with an undaunted soul, I saw likewise the solicitous, solicited
Poliphilo, who awaited (to be restored, by me), praying. And thus, promptly, transrunning the scrutatory eye to the
precognised object — not to Poliphilo, but, admonished by the monitress nurse, I humbly, before the sacred Priestess,
presented myself; from whom, with the utmost confidence, I hoped to propitiate and adapt the celestial ires, and my soul,
to the spurned love, to accommodate.

And, having integrally narrated the befallen cases of so much perturbative horror, and the apparitions, nocturnal and
diurnal, seen; and the used immanities; and to have been more dire and savaging than a Tigress, and more deaf to his
lamentations of his grave griefs and amorous pains than a stopped Asp (which, by enchantment, moves not); more displeasing
than Dictynna (Diana) to Minos; making little of his prayers and miserable weepings; with hostile hatred and rage toward my
Poliphilo; and to have been of mercy un-prompt, of pity naked, of humanity austere and alien, and of compassion unmoved.
Whence, almost of these such committed rebellions terrifying myself, acerbly reprehending myself, and repenting, tediously,
in my very self — it seemed vain to think of the excluded miseries. But, contaminated and compelled by an unmeasured
cordial agitation, and infected of perfused ardour, I re-began, much more now, to languish for love of my Poliphilo — who,
as soon as he was aware of my access, the most-avid eyes opposite converting, suddenly the mordant gaze, perpetual, ran
(such as a swift arrow, from a drawn bow directed) — into my prepared and freely-disposed heart it fixed itself, so that,
of amorous sweetness, through all me, I felt (myself) crackle and up-boil.

Then, most-placid Nymphs, to that reverend presence inclining myself, I besought pardon of the preterite, and, of the
present Agon, confirmation — offering myself, of the venerable Lady Mother (Venus), a veracious and intrepid worshipper; and
never to wish to rebel, nor to be failing, nor dissentaneous, to whatever empire of her potent son; nor to whatever coveted
desire of my amorous lord Poliphilo, to refuse — but benign, and pious, and obsequent, and graciously yielding, nor ever
disjoined; and, with the utmost observance, to his amorous vows prompt, and all most-devoted; and to live with him, with
more peace and sincere concord than the Geryones lived together. Scarce made the irrevocable espousals, than the Sacred
Priestess called Poliphilo into her presence.

> POLIA HAVING ACCUSED HERSELF, BEFORE THE TEMPLE-PRIESTESS, OF HER TRANSACTED IMPIETY — AND (SHOWN) THAT, AT
> PRESENT, ALL WAS SUFFUSED OF ARDENT LOVE — DEMONSTRATING POLIPHILO STANDING BY, THE RELIGIOUS MATRON CALLED HIM TO
> HER. WHO, SUPPLICATING (FOR) THE STABILITY OF BOTH IN ONE RATIFIED PURPOSE — POLIA, FROM IMPATIENT LOVE STRENGTHENED
> IN HER, INTERRUPTED THE RESPONSE.

Appearing, sedulous, without delay, to the venerable Priestess, Poliphilo, expeditely, and with devout inclination,
presented himself there being; and I, with affectionate and thundering sighs (which, in the vaulted Temple sounding —
lo — to our hidden ears the emulous (echo) sent them back), and with the eyes only on him fixed — then, nude and
divested of every cold hardness, but most-mild and meek and outstanding, I laid open to him the gaping opening of my
enkindled heart; and, of his enticing and festive and intent eyes, I most-often imprecated (invoked) a fated domicile
and delicious lodging. And I, as desirous, courteously made it (my heart) only of that worthy and meritorious Lord — an
adjunct, and, together, to possess all my life, and my very self, to what he arbitrarily should will. Who, to me, then,
so much the more grateful presented himself, as, more, before, hateful and displeasing I had held him — a more gracious
and most-efficacious remedy to my ardent love opportunely offering himself, and much more salutary (than) — to the
navigators, upon the estuous sea with the rainy sky — appear the lucid stars of Castor and his brother Gemini, on the
right part of the Charioteer above Orion collocated, and even the desired and secure ports.

Whence, in the last degree of love wounded, I beheld him immovably to take (in), with a gracious intuition; and this was
a sweet congeries and heap of invasive fire in my breast — and my soul, thereby, from every other solicitude excluded:
only him it pleased (me); only him, most-pleasing, it desired; only him, a solace, offered itself; and, to my
insatiable and desirous regards, a delectable object — from the vacation of which impatient, and, of avidity,
stimulated, and, by an immodest appetite impelled, and, by such amorous gratifications, taken and possessed, that
almost externated (beside myself), and in ecstasy, immovable, I beheld him — whence, already beyond measure unbridled
being my eyes — and, because I felt and experienced what thing was the new love, I, miserating, reasonably, to those
(his eyes) pardoned their scrutatory importunity. But Poliphilo, who —
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
— beyond his power the improbity of blind Cupid sustained — to come there whither he desired, panting, intended, with the
utmost work to confirm and stabilise (it), by means of the reverend Priestess (before whom he was presented), that both,
one sole bond, most-tenaciously she should make to ensnare (us). And, of my aspect relieved (encouraged), with soothing
eloquence, in this form, gladly, he said:

"Celebrated and sacred Matron: if the suppliant and devout servitors, and most-devoted worshippers of the Divine Paphian
(Venus), merit to be heard before thy holy auditory and tribunal — be now, most-pious Lady, ausculted (heard) by thee, in
the present, my expended prayers and most-devout entreaties, with confidence produced, of consequuting favour from thee,
notable Templar. Whom, to this amorous act, I judge the ultimate refuge, and, to my acerb afflictions, repute a most-
efficacious Amulet, Relief, and true and choice remedy-maker. For thou art, to this place, assumed, and, to the sacrificial
Altars of the most-holy Cytherean (Venus), with so much sanctimony, sincerely serving — to aid, by means of her grace, the
inept and discordant souls, and, into one will and consent, to re-unite the lovers. For so much, to thy majestic presence
I am confidently come — because thou alone art able to patronise the miserable lovers (like me) who languish, for the
inequality of the cruel and lictorial lancing of her (Venus's) unjust son (Cupid). Pour forth the grateful prayers, then,
to that —"

"— Mother and Lady (Venus), that she command her veiled son (Cupid), that he, licitly, re-assume his amorous arms, and
that, into that stony heart, that pricking and penetrable dart, indignant, he draw — which, in me, without any pity, thus,
lancing, he fixed; and, by such equity and mode, will (satisfaction) be, to my little sadnesses, repayingly satisfied; and
modified will be all my importunate and urgent sighs, and so many languors — which, however onerous and molesting, patient
and willing I would avail to support, if Polia likewise should feel, somewhat, what thing is intense loving, and how sweet
and delectable is the being of two hearts coming into one. Whence, most-clement Priestess, if thus thou make coequal this
displeasing dissimilitude, most-blessed I hold myself. For so much, let no admiration, sublime Lady, seize thee, that I
assume ardently a venerable daring, and, of such a cause, reluctant, to speak.

"Wherefore thou oughtest to know that too much more love than befits invades and rams me, and, stimulating, exacerbates me;
and, to this (postponed every other thing), constrains and presses me. Nor ever do I hope of so many my torments to evade,
nor quietment, nor term to consequute — save whenever I think (thou, pious mediatrix) to have placated, and, placating,
settled, and, settling, delineated (soothed) the displeasing heart, and the truculence, of her, of so sweet and divine an
aspect, feigning (deceptive) — which, with so much comely elegance, an excellent and salubrious help, by the ministry of
those enticing eyes, through the middle of my redundant heart, promises me no mediocre hope, with every voluptuousness of
mitigating my incredible griefs, and of lining somewhat my petulant and ardent fires — if, at present, I can re-unite the
will and her mind, unequal from mine, and more separated from mine (O me!) than Ossa from Olympus. For I so extremely love
her, that never have I found myself mine, but ever all hers. A just thing it is that, as I am all hers, and a humble
servant, she, uniformly, be all mine, venerable lady, and totally possessress. Then thou, excellent sacrificer — being
sole and chief, in whose sentence consists and depends the power to commune (us) under this amorous Yoke, and, with the
utmost expertise, to master and discipline those who, wholly, with sincere and pure heart, are addicted to this holy
service, of the most-holy and mysterious flames perpetually to serve — that now, if I find not myself deceived, I believe,
and (hope) that this ingenuous and comely, and of singular virtue preclear light, and of beauty celestial splendour, with
me (in this place convened) consents to such services to be received and re-numbered (enrolled)."

Already the eloquent and inflamed Poliphilo fell silent from his sweet and most-accepted narration, with most-pleasant
and sweet little words; and that most-sweet mouth soothed my soul. And, taken and circum-obsessed by his mellifluous
tongue, in me I felt not the soul, but, among the rosy lips transmigrated, delightfully to enjoy I experienced. Whose
semblances fully satisfied my most-avid eyes — more grateful than offered itself, to the scelerate Stheneboea, the son of
the king of Ephyra (Bellerophon) — and all consenting, bound, and, to his meritorious petitions, duly most-prepared. By
which supreme sweetness, universally by me circumfused, it constrained me — by superfluous love already invaded — to
fulfil (it); and, by the henceforth not-simulated pity that, at present, of him I had, all commoved to satisfy — my heart
being not, of his most-wretched life, oblivious — in me so rabidly kindled, that I no more availed, one little bit, the
importunate and vehement flame to conceal, nor suppress. Wherefore it would duly, opportunely, have been (if I, by such a
way and going, had not conceded it an exit) without doubt (a cause) to burst. And, interrupting the sacrificer's (the
priestess's) response, I, first, imperterrite and incontinent, gave a most-gaping place to the flying torches, most-mild;
and, in such a manner, to the lover Poliphilo, inflamed, I said:

> SCARCE HAD POLIPHILO TERMINATED HIS NARRATION, THAN POLIA TELLS HIM OF HER VEHEMENT LOVE, INTIMATELY WOUNDED, AND (THAT
> SHE IS) MOST-AVID TO LOVE HIM, WITH VARIOUS EXEMPLIFICATIONS. AND, TO MANIFEST HER URGENT AFFECT, SHE GAVE HIM A MOST-
> SWEET KISS, FOR A PLEDGE OF HER EXCESSIVE LOVE. AND SHE NARRATES WHAT THE VENERABLE PRIESTESS RESPONDS.

"Equally, I know not, with what remuneration, most-loving my Poliphilo — save with sincere faith, and with veracious and
ardent love, and with sweet and choice pity, conveniently supplying (it) — to recompense the cruel injury inflicted (on
thee); with equal vicissitude, and with no less pity, remunerated, of the Hyades. For, no less does thy honest petition
commove and provoke me, than thy presence, for me languishing — from hour to hour successively, judging thereby, without
fail most-certain, to be the effect. Not otherwise tormenting appearing to me than Hector, slain, dragged through the
flying dust, with great runnels of fuming blood, and with the blond hair cruented, and with the face besmeared and
dusty, before the tear-bearing eyes of the dolorous and most-beloved Andromache. O my heart! O sole my good! O sweet
hope! — thy tormented and transfixed heart being saddened, by my ferocity of soul perverse, savage, dire and impious,
and, of error deceived, so protracted a time embittered — drawing the woeful life in unceasing weepings and plaints —
and, at present, full and nautically stuffed of tribulous insults of love, to my tear-weeping eyes represented. And, to
wish to follow the greatness of thy noble and worthy soul, and, of excellence of love fervidly adorned — which now shall
not find deaf and inane audience — for this, in a little hour, thou shalt see put a mode, and salubrious end, to thy
griefs. For, a blind desire having, licitly, domesticated itself, from thy edacious eyes, of my heart, in the most-prompt
breast — I too find myself not immune, nor void, but, participant, I commune with thy ills. For which thing, I intend not
to spare my life (which lies in thy arbitrament and will), and my florid and unhurt girlhood, to thy ardent desires and
gracious vows to defer (yield). And, not using now that which, before, I reasonably ought (i.e. not persisting in my
refusal), I could easily incur the inevitable ires of my lord Cupid — where —"
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
"— with every solemn and ratified faith and most-firm loyalty, I have disposed myself, with thee, wholly amorously to
live; and to be, by nothing, condemned in the holy college of the crowned lovers, in the sight of the Divine Mother, and
of her flying God, individual son, of obstinate immanity — the ire of whom frightens me, inasmuch as he, of that, has
ominously shown me, threatening (his) part.

"But thou, who so festively and perpetually, to the furious torches, and to this angarious weight of that enormous Cupid,
a perpetual bondman, wishedst to succumb — and so many unjust agitations, and painful wounds, for me intimately hast
tolerated — I esteem it most-equitable that, also, for me, vice-versa, and really, I fulfil thy gracious and meritorious
will, and, satisfying the ardent desire, refrigerate (it); and, of my inviolate and florid person, licitly take delight
copiously. Whence, Poliphilo, my sweet and amorous little soul, my unique presidium, and triumphal Bulla of my breast,
and most-safe Asylum whither securely I take refuge, at present impelled by the insolent and impelling Cupid — my treasure,
above all the jewels of the world most-appreciated — no sooner, here, a circumspectress, saw thee, cupidinously beheld
thee, than, broken and spurned every hardness, and excluded every contradiction, I disposed myself, with my pleasant voice
to respond, and placidly, to thy precious love, with all the soul, with all the heart, with all my power, benignly to
assent. Wherefore, already, in the intrinsic of the praecordia — nay, in the base of my life, and of the soul, burnt and
scorched — deservedly, to one and the other (of us) I wish opportunely to remedy: doubting sanely (rightly) lest the
inexorable cruelty, used against those seen girls (in the vision), monstrously admonishing me, in me, for no cause, more
should be found. Most-limpidly conjecturing that Eurydice the Rhodopeian would not have been by the venomous viper bitten
— nor, then, for that, upon the three-team, by Pluto, to the infernal and tartarine seats and high Barathrum conveyed —
had she, to Aristaeus, pleasing shown herself. Nor Daphne, by the like, daughter of Peneus of Thessaly, would have vainly
repented herself of the verdant fronds (her laurel-transformation), Phoebus not attending, had she, to the newest
entreated, shown herself easy. Nor even Hesperie, likewise, from the tortuous serpent would have proved the mortal biting,
had she, to Aesacus, benign been. And Arethusa the Nymph, bathing in the Alphean waves, would not have mutated the
virginal members into flowing waters, in her subterranean channel, had she, to Alpheus, mild shown herself. And Picus,
for such-like resistance and flight, would not have clad himself of fluttering plumes, had he, to Circe, consentaneous
rendered himself. By such-like fugacities, many have experienced what it is, to the grateful loves, to be a flee-er and
refusing. And beyond —"

"— this, as much as, with acrity of wit, I can conjecture — the warm and stelliferous heavens, the spacious and fruit-
bearing and fostering earth, and the wave-sounding sea, the potent son of the Divine Venus, with Dominion strenuously
possesses; penetrable wherever he wills, without opposing contraposition. Nor do I believe that studded cuirass, nor
triple-twilled Lorica, nor steel helm, nor shield-defence — however fatal they were — could resist, nor spurn, nor
against endure, the fulgurant impetus of his arrow-shooting and Ithyrean bow; and (that there is) whatever harsh and
torve Heart, however rigid, however reluctant, however most-fugitive and pertinacious, and however of asperity imbricate,
and however of dominion endowed, that his swift and pricking darts do not perforate.

"I would doubt, then, lest, with such malefic arrows irate (against so much softness of soul), most-intemperate,
bacchant, and against me of every safeguard unarmed, he should draw (shoot), and then, never, for weeping, nor for
sighing groans, be flexible — as, to the elegant youth (Narcissus), inexorably displeasing to Echo the Nymph, over the
gelid fount, into a purpling flower, he made cruel vengeance; nor was Syrinx, displeasing and rustic, had she to Pan,
amorous, consented, perhaps to him a gracious instrument. Whereupon, still, me not being tamed in his offices, save to
feel a mordant appetite of this Poliphilo — most-pious Lady (I suddenly began) — after that, to my piteous eyes, the
bewildered presence, of facial colour obliterated, and all mournful, offered itself; and, to my most-vigilant ears, the
most-charming speeches, and sweet laments, arrived — perfused of amorous ardour, I have shattered my heart through the
middle.

"No otherwise glad and gracious to him, and pleasing rendering myself, than Atalanta to Hippomenes, and the pleasant
Queen of Carthage (Dido) to the adventitious son of Anchises (Aeneas), and the fierce Lion to captive Androcles
(sparing, not lacerating). Then return, alacritous and festive and most-jocund, my Poliphilo, my joy, my gladness, my
solace, my hope, my little Refuge, and my most-ardent love — that so much, for the future, of me thou shalt take special
delight, and solacing content shalt feel, that thy preterite torments and retrograde troubles thou shalt forget, which
now, by my blandishments and easings, shall be dispersed — neither more nor less than the fogs, born and concreted of
marshy earth, through the air, by the forceful winds, resolve themselves, and, like minute dust, through the air flying,
vanish. And now take this amorous kiss (with virginal wont embracing me), for a pledge of my inflamed heart, and of
excessive love conceived." And he strained me; and I, with the most-purple little mouth, round and moist —
— kissing, sipping, with a meeting, mutually, of the tongue's little bite, most-sweetly.

Now, having (thus) fondly kissed him, and he probably having kissed me — the venerable and sacred Matron (who saw, and
assented to, and heard the whole), commoved by sweet little sighs, and the standing-by (nymphs), and the eyes made dewy,
and marvelling, thus began to say:

"Amorous Youths — it appearing to me to know your intention, all is, of love, mutually kindled: for so much, it is not
opportune that (in) that which, in the one and the other, clearly I see composed and unanimous, I should interpose myself,
conciliating; for most-excellently, between you, you have arranged it, and wholly satisfied (it). So that, to me, it would
seem superfluous to add other help to this pleasant work — which Love (who moves all like things) has now, of himself,
called you (together) and opportunely conciliated. For which thing, having I, in part, with the utmost delightment, heard
of a certain litigation and discord of yours — and somewhat, thou Poliphilo, hast touched (on) it — which most-highly it
is grateful to me to understand: then, compendiously recite and, discoursing, tell me, how thou wast, of Lady Polia, thus
extremely, of love lancinated; and she, by a certain her harsh rite, refused so sweet an act. Because thy saying much, and
greatly, allures me and —"

— pleases (me)." Having probably finished her grave words, the charming Priestess — Poliphilo, all alacritous and content,
thus began to narrate:

> POLIPHILO LAUDS PERSEVERANCE, OBEYING THE COMMAND OF THE PRIESTESS. INTERMITTING (RESUMING) THE PARTS TOLD OF HIS
> FALLING-IN-LOVE, HE NARRATES ALSO HOW HE SAW HER AT A FEAST IN THE TEMPLE, WHERE, OF LOVE SUPREMELY AGITATED, HE THEN
> MORE GRIEVED OF HIS DEPARTURE. WHENCE HE MANIFESTS HIS TORMENT BY THE INVENTION OF SENDING HER AN EPISTLE (LETTER).

"Reverend and holy Priestess: Virtue is, in the arduous and funereal fatigues, and turbulent incommodities, and ungrateful
expense — the knowing to conserve oneself, and, with suasible hope, to the distempered soul, a bridle and temperature, with
probity and shrewd mode, to put; and not, impatient and inconsulate, to precipitate and fall, but, suffering,
perseveringly, to present oneself to the undertaking — however most-strait and difficult it be — and, to the voluble and
obstinate lot, and to its mockeries, and insidious versutia, with dissimulation to cede. Because not with fortitude (force),
but with virtue and wit, one conquers — as Bellerophon, persevering, succeeded to glory. Because, to all the stipends and
prices, the strenuous soldier prefers the glory.

"Wishing, then, I, legitimately, the honour (which is the due and expected prize of my amorous Agon) to consequute — firmly,
valorous, I disposed myself to endure (as an) object at which the violent Cupid might make, of me, a despicable, opprobrious
inconstancy. Judging it dementia and levity to be, timid and vecordious, to accede to the battle; and no thing to present
itself more valid than the fortitude of the soul; and no mediocre shame and verecundity persuading me — to the soldier
befalling that, in the begun contest, he turn tail and show the shoulders. But above all, never, to the militant, does it
appertain to despair, and, in the initiated battle, to defect (fail) — because it is better not to begin, than, having begun,
to leave the undertaking. For, if I err not, it seems to me that one cannot truly be called happy, if he has not somewhat
sustained his opposite (adversity) — because thence is born insolence, is generated confidence, from which proceeds the
unhappy exit, as to Polycrates. And therefore the perfection of the touchstone-trial is so much the better felt, by its
contrary, as, upon the index Battus, clearly is comprehended."
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
"Beyond this, holy Lady — if Polia, egregious girl, here present (whose unvisited beauties the celestial spirits would
easily contaminate), without fatigue, expense, and bitterness of heart, and imperilling of the amiable life, had drawn (me)
to my ardent desire — by immortal Jove, likewise, similarly, I could, without those (torments), lightly leave her. But who
has no repugnance (opposition), a glorious palm acquires not, nor (he) who persists not at it. Because neither glory, nor
triumph, nor any good, can be consequuted without industrious fatigue; then fatigue is cause of good, and perseverance
births it, with its Companions. And for this, a more precious thing it is (and so it is held) which troublously one
acquires, than the (thing) fittingly attained. Lucius Siccius Dentatus, therefore, of his fortitude would not be dignified
of praise and memory, had the scars, drawn-over, of his wounds, at the back been seen — because, to the degenerate
soldiers, easy presents itself the wounding from behind; but, to the strong resistant, appertains only the wounding in
front (facing the foe).

"For which thing, Love — in my contaminated, infected, and most-defiled heart (of its morbid qualities) being, unbecomingly,
risen an invader — used a more burning displeasingness than the meridional Aethon of Phoebus uses to the fresh little
flowers and soft plants and herbs; which, immoderately, it burns more than the insatiable Vulcan (fire of) Etna. For which
cause, tightly being, of such an effect, haltered, infinite accidents, and various accessories, and manifold peril, with
evident danger, showed my pitiless, collapsed, and infirm fortune against me, wrongfully mocking. Of which pernicious and
deadly cases, at present, in some part, obeying thy vow (wish), I shall begin briefly to narrate.

"Notable Priestess, and most-outstanding Lady: after that my lethal languors are quieted and somewhat settled — hastening
to satisfy thy benign precepts, more with my pleasant words than with tearful sobs, I would touch that part where I am
allotted so most-preclear a love (being silent of that which already is said) — (which) more fervid and active, wholly,
constrained me. Now, me, in thy venerable and choice, and Polia's gracious, presence, happy reputing, I shall take a modest
daring; since, with a most-humane face, thou showest thyself not to be aggrieved of this audition.

"Phoebus being risen, to re-sup the fresh tears of the weeping Aurora, with the refreshed and golden rays — every star of
the orient put to flight — illuminated, with his Eoan (dawn-light), our hemisphere, disterminated from the horizon; and,
the laborific day made, the lazy quiet dispelled, and the ponderous earth —"

— of new verdure re-vested, and whatever animal, glad, to the work of effectrice nature intent — I arrived at the sacred
Temple of chaste Diana (this one, no more hoping to re-see). In which she (Polia), and many other noble and outstanding
girls, festive, with solemn rites and celebrated offices, in that fostering day, hymning, celebrated. And, as the wood
already once having been in the fire, then, re-putting it (in), more quickly re-kindles than would that which never felt
flame — like the returning, upon the imprint, to its (former) form — not otherwise, of her being aware, quietly beholding
her, and recounted (recognised) among all those (like a Goddess eminent among her Nymphs), more outstanding, and more most-
adorned of most-comely beauties (multiplied by great desire), more ornate and elegant, to me manifestly offered itself her
angelic form; with the eyes more beautiful and lucid than the clear Sun, rutilant, by which all the place coruscated, with
the other singular virtues troop-wise stuffed. Whence, of most-sweet ardour excited, I reiterated, from head to feet and
throughout, stupid (stunned), to re-inflame myself, incandescent. And then the provoked flames, and the amorous lightnings,
from her serene forehead and placid face, and from the novelty of the admirable beauty, to proceed, I recognised. And, as
Pandora-Ceres, first, in the fertile earths, by the hooked ploughshare subverted, the yielding crops disseminated, and
Melissus, King of the Cretans, first, to the highest Gods religiously sacrificed — so I, first, to her vowed and offered my
soul and my heart. And so, first, she, in the tender heart (by the pricking arrows ploughed) sowed the amorous burnings — a
more noxious and mortal sowing than Jason scattered, and worse than Annona (famine). Suddenly I, prone to the swift and
sudden rapine, more tender than, to the ardent fire, the whitening and liquable wax (disposed then to receive the impressed
images) — whence, by diuturnal and continued ardour, my heart become a flagrant little furnace — in my mind I disposed her
eternally to love, as excessively I love. Her comely and honest presence — auxiliary, and an excellent and celestial
irroration, and remediable relief, to my burnable and fragile heart, I esteemed, and a salutary refuge. While, with
scrutatory and applied regard, I beheld, indefatigable, the divine work, with the eyes to the delicate and elegant face
ever inhering — where Cupid, foster-child, in me the frequent thunderbolts jaculating, solicits — the aspect of which face,
more ornate appearing than the amplest heaven (perspicuous, liquid, serene, and most-purged air interposed, of most-lucid
stars most-ornate seen), in which two of the more lucent illustrated, converted into two festive eyes, pre-fulgent, and, of
two most-tenuous and arched brows overstanding, blackest, decorated — in which so much —

"— (was) enticement, and incitement of love, and so-much singular beauty, as the most-workmanlike Jove could ever imagine
to put in them; and, in the residual formal and specious figment, put on her every perfect diligence — (such) that
Phianor, in the effigy of Neptune (nature's imitator), knew not, nor could, to paint. Which breathes a similitude of
purpling roses, commingled among milky and whitening lilies. And among the most-purple lips breathed a *Myropolium*
(perfumery), and Emporium of wondrous fragrance, in a little apothecary of whitest Ivory (in most-tiny teeth orderly
disposed) hedged. The head most-blond — (such that) not so is the Baetican straw matured — more beautiful to the eye than
if she had of the little river Gracis tasted. Which all things, chiefly, in her manifestly (beyond the notable occultation)
seeing — not only content, but certainly, above whatever lover, most-happy I would appreciate myself, if she should give me
her most-precious affect — with the soul, to her volitant, secretly saying: 'O highest Gods — thus, could I aptly reduce and
violate her to my inflamed desires, as Acontius reduced Cydippe (deceived by the deceitful apple), or with commodious
fortune, as the fierce Achilles conquered the most-gentle Deidamia — or by another way!' And how much the more most-intent I
stood, in immense delightment and most-jocund delight — and no other really than a celestial demonstration I seemed
presentially to enjoy — and, clearly seeing her, and, now laughing, and now mannerly speaking, some time toward me directing
her starry and most-pleasing eyes (accompanied with two vermilion roses, suffused of honesty and of elegance); and now,
expert and aptly to the sacred instituted and imposed offices ministering, with Nymphal gestures, with entire and devout
intent, and with matronal gravity; and some time, to the ears arriving that voice which, arousing, invited my soul to the
exit, and to the repudiation of its dear conjunct (its body) — all my spirits commoved themselves to me, feeling myself all
to be covered and surrounded of an inexpert sweetness — insomuch that the soul, neglecting its natural domicile, ever thus,
with Lady Polia, at pleasant feasts, it would, moribund, have persevered. Thence, then, I recognised the impetuous insult
to the amorous fire, and, of this, its quickening, by her, to contemplate. Nor, of this, knew I to redeem, with valid
forces of wit, the insanable eyes from the sweet allurement — of my heart, by the most-shapely face pedicated (led captive).
But, sighing, tacit, with most-firm purpose, I said: 'Of this notable Nymph, for certain, am I wholly. In her most-white
breast consists all my flattering hope, and in it I have reposited and —'"

"— intruded all my good. This one, decently, I revere, and her, above all, I honorifice and worship — neither more nor less
than the Athenians their Pallas, and the Thebans the pleasant Bacchus, and the Indians Dionysus, the Romans Liber, and the
Arabians Adonis, the Ephesians Diana, and the Paphians the most-holy Venus, and, by the Tyrians, Hercules, and, by the
Aricians, the *fascelis* Diana. And this one, indefatigable, I follow — as the Heliotrope, Clymene, mutated into a flower,
revoluble gyres, following the aspect of her beloved Phoebus (Sun). And thus I, with amorous sect (devotion), hers wish to
be — ever with this same state of mind, nor, for terror, nor for delightment, ever wavering; but with affectionate
performance, to her vows most-humbly wish to succumb, like the timid partridge in the taloned claws of the rapacious Eagle.
Nor other image, nor simulacrum, nor shrine, in the intimate of my heart affixable — nor painted, nor carved — do I hold.
And, by this one, I hope to restore myself, and amorously to live glad — esteeming (it) a greater adornment than, to kings,
the Diadem, the Paludamentum to Emperors, to Pontiffs the Galerus, and the Lituus to Augurs. And, Polia dominating,
Poliphilo — this shall be my praise, glory, honorification, and sublimity — offering myself, in her amorous surrender, thus
vanquished, and thus prostrated: hoping, unanimous, to permeate to the triumphal realms, and to the delectable state, of
the Divine Cytherean (Venus)."

Standing, then, variously rapt, demented, and absorbed, in these feigned, so delicious cogitations and ponderings, and
fruition of such an image, from hour to hour, and from point to point, the adventitious and blind wounds, in the consenting
soul glowing, fecundated themselves; and (Cupid) received, and, of me, usurped wholly the jurisdiction, Tyranny, and licit
power. To all such affectionate mystery, this only supremely I desired: 'O me, could I open to her and discover my soul, and
indicate my intrinsic desires — with the Socratic affect, of fenestrating the breast, and of showing her the percussion of
the amorous wound, and the immoderate love that I bear her; and tell her of my pressing snare, and of the urgent flame, by
which, liquefied, the heart consumes itself; and show her the dissipation of the amorous life; and tell her, with piteous
and mild words, and groaning laments, the ultimate (extremity) that, in loving her, I sustain.' And thus, with the mind
erratic, cross, pathless, and vague, of intemperate ardour supremely I languished — and now sighing, and now glad; now
placid, quiet, and tranquil; some time indignant, without hope, hesitant, and discontent. That little Sacred and celebrated
day, with these commingled and inverse accessories, I consumed — briefest, for more than one atom of time esteemed, and
more than an instant moment."

"And already the rubicund Sun, and beardless, at the extreme parts of Hesperia, the future serenity indicating — from the
sacred oracle, the delicate and ingenuous and promiscuous (mixed) women took leave and departure; and, to the solemn
offices and ceremonial observances (not as the Egyptians to Isis and Osiris, with wailing; nor as the barbarians, with
cymbal-, drum-, and pipe-strepitus; but as the Greeks, with choral dances, with melodious songs, and Latin consecrations of
little maidens, with devotion, and with the utmost alacrity performed) they made an end. Whence, from my unfed eyes and
vacillating senses, her choice and non-human image separated and disjoined, I found myself decocted and burnt of vehement
love, and to crackle like burnt Salt; and, with the eyes stupefied of the illustrious beauties, and of the brightness and
genial polish of her charming form — of there, I, again, with (eyes) frequently to salute her, and, within myself, saying
to her: 'Farewell, farewell, little robber and thievish (one) of my every good' — and secretly 'farewell' replicating,
frequently, with that little of heart which she, in her departure, permitted to remain in me (feeling myself to be ravished
and carried off, with her, my soul) — I made, I too, most-hardly, and sobbing, departure; her milky and whitening breast
made, of me, spoils, a high Trophy, and delicious repository.

"Not by other way (alas me), with the eyes desirously following her, than the beloved Protesilaus the ardent Laodamia,
pained, beheld his departing — and, more wretched, not discerning him, fell upon the shore, moribund, weeping, of mortal
grief, her Protesilaus frequently calling — so I, dolorous, with sweetest little tears most-richly resulting (like rain-
droplets), Polia called, invoked, re-called. 'O luckless Ariadne — foundest thou thyself thus, desolate of every hope, not
seeing thy perfid, deceiving Theseus?' — scattering his name, and, inane and vainly, calling, through the vast caverns and
hollow Rocks of deserted Dia (Naxos), calling him emptily; no other, to thy moist eyes objecting, appearing, than the gnawed
crags, the rigid mountains of Murex, the sylvan shrubs of Prinus, and the most-harsh shores, the curvings of the banks, of
the knotty waves and irruent, wave-sounding floods. As now, wretched me, relinquished by my re-found delight, by my unique
good, and most-efficacious remedy, in so much tear-weeping anguish and harsh torment — with a re-kindling of more ferocious
love, and thus laden of every grief? And, of this, I feel myself to agonise, because the relief of my anguishes,
singularly, beholding her, I felt. I persuade not myself, then, that thou, O unfortunate Io, in thy clear father Inachus,
thus afflicted sawest thyself, with the mutated form, and with the once-blond tresses made noxious and rigid horns, and the
human voice, thundering, to bellow, and the verdant meadows become an unwonted —"

"— aliment (grass)? I remained no less lamentful, disconsolate, and bewildered — for the commuted pleasures into gravest
penalities — from my eyes, of tears rainy, that preclear light detracted and taken. By which, precipitately, I gave entry,
and gaping ingress, to that holy and golden arrow (not in the least repugning, but humbly, prone, bending myself — like a
slack and tormentable willow-wand, torquing myself, and more pliable than the Amerine willow twisted into a band) — I
awaited, reputing (it) an extreme diversion and singular gift given by the Lord Cupid; nor ever fully, nor scrupulously,
would I know, and all the circumstances discourse, the received and tasted delightment which I depraeded (plundered) from
her incomparable beauties, with the other most-comely corollaries — relinquished, without that illuminating and celestial
torch which, most-efficacious, served to my obscure cogitations. O splendid light of my blind mind! Lady of the life!
Mistress of my will! Queen of the Heart! Empress-Goddess of my soul! — which, from whatever part besieged and circum-
impelled, began gravely to alter itself within the burnt breast; and, by this cause enkindled, and throughout estuated,
burning, a more sweet lowing to the gaping mouth sent back, with dolorous little sighs, from the dire torment — than the
founder and Sign-maker Perillus, in the hollow machine of the bronze Bull by the Tyrant of Agrigentum enclosed. Not by
other mode, my soul, interset, and in the furnaced breast en-closed, of unstoked and ardent love consumed itself. Because
not so much does humanity rejoice and gesticulate, using its delightments, as it grieves then, and contristates itself
more, of the privation of those.

"But, for all this, grave I esteemed not, for such-made a girl, to consume myself, nor frequently to die; but, to every
greater supplice most-prompt, I exposed myself, hastening. Then, of thence it followed, that — hoping to re-see the
disjoined beauties, to re-acquire the lost gladnesses, to restore the interrupted sweetnesses to my eyes, and the new and
pre-excellent love to reintegrate and conserve, and, conserving, to augment — she (O me, how undeservedly, and by injury,
from me, little-fugitive, wrong she did me, being, most-greatly, in the praecordia, so harsh an incitement, and mordant
desire, of her alone, poured (and) created) — nonetheless, I bemadded myself, daring (wretched me), against so most-valid
a love infirm, and against her valorous power, fragile, ingering myself, blaming her bow (Cupid's) badly — that the same,
indignant, to her he did not (do), and that he showed not himself contagious (to her) — imprecating against her, and
saying: 'O most-high supernal (gods), make this savage one die, who thus impiously makes me die! And, if I die, and she
not, at least make such vengeance, for so much immanity toward me performed, that she, living, ask to die, and, heard by
you, be not — so that this —'"

"— glorious death, miserably living, she acquire not.' Alas me — suddenly, in me the reason reciprocated (returning), all
these absurd curses, imprecated against my Polia, into me I re-torqued (turned back): 'Hey, Poliphilo — against thy good,
adverse thy soul, against thy heart, and adverse thy hope, art thou daringly, temerariously, to blaspheme? And that
sacrary of every virtue (like Herostratus, burning the temple), cursing, nefariously to invade?' I damned, then, the
amorous rage that of furor inflamed me, and that so demented me, praying the Gods, afterward, for her, all the contrary,
and all into benediction re-voking.

"Now, no more appreciating dying than thus living, I disposed myself to find a quite able and honest device, to give her
notice henceforth of my molesting and insupportable languors, and to confer to her my eternal conceit — thinking rightly
that there is no thing so hard, concreted in the human heart, that, with the little fire of love, softens not, is
conquered, and tamed; and (that) the round Ball, apt to roll, stable persists — but who gives it the impulse, knows the
office of its circled form. By such argument I cogitated to write to her, and to tempt (test) what might be the soul of so
noble and ingenuous a Nymph — a marvellous composite of every virtue and outstandingness, but, to me, a diuturnal contest,
and turbid sedition, assiduous anxieties, and continual grief, a familiar death without privation (deprivation), by the
privation of a thing so elegant, desirable, and beloved. And, of this, such an opinion persuaded me not, that in her other
should be found —"

"— than similar propriety, genteel manner, and ductile humanity." For which thing, cautiously, I made to be given her the
following Epistle.

> THE FIRST EPISTLE, WHICH POLIPHILO NARRATES HAVING WRITTEN TO HIS POLIA; AND SHE, NOT MOVING IN THE LEAST, HE SENT HER
> THE SECOND.

"Most-avid, and supremely most-cupidinous, to reveal somewhat the not-mediocre flame of the impatient Heart — which, for thy
preclear and singular love, greatly and validly inflamed, languishing, consumes itself — O, of veneration preclear, and
most-worthy Nymph, unique in earth of beauty, marvellous and perfect exemplar: with these — not little words, but profuse
and unimpeded little tears — blotting the present papyrus, I have taken this tolerable and honest daring (not temerarious,
but, beyond belief, strongly impelled by the continual stimulus, and by the molesting assiduity of infest love), to reveal
and declare my incredible passion, and sincere affection, which I, for thee, and to thee, bear — my sweet good, and my
sweet hope, and sole refrigerium of my unknown afflictions, and, by thee, unthought languors. To whom, with piteous voice,
and reverent words, and humble prayer, my estate, in peril, I recommend; and, of my arrow-shot and wound-dealt heart,
supplicating succour, to moderate the disordered burning.

"O Polia, divine light, and my venerable Goddess — insurd not thyself, I pray, now, to my opportune mendicables (beggings),
and (things) besought, with the face lowered, a deprecator, of most-warm love fervescent; thee I call, thee I invoke — that
thou hasten, timely, salubrious aid, efficacious comfort, necessary relief. Wherefore, my heart being, with the rapacious
hooks of thy stelliferous eyes, from my breast divulsed (torn), is originated the cause of this my inept and inelegant
writing — by me confused, and by love disposed. And, already in the preterite days, I would have attempted the like; but
never have I been able to find a mode so convenient and arcane. Then, for such respect, this my tormenting torment,
tacitly, I restrained, deferring. For, at present — since no more slow and suspended (was) my desire, intruded and
encloistered, I could not bridle it. For the violence of my love thus wills, and my depraved lot, to this my found mode, and
sweetest exordium, urges me, draws me — O egregious Nymph, and, of whoever ever was, most-beautiful. Then attend, and
commove thyself, pious; present thyself benign; render thyself, with placation, unible, to so much benevolence —"
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
"— affection and love, beyond every cogitation — to this mystery a necessary preserver — because now, more than the usual,
this my blind fire, refusing more to stay suppressed and covered, I have licitly attributed to it this exit and breathing-
hole, manifesting how much is the improbity and insolence of the intense love — not convenient, more from hour to hour, but
greatly and sufficiently passionate, to transfix my heart and pierce through, and to reveal, solicitously, the secret
martyrdom which I, thee loving, support; and no more to occult so many my diuturnal and unceasing pains — which, willingly,
for thy venerated love embittered, I repute, with integrity of soul, a laudable action to tolerate; most-greatly holding it
firm, that thou art of nature most-humane and softenable, noble and magnanimous, and of customs approved, in aspect most-
mild, and of wit perspicuous, and of urbanity elegant, munificent and liberal, preclear of every virtue.

"All these particular and amplest gifts, to thee communicated by the high heavens — with that innate fluency, and
conspicuous and luculent speaking, and divine aspects, and attractive semblances, with the form beyond humanity outstanding,
with decorous polish specious and noteworthy — draw me to translate the soul, and the heart, and the life, into thy
whitening bosom. They draw me, venerating, insatiably to gaze, and then, insensate, leave me. Then, more subtly those
considering, I satisfy my hoping, to consequute my desired desire — otherwise, so many choice and sublime conditions would
be hallucinated (deluded), offending, of ingratitude, the benignity of the gracious artificer (God).

"Most-comely Polia, then, may it please thee now, to these my first speeches and anxious writing, to offer thyself, with
