serene forehead, and to give not-doubtful faith, that I bear thee the greatest and most-singular love that ever, in the
world, a lover to a woman bore. And therefore excite thy benign audition to these just and honest petitions — that I only
ask thy pleasant and precious love; which, beyond the ornament, will be solace and conservation of my fugitive living, and,
to my acerb anguishes, moderation, and profitable lenitive. And, while I shall live, another never shall I be able to love,
without fail, than thee — with venerable service, and subject, to succumb, as to my sole Divine lord (thee) — whose
unthinkable outstandingness of beauties has transported me to this perilous pass, that I know not to imagine by what mode I,
wholly in thee, am alive, and in me, wholly dead — ignorant of the animadversion (attention) of my wretched life.

"For the health of which, from nowhere know I to find help, save both day and night, and at whatever hour, of thee sweetly
to think; and, thinking, to feign a most-apt remedy — which, at present, more necessitates than ever; otherwise, invalid and
infirm to resist the amplification of so much —"

"— continual flame, will succeed the rapacious and deadly lot. For which thing, one of these (fates), by every way, it will
behove me, from thee, to accept — if, to (my) health, benign and mild, henceforth thou present thyself: Behold me, felicity
present! Behold me, a triumphant victory attained! Behold me, a crown of love won! Behold me, full content! And if, by
chance (which I persuade not myself), the contrary thou shouldst do: Behold me, troublous, miserable, and discontent. The
one (way), both of us satisfied; the other, discontent — with (thee), then, vainly repenting of it. Consent not, for so much,
Polia, Nymphal adornment, and my most-loving, to incur into this infamous note: that thou consent to my soul-slaughter —
because thy sublime condition repugns and discrepates from impiety. Nonetheless, I offer thee the oblate and immolated soul,
and the slaughtered heart — of both which, licit (as Lady), and to thy liking, dispose. For, in perpetuity, affectionately,
both alive and dead, thine I am. Farewell."

Believing, Sacred Matron, that the Damsel, to my amorous words somewhat duly commoved, would assent — no otherwise than the
called Corydon, by Battus, succoured to his grief — but by no other mode I dispersed vainly my writing and speaking than to a
marble-born statue. And so much fruit, then, made my speeches, as wind-eggs (unfertile eggs). And therefore, reasonably
considering that the first blow does not split the tree — with Herculean audacity (which Love in me breathed), and by the
found way, commodiously, of writing —
— a few days thence, this second little epistle — sedulous and intently superseding to my health — I sent to tell her:

"If less were my harsh torment than thy accustomed cruelty, most-beautiful Nymph and Polia — a slaughterer of virtue —
to my long afflictions, with blandishing hope, it would persuade me to patience. But clearly, now, I recognise (by my
depraved and unpropitious Star) thy crude savagery and ferocity, whatever my incendious martyrdom to overcome and beyond
surpass. Then, what avails, what boots it, to Love, to increase and increment, every hour, to my already-consumed little
heart, so sweet a fire, if ever more atrocious and frigescent thou show thyself, more than rigid ice, and thy breast more
frigorific than are Dirce and Nomè, founts, and more than the Salamander, cold, which, with (its) contact, extinguishes
the fire? To my ancillary and servile patience, and to my notified vows and indicated affect — so much the more kindled,
as the more the contrary opposes itself, of thy displeasingness — nonetheless, I cannot unbind the amorous and solid chain,
which, under so soft and pressing a yoke, angariously (oppressively) holds me. Nay, the more I re-kick, so much the more I
implicate myself, taken and captive in this amorous fish-trap (Nassa), like a little fly involved in the inextricable work
of Arachne (a spider's web). And thus, tightly re-bound, and enslaved and captive, not valid nor apt for flight,
constrained am I, that I, bending, incline myself to thee — because in thee alone consists my precious liberty, and my every
necessary good.

"Whence, if thou openly understandest, my Lady, so sincere and consummate affection, and so much voluntary subjection, and
so active and laborious love — why, then, wilt thou not accept so freely these things given to thee (with all my life
offered), which, in thy delicate hands, ambivalent, hangs? Alas, sweetest and beautiful little Polia — succour, I pray thee,
and leave and concede to penetrate, a little, these my (not superb, not arrogant) but devout words, into thy heart; and
arouse in thee somewhat of compassion; receive the warm sighs; auscult my domestic and familiar laments; recognise the
cordial benevolence; attend to so faithful and meek a subject. For, avidly (visibly), I die, I consume myself, of thy
immoderate love — insomuch that all the world could not retract me, nor remove me (more firm than Milo), from (this): that I,
above every other most-precious thing, excessively love, worship, and revere thee, and that I, bowed, adore thee — O effigied
and true simulacrum of a Goddess before my eyes, and to my sight, publicly, so conspicuous and notable represented — in which
most-limpidly I see depicted all my health, and expressed all my peace, delight and content."
pages.note: Poliphilo's second letter to Polia:

t:
"Now, my hope — deny not to me, wholly thine, who thus piteously supplicate pity, and, to my urgent fire, a temperament —
that, without that, to live I know not, nor can; and, if I could, I would not. Because securely I hope, in that angelic
semblance, in those most-modest and ornate customs, in that graceful and illustrious aspect, (to find) help some time —
which, without doubt, is a special and preclear token that the supernal Jupiter, with exquisite and supreme diligence, has
skilfully-made thee, a miraculous ostentation, of all excellent beauties polished; which, without doubt, of all the
beautiful damsels of the world, transcend, outstanding, and, in thee alone, complexively (all together) perfect. For which
thing, in the least I doubt not that, again, that same Artificer — who so much good, and celestial gifts, in thee has feigned
and carved, benignly, of his similitude — I hold, then, a certain opinion, that likewise some fragment of clemency, in thy
human heart, he has, by every mode, collocated; and has not created thee among the Hyperborean Griffins, nor of mother
Niobe, nor of the sylvan and rough father Apulus, nor generated of the cruel Thracian Diomedes, nor of the furious Orestes,
nor of the malign Phaedra — but of most-humane parents, and, perhaps, beyond-worldly. And this is that which, chiefly,
conserves and sustains me, in so much fervour rosy and fluid. Otherwise, the carbuncled heart, and the soul, indignant,
would, henceforth, have fled. Succour, then, auxiliary and health-bringing (one) — for I supplicate not the insolent desire
of Midas, nor that of Pygmalion, but that, propitiated, thou lend favour; subvene to the need; show thyself pious; placate
thy ire; settle the soul; tranquillise the mind; mollify thy heart; embrace the amorous affect. Rule (as Lady) him who
wishes, thy most-faithful servant, eternally serving, to serve thee. Farewell."

> POLIPHILO CONTINUES HIS DOLOROUS HISTORY; AND HOW, POLIA NOT COMMOVING HERSELF FOR THE TWO EPISTLES, HE SENT HER THE
> THIRD; AND THERE, SHE STILL ENDURING MORE IN HER CRUELTY, BY CHANCE POLIPHILO FOUND HER ALONE, PRAYING, IN THE TEMPLE OF
> DIANA — WHERE HE DIED. THEN, IN HER SWEET EMBRACES, HE RESUSCITATED.

"Lady most-whole in the sacred (things), and Divine Priestess: since, of my dolorous, unpolished and inelegant narrating,
to thy holy and benign sight, up to now, it has not irked (thee) — henceforth, drawing to the end my prolix haranguing, I
shall follow briefly. Daring —"
pages.note: Chapter argument — Chapter XXXIV:

t:
"— complacenting thee (in) that which, loving, unpremeditatedly befalls, most of the times, (to) whoever intensely loves.
At present, wishing to persuade (that), in those (cases), opportune and useful is perseverance — thou shalt understand
that she, to my aforesaid epistles, no otherwise commoved herself, nor bent, than Mount Olympus, by the loosed and
unbridled winds, is quaked (i.e. not at all). But, for all this, not leaving (off) — that I could not (abandon) the begun
Agon — I sent her also the third epistle, making diligent scrutiny (of) what she held in her soul, or whether her heart
were touchstone-stone, or of human material congested; all the while the ever-vigilant Love assiduously stimulating, and
alone smearing and anointing the insolent appetite of blandishing hope. Such a tenor I wrote her:

"Sooner would I consume my tongue, ingenuous and most-noble adolescent-girl, than ever it could somewhat, upon the candid
papyrus, express how toilsome, how grave, how acerb is my bitter pain — which, day and night, in the languishing heart,
re-doubled, increases without intermission — seeing thee thus deaf and displeasing. And only because I recognise, too,
thee not to be content, and satiated, still, of my grave torments (no less, in the least — nay, excessively greater — than
those which, not much time (ago), twice I have sweetly written thee). But, since the fallacious, the forced, the savage,
and dolorific Love, with the impious fortune and my adversative star, necessarily constrain me, to thee, voluntary, to
handmaid and serve — O Nymph, above the human grasp, of wondrous beauty, and, of conspicuous and elegant filament, most-
admired; but, above all and whatever other, I dare say, excessively pitiless and cruel, like a sylvan and untamed beast,
more than the most-immense and famished Lion of Androcles, rigid and displeasing. Which things belie the human seed, and
that thy meek and divine simulacrum, of thy comely aspect pre-shining, and of that celestial and rare make, denigrate —
of humanity naked, and rebelling to the amorous little fires of Cytherea, and to the divine Empire of the shrewd Nature a
spurner. For, a juridical cause, and odious experience, alluring me, transport (me), (that I ought) to speak of so much
appreciable time vainly consumed... amorously afflicting thee, and day and night to that colloricated (heated), detained,
occupied, and useless, having lost (it) — inflamed and dried up, loving thee, sole elected to destroy my life — by that
which I manifestly see: that, the more I love thee, so much the more it seems that I, hardening thee, lapidise (turn thee
to stone). Ah, Polia — can it be that, in thee, would not be found one atom of piteous spirit, that a little gracious
audition, with internuncio (messenger) little epistles, I could find in thee — nor with pre-strepent sighs, nor with
affluent and frequent little tears, from my moist eyes vaporable, solicitous, irroring, which every hour weep —"
pages.note: Poliphilo's third letter to Polia:

t:
"— its (my heart's) guilty condition and dolorous case? — (my eyes) which so easily believed, and, with mere faith,
judged, that thy incomparable beauty had allotted and associated itself with the inextricable congestion of some sweetness
of soul; which eyes, with prompt appetence and flagrant petulance, have been the cause and primary beginning of the ruin
and captivity of my life. Nor, for this, still, can I, with any temperament, bridle them, that they extremely desire not
those (thine) to re-behold — and that most-fulgent Sun which has made them to darken, and to relapse, precipitant, into
the pernicious harm. Whence, O celestial spirit, and venerable Idol of mine — if, propitiated to my writing, now thou
concede them not entry and audience, perhaps it is for my absence. But, amiable my Lady, if in sight, and presentially,
thou sawest me consume and languish, and all liquable in tears, together with re-increasing sighs — and me sweetly giving
heed to bend thy soul, and, supplicating, to mercy thee, and to placation, deprecate; and likewise, with every reverent
and ancillary meekness, narrate the incredible love that I bear thee, and the bitterness of heart that I sustain, and the
tedium of my already-odious life, and that which, for thee, continually, miserably, I suffer — alas me, illustrious Polia,
beauty of the Nymphs: I am certain that, to pity, thou wouldst commove thyself, and limpidly wouldst recognise that I merit
to obtain favour and prompt aid from thee.

"Which (aid) whenever, persisting pertinacious and impious, thou deniedst, reluctant — and so fervid and proterve a love
spurning — so much I can conjecture: that thou tellest me to burst and die for thee. Now, what convenient cause feelest
thou, to consent to so much evil? What praise, what prize, what victory, what content, canst thou ever, of this,
consequute? Nay, a most-vulgar, infamous mark of vituperable cruelty; and, perhaps, inexorable vengeance from the avenging
Gods (which, never stumbling, lets not the previous and criminal flee-er escape). Wish not, then, to assent to so much
vituperable evil; but rather, with thy supreme crown (glory), render thyself pious, mild, and pleasant — of which thing,
and (of) the ornament of thy commendable beauty, and long-life of our caducous life, and content, and quiescence, and
sweetest fruit, to sprout and grow up in a brief little point, not ungrateful thou shalt feel. Because what other treasure,
in the world, so precious could be esteemed, as two uniform lovers? Nor a more maledict, malign, and improbable thing, than
that thou be loved, and not love. For which thing, if, at present, a preserver of my love, and health-bringing to my ills,
thou present not thyself — what wilt thou that I do more of this sad life, henceforth, for thee so noxious and dolorous?
Being certain that, if, obdurate, obstinately unmitigable, thou shalt persevere, immense and stupid — of insupportable
passion, it will behove me, out of this life, to commeate (depart); and, by this way, finally, thy —"
"— iniquitous will will cease, and the greatness of my grief. Farewell."

By this way, then, I gave heed, sedulous, to reduce and humanate, and her sweetly to blandish, and to mitigate — soliciting
the asperity received from the initiated arduous and perilous work. But neither she, nor the perfid Love, consented to my
suasive words, with high and sworn espousals, openly showing her the nod and semblance of my — of every sweetness sweetest —
flames; (that) she, in return, with requisite reciprocation, love me. And with every industrious art, and shrewd cogitation,
I forced myself to kindle her of that veracious, nude, simple, and excellent affect, and amorous fire, in which, without any
remedy, continually — like a *Pyraulus* (fire-fly/flame-moth) — I nourished myself, wretched. And, beyond this, with her,
infinite times, with the mind I feigned to have a charming colloquy; and, ratiocinating (with her), daringly — intermixed,
frequently, the tormentable wailings — I said: 'O my little Nymph, of inhuman and ferine heart — of nature a soft girl (yet)
more than solid Steel, and more than murex-stone hardest, more tenacious than a retaining Grapnel, more obstinate than a
hinged Beam; more mordant than a rapt Talon, and much more than the cruel and foul Harpies rapacious of my heart: how canst
thou persevere in so much hardness and impiety? — more impious than Mithridates, more savage than Alcmaeon, more ungrateful
of so much affection than Paris toward Oenone.' — To my prayers, remove, then, these iniquitous abjections from thy Nymphal
heart, and this vulgar mark; and assent thyself, propitiated, to my suppliant petitions; concede, my Lady, that I consequute
the desired quiet; permit to penetrate thy auditory, my tormentable little sighs; consent to my ardent loves.

And, many, and to these similar, complaints and instances performed — in the least I could not move such agitation from my
continual grief, which, in me pressed, was so much in all the viscera occupant, and had so high germinated in the heart its
most-bitter roots, that, by other art, nor way, nor mode — save by its chief hope (Polia herself) — ever, to extirpate, I
know not, nor can, nor avail. And less profitable, still, were the groaning voices, about her superb palace vainly dispersed
— (she) more deaf than Icarus to the paternal admonitions, and more displeasing than Caunus to the desperate Byblis;
abominatrix of sweet love, superseding to the false and habituated opinions, in the tender and virgin age wont to harden. And
an ardous thing it is to leave that which, some time, in the soul is impressed: enerve, not easily can one. Thence, then, was
the exordium and origin, that I, simply ensnared and implicated, in these enveloping nets, and fallacious decoy, and in
these subtle, caducous, uncertain, fugacious and momentary snares and sharpnesses of love, enslaved — that, under this
molesting Tyranny and condition, and miserable servitude, subjugated and enrolled, I found one sole pleasure and alluring
delightment: to love her extremely; nor did I repugn to the flying (arrows) —"

— little arrows of blindfold Cupid. To whom, enticed, without delay, disposing myself, humbly I accepted, and all,
indefatigable, I dedicated myself an observer of his most-turbulent, sharp, investigatrix, cross, and unbridled little
laws — relying on the confidence of her angelic aspect, and that such were, still, her heart, and that the part with the
whole should agree, and the whole, mosaic-wise, accede to the part, and not, with desperate harmony (be), so beautiful, so
elegant, so comely and marvellous, and divine, a composite. Hoping reasonably that the arrow-shooting Cupid — who thus
tormentably had wounded, intimately, the sad heart in me — was, juridically, and to my adverse and pernicious love, a most-
safe presidium, and, to the blind errors incursant, an affable and remediable propulser, and a prompt and pious succour,
and, to the superfluous blight and ardour, a congruous temperament — expecting, however, salutary aid from nowhere else than
from him: that he, equally, should draw, in her, the hard and cruel bow, with which, in me, direly, he has drawn.

And, treating the gaping wound, the more it exacerbated in asperity, and the more re-doubled the wound-dealing and mortal
grief — but, the hope of re-healing the amplified wound ever having, in him, non-hesitant confidence (that, I being his most-
vowed subject and servant, and his opulent prey, bondman, captive, plunder, and spoil, and his copious Trophy), that same
medicament which his most-pious Mother, and my Lady (Venus), made to the wounded Aeneas, still to me, following the maternal
pity, would aid. And, again, being his most-devoted — that same patronage he should lend which holy Vesta lent to her
handmaid and subject Tuccia, benignly, by the miracle of the sieve (carrying water in a sieve), the perpetrated fault
occulted, freed (her) from public opprobrium and infamous supplice.

Whence — as, to lovers, is wont manifoldly to befall — thus, desperate, in grave litigation, without judge and adverse
party, I condemned both (Love and Fortune), conjured to my deadly harm, with querulous laments weeping, inculpating them as
guilty, and choice enemies of every pious humanity; (then) now, glad and festive, I revoked in me the sentence. Some time,
excited, like a rabid and impatient dog, biting at its retaining chain, I wished to avoid and flee the hard knot of the
amorous but molesting snare, and to un-armour myself. Then, vainly imagining, I feigned many and delectable solaces and
pleasures, false vengeances, temerarious insults, perturbing perils, and impavid death — I found myself, afterward, more
tightly knotted, and solidly armoured. By such altercation, and abortive appetites, consuming my tribulous life — and,
among sighs and bitter sobs, half-consumed — there remained no place that, by me, with solicitude, perennial care, and
scrutatory vigilance, was not indagated and lustrated, ratched, and re-searched; no way, and blind-alley, and almost even
through the porticoes, unattempted, omitted —

— only, exploring, most-vigilant and frequent, and minutely and corneredly investigating, if her I could find. It befell,
lastly, that Love and Fortune, in a benign ascension finding themselves, benignly most-pacate, unforeseenly conducted me
into the Sacramentary Temple — she inadvertent — into which she frequently went, but occult. And there, having found her
alone, swiftly — the heart shaken (of) every other appetence, like a spear-armed Lion (at) the insulting prey — thus, and
by no other mode, prompt to her, most-ferocious, invading, and, with the extreme virtues (strength) derived and joined,
and having accosted (her), of a sudden liquefied — like wax, by fire, adherent and near — lifeless I became, and
consternated; and, ignorant what to do or say, at length thus I began, with pained and inelegant speaking, humbly to say
(only, of all my forces, scarce remaining the tremulous voice, and a little of spirit, almost, in the afflicted jaws,
interdicted; and the soul mourning, stupefied the eloquent tongue, and, with all the body trembling, the torpid members),
lamentful:

"Alas me, Polia — golden and precious Column of my living, sole consolable hope of my afflictions — already several days
are transacted, that thee alone, most-fervidly, not so much have I loved, but, like a Goddess, venerating, honorificated,
and, with per-injury of the Gods, adored — with burning flame of love, my holocaust heart immolated (as the Priests did,
sacrificing to Bellona), and consigned to thee my living, voluntarily, to thy arbitrament and will. And thou art made
(alas, unhappy!), undeservedly, against me cruel, and a more irritable expultress of my every good — as if thou wast, by me,
noxiously hurt — like Juno, the Trojans, with great irascence, persecuting. More noxiously to me infest than the British
little stones to the mellificating Bee; and more pugnacious, contrary, and more different from my will than the infest
Thetis to Vulcan; and more molesting than the unstable tail to Lucius (the ass); more noxious than the *scandulacea*
(darnel) to the crops, and more than the sonorous hail to the most-tender little fronds; and more than the burning Phoebus
to the springing flowers and grassy meadows.

"Finally, wishing I, with every sweetness of heart, with alluring and meek speaking, to soothe, placate, propitiate,
enticing her, and to remove her from the unmild and obstinate purpose, and to divert and retrograde the dire and truculent
will, and to tranquillise so many her turbulences, and her soul unconsentaneous and indecent, and to reflect (it) to pity
and mercy, and her ferocity to moderate, and her morbid heart, of savagery, with tears and sighs to medicate, and, to the
charity and penury of affection, with fecund love to succour — blandishing, charming and sweetly, with profuse little tears
and —"

"— penible weepings, and loosed sighs, sedulous, to reduce the rigid breast, and aptly to soften and slacken it (like a
tender wand and withy, which — however so fragile and dried it presents itself — yet, by liquid (water), and with a little
fire, and (a) measure, does not contort itself, and become a band to the others)" — but this one, however that her fragile
and soft sex be flexile, and, of love, burnable, nonetheless — neither with my enkindled love, nor with abundant tears
(that so anxiously the afflicted Isis wept not for her dear Osiris), nor with blandishing mode — to infire, nor mollify,
nor provoke her to the sweet embrace of my most-cordial love, I availed. She could not be perverted, nor changed, by any
mode — offering her, purely, the most-sincere (heart), and, of every other (love), refined (of dregs), heart, and pre-nitid
affect: (a love) which was not that which Tiberius Gracchus showed to his most-beloved consort Cornelia (credulous to the
prodigy of the two serpents); and greater than that of Alcestis the queen, who, for her dearest husband, wished to undergo
the voluntary death; and, more without comparison, was not the love which she (Portia?) showed, who, for the husband, wept
and declaimed at the ardent pyre, wished to deglutinate (swallow) the kindled coals; and (greater) than the most-loving
Panthea's to her consort; and, with more amiable affection than Pylades' toward his Orestes.

Now, to the last, wishing to dispose (her) tractable, and to conduce, I persevered, her sylvestrous and ferine heart, to
mansuefy, and to domesticate to some humanity and sweetness — which hardened itself, persisting, uncontaminated, untamed,
immovable, and crudely lapidescent (turning to stone): no otherwise ignorant of gentleness, and exempt of pity, than if she
were born in Hyrcania, or in the wood of Ida, obstruse of shadows, among the rough and knotty oaks and valid robles; or on
Mount Ismarus; or among the Anthropophagi descended; and among the horrid furies of Cyclops, and in the intercaved cavern of
Cacus a nursling, and among the Syrtes.

For which immanity, constantly persevering in the tormenting exasperations, and non-simulated ache and mourning — newly, and
more noxious, began the raucous sighs in my flammid breast, more than the lowing of a famished, or fever-sick, Lion, in a
sonorous and hidden Cavern, or cave. Re-cogitating, in vain, my every fatigue performed — by her pertinacity rightly
pondering that an imperforate cask cannot be emptied — almost diffident and desperate of so arduous an undertaking, and, in
the weeping eyes, with frequent scaturigine (gushing), infinite tears heaping, more dolorously than the tormented Myrrha,
distilling through the hard bark — whence, more than the just, improbly, without measure, beyond the beginning and quickening
of this my affectionate and invalid sickness, I found myself in the state, with multiplied increment, and re-doubled
augmentation, of my unceasing —"

— torment of the infirm heart, finding myself without any hope, considering her, most-immense (in cruelty), enduring —
after (I had) expressed many tormenting laments, and weeping and plaint, and, beyond belief, greatly embittered myself —
and she persisting rigidly frigorated, more than Styx in Arcadia, and totally deprived and divested of every benignity,
nay, without any token of propitiation — whence, with swift exit, I felt my genius (soul), of the inflicted injuries the
arbiter, to flee; and there, in the temple (she present), with the soul pertinacious, imperterrite and immovable seeing —
the immature and accelerated death, lamenting, asthmatic, over the couplings, or vertebrae, prone, mercy reluctantly
praying, and on the earth prostrated, dead I remained.

For which thing, she — perhaps instigated by the Gods, and pre-monished of her malignity, and rigid and inhuman perversity
(because none enters into new things if of the preterite he repents not) — returned, before dawn, the following morning, to
re-behold, in the violated Temple, the yesterday's soul-slaughter. And, with much virginal handling, and sweet anxieties,
and suppressed little groans, and infinite kisses, and funereal submurmurs, penitent, embracing me, and piteously tear-
weeping, and, of tears abundant, be-dewing me, she revoked (called back), sweetly, my soul — which, no sooner offered
(out) of my body, was up-borne, and sent down (presented) into the divine sight, and to the high throne of the divine Lady
Mother (Venus). Whence, into its habit and habitude reiterating, and into its inane (empty) little body — joyous, and with
charming jocundity, and with obtained grace victrix — thus, alacritously, it (the spirit) said:

> POLIPHILO CONTINUES HIS NARRATION, HOW THE SPIRIT APPEARED TO HIM, IN HIM REITERATING (RE-ENTERING), FESTIVELY SPEAKING,
> SAYING TO HIM (THAT IT HAD) BEEN IN THE PRESENCE OF THE DIVINE PAPHIAN (VENUS), PLACATED AND BENIGN — BY WHOSE OBTAINED
> GRACE IT RETURNS MOST-JOYOUSLY TO VIVIFY HIM.

"Amorously joyful, at pleasures and extreme gladness, and joy and tranquil delightment gesticulating, exult, with the utmost
jocundity, O my little body, gracious mansion, and most-loving domicile — postposing every grave perturbation, and infest
grief, and afflicting desire, thy soul festively accommodating, convert thyself, and revoke (recall thyself). And to the
consequuted sweetnesses, and to the obtained loves, and to the won victory, and to the attained Trophy-triumph, probably
attend — that never, of such Plunder and spoils, and promiscuous trophies, and superb insignia —"
pages.note: Chapter argument — Chapter XXXV:

t:
"— was a triumph adorned, like our glorious (one). And therefore the feeble anguishes, and ungrateful mourning, resect
(cut off), and totally amputate, defect (failing). And, out of so much burden and tyrannic angary, return into most-
precious liberty — un-armoured, loosed, and expedited, and (changed) into festive delights, mutated. Because, henceforth,
in the courses of the ages, more blessed and happy shall be found none than thou art become, by the obtained graces.

"For which thing I doubt not a little point, that the benign and supernal Gods, to my amorous cause miserating,
favoured, patronising. And I saw that which, a long protraction, the discoursing would wish (require), and scarce would I
know to express (it). Venus, then, was Lady there, without doubting, disjoined and distant from the cold, and torpid, and
worn Virgin Astraea, and remote from the avenger of nimbose Orion, and disjoined from the hirsute Ram — when I, to that
lofty and divine throne, at the sight of the grave, holy, and severe majesty, lancinated (wounded) and groaning, presented
myself. There, as best I could, against her malefic and law-breaking son (Cupid), inculpating, lamenting myself, I put
forth: that thus, guiltless, inculpable, and without offence, with his wound-dealing and swift arrows, he has drawn, into
my already-sieved (riddled) heart, more punctures than, in the panic Labo (?), grains are found; (and that,) with simulated
good, and feigned delight, the ordained term anticipated, from my most-pleasing and sublime Citadel (Polia) surrept and
disjoined, bitterly I was — and troublous, for love of a most-cruel damsel, erroneous and vague, a fugitive, externated,
paling, and ignorant of quiet."
pages.wcap: Cupid Shoots Arrow at Bust of Polia

t:
Having benignly heard my lamentable complaints, to herself, immediately, the glorious Goddess and sublime Lady called the
flying offspring (Cupid), demanding of him what had been the cause of so much injury. He, then, smiling and enticing, thus
took to say: "Amorous Mother — it will not be a protraction of time, that becomingly co-adapted shall be the present
litigation and discordant souls, with reciprocal vicissitude of equability." Nor had he sooner proffered, charmingly, these
little words, than the mellifluous (one) turned himself to me, saying:

"Behold diligently this noteworthy image. How many would there be, who — however great — most-content would repute
themselves, esteeming themselves blessed, beatific, and best, only to gaze on her, let alone to be loved by her — that such
a virgin Thalasio (a bride) had not, by lot, in the rape of the Sabines" (showing me that true and divine effigy of Polia).
"And attend, and with wondrous affect appreciate: these particular gifts, given by the Gods most-precious, ought not to be
spurned — because, however much we are accustomed to concede (them) to the earth-born, nonetheless, many would wish them, and
cannot consequute them. Which (gift), graciously most-precious, now I give thee; and the first-fruits of so glorious a
congeries of virtue and corporeal beauties, which I, gracious, offer thee."

And then, to the genetrix, too, thus he (Cupid) says: "Lady Mother of the warm loves, glorious nurse — this is the cause of
the ill and heart-grief, and of the pernicious exiling, and molesting Hyperoria (banishment), of this poor little and
wretched, exiled, and tormenting soul. But (in a) brief little instant, disconsolate soul, I shall make thee most-
efficaciously, of thy coveted (desire), satisfied and content, and to re-migrate unharmed where dislocated thou art. And I
wish to unite thee, and fittingly to couple thee, with thy cruel adversary (Polia); and to remove and break all the
obstacles repugning to my flying ingress." Sealed, then, the divine lips, of a sudden he re-assumed his candent, penetrable,
and barbed armatures, prependent from the most-holy flank, from the promptuary Quiver — manifestly seeing I, with the curved,
and, with rigour, corded bow — into the delicate breast of the shown image (Polia's), striking, he shot, of a golden arrow,
little-feathered of mordant thorns, and adorned of manifold colouring. Nor sooner, wounding, did that fulgurant arrow fix
itself (with a fermentous propagation of love), than the virgin girl — ductile, facile, mild, benign — gladly acclived
herself, bending; and, vanquished and prostrated, with Nymphal manner accusing herself (as those who, infirm and unarmed,
avail not to contrast) of the accustomed cruelty and ferine savagery.
Now, there being I, in the most-blessed sight of three presences — two divine, —

— the third a little less than celestial (as, without fail, I judged) — I beheld, in the open and openly, mysteries and
arcane visions, rarely to mortals and material senses permitted to discern. But I, who, by special grace, and singular
indult, and gracious privilege, was exploring the whole — and diligently and most-accurately contemplated the divine gift
granted, which, wounded, to me graciously offered the fire-born Cupid, which, with certain and secure conjecture, I hoped,
with thee (Polia), to conquer and, attained, amorously to enjoy — and there, scrupulously hallucinated and astonished, that
in one little Nymphal body were, especially, heaped all the elegancies and comely filament of beauties, and, perfectly, every
aggregate shapeliness re-beholding (the present Numina, too, provoked into admiration): I saw, among the other noteworthy and
celestial things, two coruscating and splendid eyes, more clear than the matutinal stars — that thou wouldst say Phoebus
twinned, under those brows, resplendent — scintillating little arrows of gold, without intercalation, into my so most-willing
object, communicating the splendour of every notable virtue pre-nitent; which, no less than the rays of the most-lucent Sun,
made my intent regard to vacillate. Much more, without measure, salutary and gracious than, to the shipwrecked, the near
shore; and more than recuperated health to the sick; and more than were the anxious riches to Darius, the victories to
Alexander; and more than the increment of the rainy Nile to the Egyptian fields... And there the most-beautiful Nymph,
ethereal adornment, to all the other conspicuous beauties sole outstanding, most-comely, amiable, offered herself, with milky
breast, in which Love had made his delicious Orchard, and most-pleasant little garden, a manifest seminary and vestige of
Jove — with golden interweaving of her balled-up tresses, the genial nape encompassing, and choicely constricting, and,
without Ciniflonean (curling-iron) art, crisping, unstable; and part effused, wavy, over the most-white shoulders, which
whitened of nival Candour, adulterated of rosy liquamen. More desirable offering herself than the sacred gold to the
iniquitous Atalanta... nor was so opportune the laurel-chaplet to the baldness of Caesar, nor so salubrious and efficacious was,
to the enamoured Faustina, the gore of the wretched Gladiator, as she, to my furnaced fervour, a most-opportune, salubrious,
and most-efficacious and present remedy. So much, then, is her beauty, that I believe not that of such and so much was Deiopea
promised to Aeolus (by Juno)."

Being, then, in such a manner rapt and sublimated, and, of beholding the celestial works, stupefied — and re-dried the flux
of the solicitous tears, and benignly ausculted my miserable laments — the Divine Lady Mother, with an ineffable majesty and
sanctimony, and with an unheard and venerable voice, soothing (enough to re-serene the beclouded heavens, to take the noxious
armature from Enyalian Mars, and the thunderbolts from the hand of the jaculating Jove, to in-youth the old Saturn, to
Ethiopise (darken) the most-beautiful Phoebus, to in-stammer the eloquent Cyllenian (Mercury), and to defile the chaste
Diana) — never by the terrestrials heard such (a voice) — proffered divine words, with divine afflation, and with such
Harmony, affably, as never, to the empty Syrinx (pipe), the divine lips of the talaric Mercury, (playing) to the eyed Argus,
breathed — by the sweetness of which, whatever Cotic whetstone-rock of Libya, nay, whatever Indian Diamond, contaminated and
immuted, would have been softened to every softness, tender and fresh.

And, in this manner speaking, she made me secure of my health, and of my prosperous love, and of this my most-jocund
*postliminium* (homecoming), and to thee (Polia) to return. And, with a most-charming little laugh, she said to her offspring:
"And thou — if, for the wounded Virgin girl, perhaps to turn-tail from this amorous office, and to relinquish this present
soul, thou shouldst fore-attempt — thou shalt be surety (bail)." — "Then, my little body, my lodging: remove from thee all the
most-harsh griefs, and every passion, and accept me thus entire into thee, as ever, with thee, conjoined I was — with that
most-celebrated name, in me impressed, by which, from thee, I receded; which, otherwise, is carved and impressed, and sealed,
within me, vegetable and fecund — (it) was not that of Oenone and of Paris, sculpted in the ramose trees and rugose barks,
nor thence ever shall it be erased, nor to be deleted, but eternally consigned, conservable. Now, most-loving host, receive
me, thy indigene (native), who, to remedy thy grave and insupportable tribulations, have penetrated and passed through so
many waters of weepings, and through so much fire of love, and through so many supreme fatigues; and, finally, up-borne
where thy likes cannot be, and have attained so much divine benignity, that I, thence timely sequestered, bear thy most-
valiant and most-whole health."

And I, to my re-turned and re-gathered Genius (soul), responded: "Come, indigene inhabitant, and Lady of the supreme citadel
of my mind, best rational portion. Come, my heart, domicile of irritable ardour. Come, extreme part where makes residence my
exhorter Cupid — and let us make, then, the festive Soteria (thanksgivings) for thy retrograde reformation (return)."

> POLIPHILO SAYS THAT, NO SOONER (HAD) THE SOUL, FALLING SILENT, (THAN) IN THE ARMS OF POLIA, ALIVE, HE FOUND HIMSELF.
> PRAYING THEN THE PRIESTESS THAT, PERPETUALLY, BOTH SHE SHOULD BIND OF LOVE — THEN HE MADE AN END. AND POLIA CONCLUDES
> HER NARRATING TO THE NYMPHS, HOW ENAMOURED SHE WAS, AND, OF HER, POLIPHILO.

"Venerable and holy Matron, of this Sacred Temple Priestess preclear and most-worthy: perhaps incredible it appears, and
alien of faith, that — no sooner had the soul put an end to its salutiferous reasonings, (than) in me regressed the
appetible life, (and) suddenly I found myself in the tight and sealed embraces, and juicy and most-savoury kissings, of
this Nymph, virginal flower redolent. And, with the observed order (which she, as charming, festive, eloquently has
narrated), with wondrous and amorous fomentation grew, intimately, our affection, up to the present case. Whence, being
now before thee, notable religious, and president of this sacred, holy place — to thee it appertains decently to divert,
obliquate, and, removing, avert the ill; to prosper the good; and the humble and low things to sublimate; the nodding to
direct and prop; the obscure to lucify; and the adverse to emend and correct. Then, we beseech, make equally an
indissoluble ensnaring, and, coupling, constrain our soul into one concord will, and into one desire; and confirm and
stabilise our united and concrete love — perpetually disposed to succumb and handmaid, serving to the high Empire of the
Divine Mother." And there Poliphilo made silence.

The Divine Priestess, without delay, together made us amorously kiss, and said: "As, to the immortal Gods, it has pleased,
no otherwise be it. Whence, holy and just to me it seems, that you, from the first state, ought to migrate to a more
laudable (one). Be, then, by me, blessed; and live happy, amorous; and, sedulous, visit this Holy temple, for your all
refuge and secure presidium of your mutual love and equal affection. And whichever of you shall be cause of impeding this
fatal love — be (he/she) persecuted by the noxious and fearful arrows and jaculable darts of Cupid; and wounded, the one,
of the golden (arrow), and the other be fixed of the funereal leaden."

"This, then, was the case and primordium of our falling-in-love, in the burning Cupidine flames equally burning, glorious
Nymphs — as, perhaps, fastidiously, at length I have narrated." (And, in this saying, Polia — almost weary of the prolix
sermoning — made an end.)
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
— perhaps fastidiously, at length, I have narrated. And, in this saying, Polia — almost weary of the prolix sermoning —
made an end; and, enclosed modestly in that chorus of oriental pearls that mossy (fragrant) breath, and, among the purpling
lips, detained, she quieted herself.

> POLIPHILO SAYS THAT, POLIA FALLING SILENT, SHE HAD ALSO FINISHED THE FLORAL LITTLE CHAPLET — WHICH SHE, HAVING PLACED IT
> ON (HIS) HEAD, KISSED HIM SWEETLY. AND THE NYMPHS, WHO, WITH SO LITTLE DELAY, HAD AUSCULTED THE AMOROUS HISTORY, RETURNED
> TO THEIR SOLACES, AND ASKED LEAVE. POLIA REMAINED, AND POLIPHILO, ALONE; AND, OF LOVE WITH HIM CONFERRING, POLIA, MOST-
> TIGHTLY EMBRACING HIM — SHE DISAPPEARED, AND THE SLEEP.

I in the least doubt not that the solacing Nymphs — who, for a longish delay, intently had lent benign audience — beyond the
supreme delight, took no scanty and exiguous admiration of the loves which Polia, adolescent-girl, distinctly, with such
comeliness, narrating, had prosecuted. And, the term imposed to the prolix little history, all rose from the quiet sitting.
And, just as she, enucleatedly, with supreme and wondrous fluency, narrated — neither more nor less she bound, inter-weaving
the most-odorous florets into a circular little chaplet; and, with the sweet words, it was completed — and, to my head,
affectionately genuflecting herself, cunningly she placed (it); and, with twin nectareous and cinnamon lips, dove-wise
kissing me. For which thing the Nymphs extremely lauded, approving the most-charming speaking, and the adorned fluency; and
that, with elegant procession, and outstanding gestures, and with preclear beauty, had been her most-polished eloquy — high,
and of memorable worth. Then, much more most-pleasing, the understanding of her high and noble origin, and egregious stock,
and generous lineage, and of the notable family, illustrious and ancient, and of the happy exit of her love, thus orderly
recited.

Incontinently, to their Nymphal diversions, jests, and delights, most-facetious and hilarious and all festive, they
returned — beginning the muted (many) instruments, with canorous music, to sound, and to the celestial canticles composedly
to enter, dancing in a ring around the sacred fount most-limpid, flowing sweet liquors —
pages.note: Chapter argument:

t:
— with charming whisper, through the soft and flower-bearing and rosy meadows, flowery, of diverse colours; and through the
opaque shade-canopies of the pleasant little Groves of fruit-bearing trees. And there, rapt Polia and me they drew to the
joyous Chorus, festively busy, leaping with choice alacrity, with special and Nymphal and delicious gesticulation, with
applause, solace, and ineffable delight, some little delay. And, after great feast and manifold dances and choruses, the
Nymphs, with indicible delightment, thence departed — with sweetest and mutual embracings and biting kisses; and, of both us,
amorously friendship contracted, took leave.

Now, in this holy and most-pleasant place, remained alone, I and my refined Polia — all inflamed of venereal and delectable
fires, and increments of love — thus I began to say to her: "Philareta (Virtue-loving) Polia, most-desired, and my most-
elegant Eupathia (Well-feeling): henceforth, excluded every vulgar pondering, and every turbid suspicion exploded — thou art,
by every mode, that unique, pre-elected among the mortals, first first-fruits amorous of thy inviolate, and all-flowery and
clean person, comely Nymph of choice elegance; for whom, flagellously afflicting myself, my soul, connexed and knotted to thy
most-pleasing affects, one little point has not been quiescent, nor without gravity of bitterness. At present, thou art made
more most-pleasing to me than the clear day to the terrestrials, and more opportunely now to me accommodated than the annual
harvests to human fomentation.

"Conserve, then, with amorous little custody, my soul in thy eternal Love. Because thee alone — so excessively beautiful, so
transcendently delectable as ever one could, imagining, ponder, and, pondering, chimaerise — stuffed of a chorus of all
virtue and honesty, and worthy manners, accompanied by all the species of shapeliness, from heaven, to my sight, cast, a
wondrous image, for whom, with profound love, I am bound to the eternal fetters — among infinite girls shrewdly elected,
most-choice, and chief lady of my living, and my dear preserver; sole triumphant Empress of my enkindled and abstemious
heart, precipitated into the barathrum of so much amorous ardour — of which (heart) thou alone, victorious, art, of the vital
spoils and high Trophy, a superb bearer, deserving and dignified. Thou, my singular, to-be-worshipped Goddess of my soul, and
of my every good." And, said (this), she, to me, without delay, amorously subjoined:

"Poliphilo, my delight, my sole festive refrigerium, my pleasant solace, and my delicious delight, and, of my mind, the
chief and terminated content, and licentious dominator of my sworded and transfixed little heart — to —"

"— me, above all the precious treasures and richest gem-wealth of the world, excessively most-esteemed. I pray thee — not
re-counting that which now, in the open and perspicuous, infallibly thou knowest, and which thou hast been able expressly,
undefective and ratified, to comprehend, in the divine presence placed of so many Nymphs — all thine, individual (undivided),
with every corollary, strictly I vow myself; with the tightest and juridical surrender, donatively I dedicate, and inseparably
I promise thee to bear thy precious love — ever, an intimately native and eternal inhabitant, in my tenacious and ardent
heart. And thine, most-firmly, I am; nor of another's was I ever, (even) had I lived more years than the Terebinth of Hebron.
Thou art that solid column and prop of my life, and true and most-immovable support, and my chief Philoctetes; in which I see,
perspicuously, all my refreshing, salutary hope, stabilised, and commodulated of diamantine snares and indissoluble chains,
from which I cannot divert, nor obliquate, my eyes, but, indefatigable, gazing."

And, wound (about me), embracing — the milky and immaculate arms about my throat — sweetly, biting, with the coral little
mouth kissing me, she strained (me). And I, prompt, the turgid little tongue, jesting, most-sweetly juicy, kissing her, to the
extreme demise; and I, unrestrained, into extreme sweetness fallen, with a most-honeyed little bite kissing her — more
provoked, she twiningly strained me. And, in the amorous little embraces straining me, I beheld a rosy and venerable blush, in
her snowy cheeks native, diffused, with a rosy Punic tincture, with the placid and ivory brightness of the stretched skin
shining, to supreme grace and adornment. And, provoked by extreme sweetness, in the most-lucent little eyes, little tears
emulating perspicuous crystal, and most-circular pearls (more beautiful than those of Euryalus, and than those of the
distilling Aurora over the matutinal rosy roses), sighing —

that celestial, deified image, like a fumy wand of musk-and-amber suffumigation seeking the ether, most-fragrant (with no
exiguous delightment of the celestial spirits, so unwonted a sweet-smelling little fume redolent), through the air resolving
itself — with the delightsome sleep, quickish, from my eyes, and with swift flight, took herself away, she saying:
> **"Poliphilo, my dear — loving me — Farewell."**
pages.note: THE END of the Second Book, and of the whole dream. Poliphilo's waking follows in the epilogue, chapter XXXVIII.

t:
*Poliphilo here ends his Hypnerotomachia, grieving that the sleep was no longer,
and that the Sun was envious, and made it day.*

So unlooked-for a delight snatched away, that angelic spirit taken from my eyes,
and the sweet and gentle sleeping drawn out of my drowsy limbs as I woke — in
that instant, alas, ah me, amorous readers, I ached all over from the hard
clasping of that blessed image, that happy presence, that venerable majesty,
which left me and deserted me between wondrous sweetness and piercing
bitterness. When from my gaze there departed that most joyful sleep and that
divine shade, the mysterious apparition broken off, scattered, and carried away
— by which I had been led and lifted to thoughts so high, so sublime, so
piercing.

And then, as it happened, the Sun, stirred to envy by so blessed a dream, coming
to plunder the glorious night like a public enemy and an informer against the
divine Mother, came suddenly with his shining splendours and painted the
whitening Dawn a rosy colour, the long night dispelled. And the new-made day
being lit and set between us, I was left crammed and utterly filled with a sweet
and subtle deception.

Consider, then, what livid spite he would have had, if I had truly felt, in the
enjoying of them, the very voluptuous delights of so shapely and divine a
damsel, so matchless a nymph — he who would not endure (because, I judge, with a
goddess it is not permitted) to grant me the long night of Alcmena. Ah me, why
did he not exchange a little of his swiftness for a little sloth, for the sake of
my restored rest, and overrun his appointed hour by just so much? And why was
the Stygian sleep out of curious Psyche's box not laid upon me then?

And there Philomela, weeping before daybreak, hidden among thorny brambles and
in thickets close with the dark foliage of small oaks wound about with twining
honeysuckle, was pouring out the violence of that adulterous and faithless
Tereus, saying with tuneful chatter: *Tereus, Tereus* — [?have I been wronged].
Sighing, risen and released from the sweet sleep, I woke of a sudden into the
small hours, saying: **Farewell then, Polia.**

*At Treviso, where wretched Poliphilo was held fast in the most comely little
thongs of Polia's love. 1467, on the Kalends of May.*

*The text on this leaf is Latin, not Italian. It is given here in the original
with an English rendering beneath, since the Latin is itself quotable and the
first three lines carry an acrostic.*

> F œlix Polia, quæ sepulta vivis
> C haro Marte Poliphilus quiescens
> I  am fecit vigilare te sopitam.

Happy Polia, who being buried yet live:
Poliphilo, resting from dear Mars,
has now made you, who were lulled asleep, keep watch.
*The initials set out from the margin spell* **F · C · I**.

> VIATOR FAC QUAESO MORULAM, POLIAE NYMPHAE HIC EST MYROPOLIUM.
> QUAE NAM INQUIES POLIA? FLOS ILLE OMNEM REDOLENS VIRTUTEM SPECTATISSIMUS.
> QUI OB LOCI ARITUDINEM, PLUSCULIS POLIPHILI LACHRYMUL[IS] REPULULESCERE NEQUIT.
> AT SI ME FLORERE VIDERES, EXIMIA PICTURA UNIVERSIS DECORITER PRAESTARE
> CONSPICERES, PHOEBE INQUIENS, QUEM INTACTUM URORE RELIQUERAS, UMBRA CECIDIT.
> HEU POLIPHILE DESINE. FLOS SIC EXSICCATUS, NUNQUAM REVIVISCIT. VALE.

Traveller, make a little pause, I beg you: here is the perfume-shop of the nymph
Polia. And what, you will say, is Polia? That most admired flower, fragrant with
every virtue — who, because the ground is parched, cannot put out shoots again
for all Poliphilo's little tears. But if you had seen me in flower, you would
have seen me surpass all others in beauty, like an exceptional painting; saying,
*Phoebus, the one you left untouched by your burning, a shadow has felled.* Ah,
Poliphilo, have done. A flower dried out like this never lives again.
Farewell.
